### Ali H 2026 — HLA-DR Matching in Kidney Transplantation: Ethnic Disparities in Clinical Benefit and Policy Implications From a UK Registry Analysis

Ali H 2026, *Clinical Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ctr.70429](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70429). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (Wiley, Clin Transplant 40(1):e70429; PMC full text available; tables carry a 'John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.' footer; licence not stated in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult deceased-donor kidney transplants in the UK Transplant Registry, 1 Jan 2008 - 31 Dec 2020; excluded missing HLA mismatch, primary non-function, missing graft survival; recipients 73.4% White, 14.6% Asian, 8.2% Black; donors 93.8% White |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 25,094 |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; competing-risk Cox regression (patient death as competing risk) with backward stepwise selection, HLA-A/B/DR/DQ mismatch kept a priori as 0/1/2 dummies; UK-KAS four-level grouping; ethnicity subgroup models; logistic regression for acute rejection within 3 months; sensitivity analyses truncated at 5 and 10 years and restricted to DR-0 recipients; simple imputation for missing data |
| typing resolution | low/intermediate resolution (antigen level) as used by the UK Kidney Allocation Scheme; molecular typing methods stated as standardised since 2008 |
| outcome | graft failure (eGFR low enough for relisting or return to dialysis) with death as competing risk; secondary: acute rejection within 3 months |
| follow up | median 5 years |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, dialysis at transplantation, CRF (continuous; in UK registry usage this is the calculated reaction frequency, the sensitisation measure; HR 1.003 per unit, 1.002-1.004), recipient CMV, donor CMV, donor age, donor sex, recipient ethnicity, donor ethnicity, donor hypertension, extended-criteria donor, cold ischaemia time, donor risk index, delayed graft function, PRA was collected but does not appear in the final multivariable model (Table 2) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest contemporary (tacrolimus/MMF era, 2008-2020) deceased-donor registry analysis that enters every locus (A, B, DR, DQ) as separate 1-vs-0 and 2-vs-0 terms in one model, so it answers the per-locus ranking question (DR > B > A, DQ null for graft failure) and the one-versus-two question directly: nearly all of the DR penalty arrives with the first mismatch (SHR 1.119) and the second adds little (SHR 1.148, p=0.070; 10-year 1.13 vs 1.17). The DR-0 sensitivity analysis and the rejection ORs (DQ 1.202/1.464, persisting at 1.36/1.80 in DR-matched pairs) speak to whether DQ acts independently of DR, and the UK-KAS four-level result (level 2 no worse than level 1, SHR 0.973) is evidence against a zero-mismatch premium beyond 0-DR/low-B configurations. Typing is antigen-level, which matches the one-field typing an Iranian living-donor pre-screen would have, and the model contains no DSA data, resembling an antibody-unknown screen (sensitisation enters only as continuous CRF without interaction with mismatch). Transfer is imperfect: donors are deceased (mean age 49, 36% ECD, CIT 14 h, 24% DGF), recipients and donors are predominantly White British, and living-donor grafts have shorter ischaemia and better donor quality, so absolute effects in Iran may differ. The ethnicity finding (DR effect strong in Asian recipients, absent in Black recipients, no formal interaction test) is a warning that the predictive value of antigen-level DR matching depends on population haplotype structure and should be validated locally rather than assumed for Iranian pairs.

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: SHR 1.119 (1.035-1.211), p=0.005 [main text]; HR 1.141 (1.053-1.236) [Table 2]; 10-yr sdHR 1.13 (1.04-1.23); 2 MM: SHR 1.148, CI not printed, p=0.070 [main text]; HR 1.186 (1.020-1.378) [Table 2]; 10-yr sdHR 1.17 (1.00-1.36); 5-yr sdHR 0.90 (0.74-1.10)
- DQ: 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: HR 1.031 (0.953-1.115), p=0.452 [Table 2]; 10-yr 1.02 (0.95-1.11); 2 MM: HR 1.080 (0.950-1.227), p=0.242 [Table 2]; 10-yr 1.08 (0.94-1.23)
- B: 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: HR 1.082 (0.969-1.209), p=0.163 [Table 2]; 5-yr 1.16 (1.01-1.33); 10-yr 1.07 (0.95-1.20); 2 MM: HR 1.146 (1.002-1.310), p=0.047 [Table 2]; 5-yr 1.24 (1.05-1.46); 10-yr 1.14 (0.99-1.30)
- A: 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: HR 0.911 (0.824-1.008), p=0.071 [Table 2]; 5-yr 0.88 (0.78-1.00), p=0.043; 10-yr 0.91 (0.82-1.00); 2 MM: HR 0.975 (0.876-1.086), p=0.648 [Table 2]; 5-yr 0.96 (0.84-1.09); 10-yr 0.96 (0.86-1.07)
- Shape reported: step (per locus): at DR the first mismatch carries almost all of the penalty (1.119) and the second adds little (1.148, NS; 10-yr 1.13 vs 1.17); at B the second mismatch is larger than the first (1.082 vs 1.146; 5-yr 1.16 vs 1.24) with 1-vs-0 not significant; at A no penalty (point estimates below 1). For the UK-KAS composite: no penalty at level 2 vs perfect match (0.973), then incremental 1.132 and 1.190 at levels 3 and 4 - a threshold rather than a zero-mismatch premium. No total A+B+DR count series reported.; linearity tested: not tested; each locus entered as categorical dummies (1 vs 0 and 2 vs 0), no trend test, spline or per-mismatch linear term; 2-vs-1 was not compared directly; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- recipient ethnicity x HLA-DR mismatch: DR mismatch predicts graft failure in Asian recipients but not in Black recipients (point estimate below 1 in Black); overall SHR 1.119; no formal interaction test, subgroup models only (Asian DR Level 1 SHR 1.407 (1.138-1.739), p=0.002; Black DR 'Level 2' SHR 0.693 (0.432-1.113), p=0.129) [Abstract; Results 3.2; Tables S4-S5]
- recipient ethnicity x HLA-A / HLA-B mismatch: no significant effect of A or B mismatch in either Black or Asian subgroup (p values consistently exceeding 0.4 (no estimates printed)) [Results 3.2]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x HLA-DR mismatch (linkage disequilibrium): restricted to DR-0 recipients, DQ mismatch did not independently predict graft failure; for acute rejection the DQ effect persisted in DR-0 recipients, and a DR effect on rejection appeared only among DQ-0 recipients (graft failure in DR-0: no numbers in main text (Table S2); rejection in DR-0: DQ1 OR 1.36 (p<0.001), DQ2 OR 1.80 (p=0.003); DR in DQ-0: p<0.001, OR not printed) [Results 3.1; Results 4.1.1; Tables S2, S6]
- HLA-DR x HLA-B combination (UK-KAS levels): 1 DR + 0 B or 0 DR + 0/1 B (level 2) carries no excess risk over a 000 match; 0 DR + 2 B or 1 DR + 1 B (level 3) does; 1 DR + 2 B or 2 DR (level 4) most (SHR 0.973 (0.863-1.097); 1.132 (1.010-1.269); 1.190 (1.037-1.366)) [Results section 4; Figure 5; Table S3]
- follow-up horizon (5-year vs 10-year truncation): A (protective, 1 mismatch) and B (harmful, 1 and 2 mismatches) reach significance only in the 5-year model; at 10 years only DR remains significant; DR2 flips from 0.90 (5-yr) to 1.17 (10-yr) (see Table 4 entries) [Results 4.1.2; Table 4]
- recipient ethnicity x mismatch exposure (distribution, not outcome): Black and Asian recipients receive more poorly matched kidneys at every locus (chi-square p<0.001 each locus) (2-DQ mismatch 14.83% Black vs 10.68% Asian vs 9.56% White; 2-A mismatch 44.65% / 41.25% / 27.85%; 0-B mismatch 8.75% / 7.83% / 18.82%; 2-DR mismatch 14.83% / 7.58% / 7.56%) [Results 3.2; Table 3]
- sensitisation (CRF) x HLA mismatch: CRF entered only as a continuous main effect; no interaction with mismatch reported; no DSA data (CRF HR 1.003 (1.002-1.004) per unit) [Table 2; Discussion (limitations)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C9* — "Ten‐year graft survival was 13% less with one HLA DR mismatch, and 17% less with 2 HLA DR mismatch, in comparison to zero DR mismatch." (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "Although a single DR mismatch was associated with increased risk of graft failure in the overall cohort, this benefit did not extend clearly to Black recipients." (Discussion para 1)
- *C5* — "Low‐risk borderline HLA‐B mismatch (B mismatch = 1) and high‐risk borderline mismatch (B mismatch = 2) were also independently predictive of increased failure risk" (Results 4.1.2 (5-year truncated model))
- *C4* — "However, DQ mismatches did not independently predict long‐term graft failure in our cohort, suggesting that while they may trigger early rejection, they may not have a sustained impact on allograft loss" (Discussion para 5)
- *C10* — "We observed that transitioning from HLA Levels 1 to 2 does not significantly alter graft survival outcomes, as indicated by a sub‐distribution hazard ratio of 0.973 (95% CI: 0.863, 1.097" (Results section 4, para 2)
- *C11* — "Our subgroup analysis suggests that DR mismatching may offer limited, if any, survival benefit in Black patients, while DR matching may confer advantages in Asian recipients." (Discussion para 2)

**Limitations.** deceased donors only (mean donor age 49, 36% extended-criteria, mean CIT 14 h, 24% DGF); no living-donor data; UK registry: recipients 73% White, donors 94% White; ethnicity self-reported; Black subgroup n=2056 and its DR estimate is labelled 'Level 2' without clarifying whether that means two mismatches; antigen-level (low/intermediate resolution) typing; HLA-C and HLA-DP not analysed; no eplet or two-field data; no donor-specific antibody data; sensitisation only as continuous CRF main effect (PRA collected but absent from final model); no mismatch x sensitisation interaction; two different DR estimates are printed for the same comparison (text SHR 1.119, Table 2 HR 1.141) and it is not stated which table is the competing-risk model; text says B was not significant while Table 2 gives B[2] p=0.047 and the 5-year model gives significant B effects; 2-DR-mismatch group is small (7.7% of cohort), so the 2-vs-0 estimate is imprecise and no direct 2-vs-1 contrast is reported; no trend or linearity test; ethnicity results are subgroup models without a formal interaction test; backward stepwise variable selection; simple (single) imputation of missing covariates (BMI missing 21%); delayed graft function, a post-transplant variable, is a covariate; acute rejection recorded for only 80% of patients; rejection ORs for DR/A/B and the DR-0 graft-failure sensitivity analysis are only in supplementary tables not retrieved; median follow-up 5 years; graft failure defined by relisting or return to dialysis with death treated as a competing risk (not all-cause graft loss).

### Keith D 2026 — Should the Current Zero HLA ABDR-Mismatch Priority in Kidney Allocation System Continue?: A Critical Appraisal.

Keith D 2026, *Kidney360*, [DOI 10.34067/KID.0000001132](https://doi.org/10.34067/KID.0000001132). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (Kidney360/American Society of Nephrology; full text retrieved from PMC13229415, no licence statement present in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All adult deceased-donor kidney-alone transplants in the US SRTR from the start of KAS (4 December 2014) to 6 February 2024, excluding multiorgan-with-kidney, paediatric, 98%-100% CPRA, prior living donors, medically urgent and safety-net transplants; 122,951 transplants, of which 6228 (5.1%) were zero HLA ABDR-mismatch recipients with allocation CPRA <98% and 116,723 were nonzero (1-6) HLA ABDR-mismatch recipients |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 122,951 (6228 zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs 116,723 nonzero) |
| design | retrospective national registry (SRTR) observational cohort; Cox proportional hazards with 20 covariates (12 individual plus eight KDPI 2022 components); Schoenfeld residuals for proportionality; multiple imputation (5 imputations, MCMC) for 2.4% missing donor creatinine / cold ischaemia time; chi-squared, Mann-Whitney and ANOVA for descriptive comparisons; SPSS 29.0.2.0 |
| typing resolution | not stated; by KAS definition the zero-mismatch priority is antigen-level (low-resolution) HLA-A, -B, -DR only. The paper explicitly notes that HLA-C, -DQ and -DP are not considered in the priority |
| outcome | all-cause graft failure (explicitly including graft loss due to death with graft function) and patient death; adjusted 7-year graft and patient survival |
| follow up | median follow-up not reported; accrual 4 December 2014 to 6 February 2024 (maximum ~9.2 years); survival curves and adjusted survival reported to 7 years; censoring at loss to follow-up or dataset end |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, recipient race and ethnicity (SRTR), recipient gender, recipient ABO blood type, cause of ESKD, allocation CPRA, previous organ transplant, duration of dialysis before transplant, cold ischaemia time, donor KDPI 2022 (donor age, height, weight, cause of death, CVA, diabetes, hypertension, DCD, donor creatinine), donor race (SRTR), donor gender, donor ABO blood type |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a direct, contemporary-era evaluation of the single largest 'zero-mismatch premium' policy in the world, and therefore speaks to review question C13 (how allocation schemes score HLA and whether that scoring is validated by outcomes) and to the top rung of the C2/C9 dose-response question (how much a 0-ABDR-mismatch graft is actually worth versus any mismatched graft under modern immunosuppression). Its answer is that the premium is real but small: adjusted HR for all-cause graft failure 0.898 (0.834-0.967) and an absolute 7-year graft-survival difference of only 2 percentage points, with no patient-survival benefit at all (HR 0.947, 0.865-1.037). Crucially for the review, the paper does NOT provide a dose-response: exposure is dichotomised as 0 versus 1-6 ABDR mismatches, so it can bound the size of the zero-mismatch step but says nothing about whether risk rises linearly across counts or where a threshold lies. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field (low-resolution), antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is partial: the exposure definition matches the pre-screen exactly (antigen-level A/B/DR counted 0-6, C/DQ/DP ignored), so the estimate is a fair anchor for how much a zero-ABDR-mismatch living donor is worth in expectation, but the cohort is deceased-donor, and its zero-mismatch grafts were disproportionately shipped (79% from outside 250 miles) with longer cold ischaemia (20.4 vs 18.9 hours), a penalty that does not exist in living donation and that biases this HR toward the null relative to what a living-donor zero-mismatch would deliver. Two further cautions for the Iranian pre-screen: the outcome includes death with graft function, which dilutes an immunological effect, and the comparator group is dominated by high mismatch counts (78% had 4-6 mismatches), so this is a 0-versus-mostly-badly-matched contrast, not 0 versus 1. Finally, the paper's central equity argument - that zero-ABDR-mismatch priority tracks HLA-frequency dominance in the local donor pool and therefore concentrates benefit in the majority ethnic group - transfers directly to any Iranian scheme that would rank donors by antigen-level match, and is a reason to treat a zero-mismatch bonus as a tie-breaker rather than a hard priority.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft failure (including death with graft function): zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero (1-6) HLA ABDR-mismatch, allocation CPRA <98% — HR 0.898 (0.834–0.967), p=0.004; adjusted for 20 covariates (recipient age, SRTR race/ethnicity, gender, ABO, cause of ESKD, CPRA, previous transplant, dialysis duration, cold ischaemia time; donor KDPI 2022 with eight components, donor race, gender, ABO) [Abstract (Results); Results paragraph 3]
- patient death: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero (1-6) HLA ABDR-mismatch — HR 0.947 (0.865–1.037), p=0.239; adjusted for same 20-covariate Cox model [Abstract (Results); Results paragraph 3]
- all-cause graft failure: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero, UNADJUSTED — HR 0.788 (0.737–0.841); adjusted for none (crude) [Results paragraph 3]
- patient death: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero, UNADJUSTED — HR 0.827 (0.783–0.896); adjusted for none (crude) [Results paragraph 3]
- all-cause graft failure: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero, sensitivity analysis including highly sensitised (98%-100% allocation CPRA) kidney-alone recipients in the nonzero group — HR 0.899 (0.836–0.967); adjusted for same 20-covariate Cox model [Results paragraph 3]
- patient death: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch vs nonzero, sensitivity analysis including 98%-100% CPRA recipients in the nonzero group — HR 0.934 (0.859–1.026); adjusted for same 20-covariate Cox model [Results paragraph 3]
- adjusted graft survival at 7 years, zero HLA ABDR-mismatch group: zero HLA ABDR-mismatch (absolute) — percentage 67; adjusted for Cox-adjusted survival curve [Results paragraph 3; Figure 2B]
- adjusted graft survival at 7 years, nonzero HLA ABDR-mismatch group: nonzero (1-6) HLA ABDR-mismatch (absolute); 2 percentage-point difference vs zero-mismatch — percentage 65; adjusted for Cox-adjusted survival curve [Results paragraph 3; Figure 2B]
- adjusted patient survival at 7 years: identical in zero and nonzero HLA ABDR-mismatch groups — percentage 78; adjusted for Cox-adjusted survival curve [Results paragraph 3; Figure 2A]
- share of adult deceased-donor kidney-alone transplants allocated as zero HLA ABDR-mismatch (CPRA <98%): 6228 of 122,951 — percentage 5.1 [Abstract (Methods); Results paragraph 1]
- blood type O donor kidneys shunted to nonidentical (non-O) ABO recipients under the zero-mismatch priority: 1441 of 58,654 O donors; A donors 0.18%, AB 0.07%, B 0.22% — percentage 2.46 [Abstract (Results); Results paragraph 2; Table 2]
- White recipients among zero HLA ABDR-mismatch recipients: 63.7% (3966) zero-mismatch vs 33.4% (38,966) nonzero — percentage 63.7, p=0.001 [Table 1 (recipient race and ethnicity; p reported as <0.001)]
- Black recipients among zero HLA ABDR-mismatch recipients: 10.6% (663) zero-mismatch vs 36.6% (42,747) nonzero — percentage 10.6, p=0.001 [Table 1 (p reported as <0.001)]
- Asian recipients among zero HLA ABDR-mismatch recipients: 2.9% (181) zero-mismatch vs 8% (9328) nonzero — percentage 2.9, p=0.001 [Table 1 (p reported as <0.001)]
- median time on dialysis before transplant (years): 1.85 (IQR 0.40-3.55) zero-mismatch vs 3.87 (IQR 1.70-6.18) nonzero — median years 1.85, p=0.001 [Table 1 (p reported as <0.001)]
- preemptive (no dialysis) transplants: 20.5% (1274) zero-mismatch vs 9.5% (11,085) nonzero — percentage 20.5, p=0.001 [Table 1 (p reported as <0.001)]
- previous organ transplant (retransplant recipients): 27.3% (1701) zero-mismatch vs 12.3% (14,351) nonzero — percentage 27.3, p=0.001 [Table 1 (p reported as <0.001)]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 0.898 (0.834–0.967); 1-6 pooled MM: 1.0
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. HLA ABDR mismatch enters the Cox model only as a binary indicator (zero vs nonzero). No per-count hazard ratios, no trend test, no spline, no threshold analysis. Table 1 gives the 0-6 mismatch count distribution but only as a cohort characteristic, never as an exposure with an outcome attached.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- zero HLA ABDR-mismatch x sensitisation (allocation CPRA 98%-100%): Sensitivity analysis, not a formal interaction test. Adding highly sensitised (98%-100% CPRA) kidney-alone recipients into the nonzero comparator did not materially change either estimate. (graft failure HR 0.899 (0.836-0.967) vs 0.898 (0.834-0.967) in the primary analysis; death HR 0.934 (0.859-1.026) vs 0.947 (0.865-1.037)) [Results paragraph 3]
- zero HLA ABDR-mismatch x missing data (donor creatinine, cold ischaemia time): Multiple imputation (5 imputations, MCMC) over 2.4% missing values did not change the statistical conclusions for patient or graft survival; missingness was near-identical between the two groups (donor creatinine 1.2% vs 1.2%; cold ischaemia 2.2% vs 2.1%). (no change in statistical outcomes (imputed Cox results in supplement, not in retrieved text)) [Methods; Results paragraph 3; Discussion (weaknesses)]
- zero HLA ABDR-mismatch x recipient race/ethnicity: Reported as an access disparity, not as effect modification on graft survival. Race is a covariate in the Cox model; no race-stratified hazard ratios for the HLA effect are given. (White 63.7% vs 33.4%; Black 10.6% vs 36.6%; Asian 2.9% vs 8% (all p<0.001, chi-squared)) [Table 1; Discussion paragraph 1]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "candidates without HLA mismatches to donor HLA A, B, and DR to receive offers before nonzero HLA ABDR-mismatch candidates, based on the greater utility of organ use (HLA C, DQ, and DP are not considered)" (Introduction, paragraph 2)
- *C9* — "zero HLA ABDR-mismatch confers a small graft survival benefit but no patient survival benefit" (Discussion, weaknesses paragraph)
- *C2* — "The adjusted graft survival at 7 years was 67% (zero HLA mismatch) versus 65% (nonzero HLA mismatch), whereas adjusted patient survival was the same for the two groups at 7 years, at 78%" (Results, paragraph 3)
- *C13* — "The current zero HLA ABDR-mismatch priority is highly biased against racial minority recipients, shunts a sizable number of O donors to non-O recipients, only makes a small improvement to organ utility, and should be removed from the allocation priority list." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C13* — "zero HLA DR-mismatch receives one point, while a year of waiting receives only 0.1 point in the model, even though they have almost equivalent effect on graft survival" (Discussion, paragraph on continuous-scoring models)
- *C1* — "There is evidence that the effect of HLA mismatching is decreasing due to better immunosuppression and histocompatibility testing." (Introduction, paragraph 4)

**Limitations.** Exposure is dichotomised (0 vs 1-6 ABDR mismatches). The paper contributes nothing to the shape of the dose-response: no per-count HRs, no trend test, no spline, no threshold analysis.; The comparator is dominated by badly matched grafts (78.3% of the nonzero group had 4-6 mismatches; only 1.4% had a single mismatch), so HR 0.898 is a 0-versus-mostly-4-to-6 contrast and materially overstates what would be gained by 0 versus 1.; Graft failure is all-cause and explicitly includes death with graft function; no death-censored graft survival is reported, which dilutes any immunological signal and biases the HLA effect toward the null.; Observational registry with strong allocation-driven confounding by indication: zero-mismatch recipients had half the dialysis exposure (median 1.85 vs 3.87 years), twice the preemptive rate, twice the retransplant rate, and were 63.7% vs 33.4% White. Adjustment cannot fully remove this; the crude HR (0.788) shrinks to 0.898 after adjustment, showing how much of the apparent benefit is confounding.; Zero-mismatch grafts were far more often shipped (79% vs 41.1% from outside the 250-mile radius) with longer cold ischaemia (20.4+/-7.0 vs 18.9+/-8.2 hours), a penalty that partly offsets the matching benefit and does not exist in living donation.; Priority-group membership is inferred from HLA mismatch, listing age, prior-living-donor flag, urgent status, safety-net timing and allocation CPRA, because the allocation priority group is not recorded in the SRTR dataset; the authors acknowledge possible misclassification.; No per-locus results (A vs B vs DR are only ever summed) and no data at all on HLA-C, -DQ or -DP, which the priority ignores by design.; No DSA, eplet or molecular mismatch data; HLA typing resolution is never stated; sensitisation enters only as allocation CPRA, and only as a sensitivity analysis.; No formal effect-modification testing (no interaction terms reported) for race, donor quality, sensitisation, age or era.; Deceased-donor only, US only; results do not directly speak to living donation, and the 7-year horizon truncates any late divergence between matched and mismatched grafts.; Unmeasured socioeconomic and health-literacy confounding is acknowledged by the authors as biasing in favour of the zero-mismatch (predominantly White, more preemptive) group.; The Discussion is an explicit policy argument; the outcome analysis is a modest part of a paper written to advocate removing the priority..

### Morford HJ 2026 — HLA Matching in US Kidney Transplantation Over Three Decades: Trends, Disparities, and Clinical Implications.

Morford HJ 2026, *J Am Soc Nephrol (JASN)*, [DOI 10.1681/ASN.0000001202](https://doi.org/10.1681/ASN.0000001202). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown (publisher copyright; PubMed abstract only, no PMC deposit at time of retrieval).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | US kidney transplant recipients in the Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients (SRTR), 1991-2023; living and deceased donor transplants; adults and children; analysed across racial and age subgroups. Neither the analytic inclusion/exclusion criteria (first vs repeat transplant, kidney-alone vs multi-organ) nor the adjustment set are stated in the abstract. |
| donor type | both |
| n | Total analytic N not stated in the abstract. The only counts printed are zero-mismatch transplant counts by year: 1,145 (zero HLA-ABDR) and 3,804 (zero HLA-DR) in 2023; 318 (zero HLA-ABDR) and 929 (zero HLA-DR) in 1991. |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort. Two analyses: (a) temporal trend in the proportion of zero HLA-ABDR and zero HLA-DR mismatch transplants, 1991-2023, overall and by donor type, race and age; (b) era-stratified association of HLA mismatching with graft outcomes and with peak CPRA at repeat waitlisting. The regression model class (e.g. Cox) is not named in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; the exposure is expressed as HLA-ABDR and HLA-DR mismatch counts as recorded in SRTR. Whether that is antigen-level/low-resolution is NOT stated by the paper and must not be asserted on its behalf. |
| outcome | graft survival / graft longevity (the exact endpoint definition - all-cause vs death-censored graft failure - is not stated in the abstract); secondary: peak CPRA at repeat waitlisting; descriptive: proportion of transplants with zero HLA-ABDR or zero HLA-DR mismatch |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | transplant era (1990s, 2000s, 2010s), donor type (living vs deceased), recipient race, recipient age (including children), peak calculated panel reactive antibody (CPRA) at repeat waitlisting, US kidney allocation policy changes (a narrative explanation of trend inflections; NOT stated to be a model covariate) |

**Why it is relevant.** VERIFIER-TRIMMED. This is the most recent national test of the review's central temporal question: whether HLA matching still predicts kidney graft outcome under contemporary immunosuppression, and whether the size of that benefit has shrunk. Its answer is a qualified yes - the abstract states that the associations are weaker in recent eras but that HLA matching remained significantly associated with better graft survival (note: the abstract does NOT print era-by-era significance, so 'significant in every era' cannot be asserted from it). That attenuation-not-abolition pattern is what the pre-screen must be calibrated against; keeping HLA in the score without letting it dominate is our inference, not a recommendation the paper makes. It also supplies a second, non-graft reason to match that matters for a young Iranian living-donor population: greater HLA mismatching was ASSOCIATED with significantly higher peak CPRA at repeat listing. That association is measured only among patients who lost a graft and were relisted, so it is not established as a causal sensitisation cost, and the abstract prints no effect size for it. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor setting is partial. The living-donor half of this cohort is relevant and the paper's living-donor finding - that the decline in well-matched transplants paralleled reductions in biologically related donors - is the mechanism a mostly unrelated-donor Iranian programme should expect to face, implying that better matching there must be engineered by selection rather than inherited from kinship. The exposure is HLA-A/B/DR mismatch counts from a registry; the abstract does not state typing resolution, so the assumption that this is the same low-resolution currency our pre-screen will have is ours, not the paper's. The limits are that the paper reports no antibody or DSA data at transplant beyond CPRA at relisting, so it cannot inform an antibody-status-unknown screen directly, and that from the abstract alone we obtain no era-specific hazard ratios and no per-mismatch-count series to fit a dose-response weight to.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- proportion of kidney transplants with zero HLA-ABDR mismatch: calendar year 2023 — percentage 5.0; adjusted for unadjusted descriptive proportion [Abstract, Results (n = 1,145 transplants)]
- proportion of kidney transplants with zero HLA-DR mismatch: calendar year 2023 — percentage 16.0; adjusted for unadjusted descriptive proportion [Abstract, Results (n = 3,804 transplants)]
- proportion of kidney transplants with zero HLA-ABDR mismatch: calendar year 1991 — percentage 11.0; adjusted for unadjusted descriptive proportion [Abstract, Results (n = 318 transplants)]
- proportion of kidney transplants with zero HLA-DR mismatch: calendar year 1991 — percentage 32.0; adjusted for unadjusted descriptive proportion [Abstract, Results (n = 929 transplants)]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: note MM: The abstract reports the PREVALENCE of zero HLA-DR mismatch (32% in 1991 falling to 16% in 2023) but no per-mismatch-count effect estimate for DR. No 0/1/2 effect series is printed for any locus.
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested, or not reported in the abstract; no P for trend, no spline, no threshold analysis is mentioned; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching x transplant era (1990s vs 2000s vs 2010s): VERIFIER-TRIMMED. The abstract states that the associations are weaker in recent eras, that HLA matching remained significantly associated with better graft survival, and that the magnitude of benefit has diminished in the most recent era. It does NOT report era-by-era significance, so the earlier wording ('persisted in every era', 'remained statistically significant throughout') has been removed as unsupported. (No era-specific hazard ratios, confidence intervals, P values or P for interaction are printed in the abstract. The claim is stated qualitatively as 'the associations are weaker in recent eras' and 'the magnitude of benefit has diminished in the most recent era'.) [Abstract, Results and Conclusions]
- HLA mismatch count x subsequent sensitisation (peak CPRA at repeat waitlisting): Greater HLA mismatching was associated with significantly higher peak CPRA at repeat listing. The analysis is restricted to patients who were relisted, so this is an association within a selected subgroup, not a demonstrated causal sensitisation cost. (No effect size, CI or P value is printed in the abstract; only the word 'significantly'.) [Abstract, Results]
- calendar trend in zero-mismatch share x donor type (living vs deceased): Deceased-donor declines were intermittent and temporally aligned with US allocation policy changes, whereas living-donor declines were continuous and paralleled the fall in biologically related donors. This is effect modification of the TREND in matching, not of the graft-survival association. (Not quantified in the abstract.) [Abstract, Results]
- calendar trend in zero-mismatch share x race and x recipient age: The declining trend was consistent across racial and age groups, with the lowest levels of matching currently seen in children and in racial-minority deceased-donor kidney recipients. Again a disparity in exposure prevalence, not a reported modification of the mismatch-outcome association. (Not quantified in the abstract.) [Abstract, Results and Conclusions]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "Although the associations are weaker in recent eras, HLA matching remained significantly associated with better graft survival, and greater HLA mismatching was associated with significantly higher CPRA at repeat listing." (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "Well-matched transplants experience better graft longevity, but the magnitude of benefit has diminished in the most recent era." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C13* — "In 2023, 5% (1,145) and 16% (3,804) of transplants had zero HLA-ABDR and zero HLA-DR mismatches, respectively, compared with 11% (318) and 32% (929) in 1991." (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "Trends in deceased donor transplantation were intermittent and temporally aligned with allocation policy changes, whereas declines in living donor transplantation were continuous and paralleled reductions in biologically related donors." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "These patterns were consistent across racial and age groups, with the lowest rates observed among children and racial minority deceased donor kidney recipients." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "We further examined associations between HLA mismatching and graft outcomes across transplant eras (1990s, 2000s, 2010s) and peak calculated panel reactive antibody (CPRA) at repeat waitlisting." (Abstract, Methods)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY. No PMC full text exists for this record (the verifier independently re-ran convert_article_ids on PMID 42525732 and it returned no pmcid), so every effect estimate for graft survival, every confidence interval, every P value and every P for interaction in this paper is unavailable to the review. The era comparison - the reason the paper is in the review - is currently only a qualitative statement.; No hazard ratios of any kind are printed in the abstract; the only numbers obtainable are four descriptive percentages of zero-mismatch share and their counts.; No dose-response series is reported: no per-count (0/1/2/.../6) estimates, no per-locus effect estimates, no test of linearity, no statement of whether 1 and 2 mismatches at a locus were pooled. The paper therefore cannot support claim C2 at all.; Retrospective registry design; typing resolution is not stated and cannot be confirmed from the abstract.; The adjustment set is not stated. Era-stratified comparisons of a matching effect are heavily confounded by everything else that changed between the 1990s and the 2010s - induction and maintenance immunosuppression, donor quality and donor age, cold ischaemia, recipient age and comorbidity, allocation policy - so 'the benefit has diminished' may partly reflect changing case mix or changing competing risks rather than a changed biological effect of mismatch.; The outcome definition is not given: all-cause versus death-censored graft failure matters a great deal for an era comparison, because rising recipient age inflates death-with-function in later eras and mechanically dilutes an immunological effect.; The CPRA analysis is conditioned on being relisted, a selected subgroup (patients who lost a graft and returned to the waitlist and were HLA-tested again); this is a collider-prone comparison and the abstract gives no sensitisation effect size.; US allocation environment (including the 2014 Kidney Allocation System) drives the deceased-donor trends; those inflection points do not transfer to Iran, and the deceased-donor half of the cohort is not the review's target population.; No antibody or DSA data at transplant, no eplet/molecular mismatch, no DQ or DP analysis reported in the abstract - so the paper says nothing about the antibody-unknown pre-screen problem beyond the downstream CPRA signal.; Living-donor-specific effect estimates for HLA mismatch on graft survival are not reported separately in the abstract; the living/deceased split is presented only for the matching-prevalence trend.; US racial and biological-relatedness composition differs from Iran's; the finding that living-donor matching fell as biologically related donation fell is mechanistically transferable but the absolute levels are not..

### Brosi DN 2025 — Recipient Human Leukocyte Antigen-DR Homozygosity and Access to Quality Kidneys

Brosi DN 2025, *Kidney International Reports*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ekir.2025.11.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2025.11.005). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (no Creative Commons or licence statement present in the retrieved PMC text; Kidney International Reports is an open-access journal).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 262,815 adult (>=18 y at listing), primary (no previous transplant), kidney-alone (simultaneous kidney-pancreas excluded) US deceased-donor kidney transplant candidates listed 1 January 2015 - 31 May 2024, SRTR; listings missing race/ethnicity or HLA-DR antigen pair excluded; 13% HLA-DR homozygous, 87% heterozygous; 12% of deceased kidney donors HLA-DR homozygous |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 262,815 candidates; 103,327 received a DDKT (15,237 with 0 DR MM, 48,819 with 1 DR MM, 39,108 with 2 DR MM, 163 unknown); 14% received a living-donor transplant (competing event); 23% died or were removed; 24% still waiting at censoring |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; Fine and Gray competing-risk regression (subdistribution hazard ratios) for time from listing to (a) any DDKT and (b) DDKT with exactly 0, 1 or 2 HLA-DR mismatches, each a separate model with all other DDKTs, death/removal and living-donor transplant as competing events; 8 models total (4 outcomes x with/without a race x homozygosity interaction); Bonferroni-corrected significance threshold 0.006; sensitivity analyses by pre/post COVID-19 and pre/post KAS250 listing period |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen level (one-field), explicitly resolved through the 2021 OPTN Updated Equivalency Tables; split antigens collapsed to their serologic broad equivalent (e.g. DR1 and DR101 count as homozygous; DR4 + DR401 treated as the same DR4 lineage). Discordant candidate-vs-transplant DR typings (n=296, 0.1%) and double-null DR typings (n=1297, 0.5%) were dropped (total n=1593, 0.6%); the most recent typing was used when typings were equivalent but not identical |
| outcome | ACCESS, not graft outcome: time from waitlist registration to deceased-donor kidney transplant, overall and stratified by the number of HLA-DR mismatches received (0, 1, 2). No graft-survival, rejection or DSA outcome is analysed in this paper. |
| follow up | listings 1 Jan 2015 to 31 May 2024, administratively censored 31 May 2024 (maximum ~9.4 years); no median follow-up reported. Cumulative-incidence results are reported at 1 and 5 years. |
| other factors modelled | recipient race/ethnicity (5 groups: non-Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Black, Hispanic White, non-Hispanic Asian American/Pacific Islander, Other), biological sex, age, education, primary insurance type, Distressed Community Index score (2017-2021 Economic Innovation Group, social determinants / built environment), ABO blood type, time on dialysis at waitlist placement, primary diagnosis, cPRA category at waitlist placement, diabetes status, body mass index category, UNOS region |

**Why it is relevant.** This is an ACCESS paper, not an outcome paper: it quantifies how a recipient's own HLA-DR genotype changes the probability of ever being offered a well-matched kidney, and it is the largest such quantification (262,815 candidates). It answers the review's non-additivity question (C10) from the supply side: because a DR-homozygous candidate can only score 0 DR mismatches against a donor carrying that same single DR antigen, the mismatch count is not an interchangeable integer across candidates - the same '1 DR mismatch' is a structurally different event for a homozygote than for a heterozygote, and the paper shows the resulting gradient (sHR 0.46 for a 0-MM kidney, 0.83 for 1 MM, 1.40 for 2 MM). It answers C13 by showing that an allocation rule which awards points for low DR mismatch (US: 1 point for 1 DR MM, 2 points for 0 DR MM, extra for 0-ABDR) systematically transfers those points away from homozygous and from antigen-rare candidates, and the authors conclude the scheme should be revised to incorporate homozygosity. Transfer to a LIVING-donor Iranian pre-screen is partial but real. The typing resolution is exactly ours - one-field serologic antigens read against an equivalency table - so the homozygosity definition and the DR1/DR101-style split-vs-broad trap are directly reusable; the equivalency step is a concrete requirement, since without it DR1 vs DR101 would be scored as a mismatch when it is not. Antibody status is only weakly used here (cPRA is a covariate, not a filter), which matches an antibody-unknown pre-screen, and the paper incidentally notes 3% of homozygous vs 1% of heterozygous candidates had cPRA 100%. The core mechanism transfers: in a living-donor pool an Iranian DR-homozygous recipient will more often show apparently favourable low DR mismatch counts against arbitrary donors on one DR line while being unable to reach a true 0-MM, so a ranking function must not read a homozygote's mismatch count on the same scale as a heterozygote's. What does NOT transfer is the allocation machinery itself - deceased-donor queueing, competing risks, KAS250 points and US racial/ethnic HLA-DR frequency distributions have no analogue in a directed living-donor search, and the paper reports no graft-survival evidence at all, so it can support the SCORING-DESIGN and access claims but never a compatibility or outcome claim.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- receiving any DDKT: recipient HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous — sHR 0.95 (0.93–0.97); adjusted for race/ethnicity, sex, age, education, insurance, Distressed Community Index, blood type, dialysis time, primary diagnosis, cPRA, diabetes, BMI, UNOS region [Abstract Results; Results, Competing Risks para 2 (main non-interacted model)]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: recipient HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous — sHR 0.46 (0.43–0.49); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Abstract Results; Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 1 HLA-DR mismatch: recipient HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous — sHR 0.83 (0.81–0.86); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Abstract Results (CI 0.81-0.86). NOTE: the Results body prints this CI as '0.91-0.86', an obvious typographical error; the abstract value is used here]
- receiving a DDKT with 2 HLA-DR mismatches: recipient HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous — sHR 1.4 (1.36–1.44); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Abstract Results; Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: Black vs White candidates (main effect, homozygosity in the model separately) — sHR 0.62 (0.59–0.65); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: Asian American/Pacific Islander vs White candidates (main effect) — sHR 0.66 (0.61–0.71); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 2 HLA-DR mismatches: Black vs White candidates (main effect) — sHR 1.54 (1.49–1.58); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 2 HLA-DR mismatches: Asian American/Pacific Islander vs White candidates (main effect) — sHR 1.45 (1.39–1.51); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving a DDKT with 2 HLA-DR mismatches: Other race vs White candidates (main effect) — sHR 1.41 (1.31–1.53); adjusted for same adjustment set as above [Results, Competing Risks para 2]
- receiving any DDKT: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous, WITHIN White candidates (interacted model) — sHR 0.9 (0.87–0.93); adjusted for same adjustment set, race x homozygosity interaction [Results, Competing Risks para 4]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous, WITHIN Black candidates (interacted model) — sHR 0.41 (0.35–0.47); adjusted for same adjustment set, race x homozygosity interaction [Results, Competing Risks para 4]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous, WITHIN Asian American/Pacific Islander candidates (interacted model) — sHR 0.43 (0.34–0.54); adjusted for same adjustment set, race x homozygosity interaction [Results, Competing Risks para 4]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous, WITHIN Hispanic candidates (interacted model) — sHR 0.56 (0.5–0.63); adjusted for same adjustment set, race x homozygosity interaction [Results, Competing Risks para 4]
- receiving a DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous, WITHIN White candidates (interacted model) — sHR 0.44; adjusted for same adjustment set, race x homozygosity interaction [Results, Competing Risks para 5 (quoted in text without a CI; the CI is only in the supplementary/figure tables, which were not in the retrieved text)]
- cumulative incidence of a 0-HLA-DR-mismatch DDKT at 1 year: HLA-DR heterozygous candidates — cumulative incidence (%) 2.82 (2.75–2.89); adjusted for unadjusted cumulative-incidence function [Results, Competing Risks para 1]
- cumulative incidence of a 0-HLA-DR-mismatch DDKT at 1 year: HLA-DR homozygous candidates — cumulative incidence (%) 1.55 (1.42–1.69); adjusted for unadjusted cumulative-incidence function [Results, Competing Risks para 1]
- cumulative incidence of a 0-HLA-DR-mismatch DDKT at 5 years: HLA-DR heterozygous candidates — cumulative incidence (%) 7.06 (6.94–7.71); adjusted for unadjusted cumulative-incidence function [Results, Competing Risks para 1 (the printed upper limit 7.71% is implausibly wide for a point estimate of 7.06% with a lower limit of 6.94% and is probably a typo for ~7.18%; reproduced as printed)]
- cumulative incidence of a 0-HLA-DR-mismatch DDKT at 5 years: HLA-DR homozygous candidates — cumulative incidence (%) 3.52 (3.3–3.74); adjusted for unadjusted cumulative-incidence function [Results, Competing Risks para 1]
- distribution of HLA-DR mismatch counts among DDKTs actually performed: 0 vs 1 vs 2 HLA-DR mismatches among 103,327 DDKT recipients — percentage None; adjusted for descriptive [Results, Descriptive Statistics: 15% (n=15,237) 0 DR MM, 47% (n=48,819) 1 DR MM, 38% (n=39,108) 2 DR MM, <1% (n=163) unknown]
- prevalence of HLA-DR homozygosity: candidates overall and by race/ethnicity; deceased donors — percentage 13; adjusted for descriptive [Results, Descriptive Statistics: 13% of candidates homozygous (87% heterozygous); AA/PI and Other highest at 17%, Black lowest at 11%, White 13%, Hispanic 14%; 12% of deceased kidney donors homozygous]
- cPRA 100% prevalence: HLA-DR homozygous vs heterozygous candidates — percentage 3; adjusted for descriptive [Results, Descriptive Statistics: 3% of homozygous vs 1% of heterozygous candidates had cPRA 100%; cPRA 0% in 52% of homozygous vs 55% of heterozygous]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 0.46 (0.43–0.49); 1 MM: 0.83 (0.81–0.86); 2 MM: 1.4 (1.36–1.44)
- DR: 0 MM: sHR 0.46 (0.43-0.49) for a homozygous candidate obtaining a 0-DR-MM DDKT; 1 MM: sHR 0.83 (0.81-0.86) for a homozygous candidate obtaining a 1-DR-MM DDKT; 2 MM: sHR 1.40 (1.36-1.44) for a homozygous candidate obtaining a 2-DR-MM DDKT
- A: not analysed
- B: not analysed (the Introduction notes HLA-B was removed from US allocation after it caused access disparities for Black candidates without significant additional post-transplant benefit)
- C: not analysed
- DQ: not analysed
- DP: not analysed
- Shape reported: not reported as an outcome dose-response. What the paper reports is an ACCESS gradient that is monotone and sign-reversing across DR mismatch count (0.46 -> 0.83 -> 1.40), i.e. the homozygosity penalty is concentrated almost entirely at the 0-mismatch end and becomes an excess at 2 mismatches. The authors describe the 'all DDKT' estimate (0.95) as moderate precisely because the 0/1-mismatch deficit and the 2-mismatch excess partly cancel.; linearity tested: not tested. Each mismatch count was modelled as a separate Fine and Gray competing-risk outcome (with the other counts as competing events); no trend test, no spline, no ordinal model, and no test of linearity across mismatch count was performed or reported.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- recipient HLA-DR homozygosity x recipient race/ethnicity, outcome = any DDKT: significant interaction; the homozygosity penalty for receiving ANY DDKT was present only in White candidates (sHR 0.90, 0.87-0.93) and was not significant within any racial/ethnic minority group, which the authors attribute to minorities' higher baseline likelihood of receiving a 2-DR-mismatch DDKT offsetting the deficit at 0 and 1 mismatches (joint Wald test statistic 18.0, p = 0.001 (Bonferroni-corrected threshold 0.006)) [Results, Competing Risks paras 3-4]
- recipient HLA-DR homozygosity x recipient race/ethnicity, outcome = DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches: significant interaction, but the DIRECTION is the same in every stratum: homozygosity lowered access to a 0-DR-mismatch DDKT for all races/ethnicities (Black 0.41, AA/PI 0.43, White 0.44, Hispanic 0.56). The interaction reflects a difference in magnitude, not sign - the authors explicitly warn that a higher sHR here means a less dramatic decrease, not better access (joint Wald test statistic 16.1, p = 0.003; Hispanic 0.56 significantly higher than White 0.44) [Results, Competing Risks paras 3-5]
- recipient HLA-DR homozygosity x recipient race/ethnicity, outcomes = DDKT with 1 and with 2 HLA-DR mismatches: no significant interaction; the homozygosity association did not vary by race/ethnicity for these outcomes. Homozygosity raised the likelihood of a 2-DR-mismatch DDKT irrespective of race/ethnicity (interaction not significant (no test statistic or p-value printed in the retrieved text)) [Results, Competing Risks para 3]
- HLA-DR homozygosity x allocation-policy era (pre/post KAS250) and pre/post COVID-19 listing period: sensitivity analyses confirmed the main results; significance was unchanged in all models except that in the post-KAS250 period the homozygosity effect became significant within the Other race group where it had been non-significant in the main analysis. Some post-KAS250 estimates were more extreme, possibly because that period is under 3 years (no numbers printed in the retrieved text (relegated to supplementary tables)) [Results, Sensitivity Testing]
- recipient HLA-DR antigen frequency x deceased-donor pool antigen frequency (the mechanism behind the interaction, descriptive): candidate/donor antigen-frequency mismatch, not homozygosity alone, drives the access penalty: White and Hispanic candidates' DR frequencies resemble the donor pool, while Black and AA/PI candidates carry antigens rare in donors (DR18 12% in Black candidates vs 2% of donors; DR12 25% in AA/PI vs 4% of donors), lowering their chance of a 0-DR-mismatch offer (descriptive genotype frequencies only, no test statistic) [Results, HLA-DR Antigen Prevalence; Discussion para 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Prioritization for access to transplantation should incorporate HLA-DR homozygosity to promote equity." (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C13* — "For kidney allocation, candidates receive 1 priority point (equivalent to 1 year of waiting time) for 1 HLA-DR mismatch and 2 points for a 0 HLA-DR mismatches along with extra points for a 0-ABDR mismatch." (Introduction, para 1)
- *C10* — "HLA-DR homozygous KT candidates were particularly disadvantaged for receiving DDKT with 0 HLA-DR mismatches, followed by DDKT with 1 HLA-DR mismatches." (Discussion, para 1)
- *C10* — "a candidate with 2 HLA-DR7 haplotypes or a candidate with HLA-DR1 and HLA-DR101 haplotypes would both be considered HLA-DR homozygous" (Methods, Data Sources and Measures, para 3)
- *C10* — "the frequency of HLA-DR18 in Black KT candidates is 12% compared with only 2% in the donor population" (Results, HLA-DR Antigen Prevalence)
- *C13* — "This disparity in access to highly matched HLA-DR kidneys for HLA-DR homozygous patients creates a bias in downstream outcomes that is difficult to correct after transplantation." (Conclusion)

**Limitations.** This paper measures ACCESS to transplantation, not transplant OUTCOME. It contains no graft-survival, rejection, dnDSA or mortality analysis of its own; every outcome claim it makes about DR mismatch is cited from prior literature, not estimated here. It cannot support C1, C2, C3 or C9 on its own evidence.; Deceased-donor allocation only. Living-donor transplantation is treated purely as a competing event (14% of the cohort), so the paper says nothing quantitative about HLA-DR homozygosity in a directed living-donor search - which is the KidneyMatch use case.; The mechanism is queue-and-supply specific: results are produced by the US waiting list, KAS/KAS250 point structure, UNOS regional geography and the US deceased-donor antigen-frequency distribution. None of these exist in an Iranian living-donor pre-screen; only the underlying combinatorial fact (a homozygote cannot reach 0 MM against most donors) transfers.; Race/ethnicity is used as a proxy for HLA-DR antigen frequency. The authors show frequency data descriptively but do not model antigen frequency directly, so the 'race' interaction is a coarse stand-in for the actual genetic mechanism - and US race categories have no meaning for an Iranian population.; Serologic, one-field typing resolved through the 2021 OPTN equivalency tables. Homozygosity here is SEROLOGIC homozygosity: two alleles that are serologically equivalent but molecularly distinct (e.g. DR1 vs DR101) are counted as homozygous. True allele-level homozygosity is neither measured nor distinguished, so the exposure is partly a typing artefact.; Residual confounding acknowledged by the authors: unobserved factors correlated with both race/ethnicity and HLA-DR homozygosity may drive part of the effect.; 9.2% of the sample had missing cPRA, mostly in 2023-2024; missing covariate values were carried as separate model levels rather than imputed.; Geography only partly controlled (UNOS region); centre-level offer-acceptance behaviour and local waiting times are not modelled, and the authors flag this.; DR only. HLA-A, -B, -C, -DQ and -DP homozygosity are not examined at all, so nothing can be said here about whether the same access penalty operates at other loci or about cross-locus non-additivity.; Two numerical typographical errors in the retrieved text: the 1-DR-mismatch CI is printed as '0.91-0.86' in Results (abstract gives 0.81-0.86), and the 5-year heterozygous cumulative incidence CI is printed as '6.94%-7.71%' around a 7.06% point estimate. The Methods also state the Bonferroni rule backwards ('only consider p-values > 0.006 as statistically significant').; Tables and figures were not present in the retrieved PMC text; several results (full covariate tables, unadjusted models, all sensitivity-analysis numbers, and the CI for the White 0-MM interacted estimate) are only available there and could not be extracted..

### Das R 2025 — Understanding HLA-DQ in renal transplantation: a mini-review

Das R 2025, *Front Immunol*, [DOI 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1525306](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1525306). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown from retrieved text (Frontiers in Immunology articles are normally CC BY 4.0; the licence statement was not part of the PMC text returned).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Narrative mini-review of HLA-DQ immunobiology in kidney transplantation; no primary cohort. The authors state the review focuses on kidney transplantation but that principles may apply to other solid organs; one cited PIRCHE-II result spans 'various organ and donor types'. |
| donor type | both (cited literature); one cited study is adult living-donor kidney recipients |
| n | not applicable (narrative review, no pooled data) |
| design | narrative mini-review; no search strategy, no quantitative synthesis; two authors (Das R, Greenspan NS), Case Western Reserve University |
| typing resolution | discussed explicitly: serological / low or intermediate DNA-based vs two-field high-resolution; argues two-field typing is required for HLA-DQ |
| outcome | cited qualitatively: DSA formation, rejection (TCMR/AMR), graft failure, death |
| follow up | not applicable |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a narrative mini-review, not a data source; it contributes to the review's typing-resolution question (C12) and to the qualitative case that HLA-DQ is the most immunogenic locus for DSA (C4). Its one number is the claim that low/intermediate-resolution HLA-DQ mismatch assessment was wrong in 43% of donor-recipient pairs when compared with two-field sequencing, which speaks directly to a one-field, antigen-level pre-screen in Iran: any DQ term computed from serologic or first-field typing carries substantial misclassification, and the review argues that studies built on such typing may mislead. However the 43% has been traced to its source and the review misstates it (see limitations and notes), so the reviewer must cite the primary study, not this sentence. The paper also states, citing a living-donor kidney study, that DQ mismatch is associated with graft failure, rejection and death independently of DR mismatch, which is the C4 living-donor point, but gives no effect size. The heterodimer (cis/trans, up to four DQ proteins per donor, DQA1 needed) and expression arguments explain why DQB1-only, low-resolution counting understates DQ complexity. Transfer to an antibody-status-unknown living-donor pre-screen is therefore conceptual: it justifies a cautious weight for DQ and an explicit flag that one-field DQ typing is imprecise, but it supplies no coefficients.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- misclassification of HLA-DQ donor-recipient mismatch: low/intermediate-resolution (DNA-based or serological) HLA-DQ typing vs two-field high-resolution typing by nucleotide sequencing — percentage of donor-recipient pairs assessed incorrectly (as stated by the review; the review's characterisation of this number does not match its source - see notes) 43 [Section 'HLA-DQ mismatching: typing methods and clinical implications', paragraph 2 (cited from an external study; reference number stripped in the PMC rendering)]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested (narrative review, no primary data); 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DQ mismatch x evolutionary lineage / recipient zygosity (DQalpha01 group vs DQ2/3/4 group; donor DQalpha05): Cited (Maguire et al.): a significant proportion of patients developing HLA-DQ DSA either were homozygous for one evolutionary group with a donor from the other group, or received a donor DQ protein containing DQalpha05; no estimate given [Section 'Evolutionary divergence and functional differences in HLA-DQ']
- HLA-DQ vs HLA-DR mismatch (independence, living donors): Cited: DQ mismatch, along with DR mismatch, independently associated with graft failure, rejection and death in adult living-donor kidney recipients; the authors say prioritising DQ over DR in donor selection 'could improve' outcomes but needs more data; no estimate given [Section 'Complexity of HLA-DQ protein expression and immunogenicity', paragraph 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "HLA-DQ mismatching assessed using the lower resolution typing methods was incorrect in 43% of donor-recipient pairs" (Section 'HLA-DQ mismatching: typing methods and clinical implications', paragraph 2)
- *C12* — "Consequently, studies that utilized serological or low/intermediate level DNA-based HLA typing might provide misleading conclusions regarding HLA-DQ mismatching" (Section 'HLA-DQ mismatching: typing methods and clinical implications', paragraph 2 (last sentence))
- *C4* — "Studies have highlighted that DSAs are more commonly formed against HLA-DQ compared to other HLA proteins, and these antibodies are often present in high titers and are particularly detrimental to transplant outcomes" (Introduction, paragraph 1)
- *C4* — "HLA-DQ mismatch, along with HLA-DR mismatch, is independently associated with an increased risk of graft failure, rejection, and death in adult living kidney transplant recipients" (Section 'Complexity of HLA-DQ protein expression and immunogenicity', paragraph 3)
- *C12* — "eplet-based mismatching correlates more strongly with clinical outcomes than traditional antigen-level mismatching or simply counting amino acid differences" (Section 'Molecular mismatching and immunogenicity assessment', paragraph 6)
- *C12* — "up to four different HLA-DQ proteins can be expressed by a single donor, depending on whether they are homozygous or heterozygous for the relevant alleles" (Section 'Complexity of HLA-DQ protein expression and immunogenicity', paragraph 1)

**Limitations.** Narrative mini-review: no search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no quantitative synthesis; every statement is a citation of other work.; No hazard ratios, odds ratios or confidence intervals are reported anywhere; a full-text regex sweep for percentages, HR/OR, 95% CI and p-values returned exactly one hit - the 43% sentence. This paper contributes no effect estimate of its own.; Reference numbers are stripped in the PMC full-text rendering (citations render as empty parentheses), so the reference list cannot be read from the retrieved text and the review's own numbering cannot be resolved.; The 43% statement misstates its source. The number has been traced by retrieving the candidate paper's full text: Senev A et al., Am J Transplant 2020;20:3367-3378 (PMID 32337773, PMC7754319) states in its Discussion, verbatim, 'Of all misclassified DSAs at the LR level, 43% were directed against the DQ molecule' (Results: N = 22 of 51 misclassified DSAs, 43.1%). That is the DQ share OF MISCLASSIFIED DSAs among 51 disproved antibodies, not the share of donor-recipient pairs whose DQ mismatch was wrongly assessed. In that cohort only 51/224 (22.8%) LR-suspected DSAs were disproved, only 32/140 (22.9%) DSA-positive patients had solely misclassified DSA, and 860/1000 pairs had no DSA at all. The review's sentence therefore inflates and re-frames the finding; do not cite the review for this number.; Senev 2020 is a 94.1% deceased-donor, 98.4% white Belgian single-centre cohort of sensitised-antibody analyses; its misclassification rate does not transfer directly to an Iranian living-donor population or to the first-field typing kits used there.; The living-donor DQ/DR statement is a one-sentence citation with no effect size and no identifiable reference in the retrieved text.; Molecular-mismatch algorithm comparisons are qualitative; the authors themselves caution that scores are population-level associations that may not predict individual patients and that clinical application for DQ may be premature.; Expression-level and inter-isotypic heterodimer arguments are mechanistic hypotheses, not outcome evidence.; kidney_only is true by the review's declared scope, but it is a scope declaration rather than a data restriction: one cited PIRCHE-II result spans 'various organ and donor types'..

### Gately R 2025 — Comparison Between Antigen and Allelic HLA Mismatches, and the Risk of Acute Rejection in Kidney Transplant Recipients

Gately R 2025, *HLA*, [DOI 10.1111/tan.70163](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.70163). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (full text deposited in PMC and returned in full; no licence statement in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All deceased-donor kidney-only transplants performed in Australia 1 January 2017 - 31 December 2020, captured in ANZDATA with HLA typing from OrganMatch. Living-donor and multi-organ recipients were excluded by design. Of 2841 screened, 197 (7%) excluded for missing donor/recipient HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 typing or multi-organ status, leaving 2644. Median recipient age 55 (IQR 44-63), 36% female, 66% Caucasian, 87% first graft, 69% DBD, median mPRA 0, 6.5% with pre-transplant DSA. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 2644 (521 with acute rejection; 2270 included in the 12-month classification-metric analysis) |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort. Three oblique random survival forest models for time to acute rejection: (1) antigen mismatches at HLA-A, -B, -DRB1, -DQB1; (2) allele mismatches at the same four loci; (3) extended allele mismatches at HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQA1, -DQB1. Each model also contained all donor, recipient and transplant variables with <10% missing data (random-forest imputation for those). Discrimination by concordance index and calibration/accuracy by IPCW integrated Brier score, both from fivefold cross-validation; permutation-based variable importance; confusion matrices with Youden's index at 12 months; category-less NRI vs the antigen model; competing-risk cumulative incidence curves for antigen/allele discordant DRB1 and DQB1 pairs. |
| typing resolution | mixed. Donor typing at allocation was molecular but low-to-intermediate resolution (SSO, SSP or rtPCR), reported at one- or two-field; two-field typing was available for most recipients. Where only one-field typing existed, two-field allelic equivalents were IMPUTED by a single experienced laboratory scientist using ethnic-group-specific haplotype linkage (CWD catalogue in AFND, Haplostats, IMGT/HLA). Where antigen typing was missing, two-field typing was converted back to the antigen equivalent. HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were excluded (absent loci and up to 60% missing DP typing). |
| outcome | Time from transplant to first biopsy-proven acute rejection reported to ANZDATA (cellular and antibody-mediated combined); secondarily, acute rejection within 12 months as a binary outcome for sensitivity/specificity/PPV/NPV and NRI. Censored at end of follow-up, graft loss or death. |
| follow up | median 1.7 years (IQR 0.5-2.7); 2.0 (1.2-2.8) years in those without rejection and 0.1 (0-0.4) years in those with rejection; 337/521 (65%) of rejections occurred in the first 3 months |
| other factors modelled | donor type (DCD vs DBD), recipient age at transplantation, donor age, recipient sex, donor sex, recipient ethnicity (Caucasian, ATSI, Pasifika, Asian, Other), BMI, blood group, graft number (first vs repeat), smoking status (recipient and donor), coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes (recipient and donor), donor hypertension, donor history of cancer, initial dialysis modality, dialysis duration, mPRA / calculated PRA, primary cause of kidney failure, year of transplant (era), total ischaemic time, induction with anti-CD25, induction with T-cell depletion, pre-transplant DSA |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's cleanest direct test of the typing-resolution question (C12): in the same cohort the authors computed HLA mismatch three ways - antigen level, allele level at the same four loci, and extended allele level adding HLA-C and -DQA1 - and asked whether the finer coding predicts acute rejection better. It answers the coding-scheme question of discovery angle H: mismatch counts entered a non-parametric oblique random survival forest alongside ~25 clinical covariates, and permutation importance placed HLA-DRB1 first and HLA-DQB1 among the top three in every model, above or beside donor type (DCD vs DBD) and recipient age, which is the relative-importance comparison the review wants. For a LIVING-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran the practical message transfers well: the cheap antigen-level (one-field) count was not beaten by the expensive allele-level count on either discrimination (c-index 0.63 vs 0.63 vs 0.62) or reclassification (NRI -0.091 and -0.015), so a pre-screen built on one-field typing is not obviously leaving predictive signal on the table, and the paper directly quantifies the harm of the opposite choice - allele-level scoring pushed 45% of recipients into a higher mismatch category with no clinical gain. Transfer is nonetheless limited in three ways: the cohort is deceased-donor only (living donation excluded by design), so the donor-quality gradient and the ischaemic-time distribution differ from a living-donor programme; the outcome is acute rejection within a median 1.7 years, not graft survival, so nothing here bears on the long-term dose-response the review needs; and the population is predominantly Caucasian, whereas the accuracy of one-field-to-two-field imputation - a step this study depended on - is worse in populations whose haplotype frequencies are poorly catalogued, which includes Iranian ancestries. The paper reports no hazard ratios at all, so it supports the review only as a model-performance and coding-scheme paper, not as a source of effect sizes.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- acute rejection (time to event): antigen-mismatch model (HLA-A, -B, -DRB1, -DQB1) + clinical covariates — concordance index (c-index), fivefold cross-validated 0.63; adjusted for all donor, recipient and transplant characteristics with <10% missing data [Results 3.3; point value in text, distribution shown only in Figure 2a]
- acute rejection (time to event): allele-mismatch model (HLA-A, -B, -DRB1, -DQB1) + clinical covariates — concordance index (c-index), fivefold cross-validated 0.63; adjusted for all donor, recipient and transplant characteristics with <10% missing data [Results 3.3; Figure 2a]
- acute rejection (time to event): extended allele-mismatch model (HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DQA1, -DQB1) + clinical covariates — concordance index (c-index), fivefold cross-validated 0.62; adjusted for all donor, recipient and transplant characteristics with <10% missing data [Results 3.3; Figure 2a]
- acute rejection (time to event): antigen-mismatch model — integrated Brier score (IPCW) 0.09; adjusted for as above [Results 3.3; Figure 2b]
- acute rejection (time to event): allele-mismatch model — integrated Brier score (IPCW) 0.09; adjusted for as above [Results 3.3; Figure 2b]
- acute rejection (time to event): extended allele-mismatch model — integrated Brier score (IPCW) 0.09; adjusted for as above [Results 3.3; Figure 2b]
- acute rejection within 12 months: allele-mismatch model vs antigen-mismatch model (base) — category-less net reclassification index (NRI) -0.091 (-0.123–-0.06); adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: extended allele-mismatch model vs antigen-mismatch model (base) — category-less net reclassification index (NRI) -0.015 (-0.037–0.009); adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: antigen-mismatch model at Youden-optimal threshold (highest of the three models) — sensitivity 0.9 (0.87–0.92); adjusted for as above; n = 2270 after excluding death/graft loss/censoring within 12 months [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: antigen-mismatch model at Youden-optimal threshold — specificity 0.89 (0.87–0.92); adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: antigen-mismatch model at Youden-optimal threshold — positive predictive value 0.67 (0.63–0.7); adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: antigen-mismatch model at Youden-optimal threshold — negative predictive value 0.97 (0.96–0.98); adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: antigen-mismatch model — Youden's index 0.78; adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: allele-mismatch model — Youden's index 0.79; adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection within 12 months: extended allele-mismatch model — Youden's index 0.76; adjusted for as above [Results 3.5]
- acute rejection (any, over median 1.7 y): whole cohort incidence — proportion (%) 20.0; adjusted for unadjusted; 521/2644, of which 337 (65%) in the first 3 months [Abstract; Results 3.1]
- antigen/allele mismatch-count discordance: HLA-A: allele count differs from antigen count (identical in 2439 (92%) cases) — proportion (%) of pairs discordant 8.0; adjusted for n/a (descriptive) [Abstract; Results 3.2; Table 2]
- antigen/allele mismatch-count discordance: HLA-B: allele count differs from antigen count (identical in 2402 (91%) cases) — proportion (%) of pairs discordant 9.0; adjusted for n/a (descriptive) [Abstract; Results 3.2; Table 2]
- antigen/allele mismatch-count discordance: HLA-DRB1: allele count differs from antigen count (identical in 2019 (76%) cases) — proportion (%) of pairs discordant 24.0; adjusted for n/a (descriptive) [Abstract; Results 3.2; Table 2]
- antigen/allele mismatch-count discordance: HLA-DQB1: allele count differs from antigen count (identical in 2025 (77%) cases) — proportion (%) of pairs discordant 17.0; adjusted for n/a (descriptive) [Abstract; Results 3.2; Table 2]
- reclassification into a higher HLA mismatch category by allele-level counting: allele-level vs antigen-level mismatch assignment, whole cohort — proportion (%) of recipients 45.0; adjusted for n/a (descriptive) [Discussion, paragraph beginning 'Our study showed']
- misclassification of locus mismatch load by one-field typing: recipients with 1 HLA-DRB1 ANTIGEN mismatch who in fact had 2 ALLELE mismatches — proportion (%) 35.5; adjusted for n/a (descriptive); 320 of 902 [Results 3.2 (text gives 320 (35%)); Table 2]
- misclassification of locus mismatch load by one-field typing: recipients with 1 HLA-DQB1 ANTIGEN mismatch who in fact had 2 ALLELE mismatches — proportion (%) 30.1; adjusted for n/a (descriptive); 377 of 1253 [Results 3.2 (text gives 377 (30%)); Table 2]
- misclassification of locus mismatch load by one-field typing: recipients with 0 HLA-A ANTIGEN mismatches who had 1 ALLELE mismatch — proportion (%) 12.9; adjusted for n/a (descriptive); 57 of 444 in Table 2 (text says 'In 446 recipients ... 57 (13%)') [Results 3.2; Table 2]
- misclassification of locus mismatch load by one-field typing: recipients with 1 HLA-B ANTIGEN mismatch who in fact had 2 ALLELE mismatches — proportion (%) 17.6; adjusted for n/a (descriptive); 171 of 970 [Results 3.2 (text gives 171 (18%)); Table 2]
- cumulative incidence of acute rejection (competing risks: graft loss, death with function): among 0 HLA-DRB1 ANTIGEN mismatch recipients: with vs without DRB1 ALLELE mismatch — difference in cumulative incidence curves (no point estimate printed) None, p=0.3; adjusted for competing risks of allograft failure and death with a functioning allograft [Results 3.6; Figure 6a]
- cumulative incidence of acute rejection (competing risks: graft loss, death with function): among 1 HLA-DRB1 ANTIGEN mismatch recipients: 1 vs >1 DRB1 ALLELE mismatch — difference in cumulative incidence curves (no point estimate printed) None, p=0.3; adjusted for competing risks of allograft failure and death with a functioning allograft [Results 3.6; Figure 6a]

**Dose-response.**

- note: The paper reports NO risk estimate (HR/OR/SHR) per mismatch count at any locus. The only printed 0/1/2 series is Table 2, the cross-tabulation of ANTIGEN mismatch count (rows) against ALLELE mismatch count (columns), as number (proportion) of donor/recipient pairs. Reproduced verbatim below. The other 0/1/2-shaped result is the permutation variable-importance ordering, which gives a ranking, not a per-count effect.
- A: antigen 0 MM: 0 allele MM 382 (86.0); 1 allele MM 57 (12.9); 2 allele MM 5 (1.1); antigen 1 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 1078 (88.3); 2: 143 (11.7); antigen 2 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 0 (0.0); 2: 979 (100.0)
- B: antigen 0 MM: 0 allele MM 228 (76.3); 1 allele MM 65 (21.7); 2 allele MM 6 (2.0); antigen 1 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 799 (82.4); 2: 171 (17.6); antigen 2 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 0 (0.0); 2: 1375 (100.0)
- DRB1: antigen 0 MM: 0 allele MM 374 (55.1); 1 allele MM 248 (36.5); 2 allele MM 57 (8.4); antigen 1 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 582 (64.5); 2: 320 (35.5); antigen 2 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 0 (0.0); 2: 1063 (100.0)
- DQB1: antigen 0 MM: 0 allele MM 459 (65.4); 1 allele MM 199 (28.4); 2 allele MM 43 (6.2); antigen 1 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 876 (69.9); 2: 377 (30.1); antigen 2 MM: 0: 0 (0.0); 1: 0 (0.0); 2: 690 (100.0)
- importance_ranking: Antigen model: HLA-DRB1 mismatches > HLA-DQB1 mismatches > donor type (DCD vs DBD). Allele model and extended allele model: HLA-DRB1 mismatches > donor type (DCD vs DBD) > HLA-DQB1 mismatches > recipient age at transplantation. Magnitudes are only in Figures 3-5; no numeric importance values are printed in the text.
- median_mismatch_load: Median antigen mismatches across HLA-A, -B, -DRB1, -DQB1 = 6; median allele mismatches = 7. The IQRs were lost in the PMC text conversion (printed as '6 [,,,,] and 7 [,,,]').
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. Mismatch counts entered an oblique random survival forest, which is non-parametric and imposes no functional form, but the authors report no partial-dependence plot, spline, trend test or per-count hazard, so the shape of the mismatch-risk relationship cannot be read off this paper. The only shape-relevant comparison is the competing-risk cumulative incidence in Figure 6, stratified by antigen mismatch count (0 or 1) at DRB1/DQB1.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DRB1 allele-level mismatch x HLA-DRB1 antigen mismatch count: Within the 0-antigen-mismatch stratum, recipients who were nonetheless allele-mismatched had a cumulative incidence of acute rejection similar to those with no allele mismatch; within the 1-antigen-mismatch stratum, 1 versus >1 allele mismatches made no difference. So the extra allele-level disparity carried no additional risk conditional on the antigen count. (p = 0.3 in both strata; no point estimate or CI printed) [Results 3.6; Figure 6a]
- HLA-DQB1 allele-level mismatch x HLA-DQB1 antigen mismatch count: 'Similar findings were observed for recipients who received 0 and 1 HLA-DQB1 antigen mismatched kidneys' - i.e. no difference in cumulative incidence of acute rejection between antigen-matched/allele-mismatched pairs and concordant pairs. (no p-value, point estimate or CI printed for the DQB1 strata) [Results 3.6; Figure 6b]
- HLA mismatch x clinical covariates (sensitisation, donor type, recipient age, ischaemic time, ethnicity): No formal effect-modification analysis was performed or reported. The oblique random survival forest can absorb interactions implicitly, but no interaction was extracted, plotted or tested, and no subgroup analysis (e.g. by cPRA, pre-transplant DSA, ethnicity or DCD/DBD status) is presented. (not estimated) [absent from Methods 2.5 and Results]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "Predictive performances were similar across all models, with concordance indices of 0.62-0.63 and integrated Brier scores of 0.09." (Abstract)
- *C3* — "HLA-DRB1 and -DQB1 mismatches were the strongest predictors of acute rejection across models." (Abstract)
- *C3* — "the most important variables for predicting acute rejection were HLA-DRB1 mismatches, followed by HLA-DQB1 mismatches and donor type (DCD vs. DBD)" (Results 3.4, Variable Importance for Predicting Acute Rejection (antigen model))
- *C12* — "In patients matched at the HLA-DRB1 or -DQB1 antigen, those with allelic mismatches had similar incidences of rejection compared to those without." (Abstract)
- *C12* — "A discordant number of antigenic and allelic mismatches occurred in 8%, 9%, 24% and 17% of HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 and -DQB1 loci." (Results 3.2, Discordant Antigen and Allele Mismatches)
- *C12* — "Our study showed that the calculation of allele-level mismatches resulted in reassignment into a higher HLA mismatch category in 45% of recipients." (Discussion)
