**Limitations.** Deceased-donor only by design (living-donor and multi-organ recipients excluded), so nothing here speaks directly to living-donor selection; donor-quality and ischaemic-time distributions differ from a living-donor programme.; Outcome is acute rejection over a median of only 1.7 years - and 65% of events occurred within 3 months - so the paper says nothing about graft survival or the long-term mismatch dose-response.; No hazard ratios, odds ratios or any per-mismatch effect estimate is reported anywhere; the HLA signal is expressed only as permutation variable importance and as model-level discrimination, so the paper cannot contribute effect sizes to a meta-analysis.; A substantial proportion of donor and/or recipient allele typing was IMPUTED from one-field typing (especially HLA-DQA1 and -DQB1) using ethnic-group-specific haplotype frequencies; the authors concede this may bias the true allele mismatch count, and their reassurance rests on the cohort being mostly Caucasian - the reassurance does not transfer to Iranian or other under-catalogued haplotype populations.; The comparison is therefore antigen-level vs IMPUTED allele-level, not antigen-level vs directly sequenced two-field typing; a null result may partly reflect imputation error rather than genuine equivalence of the two coding schemes.; HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were excluded entirely (absent loci; up to 60% missing DP typing), so the 'extended' model is not a full molecular-mismatch model.; No eplet or amino-acid (PIRCHE/HLA-EMMA) molecular-mismatch model was tested - only antigen counts vs allele counts - so this is not evidence about molecular mismatch scoring as such.; de novo DSA and allo-sensitisation were not captured by ANZDATA, so the authors explicitly cannot exclude that allele-level matching predicts sensitisation better even though it does not predict rejection better.; Registry residual confounding acknowledged: variation in organ acceptance, immunosuppression exposure and drug levels, and protocol vs indication biopsy practice; rejection was recorded by local clinicians/data managers, not centrally adjudicated.; Discrimination is modest in absolute terms (c-index 0.62-0.63), so no model here is a usable individual-level predictor of rejection; the classification metrics (sensitivity 0.90, specificity 0.89) come from a Youden-optimised threshold on the same data and are not externally validated.; Model performance values and permutation-importance magnitudes appear only in Figures 2-5; the text gives point values without confidence intervals for the c-index and Brier score.; Predominantly Caucasian (66%) Australian cohort with median mPRA 0 and only 6.5% pre-transplant DSA - a low-immunological-risk, well-typed setting..

### Gopal A 2025 — One Size Doesn't Fit All: A Review of International Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation Algorithms.

Gopal A 2025, *Clinical Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ctr.70402](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.70402). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown; no PMC record exists for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned pmid only, no pmcid), so the article is presumed publisher copyright (Wiley) and only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | not a patient population; the units of analysis are 21 national or regional deceased-donor kidney allocation algorithms across five continents, identified from literature searches, transplant organisation websites and policy documents, with three governance case studies (United States, Canada, Eurotransplant) |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 21 allocation algorithms (no patients; no per-scheme n reported in the abstract) |
| design | targeted comparative policy review; no statistical model, no outcome analysis, no simulation reported in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated |
| outcome | descriptive policy characteristics only (which algorithm components are present and how they are defined/weighted); no clinical outcome, no graft or patient survival endpoint reported in the abstract |
| follow up | not applicable |
| other factors modelled | wait time, recipient age, immunologic risk (panel reactive antibody), medical urgency, paediatric priority, ABO compatibility, longevity matching via donor age, Kidney Donor Profile Index (KDPI), Expected Post-Transplant Survival (EPTS), governance / sociopolitical context (centralised vs provincial) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's ANGLE F / claim C13 question - how allocation and selection schemes actually operationalise HLA - rather than any question about the biological effect of mismatch. Its value is as a map: it establishes across 21 national and regional schemes on five continents that HLA mismatch scoring is one of three donor-recipient matching strategies in routine use (alongside ABO compatibility and longevity matching via donor age, KDPI or EPTS), and that immunologic risk is more often handled through panel reactive antibody than through HLA mismatch points, which is a direct precedent for treating antibody status and HLA mismatch as separable inputs. It also documents that thresholds and implementation differ between jurisdictions even where the same component is present, which supports the design position that a national scheme may legitimately weight HLA differently from OPTN/UNOS or Eurotransplant rather than copying one of them. Transfer to a living-donor, low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is weak and indirect on three counts: every algorithm reviewed is a deceased-donor waiting-list allocation system, where HLA points trade off against accrued wait time and queue equity - trade-offs that do not exist when a single named living donor is being screened against a single recipient; the schemes assume a functioning PRA/DSA infrastructure that the Iranian pre-screen explicitly cannot assume; and the retrievable abstract gives no per-scheme HLA point values, locus weights or outcome validation, so it cannot supply a numeric weighting to imitate. It should be cited for the existence and diversity of HLA scoring in national schemes and for the framing that equity, need and utility are balanced within local constraints - never for how much any locus is worth. Note also that this is a 2025 review, so it is the most current available snapshot of the international landscape, and the full text (not retrievable here) is where any per-scheme HLA detail would live.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - this is a policy review with no outcome model; the abstract reports no mismatch-count or per-locus series of any kind; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Donor-recipient matching strategies included HLA mismatch scoring, ABO compatibility, and longevity matching via donor age, Kidney Donor Profile Index, or Expected Post-Transplant Survival." (Abstract, Results sentence 3)
- *C13* — "We conducted a targeted review of 21 allocation algorithms across five continents, identified through literature searches, transplant organization websites, and policy documents." (Abstract, Methods sentence 1)
- *C13* — "All algorithms incorporated wait time and age, with variable definitions and weighting. Most addressed panel reactive antibody, pediatric priority, and medical urgency, but thresholds and implementation differed." (Abstract, Results sentences 1-2)
- *C13* — "Core components analyzed included wait time, age, immunologic risk, medical urgency, and donor-recipient matching." (Abstract, Methods sentence 2)
- *C13* — "Grounded in shared ethical principles, kidney allocation algorithms differ in how these are operationalized." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence 1)
- *C13* — "Although many countries have formal systems, comparative analyses of their structure, context, and evolution remain scarce." (Abstract, Background sentence 2)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only access: no PMC record exists for this PMID, so every per-scheme detail - which of the 21 algorithms award HLA points, at which loci, and how many - is in full-text tables that could not be retrieved. The evidence extracted here is therefore a landscape statement, not a data source.; Zero effect sizes. This is a descriptive policy review with no cohort, no model, no hazard ratio and no outcome. It cannot support any claim about the magnitude or shape of the HLA mismatch effect (C1-C12, C14).; 'Targeted review' is the authors' own term; no systematic search protocol, no registration, no stated inclusion/exclusion criteria and no risk-of-bias assessment are described in the abstract, so selection of the 21 algorithms is not reproducible from the retrievable text.; Sources are transplant organisation websites and policy documents, which are living pages: the description of any given scheme is a snapshot that may already be stale, and no version or access date is given in the abstract.; Deceased-donor allocation only. No living-donor selection or paired-exchange scheme is in scope, which is precisely the setting the Iranian pre-screen operates in.; No outcome evaluation or simulation of the HLA components is reported in the abstract, so the review cannot validate whether any scheme's HLA weighting improves graft survival or equity - it only records that the weighting exists.; Whether Iran's own allocation scheme is among the 21 cannot be determined from the abstract; the abstract names only the three case-study jurisdictions (United States, Canada, Eurotransplant).; HLA typing resolution used by the reviewed schemes is not stated anywhere in the retrievable text, so the review says nothing about the one-field versus two-field question central to C12..

### Israeli S 2025 — Soft kidney allocation improves HLA matching and maintains allocation order.

Israeli S 2025, *Communications Medicine (Commun Med (Lond)) 5(1):526*, [DOI 10.1038/s43856-025-01232-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43856-025-01232-8). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (retrieved via PMC open access; no licence line survived text extraction; Communications Medicine is a fully open-access journal).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Two retrospective cohorts of already-performed kidney transplants, re-allocated in silico. (1) US: transplants 2015-2023 in states with >=500 transplants; 95,250 deceased-donor transplants analysed, plus non-directed and directed living donors in 25 states for the paired analysis. (2) Israel: two geographically close centres (Sheba and Rabin), 42 recent deceased-donor cases, 230 non-directed living-donor transplants, plus directed (related) living-donor pairs. Sensitised (anti-HLA antibody carrier) recipients, invalid typings and pairs with missing age/ABO were removed. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 95,250 US deceased-donor transplants; 42 Israeli deceased-donor cases; 230 Israeli non-directed living-donor transplants; plus directed living-donor pairs (n not stated in the retrieved text) |
| design | Retrospective counterfactual simulation. Historical donor-recipient pairs are re-allocated by a 'soft allocation' Top-K rule (offer each kidney to the best HLA match among the top K candidates in the existing queue, K = 1-50, policy range 5-20, with a hard guarantee that nobody is delayed more than K-1 turns) and, for paired/related donation, by an exchange-cycle optimisation (cycle size 2-5, four-month windows, alternative donor accepted only if it does not worsen any recipient's match). No clinical outcome model; no survival analysis; no comparison group other than the observed allocation. |
| typing resolution | Mixed and low. US cohort: serology (antigen) level only. Israeli cohort: first field (2-digit) typing, with missing loci imputed to two-field 5-locus genotypes by MR-GRIMM using GRIMM/EM haplotype frequencies from the Ezer Mizion Bone Marrow Donor Registry (donor/recipient ethnic origin unknown, so the whole Israeli population was treated as a single origin), then converted back to antigen level with py-ard; Israeli analyses run at both serology and 4-digit level. |
| outcome | SURROGATE ONLY: mean HLA match score. Match per locus defined as 2 - (number of donor alleles absent in the recipient); summed over A&B&DR (0-6), DQ&DR (0-4) and all five loci A,B,C,DR,DQ (0-10). Secondary outcomes: change in queue position (mean and SD) and waiting time. No graft survival, rejection, dnDSA or any patient outcome was measured. |
| follow up | none - no post-transplant follow-up; the study ends at the allocation decision |
| other factors modelled | ABO blood-type compatibility (hard constraint), donor/recipient age criteria (donor >=65 to recipient >=60; donor <18 to recipient <18), queue position / maximum delay of K-1 allocation turns, geography (within-state vs between-state exchange in the US; two geographically close centres in Israel), genotype (haplotype) frequency as a rare-HLA / population-diversity equity proxy, maximum exchange cycle size (2-5) and a four-month cycle window for paired donation, NOT modelled: sensitisation/CPRA/DSA (sensitised recipients were excluded), KDPI or donor quality, cold ischaemia, organ discard/turn-down, centre size |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's clearest demonstration that HLA match quality is a controllable output of the allocation/selection rule rather than a fixed property of the donor pool, which is exactly the question a pre-screen tool answers (C13). Its most transferable result for Iran is the living-donor arm: non-directed living donors, the group whose selection is least constrained by a queue, showed the largest gain of any group (mean A&B&DR match 1.34 out of 6 under current practice, 2.03 under best-of-top-K), i.e. current unrelated living-donor practice leaves most of the available match quality unused, and a shortlist re-ranking recovers it without any new donors, tests or costs. The design matches an Iranian pre-screen closely on three axes that usually break transferability: matching was scored at ANTIGEN (serology, one-field) level, which is the resolution Iranian typing reports carry; the cohort deliberately EXCLUDED sensitised recipients, so the algorithm is defined for exactly the antibody-status-unknown, presumed-unsensitised candidate a pre-screen sees before crossmatch; and the mechanism is a rank-then-choose rule over a small candidate pool, which is what a matching engine over a candidate registry does. The paired/related arm also transfers to Iran's related-donor and crossover setting: related pairs often already share a haplotype and cannot be improved, but where a better donor existed the A&B&DR match rose about three-fold with a constraint that no recipient ends worse off, i.e. crossover is a match-improving move only for a minority and must be evaluated pair-by-pair. Two things limit the transfer, and both matter: the paper's endpoint is the match score itself, never graft survival, so it inherits rather than supplies the evidence that a higher match helps (the authors say so explicitly and call for outcome-based work); and the Israeli match scores rest on haplotype-frequency imputation from an Israeli registry, which has no Iranian equivalent, so an Iranian implementation must score matches on printed antigens alone and cannot copy the imputation step.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- mean HLA-A&B&DR match score (0-6), US deceased donors: soft (Top-K) allocation vs current allocation — mean match score, before -> after 1.45 -> 1.77; adjusted for ABO and age compatibility enforced; no statistical adjustment, no test [Abstract, Results (this exact pair of numbers appears ONLY in the abstract; the body reports K-specific values, see next rows)]
- mean HLA-A&B&DR match score (0-6), US deceased donors, case 1 (39 states with >=500 DD transplants, exchange within state only): Top-K with K = 20 vs current allocation — mean match score, before -> after 1.45 -> 1.98; adjusted for ABO and age compatibility; within-state exchange only [Results, 'Improved HLA match in US DD']
- mean HLA-A&B&DR match score (0-6), US deceased donors, case 3 (11 states with >=3000 DD transplants): Top-K with K = 50 vs current allocation — mean match score, before -> after 1.44 -> 2.3; adjusted for ABO and age compatibility [Results, 'Improved HLA match in US DD']
- mean HLA-A&B&DR match score (0-6), Israeli deceased donors (n = 42): soft (Top-K) allocation vs current allocation — mean match score, before -> after 2.33 -> 2.54; adjusted for ABO and age compatibility [Abstract (post-value 2.54 appears only in the abstract; the 2.33 baseline is repeated in Results, 'Transplant match level')]
- mean HLA-A&B&DR match score (0-6), Israeli non-directed living donors (n = 230): soft (Top-K) allocation vs current allocation — mean match score, before -> after 1.34 -> 2.03; adjusted for ABO and age compatibility [Abstract (post-value 2.03 appears only in the abstract; the 1.34 baseline is repeated in Results, 'Transplant match level')]
- baseline mean match under current allocation, Israeli ND-LD (n = 230): observed practice, three locus groupings — mean match score A,B,DR 1.34/6; DQ+DR 1.7/4; all 5 loci 3/10; adjusted for none [Results, 'Transplant match level']
- baseline mean match under current allocation, Israeli deceased donors (n = 42): observed practice, three locus groupings — mean match score A,B,DR 2.33/6; DQ+DR 2.55/4; all 5 loci 4.36/10; adjusted for none [Results, 'Transplant match level']
- baseline mean match under current allocation, US deceased donors (n = 95,250): observed practice, three locus groupings — mean match score A,B,DR 1.45/6; DQ+DR 1.44/4; all 5 loci 2.67/10; adjusted for none [Results, 'Transplant match level']
- proportion of recipients not harmed by the re-allocation (Israel): Top-K vs current allocation, per recipient — percentage of recipients with a better or unchanged match 77-91% (maximal for A,B,DR); adjusted for none [Results, 'Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation of the queue in Israeli ND-LD and DD' (underlying figure is in Supplementary Material)]
- size of the gain at the largest policy-realistic K, Israel (ND-LD and DD): Top-K with K = 20 vs current allocation — relative improvement in mean match score typically 50-100% improvement; adjusted for none; the word 'significant' is used without any test statistic [Results, 'Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation of the queue in Israeli ND-LD and DD']
- mean HLA-A&B&DR match, ALL Israeli living donors (related + unrelated combined): current vs Top-K and cycles applied separately vs the combined Top-K + related-donor method — mean match score 1.74 (current) -> 2.29 (Top-K and cycles separately) -> 2.19 (combined method); adjusted for ABO, age, four-month cycle window [Results, 'All living donation - paired and unpaired in Israel and the US']
- match gain in RELATED (directed living) pairs re-matched by crossover/cycles, Israel: optimised crossover vs the originally intended related donor, restricted to pairs for which a better donor existed — fold increase in mean match score A&B&DR ~3-fold; class II and all 5 loci ~2-fold; no recipient's match worsened; no benefit from cycles longer than 3 pairs; adjusted for hard constraint that the alternative donor must match at least as well as the original [Results, 'Paired donations - Israel population']
- match gain in US combined living donation (ND-LD + D-LD, 25 states, within-state crossover): optimised cycles vs original pairing, among the ~half of recipients for whom a better donor was found — fold increase in mean match score A&B&DR and class II 2.5-3 fold; all 5 loci ~2-fold; about half of recipients could not be improved; adjusted for ABO, age, four-month window, cycle size 2-5 [Results, 'All living donation - paired and unpaired in Israel and the US']
- queue disturbance (equity check): position under Top-K vs current position, 1 <= K <= 25 — mean and SD of position change mean difference always 0; SD approximately K; waiting-time impact averaging less than a month for K = 10 in Israel; genotype frequency uncorrelated with change in queue position or match gain; adjusted for n/a [Results ('Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation...') and Discussion]
- BACKGROUND, NOT THIS PAPER'S ANALYSIS: 10-year graft survival by HLA mismatch count, cited from UNOS: 0 vs 3 vs 6 mismatches — 10-year graft survival percentage 82% (0 MM), 76% (3 MM), 71% (6 MM); adjusted for unstated; cited from the UNOS database in the Introduction, no reference detail retrievable from the extracted text [Introduction, first paragraph]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 82% 10-year graft survival; 3 MM: 76% 10-year graft survival; 6 MM: 71% 10-year graft survival
- note: No per-locus mismatch-count risk estimates. The paper scores MATCHES (not mismatches) in three fixed locus groupings only: A&B&DR (0-6), DQ&DR (0-4), and all five loci A,B,C,DR,DQ (0-10). No locus is weighted above another and no locus-specific effect on any outcome is estimated.
- A_B_DR: mean match 1.45/6 (US DD), 2.33/6 (Israel DD), 1.34/6 (Israel ND-LD), 1.74/6 (all Israeli living donors)
- DQ_DR: mean match 1.44/4 (US DD), 2.55/4 (Israel DD), 1.7/4 (Israel ND-LD)
- all_5_loci: mean match 2.67/10 (US DD), 4.36/10 (Israel DD), 3/10 (Israel ND-LD)
- Shape reported: not reported. The paper assumes rather than estimates a dose-response: the Introduction states that each additional matched allele incrementally enhances graft longevity, and cites the three-point UNOS series above. The authors' own analysis has no clinical outcome, so it cannot describe a shape.; linearity tested: not tested. No model of outcome against mismatch count is fitted anywhere in the paper; no spline, trend test, or categorical-vs-linear comparison. Note that no statistical test, p-value or confidence interval of any kind appears in the retrieved full text - the word 'significant' is used informally throughout.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- donor type x achievable match gain: the gain is largest exactly where the queue constraint is weakest: non-directed living donors improved most (1.34 -> 2.03 of 6), deceased donors least in Israel (2.33 -> 2.54), because the Israeli DD pool already matched relatively well; related/directed pairs are often already the best available match and cannot be improved at all (ND-LD +0.69 of 6 vs Israeli DD +0.21 of 6 (abstract values)) [Abstract; Results, 'Transplant match level' and 'Paired donations - Israel population']
- K (depth of the candidate shortlist) x match gain and waiting time: match increases monotonically with K; K = 20 still gives a typical 50-100% improvement in Israel and the largest US gain came at K = 50, but larger K lengthens waiting time, most in low-volume centres. The authors frame K as a policy dial, not an estimate. (K varied 1-25 (Israel, US case 1) and 1-50 (US cases 2, 3); US A&B&DR 1.45 -> 1.98 at K = 20, 1.44 -> 2.3 at K = 50; SD of position change is approximately K; mean position change always 0) [Results, both Top-K sections; Discussion]
- geographic pooling x match gain (US): the achievable gain depends on how wide the exchange pool is: within-state exchange in 39 states, exchange between all states, and the 11 largest states were compared, with similar results at similar K, the largest gains coming from the wider pools and larger K that only large states can absorb without lengthening waits (case 1 (within state) 1.45 -> 1.98 at K = 20; case 3 (11 largest states) 1.44 -> 2.3 at K = 50) [Results, 'Improved HLA match in US DD']
- genotype (haplotype) frequency, used as a proxy for population-level HLA variation and thus potential ethnic diversity, x algorithm effect: explicitly tested equity analysis: genotype frequency was NOT correlated with the change in queue position or with the change in HLA match score, so the authors conclude the rule does not disproportionately disadvantage rare-genotype (minority-origin) candidates. No correlation coefficient or p-value is given in the text; the evidence is a supplementary figure. ('not correlated' - no numerical estimate reported) [Results, 'Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation of the queue in Israeli ND-LD and DD' (Supplementary Material figure)]
- typing resolution x result: the Israeli conclusions were reproduced at the four-digit level as well as at serology level, i.e. the direction of the benefit did not depend on the resolution at which the match was scored ('The same results hold when the analysis is performed at the four-digit level' - no numbers in the main text (supplementary figure)) [Results, 'Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation of the queue in Israeli ND-LD and DD']
- exchange cycle size x match gain: diminishing returns above three pairs: cycle sizes 2-5 were tested and the authors conclude there is no point in cycles longer than three pairs in Israel; in the US larger cycles did not change the average gain much but included more pairs (no benefit beyond cycle size 3 (Israel)) [Results, 'Paired donations - Israel population' and 'All living donation...']
- sensitisation x applicability: NOT an interaction result but a scope boundary the reviewer must note: sensitised (anti-HLA antibody carrying) recipients were removed from both cohorts, so no DSA/CPRA interaction was estimated. The authors propose that on a mixed list sensitised patients would follow the standard protocol while non-sensitised patients use Top-K, and leave this to future work. (not estimated) [Methods, 'Data'; Discussion, final paragraph]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Analysis of 95,250 US DD transplants shows an increase in HLA-A&B&DR match scores from 1.45 to 1.77." (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "HLA match has a limited effect (0–4 points) since it was shown to bias the allocation to frequent HLA alleles." (Introduction, paragraph 2 (describing the US Kidney Allocation System))
- *C13* — "most of the recipients (77-91% with the maximal increase for A,B,DR) receive a better HLA match or with no change" (Results, 'Improved HLA matching with limited perturbation of the queue in Israeli ND-LD and DD')
- *C12* — "HLA typing (for Israel at 2-digit genetic level, and for the US at serology level)" (Methods, 'Data')
- *C2* — "average 10-year graft survival rates are 82% with 0 mismatches, 76% with 3 mismatches, and 71% with 6 mismatches" (Introduction, paragraph 1 (cited from the UNOS database, NOT this paper's own analysis))
- *C13* — "Further research is needed to directly assess the impact of soft allocation strategies on graft survival and rejection rates" (Discussion, paragraph 5)

**Limitations.** SURROGATE ENDPOINT ONLY. The paper measures the HLA match score, never a patient outcome. No graft survival, rejection, dnDSA or sensitisation result is produced; the authors concede that outcome-based prospective or retrospective work is still needed. Every clinical claim in this paper is borrowed from prior literature.; NO STATISTICS OF ANY KIND. No confidence interval, p-value, standard error or hypothesis test appears anywhere in the retrieved full text. The word 'significant' is used repeatedly in its informal sense. Differences between simulated and observed match scores therefore have no measure of uncertainty.; ABSTRACT AND BODY DISAGREE. The headline US figure 1.45 -> 1.77 and the Israeli post-values 2.54 and 2.03 appear ONLY in the abstract. The Results section instead reports 1.45 -> 1.98 at K = 20 and 1.44 -> 2.3 at K = 50 for the US. The abstract numbers presumably correspond to a smaller K, but the retrieved text never states which; cite the K-specific body values in preference.; COUNTERFACTUAL SIMULATION, NOT AN EXPERIMENT. Kidneys are re-shuffled among people who actually received a transplant. Everything that determines whether an offer is accepted is absent: the US turn-down/discard rate (stated as above 26%), donor age, terminal creatinine, comorbidities, recovery type and biopsy, KDPI, cold ischaemia, centre size and logistics. The authors state this simplification themselves.; SENSITISED RECIPIENTS EXCLUDED. Anti-HLA antibody carriers were removed from both cohorts, so the algorithm is unvalidated in exactly the population where HLA matching is hardest and matters most; adapting it to sensitised candidates is left to future work.; IMPUTATION DEPENDENCE IN THE ISRAELI ARM. Missing Israeli loci were imputed to two-field genotypes with MR-GRIMM from bone-marrow-registry haplotype frequencies, with donor and recipient origin unknown so the whole Israeli population was treated as a single origin. No imputation accuracy, error rate or sensitivity analysis is reported in the retrieved text, and the imputed genotypes feed directly into the match scores.; TINY DECEASED-DONOR SAMPLE IN ISRAEL. Only 42 recent deceased-donor cases; the 2.33 -> 2.54 gain rests on that. The Israeli cohort also comes from two geographically adjacent centres, a best case for exchange that the authors acknowledge does not generalise.; MOST EVIDENCE IS IN FIGURES AND SUPPLEMENTARY MATERIAL. The equity analysis (rare genotypes), the per-recipient improvement distribution, the four-digit replication, the age-difference distribution and all per-K curves are supplementary figures. PMC text extraction stripped every figure and table number, so those results could not be read numerically here.; SELF-SELECTED COMPARATOR. The 'current allocation' baseline for the Israeli deceased-donor arm is a simulated queue, not the observed one ('For deceased donations, we tested using the existing ND-LD queue and simulated the DD queue')..

### Khalil MAM 2025 — Donor-specific antibodies against HLA-C, HLA-DP and HLA-DQ and their implications in kidney transplantation

Khalil MAM 2025, *World J Transplant*, [DOI 10.5500/wjt.v15.i2.99952](https://doi.org/10.5500/wjt.v15.i2.99952). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown — Baishideng World Journal of Transplantation publishes open access (normally CC BY-NC 4.0), but the retrieved PMC text contains no licence statement, so the licence is unverified from the source used here..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Kidney transplant recipients only. The review synthesises published kidney-transplant studies and case reports spanning 1977-2023; cited cohorts range from 37 to 3600 recipients and include first transplants, retransplants, sensitised and unsensitised recipients. The review reports no primary cohort of its own. |
| donor type | both |
| n | not applicable — narrative review with no primary cohort; largest cited series 3600 (Mytilineos DNA typing) and 1478 (Laux retransplants); the only pooled estimate quoted is a 5-study, 1166-patient meta-analysis of HLA-DP DSA |
| design | narrative (non-systematic) review; no search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no protocol registration, no meta-analysis performed by the authors; evidence tabulated chronologically in three tables (HLA-C, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ) |
| typing resolution | mixed across cited studies — serological HLA-C specificities (Cw1-Cw10) in the older studies, allele-specific PCR / molecular DNA typing in Frohn 2001 and Mytilineos 1997, eplet-level analysis in Duquesnoy & Marrari, Laux and Sapir-Pichhadze; the review itself recommends molecular typing plus single-antigen bead DSA screening |
| outcome | antibody-mediated rejection (acute and chronic), mixed rejection, biopsy-proven acute rejection, transplant glomerulopathy, graft loss, graft survival, DSA prevalence and MFI |
| follow up | varies by cited study — 2 years (Bachelet 2016 biopsy-proven rejection; Laux 2-year survival), 2.2 years (Lim 2016), 1 year (Mytilineos graft survival); the review states no pooled follow-up |
| other factors modelled | none modelled by the review itself — it is a narrative review and fits no model, factors discussed narratively: prior sensitising events (retransplantation, pregnancy, transfusion), DSA mean fluorescence intensity (MFI) strength, antigen surface expression level (HLA-C ~10% of HLA-A/B), linkage disequilibrium between HLA-C and HLA-B, and between HLA-DQ and HLA-DR, KIR / NK-cell genotype (HLA-C1 vs HLA-C2 ligand groups), ischaemia-reperfusion injury and infection as expression triggers, denatured vs native antigen on single-antigen beads (assay artefact) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's designated source for C7 (HLA-C) and C8 (HLA-DP), and it is kidney-only, which is unusual for a C/DP/DQ review. It answers the question 'does HLA-C mismatch deserve weight in a matching score?' but it answers it almost entirely through the DSA channel rather than the mismatch channel: the paper's own framing is that HLA-C matters because HLA-C mismatches generate anti-HLA-C DSAs which then cause AMR, and the great majority of its numeric evidence is conditioned on a measured DSA. That is the wrong conditioning for a LIVING-donor, ANTIBODY-STATUS-UNKNOWN Iranian pre-screen, where no single-antigen bead result exists at the moment the score is computed, so the 27.3%-vs-9.1% AMR figure and the DP odds ratio of 3.6 cannot be carried across as mismatch weights. What does transfer is the much thinner mismatch-level evidence the review tabulates, and it is largely negative for HLA-C: Albrechtsen 1977 and Ling 2012 found no benefit from HLA-C matching, and the one positive mismatch study, Frohn 2001, reached significance only after linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B was removed and was strongest when a B mismatch was also present — which is precisely the C7 claim that HLA-C rides on HLA-B, and which implies that in a low-resolution A/B/DR pre-screen the HLA-C signal is already partly captured by the B term and should not be double-counted. The paper also supports C7's sensitisation clause, stating repeatedly that these effects are 'more pronounced in retransplants' while insisting they also occur in first transplants; an Iranian first-transplant living-donor population sits at the low-risk end of that gradient. For C8 the review is genuinely two-sided and matches the claim as written: DP mismatch per se was null in first transplants (Rosenberg, Redondo-Pachon, Mytilineos' first-transplant arm) while DP-DSA was harmful (meta-analytic OR 3.6, Seitz HR 9.57), so DP mismatch should not enter a mismatch score. Practically, HLA-C and HLA-DP are usually not typed at all in a one-field Iranian workup, so the review's central recommendation — universal molecular typing of C, DP and DQ plus bead screening — describes a capability the pre-screen does not have and should be recorded as an aspiration, not an input.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- acute transplant rejection: HLA-C mismatch vs no HLA-C mismatch (allele-specific PCR, 104 donor-recipient pairs), after exclusion of linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B — p-value only None, p=0.004; adjusted for linkage disequilibrium excluded; no other adjustment reported by the review [Results/synthesis, HLA-C section and Table 1 row Frohn/2001]
- renal allograft outcome (unspecified): routine HLA-C typing/matching vs none, 142 living-related + 311 cadaveric transplants — narrative null None; adjusted for not stated [Table 1 row Albrechtsen/1977]
- antibody-mediated rejection: anti-HLA-C DSA at day 0 (n=22) vs sensitised controls without anti-HLA-C DSA (n=88), within 608 renal transplant patients — percentage 27.3; adjusted for case-control design matched on sensitisation; no multivariable adjustment reported [Results/synthesis, 'DSAs against HLA-C' paragraph and Table 1 row Aubert/2014]
- DSA strength in AMR vs no AMR: median MFI of anti-HLA-C DSA at day 0, AMR group vs non-AMR group — MFI (median) 4966; adjusted for none [Results/synthesis, HLA-C section and Table 1 row Aubert/2014]
- sensitisation (anti-HLA class I antibody positivity): anti-HLA-Cw vs anti-HLA-A vs anti-HLA-B positivity in 60 sensitised patients — percentage 42.0; adjusted for none [Table 1 row Bryan/2010 and HLA-C synthesis paragraph]
- anti-HLA-C DSA prevalence after graft failure: sera from 45 HLA-C-mismatched recipients after allograft nephrectomy — percentage 60.0; adjusted for none [Results/synthesis, 'DSAs against HLA-C' and Table 1 row Duquesnoy and Marrari/2011]
- anti-HLA-C DSA prevalence in sensitised patients: range across cited studies — percentage range None (42.0–65.0); adjusted for none [Results/synthesis, first sentence of 'DSAs against HLA-C']
- antibody-mediated rejection: preformed isolated HLA-Cw-DSA vs preformed isolated HLA-DP-DSA, 183 recipients, multicentre — percentage 12.0; adjusted for not stated [Results/synthesis, HLA-C section and Table 1 row Laboux/2023]
- AMR and graft function: preformed anti-HLA-Cw DSA (n=12) vs preformed anti-HLA-A and/or HLA-B DSA (n=23) — p-value only None, p=1.0; adjusted for not stated [Table 1 row Santos et al/2016]
- acute AMR / chronic AMR / graft survival: anti-native HLA-Cw antibodies vs anti-denatured HLA-Cw antibodies, among 52 patients with anti-HLA-Cw DSA within 135 studied — p-value only None, p=0.006; adjusted for none [Results/synthesis, HLA-C section and Table 1 row Visentin/2020]
- graft loss or acute rejection: anti-HLA-DP DSA present vs absent — meta-analysis of 5 studies, 1166 patients — OR 3.6 (1.6–8.1), p=0.002; adjusted for pooled unadjusted; I-squared = 52% [Results/synthesis, 'HLA-DP' section, and Table 2 summary row]
- antibody-mediated rejection: pre-existing isolated HLA-DP DSA vs standard-immunological-risk controls (n=46), highly sensitised controls (n=27) and non-donor-specific HLA-DP antibody controls (n=18) — HR 9.57, p=0.012; adjusted for not stated in the review [Results/synthesis, 'HLA-DP' section (Seitz study)]
- 1-year graft survival: HLA-DPB mismatch count 0 vs 1 vs 2 in SECOND transplants (retrospective DNA typing, 3600 typed, repeated in 1300 deceased-donor transplants) — survival percentage 83.0; adjusted for not stated [Table 2 row Mytilineos/1997]
- 2-year graft survival: fewer than 2 HLA-DPB1 epitope mismatches vs 3 epitope mismatches, 1478 cadaveric retransplants — survival percentage 77.8, p=0.0112; adjusted for not stated [Table 2 row Laux/2003]
- graft function: HLA-DP antibodies present vs absent, sera from 505 patients — percentage (prevalence) with narrative null 7.3; adjusted for none [Table 2 row Pfeiffer/1995]
- graft survival: anti-HLA-DP antibodies detected by solid-phase assay vs none, 440 kidney transplant patients — narrative null None; adjusted for not stated [Table 2 row Redondo-Pachon/2016]
- isolated HLA-DP mismatch effect: isolated HLA-DP mismatches between donors and recipients, 37 patients — narrative null None; adjusted for not stated [Table 2 row Rosenberg/1992]
- anti-HLA-DP antibody prevalence before first transplant: patients awaiting a FIRST kidney transplant — percentage range None (23.0–64.0); adjusted for none ['WAY FORWARD IN VIEW OF CRITICAL REVIEW' section]
- rejection, late rejection, AMR: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches (POOLED) vs 0 HLA-DQ mismatches, 788 recipients followed 2.2 years — p-value only None, p=0.01; adjusted for not stated [Table 3 row Lim/2016]
- transplant glomerulopathy: HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch load 27-43 vs lower, case-control of 156 recipients — OR 2.84 (1.73–7.84); adjusted for logistic regression; covariates not stated in the review [Table 3 row Sapir-Pichhadze/2015]
- HLA-DQ / HLA-DR discordance: matching status at DR and DQ among 505 recipients — percentage 7.5; adjusted for none ['Underexpression of HLA-DQ and its masking by linkage disequilibrium' section (Willicombe)]

**Dose-response.**

- C: 0 MM: no count series reported anywhere in the paper; 1 MM: not reported; 2 MM: not reported; note MM: HLA-C is handled only as a binary (mismatched vs not) or via DSA presence/MFI. There is no 0/1/2 HLA-C mismatch gradient in this review.
- DPB (second transplants only, Mytilineos 1997, 1-year graft survival): 0 MM: 83% +/- 2% (reference); 1 MM: 76% +/- 2% (P = 0.02 vs 0); 2 MM: 73% +/- 3% (P = 0.003 vs 0); note MM: explicitly no effect in first transplants; each mismatch is compared with 0, never with each other, so the 1-to-2 increment is not tested
- DPB1 epitopes (Laux 2003, 2-year graft survival, retransplants): <2 epitope mismatches MM: 77.8%; 3 epitope mismatches MM: 65.8%; p MM: 0.0112; note MM: an epitope-load threshold, not an antigen count
- DQ (Lim 2016): 0 MM: reference; 1 or 2 (pooled) MM: more rejection (P < 0.01), late rejection (P = 0.03) and AMR (P = 0.01); note MM: 1 and 2 explicitly pooled
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The review performs no modelling of its own and reports no test for linear trend, no spline, no threshold analysis and no P for trend for any locus. The only quantities that behave like a gradient are the DPB 0/1/2 one-year survival figures from Mytilineos 1997 (retransplants only), and even there each level is only contrasted with zero. The one threshold-like statement in the paper is on antibody STRENGTH, not mismatch count: anti-HLA-Cw DSA pathogenicity is described as manifesting above an MFI of 3000.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-C mismatch x linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B: The HLA-C mismatch effect on acute rejection only emerged once linkage disequilibrium was removed, and was strongest when an additional HLA-B mismatch was present — i.e. the crude HLA-C signal is confounded by, and partly carried on, HLA-B. (P = 0.004 after exclusion of linkage disequilibrium (104 pairs); no effect size given) [HLA-C synthesis paragraph and Table 1 row Frohn/2001]
- HLA-C/DP DSA x concurrent DSA against HLA-A, -B, -DR, -DQ: Combined Cw/DP DSA plus classical-antigen DSA produced significantly more acute rejection episodes and immunological graft loss than either alone; the review calls this synergy and repeats it as recommendation 7. (no numeric interaction term; narrative only (Gilbert 2011: 176 with classical-antigen antibodies vs 27 (13.3%) with HLA-C and/or HLA-DP antibodies)) [HLA-C synthesis paragraph, Table 1 rows Gilbert/2011 and Bachelet/2016, RECOMMENDATIONS item 7]
- DSA locus (Cw vs DP) x DSA strength (MFI): The excess AMR risk of HLA-DP DSA over HLA-Cw DSA was significant only in the low-strength stratum (MFI < 3000); the review reads this as Cw-DSA pathogenicity being MFI-dependent and appearing above MFI 3000. (AMR 12% (Cw-DSA) vs 28% (DP-DSA); interaction significant only for MFI < 3000) [HLA-C synthesis paragraph and Table 1 row Laboux/2023]
- HLA-DPB mismatch x transplant number (first vs second transplant): HLA-DPB mismatch had no effect on first transplants but a graded effect on second transplants — the clearest effect-modification-by-sensitisation result in the paper. (second transplants: 0 MM 83% +/- 2%, 1 MM 76% +/- 2% (P = 0.02), 2 MM 73% +/- 3% (P = 0.003) 1-year survival; first transplants null) [Table 2 row Mytilineos/1997]
- anti-HLA-Cw antibody x antigen conformation (native vs denatured bead): Only anti-NATIVE HLA-Cw antibodies were pathogenic; anti-denatured antibodies were not, so a positive single-antigen bead against HLA-C is not by itself evidence of risk. (acute AMR P = 0.006, chronic AMR P = 0.03, graft survival P = 0.04; bead-fluorescence/crossmatch correlation 0.178 (classical) vs 0.289 (reduced-denatured beads)) [HLA-C synthesis paragraph and Table 1 row Visentin/2020]
- donor HLA-C ligand group (C1 vs C2) x recipient KIR genotype: Recipients of kidneys from donors homozygous for HLA-C1 had a significantly higher risk of chronic rejection than recipients of HLA-C2 homozygous/heterozygous or HLA-Bw4-bearing donors; risk was highest when both rKIR2DL1/dHLA-C2 and rKIR3DL1/dHLA-Bw4 ligand combinations were absent. (no numbers reported; 760 recipients genotyped (Hanvesakul)) ['Interaction with killer immunoglobulin like receptor' section]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x HLA-DR matching (linkage disequilibrium): DR matching does not guarantee DQ matching: 7.5% of 505 recipients were DR-matched but DQ-mismatched (and DQ is discordant in 15%-26% of DR-matched patients elsewhere in the paper), so the assumed masking of DQ by DR is incomplete. (21.4% matched at both; 56.2% mismatched at both; 7.5% DR-matched/DQ-mismatched; 14.9% DQ-matched/DR-mismatched) ['Underexpression of HLA-DQ and its masking by linkage disequilibrium' (Willicombe)]
- C/DP/DQ DSA x retransplantation vs first transplant: The review's overall position: harmful effects of these DSAs are more pronounced in retransplants, but occur in first transplants too, and several anti-HLA-C rejection cases had no identifiable prior sensitising event. (no numeric interaction; 23%-64% of patients awaiting a FIRST transplant carry anti-HLA-DP antibodies) [Abstract, 'WAY FORWARD' section, CONCLUSION]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C7* — "Initial clinical studies showed that typing for HLA-C had no beneficial effect on graft outcomes" (WAY FORWARD IN VIEW OF CRITICAL REVIEW, first paragraph)
- *C7* — "HLA-C mismatch was significantly associated with acute transplant rejection, particularly when combined with an additional mismatch on the B locus" (Results/synthesis, 'HLA-C and DSA against HLA-C', paragraph 2 (Frohn 2001))
- *C7* — "HLA-C is not routinely typed, and the frequency of anti-HLA-C antibodies is lower than that of anti-HLA-A or HLA-B. The frequency of anti-HLA-C DSAs varies between 42% and 65% in sensitized patients" (Results/synthesis, 'DSAs against HLA-C', opening sentences)
- *C7* — "AMR was observed in 27.3% of patients with DSAs against HLA-C, compared to 9.1% in the immunized control group" (Results/synthesis, 'DSAs against HLA-C', final paragraph (Aubert 2014 case-control))
- *C8* — "anti-HLA-DP DSAs showed an increased risk of graft loss or acute rejection (odds ratio = 3.6, 95%CI: 1.6–8.10" (Results/synthesis, HLA-DP section, meta-analysis paragraph immediately before Table 2)
- *C8* — "No effect on 1st transplant. In 2nd transplant, the 1-yr survival rate of transplants with no HLA-DPB mismatch was 83% ± 2%, which was significantly higher than grafts with 1 mismatch" (Table 2, row Mytilineos/1997)

**Limitations.** Narrative, non-systematic review: no search strategy, no databases or date limits stated, no inclusion/exclusion criteria, no protocol registration, no risk-of-bias assessment and no quality weighting of the tabulated studies. Study selection is therefore unauditable and probably favours positive reports.; The authors perform no analysis of their own. Every number in this evidence file is second-hand from a cited primary study, and most are reported without an effect size, a confidence interval, or a p-value.; A large share of the HLA-C evidence base is case reports (Chapman 1986, Baan 1993, Bachelet 2011, Suneja and Kuppachi 2012, Bosch 2014, Persaud 2017, Abuzeineh 2020) — seven of the sixteen Table 1 rows. Case reports cannot support a mismatch weight.; The paper conflates two different exposures throughout: HLA-C MISMATCH (a pre-transplant, antibody-free variable) and anti-HLA-C DSA (a measured antibody). Its strong conclusions rest on the DSA evidence; the mismatch evidence is thin and mostly null.; Cohorts are small where the C-specific answers are: 22 vs 88 (Aubert), 12 vs 23 (Santos), 104 pairs (Frohn), 52 with Cw-DSA (Visentin), 37 patients (Rosenberg, DP). Several 'significant'/'similar' verdicts rest on double-digit samples.; Publication span 1977-2023 with no stratification by immunosuppression era; findings from the ciclosporin era and the modern tacrolimus/MMF era are tabulated side by side.; Almost no living-donor evidence: only Albrechtsen 1977 (142 living-related, a null result) and one living-related case report (Persaud 2017). The living-donor transfer for C7/C8 is weak.; The authors declare a directional thesis in the title and abstract (these antigens are 'not benign') and end with ten recommendations advocating universal typing; the review is argumentative rather than neutral, which raises the risk of selective citation.; Internal inconsistency: anti-HLA-C antibody prevalence in sensitised patients is given as 42%-56% in the Introduction and 42%-65% in the 'DSAs against HLA-C' section, with no reconciliation.; Text-extraction artefacts in the retrieved PMC copy: inline citation markers are empty '[]' so individual claims cannot be traced to a numbered reference, italic gene symbols are dropped (e.g. 'the DQ subunit is encoded by the gene'), and the italic 'P' before p-values is stripped so the source reads '(= 0.004)'. P-values recorded here were read from that pattern; a reader should confirm against the publisher PDF.; The DP eplet category in Sapir-Pichhadze/2015 is truncated in the retrieved text: a second OR of 4.62 (1.51-14.14) is printed with no stated mismatch band.; No cost, feasibility or resource discussion accompanies the recommendation for universal molecular typing of C, DP and DQ plus routine single-antigen bead screening — a material omission for a resource-constrained programme..

### Lalji R 2025 — Association Between Donor-recipient Matchability, Access to Transplantation, and Posttransplant Outcomes.

Lalji R 2025, *Transplantation Direct*, [PMID 41069639](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41069639/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown — Transplantation Direct is an open-access journal, but no license statement appeared in the retrieved PMC text; treat quotes as short verbatim excerpts with attribution.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Australian kidney transplant candidates and recipients in the ANZDATA Registry, 1 July 2006 - 31 December 2023. HLA-A/-B/-DR data from 14 836 recipients (potential and actual) and 7708 donors (potential and actual) were used to build the M-score; 10 760 recipients with waitlist data entered the time-to-transplant model (Table 1 quartile sizes: Q1 2629, Q2 2701, Q3 2890, Q4 2908). New Zealand patients excluded (no waitlist data). Only first transplants. |
| donor type | deceased for all outcome analyses (multiorgan and living-donor recipients explicitly excluded from the posttransplant analyses); the M-score itself was built from HLA of both living and deceased donors and of non-transplanted typed candidates/donors |
| n | 14 836 recipients + 7708 donors for M-score construction; 10 760 waitlisted recipients in the models; size of the deceased-donor transplant subcohort used for graft-loss and rejection models is not stated in the retrieved text |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; a matchability score (M-score) computed by pairing every recipient against every donor, then three multivariable Cox models (time to transplant, death-censored graft loss, first acute rejection) with M-score quartile as the exposure, stratified by era and state; Kaplan-Meier plus log-rank |
| typing resolution | molecular (DNA) typing converted DOWN to HLA serotypes (antigen/broad level) for HLA-A, -B, -DR only; alleles with no WHO-assigned serotype mapped via HLA G codes, published data and a virtual-serotype computational tool; final assignment mirrors OrganMatch, the Australian deceased-donor allocation platform. HLA-C, -DQ and -DP were not used. |
| outcome | primary: time from waitlisting to deceased-donor transplantation. Secondary: time to death-censored graft loss; time to first acute rejection (cellular or antibody-mediated, per ANZDATA definitions) |
| follow up | not stated as a median; study window 1 July 2006 - 31 December 2023 (17.5 y), with 5-y death-censored graft survival reported by quartile |
| other factors modelled | recipient ethnicity (European Australian, Asian Australian, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Pasifika, Maori, Other), measured panel-reactive antibody (mPRA) dichotomised at 80%, ABO blood group, recipient sex, age at waitlisting / at transplant (<=18 vs >18 y), dialysis vintage / years from first dialysis to waitlisting, Kidney Donor Risk Index (KDRI, per unit), era and state (used as stratification variables because they violated proportional hazards) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a modern, fully specified implementation of the UK/French 'matchability' idea in a national registry, and it is the cleanest available demonstration that HLA MATCH PROBABILITY - not raw mismatch count - is the allocation-relevant quantity, which is exactly the C13 question of how a scheme should score HLA. It matters to the review in two independent ways. First, its scoring rule is an explicit non-additive weighting across loci (A=1, B=2, DR=4 points per mismatch, weights taken from the ratio of HR coefficients in a death-censored graft-survival model), so it is direct evidence for C10 that loci should not be summed with equal weight and quantifies a DR:B:A importance ordering of 4:2:1 at antigen level. Second, it shows that a candidate's position in the matchability distribution independently predicts outcome, not only access: the hardest-to-match quartile had aHR 0.56 (0.52-0.60) for ever receiving a deceased-donor kidney, 1.39 (1.01-1.92) for death-censored graft loss and 1.29 (1.09-1.52) for acute rejection. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown Iranian pre-screen is partial but favourable on the typing axis: the exposure here is deliberately LOW-resolution (molecular typing collapsed to serotypes, A/B/DR only), which is the same resolution a KidneyMatch pre-screen will have, so the 1:2:4 weighting is directly reusable and does not require two-field data. It transfers badly on the allocation axis: the access endpoint (waiting time on a deceased-donor list) has no analogue in a directed living-donor setting, and the whole equity argument - that scarce well-matched donors are rationed against minority candidates - only bites when the donor pool is shared. The graft-loss and rejection signal is the transferable half, but it is measured in deceased-donor grafts where KDRI (HR 1.69 per unit) and sensitisation (HR 13.7 for mPRA >=80%) dominate the M-score effect, and living-donor recipients were removed from those models by design. The paper is also a useful caution for Iran specifically: matchability is a property of the LOCAL donor pool, so an M-score computed on an Australian pool says nothing numerically about an Iranian one - only the method transfers, and it would have to be recomputed on Iranian HLA frequencies, where ethnic homogeneity would shift the whole distribution.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- receipt of a deceased-donor kidney transplant (time from waitlisting): M-score Q2 (harder to match) vs Q1 (easiest) — aHR 0.79 (0.74–0.84), p=<0.001 (overall M-score term); adjusted for blood group, sex, age at waitlisting, mPRA, dialysis-to-waitlisting time, ethnicity; stratified by era and state [Results, Time to Transplant; Table 4]
- receipt of a deceased-donor kidney transplant: M-score Q3 vs Q1 — aHR 0.66 (0.62–0.7), p=<0.001 (overall M-score term); adjusted for as above [Results, Time to Transplant; Table 4]
- receipt of a deceased-donor kidney transplant: M-score Q4 (hardest to match) vs Q1 — aHR 0.56 (0.52–0.6), p=<0.001 (overall M-score term); adjusted for as above [Results, Time to Transplant; Table 4; Abstract]
- median time from waitlisting to transplantation: M-score Q1 (easiest) — median days 252 (233–280); adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier) [Results, Time to Transplant]
- median time from waitlisting to transplantation: M-score Q4 (hardest) — median days 743 (673–812), p=<0.001 (log-rank across quartiles); adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier) [Results, Time to Transplant]
- death-censored graft loss: M-score Q2 vs Q1 — aHR 1.24 (0.91–1.69), p=0.2; adjusted for age at transplant, sex, dialysis vintage, KDRI, ethnicity, mPRA; stratified by era and state [Results, Death-censored Graft Loss; Table 5]
- death-censored graft loss: M-score Q3 vs Q1 — aHR 1.19 (0.87–1.63), p=0.3; adjusted for as above [Results, Death-censored Graft Loss; Table 5]
- death-censored graft loss: M-score Q4 vs Q1 — aHR 1.39 (1.01–1.92), p=0.042; adjusted for as above [Results, Death-censored Graft Loss; Table 5. NOTE: the Abstract prints the same estimate as 1.39 (1.01-1.91), P = 0.05 - the upper CI and p differ slightly between Abstract and Table 5/Results text.]
- 5-y death-censored graft survival: M-score Q1 / Q2 / Q3 / Q4 — percent surviving 96.2 / 95.2 / 94.1 / 92.7, p=<0.001 (log-rank across quartiles); adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier) [Results, Death-censored Graft Loss]
- first acute rejection (cellular or antibody-mediated): M-score Q2 vs Q1 — aHR 1.13 (0.97–1.32), p=0.12; adjusted for age at transplant, sex, dialysis vintage, KDRI, ethnicity, mPRA; stratified by era and state [Results, Acute Rejection; Table 6]
- first acute rejection: M-score Q3 vs Q1 — aHR 1.18 (1.01–1.38), p=0.042; adjusted for as above [Results, Acute Rejection; Table 6]
- first acute rejection: M-score Q4 vs Q1 — aHR 1.29 (1.09–1.52), p=0.003 (Table 6); the Abstract prints P = 0.002; adjusted for as above [Results, Acute Rejection; Table 6; Abstract]
- cumulative incidence of acute rejection across quartiles: Q1 vs Q2 vs Q3 vs Q4 (unadjusted) — log-rank p None, p=0.023; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Acute Rejection]
- proportion of non-European Australian candidates (composition, not risk): M-score Q1 / Q2 / Q3 / Q4 — percent 16 / 26 / 40 / 61, p=<0.001; adjusted for descriptive [Results, Baseline Characteristics; Table 1. NOTE: the Abstract prints Q4 as 60%, the Results text as 61%.]
- proportion sensitised (mPRA >= 80%) (composition, not risk): M-score Q1 / Q2 / Q3 / Q4 — percent (n) 5.9 (150) / 6.4 (168) / 8.2 (224) / 10 (298), p=<0.001; adjusted for descriptive [Results, Baseline Characteristics]
- death-censored graft loss - non-HLA comparators in the same model: mPRA >= 80% vs < 80% — aHR 13.7 (10.8–17.3), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model as the M-score estimates [Table 5. Included because it dwarfs the M-score effect and bounds how much a matchability term can add once antibody status is known.]
- death-censored graft loss - non-HLA comparators: KDRI, per unit — aHR 1.69 (1.34–2.12), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model [Table 5]
- death-censored graft loss - ethnicity: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander vs European Australian — aHR 2.29 (1.63–3.22), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model, i.e. over and above M-score quartile [Table 5]
- death-censored graft loss - ethnicity: Pasifika vs European Australian — aHR 2.18 (1.39–3.39), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model [Table 5]
- acute rejection - non-HLA comparator: mPRA >= 80% vs < 80% — aHR 1.9 (1.58–2.29), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model as the M-score rejection estimates [Table 6]
- receipt of a deceased-donor transplant - non-HLA comparator: mPRA >= 80% vs < 80% — aHR 0.58 (0.53–0.64), p=<0.001; adjusted for same model as the M-score access estimates [Table 4]
- narrative summary of the Q4-vs-Q1 contrast: Q4 vs Q1, all three endpoints — relative, as stated by the authors 3x longer wait, 40% more graft loss, ~30% more acute rejection; adjusted for narrative restatement of the adjusted models [Discussion, paragraph 1]

**Dose-response.**

- A: 1 mismatch point per HLA-A mismatch (weight 1)
- B: 2 mismatch points per HLA-B mismatch (weight 2)
- DR: 4 mismatch points per HLA-DR mismatch (weight 4)
- C: not used - HLA-C was not part of the M-score
- DQ: not used - the authors propose adding HLA-DQ in a future version
- DP: not used
- derivation: The 1:2:4 weighting is stated to be 'the ratio of their hazard ratio (HR) coefficients from a multivariable model of death-censored graft survival, considering only HLA mismatches', aligned with previously published Australian HLA-mismatch data and with the French MDP weighting. The underlying per-locus HRs are cited to a supplementary table and are NOT reproduced in the retrieved PMC text, so no per-locus HR/CI can be extracted from this paper.
- score_range: 0 to 14; a fully mismatched pair (2A, 2B, 2DR) scores 14, a perfect match scores 0. Recipient M-score = mean of that score across all donors in the pool; quartile IQRs Q1 9.3-10.7, Q2 10.8-11.3, Q3 11.4-12.0, Q4 12.0-13.7; cohort mean +/- SD 11.4 +/- 0.9.
- Shape reported: step (quartiles). Access falls monotonically and steeply across quartiles (0.79 -> 0.66 -> 0.56). Acute rejection rises monotonically (1.13 -> 1.18 -> 1.29). Death-censored graft loss is NOT monotonic across the middle of the range (1.24 for Q2 then 1.19 for Q3 before 1.39 for Q4), and only Q4 reaches significance - so the graft-loss dose-response is best described as a threshold/top-quartile effect rather than a graded one.; linearity tested: not tested. The M-score was modelled only as a categorical quartile variable; no linear term, trend test, spline or other functional form for the M-score is reported. The authors did explore alternative functional forms, but for the mPRA covariate rather than for the M-score, and rejected them by AIC in favour of dichotomising mPRA at 80%.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- recipient ethnicity x M-score (matchability) on time to transplantation: No effect modification. The interaction term was pre-specified, fitted, tested by likelihood ratio test and found non-significant, so it was dropped from the final model. The matchability penalty on access therefore appears to act uniformly across ethnic groups; ethnicity affects access mainly by determining WHERE a candidate sits in the matchability distribution (Q1 16% to Q4 61% non-European Australian), not by changing the slope. (P = 0.828 (likelihood ratio test)) [Statistical Methods; Results, Time to Transplant]
- recipient ethnicity as an independent predictor alongside M-score (death-censored graft loss): Not an interaction test, but relevant to C11: after adjusting for M-score quartile, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander (aHR 2.29; 1.63-3.22) and Pasifika (aHR 2.18; 1.39-3.39) recipients still had roughly double the death-censored graft loss, so matchability does not explain the ethnic outcome gap. No formal ethnicity x M-score interaction was tested for the graft-loss or rejection models (only for access). (aHR 2.29 (1.63-3.22) and 2.18 (1.39-3.39), both P<0.001) [Table 5]
- locus x locus (A x B x DR) non-additivity: NOT tested. The loci are combined by a fixed additive point sum with unequal per-locus weights (1/2/4); no interaction between loci, no haplotype term, and no non-additive combination rule was fitted or reported. The paper is evidence for unequal WEIGHTING of loci, not for interaction between them. [Materials and Methods, Creation of M-score (absence)]
- sensitisation (mPRA) x matchability: Not tested as an interaction, but sensitisation is strongly correlated with matchability quartile (mPRA >= 80% in 5.9%, 6.4%, 8.2%, 10% of Q1-Q4, P<0.001) and is by far the dominant term in the graft-loss model (aHR 13.7). The two exposures are entangled and the paper cannot separate a matchability effect from residual sensitisation. (quartile gradient P<0.001; mPRA aHR 13.7 (10.8-17.3)) [Results, Baseline Characteristics; Table 5]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Mismatch points were assigned as follows: 1 point per HLA-A mismatch, 2 points per HLA-B mismatch, and 4 points per HLA-DR mismatch." (Materials and Methods, Creation of M-score)
- *C10* — "The relative weighting of mismatch points was based on the ratio of their hazard ratio (HR) coefficients from a multivariable model of death-censored graft survival, considering only HLA mismatches" (Materials and Methods, Creation of M-score)
- *C13* — "Scores ranged from 0 to 14, with a fully mismatched donor-recipient pair (2A, 2B, 2DR MM) receiving the maximum score of 14 and a perfectly matched pair receiving a score of 0." (Materials and Methods, Creation of M-score)
- *C13* — "On average, Q4 patients waited 3 times longer for a kidney offer, experienced 40% more graft loss, and had almost 30% higher rates of acute rejection than those in the easiest group (Q1)." (Discussion, paragraph 1)
- *C11* — "The interaction term between ethnicity and matchability scores was tested but was not statistically significant" (Results, Time to Transplant)
- *C12* — "All HLA data used in the analysis were defined by molecular techniques and converted to HLA serotypes for analysis." (Materials and Methods, Conversion of HLA Data)

**Limitations.** Not a mismatch-count study. The exposure is a candidate-level match-probability quartile, so the paper gives no HR per additional mismatch, no per-locus HR and no zero-mismatch premium. It cannot answer C2, C3, C5, C6 or C9 directly; the 1:2:4 weighting is asserted from an unreported supplementary model, not demonstrated here.; The per-locus hazard ratios that justify the A:B:DR = 1:2:4 weighting are cited to supplementary material and are absent from the retrieved PMC text, so the review cannot check the weighting against the primary numbers.; M-score modelled only in quartiles; linearity/functional form of the continuous score was never tested, and the score has a narrow spread (mean 11.4, SD 0.9, quartile boundaries about 10.7 / 11.3 / 12.0 on a 0-14 scale), so the contrast between Q1 and Q4 is a difference of roughly 1.5-2 weighted mismatch points.; Death-censored graft loss is non-monotonic (Q2 1.24 > Q3 1.19) and only Q4 is significant, with a CI whose lower bound is 1.01 and a p of 0.042 (0.05 in the Abstract) - a fragile result. The rejection gradient is more consistent but modest.; Abstract and Results/tables disagree on three printed values: Q4 graft-loss CI (1.01-1.91 vs 1.01-1.92) and p (0.05 vs 0.042), Q4 rejection p (0.002 vs 0.003), and the Q4 non-European proportion (60% vs 61%).; Matchability is a property of a specific donor pool. The Australian M-score distribution is not transportable to Iran, or anywhere else, as a number; only the method is.; Only HLA-A, -B and -DR were used. HLA-C, -DQ and -DP are absent, which the authors themselves flag as a gap to be closed in a future version.; Molecular typing was deliberately collapsed to serotypes, and some historical serological typing was converted using imputation-like methods; measurement error is acknowledged, though the authors say it affected <0.1% of the dataset.; Confounding by indication and by sensitisation: mPRA rises across quartiles and has an aHR of 13.7 for graft loss, so the residual M-score effect could partly be unmeasured antibody burden. mPRA was forced into a binary <80/>=80 form.; A mid-study national switch (2016) from CDC-based PRA to Luminex-calculated PRA changed the meaning of the mPRA covariate over time.; Registry data: coding errors, only recipients with complete HLA data included (though the authors show the excluded were not enriched for ethnic minorities), no immunosuppression protocol, no cold ischaemia time, no DSA/eplet data, no PIRCHE.; Outcomes span multiple allocation-algorithm eras over 17.5 years; era and state had to be handled by stratification because they violated proportional hazards.; No median follow-up is reported, and the size of the deceased-donor transplant subcohort feeding the graft-loss and rejection models is not stated in the text.; Living-donor recipients were excluded from every outcome model, which is the single biggest limitation for a living-donor pre-screen application..

### Lee H 2025 — Eplet mismatch analysis in kidney transplantation: from concept to clinical practice

Lee H 2025, *Clinical Transplantation and Research (Clin Transplant Res) 39(3):183-199*, [DOI 10.4285/ctr.25.0046](https://doi.org/10.4285/ctr.25.0046). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - no licence statement appears in the retrieved PMC text; the journal (Korean Society for Transplantation) is open access, but the exact CC licence could not be confirmed from the retrieved text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | narrative review of the eplet / molecular-mismatch literature in kidney transplantation; the cohorts it cites span adult and paediatric, living- and deceased-donor kidney recipients (e.g. Tafulo n=151 and n=96 living donor; Ashimine n=691 living donor; Senev n=926; Lee n=347 Korean; Southeast Asian n=234; Jaeger n=439; Sapir-Pichhadze >118,000 US; Mohammadhassanzadeh n=118,313; National Kidney Registry n=5,193) |
| donor type | both (several key cited cohorts and both named eplet-using allocation programmes are living donor) |
| n | not applicable - narrative review; no pooled denominator. Individual cited cohorts range from n=42 to n>400,000 |
| design | narrative (non-systematic) review; no search strategy, no pooling, no risk-of-bias assessment |
| typing resolution | two-field / allele-level (high-resolution) typing is the premise of the whole method; the review explicitly discusses haplotype-frequency imputation as the substitute when only low-resolution typing is available |
| outcome | dnDSA formation; antibody-mediated rejection; acute and chronic rejection; death-censored and all-cause graft failure; transplant glomerulopathy; dd-cfDNA |
| follow up | not applicable (review); one cited model reports 10-year dnDSA-free survival |
| other factors modelled | tacrolimus trough level / immunosuppression exposure, recipient age, prior sensitisation status, donor-recipient race/ancestry concordance, retransplantation and repeated eplet mismatch, PIRCHE-II T-cell epitope load, donor-derived cell-free DNA |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's most current secondary source for claim C12 (molecular mismatch: thresholds, two-field typing requirement, low-resolution misclassification, imputation accuracy) and C13 (programmes that actually score HLA by eplets in allocation). It answers the question 'could a pre-screen use eplet load instead of antigen mismatch counts?' and the answer it gives is a boundary condition rather than an endorsement: eplet analysis is defined on allele-level (second-field) sequence, so it cannot be computed from one-field Iranian typing at all without haplotype-frequency imputation. The review then states that imputation accuracy is population-dependent and specifically degraded in non-European populations where population-specific HLA reference data are sparse - which is exactly Iran's situation, since no Iranian haplotype reference panel is cited anywhere in the paper. It supplies both sides of that trade-off numerically: Cohen preserved risk classification in >90% of pairs (97.1% concordance in real-world validation), while Senev found 23.3% of DSA assignments inaccurate on imputed genotypes, and the authors' own reading is that imputation 'cannot fully substitute for high-resolution data'. For C13 it documents the two living-donor programmes that already put eplets into allocation (US National Kidney Registry; Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne) and the 2022 STAR Working Group recommendation to move beyond antigen-level matching - useful precedent for a living-donor matching product, but the same paragraph stresses that standardisation and validation across diverse populations must precede allocation use. Net transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran: eplet load is out of reach as a scoring input under current typing practice, so the pre-screen must stay on antigen-level mismatch counts, and this paper is the citation for WHY that choice is forced rather than merely conservative.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- dnDSA (class II): Wiebe 2013 class II eplet mismatch thresholds DR<10, DQ<17 vs antigen-level matching — threshold (no effect estimate given) None; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation', para 1]
- dnDSA / alloimmune risk stratification: Wiebe single-molecule eplet mismatch categories: low = DR<7 and DQ<9; intermediate = DR>=7 and DQ<14; high = DR>=7 and DQ>=15 — risk category cut-points (ROC-derived, no effect estimate given) None; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation', para 2]
- class II dnDSA: HLA-DQ eplet mismatch cut-offs in a Korean cohort (n=347): single-molecule >=10, total eplet >=12, antibody-verified or antibody-verified single-molecule >=4 — threshold (no effect estimate given) None; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation', para 3]
- antibody-mediated rejection: high HLA class II eplet mismatch load (>=13) vs lower, in 151 living-donor kidney transplants — threshold, independent predictor (no effect estimate given) None; adjusted for described as 'independently predicted'; covariates not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Impact of Eplet Mismatch on Rejection and Graft Survival', para 1]
- rejection incidence: low scores on all three molecular-mismatch measures (eplet count, highly immunogenic eplets, PIRCHE-II) vs high scores, n=439 standard-risk recipients — incidence proportions 12% vs 33%, p=0.003; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Integration of Eplet Mismatch With Complementary Assessment Tools']
- dnDSA: tacrolimus trough <6 ng/mL vs higher, within intermediate- and high-risk eplet mismatch groups — fold-increase in risk 2.3; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch-Guided Immunosuppression Strategies']
- 10-year dnDSA-free survival: low-risk group defined by combined single-molecule eplet mismatch and recipient age — survival proportion 97%; adjusted for model combines eplet mismatch with recipient age [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch-Guided Immunosuppression Strategies']
- imputation accuracy - mismatch risk classification: imputed vs directly typed allele-level genotypes, racially concordant and discordant donor-recipient pairs — concordance proportion over 90% (97.1% concordance in a real-world validation cohort); adjusted for not applicable [Critical issues, 'Imputation Accuracy and Population-Specific Limitations']
- DSA assignment accuracy: DSA assignment based on imputed genotypes vs direct high-resolution typing — misclassification proportion 23.3% of DSA assignments inaccurate; adjusted for not applicable [Critical issues, 'Imputation Accuracy and Population-Specific Limitations']
- eplet antibody-verification status: eplets meeting the highest verification standard (Level A1/A2) vs all catalogued eplets — proportion 12%; adjusted for not applicable [Critical issues, 'Limitations in Eplet Immunogenicity Validation']
- proportion of dnDSA directed at HLA-DQ: DQ vs other loci among patients who developed dnDSA — proportion 77% (DeVos), 54% (Willicombe), approximately 64.6% (Korean cohort); adjusted for not applicable [Introduction/Molecular basis section on HLA-DQ]
- rejection in race-discordant donor-recipient pairs (paediatric): different-race vs same-race donor, conditional on class I eplet load >=70, n=110 — threshold-conditional association (no effect estimate given) None; adjusted for not stated in this review [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation', para 3]
- match quality in deceased-donor allocation: eplet-based matching vs conventional, National Kidney Registry dataset n=5,193 — improved match quality for Black and Hispanic/Latino candidates (no numeric estimate given) None; adjusted for not applicable [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Clinical Implementation in Transplantation Programs']

**Dose-response.**

- DR: single_molecule_low MM: DR<7; single_molecule_intermediate MM: DR>=7 (with DQ<14); single_molecule_high MM: DR>=7 (with DQ>=15); earlier_2013_threshold MM: DR<10
- DQ: single_molecule_low MM: DQ<9; single_molecule_intermediate MM: DQ<14; single_molecule_high MM: DQ>=15; earlier_2013_threshold MM: DQ<17; korean_cohort_cutoffs MM: single-molecule >=10; total eplet >=12; antibody-verified (or AV single-molecule) >=4
- class_II_combined: AMR_threshold_living_donor MM: >=13 (Tafulo, n=151)
- class_I: paediatric_race_discordance_threshold MM: >=70 (Philogene, n=110)
- Shape reported: linear (for antibody-verified HLA-DQ eplet load, as reported from Senev) combined with an operational step/category structure (Wiebe low / intermediate / high). The review's own conclusion is that risk rises monotonically with load but that no safe cut-point exists.; linearity tested: Not tested by this paper - it is a narrative review and runs no analysis. It reports, secondhand, that Senev et al. found antibody-verified HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load 'independently and linearly associated' with dnDSA, rejection and graft failure; the Wiebe thresholds are described as ROC-derived cut-points, which is a categorisation of a continuous load rather than a test of linearity.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- eplet mismatch risk group x tacrolimus trough level: Tacrolimus trough <6 ng/mL raised dnDSA risk only in intermediate- and high-risk eplet mismatch groups; no significant association in the low-risk group. The review adds that high-risk patients warrant trough >=8 ng/mL while low-risk patients permit dose reduction. (2.3-fold increased risk in intermediate/high groups; not significant in low-risk group) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch-Guided Immunosuppression Strategies' (Davis et al.)]
- eplet mismatch x tacrolimus trough (synergy): Compounded risk when both high HLA-DQ eplet mismatch and low tacrolimus trough are present, described as a synergistic increase in dnDSA development. (no numeric estimate given) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch-Guided Immunosuppression Strategies' (Lee et al.)]
- prior sensitisation status x molecular mismatch metric: In unsensitised recipients both eplet mismatch and PIRCHE-II predicted class II dnDSA; in previously sensitised recipients only PIRCHE-II and a history of T cell-mediated rejection remained significant. Directly relevant to an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen: the predictive metric that works depends on sensitisation state. (no numeric estimate given) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Integration of Eplet Mismatch With Complementary Assessment Tools' (Ashimine et al., n=691 living donor)]
- donor-recipient race discordance x class I eplet load: Rejection risk was higher with different-race donors than same-race donors, but only when the class I eplet load was >=70 - i.e. the race effect was conditional on crossing an eplet-load threshold. (threshold >=70; no effect estimate given) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation' (Philogene et al., n=110 paediatric)]
- ancestry / population x imputation accuracy: Imputation error is higher in non-European populations with limited population-specific HLA reference data; ancestry misclassification during imputation increases mismatch uncertainty (shown for Alaska Native/American Indian). Multiple imputation with ancestry-informed models improves accuracy but cannot fully substitute for high-resolution data. (no numeric estimate for the interaction itself; the marginal figures are Cohen >90% and Senev 23.3%) [Critical issues, 'Imputation Accuracy and Population-Specific Limitations' (Matern et al.)]
- recipient ancestry x matching metric (allocation equity): Race-informed molecular matching using hydrophobicity, electrostatic charge and amino acid composition improved donor compatibility for underrepresented groups; eplet-based matching improved match quality for Black and Hispanic/Latino candidates in the National Kidney Registry dataset. (n=5,193; no effect estimate given) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Clinical Implementation in Transplantation Programs' (Bekbolsynov et al. and NKR analysis)]
