- repeat mismatch (retransplantation) x eplet immunogenicity: Repeated mismatches at immunogenic eplets were associated with higher AMR rates and reduced graft survival; DSAs targeting repeated eplets were more persistent and had higher MFI. (no numeric estimate given) [Results/Clinical evidence, 'Impact of Eplet Mismatch on Rejection and Graft Survival' (Arches et al.)]
- scoring platform x eplet mismatch result (methodological, not biological): HLAMatchmaker v2.1 and One Lambda Fusion MatchMaker v4.2 gave significantly different total mismatch counts, different mismatched-eplet lists and different antibody-verification status on identical donor-recipient pairs, with some incorrect eplet-to-allele assignments. (no numeric estimate given) [Critical issues, 'Standardization and Validation Requirements' (Tassone et al.)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "established mismatch thresholds for each individual HLA-DR and -DQ molecule, enabling stratification of recipients according to whether a molecule exceeded its threshold (low: DR<7 and DQ<9; intermediate: DR≥7 and DQ<14; high: DR≥7 and DQ≥15)" (Clinical evidence, 'Eplet Mismatch and Donor-Specific Antibody Formation', para 2)
- *C12* — "Senev et al. [] showed that 23.3% of DSA assignments were inaccurate when based on imputed genotypes, highlighting the need for direct high-resolution typing whenever possible." (Critical issues, 'Imputation Accuracy and Population-Specific Limitations')
- *C12* — "Cohen et al. [] demonstrated that imputation preserved mismatch risk classification in over 90% of both racially concordant and discordant donor-recipient pairs, with 97.1% concordance in a real-world validation cohort." (Critical issues, 'Imputation Accuracy and Population-Specific Limitations')
- *C13* — "Some living donor programs, including the National Kidney Registry in the United States and the Royal Children’s Hospital Melbourne transplant program, have already integrated eplet mismatch considerations into their allocation algorithms" (Critical issues, 'Integration of Eplet Mismatch Into Clinical Practice and Allocation Systems', para 1)
- *C13* — "They recommended incorporating molecular mismatch analysis—including eplet-based and physicochemical scoring—into pre- and posttransplant risk assessment strategies." (Critical issues, 'Integration of Eplet Mismatch Into Clinical Practice and Allocation Systems', para 2 (STAR Working Group 2022 consensus meeting))
- *C12* — "The risk increases with higher mismatch load; however, no universally safe threshold has yet been defined." (Conclusion)

**Limitations.** Narrative (non-systematic) review: no stated search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no risk-of-bias assessment, no pooling. It cannot be used as an effect-size source in its own right.; Every number in this paper is secondary reporting of a cited primary study. Before any figure here is used in the review's synthesis it must be re-extracted from the primary source (Wiebe, Senev, Cohen, Tafulo, Lee, Jaeger, Davis, Philogene, Bezstarosti).; The paper reports no hazard ratio, odds ratio or relative risk anywhere, and reproduces no confidence interval at all. Exactly one p-value appears in the whole text (P=0.003, Jaeger rejection 12% vs 33%). Effect sizes are therefore almost entirely absent.; Tables and figures were not captured in the retrieved PMC text - citation markers were stripped to empty '()' and '[]'. Numeric detail that exists in the paper's tables (the summary tables of eplet studies and of molecular mismatch tools) is not represented in this extraction and may contain further figures.; Contributes nothing to antigen-level dose-response (C2, C9): there is no 0/1/2 mismatch-per-locus series in the paper. It is an eplet/molecular-mismatch source only.; Thresholds are acknowledged by the authors themselves as not validated across ethnic groups; the Korean cut-offs (DQ single-molecule >=10) differ from the Wiebe cut-offs, which shows the cut-points are cohort- and immunosuppression-dependent rather than universal.; No Iranian, Middle Eastern or West Asian data, and no Iranian haplotype reference panel is cited - so the imputation-accuracy figures (Cohen >90%, Senev 23.3%) come from European and US populations and cannot be assumed to hold in Iran.; The two cited imputation figures point in opposite directions (Cohen reassuring, Senev alarming) and the review does not reconcile them; it lands on 'cannot fully substitute for high-resolution data'.; Authors are a two-person Korean laboratory-medicine group; the evidence selection is not blinded or duplicated, and cited-study selection may be non-representative.; Eplet scores themselves are shown to be unstable across software platforms and database versions (Tassone), so even with two-field typing an eplet score is not a single well-defined quantity.; Only 12% of catalogued eplets meet the highest antibody-verification standard, so a large part of any eplet load is sequence-inferred rather than experimentally validated immunogenicity..

### Niemann M 2025 — Advancing risk stratification in kidney transplantation: integrating HLA-derived T-cell epitope and B-cell epitope matching algorithms for enhanced predictive accuracy of HLA compatibility.

Niemann M 2025, *Frontiers in Immunology*, [DOI 10.3389/fimmu.2025.1548934](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2025.1548934). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown from retrieved text; no licence statement was present in the retrieved PMC body. Frontiers in Immunology publishes under CC BY 4.0 as its standard licence, but this was not verified in the retrieved text..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | US SRTR kidney transplant recipients, transplants 1991-2022 (median 2010); 542,621 records screened, 400,935 analysed after aggregation and filtering for missing data. 60.57% male, 33.37% living-donor, 24.44% recipient black, 11.91% donor black, 74.00% tacrolimus maintenance, 86.71% first transplants, 16.99% CMV mismatch. Median recipient age 51 (IQR 22), median donor age 40 (IQR 23), median A-B-DR mismatches 4 (IQR 2). A pre-specified subgroup of 31,479 transplants performed 2014-12-04 to 2016-12-03 covered the OPTN KAS 2014 allocation change. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 400,935 (of 542,621 screened); KAS-2014 subgroup 31,479 |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; head-to-head comparison of HLA coding schemes (serological HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch, summed vs per-locus, and four molecular metrics: antibody-verified Eplets, all Eplets, Snow [Snowflake+Snowball], PIRCHE-II v3/v4, amino-acid mismatches) inside Cox proportional hazards models (BIC, Uno iAUC at 25th/50th/75th percentiles of follow-up, VIF for multicollinearity) and XGBoost accelerated-failure-time models (iAUC, Harrell C, gain-based variable importance). 70/30 train/test split repeated with 10 random seeds; no external validation cohort. Threshold optimisation of Snow and PIRCHE-II by AIC; optimal cutpoints by maximally selected rank statistics (survminer). |
| typing resolution | low resolution (antigen / first-field) HLA-A, -B, -DR only, as recorded in SRTR. Protein-level (high-resolution) typings were produced by multiple imputation against the 2007 NMDP haplotype dataset, with the individual's reported race/ethnicity used to select the reference population; HLA-C and -DQ alleles were imputed from the available A/B/DR typing. High-resolution haplotype pairs were filtered at a normalised 1% threshold and molecular scores were aggregated by frequency-weighted summation over candidate pairs. |
| outcome | death-censored graft survival / death-censored graft failure |
| follow up | median 4.85 years (25th percentile 1.98 years, 75th percentile 8.97 years); 76,077 graft losses (20%). KAS-2014 subgroup: median 5.84 years (IQR 4.28-6.16), 3,496 graft losses (9%). |
| other factors modelled | donor age, recipient age, living vs deceased donor type, donor black (donor ethnicity), recipient black (African American recipient), CMV mismatch (donor pos / patient neg), Tacrolimus-based maintenance immunosuppression, number of previous transplantations (retransplantation) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's cleanest head-to-head test of how HLA should be CODED in a pre-transplant risk model (discovery angles E and H): antigen-level HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch, summed versus per-locus, is put in direct competition with four molecular metrics inside both a semi-parametric Cox model and a non-parametric gradient-boosting model, on 400,935 kidney-only transplants with death-censored graft survival. It answers C12 directly: molecular metrics add information over antigen matching, but the gain is small and appears mainly in long-term prediction, while antigen-level HLA-A/-B/-DR matching remains the strongest single histocompatibility term in XGBoost and in the underpowered KAS-2014 subgroup. It is unusually transferable to an Iranian living-donor, one-field-typing pre-screen because the SOURCE DATA ARE LOW-RESOLUTION A/B/DR ONLY: the authors show that a haplotype-frequency imputation step (NMDP reference, ethnicity-matched, 1% threshold, frequency-weighted aggregation of candidate high-resolution pairs) is enough to compute PIRCHE-II, Snow and eplet loads from exactly the typing depth an Iranian programme would have. Two caveats limit that transfer sharply: the imputation reference is a US/NMDP population with no Iranian haplotype panel, and the authors themselves name imputation inaccuracy as a limitation; and the cohort is 33% living-donor with no separate living-donor effect estimate, so the review cannot read a living-donor-specific molecular-mismatch effect out of it. The paper is also the strongest single source on relative importance: in the XGBoost variable-importance ranking, living donation, recipient ethnicity, tacrolimus, donor age and number of previous transplants all outrank HLA-DR mismatch, which in turn outranks recipient age, PIRCHE, Snow, HLA-B and HLA-A - a direct warning that in a pre-screen, donor-quality and clinical factors dominate any HLA metric. Finally, it supplies the non-linearity evidence the review needs: molecular load is explicitly non-linear in log-hazard with a dampened increase at high load, log-transformation improved BIC for every metric, and empirically derived four-band cutpoints are given for PIRCHE-II, Snow and antibody-verified eplets.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: best UNIVARIABLE histocompatibility metric: PIRCHE-II version 4 (Cox) — median iAUC (Uno, integrated over 25th/50th/75th percentiles of follow-up) 0.5436; adjusted for nothing (univariable histocompatibility model) [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis; also Figure 4 top panel]
- death-censored graft failure: best HISTOCOMPATIBILITY-ONLY multivariable Cox model: HLA-A, -B, -DR matching + Snow + PIRCHE-II version 4 (lowest BIC of all histocompatibility-only Cox models) — median iAUC 0.5392; adjusted for the histocompatibility covariates only; no clinical covariates [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis; Figure 4 top panel]
- death-censored graft failure: clinical reference model alone (donor black, recipient black, tacrolimus maintenance, recipient age, donor age, living donor, CMV mismatch, number of pre-transplants) - NO HLA term — median iAUC (Cox) 0.6558; adjusted for the listed clinical covariates [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis; Figure 4 bottom panel]
- death-censored graft failure: clinical reference model + HLA-A, -B, -DR matching + antibody-verified Eplets + PIRCHE (lowest BIC of all clinical+histocompatibility Cox models; a model exchanging Eplets for Snow had a very similar BIC) — BIC improvement with iAUC essentially unchanged (no numeric BIC printed in the text) None; adjusted for clinical reference covariates [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis; Figure 4 bottom panel. Note: BIC values are shown only as a scaled butterfly plot, not as numbers.]
- death-censored graft failure: XGBoost histocompatibility-only models, range across variable sets: worst = PIRCHE version 3, best = HLA-A, -B, -DR matching + Snow + PIRCHE — median iAUC range None (0.545–0.557); adjusted for nothing beyond the histocompatibility variables in each set [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis (XGBoost paragraph); Figure 7 top panel. NOTE: 0.545 and 0.557 are the two ENDS of a range of model medians, not a confidence interval.]
- death-censored graft failure: XGBoost clinical risk-factor model + HLA-A, -B, -DR matching + Eplets + PIRCHE (best overall). Similar performance when Eplets were exchanged for Snow, or when molecular compatibility was dropped entirely and only HLA-A, -B, -DR matching was used — Harrell C index and median iAUC (both reported as 0.680) 0.68; adjusted for clinical reference covariates [Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis (XGBoost paragraph); Figure 7 bottom panel]
- estimated 10-year death-censored graft survival: within the 6-16 antibody-verified Eplet mismatch stratum: PIRCHE-II < 23 versus PIRCHE-II >= 69 — absolute 10-year graft survival, two ends of the gradient None (67.9–75.8); adjusted for unadjusted stratum-specific incidence based on optimal cutpoints [Figure 5 legend (worked example). NOTE: 67.9% and 75.8% are the two ends of a within-stratum gradient, not a confidence interval; the full risk-strata grid is only in Figure 5.]
- median (half-life) death-censored graft survival by predicted-risk quartile: Cox model INCLUDING molecular matching versus Cox model of HLA-A, -B, -DR matching only, high / int-high / int-low / low risk quartiles — graft half-life in years, printed as pairs None; adjusted for model-predicted risk quartile [Results 3.4 Model inference; Figure 9. Printed verbatim as '16.78y vs 17.47y, 17.65y vs 17.88y, 19.01y vs 18.76y, 22.88y vs 22.72y, for high, int-high, int-low and low risk, respectively'. The text asserts molecular matching discriminates 'slightly better' but does not label which member of each pair is which model; the reviewer should treat the assignment as ambiguous.]
- construct validity of Snow (not a clinical outcome): share of reported antibody-verified Eplets whose highly exposed amino-acid positions are captured by the optimal Snow configuration — percentage None [Results 3.1 Threshold analysis: HLA class I 50/74 = 67.6%; HLA-DRB1 12/17 = 70.6%; HLA-DQB1 21/31 = 67.7%]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: non-linear / concave in the log-hazard with respect to molecular mismatch load. Verbatim: 'Molecular incompatibility loads appear superlinear with a dampened increase in hazard at high load scores, justifying log-transformation of these metrics'. The authors' word 'superlinear' describes the score DISTRIBUTION; the hazard relationship they describe and correct for is a dampened (diminishing-returns) increase at high load, which is why the natural log of the score fitted better. In place of a smooth curve the authors report empirical risk BANDS from maximally selected rank statistics: PIRCHE-II (v4, 300 permille) intervals [0-23), [23-45), [45-69), [69-inf); Snow (0.26/0.68) intervals [0-17), [17-35), [35-47), [47-inf); antibody-verified Eplet intervals [0-6), [6-16), [16-22), [22-inf).; linearity tested: Yes, three ways. (1) Log-transformation was applied to PIRCHE-II (following Lachmann et al., scores incremented by one then natural log) and likewise to Snow, amino-acid and Eplet matching; log-transformation improved BIC for ALL molecular matching metrics with little to no impact on iAUC - this is the paper's operational test of non-linearity in the Cox model. (2) XGBoost was used explicitly as a non-parametric comparator, and its slightly higher iAUC was attributed by the authors to trees mapping 'the non-linear histocompatibility metrics better to immunologic risk'. (3) Optimal cutpoints were derived by maximally selected rank statistics (three consecutive cutpoint analyses per metric), yielding four-band step functions for PIRCHE-II, Snow and antibody-verified Eplets. No spline was fitted and no formal test for trend or P-for-non-linearity is reported.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- histocompatibility/molecular metrics x follow-up horizon (time): Effect modification by time since transplant. Adding histocompatibility to the clinical Cox model slightly WORSENED short-term prediction (AUC at 1.98 years) but IMPROVED long-term prediction (AUC at 8.97 years). In XGBoost the improvement was time-independent. (no numbers printed; shown as AUC distributions at 1.98 / 4.85 / 8.97 years) [Results 3.2, final paragraphs; Figure 6; repeated in Discussion]
- PIRCHE-II (T-cell epitope) x Snow, and PIRCHE-II x antibody-verified Eplets (B-cell epitope): Additive, not redundant: within every stratum of one metric (each row or column of the risk grid) a gradient in 10-year graft survival is seen across strata of the other metric, i.e. the two pathways carry independent information - the paper's central 'linked recognition' result. (worked example: within 6-16 Eplet mismatches, 10-year graft survival 75.8% (PIRCHE-II < 23) to 67.9% (PIRCHE-II >= 69)) [Results 3.2; Figure 5]
- Snow x Eplet (collinearity, not effect modification): Elevated variance inflation factors for both Eplet and Snow scores when entered together, confirming conceptual and statistical codependency; these covariate combinations were EXCLUDED from further analysis. PIRCHE+Eplets and PIRCHE+Snow give comparable performance, so the two B-cell metrics are interchangeable but not combinable. (VIF elevated (no numeric VIF printed)) [Results 3.2; Discussion paragraph 3]
- Snow threshold configuration x presence of PIRCHE-II and antigen matching in the model: The optimal Snow threshold depends on what else is in the model - a model-level interaction. Alone, the AIC-optimal Snowflake/Snowball configuration was 0.00/0.00 (which degenerates to a plain donor amino-acid mismatch count); combined with PIRCHE-II the optimum became more restrictive at 0.26/0.68/300, and adding HLA-A, -B, -DR serological matching improved it further (0.70/0.66/300, only slightly better than 0.26/0.68/300). Authors interpret this as each predictor being allowed to specialise for its own allorecognition pathway. (AIC-based; no numeric AIC printed) [Results 3.1 Threshold analysis; Discussion paragraph 2]
- allocation era (OPTN KAS 2014 subgroup) x molecular matching: In the 31,479-transplant KAS-2014 subgroup (median follow-up 5.84 y, only 3,496 events, 9%), complex multi-metric histocompatibility Cox models mostly LOST statistical significance although individual metrics performed well univariably; XGBoost did not benefit from molecular metrics and HLA-A, -B, -DR matching was the strongest histocompatibility predictor; augmenting the clinical model with molecular matching did not improve it. Variable importance for almost all parameters (except living donation and recipient black) failed to clearly exceed a random control variable. Authors attribute this to insufficient power and short follow-up rather than to an era effect. (no numbers printed) [Results 3.3 KAS 2014 subgroup analysis; Discussion]
- HLA metrics versus clinical/donor-quality factors (relative importance, XGBoost gain): Ranking, most to least important: living donation > recipient black > tacrolimus maintenance > donor age > number of previous transplantations > HLA-DR mismatch > recipient age > donor black > CMV mismatch > PIRCHE > Snow > HLA-B > HLA-A (least). HLA-A and Snow were lower by an order of magnitude but still above an artificially added random variable. Authors note the low apparent importance is partly an artefact of splitting histocompatibility across five input variables; in single-metric models the histocompatibility variable's importance is still low but of the same order as recipient age. (gain metric; no numeric gains printed (Figure 8 only)) [Results 3.2, variable importance paragraph; Figure 8]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "Multivariable models of histocompatibility generally outperformed univariable predictors, with a combined model of HLA-A, -B, -DR matching, Snow and PIRCHE-II yielding highest AUC in XGBoost and lowest BIC in Cox models." (Abstract, Results; repeated in Results 3.2)
- *C2* — "Molecular incompatibility loads appear superlinear with a dampened increase in hazard at high load scores, justifying log-transformation of these metrics" (Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis)
- *C12* — "The multivariable model of HLA-A, -B and -DR (A+B+DR) mismatches outperformed the univariable model of the summed number of mismatches on all three loci." (Results 3.2 Competitive model analysis)
- *C11* — "Variable importance of the best-performing XGBoost ensemble indicated that living donation was the most important variable, followed by recipient being black, Tacrolimus maintenance, donor age, number of previous transplantations, HLA-DR mismatch" (Results 3.2, variable importance paragraph (Figure 8))
- *C12* — "the histocompatibility-augmented clinical models had a slightly worse short-term prediction performance at 1.98 years post transplantation" (Results 3.2, penultimate Cox paragraph (Figure 6))
- *C12* — "reliance on the SRTR dataset, which includes only low-resolution HLA typing information, may introduce biases or limitations in the findings" (Discussion, limitations paragraph)

**Limitations.** No hazard ratios, confidence intervals or p-values are printed anywhere in the retrieved full text for any HLA mismatch term. The paper reports only model-level fit and discrimination (BIC, iAUC, C index) and gain-based variable importance. A reviewer wanting a per-mismatch effect size cannot get one from this paper.; Numeric BIC, AIC, VIF and gain values are not in the text - they exist only as butterfly plots and figures (Figures 4, 7, 8) and in cited but unretrieved supplementary material. The Results text is full of parenthetical citation stubs '()' where figure/table references were stripped.; Retrospective registry study on SRTR; the authors name this as a limitation.; HLA typing in SRTR is low resolution A/B/DR only. All molecular metrics (PIRCHE-II, Snow, Eplets, amino-acid) rest on MULTIPLE IMPUTATION to protein level using the 2007 NMDP haplotype dataset with race/ethnicity-mapped reference populations, and HLA-C and -DQ were imputed entirely from A/B/DR. The authors concede imputation 'could introduce inaccuracies affecting the predictive performance of the models'. Molecular scores in this paper are therefore imputed, not measured - the low-resolution misclassification problem is baked in rather than solved.; No external validation cohort: 'Lacking an external validation data set', models were fitted on 70% and tested on the held-out 30% with 10 random seeds. Generalisation outside the US SRTR population is untested, and the NMDP haplotype reference contains no Iranian population.; Absolute discrimination is weak: histocompatibility-only models reach iAUC ~0.54-0.56, barely above chance, and the full clinical+molecular model reaches only 0.68. The incremental value of molecular metrics over antigen-level A/B/DR matching is small; in XGBoost, dropping molecular compatibility and using HLA-A, -B, -DR matching alone gave 'similar performance'.; Effects on death-censored graft survival only. No rejection, dnDSA, ABMR or patient-survival endpoint. The authors themselves suggest clinical utility 'may be stronger for predicting upstream events, such as antibody formation and graft pathology' - which they did not measure.; Mixed donor type (33.37% living) with NO living-donor-stratified analysis. Living donation was the single most important variable in XGBoost, but no living-donor-specific HLA or molecular effect estimate is reported, so this paper cannot answer whether molecular matching earns its keep within living donation.; Wide transplant era (1991-2022, median 2010) spanning multiple immunosuppression and allocation regimes; the only era-stratified analysis (KAS 2014) was underpowered and largely null.; Sensitisation / PRA / pre-existing DSA is NOT among the covariates. Neither is cold ischaemia time, delayed graft function, or KDPI. Ethnicity enters only as the binary 'black' for donor and recipient - and it does double duty, since the same reported race/ethnicity drives the haplotype imputation reference population, so ethnicity is entangled with the molecular scores themselves.; 142,000 of 542,621 records (26%) were dropped for missing data before analysis; no attrition or missing-data-mechanism analysis is described in the retrieved text.; Conflict-of-interest relevant: the first and second authors are employed by PIRCHE AG (Research and Development), the commercial developer of the PIRCHE and Snow algorithms being evaluated. No competing-interests statement was present in the retrieved text.; Snow's AIC-optimal univariable configuration (0.00/0.00) degenerates to a plain amino-acid mismatch count, i.e. the elaborate structural modelling adds nothing unless a second metric is in the model - a fragility the authors report but do not dwell on.; The graft half-life comparison in Results 3.4 prints value pairs without labelling which model each value belongs to, so the direction of the claimed advantage cannot be verified from the text alone..

### Shin DH 2025 — Long term graft survival and rejection rate of zero-human leukocyte-antigen-mismatched deceased donor kidney transplant recipients: a retrospective multicentric cohort study.

Shin DH 2025, *Kidney Research and Clinical Practice (Kidney Res Clin Pract)*, [DOI 10.23876/j.krcp.24.238](https://doi.org/10.23876/j.krcp.24.238). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown (no PMC record exists for this PMID or DOI; only the PubMed abstract was retrievable, so the article licence could not be confirmed).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients enrolled in the Korean Organ Transplantation Registry (KOTRY), multicentre, Republic of Korea, transplanted May 2014 to December 2022 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 3,350 deceased-donor KT patients entered the propensity-score matching; 552 analysed after 1:1 matching (276 zero-mismatch vs 276 non-zero-mismatch) |
| design | multicentre registry cohort, 1:1 propensity-score matched, multivariable-adjusted Cox models (the title says 'retrospective' while the abstract Methods says 'prospective observational cohort study' - see notes) |
| typing resolution | not stated (the abstract never names the loci counted, the denominator of the mismatch count, or whether typing was antigen/low-resolution or two-field) |
| outcome | death-censored graft failure; biopsy-proven rejection; death; posttransplant infection; antibody-mediated rejection |
| follow up | mean 38.4 +/- 28.8 months (approximately 3.2 years) |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract; the propensity score covariates and the multivariable adjustment set are not listed, immunosuppressant use is reported as balanced between groups after matching, so it was checked but the abstract does not say it was modelled |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper speaks directly to the review's zero-mismatch-premium question (C9): it is one of the few recent Asian registry analyses that isolates the 0-mismatch contrast by propensity-matching rather than by regression adjustment alone, and it does so under contemporary immunosuppression, which is the modern-era condition C1 asks about. Its headline result is a genuine split: death-censored graft failure was not significantly worse for non-zero mismatch (HR 1.63, 95% CI 0.72-3.69), but antibody-mediated rejection was clearly worse (HR 4.48, 95% CI 1.52-13.25, p = 0.001), so the same dataset argues that a zero-mismatch premium survives in the immunological outcome even where the graft-survival signal is too imprecise to detect. Transfer to an Iranian LIVING-donor pre-screen is limited and mostly indirect: the cohort is deceased-donor only, where cold ischaemia, donor quality and allocation-driven confounding dominate and where zero-mismatch grafts are preferentially allocated, whereas a living-donor pre-screen selects among volunteers whose donor quality is comparatively uniform and where the HLA term therefore carries relatively more weight. The typing resolution is not stated, so the paper cannot tell us whether a one-field (low-resolution) mismatch count behaves the same way - though the fact that a registry zero/non-zero split at whatever resolution KOTRY records still tracks ABMR is weakly reassuring for a low-resolution screen. Because antibody status is not reported and no sensitisation subgroup is given, the paper cannot inform how the mismatch count should be weighted when antibody status is unknown, which is exactly the Iranian pre-screen situation. Its most usable contribution to the review is therefore a cautionary one: it shows how a small propensity-matched sample produces a null graft-survival estimate whose confidence interval is entirely compatible with a large harm, and it should not be cited as evidence that matching does not matter.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: non-zero HLA mismatch vs zero HLA mismatch (deceased donor) — HR 1.63 (0.72–3.69), p=0.24; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted within the 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample; the adjustment covariates are not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- biopsy-proven rejection (any): non-zero HLA mismatch vs zero HLA mismatch (deceased donor) — HR 1.62 (0.96–2.76), p=0.07; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted within the 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- death (all-cause mortality): non-zero HLA mismatch vs zero HLA mismatch (deceased donor) — HR 2.09 (0.87–5.0), p=0.1; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted within the 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- posttransplant infection: non-zero HLA mismatch vs zero HLA mismatch (deceased donor) — HR 1.38 (1.02–1.86), p=0.03; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted within the 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR): non-zero HLA mismatch vs zero HLA mismatch (deceased donor) — HR 4.48 (1.52–13.25), p=0.001; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted within the 1:1 propensity-score-matched sample; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; non-zero (all counts >= 1 pooled into a single 'non-zero group'; the number of mismatches is never broken out) MM: 1.63 (0.72–3.69)
- Shape reported: not reported - the paper reports only a binary zero vs non-zero contrast, so no dose-response shape (linear, concave, threshold or step) can be read off it; linearity tested: not tested - with mismatch collapsed to a two-level variable there is no per-count series to fit a trend to, and the abstract reports no test for trend, no spline and no threshold analysis; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C9* — "Multivariable-adjusted hazard ratios of non-zero group vs. zero group were 1.63 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.72-3.69; p = 0.24) for death censored graft failure" (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "1.62 (95% CI, 0.96-2.76; p = 0.07) for biopsy-proven rejection, 2.09 (95% CI, 0.87-5.00; p = 0.10) for death" (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "1.38 (95% CI, 1.02-1.86; p = 0.03) for posttransplant infection and 4.48 (95% CI, 1.52-13.25; p = 0.001) for antibody mediated rejection." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "A total of 3,350 KT patients were propensity score-matched at a 1:1 ratio and compared according to zero HLA mismatching (zero group) vs. non-zero HLA mismatching (non-zero group)." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C9* — "Over a follow-up period of 38.4 ± 28.8 months, the use of immunosuppressants was similar between the two groups." (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "This study suggests that rigid adherence to HLA matching may be less critical than previously thought, particularly due to advancements in immunosuppressive therapies." (Abstract, Conclusion)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC record exists for this PMID or DOI, so the Methods, the covariate list, the tables, the event counts and any per-locus or per-count analysis could not be read. Everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; Severely underpowered for graft failure. Only 552 of 3,350 patients survive the 1:1 propensity match, and the death-censored graft failure CI (0.72-3.69) spans everything from a 28% risk reduction to a nearly fourfold increase - the null result is uninformative, not evidence of no effect.; The paper's own conclusion ('rigid adherence to HLA matching may be less critical than previously thought') is not licensed by its data: it rests on non-significant findings in a small sample while the one immunological endpoint that was significant, ABMR at HR 4.48, points the opposite way. Cite the numbers, not the conclusion.; No dose-response at all. Every count from 1 upward is pooled into 'non-zero', so the paper cannot address whether the second mismatch at a locus costs as much as the first, and cannot distinguish a zero-mismatch premium (step) from a graded effect.; No per-locus breakdown. A, B, C, DR, DQ and DP are never separated, so the paper says nothing about DR primacy, DQ immunogenicity, B-over-A ranking, or C/DP.; Typing resolution and the mismatch denominator are not stated - it is not clear which loci are counted, whether the count is out of 6, or whether typing is antigen-level or two-field.; Deceased donor only. Donor quality, cold ischaemia and allocation priority for zero-mismatch grafts confound the contrast in ways that do not exist in living donation, and none of these are reported as balanced.; Antibody status is not reported: no PRA, no sensitisation subgroup, no DSA data. Since ABMR was the standout result, the absence of antibody data is the single largest gap for interpreting it.; Short follow-up (mean 38.4 months) for a graft-survival endpoint, in a paper whose title claims 'long term graft survival'.; Design label is internally inconsistent: the title says 'retrospective multicentric cohort study' while the abstract Methods says 'prospective observational cohort study'. KOTRY is a prospective registry analysed retrospectively, which is presumably what is meant, but the paper as indexed contradicts itself.; Korean population; HLA haplotype frequencies, allocation rules and the resulting zero-mismatch case mix differ from Iran's.; Propensity matching cannot remove unmeasured confounding, and zero-mismatch recipients in a deceased-donor allocation system are selected on characteristics (waiting time, haplotype commonness, sensitisation) that are themselves prognostic..

### Stögner VA 2025 — The role of eplet matching in solid organ transplantation.

Stögner VA 2025, *Frontiers in Transplantation (Front Transplant), 4:1710058*, [DOI 10.3389/frtra.2025.1710058](https://doi.org/10.3389/frtra.2025.1710058). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (no licence statement in the retrieved PMC text; Frontiers titles are normally CC BY 4.0 but this was not verified in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 97 studies (Methods/Results) — the Abstract and one Discussion sentence say 98 — comprising 284,540 solid-organ transplant recipients (Abstract: 286,101). Kidney subset: 72 studies, 237,700 recipients. Mean recipient age 41.3 ± 15.4 y overall; 60.8% male; 48.3% adult cohorts. PubMed search 29 July 2025; all studies used HLAMatchmaker eplet matching. |
| donor type | both — of 72 kidney studies: living-donor only 11 (15.3%), deceased-donor only 12 (16.7%), mixed 38 (52.7%), unspecified 11 (15.3%). All 11 living-donor-only studies in the whole review were kidney studies. |
| n | 97 studies / 284,540 recipients overall; kidney 72 studies / 237,700 recipients |
| design | scoping review with weighted descriptive synthesis (Covidence screening; weighting of epMM means by study size). 93.8% of included studies retrospective, 81.4% cohort, 10.3% registry-based, 5.2% prospective. No pooled effect estimate, no meta-regression, no risk-of-bias tool reported. |
| typing resolution | mixed and mostly LOW/INTERMEDIATE. Across all 97 studies only ~16% used high-resolution methods exclusively (NGS 12.3%, SBT 2.1%); SSO 28.9%, SSP 6.2%, SSOP 5.2%, serology 3.1%, OP 1%, >1 method 20.6% (30% of those included NGS), unspecified 20.6%. Kidney subset (72 studies): NGS only 8 (11.1%), SBT only 0 (0%), SSO only 20 (27.8%), SSP only 4 (5.6%), SSOP only 5 (6.9%), OP only 1 (1.4%), serology only 3 (4.2%), >1 method 16 (22.2%; 6 including NGS), unspecified 15 (20.8%). |
| outcome | de novo DSA (dnDSA), AMR, TCMR, unspecified rejection, graft dysfunction, graft loss/survival, PRA, CXCL10, CD4+ staining — reported as the fraction of studies finding a significant association per locus, and as counts of reported/significant eplet-mismatch thresholds |
| follow up | mean 4.6 ± 3 years overall (range 0.1-15); kidney mean 4.6 years (range 0.1-15) |
| other factors modelled | typing resolution / HLA typing method (NGS, SBT, SSO, SSP, SSOP, OP, serology), matching algorithm and version (HLAMatchmaker, PIRCHE-II, HLA-EMMA, SNOW, TCE), eplet library version / antibody-verified vs all eplets, recipient age (adult vs paediatric), recipient sex, donor type (living / deceased / mixed), primary vs re-transplantation, immunosuppression regimen (mono/dual/triple/steroid-free), donor-recipient race concordance (one paediatric kidney study only), transplant urgency / allocation scheme, DSA assay MFI thresholds and monitoring schedule, follow-up duration |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's best single source for claim C12 because it quantifies, across 72 kidney studies and 237,700 kidney recipients, exactly how molecular (eplet) matching behaves in practice: which loci carry the signal, how widely thresholds scatter, and — critically — what typing resolution the underlying evidence actually rests on. Its kidney-specific locus table is a direct, if indirect-design, corroboration of the antigen-level locus ordering the review argues for: class II dominates class I (68.7% vs 21.3% of kidney studies reporting a significant association), DQ outranks DR (60.7% vs 42.1%), and within class I A and B are indistinguishable (13.6% each) with C lowest (10.5%). For a LIVING-donor pre-screen the paper is directly on point in one respect: every living-donor-only study in the review was a kidney study, and the authors note that eplet matching is being adopted 'especially in the context of living donor transplants' precisely because the non-urgent timeline permits high-resolution typing. It is a warning rather than a template for a LOW-RESOLUTION (one-field) Iranian pre-screen: the authors state that all these algorithms require high-resolution NGS, that only ~16% of the evidence base used it, and that imputing high-resolution alleles from intermediate-resolution input introduces second-field errors that propagate into false-positive and false-negative eplet assignments. The practical conclusion for KidneyMatch is that eplet/PIRCHE scoring must NOT be attempted from one-field typing; the antigen-level locus weighting stays the operative rule and eplet scores remain a later, NGS-gated upgrade. For an ANTIBODY-STATUS-UNKNOWN pre-screen the paper's asymmetry finding is the useful one: eplet burden has potentially strong negative predictive value (very low counts rarely produce alloimmune injury) but only modest positive predictive value — which is the same shape as a screening filter that should exclude bad pairs rather than certify good ones. Generalisability to Iran is weak on ancestry: the review found exactly one study in the whole corpus that compared eplet results by donor-recipient race, and it calls for equity assessment across ancestries, so no threshold here is validated in a Middle Eastern population.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- any adverse transplant outcome (dnDSA/AMR/TCMR/dysfunction/graft loss): share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA class I epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 21.3; adjusted for none — vote-count across studies, unadjusted [Results 3.3, Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-A epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 13.6; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-B epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 13.6; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-C epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 10.5; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA class II epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 68.7; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-DR epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 42.1; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-DQ epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 60.7; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: share of KIDNEY studies analysing HLA-DP epMM that found a significant association — percentage of studies 25.0; adjusted for none — vote-count [Table 2, Kidney row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: ALL ORGANS: class II epMM significant in 70% (63/90) of studies vs class I in 24.1% (20/83) — percentage of studies 70.0; adjusted for none — vote-count [Results 3.3 text and Table 2, Total row]
- any adverse transplant outcome: ALL ORGANS: HLA-DQ significant in 61.8% (47/76) vs HLA-DR 38.8% (31/80) — percentage of studies 61.8; adjusted for none — vote-count [Results 3.3 text and Table 2, Total row]
- de novo DSA: pooled crude incidence among KIDNEY recipients in included studies — incidence percentage 13.7; adjusted for none — crude pooled fraction [Table 3, Kidney row]
- AMR: pooled crude incidence among KIDNEY recipients — incidence percentage 11.6; adjusted for none [Table 3, Kidney row]
- TCMR: pooled crude incidence among KIDNEY recipients — incidence percentage 23.7; adjusted for none [Table 3, Kidney row]
- graft loss: pooled crude incidence among KIDNEY recipients — incidence percentage 35.8; adjusted for none [Table 3, Kidney row]
- graft dysfunction: pooled crude incidence among KIDNEY recipients — incidence percentage 0.7; adjusted for none [Table 3, Kidney row]
- methodology (typing resolution): share of KIDNEY studies using high-resolution NGS as the sole typing method — percentage of studies 11.1; adjusted for none [Table 1, HLA Typing Methods block, Kidney column; Results 3.2 text]
- eplet mismatch burden: weighted mean epMM count in KIDNEY transplantation (total / class I / class II) — weighted mean count 24.7; adjusted for weighted by study participant fraction [Results 3.2 text and Table 1, Eplet Mismatches block, Kidney column]

**Dose-response.**

- Total/All epMM (kidney): 14 thresholds reported, 11 significant; threshold range 5-73 epMM. dnDSA thresholds: >5, >12, >16, >22, >27, and the categorical <5 / >=5-<18 / >=18-<36 / >=36; graft loss/survival: low 27-60, medium 62-72, high 73-129, and >20, >=60
- Class I (kidney): 8 thresholds reported, only 3 significant; range 8-70. Values seen: >8, >9, >=10, >70, and categorical 0-16 / 17-29 / >29
- HLA-A (kidney): >=8 — 1 threshold reported, 0 significant
- HLA-B (kidney): >=6 — 1 threshold reported, 1 significant
- Class II (kidney): 5 thresholds reported, 4 significant; range 3-48. Values: >3, >14, >=13, >=48, and categorical low <=5 / high >=13
- HLA-DR (kidney): 13 thresholds reported, 9 significant; range 3-20. Values: >3, >5, >10, >12, >13, >=6, >=15, and categorical 0-10 / 11-20 / >20. For dnDSA 5 DR cutoffs were reported but only 3 reached significance (>5, >10, >13); for AMR all 3 DR thresholds were significant (>=6, >13, >=15)
- HLA-DQ (kidney): 19 thresholds reported, 17 significant — the densest and most consistently significant locus; range 2-17. Values: >3, >5, >8, >9, >12, >17, >=2, >=6, >=7, >=11, >=15, and categorical low 0 / intermediate 1-5 / high >=6. For dnDSA 7 DQ thresholds spanning >=2 to >17 were all significant; for AMR 4 DQ thresholds all significant (>3, >=7, >9, >=15)
- HLA-DP (kidney): no separate DP threshold row in Table 4/5 (DP appears only in Table 2 locus-association counts: 4/16, 25%)
- Immunogenic epMM (kidney): 1 threshold reported (categorical 0-5 / 6-8 / 9-11 / >=12), 0 significant
- PIRCHE-II (kidney): 6 thresholds reported, all 6 significant; range 9-176. Values: >41 (class I) and >30 (class II), >176 (reported identically by two independent studies), and categorical <9 / >=9-<35 / >=35-<90 / >=90
- Combination DR+DQ (kidney): 13 thresholds reported, 9 significant. Recurring schemes: low DR<7 and DQ<9 / intermediate DR>=7 or DQ 9-14 / high DQ>=15; and low DR=0 and DQ=0 / intermediate DR=1-6 and/or DQ=1-8 / high DR>=7 or DQ>=9
- Shape reported: threshold / step — not a smooth dose-response. Every included kidney study cut a continuous epMM count at a study-specific breakpoint or into 2-4 ordered risk bands; the review tabulates those breakpoints rather than a per-unit gradient.; linearity tested: not tested. The review performs no meta-regression, no spline, no test for trend and no test for linearity; it counts how many studies reported a threshold and how many of those were statistically significant. Several individual studies used monotone ordered bands (e.g. total epMM <5 / >=5-<18 / >=18-<36 / >=36; DR 0-10 / 11-20 / >20; PIRCHE-II <9 / >=9-<35 / >=35-<90 / >=90), which imply but do not test monotonicity.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- eplet mismatch burden x HLA class (I vs II): the signal is concentrated in class II; class I associations are inconsistent (kidney: class II significant in 68.7% (46/67) of studies vs class I in 21.3% (13/61); all organs 70% vs 24.1%) [Results 3.3, Table 2]
- eplet mismatch burden x locus within class II (DQ vs DR): DQ outranks DR both in how often it is significant and in how often its thresholds hold (kidney significance 60.7% (34/56) DQ vs 42.1% (24/57) DR; kidney thresholds 19 reported/17 significant for DQ vs 13/9 for DR) [Table 2 kidney row; Table 4]
- eplet mismatch x outcome type (humoral vs cellular): class II, DR and DQ epMM individually were NOT significant for TCMR; only the DR+DQ combination predicted TCMR, whereas DR and DQ each predicted AMR and dnDSA individually (kidney TCMR: 8 thresholds reported, only 4 significant; kidney dnDSA: 34 reported, 28 significant) [Results 3.6 Rejection; Table 4]
- eplet mismatch x organ: locus significance shares differ by organ; the class II signal is present in all organs but class I is more often significant in liver (60%) and heart (37.5%) than kidney (21.3%) or lung (12.5%) (class I: kidney 13/61 (21.3%), heart 3/8 (37.5%), lung 1/8 (12.5%), liver 3/5 (60%)) [Table 2]
- eplet mismatch x recipient age (paediatric vs adult): authors argue paediatric recipients may mount stronger alloimmune responses at lower molecular mismatch (naive repertoire, longer graft exposure), while adults show more variable patterns from prior antigen exposure — a mechanistic argument, not a quantitative interaction test (no numeric interaction estimate reported) [Discussion]
- eplet mismatch x donor-recipient race concordance: one paediatric KIDNEY study found higher epMM load in different-race pairs than same-race pairs, with significantly increased epMM-predictable rejection risk; the authors state this was the only such comparison in the entire corpus (no numeric estimate reproduced in the review) [Discussion (Philogene et al. cited)]
- eplet threshold x typing resolution / imputation: imputing high-resolution alleles from intermediate-resolution typing introduces second-field errors that propagate into false-positive and false-negative eplet assignments; some tools (HLA-EMMA) will not impute intermediate-resolution input at all (benchmarked against >61,000 NGS typings by Lhotte et al.; the review reproduces no error rate) [Discussion]
- eplet threshold x eplet library / algorithm version: eplet library heterogeneity and version updates change the numeric epMM assigned to the same donor-recipient pair, limiting cross-study comparability unless algorithm version and registry snapshot are reported (qualitative) [Discussion]
- eplet burden x prior sensitisation / immune responsiveness: eplet burden has potentially strong negative predictive value but only modest positive predictive value; individual results are shaped by immunosuppression exposure, HLA expression and immune reactivity (qualitative — no PPV/NPV numbers given) [Discussion]
- eplet matching x allocation urgency / donor type: urgency-based allocation (heart, lung, liver) confounds matching quality; kidney is the organ where molecular matching is most feasible because renal replacement therapy removes urgency, and living-donor networks are where eplet-aware selection has actually been piloted (all 11 living-donor-only studies in the review were kidney studies) [Discussion; Table 1 donor-type block]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "What all aformentioned HLA matching algorithms have in common is that they require high-resolution NGS to ensure accurate results. In our review, only ∼16% of studies used NGS; the remainder relied on intermediate or low-resolution methods." (Discussion)
- *C12* — "Using >61,000 NGS typings, Lhotte et al. showed that inferring high-resolution from intermediate-resolution inputs introduces non-trivial second-field errors, and that these errors translate into false-positive/false-negative eplet assignments." (Discussion)
- *C12* — "Among those articles 70% reported significant associations between HLA class II epMMs and transplant outcomes, while only 24.1% found significant relationships with HLA class I epMMs." (Results 3.3 (Eplet mismatches & adverse transplant outcomes))
- *C4* — "Analysis of specific HLA loci revealed that HLA-DQ epMMs were most frequently significantly associated with adverse transplant outcomes (61.8%), followed by HLA-DR (38.8%)" (Results 3.3 (Eplet mismatches & adverse transplant outcomes))
- *C12* — "However, these thresholds spread over a larger range, with the lowest counting >5 and the highest counting ≥36 epMMs. Seven papers identified HLA-DQ thresholds, ranging from ≥2 to >17 epMMs, as significant predictors for dnDSA formation." (Results 3.5 (DSA formation) — kidney thresholds)
- *C12* — "eplet matching functions primarily as a complementary risk stratification tool rather than a deterministic predictor with potentially strong negative predictive value—patients with very low mismatch counts rarely develop alloimmune injury—yet modest positive predictive value" (Discussion)

**Limitations.** Scoping review, not a meta-analysis: no pooled effect estimate, no confidence intervals, no meta-regression, no heterogeneity statistic, and no risk-of-bias or GRADE assessment is reported. Every 'effect size' here is a vote-count (fraction of studies reporting a significant association) or a crude pooled incidence, both of which are vulnerable to publication bias, multiple testing within studies, and unequal study sizes.; Internal numerical inconsistency: the Abstract says 98 studies and 286,101 recipients, the Methods and Results say 97 articles and 284,540 recipients, and one Discussion sentence again says 98. The kidney counts used here (72 studies, 237,700 recipients) come from Table 1, which sums to the 97/284,540 figures.; Vote-counting denominators differ per locus (e.g. kidney DQ 34/56 but DP 4/16), so loci examined by few studies have unstable percentages; DP in particular rests on 16 kidney studies.; The evidence base is overwhelmingly retrospective (93.8%) with only 5 prospective studies in the whole corpus (4 kidney, 1 liver), and mean follow-up is only 4.6 years — short for graft survival endpoints.; The reported epMM counts and thresholds are not comparable across studies: eplet libraries and HLAMatchmaker versions change the number assigned to the same donor-recipient pair, and the review does not standardise for algorithm version, antibody-verified vs all-eplet definitions, or DSA assay MFI cut-off.; Most of the underlying eplet counts were computed from intermediate/low-resolution typing with imputation to allele level; the review itself flags that this generates false-positive and false-negative eplet assignments, so many of the tabulated thresholds are built on partly misclassified inputs.; No dose-response in the sense this systematic review needs: there is no antigen-level 0/1/2 mismatch series, no zero-mismatch reference, no per-locus HR, and no test of linearity anywhere in the paper. It cannot support C2, C9 or C10 at all.; Kidney is reported separately in all tables, but the kidney sub-analyses are descriptive counts, not a kidney-restricted quantitative synthesis; the 'kidney' rows share the same methodological heterogeneity as the whole corpus.; Populations are 60.8% male and almost entirely from North American / European / East Asian cohorts. Only one study in the entire corpus compared eplet results by donor-recipient race, and no study from Iran or the wider Middle East is identified — so none of the tabulated thresholds is validated in the target population.; Living- vs deceased-donor kidney results are not analysed separately: 52.7% of kidney studies had mixed donor cohorts, so the living-donor-specific effect of eplet burden cannot be read off this paper.; Numbers for individual studies (which cohort produced which threshold) are given only as citation markers, which the PMC text extraction rendered as empty parentheses; the specific source study behind each threshold is not recoverable from the retrieved text..

### van den Broek DAJ 2025 — Repeated HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 Mismatches Without Preformed DSA Affect Graft Survival, Rejection and DSA Development: A Multicenter Analysis

van den Broek DAJ 2025, *HLA*, [DOI 10.1111/tan.70264](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.70264). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown — full text is open in PMC (PMC12087429) but the licence statement was not present in the retrieved text; treat quotes as short verbatim excerpts with attribution.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | repeat (second or later) kidney transplant recipients at LUMC, Erasmus MC and UMCG, the Netherlands, transplanted from January 2009 onward, with complete HLA-A/B/C/DRB1/DRB3-4-5/DQB1 typing for all previous donors, and with preformed donor-specific HLA antibodies NEVER detected (confirmed by Luminex within 6 months pre-transplant); ABO-incompatible cases excluded; patients whose repeated mismatch was only HLA-DP or only HLA-DRB3/4/5, or only definable at broad-antigen level, excluded |
| donor type | both |
| n | 460 (284 no RMM, 113 HLA-class I RMM only, 63 HLA-class II RMM group [class II only plus class I+II combined]); screened from 866 identified repeat recipients |
| design | retrospective multicentre cohort; exposure = presence of a repeated HLA mismatch (RMM) at the split serological antigen level, stratified into three groups (no RMM / class I only / at least class II); Kaplan-Meier with Gehan-Breslow-Wilcoxon, Fine and Gray competing-risk model for graft loss (death competing), Cox proportional hazards for rejection and DSA development; analyses truncated at 1 and 5 years; 10-events-per-covariate rule; full-case analysis (<5% missing) |
| typing resolution | mixed / low-resolution for the exposure. RMM defined at the split serological antigen level because historic donors (pre-2009) were not second-field typed and no material remained. Recipients typed by Lifecodes Luminex SSO (to 2020) then NGS (GenDx); donors by Olerup SSP; de novo DSA assigned at second-field resolution. A sensitivity 'allelic RMM sub-cohort' retained only patients where the serological RMM was >=90% likely also a second-field RMM, inferred from regional allele frequencies and known DRB1-DQA1-DQB1 linkage (imputation-like, not measured) |
| outcome | primary: all-cause graft loss at 1 and 5 years (return to dialysis, pre-emptive retransplantation, or patient death; death also handled as competing risk in Fine-Gray); secondary: biopsy-proven acute rejection (BPAR) at 1 and 5 years, and post-transplant DSA development at 1 and 5 years (dnDSA data available for LUMC and EMC only) |
| follow up | median 4.15 years (IQR 1.77-6.89); analyses truncated at 1 and 5 years |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, donor age, donor type (living vs deceased), transplant centre, PRA level, total serological HLA-A/B/DR mismatch load, death as competing risk (Fine-Gray), immunosuppressive protocol (sensitivity analysis), DSA-screening assay (Luminex screening vs single-antigen bead; sensitivity analysis) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's re-transplant / effect-modification question (C11) and the class II locus-hierarchy question (C3, C4) in the cleanest available setting: recipients re-exposed to a previously mismatched HLA antigen but with preformed DSA excluded by contemporary Luminex assays, so the hazard cannot be attributed to circulating antibody the pre-screen would have caught. It is directly relevant to a KidneyMatch-style pre-screen because 43% of the cohort (200/460) received living donors, and the authors explicitly recommend that low-PRA living-donation candidates with a repeated DRB1/DQB1 mismatch be steered toward paired exchange or a better-matched donor — i.e. exactly the decision a donor-selection tool makes. The exposure is defined at the SPLIT SEROLOGICAL ANTIGEN level, the same one-field granularity an Iranian low-resolution typing pre-screen has, and the allelic sub-cohort sensitivity analysis shows the effect is not an artefact of low-resolution misclassification, which is the single most useful transfer property for our setting. It is also directly applicable to the antibody-status-unknown case only in the negative sense: this cohort is antibody-NEGATIVE by construction, so it establishes a floor risk that exists even when antibody screening is clean, meaning a pre-screen that cannot see antibodies should still treat a repeat DRB1/DQB1 mismatch as high risk. The important caveat for our dose-response work is that this study models RMM as a binary per-class exposure and enters total HLA-A/B/DR mismatch load only as a continuous nuisance covariate, where it was NOT significant (HR 0.84 and 0.86 for 1- and 5-year graft loss) — so it says nothing about the shape of the ordinary 0/1/2 mismatch dose-response and must not be cited for C2. Finally, the cohort is Dutch/Eurotransplant with 88-94% IL2-receptor-antagonist induction and tacrolimus-based maintenance, which is a reasonable but not identical match to Iranian practice, and repeat transplants are a minority of the Iranian living-donor caseload, so the direct applicability is to the retransplant subgroup only.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft loss, 5 years: HLA-class II RMM vs no RMM — HR (Fine-Gray) 3.96 (1.86–8.45); adjusted for recipient age, donor age, donor type, HLA-mismatch load, transplant centre, PRA; death competing [Results 3.2; Table 2 (printed as p < 0.001)]
- all-cause graft loss, 1 year: HLA-class I RMM only vs no RMM — HR (Fine-Gray) 0.85 (0.3–2.45), p=0.77; adjusted for donor type, donor age, HLA-mismatch load [Table 2]
