**Dose-response.**

- note: No per-locus or per-count RMM series is reported. The exposure is a three-level categorical: no RMM (ref) / HLA-class I RMM only (A, B and/or C) / at least HLA-class II RMM (DRB1 and/or DQB1). DRB1 and DQB1 are NOT separable in this paper, and A, B and C are not separable from each other.
- class I (A/B/C) RMM: 0 MM: ref; any MM: graft loss HR 0.85 (0.30-2.45) at 1 y; 1.36 (0.68-2.72) at 5 y; BPAR HR 0.79 (0.43-1.42) at 1 y; DSA HR 1.61 (0.58-4.43) at 5 y — all non-significant
- class II (DRB1 and/or DQB1) RMM: 0 MM: ref; any MM: graft loss HR 3.75 (1.51-9.34) at 1 y and 3.96 (1.86-8.45) at 5 y; BPAR HR 1.98 (1.04-3.76) at 1 y; DSA HR 9.89 (1.92-50.99) at 1 y univariable and 2.99 (1.00-8.91) at 5 y adjusted
- total serological HLA-A/B/DR mismatch load (ordinary, non-repeated, continuous covariate): per additional mismatch MM: graft loss HR 0.84 (0.66-1.09) at 1 y and 0.86 (0.70-1.06) at 5 y; BPAR HR 1.13 (0.97-1.31) at 5 y; DSA HR 1.08 (0.81-1.44) at 5 y — all non-significant
- baseline median mismatch counts (Table 1, no RMM / class I RMM / class II RMM): HLA-A MM: 1 [0,1] / 1 [1,2] / 1 [1,1], p < 0.001; HLA-B MM: 1 [1,2] / 1 [1,2] / 1 [1,2], p < 0.001; HLA-DRB1 MM: 1 [0,1] / 1 [1,1] / 1 [1,2], p < 0.001; HLA-DQB1 MM: 1 [0,1] / 1 [0,1] / 1 [1,2], p < 0.001
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The RMM exposure is binary within each HLA class (present vs absent), so the number of repeated mismatches (1 vs 2 vs more) is never modelled and no trend, spline or threshold analysis is presented. The only quantitative mismatch variable is total serological HLA-A/B/DR mismatch load, entered as a single continuous covariate (implicitly assuming log-linearity, never categorised, never tested for departure from linearity), and it was not significantly associated with any outcome in this cohort.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-class II RMM x additional HLA-class I RMM (non-additivity across classes): Adding class I RMM on top of class II RMM did not worsen outcome; the two class II subgroups were therefore merged. 50% of class II RMM patients also carried class I RMM, and class I RMM alone had no effect, so the authors conclude class II RMM confers independent risk. (1-year graft loss HR 0.64 (95% CI 0.16-2.64), p = 0.50; 5-year HR 1.23 (95% CI 0.41-3.66), p = 0.72 for both classes vs class II only) [Results 3.2 final paragraph; Discussion paragraph beginning 'A key question arising from our findings']
- HLA class x definition of the exposure (aggregation masking): When RMM was collapsed into a single 'any RMM vs none' variable the effect disappeared; only class-stratified analysis revealed the class II signal. Directly relevant to any scoring tool that sums mismatches without distinguishing class. (no significant difference in graft survival between all RMM patients and those without RMM (Figure 2); significant only after class stratification) [Results 3.2; Discussion, paragraph comparing with Lucisano et al.]
- RMM class x pre-transplant DSA assay sensitivity (Luminex screening vs single-antigen bead): Restricting to patients whose DSA-negativity was confirmed by SAB (the more sensitive assay) strengthened rather than weakened the class II effect, arguing the hazard is not residual undetected preformed DSA. (1-year graft loss HR 8.37 (2.73-25.64), p = 0.002; 5-year HR 4.62 (1.51-14.13), p = 0.007; 1-year DSA HR 13.42 (1.50-120.30), p = 0.02) [Results 3.3 and 3.7]
- RMM class x immunosuppressive regimen: Effect persisted within the homogeneous IL2-receptor-antagonist + tacrolimus/mycophenolate/steroid subgroup (n = 243), so it is not explained by regimen imbalance. (1-year graft loss HR 6.15 (2.07-18.31), p = 0.001; 5-year HR 3.95 (1.48-10.52), p = 0.006; 1-year DSA HR 5.71 (1.05-31.20), p = 0.04) [Results 3.3 and 3.7]
- RMM class x typing resolution of the repeated mismatch (serological split vs inferred allelic): In the sub-cohort where the serological RMM was >=90% likely also a second-field (allelic) RMM, class II effects were unchanged and class I remained null — evidence that the class I null is not caused by low-resolution misclassification of the re-exposure. (1-year graft loss HR 4.14 (1.26-13.60), p = 0.019; 5-year HR 4.90 (1.74-13.79), p = 0.008; class I not significant) [Results 3.3; Discussion, second paragraph]
- RMM class x rejection phenotype (AMR vs TCMR): No significant effect of RMM class on either AMR-free or TCMR-free survival separately in the Banff-reclassified LUMC sub-cohort, though a non-significant trend toward AMR was seen with class II RMM; the authors attribute the graft-loss signal to a B-cell/memory mechanism but the analysis was underpowered. (no estimates printed for the AMR/TCMR split (referred to supplementary Chapter III)) [Results 3.5; Discussion]
- RMM class x centre / DSA-screening protocol: DSA screening was routine at LUMC and indication-driven at EMC; restricting to the prospectively screened LUMC cohort preserved the class II DSA signal. (HR 12.19 (95% CI 1.11-134.51), p = 0.04) [Results 3.7; Discussion limitations]
- RMM class x PRA (cited from other work, NOT tested here): The authors cite a US registry study reporting a class II mismatch hazard only in recipients with PRA > 0%, and contrast their own result; they did NOT themselves test an RMM x PRA interaction — PRA was only entered as an adjustment covariate. Do not attribute this stratification to this paper. (not estimated in this study) [Introduction (citing US registry); Table 2/3 (PRA as covariate only)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "A competing risk model, adjusting for demographic factors and total HLA‐mismatch load while accounting for death as a competing risk, showed that HLA‐DRB1 and/or HLA‐DQB1 RMM significantly increased the risk of graft loss within 1 year post‐transplant" (Abstract)
- *C3* — "Importantly, multivariable analysis revealed a significant risk of early biopsy‐proven rejection at 1 year for HLA‐class II RMM" (Results 3.4.1 Total Biopsy-Proven Rejections)
- *C4* — "Patients with HLA‐class II RMM had a significantly higher risk to develop DSA within both the first‐year post‐transplant" (Results 3.6 DSA Development)
- *C11* — "We detected no significant effects on any transplant outcome of HLA‐class I RMM, perhaps indicating they are less relevant in a cohort of our size." (Discussion, paragraph on whether repeated mismatches should be avoided)
- *C10* — "Although 50% of patients with HLA‐class II RMM also had HLA‐class I RMM, outcomes did not differ between those with and without additional HLA‐class I RMM, and HLA‐class I RMM alone did not significantly affect transplant outcomes." (Discussion, paragraph beginning 'A key question arising from our findings')
- *C11* — "Notably, when patients were simply categorised as having any RMM (regardless of class), no significant difference was observed" (Discussion, paragraph comparing with Lucisano et al.)

**Limitations.** Exposure is a REPEATED mismatch (re-exposure to a previously mismatched antigen), not an ordinary mismatch count; the paper therefore cannot be cited for the shape of the ordinary 0/1/2 dose-response, and in fact total HLA-A/B/DR mismatch load was NOT associated with graft loss here (HR 0.84 and 0.86, both non-significant).; HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 are pooled into a single 'class II RMM' variable, so the paper cannot separate a DR effect from a DQ effect; likewise A, B and C are pooled into 'class I RMM'. It supports C3 and C4 jointly, neither individually.; Small numbers drive very wide confidence intervals, especially for DSA (1-year class II HR 9.89, CI 1.92-50.99; SAB sensitivity HR 13.42, CI 1.50-120.30; LUMC-only HR 12.19, CI 1.11-134.51). The 5-year adjusted DSA CI touches unity (1.00-8.91, p = 0.049). These estimates are unstable and should not be pooled at face value.; Only 63 patients in the class II RMM group and 10 first-year graft losses in it; the 10-events-per-covariate rule forced different (fewer) covariates into the 1-year and 5-year models, so the 1-year graft-loss model omits recipient age, centre and PRA — the 1-year HR 3.75 is less adjusted than the 5-year HR 3.96.; Unadjusted Kaplan-Meier rejection curves were NOT significant (p = 0.21 and 0.20); the rejection finding exists only after multivariable adjustment, and the 5-year adjusted HR (1.60) is also non-significant. The rejection signal is the weakest of the three outcomes.; RMM defined at the split serological antigen level because historic donors were not second-field typed; the 'allelic' sub-cohort is an inference from regional allele frequencies and DRB1-DQA1-DQB1 linkage (>=90% certainty), not measured second-field typing.; HLA-DPB1 and HLA-DRB3/4/5 repeated mismatches could not be assessed at all (DPB1 typing missing in >90% of the cohort); patients whose only RMM was at these loci were excluded, so the paper says nothing about C8.; Preformed DSA cannot be fully excluded: the mandatory Eurotransplant screening interval leaves up to ~3 months between the last antibody assay and transplant, and cell-based crossmatches do not exclude low-strength DSA. Residual undetected class II DSA remains a plausible partial explanation, though the SAB sensitivity analysis argues against it.; Eplet / shared-epitope and PIRCHE-style molecular analyses were explicitly precluded by sample size and typing limitations, so the mechanism (identical molecule vs shared epitope) is unresolved.; Post-transplant DSA surveillance protocol differed by centre (routine at LUMC, indication-only at EMC, absent at UMCG), so DSA incidence is ascertainment-biased; biopsies were Banff-2022 re-read only at LUMC.; Retrospective, observational, three Dutch centres, Eurotransplant allocation, contemporary tacrolimus-based immunosuppression with 88-94% IL2-receptor-antagonist induction — not generalisable to different immunosuppression or allocation environments without caution.; Internal numerical inconsistency in the rendered text: the Results state 37 patients with only class II RMM plus 36 with both classes (= 73), but Table 1 and the stated cohort total give a class II group of n = 63 (284 + 113 + 63 = 460). The 63 figure is the one consistent with the reported cohort size.; Graft loss is defined all-cause (including patient death) in the Kaplan-Meier figure legend while death is simultaneously treated as a competing risk in the Fine-Gray models; the two definitions are in tension and the paper does not reconcile them.; Median follow-up 4.15 years (IQR 1.77-6.89) with analyses truncated at 5 years; nothing beyond 5 years is estimable..

### Caldwell JS 2024 — Immunologic Benefits of 0-antigen Mismatched Transplants: No Added Boost for Racial and Ethnic Minorities

Caldwell JS 2024, *Transplantation Direct*, [PMID 38881747](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38881747/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (no licence statement in the retrieved PMC text; Transplantation Direct is an open-access journal, but the specific licence was not visible in the retrieved body).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult, single-organ, deceased-donor kidney transplants in the United States (SRTR/OPTN), 1 January 2007 to 31 December 2016. 102 114 transplants: 59 254 White recipients (7628 with 0-antigen mismatch, 51 626 with >=1) and 42 860 non-White recipients (1439 with 0-antigen mismatch, 41 421 with >=1). The non-White group was 80% Black and 16% Asian-American. Living donors were deliberately excluded. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 102,114 |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort. Multivariable parametric Weibull survival regression for time-to-allograft-failure, with death as a competing event handled by Kaplan-Meier imputation; missing covariates imputed 5-fold by MICE, then each imputed set further imputed 5-fold for censoring times (25 datasets), coefficients averaged and SEs by Rubin's rule; models built sequentially (Model 1 base; +medical/transplant; +immunologic; +socioeconomic); analysis stratified by recipient race (White vs non-White) with a mismatch x race interaction term tested by Z-test; goodness of fit by Cox-Snell residuals and calibration plots. |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen level (broad antigen mismatches at HLA-A, -B and -DR as recorded by OPTN/SRTR); the resolution is not stated explicitly in the text, and HLA-C, -DQ and -DP were not assessed |
| outcome | primary: time-to-allograft failure from transplantation (death-censored graft failure) with death as a competing event; secondary: time to death. Acute rejection was explicitly NOT studied because of the poor sensitivity of OPTN rejection data. |
| follow up | median 5.6 y (16 862 graft losses, 18 994 deaths) |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, recipient sex, dialysis vintage, diabetes, hypertension, kidney donor risk index (KDRI, normalised to 2021), cold ischaemia time, year of transplant (proxy for allocation policy), calculated panel-reactive antibody (0-80%, 81-98%, 99-100%), induction immunosuppression (lymphocyte-depleting vs non-depleting), recipient ethnicity (Latino vs non-Latino), education (some college vs none), insurance (private/Medicare/VA vs underinsured) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a modern-era (2007-2016), registry-scale quantification of the zero-mismatch premium itself, which is the single sharpest feature of the ABDR dose-response the review is trying to characterise: a 0-ABDR graft carries an adjusted sHR of 0.80 for death-censored graft loss against everything else pooled together, i.e. roughly a 20% risk reduction that survives adjustment for donor quality, cold ischaemia, cPRA, induction and socioeconomic factors. It answers ANGLE A only in part, because the main exposure is dichotomous (0 vs >=1) and the only per-count information is an unadjusted linear slope, so the paper fixes the height of the 0-vs-rest step but says nothing about whether the curve between 1 and 6 mismatches is linear, stepped or threshold-shaped. Its supplemental DR-only slope (unadjusted sHR 1.16 per DR mismatch in White, 1.11 in non-White recipients) is markedly steeper than the all-ABDR slope (1.07 / 1.04), which is consistent with DR carrying more weight per antigen than A or B, though the paper never compares loci head to head. Transfer to a living-donor Iranian pre-screen is limited in one important way and useful in another: the authors excluded living donors precisely because relatives share more genetic material, so the absolute magnitudes here are for an unrelated deceased-donor pool and should not be carried across, but the typing basis is exactly the low-resolution one-field A/B/DR antigen count that an Iranian pre-screen would have, which makes the effect sizes directly interpretable in that data format. Antibody status is measured here (cPRA is a covariate, and 0-mismatch recipients were far more sensitised: 9-12% at cPRA 99-100% versus 3%), so this paper cannot tell an antibody-status-unknown screen what happens when sensitisation is unobserved; it does, however, show that the 0-mismatch benefit persists after cPRA adjustment, which is reassuring for a screen that cannot condition on it. Finally, the paper's own explanation for the weaker benefit in non-White recipients, that a 0-ABDR pair may still be mismatched at HLA-C, -DQ and -DP and at minor antigens, is a direct warning that 'zero mismatch' at one-field A/B/DR is a coarse label in genetically diverse populations, which is the Iranian situation.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1-antigen mismatch, all recipients — sHR 0.8 (0.75–0.85); adjusted for fully adjusted (Model 4: medical/transplant + immunologic + socioeconomic factors); the Results text notes the estimate was the same with and without adjustment [Abstract, Results; Results, 'Main Analysis: ABDR Mismatch, 0- Versus >=1-antigen'; Figure 2A]
- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, White recipients — sHR 0.78 (0.72–0.83); adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2A]
- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, non-White recipients — sHR 0.88 (0.79–0.99); adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2A]
- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, White recipients — sHR 0.78 (0.73–0.84); adjusted for adjusted for medical/transplant, immunologic and socioeconomic covariates [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2A]
- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, non-White recipients — sHR 0.87 (0.77–0.98); adjusted for adjusted for medical/transplant, immunologic and socioeconomic covariates [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2A]
- death-censored graft failure: 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, Black recipients only (supplemental) — sHR 0.88 (0.77–0.99); adjusted for adjusted [Results, Main Analysis (supplemental analysis limited to Black recipients)]
- death (all-cause mortality): 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, full cohort — sHR 0.91 (0.87–0.96); adjusted for unadjusted; the text states the effect was fully attenuated with adjustment [Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2B]
- death (all-cause mortality): 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, White recipients — sHR 0.9 (0.85–0.95); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2B]
- death (all-cause mortality): 0-antigen ABDR mismatch vs >=1, non-White recipients — sHR 0.99 (0.87–1.12); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2B]
- death-censored graft failure: per additional ABDR mismatch (continuous, range 0-6), White recipients — sHR 1.07 (1.05–1.08); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death-censored graft failure: per additional ABDR mismatch (continuous, range 0-6), non-White recipients — sHR 1.04 (1.02–1.06); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death (all-cause mortality): per additional ABDR mismatch (continuous, range 0-6), White recipients — sHR 1.03 (1.02–1.04); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death (all-cause mortality): per additional ABDR mismatch (continuous, range 0-6), non-White recipients — sHR 1.03 (1.01–1.05); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death-censored graft failure: per additional DR mismatch (continuous, range 0-2), White recipients — sHR 1.16 (1.13–1.2); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death-censored graft failure: per additional DR mismatch (continuous, range 0-2), non-White recipients — sHR 1.11 (1.07–1.14); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death (all-cause mortality): per additional DR mismatch (continuous, range 0-2), White recipients — sHR 1.09 (1.06–1.11); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']
- death (all-cause mortality): per additional DR mismatch (continuous, range 0-2), non-White recipients — sHR 1.08 (1.04–1.12); adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'Supplemental Analysis']

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 0.8 (0.75–0.85); >=1 (1-6 pooled) MM: 1.0
- DR: series MM: continuous 0-2, no per-count categories; White MM: unadjusted sHR 1.16 (1.13-1.20) per additional DR mismatch, graft loss; non-White MM: unadjusted sHR 1.11 (1.07-1.14) per additional DR mismatch, graft loss
- A: not reported separately
- B: not reported separately
- C: not typed or analysed; named in the Discussion only as unmeasured residual mismatch
- DQ: not typed or analysed; named in the Discussion only as unmeasured residual mismatch
- DP: not typed or analysed; named in the Discussion only as unmeasured residual mismatch
- Shape reported: step (0 vs >=1) in the main analysis; a log-linear slope was imposed, not demonstrated, in the supplemental continuous analysis. The paper reports no 0/1/2/3/4/5/6 series and therefore no empirical shape.; linearity tested: not tested. The authors cite prior work for a dose-response and then simply enter the mismatch count as a single linear term (range 0-6, and DR 0-2) in the Weibull model. No categorical per-count model, no spline, no test for departure from linearity, and no test comparing the step model with the linear model. Model fit was checked only globally (Cox-Snell residuals, calibration plots), not for the functional form of the mismatch term.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- 0-antigen ABDR mismatch x recipient race (White vs non-White), graft loss, unadjusted: the protective effect of 0-antigen mismatch was significantly stronger in White recipients (sHR 0.78 (0.72-0.83) in White vs 0.88 (0.79-0.99) in non-White; P for interaction = 0.04) [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis]
- 0-antigen ABDR mismatch x recipient race, graft loss, adjusted: the differential effect was attenuated and no longer significant after adjustment; the review's hypothesis (a larger benefit in minorities) was refuted, the point estimates trending the other way (sHR 0.78 (0.73-0.84) in White vs 0.87 (0.77-0.98) in non-White; P for interaction = 0.10) [Abstract; Results, Main Analysis]
- continuous ABDR mismatch count x recipient race, graft loss, unadjusted: steeper per-mismatch slope in White recipients (sHR 1.07 (1.05-1.08) vs 1.04 (1.02-1.06) per mismatch; P for interaction = 0.01) [Results, Supplemental Analysis]
- continuous ABDR mismatch count x recipient race, death, unadjusted: no effect modification on mortality (sHR 1.03 (1.02-1.04) vs 1.03 (1.01-1.05); P for interaction = 0.82) [Results, Supplemental Analysis]
- continuous DR mismatch count x recipient race, graft loss, unadjusted: steeper per-DR-mismatch slope in White recipients (sHR 1.16 (1.13-1.20) vs 1.11 (1.07-1.14) per DR mismatch; P for interaction = 0.01) [Results, Supplemental Analysis]
- continuous DR mismatch count x recipient race, death, unadjusted: no effect modification on mortality (sHR 1.09 (1.06-1.11) vs 1.08 (1.04-1.12); P for interaction = 0.75) [Results, Supplemental Analysis]
- 0-antigen mismatch x outcome type (graft loss vs death): the benefit is specific to graft survival; the crude mortality association disappeared entirely on adjustment (graft loss adjusted sHR 0.80 (0.75-0.85) vs death unadjusted sHR 0.91 (0.87-0.96), fully attenuated after adjustment) [Results, Main Analysis; Figure 2B; Conclusion]
- 0-antigen mismatch x sensitisation and donor quality (baseline imbalance, not a formal interaction test): 0-mismatch recipients were more highly sensitised but received better organs, so the crude comparison confounds immunology with allocation; these were entered as covariates rather than tested as modifiers (cPRA 99-100%: 9% vs 3% in White, 12% vs 3% in non-White recipients; median KDRI 0.83 (0.68-1.00) vs 0.93 (0.76-1.16) in White, 0.86 (0.71-1.07) vs 0.95 (0.77-1.17) in non-White) [Results, Baseline Characteristics; Table 1]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "Zero-antigen mismatch was associated with improved allograft survival (adjusted subdistribution hazard ratio [sHR] 0.80; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.75-0.85)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "Unadjusted analyses treating ABDR mismatch as a continuous variable demonstrated a 7% increase in the risk of graft loss for White recipients with each additional degree of mismatch compared with 4% in non-White recipients" (Results, Supplemental Analysis)
- *C3* — "Each additional DR mismatch was associated with a 16% increase in graft loss in White recipients compared with an 11% increase in non-White recipients" (Results, Supplemental Analysis)
- *C9* — "In an era of contemporary immunosuppression, 0-antigen mismatched transplants are associated with protection against graft loss but not against death." (Conclusion)
- *C11* — "non-White individuals may have a greater number of mismatches at other HLA alleles (eg, HLA-C, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DP), as well as minor antigen mismatches not routinely tested for" (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C14* — "We limited the cohort to deceased donors because living donation kidney transplants are frequently from related donors who often share more genetic similarity with the recipient than do transplants from deceased donors." (Materials and Methods, Cohort)

**Limitations.** Retrospective, observational registry analysis; the authors explicitly state they cannot rule out unmeasured confounding.; Deceased donors only, by design: living-donor transplants were excluded because related donors share more genetic material. Nothing in this paper estimates the mismatch effect within living donation, so the 0.80 sHR should not be transported to a living-donor programme without discount.; The main exposure is dichotomous (0 vs >=1). Mismatch counts 1 through 6 are pooled into one reference category whose mean is 4.2-4.6 mismatches, so the paper cannot say anything about the shape of the curve between 1 and 6, nor about the size of the first mismatch relative to the second.; The only per-count information is a single linear term in an UNADJUSTED model. The per-mismatch slopes (1.07, 1.04) and per-DR slopes (1.16, 1.11) are not adjusted for donor quality, cold ischaemia, cPRA or transplant year, and higher mismatch counts are systematically allocated worse organs, so those slopes are upper bounds contaminated by allocation.; Linearity of the dose-response was assumed, never tested; no categorical, spline or threshold model was fitted.; Antigen-level (broad, one-field) A/B/DR matching only. HLA-C, -DQ and -DP were not typed or analysed, and no molecular/eplet mismatch was computed; the authors themselves invoke unmeasured mismatch at these loci to explain their negative interaction result, which means residual immunologic mismatch is a live confounder of the 'zero mismatch' label.; Acute rejection was deliberately not an outcome because OPTN rejection data are insensitive, so the paper speaks only to graft failure, not to the rejection endpoint.; Race was collapsed to White vs non-White for statistical power; the authors note SRTR race collection is not standardised between centres and 'mixed and problematic'. The non-White group is 80% Black, 16% Asian-American, so it is not a proxy for a Middle Eastern population.; Baseline imbalance: 0-mismatch recipients were younger, had shorter dialysis vintage and much better donor organs (lower KDRI) but were far more sensitised (9-12% at cPRA 99-100% vs 3%). Adjustment is by covariate entry only; no propensity or matched design.; Sequential model estimates (Models 1-4) are shown only in a forest plot (Figure 2); the numeric values in prose are the unadjusted and the fully adjusted estimates. The supplemental tables (Table S1) and calibration plots (Figure S1) were not retrieved.; US allocation policy over 2007-2016 is handled only by adjusting for transplant year; 0-ABDR grafts were nationally prioritised throughout, so the exposure is not exchangeable with a matching decision made inside a single centre.; Antibody status is measured here (cPRA is a covariate), which is the opposite of the antibody-status-unknown setting the review is designing for; the paper cannot tell us how the estimate behaves when sensitisation is unobserved..

### Charnaya O 2024 — The Impact of HLA-DQαβ Heterodimer Mismatch on Living Donor Kidney Allograft Outcomes

Charnaya O 2024, *Transplantation (online 2024-09-05; print 2025;109(4):720-728)*, [PMID 39233325](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39233325/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, author manuscript (PMC11880352 is the NIH author manuscript). Confidence intervals are absent from the PMC manuscript body and from its abstract; the only CIs available are in the PubMed abstract of the published version, where the Methods state 'Confidence intervals are reported as per the method of Louis and Zeger' and they render as bare 'lower estimate upper' triplets (e.g. 'aHR DQ = 1.03 1.14 1.28') with no parentheses or dashes..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult (>18 y) recipients of a primary living-donor kidney transplant at 11 US centres, transplanted 2010-01-01 to 2022-03-31, follow-up to 2023-07-31; 4431 pairs with two-field typing and DQαβ pairing initially included, 3916 in the final analysis cohort; 61.9% male, median recipient age 51 (IQR 38-61), 74.5% cPRA 0%, 72.6% Caucasian, 60.4% private insurance; donors 62.7% female, median age 44 (IQR 34-54), 42.5% related to the recipient |
| donor type | living |
| n | 3,916 donor-recipient pairs |
| design | retrospective multicentre cohort; Cox proportional hazards for all-cause and death-censored graft failure (Model A DQαβ only, Model B DR only, Model C both; AIC used to pick the best-fitting model); multilevel logistic regression with individual-level random intercepts for rejection (sensitivity analysis: discrete-time Cox); subgroup analysis in recipients >60 y; supplementary analysis substituting UNOS-style DQ antigen mismatch for the heterodimer allele mismatch |
| typing resolution | two-field (NGS, or SSOP where only one common and well-documented allele was present) for DQA1/DQB1, paired into cis DQαβ heterodimers using NMDP 9-locus high-resolution haplotype frequencies (trans heterodimers not considered); HLA-DR compared at antigen (DRB1) level; HLA-A/B not modelled. DR antigen and DQαβ allele mismatch were given equal weight in the statistical models. |
| outcome | all-cause graft failure (graft failure, retransplant, or death); death-censored graft failure; rejection (SRTR-reported acute rejection episode / biopsy-proven / treated / failure due to rejection, first episode; 577 events, at least 420 treated) |
| follow up | median 5.86 y |
| other factors modelled | donor age per 10 y (splined at 50), donor sex, recipient age per 10 y (splined at 50), recipient sex, recipient race, primary diagnosis, HLA-DR antigen (DRB1) mismatch 0/1/2 (Models B and C), HLA-DQαβ heterodimer allele mismatch 0/1/2 (Models A and C) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest living-donor-only cohort with two-field class II typing that tests whether DQ mismatch carries information beyond DR, and it is the source of the 'prioritise DQ over DR' recommendation; it answers the review's questions on DQ independence from DR (C4), the first-versus-second mismatch at a locus (C9), DR-DQ non-additivity through linkage (C10) and the typing resolution at which the DQ signal survives (C12), all within living donation (C14). The population is directly comparable to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen on donor type, adult age, first transplant and predominantly unsensitised recipients (74.5% cPRA 0%), and the covariate set (donor age, recipient age, sex, race, diagnosis) is the kind of data such a pre-screen would actually hold. Transfer to a one-field, antibody-status-unknown Iranian screen is limited on two counts: the DQ effect that survived joint modelling was for two-field DQαβ heterodimer alleles, and this same cohort shows that UNOS-style DQ antigen mismatch - the only DQ quantity a low-resolution typing can supply - loses significance once DR antigen is in the model; and DR itself was scored at antigen level, so the paper cannot say what a one-field DQB1 count adds over a one-field DRB1 count. The per-count ORs for rejection (DQαβ 1.82 then 2.25; DR 1.86 then 2.17) are nevertheless directly usable as the shape of the locus-level dose-response in living donors, with the caution that the graft-failure hazards were modest (aHR 1.14-1.19) and that the authors themselves conclude DR and DQ have equal ability to predict failure, DQ adding only for rejection. The US, 72.6% Caucasian cohort with NMDP-haplotype-based cis heterodimer imputation may not reproduce Iranian DQA1-DQB1 haplotype structure, so the heterodimer construct would need local haplotype frequencies before it could be computed at all.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DQαβ heterodimer allele mismatch, Model A (DQ only); scale per mismatch not explicitly printed — aHR 1.14 (1.03–1.28); adjusted for donor age per 10 y (splined at 50), donor sex, recipient age per 10 y (splined at 50), recipient sex, race, diagnosis [PubMed abstract (Results; CI as Louis-Zeger triplet '1.03 1.14 1.28'); Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DR antigen mismatch, Model B (DR only) — aHR 1.15 (1.03–1.328); adjusted for as Model A covariates [PubMed abstract (triplet '1.03 1.15 1.328'; upper bound almost certainly a typographic error for 1.28 - 1.28 would make the interval log-symmetric, 1.328 does not); Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DQαβ allele mismatch, Model C (DQ and DR together) — aHR 1.08; adjusted for Model A covariates plus HLA-DR antigen mismatch [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2 (stated to have lost statistical significance; CI wider than Models A/B, value not printed)]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DR antigen mismatch, Model C (DQ and DR together) — aHR 1.08; adjusted for Model A covariates plus HLA-DQαβ allele mismatch [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2 (lost statistical significance)]
- all-cause graft failure: 2 DQαβ allele mismatches vs 0, DQ as categorical variable, unadjusted — HR 1.12; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2]
- all-cause graft failure (Kaplan-Meier, 0 vs 1 vs 2 DQαβ mismatches): log-rank across the three DQαβ mismatch groups — log-rank p None, p=0.1; adjusted for none [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 1 (curve described as dose-dependent but the three groups did not differ significantly)]
- death-censored graft failure: HLA-DQαβ allele mismatch, Model A (DQ only) — aHR 1.19 (1.01–1.4); adjusted for as Model A covariates [PubMed abstract (triplet '1.01 1.19 1.40'); Results, Death-Censored Graft Failure]
- death-censored graft failure: HLA-DR antigen mismatch, Model B (DR only) — aHR 1.18 (0.099–1.39); adjusted for as Model A covariates [PubMed abstract (triplet '0.099 1.18 1.39'; lower bound almost certainly a typographic error for 0.99, which is both log-symmetric and consistent with the Results text stating DR was NOT significantly associated with DCGF); Results, Death-Censored Graft Failure]
- death-censored graft failure: HLA-DQαβ allele mismatch, Model C (DQ and DR together) — aHR 1.12; adjusted for Model A covariates plus DR antigen mismatch [Results, Death-Censored Graft Failure (not statistically significant, but retained the higher point estimate than DR)]
- death-censored graft failure: HLA-DR antigen mismatch, Model C (DQ and DR together) — aHR 1.07; adjusted for Model A covariates plus DQαβ allele mismatch [Results, Death-Censored Graft Failure (not statistically significant)]
- rejection: 1 DQαβ allele mismatch vs 0 (DQ-only model) — OR 1.82; adjusted for multilevel logistic regression with individual-level random intercepts; the covariate set is not restated in the rejection paragraph [Results, Rejection para 1]
- rejection: 2 DQαβ allele mismatches vs 0 (DQ-only model) — OR 2.25; adjusted for as above [Results, Rejection para 1]
- rejection: 1 DR antigen mismatch vs 0 (DR-only model) — OR 1.86; adjusted for as above [Results, Rejection para 1 (sentence says 'the hazard of rejection' but prints OR=1.86)]
- rejection: 2 DR antigen mismatches vs 0 (DR-only model) — OR 2.17; adjusted for as above [Results, Rejection para 1]
- rejection: 2 DQαβ allele mismatches vs 0, Model C (DQ and DR together) — OR 1.68 (1.03–2.74); adjusted for covariates plus HLA-DR antigen mismatch [PubMed abstract (labelled aHR, triplet '1.03 1.68 2.74'); Results, Rejection para 1 (OR=1.68; the ONLY term in the joint model that retained statistical significance)]
- rejection: 1 DQ antigen mismatch vs 0 (UNOS-style DQ antigen, DQ-only model) — OR 1.39; adjusted for as above [Results, Rejection para 3 (supplementary antigen-vs-allele analysis)]
- rejection: 2 DQ antigen mismatches vs 0 (UNOS-style DQ antigen, DQ-only model) — OR 1.55; adjusted for as above; in Model C with DR antigen, DQ antigen LOST significance while DR antigen remained associated (no numbers printed) [Results, Rejection para 3]

**Dose-response.**

- DQαβ heterodimer allele (rejection, DQ-only model): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: OR 1.82 (CI not in retrieved text); 2 MM: OR 2.25 (CI not in retrieved text)
- DQαβ heterodimer allele (rejection, joint model with DR): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: not significant, value not printed; 2 MM: OR 1.68 (1.03-2.74)
- DR antigen / DRB1 (rejection, DR-only model): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: OR 1.86; 2 MM: OR 2.17
- DQ antigen, UNOS-style low-resolution (rejection, DQ-only model): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: OR 1.39; 2 MM: OR 1.55
- DQαβ heterodimer allele (all-cause graft failure): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: not printed; 2 MM: unadjusted HR 1.12 (categorical); the adjusted models report a single aHR 1.14 (1.03-1.28) for DQ mismatch rather than a per-count series
- DR antigen (all-cause graft failure): 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: not printed; 2 MM: not printed; single aHR 1.15 (1.03-1.328 as printed)
- Shape reported: monotone increasing ('dose-dependent', the authors' word) for rejection at DQαβ allele, DR antigen and DQ antigen. In every one of the three rejection series the SECOND mismatch adds less than the first on the OR scale (1.82 then 2.25; 1.86 then 2.17; 1.39 then 1.55), i.e. concave / diminishing increments, with the largest step from 0 to 1. The ACGF Kaplan-Meier curves were described as dose-dependent but the three groups did not differ significantly (log-rank p=0.1); the DCGF Kaplan-Meier showed no significant difference across 0/1/2.; linearity tested: not formally tested for HLA mismatch: no P for trend, no P for interaction, and no spline on mismatch count (splines were fitted only to donor and recipient age, knotted at 50 y). Mismatches were entered as 0/1/2 categories for rejection; the graft-failure models report a single term per locus plus one separate unadjusted categorical check (2 vs 0, HR 1.12). AIC was used to choose between Models A, B and C, not to test the shape of the dose-response.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- DQαβ allele mismatch x DR antigen mismatch (mutual adjustment, Model C): For ACGF and DCGF both terms lose statistical significance when entered together, with nearly unchanged point estimates and wider CIs; the authors attribute this to collinearity from DR-DQ linkage disequilibrium rather than to absence of effect. For rejection, only 2 DQαβ mismatches stays significant (OR 1.68) while 'the contribution of DR mismatch is diminished'. No formal interaction term and no P for interaction were reported - this is mutual adjustment, not a tested interaction. (ACGF Model C aHR DQ 1.08, DR 1.08; DCGF Model C aHR DQ 1.12, DR 1.07; rejection Model C 2-DQ OR 1.68 (1.03-2.74)) [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2; Death-Censored Graft Failure; Rejection para 1]
- recipient age >60 y subgroup: ACGF/DCGF: similar findings overall, with DQ keeping the higher point estimate in Model C but not reaching significance. Rejection: both DR and DQαβ were associated with rejection when alone in the model, but BOTH lost statistical significance in the combined model; the authors state this subgroup had fewer rejection events and was underpowered. (no numbers printed in the retrieved text (supplementary tables not in the PMC manuscript)) [Results, All-Cause Graft Failure para 2; Death-Censored Graft Failure; Rejection para 2]
- DQ categorisation resolution (two-field heterodimer allele vs UNOS-style DQ antigen) x adjustment for DR: This is the single most transfer-relevant result for a low-resolution screen. DQ ANTIGEN mismatch predicts rejection when alone in the model (OR 1.39 for 1 MM, 1.55 for 2 MM, dose-dependent) but loses statistical significance once DR antigen is added, while DR antigen remains associated. By contrast the two-field DQαβ ALLELE mismatch (2 mismatches) survives DR adjustment. The DQ signal beyond DR is therefore a property of high-resolution typing, not of DQ as a locus. (DQ antigen 1 MM OR 1.39, 2 MM OR 1.55 (DQ-only model); joint-model numbers not printed, only the direction stated) [Results, Rejection para 3; Discussion para 3]
- sensitisation (PRA/cPRA), induction agent, cold ischaemia, donor age, donor relatedness, ethnicity: None was tested as an effect modifier and none except age/sex/race/diagnosis was adjusted for, yet several differed systematically across DQ mismatch groups: more 0-mismatch recipients had PRA>0; more 2-mismatch recipients received lymphocyte-depleting induction while the 0-mismatch group had the highest rate of no induction; and the 0-DQαβ mismatch group contained a higher proportion of related donors with fewer A, B and DR mismatches. This last point is confounding by haplotype sharing that the models do not remove. (none reported) [Results, Study Population; Methods, Graft failure]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C4* — "Our study shows that both HLA-DR antigen and HLA- DQαβ allele mismatch have equal ability to predict failure but that HLA- DQαβ allele mismatch adds additional in prediction of rejection." (Discussion (paragraph before the limitations paragraph))
- *C9* — "Compared to 0-mismatch the odds of rejection with 1-DQ and 2-DQ mismatches was 1.82-fold (OR=1.82) and 2.25-fold (OR=2.25) higher, respectively" (Results, Rejection para 1)
- *C10* — "Given the high degree of linkage disequilibrium in inheritance of Class II alleles, the loss of statistical significance when both were included in the analysis was suspected to be due to collinearity" (Results, Death-Censored Graft Failure, final para)
- *C12* — "Our study showed that HLA-DQαβ allele and not HLA-DQ antigen mismatch inferred higher odds of rejection after controlling for DR antigen, thereby highlighting the improved precision when using the heterodimer categorization." (Discussion para 3)
- *C14* — "Finally, using a living donor cohort limits the extrapolation to deceased donor allocation but provides insight into selection between multiple living donor options and allocation of organs in paired-exchange programs." (Discussion, limitations para)
- *C4* — "we suggest that HLA-DQαβ should be prioritized over HLA-DR in donor selection" (Abstract (Conclusions))

**Limitations.** The PMC copy is an NIH author manuscript with all in-text confidence intervals and tables stripped (figure/table citations render as empty '()'); the only recoverable CIs are the four in the PubMed abstract, two of which are visibly mistyped ('1.328', '0.099'), and no per-count CI for any rejection OR is available anywhere in the retrieved text; Resolution asymmetry: DQ was compared at two-field heterodimer level while DR was compared at antigen level, and the two were given equal weight in the models. A finer-grained variable can outperform a coarser one for that reason alone, so the paper cannot support a one-field DQB1 vs one-field DRB1 comparison; The UNOS-style DQ antigen mismatch - the only DQ quantity a low-resolution screen could actually compute - lost statistical significance once DR antigen was in the model, which is the directly relevant result for a one-field Iranian pre-screen and it is negative; DQ and DR are strongly collinear through linkage disequilibrium; in the joint model both graft-failure associations became non-significant, so DQ 'independence' is demonstrated only for rejection and only for the 2-mismatch category; Rejection was ascertained from SRTR, which the authors say is not consistently captured, lacks granularity, and cannot separate cell-mediated from antibody-mediated rejection; there is no dnDSA data in SRTR, so the paper's central mechanistic premise (DQ drives dnDSA) is imported from other studies, not tested here; Intermediate follow-up only (median 5.86 y) by design, since transplants had to fall in the modern typing era; this limited outcome events and widened the CIs, and the KM curves did not separate significantly (ACGF log-rank p=0.1, DCGF not significant); Models adjusted only for donor age/sex, recipient age/sex/race and diagnosis: no adjustment for HLA-A/B mismatch, PRA/cPRA, induction or maintenance immunosuppression, or donor relatedness, several of which differed across DQ mismatch groups (0-mismatch group had more related donors and fewer A/B/DR mismatches; 2-mismatch group had more depleting induction); DQαβ heterodimers were assigned in cis using NMDP 9-locus haplotype frequencies and trans heterodimers were ignored - an imputation step whose accuracy depends on the reference population's haplotype structure and which was not validated against measured heterodimers; US cohort, 72.6% Caucasian, 74.5% cPRA 0%, 60.4% privately insured, single era (2010-2022) living donors, 11 academic centres; the authors themselves call for studies in more diverse populations; The scale of the graft-failure models (per additional mismatch vs categorical) is never stated explicitly in the text, so the aHR 1.14/1.15/1.19/1.18 estimates cannot be unambiguously interpreted as per-mismatch effects.

### Mangiola M 2024 — HLA EPLET Frequencies Are Similar in Six Population Groups and Are Expressed by the Most Common HLA Alleles

Mangiola M 2024, *HLA*, [DOI 10.1111/tan.70000](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.70000). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (PMC deposit of an NIH-funded article, 'Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural'; PMC copy has figures/tables stripped and reads as an accepted author manuscript).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | No patients followed. Two reference datasets: (a) the CIWD 3.0.0 catalogue of HLA alleles observed in more than 8 million typed individuals across six population groups (African-American, Asian-Pacific Islander, European/European descent, Middle East/North Coast of Africa, Hispanic/Latino, Native-American) crossed with IPD-IMGT/HLA 3.39.0 (11,952 alleles); (b) a real-world validation set of two-field HLA genotypes of 1196 kidney transplant candidates and 4000 potential living donors from the US National Kidney Registry |
| donor type | both |
| n | 491 HLA eplets (HLA-A/B/C/DRB/DQB1/DPB1); 11,952 IPD-IMGT/HLA alleles, of which 6485 (54.3%) observed in CIWD 3.0.0 and 3055 CIWD-classified; NKR validation cohort 1196 candidates and 4000 donors (934 unrelated donors) |
| design | cross-sectional descriptive frequency analysis of HLA eplets computed from HLA allele frequencies, with CIWDR status assignment mirroring the CIWD 3.0.0 rules, plus replication in an NKR candidate/donor genotype set; descriptive statistics only, no regression, no survival model, no hypothesis test of effect |
| typing resolution | two-field (allele-level) throughout, using CIWD 3.0.0 two-field P-group assignments and NKR two-field genotypes; the paper explicitly contrasts three resolutions (antigen-level/serologic, allele-level, eplet/molecular level) |
| outcome | none clinical. Outcomes are (i) the proportion of HLA eplets expressed by 'Common' HLA alleles in each population group, (ii) CIWDR status assignment of each eplet, (iii) equity of a hypothetical eplet-based allocation metric across ethnic groups |
| follow up | not applicable (no patients followed; no graft or rejection outcome) |
| other factors modelled | ethnicity / population group (AFA, API, EURO, MENA, HIS, NAM), HLA typing resolution (antigen-level vs allele-level vs eplet-level), donor relatedness in the living-donor cohort (related vs unrelated) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review for two narrow purposes and nothing else. First (C13), it is a current, citable statement of what a real national allocation scheme actually scores: the US deceased-donor kidney allocation system awards priority points only for antigen-level zero-ABDR, zero-DR and one-DR mismatch, HLA-B points having been removed for ethnic-disparity reasons, and a proposed revision would narrow this further to zero- and one-DR only. That is direct evidence that a working allocation scheme does not use a full 0-6 mismatch gradient but a small number of coarse antigen-level tiers concentrated on DR, which is the design question a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen faces. Second (C12), it bears on whether molecular (eplet) matching is a feasible or equitable alternative: the authors show 98.6% (484/491) of eplets are common in all six population groups, but they also show that only 2.25%-10.75% of HLA alleles are common within any population group and state that allele-level matching is likely to increase ethnic disparity. For a living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran this cuts against attempting eplet or allele-level matching at all, because every eplet result here presupposes two-field typing that such a pre-screen does not have and cannot obtain without imputation. Two features do transfer: the validation cohort is a living-donor registry (1196 candidates, 4000 donors, 934 of them unrelated), so the equity finding is demonstrated in the living-donation setting we care about; and Middle East/North Coast of Africa (MENA) is one of the six named population groups, the closest published proxy to an Iranian population in this literature, although no Iranian data are used and MENA frequencies come from volunteer bone-marrow registries rather than transplant cohorts. Nothing in the paper speaks to whether HLA mismatch predicts graft outcome, so it cannot support any dose-response, per-locus-effect or survival claim.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- proportion of HLA eplets expressed by 'Common' HLA alleles in all six population groups: all 491 HLA-A/B/C/DRB/DQB1/DPB1 eplets — percentage 98.6; adjusted for none (descriptive frequency) [Abstract; Results 3.4 'Less Common HLA eplets'; Conclusions. Reported as 484/491.]
- proportion of eplets expressed by Common alleles in all population groups: HLA-A/B/C (Class I) eplets, loci pooled — percentage 99.6; adjusted for none [Results 3.3. Reported as 'on average 222/223 (99.6%)'.]

- proportion of eplets expressed by Common alleles in all population groups, locus considered alone: HLA-A alone 64.5%; HLA-B alone 70.4%; HLA-C alone 48.4% — percentage (three values) None; adjusted for none [Results 3.2. These single-locus figures rise to 99.73% for Class I eplets when HLA-A/B/C are considered together, because eplets are shared across loci.]

- proportion of HLA alleles designated 'Common' within a population group: range across the six population groups — percentage range None (2.25–10.75); adjusted for none [Results 3.2 and Conclusions. Range 2.25% to 10.75%; the reviewer must read these as a min-max range, NOT a confidence interval.]

NKR cohort is 62% unrelated, 38% related donors (32% first-degree, 3% second-degree, 3% third-degree).]

The PMC text strips the citation number, so the source study is not identifiable from the retrieved text.]
- coverage of the IPD-IMGT/HLA database by the CIWD catalogue: 11,952 IPD-IMGT/HLA 3.39.0 alleles — percentage None; adjusted for none [Results 3.1: 6485 (54.3%) observed in CIWD 3.0.0; 3055 of these (47.1%) CIWD-classified; only 545 (17.83%) 'Common', 513 (16.79%) 'Intermediate', 57 (1.87%) DRB3/4/5 'Well-Documented', 1940 (63.51%) Rare]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The paper contains no outcome model of any kind, no mismatch-count exposure variable and no survival or rejection endpoint, so there is no dose-response to characterise. The only 'dose-like' structure is the allocation policy it describes, which is a step function on antigen-level counts: points for zero-ABDR, zero-DR and one-DR mismatch and nothing else.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- ethnicity (population group) x choice of matching metric (antigen-level vs allele-level vs eplet-level): The paper's central claim is that ethnicity modifies access under antigen-level and allele-level matching but not under eplet-level matching. Antigen-level zero-ABDR matching is stated to be ethnically disparate (HLA-B points were removed for that reason); allele-level matching is expected to worsen disparity because only 2.25%-10.75% of alleles are common in any group; eplet-level matching is argued to be neutral because 484/491 eplets are common in all six groups. (484/491 (98.6%) eplets common in all six population groups vs 2.25%-10.75% of alleles common per group. No interaction test, no p-value, no confidence interval; this is a descriptive contrast of frequency distributions, not a statistical test of effect modification.) [Introduction; Results 3.2, 3.3, 3.4; Conclusions]
- donor relatedness x eplet commonness (living-donor setting): The equity result held when candidates were compared against unrelated donors only, i.e. it is not an artefact of family relatedness inflating shared eplets. 99.6% of eplets were common in both candidates and the 934 unrelated donors, with only 59H and 163LG less common. (99.6% (candidates vs unrelated donors); all but 163LG when all 4000 donors included) [Results 3.5; Conclusions]
- population group x specific uncommon eplet: The seven non-common eplets are unevenly distributed by group rather than uniformly rare. MENA (the closest proxy to Iran in this dataset) has the highest listed frequency for eplet 103M via B*73:01 (f=0.00387); AFA is highest for 56E via A*80:01 (f=0.00712), 59H via B*27:03 (f=0.00367) and 162DLS via B*82:01 (f=0.00238); API is highest for 145HT via A*02:03 (f=0.01994), 163LG via B*15:12 (f=0.00152) and the Class II eplet 23L via DQB1*04:01 (f=0.00526). (frequencies as listed; no test of difference) [Results 3.4.1-3.4.7]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Currently, antigen-level zero-ABDR, zero-DR, and one-DR mismatches are awarded points in the US deceased-donor kidney allocation system." (Introduction, paragraph 1)
- *C13* — "Therefore, a newly proposed allocation policy would include priority points only for zero- and one-DR antigen mismatches." (Introduction, paragraph 1)
- *C13* — "In the United States, points for HLA-B antigen match were removed because of increased ethnic disparities while showing only a modest correlation with graft survival." (Introduction, paragraph 1)
- *C12* — "We determined that 98.6% (484/491) of HLA eplets are expressed by the common HLA alleles in all population groups." (Abstract)
- *C12* — "Therefore, matching organs based on allele-level HLA genotype is likely to increase the ethnical disparity, especially in the unbalanced US donor population." (Conclusions, paragraph 2)

**Limitations.** No clinical outcome of any kind. There is no graft survival, rejection, dnDSA or patient endpoint, no cohort followed, no hazard ratio, no odds ratio, no confidence interval and no p-value anywhere in the paper. It cannot support any claim that HLA or eplet mismatch predicts outcome; it only describes how frequently eplets occur.; Every result presupposes two-field (allele-level) typing. Eplet frequency and eplet mismatch load cannot be computed from one-field or serologic typing without imputation, and the paper does not evaluate imputation accuracy or low-resolution misclassification at all.; Author-acknowledged: about 68% of the volunteers in the CIWD catalogue come from the German and USA registries, which can skew the allele frequencies so that the catalogue 'may not match the World population'. The authors say an Allele Frequency Net Database analysis would probably be more accurate.; Author-acknowledged: CIWD 3.0.0 contains no HLA-DQA1 or HLA-DPA1 alleles, so eplets on those chains were excluded entirely; the DQ heterodimer is therefore only half assessed.; Author-acknowledged: results depend on total P-group two-field HLA assignments and on frozen database versions (IPD-IMGT/HLA 3.39.0 of January 2021, CIWD 3.0.0, HLAMatchmaker 3.0) that IPD-IMGT/HLA continues to update.; Author-acknowledged: the analysis uses the HLAMatchmaker eplet dataset 3.0 rather than the HLA Eplet Registry, so eplet definitions may not match other studies.; All seven of the less-common eplets are described as 'provisional', i.e. not verified with a monospecific alloserum or monoclonal antibody, and for 103M the authors say the methionine maps under the antigen-binding site so 'the true nature of this eplet is equivocal'. Their immunological reality is uncertain.; Eplet frequency is not eplet mismatch load. The authors themselves flag that individual eplet commonness does not settle whether eplet distributions within haplotypes (combinations of up to 18 alleles) are equitable; the haplotype-level question remains open despite the NKR check.; MENA is a coarse and heterogeneous grouping drawn from volunteer donor registries; there are no Iranian data, no Iranian allele frequencies, and no transplant-cohort data from the region. Transfer to Iran is by assumption only.; The NKR validation cohort is a US living-donor paired-exchange registry whose candidate and donor pools are not representative of Iranian living donors, and it is used only to check eplet commonness, not to link matching to any outcome.; The 6x/9x zero-ABDR offer disparity figure is quoted from another study, not computed here; the PMC text strips citation numbers so the source cannot be identified from the retrieved text.; The PMC deposit has figures and tables removed, leaving empty '(see "")' placeholders; several per-eplet and per-group frequencies live in supplementary files (Supinfo1-7) that were not retrieved. Only the numbers printed in the running text could be extracted..

### Mankowski MA 2024 — Balancing equity and human leukocyte antigen matching in deceased-donor kidney allocation with eplet mismatch.

Mankowski MA 2024, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ajt.2024.11.030](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2024.11.030). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown (no PMC record; Elsevier/AJT publisher copyright presumed).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 5193 individuals with high-resolution allele-level HLA genotypes from the US National Kidney Registry; donor-recipient genotype pairings were then simulated by repeated random sampling weighted to the ethnic composition of the historical US deceased-donor pool |
| donor type | deceased (the allocation being simulated is US deceased-donor allocation); the underlying genotype cohort is the National Kidney Registry, i.e. a living-donor kidney-exchange population |
| n | 5193 genotyped individuals (number of simulated pairings not stated in the abstract) |
| design | in silico allocation simulation. Repeated random sampling of donor-recipient genotype pairs; the reported quantity is the percentage/prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate, stratified by candidate ethnicity, under alternative definitions of a well-matched (low-risk) donor. No transplant outcomes, no survival analysis, no regression model. |
| typing resolution | high-resolution allele-level (two-field) HLA genotypes; the abstract states this resolution was required to assign eplets unambiguously |
| outcome | prevalence (percentage) of well-matched donors available per candidate under each match definition (0-ABDR antigen mismatch; 0-DR antigen mismatch; 0-DR eplet mismatch; 0-DQ eplet mismatch; 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch), and the ratio of that prevalence between ethnic groups, expressed as a fold-difference in racial disparity. NOT graft survival, rejection or dnDSA. |
| follow up | not applicable (simulation; no clinical follow-up) |
| other factors modelled | candidate ethnicity (Black, Asian, Latino, and by implication White as the reference), ethnic composition of the historical US deceased-donor pool (used to weight the simulated donor sampling) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers review question C13 - how allocation schemes score HLA and what happens to equity when the scoring rule changes - and it is the rare paper that quantifies the equity cost of a matching rule rather than its outcome benefit. Its direct message for any pre-screen design is that the choice of which loci and which granularity define a 'good match' is itself a policy lever with distributional consequences: 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch delivered a well-matched-donor prevalence that was 3-fold less racially disparate for Black and Asian candidates than the 0-ABDR antigen rule, while 0-DR eplet mismatch alone was more disparate than 0-DR antigen for Asian (1.33-fold) and Latino (1.28-fold) candidates. That non-monotonicity is the transferable lesson: moving from antigen to molecular matching does not uniformly improve equity, it improves or worsens it depending on the locus set, and it must be measured in the local population rather than assumed. Transfer to a living-donor, low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is nonetheless weak on three counts. First, the entire method presupposes high-resolution allele-level typing of both parties, which an Iranian one-field pre-screen does not have; eplet assignment from one-field typing would require haplotype imputation against a reference panel that does not exist for the Iranian population, so this paper's match definitions cannot be computed by our system at all. Second, the disparity ratios are properties of US haplotype frequency structure and of a deceased-donor pool with a specific ethnic composition; neither the numbers nor their sign carry to Iran, where the relevant heterogeneity is ethnic groups such as Persian, Azeri, Kurd, Lorish, Arab and Baloch, and where donation is directed rather than pool-allocated. Third, in a living-donor setting the candidate does not draw from a pool at all, so 'prevalence of well-matched donors available' - the paper's only outcome - has no analogue in a one-donor-at-a-time pre-screen. The paper is therefore best used as method and framing evidence: it justifies reporting the ethnic distribution of whatever match grade our pre-screen assigns, and it warns against adopting a DR-only or DQ-only rule without checking its distributional effect.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch vs 0-ABDR antigen mismatch, Black candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity (ratio of disparity ratios) 3.0; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulated sampling weighted to the ethnic composition of the historical US deceased-donor pool [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch vs 0-ABDR antigen mismatch, Asian candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity 3.0; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch vs 0-ABDR antigen mismatch, Latino candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity 2.0; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR eplet mismatch vs 0-DR antigen mismatch, Asian candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity 1.33; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR eplet mismatch vs 0-DR antigen mismatch, Latino candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity 1.28; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DR eplet mismatch vs 0-DR antigen mismatch, Black candidates — fold-difference in racial disparity None; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DQ eplet mismatch vs antigen-level matching, Black candidates (see notes: the abstract does not restate the antigen comparator for the DQ clause; the sentence opens 'Compared to 0-DR antigen mismatch') — fold-difference in racial disparity 1.26; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DQ eplet mismatch vs antigen-level matching, Latino candidates (comparator ambiguity as above) — fold-difference in racial disparity 1.14; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]
- prevalence of well-matched donors available to a candidate: 0-DQ eplet mismatch vs antigen-level matching, Asian candidates (comparator ambiguity as above) — fold-difference in racial disparity 1.26; adjusted for not a regression estimate; simulation [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- note: No graded mismatch-count series is reported anywhere in the retrievable text. The paper works exclusively at the zero-mismatch threshold, and what it varies is WHICH loci and WHICH granularity define that zero.
- match_definitions_compared: ['0-ABDR antigen mismatch (the historical US well-matched definition)', '0-DR antigen mismatch', '0-DR eplet mismatch', '0-DQ eplet mismatch', '0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (combined)']
- DR: 0 vs >0 only, at both antigen and eplet level; no 1-vs-2 contrast
- DQ: 0 vs >0 only, at eplet level; no 1-vs-2 contrast
- A: enters only inside the composite 0-ABDR antigen definition; not reported separately
- B: enters only inside the composite 0-ABDR antigen definition; not reported separately
- Shape reported: not reported (binary zero-mismatch threshold used throughout; no 0/1/2 series and no continuous eplet-load gradient in the retrievable text); linearity tested: not tested; no dose-response model, no trend test, no spline. The design is a prevalence simulation, not a regression.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- match definition (eplet vs antigen) x candidate ethnicity: The equity effect of switching from antigen to eplet matching is not uniform across ethnic groups; it reverses sign depending on the group. Moving to 0-DQ eplet mismatch reduced disparity for Black and Latino candidates but increased it for Asian candidates. (0-DQ eplet: 1.26-fold less disparity for Black, 1.14-fold less for Latino, 1.26-fold higher for Asian) [Abstract]
- locus set chosen (DR alone vs DQ alone vs DR/DQ combined) x candidate ethnicity: The combined 0-DR/DQ eplet definition was substantially less disparate than 0-ABDR antigen for all three minority groups, yet 0-DR eplet alone was MORE disparate than 0-DR antigen for Asian and Latino candidates. Which molecules define the low-risk match therefore drives the equity result more than the antigen-to-eplet switch itself. (0-DR/DQ eplet vs 0-ABDR antigen: 3-fold less disparate (Black, Asian), 2-fold less (Latino). 0-DR eplet vs 0-DR antigen: 1.33-fold more disparate (Asian), 1.28-fold more (Latino).) [Abstract]
- definition of a well-matched donor x candidate ethnicity (authors' own summary): The authors state the general form of the interaction explicitly as their conclusion: availability of well-matched donors by ethnicity depends on which molecules are chosen to define a low-risk match. (qualitative; no number attached to this statement) [Abstract, final sentence]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Human leukocyte antigen-level matching in US kidney allocation has been deemphasized due to its role in elevating racial disparities." (Abstract, opening sentence)
- *C12* — "To assign eplets unambiguously, we utilized a cohort of 5193 individuals with high-resolution allele-level human leukocyte antigen genotypes from the National Kidney Registry." (Abstract, methods sentence)
- *C13* — "The prevalence of well-matched donors with 0-DR/DQ eplet mismatch was 3-fold less racially disparate for Black and Asian candidates and 2-fold less for Latino candidates compared to 0-ABDR antigen mismatches." (Abstract, principal result)
- *C13* — "Compared to 0-DR antigen mismatch, 0-DR eplet mismatch was 1.33-fold more racially disparate for Asian and 1.28-fold more for Latino, with similar disparity for Black candidates" (Abstract, secondary result)
- *C13* — "0-DQ eplet mismatch reduced disparities, showing 1.26-fold less disparity for Black, 1.14-fold less for Latino, but 1.26-fold higher for Asian candidates." (Abstract, secondary result)
- *C13* — "The prevalence of well-matched donors for candidates of different ethnicities varied according to which molecules were chosen to define a low-risk match." (Abstract, conclusion)

**Limitations.** Simulation, not outcome evidence. No graft survival, rejection, dnDSA or any clinical endpoint is measured. The paper shows how many well-matched donors a candidate would find, never that those matches transplant better. It cannot support C1, C2 or any locus-ranking claim.; The paper does not validate that 0 eplet mismatch is in fact a low-risk match; the threshold is imported as an assumption from the molecular-matching literature. Its own conclusion calls it a 'low-risk match' only descriptively.; The genotype source is the National Kidney Registry, a US living-donor kidney-exchange cohort of 5193 people. This is almost certainly not representative of the US deceased-donor waiting list in ethnicity, health or socioeconomic profile, yet donor sampling was weighted to the deceased-donor pool. The mismatch between the genotype source and the pool being simulated is a structural limitation.; Requires high-resolution allele-level (two-field) typing of both donor and candidate. The authors say so explicitly - it is why they needed this particular cohort. Nothing in the paper can be executed on one-field/serologic typing without haplotype imputation, and imputation accuracy is not addressed in the retrievable text.; All results are properties of US haplotype frequency structure and US ethnic categories (Black, Asian, Latino). Neither the magnitudes nor the directions transfer to Iranian populations, for which no comparable high-resolution reference data are used here.; No antibody, DSA or PRA data enter the match definition; sensitisation is not modelled. A pre-screen that ignores antibody status is not addressed by this paper either way.; Deceased-donor pool allocation is the setting. There is no living-donor or directed-donation analysis, and the outcome metric (prevalence of well-matched donors in a pool) has no analogue in one-donor-at-a-time living-donor assessment.; ACCESS LIMITATION: abstract only. PMC holds no full text for this PMID or DOI. Sample sizes per ethnic group, the number of sampling iterations, the exact definition and denominator of the disparity ratio, all confidence intervals, all p-values, and every table and figure are unretrieved. No number beyond the nine fold-changes in the abstract could be extracted, and none of those has a CI or a p-value printed.; The abstract's DQ sentence does not restate its antigen comparator, so the 1.26 / 1.14 / 1.26 DQ figures are reported here with that ambiguity flagged rather than resolved..

### Pipeleers L 2024 — Impact of repeat human leukocyte antigen mismatches on kidney graft survival: A contemporary Collaborative Transplant Study analysis.

Pipeleers L 2024, *American Journal of Transplantation (Am J Transplant) 2025;25(7):1481-1490, epub 2024-12-22*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ajt.2024.12.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2024.12.014). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier / American Journal of Transplantation); abstract retrieved from PubMed. PMID->PMCID conversion returned no PMC record, so no open-access full text was available..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 6711 recipients of a SECOND kidney transplant, transplanted 2010-2021, each with at least 1 HLA-A, HLA-B or HLA-DR mismatch; Collaborative Transplant Study (CTS) database (multinational, predominantly European centres). Adult/paediatric split not stated in the retrieved abstract. |
| donor type | not stated in the retrieved abstract |
| n | 6711 |
| design | retrospective multinational registry cohort; time-to-event (hazard ratios reported), with a separately reported first-post-transplant-year window and a sensitisation-stratified analysis |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved abstract (exposure is defined at the HLA-A / HLA-B / HLA-DR antigen level, i.e. a repeat mismatch of a donor antigen already mismatched in the first transplant; no allele-level or two-field typing is described in the retrieved text) |
| outcome | graft loss / graft survival after the second kidney transplant. Whether the endpoint is death-censored or all-cause is NOT stated in the retrieved abstract. |
| follow up | transplants performed 2010-2021; the headline estimates are restricted to the first year after transplantation. Median follow-up is not stated in the retrieved abstract. |
| other factors modelled | sensitization status (latest complement-dependent cytotoxicity panel reactive antibodies, >0% vs 0%), time since transplantation (the reported HLA-DR effect is specific to the first post-transplant year), NOTE: the full covariate adjustment set is not visible in the retrieved abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the most contemporary large registry test of whether an HLA mismatch that the recipient has already been exposed to (a repeat mismatch, RMM) still damages a kidney graft in the Luminex era, and it answers the review's locus-hierarchy question (C3) and its effect-modification question (C11) in the same analysis. Its answer is asymmetric and therefore informative: repeating a class I (HLA-A/B) antigen carried no measurable excess risk regardless of sensitisation, whereas repeating an HLA-DR antigen raised first-year graft loss (HR 1.61, 95% CI 1.16-2.23) and roughly doubled it in recipients with any historic CDC-PRA (HR 2.21, 95% CI 1.24-3.63). That places DR above the class I loci at antigen-level resolution even in a cohort where sensitive solid-phase antibody testing was routinely available, which is the strongest form of the C3 claim, and it makes prior immunological exposure the effect modifier rather than the mismatch count itself (C11). For the Iranian living-donor, one-field (low-resolution), antibody-status-unknown pre-screen the transfer is partial but pointed: the population here is RE-transplant, so the finding applies directly only to the minority of Iranian candidates who have lost a previous graft, and for those candidates a prior-transplant HLA record is exactly the kind of low-resolution, antigen-level datum a pre-screen can hold and act on. Crucially, the risk was concentrated in recipients whose antibody status was NOT reassuringly negative, which is the default state of an Iranian pre-screen: with antibody status unknown, the safe reading of this paper is the sensitised estimate (HR ~2.2), not the pooled one, so a repeat DR antigen in a re-transplant candidate is a strong deprioritisation signal even without DSA testing. The paper does NOT support down-weighting DR generally, and it says nothing about first transplants, about mismatch counts, or about living donors specifically, so it cannot be used to calibrate the primary first-transplant ranking rule.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft loss in the first year after the second kidney transplant: HLA-DR repeat mismatch (RMM) present vs no repeat mismatch — HR 1.61 (1.16–2.23), p=.004; adjusted for not stated in the retrieved abstract [Abstract (Results sentence)]
- graft loss in the first year after the second kidney transplant: HLA-DR repeat mismatch (RMM) present vs no repeat mismatch, in SENSITIZED recipients (latest complement-dependent cytotoxicity panel reactive antibodies >0%) — HR 2.21 (1.24–3.63), p=.002; adjusted for not stated in the retrieved abstract [Abstract (Results sentence)]

**Dose-response.**

- class I (HLA-A and/or HLA-B) repeat mismatch: no increased risk of graft loss, regardless of sensitization status; NO hazard ratio, confidence interval or p value for the class I null result is printed in the retrieved abstract
- DR: repeat mismatch vs none: HR 1.61 (95% CI 1.16-2.23; P = .004) for graft loss in the first year; in sensitized recipients HR 2.21 (95% CI 1.24-3.63; P = .002)
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported in the retrieved abstract. The exposure is binary (repeat mismatch present vs absent) within a class or locus, not a 0/1/2 mismatch count, so no dose-response in the review's usual sense is estimable from this paper. The only graded structure reported is temporal (the DR effect is stated for the first post-transplant year) and by sensitisation stratum (1.61 overall vs 2.21 in sensitised).; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR repeat mismatch x sensitisation (latest CDC panel reactive antibodies >0%): the first-year graft-loss hazard of a repeat DR mismatch is larger in sensitised recipients than in the cohort overall (HR 1.61 (95% CI 1.16-2.23; P = .004) overall vs HR 2.21 (95% CI 1.24-3.63; P = .002) in sensitised recipients. NO formal test of interaction (no P for interaction) is reported in the retrieved abstract; this is a stratum-vs-overall comparison, and the two estimates' confidence intervals overlap widely.) [Abstract (Results sentence)]
- class I (HLA-A / HLA-B) repeat mismatch x sensitisation: no increased risk of graft loss for a class I repeat mismatch in either sensitisation stratum, i.e. no effect to be modified (no numeric estimate, confidence interval or p value printed in the retrieved abstract) [Abstract (Results sentence)]
- HLA-DR repeat mismatch x time since transplantation: the reported DR repeat-mismatch hazard is specified for the first year after transplantation, implying an early/time-limited effect; later-period estimates are not given in the retrieved abstract (HR 1.61 (95% CI 1.16-2.23; P = .004), first year) [Abstract (Results sentence)]
- repeat mismatch x era / availability of solid-phase antibody testing (Luminex): the authors' framing: despite routine sensitive antibody assays in the 2010-2021 era, the DR repeat-mismatch penalty persisted while the class I penalty did not (qualitative; no era-stratified estimate printed in the retrieved abstract) [Abstract (Conclusion sentence)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "For the second KT with a HLA-DR RMM, the hazard ratio for graft loss in the first year after transplantation was 1.61 (95% CI 1.16-2.23; P = .004) compared to recipients without an RMM" (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C11* — "increased to 2.21 (95% CI 1.24-3.63: P = .002) in sensitized recipients (latest complement-dependent cytotoxicity panel reactive antibodies >0%)" (Abstract, Results sentence (continuation of the HLA-DR RMM result))
- *C3* — "No increased risk for graft loss was observed for the second KT with a class I RMM, regardless of sensitization status." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C1* — "In contrast, HLA-DR RMM still had a negative impact on graft survival in this contemporary cohort, despite the widespread availability of Luminex." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)
- *C11* — "Our observations suggest that class I RMM do not need to be systematically avoided." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)
- *C11* — "a registry analysis of the Collaborative Transplant Study database including 6711 patients who received a second kidney transplant (KT) between 2010 and 2021, with at least 1 HLA-A, HLA-B, or HLA-DR mismatch" (Abstract, Methods sentence)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY.
