There is no PMC record for this PMID, so nothing beyond the PubMed abstract was retrieved; every field marked 'not stated' could not be checked against the paper.; The class I null result is asserted without any printed hazard ratio, confidence interval or p value in the abstract, so its precision is unknown; 'no increased risk' here may mean a wide interval compatible with a real but undetected effect, not a demonstrated absence.; No formal interaction test (no P for interaction) is reported for DR RMM x sensitisation; 1.61 vs 2.21 is an overall-vs-stratum comparison with widely overlapping confidence intervals, so the effect modification is suggestive, not established.; The covariate adjustment set is not visible; whether the hazard ratios are unadjusted, or adjusted for donor age, cold ischaemia, dialysis vintage, era, immunosuppression or the total mismatch load, cannot be determined from the abstract.; The endpoint is not defined as death-censored or all-cause graft loss in the abstract.; Selection by design: the cohort is restricted to second transplants that were actually performed with at least one A/B/DR mismatch, i.e. after DSA-based exclusion. Recipients whose repeat mismatch carried detectable DSA were largely never transplanted, so this cohort estimates the residual risk of repeat mismatch AFTER antibody screening removed the worst cases - the risk without screening is likely larger. This is the single most important caveat for an antibody-status-unknown Iranian pre-screen.; Sensitisation is graded by latest CDC panel reactive antibodies >0%, a coarse and relatively insensitive marker; recipients with Luminex-detectable but CDC-negative antibodies fall in the 'non-sensitised' stratum, which would bias the stratum contrast toward the null.; Repeat mismatch is defined at antigen level; typing resolution, allele-level detail, eplet/molecular mismatch and HLA-C, -DQ and -DP are absent from the retrieved text entirely, so this paper says nothing about C4 (DQ), C7 (C), C8 (DP) or C12 (molecular mismatch).; Donor type is not stated, so the living-donor relevance (C14) cannot be assessed; CTS is predominantly European and deceased-donor weighted, which does not match the Iranian living-donor setting.; Population is RE-transplant only. The findings do not transfer to first transplants, which are the bulk of any pre-screen caseload, and no mismatch-count dose-response is reported.; Registry data: HLA typing, PRA and outcome ascertainment are centre-reported and heterogeneous across countries and eras..

### Bezstarosti S 2023 — HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load may identify kidney transplant patients eligible for tacrolimus withdrawal without donor-specific antibody formation after mesenchymal stromal cell therapy.

Bezstarosti S 2023, *HLA*, [DOI 10.1111/tan.15008](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.15008). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown - no PMC record exists for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid for either the PMID or the DOI), so no open-access full text was retrievable; all content below is from the PubMed abstract.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult living-donor kidney transplant recipients enrolled in the randomised phase-II Triton study, Leiden University Medical Center, The Netherlands; sub-study analysing de novo donor-specific HLA antibody formation against HLA eplet mismatch load |
| donor type | living |
| n | 56 analysed at the 6-month protocol biopsy (29 MSC arm, 27 control arm) |
| design | sub-study of a randomised phase-II trial; Cox regression of dnDSA on HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load, plus a dichotomous eplet threshold evaluated as a diagnostic test (sensitivity/specificity) |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; eplet mismatch load (HLAMatchmaker-type analysis) is computable only from two-field / allele-level HLA typing, so two-field typing is implicit |
| outcome | de novo donor-specific HLA antibody (dnDSA) at the 6-month protocol biopsy; secondary: eGFR (CKD-EPI), proteinuria, antibody-mediated rejection, rejection episodes, drug discontinuation |
| follow up | dnDSA assessed at 6-month protocol biopsy; eGFR and proteinuria compared to 2 years post-transplant |
| other factors modelled | immunosuppression regimen / trial arm (MSC + early tacrolimus withdrawal with everolimus vs control tacrolimus), abstract states the HLA-DQ eplet association was 'independently associated' and gives an 'adjusted hazard ratio', but the covariates in the adjustment set are NOT named in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is one of the review's THRESHOLD papers for claim C12: it reports a molecular-mismatch cut-off (>=11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches) alongside the continuous per-eplet effect from the same cohort, so it lets the review contrast a linear dose-response with a dichotomised rule computed on the same data. It answers the question 'does a molecular-mismatch threshold discriminate?' with an honest negative: the threshold caught every dnDSA case but its specificity was only 44%, meaning most recipients above the cut-off never formed dnDSA - the classic sensitive-but-unspecific screening rule, which is exactly the failure mode a pre-screen must avoid if it is used to exclude donors. The population is directly on-target for the Iranian setting in one respect - LIVING-donor kidney transplantation - and the outcome (dnDSA, all anti-HLA-DQ in the MSC arm) supports C4, that DQ is the dominant locus for de novo antibody formation. Transfer to a LOW-RESOLUTION (one-field) Iranian pre-screen is nevertheless poor and the paper is best used as a cautionary citation rather than an input: eplet load cannot be computed from one-field/serologic typing at all, so this threshold is simply not calculable on the data KidneyMatch will hold, and any attempt to reach it through imputation would import exactly the misclassification problem C12 names. The effect is also conditional on an experimental immunosuppression regimen (MSC therapy with early tacrolimus withdrawal) that no Iranian programme uses, and antibody status here was measured serially rather than unknown, so the paper cannot be read as evidence about a pre-transplant, antibody-status-unknown screen. Its usable contribution to the review is therefore methodological - a documented instance where a molecular threshold was sensitive and poorly specific, and where the underlying association was reported as a smooth per-eplet hazard rather than a step.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- de novo donor-specific HLA antibody (dnDSA) at 6-month protocol biopsy: HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load, per one additional eplet mismatch (continuous) — HR (adjusted) 1.07, p=0.008; adjusted for described only as 'independently associated' with an 'adjusted hazard ratio'; the covariate set is not named in the abstract and the full text was not retrievable [Abstract (results sentence)]
- dnDSA at 6-month protocol biopsy: MSC arm (early tacrolimus withdrawal) - absolute incidence — proportion (%) 24.0; adjusted for unadjusted; raw counts 7/29 [Abstract]
- dnDSA at 6-month protocol biopsy: control arm (standard tacrolimus) - absolute incidence — proportion (%) 3.7; adjusted for unadjusted; raw counts 1/27. No between-arm p-value or CI is printed in the abstract [Abstract]
- prediction of subsequent dnDSA: >=11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches vs <11 (dichotomous threshold), evaluated in the MSC group — specificity (%) 44.0; adjusted for unadjusted diagnostic-test metric [Abstract (final results sentence)]
- prediction of subsequent dnDSA: >=11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches vs <11 (dichotomous threshold), evaluated in the MSC group — sensitivity - NOT printed as a number None; adjusted for the abstract states the threshold 'predicted subsequent dnDSA in all 11 patients in the MSC group'; a sensitivity percentage is not printed, so no number is recorded here. See notes for the ambiguity in what 'all 11 patients' counts [Abstract (final results sentence)]

**Dose-response.**

- DQ: continuous MM: adjusted HR 1.07 per HLA-DQ eplet mismatch, p = 0.008 (no CI printed); threshold MM: >=11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches: predicted subsequent dnDSA in all 11 patients in the MSC group; specificity 44%
- A: not reported
- B: not reported
- C: not reported
- DR: not reported as an eplet count; anti-HLA-DR dnDSA occurred only in combination with anti-DQ
- DP: not reported as an eplet count; anti-HLA-DP dnDSA occurred only in combination with anti-DQ
- Shape reported: linear (continuous per-eplet hazard) AND a dichotomous threshold reported side by side; the abstract does not report a comparison of the two, nor a step/plateau shape; linearity tested: not tested - the eplet load enters the Cox model as a single linear continuous term (HR per eplet mismatch); no spline, fractional polynomial, categorised-quantile series or test for non-linearity/trend is reported in the abstract, and the full text was not retrievable to check; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load x immunosuppression regimen (MSC therapy with early tacrolimus withdrawal vs control tacrolimus): dnDSA formation was concentrated in the tacrolimus-withdrawal arm (7/29, 24%) versus the control arm (1/27, 3.7%), and the eplet threshold was evaluated within the MSC group only; the whole premise of the paper is that eplet load may identify who can safely have tacrolimus withdrawn, i.e. that the eplet effect is expressed when immunosuppression is reduced (7/29 (24%) MSC vs 1/27 (3.7%) control; NO formal interaction test, p-for-interaction, or subgroup HR comparison is reported in the abstract) [Abstract]
- HLA locus x dnDSA specificity: in the MSC group every dnDSA was anti-HLA-DQ (two anti-DQ alone, five anti-DQ combined with anti-class I, HLA-DR or -DP); no isolated non-DQ dnDSA occurred in that arm (7/7 dnDSA in the MSC arm involved HLA-DQ) [Abstract]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "A threshold of ≥11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches predicted subsequent dnDSA in all 11 patients in the MSC group, but specificity was low (44%)." (Abstract, final results sentence)
- *C12* — "The HLA-DQ eplet mismatch load independently associated with dnDSA (adjusted hazard ratio = 1.07 per eplet mismatch, p = 0.008)." (Abstract, results)
- *C4* — "In the MSC group, all dnDSA were anti-HLA-DQ; two patients had anti-DQ alone and five patients combined with anti-class I, HLA-DR or -DP." (Abstract, results)
- *C11* — "At the time of protocol biopsy at 6 months, 7/29 patients (24%) in the MSC group and 1/27 patient (3.7%) in the control group had developed dnDSA." (Abstract, results)
- *C4* — "All dnDSA were complement-binding and three patients had antibody-mediated rejection in the protocol biopsy, but overall rejection episodes were not increased." (Abstract, results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only - no PMC record exists for this PMID or DOI, so no full text, no tables, no confidence interval for the 1.07 hazard ratio, and no covariate list for the 'adjusted' model could be retrieved.; Very small sample: 56 recipients (29 MSC, 27 control) with 7 events in the MSC arm; an adjusted Cox model on so few events is fragile and the reported HR is imprecise in an unquantified way (no CI printed).; The >=11 eplet threshold appears to be derived and evaluated in the same small MSC arm, with no external or internal validation reported - a textbook setting for an optimistic cut-off.; Specificity 44% means the majority of recipients above the threshold never formed dnDSA; used as an exclusion rule this cut-off would reject many donors needlessly.; The reported sensitivity wording ('all 11 patients in the MSC group') is ambiguous in the abstract and is not printed as a percentage; the count 11 does not match the 7/29 dnDSA at the 6-month biopsy, so the denominator/timeframe for the threshold analysis cannot be established from the abstract.; The outcome is dnDSA at 6 months, a surrogate - not graft failure or death-censored graft loss. eGFR and proteinuria were reported as comparable at 2 years despite the excess dnDSA, so no hard-outcome harm was demonstrated over the observed follow-up.; The effect is conditional on an experimental regimen (mesenchymal stromal cell therapy enabling early tacrolimus withdrawal, everolimus-based) that is not standard care anywhere and is not used in Iran; the eplet-load association may not carry to conventional tacrolimus maintenance.; Eplet mismatch load requires two-field (allele-level) HLA typing. It cannot be computed from one-field/serologic typing, so this threshold is not calculable in a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen without imputation, which reintroduces the misclassification problem the review is testing.; Only HLA-DQ eplet load is reported; the abstract gives no eplet counts or thresholds for HLA-A, -B, -C, -DR or -DP, so the paper says nothing about class I molecular thresholds.; Single centre, Dutch/European donor-recipient population; allele and haplotype frequencies, and therefore eplet mismatch distributions, differ from an Iranian population..

### Dasariraju S 2023 — HLA Amino Acid Mismatch-Based Risk Stratification of Kidney Allograft Failure Using a Novel Machine Learning Algorithm

Dasariraju S 2023, *Journal of Biomedical Informatics (J Biomed Inform) 142:104374*, [DOI 10.1016/j.jbi.2023.104374](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbi.2023.104374). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, author manuscript (NIH-funded, deposited in PMC as PMC10286565); no explicit Creative Commons statement appears in the retrieved PMC text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | multiethnic US cohort of deceased-donor, kidney-alone transplants (first transplants and re-transplants), SRTR, 2000-2017 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 166,574 |
| design | retrospective registry cohort. FIBERS (Feature Inclusion Bin Evolver for Risk Stratification), an evolutionary/genetic algorithm, evolves 'bins' of amino-acid mismatch positions; bin fitness is the log-rank score separating pairs with 0 vs 1+ AA-MM in the bin. Top bins then evaluated in a separate Cox proportional-hazards model adjusted for A/B/C/DRB1/DQB1 antigen mismatches plus donor and recipient covariates, with Bonferroni correction. Generalizability assessed by 3-fold (and 10-fold) cross-validation. A 20% 'risk strata minimum' hyperparameter forces each risk group to hold at least 20% of the cohort. |
| typing resolution | SRTR holds serologic/antigen-level (one-field) typing only. Two-field (high-resolution) HLA-A, B, C, DRB1 and DQB1 alleles were MULTIPLY IMPUTED (10 replicates) from the serologic specificities using NMDP haplotype-frequency imputation, then translated to amino-acid sequences with IMGT/HLA release 3.48.0. 786 AA positions initially; 308 with no mismatches excluded; 478 analysed, 192 (~40%) with a mean mismatch count above 1% across transplants. No amino-acid-level typing was actually performed. |
| outcome | graft failure (GF), analysed as a right-censored time-to-event outcome. The retrieved text does not state whether graft failure was death-censored. |
| follow up | not reported as a median. Transplants performed 2000-2017 with graft and patient status reported at discharge, six months and annually through November 2018 (so up to ~19 years of potential follow-up). |
| other factors modelled | HLA-A, B, C, DRB1 and DQB1 antigen-level mismatches (as covariates), 0-ABDR antigen-mismatch indicator, donor characteristics (the full covariate list is in a supplementary table that is not present in the retrieved text), recipient characteristics (same; specific covariates such as donor age, cold ischaemia time, KDPI, PRA and ethnicity are NOT named anywhere in the retrieved body text) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is squarely on ANGLE H: it is a machine-learning model of kidney graft survival in which HLA is coded not as a mismatch count but as an algorithm-discovered BIN of amino-acid mismatch positions, dichotomised at zero (0 vs 1+ AA-MM in the bin), and then tested for incremental predictive power on top of conventional antigen mismatches and donor/recipient covariates. It answers two review questions directly: (C12) whether molecular/amino-acid mismatch adds anything beyond antigen matching, and (C3) which single locus matters most, since when the algorithm was restricted to one locus at a time DRB1 gave the strongest stratification (HR 1.11) while B and C were explicitly weaker. Its most transferable finding for a LOW-RESOLUTION (one-field) pre-screen is methodological rather than clinical: the amino-acid mismatches were never typed, they were imputed from serologic antigen assignments, and the authors argue the winning DRB1 (13, 26) and DQB1 (30, 55) residues are near-invariant within a serologic specificity, so these molecular mismatches are in principle recoverable from one-field typing. That is exactly the manoeuvre an Iranian pre-screen would need, but it depends on a population-appropriate haplotype-frequency reference; the imputation here uses US NMDP frequencies, and no equivalent Iranian panel of that size is cited, so the transfer is unproven and the residual uncertainty at DRB1 57/71/74/86 would be worse in an unmodelled population. Transfer is further limited because the cohort is DECEASED-donor only, has no DSA or antibody data at all (so it says nothing about an antibody-status-unknown screen), and the effect is small in absolute terms (HR ~1.10), meaning HLA cannot be the dominant term against donor-quality factors in a ranking. The one number a pre-screen designer should carry over is the low-risk yield: the amino-acid bin called ~24.4% of pairs low-risk versus ~9.1% for 0-ABDR antigen matching, i.e. a molecular rule enlarges the pool of acceptable pairs at similar separation, which is the shape of gain a donor-scarce programme cares about.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft failure: 1 or more amino-acid mismatches in the best cross-locus FIBERS bin vs zero AA-MM in that bin — HR 1.1, p=<0.001 (Bonferroni adjusted); adjusted for HLA-A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1 antigen mismatches plus donor and recipient characteristics [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure: same comparison as above, as reported in the Results body text — HR 1.1, p=<0.005 (adjusted); adjusted for HLA-A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1 antigen mismatches plus donor and recipient covariates [Results 3.2. NOTE: the abstract states adj. p < 0.001 for this same HR while Results 3.2 states adj. p < 0.005; the paper is internally inconsistent on the p threshold.]
- graft failure: 1+ vs 0 AA-MM in the top cross-locus bin, repeated on each of the ten imputation replicates — HR (range across 10 imputation replicates) None, p=<0.00001 (adjusted); adjusted for covariate-adjusted (antigen mismatches + donor/recipient characteristics) [Results 3.1]
- graft failure: 1+ vs 0 AA-MM in the best DRB1-only FIBERS bin — HR 1.11, p=<0.005; adjusted for fully adjusted Cox model (A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1 antigen mismatches + donor/recipient covariates) [Abstract and Results 3.3]
- graft failure: 1+ vs 0 AA-MM in the best DRB1-only FIBERS bin (same result restated in the Discussion) — HR 1.11, p=<0.001; adjusted for fully adjusted Cox model [Discussion. NOTE: p reported as <0.001 here but <0.005 in Results 3.3 and the abstract for the same estimate.]
- graft failure: 1+ vs 0 AA-MM in single-locus bins for HLA-A, B, C and DQB1 — HR None; adjusted for fully adjusted Cox models [Results 3.3]
- graft failure: top bins trained on training folds, evaluated on held-out test folds (3-fold cross-validation) — HR (range across folds) None, p=all significant after full covariate adjustment (threshold not printed); adjusted for full covariate adjustment [Results 3.4]
- proportion of transplants classified low-risk: best cross-locus FIBERS AA-MM bin (0 AA-MM in bin) — percentage 24.4; adjusted for not applicable (descriptive) [Results 3.2]
- proportion of transplants classified low-risk: traditional 0-ABDR antigen matching (zero antigen mismatch at HLA-A, B, DRB1) — percentage 9.1; adjusted for not applicable (descriptive) [Results 3.2 and Methods 2.2]
- graft failure model fit: adding the 0-ABDR antigen-mismatch indicator to a model with donor and recipient covariates only — AIC difference 151; adjusted for donor and recipient characteristics (no antigen mismatch terms) [Results 3.2]
- graft failure model fit: adding the top FIBERS AA-MM bin to a model already containing donor factors, recipient factors and ALL antigen mismatch variables including the 0-ABDR indicator — AIC difference 25; adjusted for donor factors, recipient factors, all antigen mismatch variables [Results 3.2]
- composition of the FIBERS low-risk group by HLA-DR antigen mismatch: distribution of DR antigen mismatch counts within pairs called low-risk (0 AA-MM) by the top bin, imputation replicate 1 — percentage None; adjusted for not applicable (descriptive) [Results 3.2]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; 1 or more (pooled) MM: 1.1
- DRB1: 0 MM: ref; 1 or more (pooled) MM: HR 1.11, p<0.005 (Results 3.3) / p<0.001 (Discussion), no CI printed; note MM: strongest of the five single-locus bins; DRB1 peptide-contact positions (notably beta13, beta26, and beta11/28/30) contributed most
- DQB1: 0 MM: ref; 1 or more (pooled) MM: significant but numeric HR not in the retrieved text; note MM: positions 30 and 55 consistently binned; 55 and 89 highlighted; authors argue DQB1 AA-MM confers incremental risk even though a recent SRTR report found DQB1 ANTIGEN mismatch was not associated with graft failure after adjusting for A, B, DRB1
- A: 0 MM: ref; 1 or more (pooled) MM: statistically significant, numeric HR not in the retrieved text
- B: 0 MM: ref; 1 or more (pooled) MM: statistically significant but explicitly a 'weaker effect', numeric HR not in the retrieved text
- C: 0 MM: ref; 1 or more (pooled) MM: statistically significant but explicitly a 'weaker effect', numeric HR not in the retrieved text
- DP / DRB3-4-5 / DQA1: not analysed; named as future work
- Shape reported: step (dichotomous) by construction. FIBERS assigns pairs to low vs high risk on 0 vs 1+ mismatches in the bin, mirroring the 0-ABDR zero-mismatch premium. A separate secondary analysis evaluated incremental risk per additional AA-MM within the top single-locus bins using different risk strata and reports 'a general trend of increasing GF risk with increasing count of MMs' at the DRB1 bin positions, but the underlying per-count estimates live in a figure/table that is absent from the retrieved text.; linearity tested: not formally tested. No test for trend, no spline, no fractional polynomial, no likelihood-ratio comparison of linear vs categorical coding is reported. The authors explicitly note that alternative cut-offs, more than two risk groups, and learned per-position weights were NOT explored and are left to future work. The 'general trend of increasing risk with increasing count' at DRB1 is stated qualitatively only.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- DRB1 amino-acid mismatch x DQB1 amino-acid mismatch (linkage disequilibrium / multicollinearity): Not a formal effect-modification test. The authors report that in the FIBERS high-risk groups isolated DQB1 AA-MMs are less frequent than isolated DRB1 AA-MMs, offered as a potential explanation for DRB1's stronger apparent effect; and that positions with Pearson correlation >0.5 are interchangeable inside top bins because they carry high mutual information (e.g. DRB1 13 correlates with 10 r=0.54, 11 r=0.85, 12 r=0.53, 30 r=0.53). (Pearson r values above; no interaction p-value reported) [Results 3.1 and Discussion]
- FIBERS AA-MM bin x 0-ABDR antigen matching (overlap, not effect modification): The bin's low-risk group is heavily enriched for DR-matched pairs: 77.92% are 0-DR antigen mismatch, 20.12% are 1-DR, only 1.96% are 2-DR. The authors say this 'strongly suggest[s]' the AA-MM low-risk group correlates with 0-DR Ag-MM and that the 2-DR-mismatch pairs called low-risk warrant further analysis. (77.92% / 20.12% / 1.96%) [Results 3.2]
- HLA locus x time since transplant: Raised as a hypothesis citing other work, NOT tested in this paper: highest risk from DRB1 AA-MM said to occur within 12 months, while DQB1 AA-MM may confer long-term risk through antibody-mediated chronic rejection. [Discussion (cited from other studies, not a result of this paper)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "relative to zero MM at the AA positions in the bin, one or more AA-MMs conferred a significant incremental GF risk (HR = 1.10, adj. p < 0.005), independent of the well-established association of antigen MMs" (Results 3.2)
- *C3* — "The bin for DRB1 exhibited the strongest risk stratification; relative to zero AA-MM, one or more MMs in the bin yielded HR = 1.11, p < 0.005 in a fully adjusted Cox model." (Results 3.3 (also Abstract))
- *C12* — "only ~9.1% of transplants in this population had zero antigen MM at the HLA-A, B, and DRB1 loci, in contrast with the ~24.4% that had 0 MM at the AA positions in the FIBERS bin" (Results 3.2)
- *C2* — "We found a general trend of increasing GF risk with increasing count of MMs at AA positions included in FIBERS’s top DRB1 bin" (Results 3.3)
- *C3* — "Covariate-adjusted Cox models showed bins for each locus were statistically significant, though bins for the B and C loci had weaker effects." (Results 3.3)
- *C12* — "Imputation of AA-MMs from HLA antigen level typing has some limitations, however many AA residues identified by FIBERS are invariant within a given HLA-DRB1 and DQB1 serologic specificity." (Discussion)

**Limitations.** DECEASED-donor kidney-alone transplants only. No living-donor cohort, so the living-donor selection question of this review is not addressed directly and the confounding structure (cold ischaemia, donor quality) is not that of living donation.; Amino-acid mismatches were never typed. They were multiply imputed (10 replicates) from serologic antigen typing using NMDP US haplotype frequencies and IMGT/HLA 3.48.0 alignments. Residual uncertainty remains at DRB1 positions 57, 71, 74 and 86 and at some DQB1 positions; the authors concede intermediate/high-resolution typing might reveal further relevant positions.; No confidence interval is printed anywhere in the retrieved body text - only point HRs and p-value thresholds. The per-locus HR table and the full covariate list are in tables/supplements not present in the retrieved PMC text, so donor age, cold ischaemia, KDPI, PRA and ethnicity cannot be compared against HLA in effect size, which is what ANGLE H asks for.; The paper is internally inconsistent on p-values: the cross-locus bin is adj. p<0.001 in the abstract but adj. p<0.005 in Results 3.2; the DRB1 bin is p<0.005 in Results 3.3 and the abstract but p<0.001 in the Discussion.; Effect sizes are small (HR ~1.06-1.11) and the main-analysis bins were discovered and evaluated on the same data; only the cross-validation analysis holds out test folds.; Risk stratification is dichotomous (0 vs 1+ AA-MM in the bin) by design, so the paper gives no per-count dose-response estimates and tests no non-linearity; the 20% 'risk strata minimum' hyperparameter mechanically constrains the size of the low-risk group and therefore the 24.4% figure.; DRB3/4/5, DQA1, DPA1 and DPB1 were not analysed, and amino-acid sites outside the antigen recognition domain were not interrogated.; First transplants and re-transplants were pooled and not compared, despite different expected sensitisation.; No donor-specific antibody, PRA or rejection data at all; the endpoint is graft failure only, and the retrieved text does not state whether it is death-censored.; US multiethnic population with US haplotype-frequency references. Imputation accuracy for an Iranian population is not established anywhere in this paper, which is the central barrier to reusing its DRB1 13/26 and DQB1 30/55 result on one-field Iranian typing..

### Hafeez MS 2023 — HLA mismatch is important for 20-year graft survival in kidney transplant patients.

Hafeez MS 2023, *Transplant Immunology*, [DOI 10.1016/j.trim.2023.101861](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.trim.2023.101861). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier, Transplant Immunology 2023;80:101861). convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 37302557, so no PMC deposit exists and no full text could be retrieved; everything below comes from the PubMed abstract record, cached at fulltext/37302557_abstract.txt..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | index (first) kidney transplant recipients in the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) registry, United States, transplanted 1990-1999, restricted to those with one-year graft survival |
| donor type | both |
| n | 76,530 (23,914 living donor; 52,616 deceased donor) |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort with landmark analysis conditional on one-year graft survival, multivariable ('multivariate') modelling; the model family (Cox vs logistic) is not named in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated. UNOS 1990-1999 mismatch counts are HLA-A/B/DR antigen-level (serologic, one-field) in that era, but the abstract does not say so, does not name the loci counted, and does not state the mismatch range (0-6 assumed but not printed). |
| outcome | graft survival beyond 10 years (stated primary outcome); the title claims 20-year graft survival. Whether failure is death-censored or all-cause is not stated in the abstract. |
| follow up | transplants performed 1990-1999 with landmarks 'at established time points' beyond 10 years and a 20-year horizon per the title; no median follow-up is reported in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract - the abstract says 'On multivariate analysis' but never names a single covariate, so the adjustment set is unknown, donor type is handled by stratification rather than adjustment: living-donor and deceased-donor allografts are reported separately, one-year graft survival is an entry condition, not a modelled covariate (landmark design) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review only for C2 - the shape and persistence of the total-mismatch-count dose-response - and it is the single longest-horizon look at that question, asking whether mismatch still separates grafts once the early attrition is past. Its landmark design is the right design for that question: by conditioning on one-year graft survival it removes early technical and acute-rejection failures and asks whether the mismatch signal is a front-loaded early-rejection effect or a durable one, and the answer it reports is durable, out beyond ten and toward twenty years. It is directly relevant to a living-donor pre-screen because 23,914 of the 76,530 transplants are living-donor and the abstract states the association held for living as well as deceased donor allografts - most registry mismatch papers are deceased-donor-only, so a living-donor stratum this large is worth having. The transfer to a low-resolution, one-field Iranian pre-screen is unusually good on the exposure side: 1990-1999 UNOS typing is serologic antigen-level A/B/DR, which is the same coarse currency an Iranian pre-screen would use, so this is evidence generated at the resolution we would actually deploy rather than evidence borrowed down from two-field or eplet work. Antibody status is the honest gap: the era predates routine solid-phase DSA testing, so the cohort is closer to an antibody-status-unknown screen than a modern DSA-informed one, which helps external validity but means the estimate is a total effect of mismatch that silently contains sensitisation. The fatal practical limitation for this review is that the abstract contains no numbers at all for the exposure - no hazard ratio, no confidence interval, no per-count series - so the paper can support the DIRECTION and the PERSISTENCE of C2 but cannot contribute a single quantitative point to the dose-response shape without the full text.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: monotone worsening with increasing mismatch count, asserted qualitatively only ('more HLA mismatches were associated with worse graft survival', 'a greater number of HLA mismatches was associated with progressively worse long-term graft survival'). 'Progressively' is the authors' word and is the only shape language in the retrieved text; no functional form (linear, threshold, step, zero-mismatch premium) is named and no numeric series is printed in the abstract.; linearity tested: not reported in the abstract. No test for trend, no spline, no comparison of a categorical against a continuous mismatch term, and no P for trend appears in the retrieved text.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x donor type (living vs deceased): the association of more mismatches with worse graft survival beyond 10 years was present in both living-donor and deceased-donor allografts; the abstract reports this as a shared direction across the two strata and does not claim a difference between them (no estimate printed; no formal interaction term or P for interaction is reported in the abstract - this is stratified reporting, not a tested effect modification) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- HLA mismatch x time since transplant (early vs late): the study's central claim is time-related effect modification in the weak sense that the mismatch effect does not disappear after the first year: conditional on one-year graft survival, mismatch 'continued to remain an essential factor in the long term'. Landmarking 'at established time points' is the method used, but which landmarks and what happened at each is not stated in the abstract. (no estimate printed; no landmark-by-landmark numbers in the retrieved text) [Abstract, Methods and Results sentences]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "On multivariate analysis, more HLA mismatches were associated with worse graft survival beyond 10 years for both living and deceased donor allografts." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C2* — "A greater number of HLA mismatches was associated with progressively worse long-term graft survival for patients." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)
- *C2* — "The primary outcome of the analysis was graft survival beyond 10 years. We explored the long-lasting impact of HLA mismatches by landmarking the analysis at established time points." (Abstract, Methods sentences)
- *C14* — "We identified 76,530 patients receiving renal transplants in the time frame, 23,914 from living donors and 52,616 from deceased donors." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C13* — "Human leukocyte antigens (HLA) matching is gradually being omitted from clinical practice in evaluation for renal allograft transplant." (Abstract, Background sentence)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY, and the abstract is entirely qualitative for the exposure of interest: not one hazard ratio, odds ratio, survival percentage, confidence interval or p-value for HLA mismatch appears in the retrieved text. The only numbers in the whole record are the three cohort counts (76,530 / 23,914 / 52,616). This paper therefore cannot contribute an effect size or a dose-response point to the review as retrieved; the full text (Elsevier, no PMC deposit) would have to be obtained separately.; The mismatch exposure is never defined in the abstract: which loci are counted (presumably A, B, DR), what the range is (presumably 0-6), whether counts were analysed as a continuous term or as categories, and whether 1 and 2 mismatches at a locus were pooled are all unknown. 'pooled_1_and_2' is therefore null, not false.; Era mismatch with the review's C1 question. Transplants are 1990-1999 - the cyclosporine/azathioprine era, largely before tacrolimus, mycophenolate and modern induction became standard. The paper is strong evidence that mismatch mattered under THAT immunosuppression over 20 years; it is weak evidence about mismatch under modern immunosuppression, and it should not be cited for C1.; Era mismatch on antibody testing. The cohort predates routine single-antigen-bead DSA screening, so the reported mismatch effect is a total effect that includes whatever sensitisation and undetected DSA travelled with higher mismatch counts. This is not separable in this paper.; The landmark design conditions on one-year graft survival, which is a selection: the ~76,530 analysed are survivors of the first year, so early mismatch-driven failures are removed by construction. This is appropriate for the 'does it persist' question but means the estimates are conditional and are NOT the total effect of mismatch from transplant; they will understate mismatch's overall burden.; The adjustment set is not stated. 'On multivariate analysis' with no named covariates means we cannot tell whether donor age, cold ischaemia, race/ethnicity, PRA, retransplant status or centre were controlled, so residual confounding cannot be assessed. In particular, in UNOS data of this era better-matched deceased-donor kidneys were preferentially shared and often had longer cold ischaemia, a confounder pushing in the opposite direction that we cannot confirm was handled.; No per-locus results. The abstract gives no DR-, B-, A-, DQ- or C-specific estimates, so the paper says nothing about C3, C5, C6, C7 or C8, and nothing about which locus drives the total-count effect.; The title claims '20-year graft survival' while the stated primary outcome is 'graft survival beyond 10 years'; the 20-year figures are not in the retrieved text, so the title's claim cannot be verified from the abstract.; Failure definition (death-censored vs all-cause graft failure) is not stated. Over a 20-year horizon with a cohort ageing from 1990-1999, death with a functioning graft is a large competing risk, and whether it was censored materially changes the interpretation.; US registry population; Iranian living-donor demography, HLA haplotype frequencies and consanguinity patterns differ, so the mismatch distribution and any haplotype-sharing effects will not transfer unchanged..

### Johnson AC 2023 — Belatacept with time-limited tacrolimus coimmunosuppression modifies the 3-year risk of eplet mismatch in kidney transplantation

Johnson AC 2023, *Am J Transplant 2024;24(2):260-270 (epub 2023-09-29)*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ajt.2023.09.011](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajt.2023.09.011). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - PMC author manuscript (PMC10842047); no license statement present in the retrieved text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult kidney-alone transplant recipients at a single US centre (Emory University), 05/2016-12/2019. Repeat transplants, EBV-seronegative, HIV-positive, HLA-identical pairs and patients with pre-existing DSA were excluded. Ethnically diverse: 55% (Bela/Tac) and 57% (tacrolimus) African-American; mostly male (53% / 59%). Tacrolimus controls were restricted to the 04/2017-11/2018 world-wide belatacept shortage window to remove physician selection. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 588 analysed (294 Bela/Tac, 294 tacrolimus), 1:1 propensity-matched from 594 eligible of 949 screened; deceased donor 59% Bela/Tac and 66% tacrolimus |
| design | Retrospective single-centre cohort exploiting the 2017-2018 belatacept shortage as a natural experiment; 1:1 propensity-score matching (MatchIt) on sex, race, donor type and eplet risk level to standardized difference <0.15; Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, and Cox proportional hazards STRATIFIED by eplet risk level (a non-stratified model with eplet risk as a covariate is said to give similar HRs) |
| typing resolution | Low and intermediate (primarily) resolution HLA typing, IMPUTED to 9-locus high resolution using NMDP haplotype frequency data plus recipient ethnicity; a single high-resolution haplotype pair drawn per person by random weighted choice from the imputed distribution. Eplets computed with HLAMatchmaker version 2 tables via hlaR. Class II only (DR, DQ) for the risk score. |
| outcome | DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA (novel DSA with MFI >=2000; protocol testing at months 1, 6, 12 and at for-cause biopsy), biopsy-proven acute rejection (Banff >= grade 1A, for-cause biopsies only), DR/DQ-associated AMR (Banff, restricted to patients with DR/DQ DSA), and the combined outcome death or graft loss (non-death-censored). Secondary: eGFR (CKD-EPI) at 36 months. |
| follow up | 3 years post-transplant; median follow-up 36 months in the Bela/Tac cohort and 45 months in the tacrolimus cohort |
| other factors modelled | immunosuppression regimen: belatacept + time-limited tacrolimus (Bela/Tac) vs tacrolimus - the exposure of interest, recipient sex (propensity-matching variable), recipient race/ethnicity (propensity-matching variable; also an input to HLA imputation), donor type living vs deceased (propensity-matching variable), single-molecule DR/DQ eplet risk level (propensity-matching variable AND the Cox stratification variable), recipient age - NOT matched; differed significantly (mean 53 Bela/Tac vs 50 tacrolimus) and was not adjusted for |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review for discovery angle D (effect modification of the HLA mismatch effect) and it is the cleanest available demonstration that the SIZE of a molecular HLA mismatch effect depends on the maintenance immunosuppression regimen: the same single-molecule DR/DQ eplet score stratifies immune events under both regimens, but belatacept + time-limited tacrolimus roughly halves-to-quarters the event rates at every stratum (stratified Cox HR 0.4 DSA, 0.2 AMR, 0.45 rejection), so any absolute risk attached to a mismatch level is regimen-conditional and cannot be transported between eras or centres without knowing the drugs. It answers C11 (immunosuppression as a modifier) directly and C12 (molecular-mismatch thresholds, and what low-resolution typing can and cannot support) indirectly but importantly. For the Iranian living-donor pre-screen its transfer is mixed and mostly cautionary. The methodological half transfers well and is the most useful part: the authors did exactly what a low-resolution registry must do - take low/intermediate-resolution typing plus recipient ethnicity, impute high-resolution haplotypes against population haplotype frequencies, and compute eplets - and they explicitly warn that this is defensible for population-level discovery but that individual allocation or treatment decisions need real high-resolution typing, which is a direct argument against putting an imputed eplet score in front of an individual Iranian donor-recipient pair (and Iranian haplotype frequency reference data of NMDP quality does not exist). The clinical half transfers poorly: 59-66% of these transplants were deceased-donor, no living-donor subgroup is reported, the modifier is belatacept - which is not the standard maintenance regimen in Iran - and patients with pre-existing DSA were excluded, so the paper says nothing about the antibody-status-unknown recipient the pre-screen must handle. The practical lesson for the tool is negative and useful: an eplet or molecular score is out of reach at one-field typing, the antigen-level count remains the only defensible input, and any risk label the pre-screen shows must be presented as regimen- and population-conditional rather than as an absolute probability.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: single-molecule DR/DQ eplet LOW risk (DR<7 and DQ<9), tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 100, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier within the propensity-matched tacrolimus cohort; p is the 3-category log-rank across low/intermediate/high [Results 3.2.1 Stratification of Tacrolimus Cohort]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk (DR>=7 or DQ 9-14), tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 93, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: eplet HIGH risk (DQ>=15), tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 89, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet LOW risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 100, p=0.1; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories (not significant, authors call it a trend) [Results 3.2.1]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 94, p=0.1; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet HIGH risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 93, p=0.1; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet LOW risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 80, p=0.08; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories (trend only) [Results 3.2.1]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 73, p=0.08; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet HIGH risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 66, p=0.08; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.1]
- death or graft loss (non-death-censored patient and graft survival): eplet LOW risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 89; adjusted for unadjusted KM; no p reported - authors state stratification of this outcome 'was not seen' and the ordering is NON-monotone [Results 3.2.1]
- death or graft loss: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 94; adjusted for unadjusted KM; no p reported; intermediate risk had the BEST survival - out of order [Results 3.2.1]
- death or graft loss: eplet HIGH risk, tacrolimus cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 90; adjusted for unadjusted KM; no p reported [Results 3.2.1]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: eplet LOW risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 100, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted KM within the propensity-matched Bela/Tac cohort; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2 Stratification of Bela/Tac Patients]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 99, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: eplet HIGH risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year DSA-free survival (%) 93, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet LOW risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 100, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories (not significant) [Results 3.2.2]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 100, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: eplet HIGH risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year AMR-free survival (%) 98, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet LOW risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 93, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories (not significant, expected ordering) [Results 3.2.2]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 85, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: eplet HIGH risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year rejection-free survival (%) 82, p=0.19; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- death or graft loss: eplet LOW risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 98, p=<0.01; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories - monotone here, unlike the tacrolimus cohort [Results 3.2.2]
- death or graft loss: eplet INTERMEDIATE risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 95, p=<0.01; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- death or graft loss: eplet HIGH risk, Bela/Tac cohort — cumulative 3-year survival (%) 88, p=<0.01; adjusted for unadjusted KM; log-rank across the 3 categories [Results 3.2.2]
- DR/DQ-specific de novo DSA: Bela/Tac vs tacrolimus immunosuppression — HR 0.4; adjusted for Cox proportional hazards STRATIFIED by single-molecule DR/DQ eplet risk category; no CI and no p printed in the retrieved text (a non-stratified model with eplet risk as a covariate is said to give similar HRs; both models are in Supplementary Table 2, which was not retrievable) [Abstract and Results 3.3.1]
- DR/DQ-associated AMR: Bela/Tac vs tacrolimus immunosuppression — HR 0.2; adjusted for Cox stratified by eplet risk category; no CI or p in the retrieved text [Abstract and Results 3.3.2]
- biopsy-proven acute rejection: Bela/Tac vs tacrolimus immunosuppression — HR 0.45; adjusted for Cox stratified by eplet risk category; no CI or p in the retrieved text [Abstract and Results 3.3.3]
- death or graft loss: Bela/Tac vs tacrolimus immunosuppression — HR 0.96, p=0.87; adjusted for Cox stratified by eplet risk category; null result - the regimen benefit on hard endpoints did NOT survive the Cox model even though the low-risk KM comparison was significant [Results 3.3.4]

**Dose-response.**

- DR (eplet): definition MM: maximum single-molecule DR eplet mismatch count; threshold MM: DR < 7 required for low risk; DR >= 7 alone makes the pair intermediate risk; outcome_series_by_count MM: not reported - no per-count series is printed, only the 3-level category
- DQ (eplet): definition MM: maximum DQ alpha + maximum DQ beta eplet mismatch count (summed because DQ loci form multiple heterodimers); threshold MM: DQ < 9 low; DQ 9-14 intermediate; DQ >= 15 high; outcome_series_by_count MM: not reported - only the 3-level category
- antigen-level A/B/DR mismatch counts: NOT analysed anywhere in this paper
- Shape reported: step / ordered 3-level categories. Monotone and in the expected direction for DSA, AMR and rejection in BOTH cohorts. Non-monotone for the hard endpoint under tacrolimus (low 89%, intermediate 94%, high 90% - the authors say patients 'did not stratify as expected'), but monotone under Bela/Tac (98/95/88%). The biggest single step is the DQ>=15 high-risk boundary. No shape is claimed for the underlying continuous eplet count.; linearity tested: not tested. No trend test, no spline, no continuous eplet-count model, and no comparison of alternative cut-points is reported anywhere. The authors used previously published thresholds (DR<7/DQ<9; DQ>=15) and explicitly flag in the Discussion that optimal thresholds may differ in their population and under belatacept - 'If higher thresholds are tolerable on belatacept, more patients could be considered low risk'.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- single-molecule DR/DQ eplet risk level x immunosuppression regimen (Bela/Tac vs tacrolimus) - outcome de novo DR/DQ DSA: The belatacept advantage is confined to the intermediate-risk stratum. Low-risk patients had NO DSA events on either regimen (nothing to modify), and high-risk patients showed no significant difference - the authors read this as the mismatch burden being potent enough to cause events despite belatacept. (intermediate-risk log-rank p=0.02; high-risk p=0.22; low-risk no events either arm; stratified Cox HR 0.4 overall) [Results 3.3.1 Donor Specific Antibodies]
- eplet risk level x immunosuppression regimen - outcome DR/DQ-associated AMR: Both intermediate- and high-risk patients had lower AMR rates on Bela/Tac, but only the intermediate-risk difference reached significance; low-risk was 100% AMR-free on both regimens. (intermediate-risk log-rank p=0.02; stratified Cox HR 0.2 overall) [Results 3.3.2 Antibody Mediated Rejection]
- eplet risk level x immunosuppression regimen - outcome biopsy-proven acute rejection: The only outcome where the regimen benefit holds at EVERY eplet risk level - i.e. for rejection the regimen effect looks additive rather than modified by mismatch burden. (low-risk p=0.04, intermediate-risk p=0.04, high-risk p<0.01; stratified Cox HR 0.45 overall) [Results 3.3.3 Acute Rejection]
- eplet risk level x immunosuppression regimen - outcome death or graft loss: Direction of modification REVERSES for the hard endpoint: the regimen benefit appears only in the LOW eplet-risk stratum, which the authors interpret as drug toxicity mattering more than immunological efficacy when immune risk is low. Intermediate and high strata were similar between regimens, and the effect did not survive the Cox model. (low-risk 98% (Bela/Tac) vs 89% (tacrolimus), log-rank p=0.02; stratified Cox HR 0.96, p=0.87) [Results 3.3.4 Patient and Graft Survival]
- formal statistical test of the eplet x regimen interaction: NONE REPORTED. There is no interaction term, no P-for-interaction, and no ratio-of-hazard-ratios anywhere in the paper. Effect modification is inferred entirely from (a) stratum-specific log-rank tests and (b) Cox models that STRATIFY on eplet risk rather than interact with it - a stratified Cox estimates one common regimen HR and by construction cannot test whether that HR varies across strata. (not reported) [Methods 2.3 Outcomes and Analysis; Results 3.3]
- eplet mismatch x recipient race/ethnicity: The paper is explicitly motivated by prior eplet studies under-representing diverse populations and its cohort is 55-57% African-American, but race enters only as a propensity-matching variable and as an input to HLA imputation. No race-stratified estimate is reported; the authors state cohort size 'limited our ability to perform subpopulation analyses'. (not reported) [Methods 2.1; Results 3.1; Discussion (limitations)]
- eplet mismatch x donor type (living vs deceased): Donor type was a propensity-matching variable only (deceased donor 59% Bela/Tac, 66% tacrolimus). No living-donor subgroup result is reported, so this paper provides no living-donor-specific estimate. (not reported) [Methods 2.1; Results 3.1]
- eplet mismatch x sensitisation / pre-existing antibody: Cannot be assessed - patients with pre-existing DSA were an explicit EXCLUSION criterion, as were HLA-identical pairs and repeat transplants. The paper therefore says nothing about the sensitised or antibody-unknown recipient. (not reported (excluded by design)) [Methods 2.1 Patient Selection]
- individual eplet identity x regimen (eplet-level immunogenicity): Of 202 DR/DQ eplets, 196 were mismatched in both cohorts; 184 of 196 had a lower immune event rate under Bela/Tac, but only 106 of 196 were more enriched among Bela/Tac patients with events - the authors offer this asymmetry as a way to separate genuinely immunogenic eplets from linked passengers. Weighted correlation network analysis found 33 co-expressed eplet communities (2-13 eplets each), and linkage disequilibrium prevents attributing risk to any single eplet within a community. (184/196 lower event rate; 106/196 more enriched; 33 communities; Pearson r>0.8 defined interrelatedness) [Results 3.4 Immunogenicity of Particular Eplets]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "In cox regression analysis stratified by eplet risk level, Bela/Tacimmunosuppression was associated with decreased rate of DSA (HR=0.4), AMR (HR=0.2), and rejection (HR=0.45)." (Abstract (PMC author manuscript))
- *C11* — "By cox regression analysis, Bela/Tacshowed a moderating effect for all immune events, with tacrolimus immunosuppression associated with more than double the risk of DSA, AMR, and rejection" (Discussion, paragraph 1)
- *C11* — "in the low-risk group, Bela/Tactreatment was associated with improved 3-year survival (98%) when compared with tacrolimus treatment (89%), significant by log-rank testing (p=0.02)" (Results 3.3.4 Patient and Graft Survival)
- *C12* — "Low and intermediate (primarily) resolution HLA typing and patient ethnicity were used as input to 9-locus high-resolution HLA imputation with National Marrow Donor Program (NMDP) haplotype frequency data." (Methods 2.2 Eplet Risk Calculation)
- *C12* — "assessments at the individual level are higher risk for variability, so applications for individual allocation or treatment decisions would benefit from high resolution typing to overcome this uncertainty" (Discussion (limitations paragraph))
- *C12* — "Rejection-free survival was similarly ordered with 80% of the low-risk group event-free at 3 years compared to 73% of intermediate-risk and 66% of high-risk patients." (Results 3.2.1 Stratification of Tacrolimus Cohort)

**Limitations.** Single centre, retrospective, n=588 after matching - small for time-to-event analysis, and the authors say cohort size prevented any subpopulation analysis.; NO confidence intervals and, for three of the four headline HRs, no p-values are printed anywhere in the retrieved text. The precision of HR 0.4 / 0.2 / 0.45 cannot be assessed; the supporting Supplementary Table 2 was not retrievable.; Effect modification is asserted but never formally tested: a Cox model STRATIFIED by eplet risk estimates a single common regimen HR and cannot by construction test whether that HR differs across strata. The modification claim rests on stratum-wise log-rank tests, which is a weak design for interaction and is vulnerable to multiplicity across 4 outcomes x 3 strata.; The eplet exposure is derived from IMPUTED high-resolution HLA (low/intermediate-resolution typing plus ethnicity, NMDP haplotype frequencies, a single haplotype pair drawn by random weighted choice). Imputation error is not propagated into any standard error, and the authors themselves say individual-level assignments are the higher-risk use.; Confounding by indication is reduced but not eliminated: the tacrolimus arm is a shortage-era cohort (04/2017-11/2018), so regimen is partly confounded with transplant era, allocation changes and rising DGF rates that the authors themselves invoke to explain a 25% rejection rate.; Recipient age was NOT a matching variable, differed significantly (53 vs 50 years) and was not adjusted for in the reported models.; Rejection was ascertained by FOR-CAUSE biopsies only, and protocol DSA testing stopped at 1 year, so 3-year outcomes rest on incomplete ascertainment; the authors note events were heavily weighted to the first year.; Belatacept regimens involve monthly infusions, so the comparison is confounded by a different level of health-system contact; adherence and MMF/prednisone dose changes could not be assessed.; AMR was defined only in patients with DR/DQ-specific DSA, which builds the exposure into the outcome definition and guarantees low-risk patients look AMR-free; two AMR cases per group without DR/DQ DSA were excluded from that endpoint.; Risk thresholds were taken from prior literature, not derived or validated here, and the authors concede the optimal thresholds may differ in their population and under belatacept.; Class II (DR/DQ) only - no class I eplet, no HLA-A/B/C or DP analysis, and no antigen-level mismatch comparison, so the paper cannot speak to antigen-count matching at all.; Excludes pre-existing DSA, repeat transplants and HLA-identical pairs; 3-year horizon only, which is short for graft survival..

de Fijter J 2023, *Kidney International*, [DOI 10.1016/j.kint.2023.05.025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2023.05.025). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier, Kidney International); no PMC record found via PubMed metadata or ID converter; extraction is from the PubMed abstract only.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Kidney transplants within the Eurotransplant Senior Program (old-for-old): kidneys donated after brain death from donors 65 years and older to candidates 65 years and older; paired allocation of both kidneys of one donor, the first via the Eurotransplant Senior DR-compatible Program (HLA-DR antigen matching) and the contralateral kidney via ESP without HLA-DR matching. Eurotransplant countries; the abstract does not name them, but the author affiliations are in Germany, Austria, the Netherlands and Belgium (inferred from affiliations, not from the abstract text). Calendar period not stated in the abstract ('the period within ESP with paired allocation'). |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 675 kidneys from paired donors: 341 HLA-DR-compatible (ESDP) and 334 contralateral kidneys allocated without HLA-DR matching (ESP) |
| design | paired-kidney (contralateral kidney) allocation cohort study; Kaplan-Meier estimates for all-cause mortality, competing-risk analysis for graft failure; log-rank test and Cox proportional hazards regression for comparisons |
| typing resolution | HLA-DR antigen level (abstract says 'matching for HLA-DR antigens'; serologic/broad-antigen equivalent); typing method not stated in the abstract |
| outcome | all-cause mortality (5-year); kidney graft failure / return to dialysis (cause-specific hazards at 1 and 5 years, competing-risk framework); cold ischaemia time and dialysis vintage as allocation consequences |
| follow up | outcomes reported at 1 and 5 years post-transplant; median follow-up not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | donor age (by design all donors 65 years and older), recipient age (by design all candidates 65 years and older), cold ischaemia (reported as a consequence of DR-matched allocation: mean difference 1.00 h), dialysis vintage (reported difference between arms: median 2.4 vs 4.1 years), Cox model covariates not stated in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's only quasi-experimental test of HLA-DR matching: both kidneys from one donor were allocated, one with DR-antigen matching (ESDP) and the contralateral without (ESP), which removes donor-side confounding and isolates the value of a single-locus, antigen-level DR match; it therefore speaks to C3 (DR as the key locus), the zero-DR-mismatch premium (C9) and allocation-scheme validation (C13). The matching criterion is HLA-DR at antigen (broad-specificity) level, which is exactly the information a one-field / serologic-equivalent typing provides, so the exposure definition transfers directly to a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen. Transfer is weaker on population: donors and recipients were all 65 years or older in a deceased brain-death-donor European programme, whereas the Iranian target is living donation with younger, better-quality kidneys, where the absolute benefit of DR matching may differ and cannot be read off these numbers. The main cost of DR-matched allocation here (about one hour more cold ischaemia) is a deceased-donor logistics effect that does not arise when choosing among living donors, so the net benefit of DR matching in a living-donor selection tool would if anything be cleaner than in this study. Sensitisation status is not described in the abstract, so nothing can be said about antibody-unknown candidates. The paper cannot inform per-mismatch dose-response or the contribution of loci other than DR.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause mortality, five-year: HLA-DR antigen-compatible allocation (ESDP kidney) vs contralateral kidney allocated without HLA-DR matching (ESP) — HR 0.71 (0.53–0.95); adjusted for Cox proportional hazards regression; covariates not stated in the abstract (full text not retrieved) [Abstract (results sentence)]
- kidney graft failure and return to dialysis, one-year (cause-specific hazard, competing-risk analysis): HLA-DR antigen-compatible allocation (ESDP kidney) vs contralateral kidney allocated without HLA-DR matching (ESP) — cause-specific HR 0.55 (0.35–0.87); adjusted for Cox proportional hazards regression; covariates not stated in the abstract [Abstract (results sentence)]
- kidney graft failure and return to dialysis, five-year (cause-specific hazard, competing-risk analysis): HLA-DR antigen-compatible allocation (ESDP kidney) vs contralateral kidney allocated without HLA-DR matching (ESP) — cause-specific HR 0.73 (0.53–0.99); adjusted for Cox proportional hazards regression; covariates not stated in the abstract [Abstract (results sentence)]
- cold ischaemia time (cost of DR-matched allocation; not an HLA-effect estimate): allocation based on HLA-DR matching vs ESP allocation without matching — mean difference (hours) 1.0 (0.32–1.68); adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract]
- median dialysis vintage at transplant (recipient-selection difference between arms; not an HLA-effect estimate): DR-compatible arm 2.4 years vs ESP without matching 4.1 years (abstract: 'significantly shorter') — median (years) in the DR-compatible arm; comparator median 4.1 years 2.4; adjusted for unadjusted descriptive comparison [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: not matched for HLA-DR (contralateral kidney, ESP; mismatch count not stratified) MM: ref; matched for HLA-DR antigens (ESDP) MM: mortality 5 y HR 0.71 (0.53-0.95); graft failure/return to dialysis cause-specific HR 1 y 0.55 (0.35-0.87), 5 y 0.73 (0.53-0.99)
- Shape reported: not reported (binary DR-compatible vs not-DR-matched comparison only; no 0/1/2 mismatch series in the abstract); linearity tested: not tested / not applicable: no per-count series is reported in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3: antigen-level HLA-DR matching improves patient survival* — "Within ESP, matching for HLA-DR antigens was associated with a significantly lower five-year risk of mortality (hazard ratio 0.71; 95% confidence interval 0.53-0.95)" (Abstract)
- *C3 / C9: DR-compatible (zero-DR-mismatch) kidneys have lower graft failure at 1 and 5 years* — "significantly lower cause-specific hazards for kidney graft failure and return to dialysis at one year (0.55; 0.35-0.87) and five years (0.73; 0.53-0.99) post-transplant." (Abstract)
- *C13: cost of DR-matched allocation (cold ischaemia) and recipient-selection difference (dialysis vintage)* — "Allocation based on HLA-DR matching resulted in longer cold ischemia (mean difference 1.00 hours; 95% confidence interval: 0.32-1.68) and kidney offers with a significantly shorter median dialysis vintage of 2.4 versus 4.1 yrs. in ESP without matching." (Abstract)
- *C13: paired-kidney design within an old-for-old allocation programme* — "This cohort study evaluated the period within ESP with paired allocation of 675 kidneys from donors 65 years and older to transplant candidates 65 years and older" (Abstract)
- *C13: the two allocation arms compared (DR-compatible programme vs ESP without DR matching)* — "the first kidney to 341 patients within the Eurotransplant Senior DR-compatible Program and 334 contralateral kidneys without (ESP) HLA-DR antigen matching" (Abstract)
- *C3 / C13: authors' conclusion that DR matching gives superior outcomes in old-for-old allocation* — "Hence, our paired allocation study suggests a superior outcome of HLA-DR matching in the context of old-for-old kidney transplantation." (Abstract (final sentence))

**Limitations.** Abstract only: PMC has no full text, so the Cox covariates, follow-up duration, typing method, calendar period and the exact operational definition of 'DR-compatible' (zero DR antigen mismatch vs broader compatibility) could not be verified.; Non-randomised allocation: recipients of DR-compatible kidneys had a much shorter dialysis vintage (median 2.4 vs 4.1 years), itself a strong prognostic factor, so part of the survival benefit may reflect recipient selection rather than histocompatibility.; Old-for-old deceased (brain-death) donor population, donors and recipients 65 years and older, Eurotransplant only; generalisability to younger living-donor recipients is untested.; Binary DR-compatible vs not-DR-matched comparison; no 0/1/2 DR mismatch series, no HLA-A, -B, -C, -DQ or -DP analysis, no molecular/eplet analysis.; No interaction or subgroup analyses in the abstract; sensitisation/PRA, ethnicity and immunosuppression are not described.; DR-matched allocation lengthened cold ischaemia by a mean 1.00 h, which works against the matched arm; this bias favours the paper's conclusion but the ischaemia effect is not separated from the matching effect.; Moderate sample (675 kidneys); the upper confidence limit for five-year graft failure reaches 0.99, and no p-values are printed in the abstract..

### de Marco R 2023 — The Problem and the Solution for Equitable Access of HLA-DR Homozygous Patients to Kidney Transplantation.

de Marco R 2023, *Transplantation*, [PMID 37749814](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37749814/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown; presumed publisher copyright (Wolters Kluwer / Transplantation), no PMC deposit, no open-access text seen.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | not retrievable - no abstract, no full text |
| donor type | not retrievable (the review's tasking implies deceased-donor allocation in Sao Paulo State, but this was NOT confirmed from the source) |
| design | not retrievable; article type is a Letter, so most likely a policy/allocation commentary or a short data letter rather than a full cohort report |
| typing resolution | not retrievable |
| outcome | not retrievable |

**Why it is relevant.** The review needs C13 (how allocation and living-donor selection schemes actually score HLA, and whether the scoring was validated against outcome) and C10 (non-additivity between loci, including what happens when a candidate is homozygous at a locus). This Letter was targeted because its title states the exact structural problem: a candidate homozygous at HLA-DR can at most be counted as carrying one DR antigen, so under a mismatch-counting or point-scoring allocation rule such candidates are systematically advantaged or disadvantaged relative to heterozygous candidates by an artefact of counting rather than by immunological risk. That question transfers directly to an Iranian living-donor, one-field (low-resolution) pre-screen: at antigen level, homozygosity and a failed/undetected second allele are indistinguishable, so a one-field pre-screen will score an apparently homozygous candidate as better-matched than they may truly be, and any points-based ranking inherits that bias. It also bears on C10 because homozygosity makes the per-locus mismatch count non-exchangeable across candidates - a 0-mismatch at DR means something different for a DR-homozygous recipient than for a heterozygous one. HOWEVER, none of this is evidence FROM this paper: no sentence, number, or point weight was retrieved, so this reasoning states why the paper was sought, not what it was found to show. Its transferability also has a hard limit even if obtained - a Letter about deceased-donor waiting-list allocation in Sao Paulo speaks to queue equity, not to the graft-outcome question that drives a living-donor pre-screen, where the donor is pre-specified and there is no queue to be advantaged in.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported (nothing retrieved); linearity tested: not retrievable - no text obtained; 1 and 2 pooled: None
