### Audry B 2022 — The new French kidney allocation system for donations after brain death: Rationale, implementation, and evaluation.

Audry B 2022, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.17180](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.17180). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown - no PMC record exists for this PMID or DOI (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid on 2026-09-08); only the PubMed abstract could be retrieved. Full text is behind publisher copyright..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult recipients of kidneys from donation after brain death in France, under the national kidney allocation system (KAS) implemented in 2015 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | not stated in the retrieved abstract |
| design | description of a national allocation policy and its rationale, with evaluation of post-implementation results (analytic design, comparison periods and statistical methods are not described in the retrieved abstract; PubMed keywords include 'simulation') |
| typing resolution | not stated |
| outcome | allocation-process outcomes: degree of HLA matching achieved, access to transplantation / transplant rate by recipient age band, cold ischaemia time, degree of national organ sharing. NOT graft survival, rejection or dnDSA. |
| follow up | not stated |
| other factors modelled | dialysis duration, waiting time / listing delay, recipient age, donor age (longevity / age matching), geography (local vs national allocation area, replacement of regional borders), cold ischaemia time (reported as a consequence, not a score criterion) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is an ANGLE F allocation-scheme description: it answers the review question of how national kidney allocation algorithms score HLA and whether the HLA component achieves what it was designed to achieve (claim C13). Its distinctive contribution is architectural rather than epidemiological: France's unified allocation score (UAS) does not add HLA points to age points but combines HLA matching and age matching through multiplicative interactions between criteria, so the value of a good HLA match is conditional on the donor-recipient age pairing (longevity matching) rather than fixed. The evaluation is a process evaluation - it reports that HLA matching improved for young recipients and access became faster for older recipients, and that access fell for recipients aged 60-69 so score parameters had to be retuned - which is direct evidence that an HLA term inside an allocation score has predictable and monitorable distributional consequences. Transfer to a living-donor, low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is INDIRECT and structural, not quantitative: the population is deceased brain-death donors under national sharing, where the scarce good being rationed is a deceased organ across a queue, whereas an Iranian living-donor pre-screen ranks candidate donors for one recipient with no waiting list, no cold-ischaemia penalty and no geographic sharing problem. Two design lessons do transfer - that HLA should enter a ranking score as a term interacting with recipient/donor age rather than as a standalone additive bonus, and that any weighting must be monitored for unintended access loss in specific subgroups and retuned - but the paper supplies no mismatch-count effect sizes, no per-locus weights and no graft-outcome estimates, so it cannot inform how many mismatches or which loci should be penalised. Because the abstract carries no numbers and no PMC full text exists, the actual HLA term of the UAS (its functional form and coefficients) was not retrievable and must be obtained from the paywalled article before this paper can be used for anything beyond a qualitative design precedent.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - the retrieved abstract contains no mismatch-count or per-locus analysis at all; HLA matching is described only qualitatively as 'better HLA matching' / 'improved HLA matching for young recipients'; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching x age matching (donor-recipient age), inside the allocation score: The allocation score is built with multiplicative rather than additive interactions between criteria, so HLA matching and age matching are combined for longevity matching; the authors present this as the mechanism that allowed multivariate optimisation of allocation. This is a SCORE-DESIGN interaction, not a measured effect-modification statistic. [Abstract (design rationale and conclusion)]
- policy effect x recipient age band: The effect of the new system on access differed by recipient age: young recipients gained both better HLA matching and better access, older recipients gained faster access, but recipients aged 60-69 lost access, which required tuning of the KAS parameters. This is heterogeneity in ALLOCATION ACCESS, not in graft outcome. [Abstract (results)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "was principally designed to introduce a unified allocation score (UAS) to be applied locally for one kidney and nationally for the other and to replace regional borders by a new geographical model" (Abstract)
- *C13* — "The new KAS balances dialysis duration and waiting time to compensate for listing delays and provides more effective longevity matching between donors and recipients with better HLA and age matching." (Abstract)
- *C13* — "national or adequately broad geographic allocation areas, combined with multiplicative interactions between allocation criteria, permit multivariate optimization of organ allocation" (Abstract (conclusion))
- *C13* — "Results show improved HLA matching for young recipients and more rapid access to transplant for older recipients." (Abstract (results))
- *C13* — "Transplant access decreased for recipients aged 60-69 and required tuning of KAS parameters." (Abstract (results))
- *C13* — "improve national kidney sharing and balance HLA matching and age matching, at the price of longer cold ischemic times and more logistical constraints than with local allocation" (Abstract (conclusion))

**Limitations.** Abstract-only: no PMC deposit exists for this PMID or DOI, so the full text, tables and the actual HLA term of the unified allocation score were not retrievable.; The abstract reports no numbers whatsoever - no hazard ratios, odds ratios, rate ratios, percentages, confidence intervals or p-values - so effect_sizes is empty and no quantitative claim can be drawn from this record.; No graft-survival, rejection, dnDSA or patient-survival outcome is reported; the evaluated outcomes are allocation-process outcomes (matching achieved, access, cold ischaemia, sharing).; The functional form and weights of the HLA component within the UAS, and the definition of an HLA mismatch used (loci counted, resolution), are not stated in the abstract.; Deceased brain-death donors under national sharing; the paper says nothing about living donors, so it does not directly inform living-donor selection.; HLA typing resolution used by the French system is not stated in the abstract, so it is unknown whether the matching term is antigen-level, allele-level or eplet/epitope-based.; A national before/after policy evaluation is confounded by secular trends in donor and candidate characteristics, and the abstract does not describe how (or whether) this was addressed.; The system needed post-hoc parameter tuning because access fell for recipients aged 60-69 - i.e. the reported version of the score is not the version whose consequences are described.; Single-country (France); the organ-scarcity, waiting-list and geography constraints that dominate the score's design do not exist in a living-donor pre-screen.; No sensitisation / PRA, ethnicity, imputation or molecular-mismatch analysis is reported in the retrieved text..

### Frischknecht L 2022 — The impact of pre-transplant donor specific antibodies on the outcome of kidney transplantation - Data from the Swiss transplant cohort study

Frischknecht L 2022, *Frontiers in Immunology*, [DOI 10.3389/fimmu.2022.1005790](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2022.1005790). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (Frontiers open access).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult (>=18 y) single-organ, ABO-compatible kidney transplants performed in the six Swiss transplant centres May 2008 - December 2017, all with a complete pre-transplant virtual cross-match; multi-organ, paediatric, ABO-incompatible and incomplete-vXM transplants excluded |
| donor type | both |
| n | 2215 transplants in 2179 patients; 411 with pre-transplant DSA vs 1804 without. Donor type: DSA group 294 deceased / 117 living (71.5% / 28.5%); no-DSA group 1118 deceased / 686 living (62.0% / 38.0%) |
| design | prospective national cohort sub-study; exposure = pre-transplant DSA assigned by virtual cross-match (donor HLA typing vs recipient SAB specificities), stratified by HLA class, by HLA locus, and by MFI band; outcomes compared by Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, ANOVA for eGFR slope, univariate Cox for graft loss, and an exploratory partial least squares (PLS) regression for the multivariable step |
| typing resolution | DNA-based donor and recipient HLA typing by SSO or SSP; the introduction describes 'modern qPCR based donor intermediate resolution HLA typing'. DSA assignment and both cumulative and highest-single MFI are computed at HLA antigen resolution. Additional loci were typed only 'if needed' when the recipient had antibodies against a locus not previously typed, so HLA-C/DQ/DP donor typing is conditional rather than universal. No two-field/allele-level or eplet analysis. |
| outcome | biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR, Banff 2017; borderline changes and isolated C4d not counted), death-censored graft loss (return to dialysis or pre-emptive re-transplant), eGFR slope (CKD-EPI 2009; mean annual slope and mean total slope, baseline = 1-year eGFR); TCMR and patient survival as secondary |
| follow up | median 6.1 years; long-term outcome data described as available for up to 12 years; 62% (n=1372) underwent a biopsy during follow-up |
| other factors modelled | recipient sex, recipient age, donor sex, donor age, previous transplantation, previous pregnancy, previous blood transfusion, maintenance immunosuppression regimen, induction therapy (ATG vs basiliximab), underlying renal disease, cold ischaemia time (deceased donors), donor type (deceased vs living), HLA-A/B/DRB1 mismatch counts (baseline table only), DSA MFI (cumulative and highest single), DSA count, DSA HLA class and locus |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper does not test HLA mismatch counts against outcome; its exposure is pre-transplant donor-specific antibody, so for this review it answers the mechanism question rather than the matching-dose question - which HLA loci actually cause harm, and through what pathway. That makes it the strongest available evidence for C7 and C8: HLA-C DSA raised ABMR risk but not graft loss, while isolated HLA-DP DSA tracked HLA-DR and HLA-DQ DSA for graft loss, i.e. the loci that a low-resolution antigen pre-screen usually ignores (C, DQ, DP) matter chiefly when an antibody is already present. It is directly relevant to a living-donor Iranian pre-screen in a negative way: 36% of the cohort were living-donor transplants, yet the entire risk stratification rests on knowing recipient antibody specificities and MFI, which is exactly the input our pre-screen does not have. The Swiss system had a complete virtual cross-match for every included transplant and still performed 19% of transplants across a DSA, with 10-year death-censored graft survival of 70% versus 90% - so the quantity our tool cannot see dominates the quantity it can. Transfer is further limited because the DSA-positive transplants were deliberately selected and heavily protected (ATG induction in 67% vs 16%), so the observed penalty is an attenuated, treated one; and because DSA assignment was at antigen resolution with DP/DQ donor typing performed only when antibody findings demanded it, which mirrors low-resolution practice but also means DP/DQ ascertainment is conditional. The practical consequence for our design is that HLA mismatch count must be presented as a ranking aid only, and antibody/PRA status must be carried explicitly as UNKNOWN rather than treated as absent, because a mismatch that is harmless without antibody becomes the dominant risk factor with it.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft survival at 10 years: any pre-transplant DSA vs no DSA — percentage (Kaplan-Meier) 70.0; adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank) [Results, 'The presence of pre-transplant DSA negatively affects transplant outcome'; Figure 2. Reference group 90% at 10 years.]
- cumulative incidence of ABMR at 4 years: combined Class I + Class II DSA (DSA I+II) — percentage (cumulative incidence) 60.0; adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier, log-rank) [Results, 'Pre-transplant DSA directed against HLA Class II antigens is coupled to decreased graft survival'; Figure 3. Reported as '>60%'.]
- presence of pre-transplant DSA (exposure distribution, not a graft outcome): HLA-DRB1 mismatch 0/1/2, DSA-positive vs DSA-negative transplants — percentage distribution None, p=0.002; adjusted for unadjusted baseline comparison [Table 1, 'HLA mismatch'. DSA group 10/56/34%; no-DSA group 18/53/29%. Fewer zero-DRB1-mismatch transplants among DSA-positive recipients.]
- presence of pre-transplant DSA (exposure distribution, not a graft outcome): HLA-B mismatch 0/1/2, DSA-positive vs DSA-negative transplants — percentage distribution None, p=0.18; adjusted for unadjusted baseline comparison [Table 1, 'HLA mismatch'. DSA group 6/41/53%; no-DSA group 9/40/51%.]
- presence of pre-transplant DSA (exposure distribution, not a graft outcome): HLA-A mismatch 0/1/2, DSA-positive vs DSA-negative transplants — percentage distribution None, p=0.8; adjusted for unadjusted baseline comparison [Table 1, 'HLA mismatch'. DSA group 14/47/39%; no-DSA group 16/46/38%.]
- prevalence of pre-transplant DSA despite complete virtual cross-match: DSA-positive transplants / all included transplants — percentage 19.0; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Study population characteristics'. 411 of 2215 transplants (19%); anti-HLA antibodies detected in 1139 patients (51%) pre-transplant.]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported for HLA mismatch count - no mismatch-count dose-response for any outcome is presented. A monotone dose-response IS reported for DSA strength (MFI): ABMR risk, graft loss and eGFR decline all worsen across ascending cumulative-MFI bands, with the worst outcome in the highest band.; linearity tested: not tested. MFI was analysed only as pre-specified categorical bands (cumulative MFI <1k / 1k-5k / 5k-10k / >10k; highest single DSA MFI <1k / 1k-2k / 2k-5k / >5k) compared by Kaplan-Meier and log-rank. No linear, trend, spline or threshold test is reported, and no p for trend is given.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- DSA HLA class x DSA MFI (low-MFI band): at cumulative MFI <1000 (n=84) isolated Class II DSA significantly increased ABMR risk while isolated Class I DSA did not; graft survival showed a clear trend to be worse only for Class II, detectable more than 6 years post-transplant. The authors turn this into different clinical cut-offs by class. (no numeric estimate printed; 'DSA II ... significantly increased' vs 'DSA I did not markedly affect long-term ABMR risk'; suggested cut-offs >1000 MFI for Class I, 500-1000 MFI acceptable to consider for Class II) [Results, 'Differential impact of MFI on Class I and Class II DSA'; Figure 5; Discussion]
- DSA HLA class x outcome type (ABMR vs graft loss): effect modification by endpoint: Class I and Class II DSA raised ABMR risk comparably, but only Class II DSA (alone or with Class I) was associated with graft loss and with accelerated eGFR decline. Class I DSA alone did not significantly affect long-term graft survival at any MFI stratum tested. (no numeric estimate printed) [Results, 'Pre-transplant DSA directed against HLA Class II antigens is coupled to decreased graft survival' and 'Differential impact of MFI on Class I and Class II DSA'; Figures 3 and 5]
- HLA-B DSA x co-existing Class II DSA (locus confounding in the multi-DSA analysis): when all 674 locus-specific DSA events were analysed, HLA-B DSA showed the highest ABMR risk, but the authors state this trend was driven by recipients whose HLA-B DSA co-occurred with Class II DSA - i.e. the apparent class I locus signal is carried by linked class II antibody. (no numeric estimate printed) [Results, 'Impact of DSA directed at different HLA loci'; Figure 6]
- pre-transplant DSA x subsequent ABMR (mediation): DSA-positive recipients who never developed ABMR had long-term graft survival comparable to DSA-negative, ABMR-free recipients; DSA-negative recipients who developed ABMR had outcomes comparable to DSA-positive recipients with ABMR. The harm of pre-transplant DSA runs through ABMR rather than being independent of it. (no numeric estimate printed) [Results, 'Pre-transplant DSA directed against HLA Class II antigens is coupled to decreased graft survival'; Figure 3]
- DSA locus x outcome (HLA-C and HLA-DP): among single-locus DSA (n=260), HLA-C DSA raised late ABMR risk but was NOT significantly associated with reduced graft survival, whereas isolated HLA-DP DSA produced a marked graft-survival decline comparable to HLA-DQ DSA over the first 6 years. The strongest correlation with both ABMR and graft loss was for HLA-DQ DSA. (no numeric estimate printed; HLA-C explicitly flagged as 'based on fewer observations') [Results, 'Impact of DSA directed at different HLA loci'; Figure 6; correlation heat map Figure 6]
- Class I DSA x high MFI (>7000): graft-loss risk for Class I DSA did not rise dramatically at MFI >7000, but the authors warn this rests on very few transplants performed against a high-MFI Class I DSA - an apparent absence of a dose-response that is most likely a power problem. (no numeric estimate printed) [Results, 'Differential impact of MFI on Class I and Class II DSA'; Figure 5]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C7* — "In summary, both Class I and Class II directed DSA are associated with increased risk for ABMR but only patients with Class II DSA show evidence of accelerated decline of graft function as well as increased risk of graft loss." (Results, end of 'Pre-transplant DSA directed against HLA Class II antigens is coupled to decreased graft survival')
- *C8* — "Surprisingly, DSA directed at HLA DP were associated with a marked decline in graft survival that was comparable to the diminished survival seen in the setting of HLA-DQ DSA during the first 6 years post-transplant" (Results, 'Impact of DSA directed at different HLA loci')
- *C7* — "HLA-C DSA were, however, not significantly associated with decreased graft survival in our cohort, and only patients with DSA directed at Class II antigens showed a decreased graft survival" (Results, 'Impact of DSA directed at different HLA loci')
- *C11* — "Here, our suggestion would be to only consider Class I DSA with an MFI >1000, whereas Class II DSA MFI could be taken into account also in the 500-1000 MFI range." (Discussion)
- *C4* — "the strongest association with ABMR and graft loss was seen for DSA targeting HLA-DQ" (Results, 'Impact of DSA directed at different HLA loci' (correlation matrix, Figure 6))
- *C11* — "DSA also significantly affected death censored graft survival, with a 70% graft survival at 10 years as compared to 90% in patients without DSA" (Results, 'The presence of pre-transplant DSA negatively affects transplant outcome'; Figure 2)

**Limitations.** The exposure is pre-transplant DSA, not donor-recipient HLA mismatch. Mismatch counts appear only in the Table 1 baseline comparison and are never modelled against ABMR, graft loss or eGFR slope, so the paper cannot support any mismatch dose-response claim (C2, C9) and supports locus claims only through the antibody pathway.; No numeric effect estimates are recoverable from the PMC full text. Hazard ratios, 95% CIs and p values are stated in Methods to have been computed by univariate Cox regression, but the values live in a table/figure that the retrieved text does not carry; all outcome comparisons in the narrative are Kaplan-Meier curves with log-rank significance stars only. Every quantitative comparison in this record is therefore a percentage read from the text, not a modelled estimate.; The multivariable step is an exploratory partial least squares (PLS) regression, chosen because of collinearity. It yields a biplot of relative proximity, not adjusted effect sizes, and the authors themselves note PLS 'has not been previously employed in the analysis of transplant immunological risk factors and the results should be interpreted accordingly'. There is thus no confounder-adjusted estimate for any locus.; Severe confounding by indication and by treatment: DSA-positive transplants were knowingly accepted after a complete virtual cross-match and were far more heavily immunosuppressed (ATG/thymoglobulin induction 67% vs 16%; tacrolimus-based maintenance 86% vs 77%). The observed DSA penalty is an attenuated, actively treated penalty, not the natural risk of an unrecognised DSA.; DSA-positive recipients differed systematically at baseline (48% vs 34% female, 44% vs 12% previously transplanted, 50% vs 27% prior transfusion, more deceased donors, fewer zero-DRB1-mismatch grafts), and these differences are not adjusted away in the outcome analyses.; Locus-specific subgroups are small. The clean single-locus analysis rests on 260 patients spread over six loci; the authors explicitly caution that the HLA-C finding is 'based on fewer observations', and the Class I MFI >7000 stratum contains very few patients. Many pairwise Kaplan-Meier comparisons are made with no stated correction for multiplicity.; Donor typing beyond the standard loci was performed only 'if needed' when the recipient carried antibodies to an untyped locus, so HLA-C, DQ and DP donor typing is conditional on the antibody result. DP-DSA and DQ-DSA ascertainment is therefore not uniform across the cohort.; Antigen-level (low-resolution) DSA assignment and MFI summation; no allele-level typing, no eplet or PIRCHE molecular-mismatch analysis, so the paper says nothing about C12.; De novo DSA and post-transplant antibody kinetics are not captured in the STCS database, which the authors state prevents assessing these markers. The 'no pre-transplant DSA but ABMR' group is presumed by the authors to be largely de novo DSA, but this is inference, not measurement.; Multicentre design over a 10-year inclusion period with centre-specific MFI cut-offs (500-1000), centre-specific biopsy and rejection-treatment practice, and locally graded biopsies later retro-translated to Banff 2017. 27% of transplants were called antibody-negative on a mixed-bead screen alone, without single-antigen bead confirmation, so some low-level DSA will have been missed.; Complete-case analysis - 'Missing values were omitted' - with no description of the amount or pattern of missingness; 69 patients were additionally dropped from eGFR analyses for out-of-range values.; Swiss population, six centres, near-universal access to SAB testing and virtual cross-match, ABO-incompatible transplants excluded. Neither the population nor the diagnostic infrastructure resembles an Iranian living-donor programme, and no living-donor-specific subgroup analysis is reported..

### Gramlick ME 2022 — Time to Move on: HLA Matching Should Be Reconsidered in Modern Deceased Donor Kidney Allocation

Gramlick ME 2022, *Transplantation Direct*, [PMID 35368986](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35368986/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - Transplantation Direct is an open-access journal and the article is deposited in PMC, but the specific licence string was not present in the retrieved text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adults (>=18 y) receiving a deceased-donor kidney-alone transplant in Australia (NSW, VIC, QLD, SA) recorded in ANZDATA, 2000-2018. Living-donor recipients, multi-organ recipients and paediatric patients were excluded. Western Australia (N = 867) excluded because its allocation score could not be split into cohorts; 460 excluded for missing OrganMatch score; 159 excluded for graft loss from nonimmunological causes. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 7440 transplant events in 7291 adult recipients (2965 matched, 40%; 4475 nonmatched, 60%) |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; exposure is the ALLOCATION COHORT (HLA-matched vs nonmatched) reconstructed from the OrganMatch score and the TSANZ national/state allocation algorithms, not an individual mismatch count. Linear mixed models for GFR; logistic and negative binomial regression for rejection; Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression for time to graft failure and patient survival; Fine and Gray for competing risk of death; formal mediation analysis of the effect of allocation group through months on dialysis. |
| typing resolution | not stated. The allocation cohorts rest on HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts out of 6 as scored by OrganMatch; the paper never states whether typing was serologic/antigen-level or molecular, and reports no allele-level, DQ, DP or C data. |
| outcome | graft function (Cockcroft-Gault GFR 3 mo to 10 y), acute rejection (any episode; rate per viable graft year; early rejection <3 mo), time to graft failure (immunological causes; death-censored analyses plus a competing-risk model), recipient survival |
| follow up | not stated as a median. Transplants 2000-2018 with GFR reported to 10 y; median time to graft failure estimable at 15.9 y (matched) and 12.7 y (nonmatched). |
| other factors modelled | time on dialysis (also modelled as a mediator), year of transplant, graft number, recipient age (and age squared), recipient gender, race (Caucasian vs not), diabetes, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, chronic lung disease, competing risk of death (Fine and Gray) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's clearest example of claim C13: a national allocation scheme that scores HLA heavily, evaluated against real long-term outcomes, with the exposure defined as the allocation cohort a recipient actually landed in rather than a mismatch count. It answers the policy-level question - what does an HLA-first allocation rule buy, and what does it cost - and the answer is a real but modest graft benefit (HR 0.72 for graft failure, 3.2 extra years of median graft survival) that shrinks to HR 0.76 once the shorter waiting time enjoyed by matched recipients is accounted for, and a survival benefit (HR 0.83) that disappears entirely (HR 0.89, P = 0.07) under the same adjustment. That mediation finding transfers to an Iranian LIVING-donor pre-screen in an unusual way: 47.6% of the graft-failure benefit and 57.4% of the survival benefit ran through dialysis time, a queue-position mechanism that simply does not exist when a specific willing living donor is being assessed, so the honest living-donor analogue of this paper's benefit is the smaller direct effect, not the crude registry contrast. The exposure granularity is nevertheless a good fit for a low-resolution pre-screen: the operative unit is an antigen-level A/B/DR mismatch count out of six, banded into 0-2 (up to 3 in Victoria) versus the rest, which is exactly the resolution a one-field Iranian typing report supports. The equity result - Caucasian recipients took 87% of matched kidneys while making up 76% of transplants, and every minority group waited longer - is a direct warning for a multi-ethnic Iranian donor pool, where an HLA-weighted rule would predictably favour the majority haplotypes. Its limits for this review are sharp: deceased-donor only with living donors explicitly excluded, no sensitisation, PRA, DSA or crossmatch data at all, and no per-locus or per-mismatch-count breakdown, so it cannot inform locus weighting (C3-C8) and cannot substitute for the antibody step that an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen must still defer to a laboratory.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- time to graft failure (immunological causes): HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — HR 0.71 (0.62–0.81), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (continuous), graft number, race (Caucasian) [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2]
- time to graft failure (immunological causes), competing risk of death accounted for: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — HR 0.72 (0.63–0.83), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (continuous), graft number, race (Caucasian); Fine and Gray competing risk of death [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2; Table 7]
- time to graft failure - DIRECT effect after mediation through months on dialysis: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — HR 0.76 (0.66–0.88), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (continuous), graft number, race (Caucasian); competing risk of death; mediated by time on dialysis (mo). Percentage of the indirect effect mediated by time on dialysis: 47.6% [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2; Table 7 and footnote]
- recipient death: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — HR 0.83 (0.73–0.94), p=0.003; adjusted for year (continuous), graft number, age, gender, Caucasian, lung disease, coronary artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes [Results, Recipient Survival; Table 7; Abstract]
- recipient death - DIRECT effect after mediation through months on dialysis: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — HR 0.89 (0.78–1.01), p=0.07; adjusted for same covariates as the recipient-survival model; mediated by time on dialysis. Percentage of the indirect effect mediated by time on dialysis: 57.4%. No longer statistically significant. [Results, Recipient Survival; Table 7 and footnote]
- at least one acute rejection episode at any time post-transplant: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — OR 0.71 (0.65–0.77), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (categorical), graft number, race (Caucasian) [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 1; Table 7]
- rate of acute rejection episodes per viable graft year: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort — IRR (incident rate ratio) 0.7 (0.63–0.78), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (categorical), graft number, race (Caucasian); offset for log time graft viable [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 1; Table 7]
- GFR (Cockcroft-Gault), averaged over 3 mo to 10 y: HLA-matched allocation cohort vs nonmatched allocation cohort (mean difference, mL/min/1.73 m2) — adjusted mean difference 1.76 (0.81–2.7), p=<0.001; adjusted for year (categorical), graft number, age, age squared, gender, Caucasian, lung disease, artery disease, peripheral vascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, diabetes [Results, Graft Function; Table 6; Abstract]
- median time to graft failure (crude, accounting for censoring), years: matched 15.9 (95% CI 14.2-17.7) vs nonmatched 12.7 (95% CI 12.3-13.8) — median survival time (years) 15.9 (14.2–17.7), p=<0.001; adjusted for crude (unadjusted); nonmatched comparator 12.7 (12.3-13.8) [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2; Table 7; Abstract]
- median recipient survival (crude, accounting for censoring), years: matched not estimable / stated as >17.6 y vs nonmatched 16.9 y (95% CI 16-NE) — median survival time (years) 16.9; adjusted for crude; the matched group never reached 50% survival, so its median is 'not estimable' in Table 7 although the Results text asserts >17.6 y [Results, Recipient Survival; Table 7 (NE) - internal inconsistency, see notes]
- incidence of at least one rejection episode (crude percentages): matched 23% (670/2965) vs nonmatched 30% (1356/4475) — percentage 23.0, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted; model-estimated proportions were 0.26 (0.23-0.28) matched vs 0.36 (0.33-0.40) nonmatched [Table 5 and Table 7]
- early rejection (<3 mo) among transplants that had any rejection: matched 59% (393/670) vs nonmatched 68% (920/1356) — percentage 59.0, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 1; Table 5]
- delayed graft function (dialysis within 7 d): matched 4.5% (132/2965) vs nonmatched 7.3% (322/4475) — percentage 4.5, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted; the P value is for the whole immediate-graft-function category, not for DGF alone [Table 5]
- graft still functioning at last follow-up: matched 88% (2624/2965) vs nonmatched 86% (3864/4475) — percentage 88.0, p=0.0065; adjusted for unadjusted [Table 5; Results text quotes P = 0.007]
- mean GFR at fixed time points (mL/min/1.73 m2), matched vs nonmatched: 3 mo 63 vs 62 (P<0.001); 6 mo 64 vs 63 (P=0.0018); 12 mo 66 vs 64 (P<0.001); 5 y 65 vs 63 (P<0.001); 10 y 65 vs 61 (P=0.0035) — mean (SD) by time point 66.0, p=<0.001 at 12 mo; adjusted for unadjusted cross-sectional comparisons [Table 5]
- months on dialysis before transplant (the mediator): matched median 28 mo (IQR 16-48) vs nonmatched 45 mo (IQR 26-73); abstract states 28.1 vs 44.8 mo; Discussion states nonmatched waited a median 17 mo longer — median difference (months) 17.0, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Demographics and Race; Table 3; Discussion para 3]
- access to a matched kidney by ethnicity (equity outcome, not a graft outcome): Caucasians were 76% of all transplants but received 87% of matched kidneys (2566/2965) vs 69% of nonmatched (3065/4475); Caucasian median dialysis 36 mo vs non-Caucasian 43 mo — percentage 87.0, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Demographics and Race; Table 2; Table 4]
- HISTORICAL, CITED FROM ANOTHER STUDY - 1-year graft survival, Australian deceased-donor transplants 1971-1980: 0/4 HLA mismatch (matched) 63% vs >=3/4 HLA mismatches (nonmatched) 50%; overall 1-y 54%, 5-y 38% — percentage 63.0; adjusted for not this cohort - these figures are quoted in the Discussion from a cited 1971-1980 Australian series to contrast with the modern era [Discussion, para 6 (cited literature, NOT a result of this study)]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The exposure is a binary allocation cohort, not a mismatch count. The authors state explicitly that the study 'looks at long-term graft and patient outcomes based on allocation cohorts rather than individual number of HLA mismatches'. No 0/1/2/3/4/5/6 mismatch series, no per-locus series, and no test for trend, linearity, threshold or spline appears anywhere in the paper.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- allocation group x months post-transplant (trend in GFR over time): No difference in the trend of graft function over time between matched and nonmatched transplants; the matched advantage is a level shift, not a divergence. The authors state there was no difference in the trend. (interaction P = 0.2528 crude (n = 29 897 observations); P = 0.3118 adjusted (n = 26 918)) [Results, Graft Function; Table 6]
- allocation group x months post-transplant x year of transplant (3-way): The change in GFR over time was not modified by the era of transplantation, i.e. no evidence that the matching benefit on graft function has waned across 2000-2018. (P = 0.978) [Results, Graft Function, last sentence]
- allocation group x year of transplant, for time to graft failure and for patient death: The Methods state that such an interaction model was fitted to test whether the matched-vs-nonmatched difference changed over the era of transplantation, but NO result for it is reported anywhere in the retrieved full text. Treat as an unreported analysis. [Methods, Statistical Analysis (model described); no corresponding Results entry]
- allocation group x recipient ethnicity, for clinical outcomes: Not tested. Ethnicity was used only as a covariate (Caucasian yes/no) and as an access/equity descriptor. The authors state that they did not evaluate clinical outcomes by racial group and call it an urgent area for future research. [Discussion, strengths and limitations paragraph]
- mediation of allocation group through months on dialysis (formal mediation, not effect modification): Time on dialysis carried roughly half of the apparent benefit of matched allocation. Graft failure: 47.6% of the effect was indirect and the direct effect remained significant (HR 0.76). Recipient survival: 57.4% was indirect and the direct effect lost significance (HR 0.89, P = 0.07). (47.6% mediated for graft failure; 57.4% mediated for recipient survival) [Table 7 footnotes; Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure and Recipient Survival]
- comorbidity burden x allocation group: Nonmatched recipients had more coronary artery disease (19% vs 15%) and diabetes (23% vs 17%). The authors considered these might explain the poorer nonmatched outcomes but report that this was not borne out in adjusted modelling for graft function and recipient survival. (both P < 0.001 for the baseline imbalance; no interaction test reported) [Results, Demographics and Race; Discussion, para 2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "The national allocation algorithm has been uniformly adopted by all the states in Australia to ensure that very well-matched kidneys (0-2 HLA mismatches) are distributed across state borders." (Materials and Methods, Cohorts)
- *C13* — "The median time to graft failure, accounting for censoring, was 15.9 y for matched transplants and 12.7 y for nonmatched transplants" (Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2)
- *C13* — "After accounting for time on dialysis, the direct effect of allocation group showed slightly less graft survival benefit for the Matched group but was still significant" (Results, Graft Rejection and Graft Failure, para 2)
- *C13* — "However, after accounting for time on dialysis, the direct effect of allocation group on recipient survival was no longer significant" (Results, Recipient Survival)
- *C13* — "Our study has demonstrated that though there continue to be advantages for recipients of well-matched kidneys, the clinical benefit is of small magnitude and is due in part to a reduction in time spent on dialysis." (Conclusions)
- *C4* — "matching at HLA-DR and HLA-DQ seems to be more important in reducing donor-specific antibody formation and its complications compared with matching at HLA-A and HLA-B" (Discussion, para 8 - NARRATIVE ASSERTION citing other literature; this study reports no per-locus or DQ data of its own)

**Limitations.** Deceased-donor only. Living-donor recipients were explicitly excluded, so the paper does not directly address living-donor selection (C14) and its central mediator - queue time on dialysis - has no analogue in a living-donor pre-screen.; The exposure is a reconstructed allocation cohort, not a recorded allocation arm and not an individual mismatch count. ANZDATA did not record the allocation arm, so the authors inferred it from OrganMatch scores and successive state/national algorithms. Misclassification is plausible, especially across the 2000-2018 policy changes.; 0, 1 and 2 mismatches are pooled into one 'matched' band (up to 3 in Victoria, which did not penalise HLA-A). No dose-response, no per-locus result, no zero-mismatch premium, no test of linearity or threshold - so the paper cannot inform claims C2, C3, C5, C6 or C9.; Selective exclusions: all 867 Western Australian transplants dropped because the WA score could not be split into cohorts, 460 dropped for a missing OrganMatch score, and 159 dropped for nonimmunological graft loss. WA weighted dialysis time more heavily, so excluding it removes the state whose policy most resembles the equity-weighted alternative the paper argues for.; Strong confounding by indication that adjustment cannot fully remove: matched recipients were healthier at baseline (coronary artery disease 15% vs 19%, diabetes 17% vs 23%, less diabetic nephropathy) and had waited far less time. Allocation is not random and dialysis time is simultaneously a confounder, a mediator and a consequence of the exposure.; The mediation analysis rests on untestable assumptions (no unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding) and no sensitivity analysis for them is reported. Mediation was run only for graft failure and recipient survival; the authors state that budget and time prevented mediating the rejection outcome, which was their largest effect.; No immunological data beyond the mismatch band: no PRA, no sensitisation status, no DSA or dnDSA, no crossmatch, no eplet or PIRCHE molecular mismatch, no HLA-C, -DQ or -DP. The paper therefore says nothing about claims C4, C7, C8 or C12 from its own data.; HLA typing resolution is never stated.; GFR is Cockcroft-Gault estimated, not measured, and is a cross-sectional value at each time point among surviving grafts, so the later time points are subject to survivor bias.; Equity findings are about ACCESS only. The authors did not analyse clinical outcomes by racial group, so the claim that HLA-first allocation harms minority recipients rests on waiting time and match rate, not on measured worse graft or patient outcomes in those groups.; Internal inconsistencies in the published tables (see notes) mean some baseline numbers should not be quoted without checking the source PDF.; The interaction of allocation group with year of transplant for graft failure and death was pre-specified in the Methods but its result is never reported, so the key 'is matching losing significance over time' question is left unanswered for the survival outcomes.; Australian/New Zealand deceased-donor practice, modern immunosuppression, universal-access health system - transfer to Iranian practice is by analogy only..

### Isaacson D 2022 — HLA-DQ Mismatches Lead to More Unacceptable Antigens, Greater Sensitization, and Increased Disparities in Repeat Transplant Candidates

Isaacson D 2022, *Journal of the American Society of Nephrology (JASN) 33(12):2293-2305*, [DOI 10.1681/ASN.2022030296](https://doi.org/10.1681/ASN.2022030296). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright (Copyright 2022 by the American Society of Nephrology); PMC deposit, no Creative Commons licence statement found on the PMC page. The PMC full-text API and E-utilities efetch returned no body text (publisher-restricted XML); the full text used here was taken from the PMC article page (pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9731640/) and saved to fulltext/36450598.txt..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult (>=18 y) recipients of a first single deceased- or living-donor kidney transplant in the US SRTR, transplanted 1 Jan 2010 to 2 Mar 2021, who lost the graft (>30 days post-transplant) and were relisted; complete split-level donor/recipient HLA-A/B/C/DR/DQ typing and unacceptable-antigen data required; multi-organ recipients and pre-emptive relisting excluded. 34,891 graft failures -> 6,338 relisted -> 4,867 included. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 4,867 (3,443 deceased-donor and 1,424 living-donor first grafts) |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; multiple linear regression (linear probability models) of per-locus mismatch count (0-2) on new unacceptable antigens corresponding to the previous donor's typing (UA-PD, proxy for de novo DSA), and of UA-PD at each locus on cPRA increase; stratified by donor type and race/ethnicity; DR/DQ interaction models |
| typing resolution | serologic-equivalent antigen level (1-field), split (private) antigen level; broad-typed records excluded; HLA-A/B/C/DR/DQ (DQ = DQB serologic specificities only) |
| outcome | (1) probability of relisting with a new UA-PD at the mismatched locus (proxy for dnDSA); (2) increase in cPRA from pretransplant value to peak after relisting, given a new UA-PD at that locus. No graft-survival or rejection endpoint. |
| follow up | not reported as a median follow-up; median days from graft failure to relisting were 1261 vs 620.5 (deceased donor, with vs without new DQ UA-PD) and 1569 vs 1246 (living donor) (Table 1) |
| other factors modelled | mismatches (0-2) at every other HLA locus (A, B, C, DR, DQ) as covariates, unacceptable antigens at every other locus (cPRA models), pretransplantation cPRA (covariate and 0% / 1-50% / 51-100% strata), time between graft failure and relisting, time between relisting and final follow-up, donor type of the failed graft (deceased vs living; stratified, not pooled), recipient race and ethnicity (African American, Hispanic, White; stratified), HLA-DR x HLA-DQ interaction terms (secondary models) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's locus-ranking question for sensitisation (C4): using 4,867 SRTR patients relisted after a failed first kidney graft, it shows that a DQ mismatch is the mismatch most likely to leave a donor-specific unacceptable antigen behind (25.2% per mismatch after deceased-donor and 28.9% after living-donor grafts, significantly more than every other locus), and that DQ unacceptable antigens raise cPRA as much as or more than any other locus. The DR x DQ interaction models directly address the linkage-disequilibrium objection (C10): DQ effects were largely independent of DR, so DR matching does not substitute for DQ matching. It bears on C11 in three ways: the living-donor stratum showed at least as large DQ effects as the deceased-donor stratum; the effects were greatest in African American and Hispanic recipients (a proxy for allele-frequency divergence between donor and recipient populations); and sensitisation effects were driven by patients unsensitised (cPRA 0%) before transplant, which is exactly the antibody-status-unknown, mostly unsensitised first-transplant population an Iranian living-donor pre-screen would face. Transfer is helped by the typing: all analyses use 1-field serologic-equivalent split-antigen typing with DQ at the DQB serologic level, the same resolution a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen would have, so the DQ effect is demonstrable without two-field typing. Limits on transfer: the outcome is sensitisation after graft loss (a barrier to retransplantation), not graft survival; the cohort is US with US race categories; and the model is a linear probability model of a 0-2 count without a formal test of shape, so it supports weighting DQ but does not settle the shape of the dose-response.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- new HLA-DQ UA-PD at relisting (proxy dnDSA): each additional HLA-DQ mismatch (0-2), deceased-donor first graft — absolute probability increase per mismatch (linear regression, percentage points) 25.2, p=P<0.05 vs each other HLA locus; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Abstract; Results 'Probabilities of New Unacceptable Antigens Corresponding to Previous Donor Typing'; Figure 2A]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD at relisting (proxy dnDSA): each additional HLA-DQ mismatch (0-2), living-donor first graft — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 28.9, p=P<0.05 vs each other HLA locus; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Abstract; Results; Figure 2B]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, deceased donor, African American recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 29.3, p=P<0.05 vs every other locus; P<0.05 vs Hispanic and White recipients; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results 'Probabilities ... by Recipient Race and Ethnicity'; Figure 3A]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, deceased donor, Hispanic recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 24.0, p=significantly different only from HLA-C; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3C]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, deceased donor, White recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 21.6, p=P<0.05 vs HLA-B, -C, -DR; comparable to HLA-A (22.2%); adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3B]
- new HLA-A UA-PD, deceased donor, White recipients: each additional HLA-A mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 22.2; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3B]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, living donor, African American recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 34.1, p=significantly greater than HLA-C only; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3D]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, living donor, Hispanic recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 33.0, p=P<0.05 vs all loci except HLA-A (26.9%); adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3F]
- new HLA-DQ UA-PD, living donor, White recipients: each additional HLA-DQ mismatch — absolute probability increase per mismatch (percentage points) 27.6, p=P<0.05 vs all other loci; adjusted for mismatches at all other HLA loci [Results; Figure 3E]
- cPRA increase (pretransplant to peak after relisting): new HLA-DQ UA-PD vs none, deceased donor, all recipients — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 23.5, p=P<0.05 vs HLA-B, -C, -DR; not vs HLA-A; adjusted for unacceptable antigens at other loci, HLA mismatches (0-2), pretransplant cPRA, time graft failure to relisting, time relisting to follow-up [Abstract; Results 'HLA Unacceptable Antigens and Increases in cPRA'; Figure 4A]
- cPRA increase: new HLA-A UA-PD vs none, deceased donor, all recipients — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 23.1, p=not significantly different from HLA-DQ; adjusted for as above [Abstract; Results; Figure 4A]
- cPRA increase: new HLA-DQ UA-PD vs none, deceased donor, pretransplant cPRA 0% — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 27.9, p=P<0.05 vs HLA-B, -C, -DR; not vs HLA-A (28.3%); adjusted for as above [Results; Figure 4B]
- cPRA increase: new HLA-A UA-PD vs none, deceased donor, pretransplant cPRA 0% — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 28.3; adjusted for as above [Results; Figure 4B]
- cPRA increase: new HLA-DQ UA-PD vs none, living donor, all recipients — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 29.0, p=P<0.05 vs all other HLA loci; adjusted for as above [Abstract; Results; Figure 4E]
- cPRA increase: new HLA-DQ UA-PD vs none, living donor, pretransplant cPRA 0% — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) 33.2, p=P<0.05 vs every other HLA locus; adjusted for as above [Results; Figure 4F]
- cPRA increase, unsensitised deceased-donor recipients by race: new HLA-DQ UA-PD: African American 27.5% (HLA-A 30.6%), Hispanic 23.9%, White 29.9% (HLA-A 25.6%) — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) None, p=AA: P<0.05 vs B, C, DR, not A; Hispanic: P<0.05 vs DR only; White: P<0.05 vs all except A; no significant difference in DQ effect between race groups; adjusted for as above [Results 'by Recipient Race and Ethnicity'; Figure 6A-C]
- cPRA increase, unsensitised living-donor recipients by race: new HLA-DQ UA-PD: African American 30.4% (HLA-A 27.6%), Hispanic 46.1%, White 32.0% — mean absolute cPRA increase (percentage points) None, p=AA: P<0.05 vs all except A; Hispanic and White: P<0.05 vs all other loci; no significant difference in DQ effect between race groups; adjusted for as above [Results; Figure 6D-F]
- probability of HLA-DQ UA-PD (DR x DQ interaction model, deceased donor): 0 DR mismatch + 1 DQ mismatch vs 0 DR + 0 DQ — absolute probability (percentage points) 40.2 (35.0–45.5); adjusted for other loci; DR/DQ interaction term [Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Supplemental Figure 1A; Supplemental Table 3]
- probability of HLA-DR UA-PD (DR x DQ interaction model, deceased donor): 0 DR mismatch + 1 DQ mismatch vs 0 DR + 0 DQ — absolute probability (percentage points) 9.5 (4.1–14.8); adjusted for other loci; DR/DQ interaction term [Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Supplemental Figure 1A]
- probability of HLA-DQ UA-PD (DR x DQ interaction model, deceased donor): 1 DR mismatch + 1 DQ mismatch vs 0 DR + 0 DQ — absolute probability (percentage points) 41.5 (36.3–46.7); adjusted for other loci; DR/DQ interaction term [Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Supplemental Figure 1A]
- probability of HLA-DR UA-PD (DR x DQ interaction model, deceased donor): 1 DR mismatch + 1 DQ mismatch vs 0 DR + 0 DQ — absolute probability (percentage points) 29.0 (23.7–34.2); adjusted for other loci; DR/DQ interaction term [Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Supplemental Figure 1A]

**Dose-response.**

- DQ: per additional mismatch (0-2), deceased donor MM: +25.2 percentage points probability of DQ UA-PD; per additional mismatch (0-2), living donor MM: +28.9 percentage points; 0/1/2 separately MM: not reported; a single linear slope per locus
- A: per additional mismatch MM: numeric value only in Figure 2 for the whole cohort; 22.2% in White deceased-donor recipients and 26.9% in Hispanic living-donor recipients (Figure 3); cPRA increase with A UA-PD 23.1% (deceased donor overall) and 28.3% (unsensitised deceased donor), not distinguishable from DQ
- B: per additional mismatch MM: Figure 2 only; significantly lower than DQ in both donor types
- C: per additional mismatch MM: Figure 2 only; significantly lower than DQ in both donor types
- DR: per additional mismatch MM: Figure 2 only; significantly lower than DQ in both donor types; in the interaction model a DR mismatch raised DR UA-PD probability from 9.5% to 29.0% (deceased donor)
- Shape reported: not reported (linear probability model: one slope per locus for a 0-2 count); linearity tested: not tested; the regression enters each locus mismatch count (0-2) as a single linear term and reports the per-mismatch increment; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR mismatch x HLA-DQ mismatch on DQ UA-PD: largely independent effects of DQ; adding a DR mismatch to an existing DQ mismatch produced only a small absolute increase in DQ UA-PD probability, proportional to the uncertainty of the estimates (deceased donor: DQ UA-PD 40.2% (95% CI 35.0-45.5) with 0 DR + 1 DQ mismatch vs 41.5% (95% CI 36.3-46.7) with 1 DR + 1 DQ mismatch; living-donor analogue in Supplemental Figure 1B (numbers not in text)) [Abstract; Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Discussion para 3; Supplemental Figure 1, Supplemental Table 3]
- HLA-DR UA-PD x HLA-DQ UA-PD on cPRA increase: adding a DR UA-PD to an existing DQ UA-PD resulted in only small changes in overall cPRA; negative interaction term, so the additive effect can be slightly lower than the individual effects (numbers in Supplemental Figures 2-3 and Supplemental Table 4 only) [Results 'Interactions of HLA-DR/DQ'; Discussion]
- donor type (living vs deceased first graft): stratified, not formally tested against each other; DQ mismatch effect on DQ UA-PD 28.9% (living) vs 25.2% (deceased); DQ UA-PD effect on cPRA 29.0% (living) vs 23.5% (deceased); in living-donor recipients DQ exceeded every other locus, whereas in deceased-donor recipients HLA-A was not distinguishable from DQ (P<0.05 vs other loci within each stratum; no between-stratum P reported) [Abstract; Results; Figures 2 and 4]
- recipient race/ethnicity x DQ mismatch on DQ UA-PD: African American deceased-donor recipients more likely than Hispanic and White recipients to develop DQ UA-PD; among living-donor recipients African American and Hispanic more likely than White; no difference between Hispanic and White (deceased) or between African American and Hispanic (living) (deceased donor: 29.3% (AA) vs 24.0% (Hispanic) vs 21.6% (White), P<0.05; living donor: 34.1% (AA), 33.0% (Hispanic) vs 27.6% (White), P<0.05) [Abstract; Results 'Probabilities ... by Recipient Race and Ethnicity'; Figure 3]
- recipient race/ethnicity x DQ UA-PD on cPRA increase: no significant differences in the magnitude of cPRA increase with DQ UA-PD between race/ethnicity groups, overall or in initially unsensitised recipients (not significant (P>=0.05)) [Results; Figures 5 and 6]
- pretransplant sensitisation (cPRA 0% vs 1-50% vs 51-100%) x UA-PD on cPRA increase: effects driven by initially unsensitised recipients (63.1% deceased, 72.8% living); in previously sensitised strata results were less consistent (smaller samples) but no locus had a significantly greater effect than DQ (unsensitised: DQ 27.9% (deceased), 33.2% (living)) [Results; Discussion; Figure 4B-D, F-H]
- time from graft failure to relisting and relisting to follow-up: no effect on overall sensitisation in the adjusted models; UA-PD effects on cPRA were largely independent of overall HLA mismatches and these intervals (Supplemental Table 2 (numbers not in text)) [Results; Discussion para 2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C4* — "Each additional HLA-DQ mismatch increased the probability of relisting with an HLA-DQ UA-PD by 25.2% in deceased donor recipients and 28.9% in living donor recipients." (Results, 'Probabilities of New Unacceptable Antigens Corresponding to Previous Donor Typing', para 1)
- *C10* — "Models evaluating interactions between HLA-DR/DQ mismatches revealed largely independent effects of HLA-DQ mismatches on HLA-DQ UA-PD." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "In living donor recipients (Figure 4, E–H), DQ UA-PD resulted in an average overall cPRA increase of 29.0%, significantly greater than all other HLA loci (P<0.05, Figure 4E)." (Results, 'HLA Unacceptable Antigens and Increases in cPRA', para 2)
- *C6* — "patients who developed new HLA-DQ UA-PD experienced mean overall cPRA increases of 23.5%, significantly greater than HLA-B, -C, and -DR but not HLA-A (23.1%, Figure 4A)." (Results, 'HLA Unacceptable Antigens and Increases in cPRA', para 2)
- *C11* — "Both African American and Hispanic living donor recipients were more likely to be relisted with new DQ UA-PD compared with White recipients (P<0.05)." (Results, 'Probabilities of New Unacceptable Antigens by Recipient Race and Ethnicity', para 3)
- *C12* — "Our analyses were reliant on low-resolution, serologic-equivalent HLA typing, in which multiple common HLA alleles are indistinguishable within antigenic groups." (Discussion, limitations paragraph)

**Limitations.** Outcome is a proxy: a new unacceptable antigen matching the previous donor's typing stands in for de novo DSA; listing of unacceptable antigens depends on centre practice and the SRTR records no DSA, ABMR or biopsy data; Selected population: only relisted patients (6,338 of 34,891 graft failures, 18.2%) and 4,867 of those; not representative of all graft losses, and no graft-survival or rejection endpoint is analysed; Registry, retrospective; unmeasured confounders including immunosuppression withdrawal after graft failure (not recorded in SRTR); Typing is 1-field serologic-equivalent antigen level; DQ is DQB serologic specificity only (no DQA1, no allele-level, no eplet analysis); apparent antigen matches may be allelic mismatches; cross-reactive-group contributions to cPRA could not be separated; Linear probability models with a single 0-2 mismatch slope per locus; no test of linearity, no 0/1/2 categories, no total-count model; 95% CIs are printed only for the DR x DQ interaction scenarios, and per-locus estimates for HLA-A/B/C/DR are shown only in Figures 2-6; Living vs deceased donor strata are analysed separately without a formal test of the difference between them; HLA-A's large cPRA effect may be an artefact of the high frequency of HLA-A2 (48% of US donors); only seven DQ serologic specificities exist, which may cap the DQ effect in already-sensitised patients; US cohort with SRTR self-declared race/ethnicity categories; Asian/Pacific Islander and other groups too small to analyse; transfer to Iranian allele frequencies is by analogy only.

### Lee H 2022 — Combined Analysis of HLA Class II Eplet Mismatch and Tacrolimus Levels for the Prediction of De Novo Donor Specific Antibody Development in Kidney Transplant Recipients

Lee H 2022, *International Journal of Molecular Sciences*, [DOI 10.3390/ijms23137357](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23137357). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (MDPI open access; licence string not printed in the retrieved PMC text, inferred from publisher).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult kidney transplant recipients without pre-transplant DSA, single centre (Seoul St. Mary's Hospital, Korea), consecutive transplants December 2016 - December 2020 |
| donor type | both |
| n | 347 analysed (415 consecutive KTs enrolled, 68 excluded for pre-transplant DSA with MFI>1000); tacrolimus sub-analysis n=175 (>=3 TAC measurements); HLA-DQ subgroup n=295 (HLA-mismatched only) |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; ROC/Youden-derived eplet thresholds, Kaplan-Meier with log-rank, Cox proportional-hazards univariate and multivariable (4 covariates) |
| typing resolution | two-field (high-resolution) SSO typing of HLA-DRB1, DQB1 and DQA1; DRB3/4/5 NOT typed; the traditional antigen-mismatch analysis counted mismatches at split-antigen level |
| outcome | de novo HLA class II DSA (against DRB1/DQB1/DQA1, single-antigen bead MFI>1000, monitored at 1, 3, 6, 12 months then yearly); secondary outcome biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR). No graft-survival endpoint. |
| follow up | median 20.3 months for dnDSA monitoring (95% CI 18.5-22.2) |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, sex, induction type (basiliximab vs thymoglobulin), ABO compatibility, time-weighted tacrolimus trough level (TAC-C0, 5 ng/mL cut-off), tacrolimus time-weighted coefficient of variability (TWCV, 20% cut-off) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a threshold paper: it asks not whether HLA class II mismatch matters but at what molecular load it starts to matter, and it derives four different HLA-DQ cut-offs (single-molecule eplet >=10, total eplet >=12, antibody-verified eplet >=4, antibody-verified single-molecule eplet >=4) on one 347-patient cohort, which speaks directly to review question C12 on whether molecular mismatch behaves as a threshold or as a smooth dose-response. Its most transferable finding for a pre-screen is the contrast inside the same cohort between the antigen-level and the eplet-level gradient: at split-antigen level only the zero-mismatch group separated (0 vs 1-2 p=0.035, 0 vs 3-4 p=0.005) while 1-2 and 3-4 antigen mismatches were statistically indistinguishable, whereas eplet load did separate intermediate from high risk - i.e. a counted antigen mismatch score saturates after the first mismatch in a DR/DQ dnDSA model. Because DSA-positive patients were excluded at baseline, this is a genuinely antibody-negative starting population, which matches an Iranian pre-screen where donor-specific antibody status will usually be unknown or presumed negative. Transfer is nevertheless limited in the direction that matters most to us: the entire eplet machinery here rests on verified two-field typing of DRB1, DQA1 and DQB1, and the authors explicitly claim high-resolution typing as their methodological advance over prior eplet work precisely because low- or intermediate-resolution typing must be imputed from population allele and haplotype frequencies - imputation the authors say they avoided, and that an Iranian one-field pre-screen could not avoid and could not calibrate, since Korean and Iranian haplotype frequencies differ. The cohort mixes living and deceased donors without reporting the split in the retrieved text, so the paper cannot be read as living-donor-specific evidence, and its outcome is dnDSA at a median 20 months rather than graft failure. It is also the clearest paper in this set for C11 effect modification by drug exposure: the same eplet load carries a very different dnDSA hazard depending on whether the tacrolimus trough sits above or below 5 ng/mL, which means any static HLA risk score - ours included - is describing a hazard that post-transplant immunosuppression can substantially move.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA class II dnDSA (incidence): whole cohort — proportion 7.2; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.1 (25/347 patients)]
- biopsy-proven ABMR (incidence): whole cohort — proportion 5.8; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.1 (20/347); the Discussion restates the same 20 recipients as 5.7% - internal inconsistency]
- HLA class II dnDSA: mean number of HLA class II antigen mismatches, dnDSA developers (2.4 +/- 0.9) vs non-developers (1.9 +/- 1.2) — group means (Mann-Whitney) 0.5, p=0.018; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.1]
- dnDSA-free survival: traditional HLA-DR/DQ split-antigen mismatch level, three categories (0 vs 1-2 vs 3-4), overall test — log-rank p only (no HR reported) None, p=0.016; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.2]
- dnDSA-free survival: 0 HLA-DR/DQ antigen mismatches vs intermediate (1-2) — log-rank p only (no HR reported) None, p=0.035; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.2]
- dnDSA-free survival: 0 HLA-DR/DQ antigen mismatches vs high (3-4) — log-rank p only (no HR reported) None, p=0.005; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.2]
- dnDSA-free survival: intermediate (1-2) vs high (3-4) HLA-DR/DQ antigen mismatches — no statistical difference (no p printed) None; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.2 and Discussion para 3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DR single molecular eplet mismatch, threshold >7 — AUC 0.7; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DQ single molecular eplet mismatch, threshold >9 — AUC 0.77; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DR total eplet mismatch, threshold >13 — AUC 0.59; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DQ total eplet mismatch, threshold >9 (second-stage cut-off >11) — AUC 0.73; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DR antibody-verified eplet mismatch, threshold >2 — AUC 0.61; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DQ antibody-verified eplet mismatch, threshold >1 (second-stage cut-off >3) — AUC 0.72; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DR antibody-verified single molecular eplet mismatch, threshold >2 — AUC 0.68; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- HLA class II dnDSA (discrimination): HLA-DQ antibody-verified single molecular eplet mismatch, threshold >1 (second-stage cut-off >3) — AUC 0.73; adjusted for unadjusted ROC, Youden index [Results 2.3]
- dnDSA-free survival: single molecular eplet risk categories (low/intermediate/high), overall — log-rank p only None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.4; printed as < 0.001]
- dnDSA-free survival: total eplet risk categories, high vs intermediate — log-rank p only None, p=0.002; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.4]
- dnDSA-free survival: total eplet risk categories, high vs low — log-rank p only None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.4; printed as < 0.001]
- dnDSA-free survival: antibody-verified eplet risk categories, high vs low — log-rank p only None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.4]
- dnDSA-free survival: antibody-verified single molecular risk categories, high vs low — log-rank p only None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.4; printed as < 0.001]

- ABMR-free survival: antibody-verified single molecular, high vs low risk — log-rank p only None, p=0.037; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 2.9]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 HLA-DR/DQ split-antigen mismatches MM: reference (best dnDSA-free survival); 1-2 (pooled, 'intermediate') MM: worse than 0, log-rank p=0.035; no HR reported; 3-4 (pooled, 'high') MM: worse than 0, log-rank p=0.005; NOT different from 1-2
- DR: no antigen-level 0/1/2 series reported. Eplet ranges: single molecular 0-20, total 0-45, antibody-verified 0-14, antibody-verified single molecular 0-7. ROC cut-offs >7, >13, >2, >2 with AUC 0.70, 0.59, 0.61, 0.68. No second-stage DR cut-off could be identified in either the single molecular or the total eplet analysis. The authors state HLA-DRB1 played little or no role because only 6 patients developed DR-DSA.
- DQ: no antigen-level 0/1/2 series reported. Eplet ranges: single molecular 0-21, total 0-29, antibody-verified 0-11, antibody-verified single molecular 0-11. First-stage ROC cut-offs >9, >9, >1, >1 with AUC 0.77, 0.73, 0.72, 0.73; second-stage cut-offs within the high group >9, >11, >3, >3, giving the abstract's four high-risk definitions DQ>=10, DQ>=12, DQ>=4 and DQ>=4.
- DQ_subgroup: in the HLA-mismatched DQ-dnDSA subgroup (n=295) the ROC cut-offs shifted to >9, >11, >2 and >2 with AUC 0.72, 0.68, 0.67 and 0.68 - i.e. two of the four thresholds moved when the endpoint and denominator changed.
- Shape reported: threshold / step - and two different shapes in the same cohort. At split-antigen level the dose-response is a single step: a zero-mismatch premium (0 vs 1-2 p=0.035, 0 vs 3-4 p=0.005) and then a flat plateau, with 1-2 and 3-4 antigen mismatches statistically indistinguishable. At eplet level the risk categories did separate intermediate from high, but only above the DQ cut-offs; in the single molecular analysis the low and intermediate eplet categories were themselves not significantly different, so the eplet response is also a step (below-threshold vs above-threshold) rather than a graded slope.; linearity tested: not tested. No continuous-eplet model, no trend test, no spline, no interaction test is reported anywhere in the paper. Every mismatch variable was dichotomised or trichotomised at ROC/Youden-derived cut-points, and the cut-points were derived and evaluated in the same 347-patient cohort with 25 events - so the thresholds carry optimism bias and no internal or external validation is presented. The only 'shape' evidence is the pattern of pairwise log-rank p values between adjacent categories.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA class II eplet mismatch load x time-weighted tacrolimus trough (TAC-C0, cut-off 5 ng/mL): the paper's central claim. Four groups were formed by crossing low/high eplet mismatch with TAC-C0 above/below 5 ng/mL; group 4 (high eplet mismatch + low TAC-C0) had the worst dnDSA-free survival and the highest adjusted hazard ratio in every analysis. In the whole cohort the group-4 HR reached 16.10 (single molecular) and in the HLA-DQ subgroup 8.03 (95% CI 2.62-24.66). (whole cohort single molecular: group 3 HR 9.14, group 4 HR 16.10 vs group 1. DQ subgroup: group 3 HR 3.77 (1.41-10.09, p=0.008), group 4 HR 8.03 (2.62-24.66, p<0.001)) [Results 2.5, 2.7, 2.8; Abstract]
- HLA class II eplet mismatch load x tacrolimus time-weighted coefficient of variability (TWCV, cut-off 20%): REPORTED INCONSISTENTLY. The Abstract states 'No significant combined effect was observed in dnDSA development according to TWCV', but Results 2.6, 2.7 and 2.8 report significant log-rank separations and significant adjusted HRs for the TWCV four-group models (whole cohort HRs up to 13.72; DQ subgroup single molecular group 3 HR 5.17, 95% CI 1.79-14.85, p=0.002). The Discussion sides with the Results ('eplet mismatch load and low TAC-T0 or high TWCV had a combined effect'). Treat the abstract sentence as unreliable and cite the Results numbers. (DQ subgroup, single molecular x TWCV: group 3 HR 5.17 (1.79-14.85, p=0.002), group 4 HR 4.16 (1.39-12.47, p=0.011); total eplet x TWCV: group 3 HR 4.56 (1.57-13.26, p=0.005), group 4 HR 3.42 (1.17-9.97, p=0.024). Only 2 of 4 eplet methods showed the effect in the DQ subgroup.) [Abstract vs Results 2.6/2.7/2.8 vs Discussion para 6]
- Wiebe et al. published HLA-DQ thresholds x this cohort (external threshold transportability): when the authors imported Wiebe's single-molecule HLA-DQ cut-offs (low <=8, intermediate 9-14, high >=15) instead of their own, the categories still correlated with class II dnDSA (p=0.005) and high vs low remained significant (p<0.001), but intermediate vs high was NOT significant (p=0.263) and the combined tacrolimus effect disappeared entirely ('the significance was lost in the tacrolimus trough level and TWCV analysis (data not shown)'). The authors attribute their own lower cut-offs to not typing DRB3/4/5, ethnic variation in HLA typing, a smaller cohort and a different HLA Matchmaker version (3.1 vs 2.0). (overall p=0.005; high (DQ>=15) vs low (DQ<=8) p<0.001; low vs intermediate p=0.005; intermediate vs high p=0.263) [Discussion para 2]
- antigen-level mismatch x eplet-level mismatch (complementarity rather than statistical interaction): no formal interaction was tested, but the authors argue the two scales carry different information: antigen mismatch separated 0 from any mismatch and then plateaued, whereas eplet load separated intermediate from high inside the mismatched population. They propose combining both to find high-dnDSA-risk patients among those with moderate or high antigen mismatch who 'are difficult to distinguish using the conventional HLA Ag mismatch method'. (no interaction estimate reported) [Discussion para 3]
- eplet mismatch method x eplet mismatch method (head-to-head): the four methods (single molecular, total, antibody-verified, antibody-verified single molecular) gave concordant results and no method was superior; the authors conclude the choice 'would be made according to familiarity and availability, as no evidence of superiority of one method over the others exists'. DQ AUCs were close (0.77, 0.73, 0.72, 0.73) and all exceeded the corresponding DR AUCs (0.70, 0.59, 0.61, 0.68). (DQ AUC range 0.72-0.77 vs DR AUC range 0.59-0.70) [Results 2.3, Discussion final paragraph]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "A high level of mismatch for single molecular eplet (DQ ≥ 10), total eplet (DQ ≥ 12), Ab-verified eplet (DQ ≥ 4), and Ab-verified single molecular eplet (DQ ≥ 4) significantly correlated with HLA class II dnDSA development." (Abstract)
- *C12* — "However, there was no statistical difference in dnDSA-free survival between the intermediate (1–2 mismatches) and high-risk (3–4 mismatches) groups." (Results 2.2, Traditional HLA DR/DQ Antigen Mismatch)
- *C12* — "Eplet analysis of low- or intermediate-resolution typing may present with inaccuracies caused by imputational methods that utilize general-population-based allele and haplotype frequencies" (Discussion, paragraph 4)
- *C12* — "We used different cut-off values for eplet mismatch risk compared to those used by Wiebe et al." (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C11* — "the tendency for worst dnDSA-free survival was observed in groups with high eplet mismatch and low TAC-T0 or high TWCV, and highest dnDSA-free survival was observed in groups with low eplet mismatch and high TAC-T0 or low TWCV" (Discussion, paragraph 6)
- *C11* — "Finally, most of the DSA detected in our group was the DQ locus. HLA-DRB1 plays little or no role in patient risk stratification, as only six patients developed DSA against HLA-DR." (Discussion, limitations paragraph)

**Limitations.** Very few events: only 25 class II dnDSA in 347 patients (7.2%) and 20 ABMR, of which only 6 were DR-DSA. Every hazard ratio in the paper rests on this event count, which is why the confidence intervals in the DQ subgroup are so wide (e.g. 2.62-24.66).; Cut-points were derived by ROC/Youden and then evaluated in the same cohort, with a second ROC pass inside the already-selected high-mismatch group. No internal validation (bootstrap, cross-validation) and no external cohort. The four DQ thresholds in the abstract are therefore optimistic and should not be transported as fixed decision rules.; Linearity was never tested. No continuous eplet model, no trend test, no spline, no formal interaction p-value anywhere in the paper - the 'combined effect' is inferred from four-group comparisons and from HRs sharing a single reference group.; Short follow-up: median 20.3 months for dnDSA monitoring. The authors concede this made chronic ABMR association hard to detect. There is no graft-survival or graft-failure endpoint at all, so nothing in this paper speaks to C1 or C2 for hard outcomes.; HLA-DRB3/4/5 was not typed, which the authors themselves call a major limitation and the likely reason their thresholds sit lower than Wiebe's. DQ eplet loads are therefore computed on an incomplete class II picture.; The multivariable model carries only four covariates (age, sex, induction type, ABO compatibility) to avoid overfitting. Donor age, cold ischaemia, donor type, PRA level, retransplant status and CYP3A5 genotype are not adjusted for; the authors flag CYP3A5 explicitly.; The tacrolimus analyses use a subset (n=175 with >=3 TAC measurements), not the full 347, and the retrieved text never states how many of that subset had low TAC-C0 or high TWCV.; Living vs deceased donor split is never given in the retrieved text (Table 1 was not retrieved). The paper cannot be used as living-donor-specific evidence.; Single centre, single ethnicity (Korean). The authors invoke 'ethnic variations in HLA typing' as the reason their cut-offs differ from a Canadian cohort's - the same argument applies with equal force to transporting either set of cut-offs to Iran.; Internal inconsistencies in the text: the abstract says no significant combined effect for TWCV while the Results report significant TWCV HRs; ABMR is 5.8% in Results 2.1 and 5.7% in the Discussion; the antibody-verified single molecular TAC-C0 HRs (9.14, 16.10) are numerically identical to the single molecular ones, which looks like a copy error; and Results 2.2 says 0 mismatches had 'significantly lower dnDSA-free survival' where the figure legend and the whole argument say higher.; Numbers reported only in tables/figures were not recoverable from the PMC full text: confidence intervals and p-values for all whole-cohort multivariable HRs, the exact definitions of TAC/TWCV groups 2 and 3, and Table 1 baseline characteristics. Two whole-cohort HRs are printed as bare integers ('10', '13') and are probably truncated decimals..

### Lemieux W 2022 — Dissecting the impact of molecular T-cell HLA mismatches in kidney transplant failure: A retrospective cohort study

Lemieux W 2022, *Frontiers in Immunology*, [DOI 10.3389/fimmu.2022.1067075](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2022.1067075). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (Frontiers standard licence; no explicit licence statement in the retrieved PMC text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First kidney-alone transplant recipients in the US SRTR, transplanted 1 Jan 2000 - 1 Jan 2015. Multi-organ transplants, prior transplants, primary graft non-function, and anyone with peak PRA above 0% or missing PRA were excluded, so the cohort is deliberately unsensitised. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 118,309 donor:recipient pairs |
| design | Retrospective registry cohort. Per-TcEMM multivariable Accelerated Failure Time (Weibull) models (Cox rejected because proportional hazards was violated for some TcEMM), Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control, then Lasso-penalised Cox regression with 10-fold cross-validation and post-selection inference for feature selection, plus WGCNA for co-expression. |
| typing resolution | Serologic/antigen-level SRTR types imputed to allele level (two-field) with the NMDP algorithm; HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1 and -DQB1 only. HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DQA1, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were unavailable. PIRCHE-II v3.2 on IMGT/HLA v3.46. |
