| outcome | death-censored graft failure (return to dialysis or re-transplantation) |
| follow up | median 6.39 years (IQR 3.12-10.01); 19,945 DCGF events (~17%) at a median of 3.12 years (IQR 1.42-6.54); administratively censored 31 May 2015 |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, recipient sex, time on dialysis, insurance coverage, recipient HLA-DRB1 (as presenting molecule), donor age, donor sex, donor type, transplant era, induction agent, calcineurin inhibitor type, steroid use, cold ischaemia time, donor-recipient weight ratio |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper sits at the far end of ANGLE H's 'how was HLA coded' axis: instead of a total antigen mismatch count or per-locus terms, the donor-recipient incompatibility is decomposed into 1,935 binary predicted T-cell epitope (PIRCHE-II) features, and a Lasso with post-selection inference is used to find which ones actually carry the graft-failure signal. It therefore answers the review's question about feature-selection alternatives to count-based HLA coding, and it demonstrates that a molecular mismatch load does predict death-censored graft failure in a large modern registry cohort (adjusted HR 1.14 per unit of log PIRCHE-II score, adjusted for era, induction, CNI and steroid use). Its transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown Iranian pre-screen is however almost entirely cautionary. The exposure requires two-field allele-level typing that Iranian one-field data cannot supply, and the authors' own workaround - NMDP imputation from serologic types - is named as a limitation, with the absence of DRB3/4/5, DQA1, DPA1 and DPB1 flagged as a source of under- or over-estimation of the mismatch; this is direct evidence for C12's low-resolution misclassification and imputation-accuracy concerns. The cohort is also the wrong side of the antibody question for an antibody-unknown pre-screen: everyone with peak PRA above 0% was excluded, so the result speaks only to unsensitised recipients and says nothing about how molecular mismatch behaves when antibody status is unknown. Donor type was only a covariate and no living-donor result is reported, so the paper cannot be used to argue anything specific about living donation, and it reports no antigen-count or per-locus dose-response at all, so it cannot inform C2, C3, C5, C6 or C9. Its practical message for the Iranian pre-screen is the authors' own: the individual TcEMM findings are not ready for clinical use and would need allele-level genotypes to apply.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: per one-unit increase in log-transformed PIRCHE-II score (score+1 log-transformed), univariable — HR 1.16 (1.14–1.17); adjusted for none (univariable AFT, Weibull) [Results, first paragraph]
- death-censored graft failure: per one-unit increase in log-transformed PIRCHE-II score (score+1 log-transformed), multivariable — HR 1.14 (1.12–1.15); adjusted for recipient age, sex, time on dialysis, insurance coverage, recipient HLA-DRB1; donor age, sex, type; transplant era, induction agent, calcineurin inhibitor type, steroid use, cold ischaemia time, donor-recipient weight ratio [Results, first paragraph]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: Not tested. The functional form was imposed, not examined: the PIRCHE-II score was log-transformed after adding 1 'in accordance with previous studies with PIRCHE-II score', so the reported HR is per unit of log score and implies a diminishing-returns (concave) relation on the raw score scale, but no spline, categorical or trend test was fitted to justify it. Individual TcEMMs were modelled as binary present/absent, so no per-feature dose-response exists. The proportional hazards assumption was tested and found violated for some TcEMMs, which is why AFT (Weibull) models replaced Cox; AIC was used to pick the distribution. That is a check on the survival model, not on the shape of the mismatch effect.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "log-transformed PIRCHE-II scores were associated with an increased risk for DCGF, with significant HRs of 1.16 (95% Confidence Interval [95%CI] = 1.14-1.17) and 1.14 (95%CI = 1.12-1.15) for univariable and multivariable models, respectively" (Results, first paragraph)
- *C12* — "Allele-level HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, and -DQB1 genotypes were imputed using the National Marrow Donor Program algorithm as previously described" (Methods, HLA typing and PIRCHE-II assignment)
- *C12* — "Of these, 56 Class I and 30 Class II derived TcEMM were significant by the post-selection inference test." (Results, Dissecting TcEMM most predictive of DCGF risk)
- *C12* — "Unavailability of HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DQA1, -DPA1, and -DPB1 could lead to under- or over-estimation of TcEMM." (Discussion, limitations)
- *C12* — "the TcEMM estimation is dependent on IMGT/HLA version considered and in the case of our analytic cohort relies on imputation" (Discussion, limitations)
- *C12* — "While TcEMM is not ready for clinical application, our observations provide the foundation for future studies" (Discussion, conclusion paragraph)

**Limitations.** Exposure is a predicted, not a measured, quantity: PIRCHE-II peptides are theoretical T-cell epitopes and the authors state there is currently no direct measure of response to TcEMM, so immunogenicity is unverified.; HLA types were imputed from serologic (antigen-level) SRTR data with the NMDP algorithm rather than genotyped at allele level; the authors name imputation as a limitation and note it matters more for Class II than Class I.; HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DQA1, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were unavailable, which the authors say could under- or over-estimate TcEMM; the recipient presenting molecule was restricted to HLA-DRB1 alone.; The TcEMM set is version-dependent: moving from IMGT/HLA 3.46 to 3.47 changed 144 TcEMMs, although this touched only 171 pairs (0.14%) of the cohort.; No external or internal validation cohort; the authors say validation may be challenging because rare peptide identity varies between cohorts, and rare high-risk TcEMMs give imprecise estimates.; Severe multiple-testing and collinearity burden: 1,935 correlated features, 38.14% of them inside highly co-expressed profiles, so the Lasso-selected feature may be a proxy rather than the causal one - the authors say so explicitly.; Individual TcEMM hazard ratios are shown only in Figures 2 and 3 and a supplementary file; no numeric per-TcEMM estimate or CI is recoverable from the retrieved text.; Selection restricts generalisability: peak PRA above 0%, missing PRA, retransplants, multi-organ recipients and primary non-function were all excluded, so the cohort is unsensitised first-graft recipients only.; No antigen-level mismatch count, per-locus (A/B/C/DR/DQ) or 0/1/2 mismatch analysis is reported, so the paper cannot speak to conventional HLA matching dose-response.; No effect-modification or subgroup analysis at all - no living versus deceased donor, sensitisation, age, ethnicity, cold ischaemia or era interaction is reported.; Registry data: immunosuppression is captured only at baseline, adherence and longitudinal exposure are unknown, and the authors call for prospective multicentre cohorts with longitudinal immunosuppression data.; One author is an employee of PIRCHE AG, which commercialises the PIRCHE web portal..

### Mohammadzadeh S 2022 — Evaluation of the Iranian panel reactive antibody calculator and potential usefulness: A retrospective study.

Mohammadzadeh S 2022, *Clin Transplant*, [DOI 10.1111/ctr.14789](https://doi.org/10.1111/ctr.14789). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley, Clinical Transplantation 2022;36(11):e14789). convert_article_ids returned no PMC id, so no open-access full text was retrievable; all quotes below are from the PubMed abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Two sets at Shiraz Transplant Center, Iran: (a) 523 deceased Iranian kidney donors whose HLA typing was used to estimate the reference allele and haplotype frequencies; (b) 100 sensitised adults on the kidney waiting list with a determined anti-HLA antibody profile, in whom cPRA was computed by each calculator. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 523 deceased donors (frequency panel); 100 sensitised waiting-list candidates (cPRA comparison) |
| design | Retrospective methodological / validation study. Allele and haplotype frequencies estimated from the deceased-donor typing pool; cPRA generated with the OPTN (UNOS) formula; the resulting Iranian calculator compared against the UNOS and Canadian Transplant Registry online calculators in the same 100 sensitised candidates; a second, frequency-free method (a script filtering the donor pool by the candidate's unacceptable antigens) compared against the formula by Lin's concordance correlation coefficient. No survival analysis and no comparison group of transplanted patients. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract. The abstract does not name the loci typed, the number of fields, or the typing platform, and no full text was retrievable to check. The companion report from the same centre (Jamshidian Tehrani, Int J Organ Transplant Med 2021, PMID 34987737, PMC8717962) states that its donor set had 'HLA typing results for A, B, and DR locus', which is indirect evidence that routine deceased-donor typing at this centre covered A, B and DR only; that statement is from the companion paper, NOT from this one. |
| outcome | calculated PRA (cPRA) value in sensitised candidates; agreement of the Iranian calculator with the UNOS and CTR calculators; agreement between cPRA(frequency) and cPRA(filtering). No clinical outcome (no graft survival, rejection, DSA or crossmatch outcome). |
| follow up | not applicable - no clinical follow-up; this is a calculator-development and agreement study |
| other factors modelled | ethnicity / population heterogeneity of the reference donor panel (Iranian vs UNOS vs Canadian), method of cPRA computation (OPTN frequency formula vs donor-filtering script) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review for discovery angle G (Iran and the region) and it answers only one question: what HLA reference data actually exist for the Iranian donor population, and how they are used operationally. It is the closest thing found to a published Iranian deceased-donor HLA allele and haplotype frequency panel built for allocation and virtual crossmatch, which is exactly the input a national matching tool would need for cPRA, haplotype-frequency imputation, or expected-mismatch calculations. It answers none of the review's dose-response questions (C1-C12): there is no graft outcome, no mismatch count, no hazard ratio, and no per-locus comparison anywhere in the paper. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is therefore indirect and partial. The frequency panel was derived from deceased donors, while the Iranian programme is dominated by living unrelated donation, so the panel is a proxy of unproven fit for living-donor pools; and because our pre-screen assumes antibody status is unknown, the paper's entire subject matter (cPRA, unacceptable antigens, virtual crossmatch) sits downstream of where our tool operates. Its most usable contributions to us are three: it establishes that a usable Iranian donor HLA frequency estimate exists at all, it demonstrates that a frequency-free donor-filtering script reproduces the formula-based answer almost exactly (CCC 0.98), which is the cheaper and more maintainable architecture for a small national pool, and its companion paper documents that routinely available Iranian donor typing may cover only A, B and DR, which directly constrains what loci any Iranian matching tool can assume are present.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- agreement between cPRA computed by the OPTN frequency formula and cPRA computed by the donor-filtering script, in 100 sensitised candidates: cPRA(frequency) vs cPRA(filtering), same candidates — Lin's concordance correlation coefficient 0.98; adjusted for not applicable (agreement statistic, unadjusted) [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - the paper contains no mismatch-count variable and no outcome model, so there is nothing whose shape could be tested; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- reference-population ethnicity x cPRA calculator: Allele frequencies differed between the Iranian, UNOS and Canadian donor panels because the underlying populations differ, but the cPRA values those calculators produced for the same 100 sensitised Iranian candidates did not differ significantly. The authors set out expecting ethnicity to modify the cPRA and report a null. (no significant difference between the Iranian, UNOS and Canadian calculators; no test statistic, effect size, confidence interval or equivalence margin is given in the abstract) [Abstract, Introduction sentence 2 and Results sentences 1-2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "The allele and haplotype frequencies of the Iranian donor pool were estimated using the HLA typing of 523 deceased Iranian kidney donors." (Abstract, Methods sentence 1)
- *C15* — "Variable allelic frequencies were obtained from population heterogeneity in each calculator's donor panel." (Abstract, Results sentence 1)
- *C15* — "those calculators can differ based on the ethnicity to which they are applied" (Abstract, Introduction sentence 2)
- *C15* — "no significant changes in cPRA were identified between the Iranian calculator, UNOS, and the Canadian online calculators" (Abstract, Results sentence 2)
- *C15* — "Lin's concordance correlation coefficient of .98 showed that cPRA (freq) and cPRA (filter) values had almost perfect agreement." (Abstract, Results sentence 3)
- *C13* — "The donor filtering method was more useful because of factors like cost and flexibility." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence 2)

**Limitations.** The paper reports no graft outcome of any kind - no survival, rejection, DSA or crossmatch result - and no HLA mismatch variable. It therefore cannot support any claim about whether or how much HLA mismatch matters (C1-C12); it is admissible for C15 and, weakly, C13 only.; Abstract only. No PMC record exists, so the actual allele and haplotype frequency tables, the loci typed, the number of fields, the typing platform, the haplotype-estimation method (EM/expectation-maximisation or otherwise) and any confidence intervals could not be inspected. Every quantitative detail of the frequency panel - the part of the paper most useful to this review - is unverified.; The frequency panel rests on 523 deceased donors from a single centre (Shiraz). That is small for haplotype-frequency estimation, especially at three or more loci, and rare alleles will be poorly estimated or absent. No sampling or representativeness analysis is reported in the abstract.; Iran is ethnically heterogeneous (Persian, Azeri, Kurd, Lur, Arab, Baloch, Turkmen and others). The abstract reports a single national panel and gives no subpopulation breakdown, yet the paper's own premise is that population differences change allele frequencies. A single 523-donor Shiraz panel may not represent the country.; The panel is deceased-donor. The Iranian programme is dominated by living unrelated donation, and the paper offers no evidence that deceased-donor allele and haplotype frequencies match the living-donor pool.; The headline comparison is a null in 100 sensitised candidates with no test statistic, no confidence interval and no pre-specified equivalence margin reported in the abstract. 'No significant difference' at n=100 is weak evidence of true equivalence between the Iranian, UNOS and CTR calculators, and it is reported as though it confirmed equivalence.; cPRA measures recipient sensitisation against a donor pool. It is an antibody quantity, not a mismatch quantity, so nothing in this paper speaks to mismatch burden or to an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen.; Single centre, retrospective, no external validation of the calculator against observed crossmatch or transplant results..

### Seitz A 2022 — Isolated Pre-existing HLA-DP Donor-Specific Antibodies are Associated With Poorer Outcomes in Renal Transplantation

Seitz A 2022, *Kidney Int Rep*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ekir.2022.07.014](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2022.07.014). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY-NC-ND (Kidney Int Rep is fully open access); the licence statement itself was not present in the retrieved PMC text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult renal transplant recipients, single centre (St James's University Hospital, Leeds, UK), transplanted January 2013 - February 2020. 1355 adult kidney transplants performed in the era; 114 analysed in four groups: 23 with isolated pre-existing HLA-DP DSA (DPDSA), 18 with non-donor-specific HLA-DP antibodies (DPnDSA), 27 highly sensitised with cRF > 85% and no HLA-DP antibodies (HSP), 46 contemporaneous standard-immunological-risk controls matched 2:1 to DPDSA by donor type. Excluded: historical DSA not present in the time-of-offer sample, regrafts repeating previous mismatches, ABO-incompatible and all other HLA antibody incompatible transplants. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 114 analysed (23 DPDSA, 18 DPnDSA, 27 HSP, 46 control), drawn from 1355 adult kidney transplants; predominantly deceased donor - the paper states there was only 1 living donor in the DPDSA group |
| design | retrospective single-centre observational cohort with three comparison groups; Kaplan-Meier survival estimates and univariable then multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Final multivariable models contained patient group, % cRF, BFXM positivity and regraft status. |
| typing resolution | molecular typing to UK allocation scheme requirements (minimum HLA-A, B, C, DRB1, DRB3/4/5, DQB1 until September 2019; HLA-DQA1, DPB1 and DPA1 added from September 2019). For DPDSA pairs, donor and recipient HLA-DPB1 and HLA-DPA1 were confirmed by reverse SSO (LABType) to separate DPA1 from DPB1 DSA. HLA-A/B/DR mismatch reported only at antigen level as UK NHSBT mismatch levels 1-4. |
| outcome | biopsy-proven antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR)-free survival (primary); overall rejection-free survival (ABMR + TCMR + mixed); death-censored graft survival; Banff 2017 biopsy lesion scores (microvascular inflammation, C4d, transplant glomerulopathy cg, tubular atrophy, fibrosis); eGFR at 3 months, 1 year, 3 years |
| follow up | median 1197 days (range 1-2517) |
| other factors modelled | calculated reaction frequency (cRF) > 85%, B-cell flow crossmatch (BFXM) positivity, regraft / retransplant status, delayed graft function, high calcineurin inhibitor variability > 3 months post-transplant, donor type (DBD/DCD/living), cold ischaemia time (described, not modelled), augmented immunosuppression (described, not modelled), inferred donor HLA-DPB1 expression level (rs9277534G, rs2281389A/G), HLA-DPB1 epitope mismatch (HLAMatchmaker 84DEAV, 96R), DPB1 T-cell epitope permissive/non-permissive classification |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers only the antibody half of review question C8: it tests whether a pre-existing, isolated HLA-DP donor-specific antibody harms kidney outcomes, and finds a large, statistically robust signal for early ABMR (multivariable HR 9.578, P = 0.012; 15 of 23 recipients rejected, median 22 days) alongside a graft-loss signal that survived only univariable analysis (HR 5.218, P = 0.048) and vanished on adjustment. It does NOT test the other half of C8 - HLA-DP mismatch as an exposure is never modelled here, so this paper cannot be cited for whether DP mismatch counts predict outcome; its only statement on that is a cited registry result, not its own data. For a LIVING-donor Iranian pre-screen the design transfers poorly on population: this is a deceased-donor, UK-allocation, highly sensitised, heavily regrafted cohort (65% of the DPDSA group were regrafts, cold ischaemia times were long, and there was only one living donor in the entire index group), so the absolute event rates cannot be carried across. It transfers poorly on exposure measurement too: the entire signal is measured by single-antigen-bead antibody testing plus DPB1/DPA1 allele-level typing, which is exactly the information a low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen does not have. Its practical value to the review is as a boundary marker - it shows that the risk this paper detects is invisible to a matching algorithm that only counts antigens, and even invisible to the flow crossmatch (BFXM added nothing within the DPDSA group), so an Iranian one-field pre-screen must be presented as not excluding DP-mediated risk rather than as ruling it out. Its secondary contribution is to C12: HLAMatchmaker epitope mismatch and the T-cell epitope permissive/non-permissive algorithm both failed to risk-stratify these transplants, which is evidence against relying on molecular-mismatch thresholds at DP in small cohorts.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- ABMR-free survival: isolated pre-existing HLA-DP DSA (DPDSA, n=23) vs standard-risk control (n=46) — HR 19.026, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier / univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: DPDSA vs control (multivariable) — HR 9.578, p=0.012; adjusted for patient group, % cRF, BFXM positivity, regrafts [Abstract Results; Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: non-donor-specific HLA-DP antibodies (DPnDSA, n=18) vs control — HR 4.54, p=0.081; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: cRF more than 85% vs not — HR 3.37, p=0.01; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: regraft vs first graft — HR 2.76, p=0.016; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: B-cell flow crossmatch positive vs negative (whole cohort) — HR 3.655, p=0.03; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- ABMR-free survival within the DPnDSA group: BFXM positive vs negative among recipients with non-donor-specific HLA-DP antibodies (median survival 276 days) — HR 8.483, p=0.0253; adjusted for unadjusted (Kaplan-Meier / Cox within stratum) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- overall rejection-free survival (ABMR + TCMR + mixed): DPDSA vs control — HR 6.129, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- overall rejection-free survival (ABMR + TCMR + mixed): DPDSA vs control (multivariable) — HR 2.855, p=0.093; adjusted for patient group, % cRF, BFXM positivity, regrafts [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival]
- death-censored graft survival: DPDSA vs control — HR 5.218, p=0.048; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, Graft Survival]
- death-censored graft survival: delayed graft function vs none — HR 3.376, p=0.016; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, Graft Survival]
- death-censored graft survival: regraft vs first graft — HR 7.461, p=0.002; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, Graft Survival]
- death-censored graft survival: high calcineurin inhibitor variability more than 3 months post-transplant — HR 9.505, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable Cox) [Results, Graft Survival]
- death-censored graft survival: regraft vs first graft (multivariable; DP-DSA was NOT associated with graft loss in this model and no adjusted HR for DP-DSA is printed) — HR 5.135, p=0.028; adjusted for patient group, % cRF, BFXM positivity, regrafts [Results, Graft Survival]
- ABMR-free survival: HLA-DPB1 84DEAV epitope mismatch vs not, within DPDSA pairs — HR 1.867, p=0.3308; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- graft survival: HLA-DPB1 84DEAV epitope mismatch vs not, within DPDSA pairs — HR 2.979, p=0.288; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- ABMR-free survival: HLA-DPB1 96R epitope mismatch vs not, within DPDSA pairs — HR 10.47, p=0.004; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- graft survival: HLA-DPB1 96R epitope mismatch vs not, within DPDSA pairs (direction OPPOSITE to the ABMR result) — HR 0.33, p=0.4435; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- graft survival: high vs low inferred donor HLA-DPB1 expression, within DPDSA pairs — HR 2.505, p=0.3578; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, Donor HLA-DPB1 Expression Levels]
- biopsy-proven ABMR (cumulative incidence over median 1197 days): DPDSA group, 15 of 23 recipients — proportion 65; adjusted for none (crude) [Abstract Results; Results first paragraph (counts 15 DPDSA, 4 DPnDSA, 3 HSP, 2 control of 24 total ABMR)]
- graft loss (death-censored): DPDSA group, 7 of 23 recipients — proportion 30; adjusted for none (crude) [Abstract Results; Results first paragraph (20 grafts failed: 7 DPDSA, 6 DPnDSA, 4 HSP, 3 control)]
- biopsy-proven ABMR and graft loss, counts by group (percentages other than the two above are NOT printed by the paper): ABMR: 15/23 DPDSA, 4/18 DPnDSA, 3/27 HSP, 2/46 control. Graft failure: 7/23 DPDSA, 6/18 DPnDSA, 4/27 HSP, 3/46 control. Any biopsy-proven rejection: 15 DPDSA, 6 DPnDSA, 5 HSP, 7 control (33 total) — counts None; adjusted for none (crude) [Results, first paragraph]
- B-cell flow crossmatch positivity: recipients with HLA-DP antibodies (DPDSA + DPnDSA) vs recipients without HLA-DP antibodies; 32% of DPDSA patients were BFXM positive; 19 of 95 wet crossmatches positive overall — proportion 32, p=0.0776; adjusted for none (chi-squared) [Introduction (32% figure); Results, Complement Dependent Cytotoxicity/FXM Testing; Discussion]
- rejection on indication biopsy (proportion of biopsies): 81% of DPDSA biopsies vs 68.75% of DPnDSA biopsies showed rejection; 109 for-cause biopsies performed (33 DPDSA, 16 DPnDSA, 30 HSP, 30 control) — proportion 81; adjusted for none (crude) [Results, Biopsy Results]
- Banff biopsy lesion scores, DPDSA vs control: higher microvascular inflammation, higher C4d, higher transplant glomerulopathy in DPDSA biopsies; no effect estimate printed, P values only — P value only None, p=MVI 0.0346; C4d <0.0001; transplant glomerulopathy 0.015; adjusted for none (rank test) [Abstract Results; Results, Biopsy Results]

**Dose-response.**

- DP: HLA-DP MISMATCH is never used as an exposure in any model in this paper. The exposure is the presence of a pre-existing isolated HLA-DP donor-specific ANTIBODY. The paper's only statement about DP mismatch as a dose is a cited registry result, not its own analysis: a study of 4900 cadaveric renal transplants in which DP mismatch had no deleterious effect in first transplants but each DP mismatch gave a step-wise reduction in 1-year graft survival in retransplants, particularly in sensitised recipients.
- A_B_DR: Reported only as a baseline characteristic, tabulated as UK NHSBT mismatch levels 1-4 (level 3 = A/B/DR 001, 011, 101, 111, 201, 211, 120, 020, 220; level 4 = 021, 121, 221, 002, 102, 202, 012, 112, 212, 022, 122, 222). DPnDSA and control patients were more likely to receive a level 3 or 4 kidney than DPDSA and HSP patients. No outcome model uses mismatch count or level.
- DQ: not analysed as an exposure; 3 DPDSA patients received a kidney fully matched at HLA-A, B, C, DR and DQ
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - no mismatch-count exposure exists in this paper, so no test of trend, no linearity test, no spline, no threshold analysis and no 'P for trend' is reported anywhere. The only dose-like analyses are at the DP epitope level (84DEAV and 96R mismatch present vs absent, i.e. binary, not graded) and donor DPB1 expression (high vs low, binary).; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- BFXM positivity x patient group: Effect modification: a positive B-cell flow crossmatch predicted ABMR only among recipients with NON-donor-specific HLA-DP antibodies. Within the DPDSA group and within controls, BFXM positivity made no significant difference to ABMR-free survival; in the HSP group there was a non-significant trend. (DPnDSA HR 8.483, P = 0.0253 (median survival 276 days); HSP P = 0.192; DPDSA and control not significant) [Results, HLA-DP Antibodies and Rejection Free Survival; restated in Abstract Results and Discussion]
- cumulative DP-DSA MFI x B-cell flow crossmatch result: No relationship - antibody strength did not predict crossmatch reactivity, so MFI cannot be used to grade DP risk via the crossmatch (R = 0.28 (not correlated); BFXM-negative median DP-DSA MFI 9931.5 (range 2141-22,252) vs BFXM-positive median 11,277 (range 2788-47,349), P = 0.2666) [Results, Complement Dependent Cytotoxicity/FXM Testing]
- inferred donor HLA-DPB1 expression level (high vs low) x crossmatch and outcome: No effect modification detected: positive crossmatch in 31% of high-expression donors vs 33% of low-expression donors (n = 6 low); expression level was not associated with rejection-free survival; only a non-significant trend to worse graft survival with high expression (graft survival HR 2.505, P = 0.3578) [Results, Complement Dependent Cytotoxicity/FXM Testing; Results, Donor HLA-DPB1 Expression Levels]
- HLA-DPB1 epitope mismatch x DP-DSA (attempt to stratify risk within DP-incompatible transplants): Discordant and unstable: 96R mismatch was associated with worse ABMR-free survival but a (non-significant) trend to BETTER graft survival; 84DEAV mismatch showed non-significant trends in both. The authors state firm conclusions could not be drawn because of small numbers and multiple epitope mismatches per pair. (96R: ABMR-free HR 10.47, P = 0.0040; graft survival HR 0.33, P = 0.4435. 84DEAV: ABMR-free HR 1.867, P = 0.3308; graft survival HR 2.979, P = 0.2880) [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- DPB1 T-cell epitope permissive/non-permissive classification x outcome: No stratification achieved - the permissive/non-permissive algorithm did not separate risk among DP-DSA transplants (no estimate printed (qualitative negative result)) [Results, Epitope Analysis]
- HLA-DP mismatch x retransplant status and x sensitisation (CITED BACKGROUND, not this paper's own data): The authors summarise an earlier registry of 4900 cadaveric renal transplants in which DP mismatch was not deleterious in first transplants but each DP mismatch reduced 1-year graft survival step-wise in retransplants, particularly in sensitised recipients with 50% reactivity of preformed lymphocytotoxic antibodies; and DPB epitope-level mismatches reduced graft survival in retransplants only. Record as second-hand. (no estimate reproduced in this paper) [Introduction paragraph 3; restated in Discussion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C8* — "A study of 4900 cadaveric renal transplants showed that whereas HLA-DP mismatch was not associated with a deleterious effect in first transplant recipients, each HLA-DP mismatch was associated with a step-wise reduction in 1-year graft survival rates for retransplants." (Introduction, paragraph 3 (this paper reporting a cited registry study, not its own result))
- *C8* — "Consequently, there is an 80% chance of a DP mismatch even if an unrelated donor and recipient pair are fully matched at the A, B, C, DR and DQ loci." (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C8* — "DP-DSAs were associated with significant episodes of ABMR with more than half (15 of 23) suffering from ABMR (median time to ABMR 22 days, twenty-fifth centile 14, seventy-fifth centile 125 days)." (Discussion)
- *C8* — "After multivariate analysis, HLA-DP-DSA was the single factor that was associated with the development of clinical ABMR (HR = 9.6)." (Discussion)
- *C8* — "In the multivariable analysis, DP-DSA was not associated with graft loss." (Results, Graft Survival)
- *C12* — "Classification of permissive and nonpermissive donor and recipient pairs using the T-cell epitope algorithm did not risk stratify DPDSA transplants." (Results, Epitope Analysis)

**Limitations.** Very small index group: 23 recipients with isolated DP-DSA, 24 ABMR events and 20 graft losses in the whole study. The multivariable Cox models carry four covariates on these event counts and are almost certainly overfitted; the ABMR HR of 9.578 should be read as directionally strong but numerically unstable.; No confidence interval is printed for ANY hazard ratio anywhere in the retrieved full text - only point estimates and P values. Precision cannot be assessed and these estimates cannot be meta-analysed as reported.; Single centre, single national allocation system (UK NHSBT), 2013-2020, with a policy change mid-study (CDC crossmatch removed; DQA1/DPB1/DPA1 typing added September 2019).; Groups are not exchangeable and confounding is severe and in the direction of the finding: the DPDSA group had far more regrafts (65%), higher cRF, longer cold ischaemia, more DBD grafts and 74% received augmented immunosuppression. Controls were matched only 2:1 on donor type.; Indication ('for cause') biopsies only, no protocol biopsies. The authors themselves concede there may have been a lower threshold to biopsy DPDSA patients, so the ABMR rate difference is partly ascertainment.; Only 1 living donor in the entire DPDSA group - the paper carries essentially no living-donor evidence.; Additional HLA-DPA1 DSA could not be excluded in 5 of the 23 DPDSA recipients, so the exposure is not purely DPB1.; Assay dependence: only 16 of 21 retested time-of-offer sera confirmed DP-DSA on a second manufacturer's kit (2 discordant for kit content, 3 negative on Immucor). The exposure definition is not reproducible across platforms at low MFI.; Graft-loss result is fragile: significant univariably (HR 5.218, P = 0.048) and null after adjustment. The paper's own conclusion for graft survival is a 'trend', not an effect.; Epitope analysis is internally contradictory (96R mismatch: worse ABMR-free survival, HR 10.47, but HR 0.33 for graft survival) and the authors say numbers were insufficient.; Internal inconsistency in the paper: the Results state 2 of 46 control patients and 3 of 27 HSP patients had biopsy-proven ABMR, but the Discussion states 'a 10% rate of ABMR in the control (standard immunological risk) group, however there was no ABMR in the HSP group'. These cannot both be right; the reviewer should treat the group-level ABMR counts with caution.; HLA mismatch itself is never an exposure - the paper cannot support or refute any claim about mismatch counts, per-locus effects or dose-response.; Non-HLA antibodies were not investigated and are acknowledged as a possible explanation for BFXM positivity in the DPnDSA group..

### Senev A 2022 — Association of Predicted HLA T-Cell Epitope Targets and T-Cell-Mediated Rejection After Kidney Transplantation.

Senev A 2022, *Am J Kidney Dis*, [DOI 10.1053/j.ajkd.2022.04.009](https://doi.org/10.1053/j.ajkd.2022.04.009). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier / National Kidney Foundation); no PMC record found via convert_article_ids on the DOI and no pmc identifier in the PubMed metadata, so no open-access full text was retrievable. All extraction below is from the PubMed structured abstract and plain-language summary only..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All kidney transplant recipients at a single centre (University Hospitals Leuven, Belgium) transplanted between 2004 and 2013 who had available biopsy data and a stored DNA sample allowing high-resolution donor/recipient HLA typing; N = 893 |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract |
| n | 893 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort with protocol/indication biopsy histology; multivariable cause-specific hazards models |
| typing resolution | two-field (high-resolution) DNA typing of both donor and recipient - required to compute PIRCHE-II and eplet mismatch |
| outcome | T-cell-mediated rejection (TCMR); borderline changes suggestive of TCMR; allograft failure |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | HLA-DSA (donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies) - explicitly accounted for; the conclusion is framed 'in the absence of HLA-DSA', unspecified further covariates in the multivariable cause-specific hazards models (the abstract says 'multivariable' but does not list the adjustment set) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper addresses the review's molecular-mismatch question (C12) and the locus-hierarchy questions (C3, C4) in a single outcome model: among 893 kidney-only recipients it asks which donor HLA loci, expressed as predicted indirectly-presented T-cell epitope load (PIRCHE-II), drive T-cell-mediated rejection and graft failure. Its answer is a clean class II versus class I separation - only the HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 PIRCHE-II scores were independently associated with TCMR and with allograft failure, and the same two loci alone predicted early (first 3 months) acute TCMR - which is direct support for DR and DQ outranking class I for cellular rejection, and which is corroborating evidence for the review's decision to weight DRB1 and DQB1 above HLA-A/B/C. It also matters as a negative control for our own design: the result is conditioned on the absence of HLA-DSA, so it isolates the cellular arm rather than the antibody arm. Transfer to a LIVING-donor, LOW-resolution (one-field), antibody-status-unknown Iranian pre-screen is, however, weak and mostly directional rather than operational. First, PIRCHE-II is computable only from two-field donor and recipient typing; a one-field Iranian pre-screen cannot produce the exposure this paper measures, so the paper can justify weighting DR/DQ but cannot be used to set a numeric molecular threshold in our tool. Second, the donor type is not stated in the abstract and the cohort is a European deceased-donor-dominant transplant programme era (2004-2013), so the living-donor generalisation is an assumption, not a finding. Third, our pre-screen has unknown antibody status, whereas this paper's headline is explicitly restricted to the DSA-negative situation; in an antibody-unknown setting the class I effects this paper found absent could reappear through the DSA pathway that the design removed. The practical carry-over is therefore the ranking (DRB1 and DQB1 first) and the explicit caveat that a one-field pre-screen is a coarse proxy for what actually drives TCMR.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- TCMR (any biopsy-proven T-cell-mediated rejection): median class II PIRCHE-II score, patients with TCMR vs patients without TCMR — median (IQR), between-group comparison 129 (IQR 60-240) vs 201 (IQR 96-298), as printed, p=<0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted between-group comparison [Abstract, Results]
- TCMR (any) and allograft failure: PIRCHE-II score for HLA-DRB1, and separately for HLA-DQB1, as continuous exposures — cause-specific hazard ratio (multivariable) None; adjusted for multivariable cause-specific hazards model, covariate list not given in the abstract [Abstract, Results (numeric HRs are in the full text, which is not open access)]
- TCMR (any) and allograft failure: PIRCHE-II scores for HLA class I molecules (A, B, C) as continuous exposures — cause-specific hazard ratio (multivariable) None; adjusted for multivariable cause-specific hazards model, covariate list not given in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- early acute TCMR within the first 3 months after transplantation: donor HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 derived T-cell epitope targets vs class I derived targets — cause-specific hazard ratio (multivariable) None; adjusted for multivariable cause-specific hazards model, covariate list not given in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- event counts (denominators for the above): cohort event frequencies, N = 893 — count 277 patients developed TCMR; 134 developed only borderline changes suggestive of TCMR on at least 1 biopsy [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- DRB1: PIRCHE-II score independently associated with TCMR and with allograft failure; no numeric HR in the retrieved abstract
- DQB1: PIRCHE-II score independently associated with TCMR and with allograft failure; no numeric HR in the retrieved abstract
- class I (A, B, C): not independently associated with TCMR or allograft failure; not associated with early acute TCMR either
- DP: not reported in the abstract
- eplet mismatch: listed as a measured exposure alongside PIRCHE-II, but the abstract reports no separate eplet result
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported in the retrieved abstract. The exposure is a continuous predicted-epitope score (PIRCHE-II), not a 0/1/2 antigen-mismatch count, so no per-count dose-response series, no threshold, no spline and no categorisation is described in the abstract. Whether the full text modelled the score linearly, in tertiles, or with a cut-off cannot be determined from the retrieved text.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA class II PIRCHE-II x HLA-DSA status: The design conditions on the antibody arm: the conclusion is stated 'In the absence of HLA-DSA', i.e. the class II > class I result is established after taking donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies into account, isolating the T-cell (indirect allorecognition) pathway. This is a stated conditioning, not a formally reported interaction term. (no interaction estimate or P for interaction printed in the abstract) [Abstract, Conclusions; Plain-language summary]
- HLA locus (class II vs class I) x time since transplantation: Effect modification by timing: when the analysis is restricted to rejection episodes in the first 3 months, only the donor DRB1- and DQB1-derived T-cell epitope targets are associated with early acute TCMR; class I targets are not associated in that early window either. (no interaction estimate or P for interaction printed in the abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- HLA class I epitope load x immunosuppression era: Interpretive, not a tested interaction: the authors attribute the null class I result to modern immunosuppression being sufficient to abort class I-directed alloimmunity while leaving DRB1/DQB1 alloresponses insufficiently suppressed. No era comparison or formal test is reported. (none) [Abstract, Conclusions]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "only the PIRCHE-II scores for HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 were independently associated with the occurrence of TCMR and with allograft failure; this was not the case for HLA class I molecules" (Abstract, Results)
- *C4* — "In the absence of HLA-DSA, HLA class II but not class I mismatches are associated with early episodes of acute TCMR and allograft failure." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C3* — "If restricted to rejection episodes within the first 3 months after transplantation, only the T-cell epitope targets originating from the donor's HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1, but not class I molecules, were associated with the early acute TCMR." (Abstract, Results)
- *C12* — "the median PIRCHE-II score for HLA class II was statistically different between the patients with TCMR compared to the patients without TCMR (129 [IQR, 60-240] vs 201 [IQR, 96-298], respectively; P < 0.0001)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C12* — "All kidney transplant recipients at a single center between 2004 and 2013 with available biopsy data and a DNA sample for high-resolution HLA donor/recipient typing (N = 893)." (Abstract, Setting and Participants)
- *C4* — "current immunosuppressive therapies are largely able to abort the most deleterious HLA class I-directed alloimmune processes; however, alloresponses against HLA-DRB1 and HLA-DQB1 molecular mismatches remain insufficiently suppressed." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only extraction. No PMC full text exists for this DOI (convert_article_ids on 10.1053/j.ajkd.2022.04.009 returned no PMCID and the PubMed metadata carries no pmc identifier), so every hazard ratio, confidence interval and P value in the paper's tables is unavailable. Only one numeric result and one set of event counts could be extracted.; The one numeric comparison that IS printed appears to have its group labels transposed: the TCMR group is given the LOWER median class II PIRCHE-II score (129) and the no-TCMR group the HIGHER one (201), which contradicts the paper's own conclusion. Do not use this number directionally without the full text.; The authors' own stated limitation: observational clinical data and residual confounding.; Single centre (Leuven, Belgium), single era (2004-2013), European donor and recipient HLA allele frequencies. Haplotype structure and allele frequencies differ substantially in an Iranian population, and PIRCHE-II scores are population-dependent.; Donor type (living vs deceased) is not stated in the abstract, so the applicability to a living-donor programme cannot be established from the retrieved text.; The exposure requires two-field (high-resolution) DNA typing of BOTH donor and recipient. It is not computable in a one-field antigen-level pre-screen, and the paper gives no low-resolution equivalent, no imputation accuracy figure and no antigen-count fallback.; The multivariable adjustment set is not described in the abstract, so it is unknown whether donor age, cold ischaemia, induction therapy, retransplant status or PRA were controlled.; The paper measured HLA eplet mismatch as well as PIRCHE-II, but the abstract reports no eplet result, so the PIRCHE-II vs eplet comparison cannot be extracted.; Nothing is reported for HLA-DP, and nothing for antigen-level (broad) mismatch counts, so this paper contributes nothing to claims C2, C5, C6, C8 or C9.; Follow-up duration is not stated, which matters for the allograft-failure endpoint..

### Jamshidian Tehrani N 2021 — Virtual Crossmatching in Kidney Transplantation, Shiraz Experience in Development of a Web-Based Program

Jamshidian Tehrani N 2021, *International Journal of Organ Transplantation Medicine*, PMID 34987737. Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 100 potential kidney-transplant recipients on the Shiraz waiting list, all with a complete HLA antibody profile, compared against 10 potential donors from previous 2020 kidney transplants; Shiraz Transplant Center, Abu-Ali Sina Hospital, Iran |
| donor type | not stated |
| n | 100 recipients x 10 donors (1000 recipient-donor virtual crossmatch comparisons) |
| design | single-centre method comparison: virtual crossmatch (VXM) performed by a new web-based program versus manually by an experienced immunologist; agreement, error count and time per patient compared |
| typing resolution | not stated; donors had HLA typing available for A, B and DR loci only (no C, DQ or DP reported) |
| outcome | VXM turnaround time per patient, manual-VXM error rate, and proportion of cases improved by secondary review; no clinical graft outcome |
| follow up | not applicable (no follow-up; cross-sectional method comparison) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper was pulled for C15 as a direct description of contemporary Iranian HLA practice, and that is the only review question it answers. Its most transferable fact is the locus panel actually available at a major Iranian transplant centre: donor typing existed for A, B and DR only, with no HLA-C, DQ or DP reported anywhere in the abstract, which corroborates the assumption that an Iranian pre-screen must operate on a three-locus, low-resolution donor record rather than on C/DQ/DP or two-field data. It also shows that the compatibility step at this centre is antibody-driven (every one of the 100 candidates had a complete HLA antibody profile and the crossmatch, not the mismatch count, is treated as the decisive compatibility test), which is the opposite of the antibody-status-unknown setting our pre-screen targets, and therefore marks a real gap rather than a supporting precedent. The paper transfers as engineering evidence, not clinical evidence: it demonstrates that a web-based tool consuming stored HLA and antibody data reduced per-patient assessment from 30 to 5 minutes and removed human matching errors that a manual reviewer made, which supports building a deterministic software pre-screen over manual immunologist review. It does not transfer as outcome evidence at all, because it reports no graft survival, rejection or dnDSA endpoint and no HLA-mismatch effect size of any kind. It says nothing about living donation specifically, and the waiting-list framing suggests deceased-donor allocation, so it cannot inform the living-donor question (C14) either.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested (the study reports no HLA-mismatch-to-outcome model of any kind); 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "10 potential donors from previous kidney transplants (2020), with available HLA typing results for A, B, and DR locus, were also selected" (Abstract, Methods)
- *C15* — "One hundred potential recipients in the waiting list of renal transplants were selected. The included patients all had a complete HLA antibody profile." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C15* — "In two manual virtual crossmatches, the VXM results had errors in matching recipient antibodies with the donor HLA typing that could affect the final decision for transplantation." (Abstract, Results)
- *C15* — "The average time for a manual VXM was 30 minutes per patient, while the virtual cross web-based program took 5 minutes per patient." (Abstract, Results)
- *C15* — "In 12% of the manual VXM cases, a secondary review of data improved final results." (Abstract, Results)
- *C15* — "a web-based VXM program that assesses HLA data can accurately perform a VXM with fewer human errors. It is especially true for highly sensitized candidates." (Abstract, Conclusion)

**Limitations.** No clinical outcome of any kind: no graft survival, rejection, dnDSA or patient survival endpoint, so the paper contributes zero effect sizes to the review's outcome questions (C1-C12).; Not a study of HLA mismatch burden at all; it studies antibody-versus-donor-antigen crossmatch prediction, so it cannot speak to per-locus or per-count mismatch effects.; PMC holds the record (PMC8717962) but returned an empty full-text body, so only the structured abstract could be retrieved; any numbers, tables, typing methods or assay platforms in the body are unseen.; No DOI is registered in the PubMed or PMC ID converter for this record, so the citation rests on PMID/PMCID alone.; Very small and non-random sample: 10 donors and 100 pre-selected recipients who all already had a complete antibody profile, which is not representative of the general Iranian candidate pool.; The comparator is a single 'experienced immunologist', so the reported manual error rate is one operator's performance and has no confidence interval or inter-rater replication.; Donor type (living versus deceased) is never stated, and no HLA typing resolution, antibody assay platform, MFI cut-off or PRA distribution is given in the abstract.; Single centre (Shiraz), single year of donors (2020); the A/B/DR-only donor panel may reflect that centre and era rather than current national practice.; The study's own tool is evaluated by its developers against a manual baseline, with no blinding described and no external gold standard such as an actual physical crossmatch result..

### Mohammadhassanzadeh H 2021 — On Path to Informing Hierarchy of Eplet Mismatches as Determinants of Kidney Transplant Loss

Mohammadhassanzadeh H 2021, *Kidney International Reports*, [DOI 10.1016/j.ekir.2021.03.877](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ekir.2021.03.877). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (Kidney International Reports is a fully open-access journal; no licence statement appeared in the retrieved PMC text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First (primary) adult and paediatric kidney-alone transplant recipients in the United States, 1 Jan 2000 - 1 Jan 2015, with peak PRA 0% (no evidence of pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies). Multi-organ recipients and primary graft non-function excluded. Independent sensitivity cohort of 48,384 PRA >0% donor-recipient pairs. Eplet frequencies estimated in 169,416 donors and 176,316 recipients. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 118,313 (primary 0% PRA cohort); 48,384 (independent PRA >0% validation cohort) |
| design | Retrospective SRTR registry cohort. Cox proportional hazards models fitted one eplet mismatch at a time, adjusted for recipient/donor/transplant characteristics, with Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control and a permutation check; Weibull accelerated failure time (AFT) models fitted because the proportional hazards assumption was violated for many eplets; weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA) to identify co-occurring eplet 'profiles'; Lasso-penalised Cox regression for variable selection on a 70% training split with replication in the held-out 30%; multiple imputation (Fully Conditional Specification) for missing covariates. |
| typing resolution | Low-resolution input imputed to allele level. Allele-level HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1 and -DQB1 genotypes were imputed from SEROLOGIC (antigen-level) HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 types using the National Marrow Donor Program algorithm, with haplotypes imputed by maximum likelihood independent of self-reported race. No measured two-field typing. HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DQA1, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were not available and are excluded. |
| outcome | Death-censored graft failure (DCGF), defined as return to dialysis or re-transplantation |
| follow up | median 6.39 years (IQR 3.12-10.01); 19,946 graft failures; administrative censoring 31 May 2015 |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, recipient sex, recipient race, dialysis vintage, insurance coverage, donor age, donor sex, donor race, donor type (living / deceased), transplant era, induction agent, calcineurin inhibitor type, steroids (yes vs no), donor-recipient weight ratio, cold ischaemia time (in a supplementary variable-selection model only) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the primary source for the review's heterogeneity-of-immunogenicity claim: it is the largest analysis to date that tests each individual eplet mismatch separately rather than summing them into a load, and it shows that only about half of the 412 observed eplet mismatches carry any death-censored graft failure risk, and that only 15 survive Lasso selection plus replication in held-out data. That directly contradicts the assumption behind any linear per-eplet or per-mismatch dose that a pre-screen might apply, and it is the empirical basis for the review's argument (C12, C4) that molecular mismatch risk is concentrated in a small immunodominant subset rather than spread uniformly. The population transfers only partly to Iran: it is a first-transplant, unsensitised (peak PRA 0%) cohort, which is the closest registry analogue to an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen, but 0% PRA is a measured fact here whereas an Iranian pre-screen simply does not know the antibody status, so the paper cannot speak to sensitised candidates except through the PRA >0% replication. Living donors are included in the cohort and donor type was carried in the models, and the authors state the selected eplet set was similar when donor type (living, SCD, ECD) and cold ischaemia time were included, but no living-donor-specific estimates are reported, so the paper supports rather than demonstrates transfer to living donation. The most operationally important element for KidneyMatch is the typing pathway: the authors derived every eplet from IMPUTED allele-level genotypes built out of serologic HLA-A, -B and -DRB1, which is exactly the one-field input an Iranian pre-screen would have, so the paper is simultaneously the best proof that eplet analysis is computable from low-resolution typing and the sharpest warning against it, since the imputation depends on National Marrow Donor Program haplotype frequencies from 21 U.S. populations with no Iranian reference and the authors themselves ran a Caucasian-only sensitivity analysis because imputation is known to be less accurate in non-Caucasian populations. On the review's practical question, the paper argues against deploying a cumulative eplet-load threshold in allocation and in favour of identifying specific higher-risk eplets, but it does not itself provide a usable scoring rule, and none of its hazard ratios are recoverable from the open-access text.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: each of 412 observed single eplet mismatches (present vs absent), one at a time — count of statistically significant associations (Cox) 243; adjusted for donor, recipient and transplant characteristics; Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control [Results, 'DCGF Risk Associated With Single EMM'. Breakdown: 121 class I (46 antibody-verified, 75 non-verified) and 122 class II (48 antibody-verified, 74 non-verified). No hazard ratio values are printed in the retrieved text.]
- death-censored graft failure: each of 412 observed single eplet mismatches (present vs absent), one at a time — count of statistically significant associations (Weibull AFT) 237; adjusted for same covariates as the Cox models; false discovery rate controlled [Results, 'DCGF Risk Associated With Single EMM'; also the Abstract ('119 class I and 118 class II EMM were associated with DCGF'). Breakdown: 119 class I (44 antibody-verified, 75 non-verified) and 118 class II (46 antibody-verified, 72 non-verified). All 237 AFT-identified eplets were a subset of the 243 identified by Cox.]
- death-censored graft failure: proportion of observed eplet mismatches carrying any measurable risk — proportion 0.58; adjusted for as above [Results / Discussion, stated qualitatively as 'only half of the observed EMMs were associated with an increased risk for DCGF'. The 0.58 is the arithmetic ratio 237/412 (and 243/412 = 0.59) implied by the printed counts; the paper itself prints only the counts and the word 'half'.]
- death-censored graft failure: eplet mismatch profiles (sets of 2 to 12 simultaneously occurring eplet mismatches) vs absence of the profile — count of significant profiles 33; adjusted for same covariates as the single-eplet models [Results, 'Profiles of EMM and Risk for DCGF': 'only 33 of the 67 EMM profiles identified in the study cohort associated with DCGF'. Network structure: 202 eplets were singletons, 210 fell within 67 profiles; profiles never mixed HLA class I with class II.]
- death-censored graft failure: Lasso-penalised Cox variable selection on the 70% training split — count of selected eplet mismatches 55; adjusted for penalised selection among all candidate eplets; hazard ratios then re-estimated by multivariable Cox with false discovery rate control [Results, 'Addressing Interrelatedness of EMMs'. The Discussion adds that 49 of these 55 were also associated with DCGF in the AFT models, describing this as an at-least-8-fold reduction from 412.]
- death-censored graft failure: replication of the 55 selected eplet mismatches in the held-out 30% of the 0% PRA cohort — count replicating 15; adjusted for recipient, donor and transplant characteristics; false discovery rate controlled [Abstract and Results, 'Addressing Interrelatedness of EMMs'. The Abstract specifies the composition: 9 singleton eplets and 6 that sit within profiles. This is the review's '15 eplets' figure, published 2021. The identity of the 15 eplets is given only in a table that PMC's text extraction did not return.]
- death-censored graft failure: eplet mismatches significant in the 0% PRA cohort, re-tested in the independent PRA >0% cohort (n=48,384) — proportion replicating 0.9; adjusted for as in the main analysis [Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses': '90% (144 of 161) of EMMs originally observed in the 0% PRA cohort were also predictive of DCGF in the PRA >0% cohort'. Note the denominator 161 is smaller than the 237/243 of the main analysis and the paper does not explain the discrepancy in the retrieved text.]
- death-censored graft failure: eplet mismatches significant in the self-reported Caucasian subgroup, re-tested against the full race-independent 0% PRA cohort — proportion overlapping 0.88; adjusted for as in the main analysis [Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses': 'Of 188 EMM associated with DCGF in the Caucasian subgroup, 165 (88%) were also associated with DCGF in the 0% PRA cohort independent of self-reported race and ethnicity.' Run specifically because allele-level imputation is less accurate in non-Caucasian populations.]
- eplet frequency (not a clinical outcome): eplet frequency in the donor population vs the recipient population — intraclass correlation coefficient 0.998; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Frequencies of Eplets in Donor and Recipient Populations and Risk of DCGF'. Reported as '0.998 or higher'. Used to argue that the risk attached to particular eplets is a property of the eplets themselves, not of differential donor-versus-recipient frequency.]
- death-censored graft failure: previously non-antibody-verified eplet mismatches at the HLA-DRB1 locus — count 40; adjusted for as in the AFT models [Discussion: 'more than 40 previously non-AbVer EMMs related to HLA-DRB1 locus are associated with DCGF in AFT models'. This is the only locus-specific count in the paper. Reported as 'more than 40', so 40 is a lower bound.]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The paper does not model a mismatch count at all: the exposure is the presence or absence of each individual eplet mismatch, modelled one at a time and then jointly via Lasso. No cumulative eplet load, no antigen-level 0/1/2 mismatch series, and no per-locus dose-response is fitted or reported. The paper is instead a direct argument against treating a cumulative load as a sufficient exposure: the Discussion notes that thresholds of acceptable cumulative eplet load have been proposed for allocation and then states that opponents object because eplets summing to the same load may differ in immunogenicity. The finding that only about half of eplets carry risk, and only 15 of 412 replicate, is the paper's evidence for that objection.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- eplet mismatch x pre-existing sensitisation (peak PRA 0% vs PRA >0%): The eplet mismatches identified in the unsensitised cohort remained predictive of death-censored graft failure in an independent sensitised cohort, and the co-occurrence profiles were also reproduced. This is a replication across strata, not a formal test of effect modification; no interaction p-value is reported. (90% (144 of 161) replicated in the PRA >0% cohort (n=48,384)) [Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses']
- eplet mismatch x self-reported race / ethnicity (imputation accuracy): Because allele-level HLA imputation is known to be less accurate in non-Caucasian populations, the main analysis was repeated in self-reported Caucasian donor-recipient pairs. Most but not all eplets overlapped, i.e. roughly 12% of the eplets significant in the Caucasian subgroup were not significant in the race-independent cohort. Presented as a robustness check on genotype misclassification rather than as biological effect modification. (165 of 188 (88%) overlap) [Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses'; Discussion]
- eplet mismatch x donor type (living vs standard-criteria vs expanded-criteria deceased) and cold ischaemia time: Adding cold ischaemia time and donor type to the variable-selection model produced a similar set of eplet mismatches associated with death-censored graft failure. No living-donor-specific hazard ratios, counts or stratified estimates are reported, so this is only weak evidence that the eplet hierarchy is stable across donor type. (not quantified ('A similar selection of EMMs')) [Methods, 'Statistical Analysis']
- eplet x eplet non-additivity (co-occurring eplet profiles; linkage disequilibrium; cross-locus eplet sharing): Eplet mismatches are not independent exposures. Weighted correlation network analysis found 210 of 412 eplets clustered into 67 profiles of 2 to 12 simultaneously occurring mismatches, always within a single HLA class but sometimes spanning loci. Only 33 of 67 profiles were associated with graft failure, and profiles that were not associated were typically composed of eplets individually not associated. The authors state that an apparent association for any single eplet may be confounded by another eplet co-occurring with it, and that for the 6 of the 15 final eplets that sit inside profiles they cannot rule out that a different eplet in the profile, or the whole profile, carries the risk. (202 singleton vs 210 in-profile eplets; 33 of 67 profiles associated with DCGF) [Results, 'Profiles of EMM and Risk for DCGF'; Discussion]
- antibody verification status (AbVer vs non-AbVer) x association with graft failure: Antibody verification and graft-failure risk are dissociated in both directions: many previously non-antibody-verified eplets (including more than 40 at HLA-DRB1) were associated with death-censored graft failure, while some already antibody-verified eplets were not. The authors attribute this partly to the heterogeneous strength of experimental verification in the HLA Epitope Registry and partly to unrecorded clinical intervention after donor-specific antibody detection. (AFT-significant set included 75 non-verified class I and 72 non-verified class II eplets) [Results, 'DCGF Risk Associated With Single EMM'; Discussion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "Allele-level donor-recipient HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, and -DQB1 types were imputed from serologic HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 types using an algorithm provided by the National Marrow Donor Program" (Methods, 'Allele-level HLA type imputation and EMM estimation')
- *C12* — "Taken together, these survival analyses demonstrated that only half of the observed EMMs were associated with an increased risk for DCGF" (Results, 'DCGF Risk Associated With Single EMM')
- *C12* — "Of those, 15 were also statistically significantly associated with DCGF in the remaining dataset when using Cox regression models adjusting for recipient, donor, and transplant characteristics and controlling for false discovery rate." (Results, 'Addressing Interrelatedness of EMMs as Determinants of DCGF')
- *C12* — "Opponents of this approach suggest that the composition of eplets giving rise to similar mismatch loads may include single EMMs of varying immunogenicity and antigenicity, rendering the risk profile insufficiently consistent to apply in clinical care." (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C4* — "these findings may also support the notion that not all eplets are created equal and this relates to their tendency to induce donor-specific antibodies, result in tissue injury, and/or respond to therapeutic interventions." (Discussion, paragraph 3)
- *C12* — "Of 188 EMM associated with DCGF in the Caucasian subgroup, 165 (88%) were also associated with DCGF in the 0% PRA cohort independent of self-reported race and ethnicity" (Results, 'Sensitivity Analyses')

**Limitations.** No hazard ratios, confidence intervals or p-values are recoverable. Every numeric effect estimate lives in the paper's tables and figures, which PMC's full-text extraction dropped; the retrieved body text contains counts and proportions only. The review cannot pool this paper quantitatively without the tables or supplement.; Eplets were derived from IMPUTED allele-level genotypes, not measured two-field typing. The input was serologic HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 only; HLA-C and -DQB1 were entirely imputed. The authors themselves call validation in datasets with measured allele-level genotypes a prerequisite before their eplets are used in allocation.; The imputation algorithm relies on National Marrow Donor Program haplotype frequencies from 21 U.S. populations. There is no Iranian reference panel, and the authors ran a Caucasian-only sensitivity analysis precisely because imputation is less accurate in non-Caucasian populations. Transfer of the eplet identities to an Iranian population is unvalidated.; HLA-DRB3/4/5, -DQA1, -DPA1 and -DPB1 were unavailable and excluded. The authors state this can both under- and overestimate eplet mismatch counts, and note that the HLA-DQ eplet repertoire was still in flux.; The proportional hazards assumption was violated for many single-eplet Cox models, which is why Weibull AFT models were added. Yet the headline set of 15 replicated eplets comes from Cox models in the held-out data, so the assumption problem is not fully resolved for the paper's central result.; 412 separate single-eplet models is extreme multiple testing. Benjamini-Hochberg FDR control and a permutation check were applied, but the Cox and AFT models disagree on 6 eplets and the sensitivity-analysis denominator (161) does not match the main-analysis counts (237/243) without explanation in the retrieved text.; Eplet mismatches are strongly correlated through linkage disequilibrium and cross-locus eplet sharing. For the 6 of 15 final eplets that lie inside co-occurrence profiles, the authors explicitly cannot attribute risk to the named eplet rather than to a co-occurring eplet or to the profile as a whole.; No head-to-head comparison against antigen-level mismatch counts, cumulative eplet load, PIRCHE-II or any other metric. The paper cannot tell the review whether eplet-level matching outperforms conventional HLA-A/B/DR antigen matching.; Living donors are included in the cohort but no living-donor-specific results are reported. The only evidence of stability across donor type is the unquantified statement that a similar eplet set was selected when donor type and cold ischaemia time were included.; The main cohort is restricted to peak PRA 0%, first transplants, in the United States. Retransplants and sensitised candidates enter only through the separate PRA >0% replication.; SRTR does not longitudinally capture donor-specific antibodies, rejection episodes, immunosuppression adherence, or treatment given after DSA detection. The authors offer this as an explanation for why some antibody-verified eplets showed no graft-failure risk, which means unmeasured intervention confounds the eplet hierarchy.; Observational registry design with residual confounding; covariate missingness handled by multiple imputation.; Entirely U.S. data, no external validation in another country or health system..

### Niemann M 2021 — Computational Eurotransplant kidney allocation simulations demonstrate the feasibility and benefit of T-cell epitope matching

Niemann M 2021, *PLoS Computational Biology*, [DOI 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009248](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009248). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (PLOS Computational Biology open access). Note: the PMC full text retrieved contained the body only, not the abstract, so every quote below is taken from and verified against the body text..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Virtual (synthetic) Eurotransplant population: 400,000 individuals generated from the NMDP 2011 European Caucasian (EURCAU) haplotype frequency dataset assuming random mating; a 10,400-patient waiting list bootstrapped to match the Eurotransplant Annual Report 2015; no real patients. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 400,000 virtual individuals; 10,400-patient waiting list maintained throughout; over 22,600 kidneys allocated over 10 simulated years, in triplicate; ~6.2 kidneys allocated/day, ~16.7 registrations/day, ~10.5 deregistrations/day; >33 million PIRCHE-II calculations per PIRCHE-based simulation run |
| design | In silico Markov Chain Monte Carlo (Gibbs sampler) simulation of the Eurotransplant Kidney Allocation System (ETKAS), daily time step, 10 simulated years; baseline ETKAS run in triplicate and compared with six PIRCHE-II-modified allocation scenarios (ETKASPIR-A to -F); ETKASPIR-E run in triplicate, others once. No patient outcomes were observed; graft survival was IMPUTED by multiplying simulated PIRCHE-II stratum frequencies by univariate 10-year graft survival incidences reported in earlier cohort studies. |
| typing resolution | Mixed by design. Virtual genotypes come from allele-level NMDP haplotypes. The ETKAS match grade itself is scored at LOW resolution: HLA-A and -B at serological broad level and HLA-DR at split level. PIRCHE-II was computed from HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1 and -DQB1 as peptide sources with DRB1 as the only presenting locus; the authors state that with multiple imputation enabled, A, B and DRB1 alone suffice for reasonably accurate PIRCHE-II scores. |
| outcome | Simulated allocation metrics: HLA match-grade (0-6 A-B-DR mismatch) distribution; PIRCHE-II score distribution summarised as distribution-weighted mean log(PIRCHE-II) per risk stratum (WML) and their sum (SWML); waiting time of transplanted patients and of the waiting list; waiting list size and country balance; cross-border kidney exchange; recipient age; histocompatibility points. Secondary, derived: estimated 10-year graft survival. |
| follow up | 10 simulated years per run (burn-in 2-3 years for match grade; 4-5 years for international exchange); no real follow-up. |
| other factors modelled | waiting time (since start of dialysis), urgency status, country balance / international exchange, distance between donor centre and transplant centre (national level only), blood group (ABO identity as a filter), PRA and unacceptable antigens (assigned via HLAMatchmaker eplets), HLA mismatch probability (MMP) / PIRCHE-II Risk Profile, paediatric bonus, recipient age, donor type (brain death vs cardiac death), 10% constant probability of an offer being declined |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the primary peer-reviewed description-plus-simulation of how Eurotransplant's largest deceased-donor kidney programme scores HLA, and so answers the review's ANGLE F / C13 question directly: ETKAS filters on blood-group identity and avoided unacceptable antigens, then sorts first by full HLA A-B-DR match and homozygosity and then by a point score in which the HLA A-B-DR match grade is worth a maximum of 400 points, alongside waiting time, urgency, country balance, distance and an HLA mismatch probability term that protects hard-to-match phenotypes. It is the clearest published statement that a real national allocation system deliberately scores HLA at LOW resolution (A and B at serological broad level, DR at split level), which is exactly the resolution available to an Iranian pre-screen, and that this low-resolution grade is nonetheless treated as a first-order allocation criterion rather than a tie-break. The paper then quantifies the trade-off of replacing that antigen count with a molecular (PIRCHE-II) score: the epitope score can be improved substantially while the antigen match grade degrades only slightly, and the estimated graft-survival gain is roughly equivalent to one extra classical HLA match. Transfer to the KidneyMatch setting is nevertheless limited and must be stated: the population is deceased-donor and waiting-list-driven, whereas the Iranian pre-screen is living-donor and pairwise, so the scarcity, queueing, country-balance and mismatch-probability machinery that dominates this paper has no analogue there. It is also a synthetic European-Caucasian population with no real outcomes, so it cannot supply a hazard ratio for any mismatch count. Its two directly usable transfers are (a) the precedent that a working national algorithm ranks candidates on a bounded low-resolution A-B-DR mismatch score with an explicit zero-mismatch priority tier, and (b) the caution for C12 that molecular matching presupposes two-field typing or accepted imputation from A, B and DRB1 - a step the review must treat as unvalidated for Iranian haplotype frequencies.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- Sum of distribution-weighted mean log(PIRCHE-II) (SWML; lower is better): ETKASPIR-E (full-HLA-match priority kept, match grade replaced by PIRCHE-II, MMP replaced by epitope MMP) vs baseline ETKAS simulation — SWML score 3.083, p=<0.001; adjusted for not applicable (simulation output; Wilcoxon rank sum test vs ETKAS reference SWML 3.391) [Results, 'Construction of an improved allocation model (ETKASPIR-E)' and Table 2]
- SWML: ETKASPIR-F (PIRCHE-II-based prioritisation instead of full-HLA-match priority, plus PIRCHE-II match score and epitope MMP) vs baseline ETKAS — SWML score 3.034, p=0.001; adjusted for not applicable (simulation output) [Results, Table 2 and 'Construction of an optimal allocation model (ETKASPIR-F)']
- SWML: PROCARE real-life ETKAS-allocated transplant cohort vs baseline ETKAS simulation — SWML score 3.657, p=<0.001; adjusted for not applicable [Table 2 (baseline ETKAS reference SWML 3.391)]
- Proportion of simulated transplants in PIRCHE-II group 1 (score 0-9, lowest risk): PROCARE 10.87% / ETKAS 15.52% / ETKASPIR-E 17.17% / ETKASPIR-F 27.12% — percentage of transplants 17.17; adjusted for not applicable [Table 2 (WML in parentheses: 0.095 / 0.112 / 0.116 / 0.353)]
- Proportion of simulated transplants in PIRCHE-II group 2 (score 9-35): PROCARE 21.62% / ETKAS 25.08% / ETKASPIR-E 41.66% / ETKASPIR-F 30.93% — percentage of transplants 41.66; adjusted for not applicable [Table 2 (WML 0.672 / 0.784 / 1.308 / 0.993)]
- Proportion of simulated transplants in PIRCHE-II group 3 (score 35-90): PROCARE 47.71% / ETKAS 46.30% / ETKASPIR-E 36.13% / ETKASPIR-F 37.02% — percentage of transplants 36.13; adjusted for not applicable [Table 2 (WML 1.937 / 1.871 / 1.404 / 1.444)]
- Proportion of simulated transplants in PIRCHE-II group 4 (score >90, highest risk): PROCARE 19.81% / ETKAS 13.10% / ETKASPIR-E 5.04% / ETKASPIR-F 4.92% — percentage of transplants 5.04; adjusted for not applicable [Table 2 (WML 0.953 / 0.624 / 0.256 / 0.244)]
- Fraction of transplants with 0 HLA-A,-B,-DR mismatches: ETKASPIR-E vs baseline ETKAS (both retain the full-HLA-match priority tier) — percentage of transplants (means of triplicate runs) 21.5; adjusted for not applicable (ETKAS reference 22.1%; described by the authors as a negligible reduction) [Results, 'Increased number of HLA mismatches with ETKASPIR-E']
- Fraction of transplants with 0 HLA-A,-B,-DR mismatches: ETKASPIR-A (12.1%) and ETKASPIR-F (11.9%), which replace full-HLA-match prioritisation with PIRCHE-II prioritisation, vs baseline ETKAS 22.1% — percentage of transplants 11.9, p=reported as 'significantly reduce'; exact p not printed; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Increased number of HLA mismatches with ETKASPIR-E']
- Estimated absolute incidence of a functioning graft at 10 years post transplant: PIRCHE-II-based allocation vs current ETKAS — absolute percentage-point increase (derived, not observed) 1.1% to 1.5%; adjusted for univariate only: simulated PIRCHE-II group frequencies multiplied by univariate 10-year graft survival incidences reported in earlier studies [Discussion]
- Estimated relative improvement in 10-year graft survival: PIRCHE-II-based allocation vs current ETKAS — relative percentage improvement (derived) 12.9% to 13.5%; adjusted for univariate, as above [Discussion; restated in the summary as 'the relative benefit in graft survival is around 13%']
