- Spread in 10-year graft survival between the lowest and highest PIRCHE-II score strata (the input assumption behind the estimate above): low vs high PIRCHE-II score — absolute difference in 10-year graft survival, taken from cited literature 8% to 12%; adjusted for univariate, from cited cohorts, not estimated in this paper [Discussion]
- Proportion of kidneys crossing national borders: ETKASPIR-F vs ETKAS and ETKASPIR-E, simulated years 5-10 — absolute difference in percentage of organs exchanged ~2-3% higher for ETKASPIR-F, p=<0.001 at all time points in the range of 5-10 years; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'International exchange']
- Fidelity of the baseline ETKAS simulation to observed HLA match-grade distributions (Jensen-Shannon distance; lower is closer): simulated year 10 vs 1998 observations (JSD 0.069) and vs 2015 ETKAS observations (JSD 0.135) — Jensen-Shannon distance 0.135, p=<0.001 for both comparisons; adjusted for not applicable [Fig 5 legend (A)]
- Bootstrap fidelity: number of waiting-list patients with 0-1 year waiting time: bootstrapped virtual waiting list (2334) vs Eurotransplant reported average 2013-2017 (2159) — count 2334, p=<0.01; adjusted for not applicable (Student's t-test; blood group, PRA, age and country showed no significant differences) [Results, 'Baseline results after bootstrapping'; Fig 4]
- Historical context reported by the authors, not a result of this study: 1-year graft survival gain predicted by the original pre-ETKAS simulations from introducing HLA matching into allocation: HLA-matched allocation vs no HLA matching (Eurotransplant, cited prior work) — absolute increase in 1-year graft survival 7% to 12%; adjusted for not applicable; cited from an earlier simulation, reference number stripped in the PMC text [Discussion]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: ETKAS 22.1% of transplants; ETKASPIR-E 21.5%; ETKASPIR-A 12.1%; ETKASPIR-F 11.9%; 1 MM: not printed numerically; increased in ETKASPIR-A and -F, counterbalancing their loss of 0-mismatch transplants; 2 MM: not printed numerically; 'decreased slightly' vs baseline ETKAS in ETKASPIR-B, -C, -D, -E and -F; 3 MM: not printed numerically; 'decreased slightly' vs baseline ETKAS in ETKASPIR-B, -C, -D, -E and -F; 4 MM: not printed numerically; increased when PIRCHE-II was included in the match grade algorithm; 5 MM: not printed numerically; increased; 6 MM: not printed numerically; increased
- note: No per-locus (A vs B vs DR vs DQ vs C) outcome or allocation result is reported. ETKAS counts HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatches together as a single match grade; the paper never separates the loci. PIRCHE-II used HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1 and -DQB1 as peptide sources with HLA-DRB1 as the sole presenting locus, but no locus-specific effect is quantified.
- Shape reported: not reported as an outcome dose-response. What the paper reports is a POINTS dose-response in the allocation algorithm itself: the ETKAS match grade is worth a maximum of 400 points, and the PIRCHE-II replacements distribute those same 400 points either as a step function (PIRCHE-II <9: 400 points; 9-35: 266; 35-90: 133; >90: 0, model ETKASPIR-B), as a weighted negative exponential (ETKASPIR-C, 400 x 0.958^PIRCHE-II), or as an inverse-linear ramp over 0-90 with zero points above 90 (ETKASPIR-D, -E, -F). The exact ETKAS points per mismatch count are shown in a figure rather than printed in the text.; linearity tested: not tested. No regression, no hazard model and no test for trend or non-linearity across mismatch counts was performed; the paper compares distributions between simulation scenarios with Wilcoxon signed-rank / rank sum tests and Jensen-Shannon distances only. The linear, exponential and step point-assignment functions were compared for their effect on the resulting PIRCHE-II distribution (SWML), not for goodness of fit to any outcome.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- PIRCHE-II-based match scoring x retention of the full-HLA-match priority tier: The cost of epitope-based scoring in antigen match grade depends entirely on whether the zero-mismatch priority tier is kept. Models that keep it (ETKASPIR-B, -C, -D, -E) lose almost no 0-mismatch transplants (21.5% vs 22.1%); models that replace it with PIRCHE-II prioritisation (ETKASPIR-A, -F) roughly halve the 0-mismatch fraction. (0-mismatch fraction 21.5% (priority kept) vs 12.1% and 11.9% (priority replaced), against ETKAS baseline 22.1%) [Results, 'Increased number of HLA mismatches with ETKASPIR-E']
- PIRCHE-II-based prioritisation x international (cross-border) kidney exchange: Cross-border exchange rose only in the models where low PIRCHE-II scores drove prioritisation (ETKAS vs ETKASPIR-F), not when prioritisation remained full HLA match (ETKASPIR-E vs -F); the authors flag that increased exchange may mean longer cold-ischaemic times. (difference of ~2-3%, p<0.001 at all time points in simulated years 5-10) [Results, 'International exchange'; Discussion]
- Mismatch-probability term x genotype frequency (equity of access for rare phenotypes): The ETKAS HLA MMP benefits only a limited number of patients with rare genotypes; a naive linear mapping of the PIRCHE-II Risk Profile gave a disproportionate number of patients high MMP points, so a fitting polynomial (including blood group and PRA) was required to reproduce the same equity profile. (no numeric estimate printed; shown as distribution curves in Fig 3B) [Materials and methods, 'HLA mismatch probability'; Fig 3B]
- Allocation model x recipient age: No effect modification detected: no impact on transplanted recipients' age was observed across the individual PIRCHE-II score groups in the different allocation simulations. (reported as no impact; no numeric estimate printed (Fig 5F)) [Results, 'Validation of the ETKAS simulation model'; Fig 5F]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "Currently, ETKAS considers the number of serological HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatches as a factor in their scoring system." (Introduction)
- *C13* — "the waiting list was prioritized by full HLA match (A and B at serological broad level, DR at split level), homozygosity status and descending by point score" (Materials and methods, 'ETKAS allocation simulation')
- *C13* — "ETKAS assigns a maximum of 400 points depending on the HLA match" (Materials and methods, 'HLA match grade replacements')
- *C13* — "The ETKASPIR-A and ETKASPIR-F models significantly reduce the fraction of 0-mismatched transplants to 12.1% and 11.9% respectively." (Results, 'Increased number of HLA mismatches with ETKASPIR-E')
- *C13* — "an increasing absolute incidence of a functioning graft 10 years after transplantation by 1.1% to 1.5%. This absolute increase translates into a relative improvement of 12.9% to 13.5%" (Discussion)
- *C12* — "With multiple imputation enabled, providing HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 is sufficient to calculate reasonably accurate PIRCHE-II scores." (Discussion)

**Limitations.** No real patients and no observed outcomes. The entire population is synthetic, generated from NMDP 2011 European Caucasian haplotype frequencies under an assumption of random mating; every 'result' is a simulation output, not a clinical measurement.; The graft-survival benefit is not measured but imputed: simulated PIRCHE-II stratum frequencies were multiplied by univariate 10-year graft survival incidences taken from earlier cohort studies. It is therefore unadjusted for donor age, cold ischaemia, immunosuppression or any other covariate, and carries no confidence interval.; No hazard ratio, odds ratio or any adjusted association between HLA mismatch count and graft outcome is estimated anywhere in the paper. It cannot contribute an effect size for C1-C11.; European Caucasian haplotype frequencies only. The authors explicitly list increasing genetic diversity from migration as an absent factor. Transfer to Iranian haplotype structure is untested, and both the mismatch-probability term and PIRCHE-II imputation depend on population haplotype frequencies.; Deceased-donor, waiting-list allocation only. There is no living-donor arm and no pairwise donor-selection analogue.; Baseline simulation fidelity is imperfect: the bootstrapped waiting list under-represented waiting time (2159 vs 2334 cases at 0-1 year, p<0.01), and simulated year-10 match grade distributions differed significantly from both 1998 and 2015 observed ETKAS distributions (JSD 0.069 and 0.135, both p<0.001), although the authors argue the error is systematic and therefore cancels between scenarios.; Other factors absent or incomplete by the authors' own account: temporal aspects of immunisation, centre-specific policies, offers rejected for a positive crossmatch, organ quality, accuracy of demographic parameters, dependency of HLA type on blood group, and spatial resolution defined at country rather than regional level.; Offer refusal was modelled as a flat 10% probability across all countries, match grades and age groups - an admitted simplification of centre behaviour.; Unacceptable antigens were assigned at random in proportion to eplet frequency to hit a target PRA, so the antibody profile of the virtual recipients is synthetic rather than clinically observed.; Statistical power is limited by run count: baseline ETKAS and ETKASPIR-E were run three times each, ETKASPIR-A to -D and -F only once, because each PIRCHE-II run took roughly 8 days of 32-core computing.; PIRCHE-II is proprietary (first author's affiliation is PIRCHE AG, Berlin; scores computed via the www.pirche.com portal), which is a relevant conflict-of-interest and reproducibility consideration.; The numeric mismatch-count distribution for 1 through 6 mismatches is shown only in Fig 8 and never printed in the text, so only the 0-mismatch fractions are extractable as numbers..

### Tambur AR 2021 — Significance of HLA-DQ in kidney transplantation: time to reevaluate human leukocyte antigen-matching priorities to improve transplant outcomes? An expert review and recommendations.

Tambur AR 2021, *Kidney International*, [DOI 10.1016/j.kint.2021.06.026](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2021.06.026). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier, Kidney International); not open access in PMC.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Not a patient cohort. Expert review of kidney allocation policy and the HLA-matching literature, centred on the United States allocation algorithm; author group from the USA, UK, Netherlands, Belgium and Canada. |
| donor type | deceased |
| design | narrative expert review with recommendations; no original cohort, no statistical analysis, and no effect estimates reported in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract |
| outcome | graft loss via chronic antibody-mediated rejection; de novo donor-specific HLA antibody (most often anti-DQ); sensitisation measured by panel-reactive antibody; access to a second transplant |
| other factors modelled | none modelled - narrative review, no statistical model reported, modern immunosuppression era (discussed as the justification for de-emphasising HLA), recipient ethnicity/race and disparity in access to transplantation (discussed), sensitisation / panel-reactive antibody (discussed as a downstream consequence), retransplantation and waitlist access (discussed), financial burden and long-term health consequences (discussed) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a position/framing source for the review, not a quantitative one: it is the flagship expert statement behind C4 (DQ as the dominant target of de novo DSA and therefore of chronic AMR and sensitisation) and C13 (how allocation schemes score HLA, and what happened when the United States progressively removed that weight). Its causal chain - mismatched donor HLA-DQ leads to de novo DSA, which leads to chronic AMR and graft loss, and which separately raises panel-reactive antibody and blocks the next transplant - is biological and donor-type agnostic, so it transfers to a living-donor programme with at least equal force: living-donor recipients are typically younger, expect a longer graft life, and are correspondingly more likely to need the second transplant that a sensitising DQ mismatch would jeopardise. That second-transplant argument is the most usable part for an Iranian pre-screen, because it justifies penalising an avoidable DQ mismatch at selection time even when the near-term graft-survival difference is small, and it applies precisely when donor choice is still open, as it is in living donation. The antibody-status-unknown setting is also a reasonable fit in one direction: the paper's subject is de novo antibody formation after transplant, which is exactly the future risk a pre-screen wants to minimise when it cannot measure antibody, so mismatch-as-proxy is the mechanism the authors themselves endorse. The fit fails on the instrument, however: the specific metric recommended, DQalphabeta (the DQA1/DQB1 heterodimer), cannot be computed from one-field typing, so a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen can at best count DQB1 antigen mismatches and must treat this paper as supporting the direction ('weight DQ') rather than the measure. Finally, the paper's equity argument - that the US de-emphasised HLA matching partly because matching reduced access for African American patients - is the standing warning for any pre-screen that ranks candidates by matching, and should be examined against the different structure of Iran's living-donor pool rather than imported.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported (narrative review, no model); 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching x recipient ethnicity/race - effect on ACCESS to transplantation, not on graft outcome: The abstract states that HLA matching was associated with decreased access to transplantation for African American patients, and that reducing this ethnic/racial disparity was part of the intent behind devaluing HLA matching in US allocation. This is a narrative policy statement, not a tested effect-modification result. [Abstract, sentences 1-2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "The weight of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching in kidney allocation algorithms, especially in the United States, has been devalued in a stepwise manner, supported by the introduction of modern immunosuppression." (Abstract, opening sentence)
- *C13* — "The intent was further to reduce the observed ethnic/racial disparity, as data emerged associating HLA matching with decreased access to transplantation for African American patients." (Abstract, sentence 2)
- *C4* — "a leading cause of graft loss is chronic antibody-mediated rejection, attributed to the development of de novo antibodies against mismatched donor HLA expressed on the graft. These antibodies are most frequently against donor HLA-DQ molecules." (Abstract, sentences 3-4)
- *C4* — "Beyond their impact on graft survival, generation of de novo donor-specific HLA antibodies also leads to increased sensitization, as measured by panel-reactive antibody metrics." (Abstract, sentence 5)
- *C4* — "Consequently, access to transplantation for patients returning to the waitlist in need of a second transplant is compromised." (Abstract, sentence 6)
- *C13* — "We highlight the observed diminished outcome data, the significant financial burden, the long-term health consequences, and, more important, the unintended consequences." (Abstract, penultimate sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only access: no PMC full text exists, so the body, all recommendations in their actual wording, every cited effect size, and any figure or table were not read. Conclusions here rest on roughly 250 words of abstract.; No original data and no numbers: this is expert opinion, the lowest quantitative tier in the review. It cannot supply an effect size for DQ, for any locus, or for any mismatch count.; Advocacy framing: the title asks whether it is 'time to reevaluate' matching priorities, and the author group are histocompatibility specialists arguing for restoring weight to HLA. The piece is not a systematic review and reports no search strategy, so selection of supporting evidence is not auditable.; US deceased-donor allocation is the frame. Applicability to a living-donor programme, and to any non-US allocation context, is not established in the abstract.; The recommended DQalphabeta (DQA1/DQB1 heterodimer) metric requires class II typing at allele-group resolution or better, which a one-field pre-screen cannot produce; the paper's actual instrument is therefore out of reach in the target setting.; The argument presumes a working DSA/antibody testing infrastructure (panel-reactive antibody monitoring, de novo DSA detection). It does not address what to do when antibody status is unknown, which is the target setting.; Cannot be checked for a living-donor subgroup, for any Iranian or regional data, or for discussion of low-resolution typing error, because the full text is unavailable.; Published 2021 and describing US policy as of then; the 2021 US kidney allocation change (KAS250 / continuous distribution work) may have moved since..

### Tang C 2021 — Analysis of de novo donor-specific HLA-DPB1 antibodies in kidney transplantation.

Tang C 2021, *HLA*, [DOI 10.1111/tan.14422](https://doi.org/10.1111/tan.14422). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley, journal HLA); not in PMC; only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 366 kidney transplant recipients at Heidelberg University Hospital, Germany, selected for having pre- and post-transplant HLA antibody results by single-antigen bead testing and donor plus recipient HLA-DPB1 high-resolution typing |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract (deceased vs living not distinguished) |
| n | 366 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; three competing definitions of HLA-DPB1 incompatibility (allele mismatch, eplet mismatch, Terasaki epitope [TerEp] mismatch) plus donor HLA-DPB1 expression tested against (a) formation of de novo donor-specific anti-HLA-DPB1 antibodies and (b) graft survival. The statistical models, mismatch cut-offs, and covariate adjustment are not described in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | HLA-DPB1 high-resolution (allele/two-field) typing of both donor and recipient; resolution at other loci not stated. Eplet and TerEp mismatch loads are derived from that high-resolution typing. |
| outcome | de novo donor-specific HLA-DPB1 antibodies (dnDSA) detected by single-antigen bead testing; graft survival |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | HLA-DPB1 expression level predicted by the linked dimorphism rs9277534 A/G (donor high-expression exposure), no other covariates are named in the abstract; whether the graft-survival analysis was adjusted is not stated |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's dedicated DP paper and it answers two distinct questions at once: whether HLA-DPB1 incompatibility drives DP-directed de novo DSA, and whether the WAY DP incompatibility is counted changes its association with graft survival. It supports C8 in a specific and slightly awkward form: in 366 kidney recipients, DPB1 mismatch counted at the allele level was not significantly associated with dnDSA-DPB1 formation, yet DPB1 mismatch counted at eplet or Terasaki-epitope level was significantly associated with worse graft survival (p < 0.001 and p = 0.003). For C12 it is a direct molecular-mismatch-versus-allele-matching comparison inside one cohort, and the authors' own conclusion is that epitope-level matching, not allele-level matching, is the version of DP matching worth doing. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is weak and mostly cautionary: every exposure in this paper requires donor and recipient HLA-DPB1 two-field typing, which a low-resolution pre-screen does not have and cannot impute reliably for DPB1, and the outcome definition depends on serial single-antigen bead testing, which an antibody-unknown screen by definition lacks. The practical reading for the Iranian pre-screen is therefore negative rather than positive: this paper gives no basis for scoring DP at antigen or one-field level, and it argues that the crude DP mismatch count a low-resolution screen could compute is not the quantity that carried the graft-survival signal. It is a German single-centre cohort of unstated donor type, so its case mix is not the living-donor-dominant Iranian population, and n = 366 with an unreported event count makes even the significant graft-survival findings fragile.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- de novo donor-specific anti-HLA-DPB1 antibody (dnDSA): HLA-DPB1 allele-level mismatch vs no allele-level mismatch (categories/cut-offs not given in the abstract) — reported as not statistically significant; no effect estimate given None; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- de novo donor-specific anti-HLA-DPB1 antibody (dnDSA): HLA-DPB1 eplet mismatch vs none (load cut-off not given in the abstract) — reported as not statistically significant; no effect estimate given None; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- de novo donor-specific anti-HLA-DPB1 antibody (dnDSA): HLA-DPB1 Terasaki epitope (TerEp) mismatch vs none (load cut-off not given in the abstract) — reported as not statistically significant; no effect estimate given None; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- de novo donor-specific anti-HLA-DPB1 antibody (dnDSA): exposure to a donor with predicted high HLA-DPB1 expression (linked dimorphism rs9277534 A/G) vs not — reported as not statistically significant; no effect estimate given None; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- graft survival: HLA-DPB1 eplet mismatch vs none/lower (grouping not given in the abstract) — p-value only (test not named in the abstract; wording is 'significant negative impact on graft survival') None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- graft survival: HLA-DPB1 Terasaki epitope (TerEp) mismatch vs none/lower (grouping not given in the abstract) — p-value only (test not named in the abstract) None, p=0.003; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]

**Dose-response.**

- DPB1: allele-level mismatch MM: not significantly associated with dnDSA-DPB1; the corresponding graft-survival result is NOT stated in the abstract (see notes); eplet mismatch MM: not significantly associated with dnDSA-DPB1; significant negative impact on graft survival, p < 0.001; TerEp mismatch MM: not significantly associated with dnDSA-DPB1; significant negative impact on graft survival, p = 0.003
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported in the abstract. No 0 vs 1 vs 2 HLA-DPB1 mismatch series is given, no eplet-load or TerEp-load threshold or cut-point is stated, and no spline or trend test is mentioned. Whether the eplet/TerEp exposures were analysed as continuous loads or as dichotomised categories cannot be determined from the abstract.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DPB1 mismatch x donor HLA-DPB1 expression level (linked dimorphism rs9277534 A/G): Exposure to a donor predicted to have high HLA-DPB1 expression was not significantly associated with the risk of developing dnDSA against HLA-DPB1; the expression-level hypothesis was not confirmed in this cohort. (reported as not significant; no estimate or p-value printed in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- mismatch DEFINITION (allele vs eplet vs TerEp) x outcome (dnDSA vs graft survival): The definition of HLA-DPB1 incompatibility changes the conclusion: all three definitions were null for dnDSA-DPB1, but the two epitope-based definitions (eplet, TerEp) were significantly associated with worse graft survival. The authors conclude epitope-level rather than allele-level DP matching has the potential to improve graft survival. (eplet p < 0.001; TerEp p = 0.003 for graft survival; all three definitions non-significant for dnDSA) [Abstract, Results and Conclusion sentences]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C8* — "The impact of HLA-DPB1 incompatibility on the outcomes of kidney transplantation is not fully understood." (Abstract, Background sentence)
- *C12* — "A cohort of 366 patients who received a kidney transplant at the Heidelberg University Hospital, Germany" (Abstract, Methods sentence)
- *C12* — "Susceptibility to increased HLA-DPB1 expression was predicted by the linked dimorphism rs9277534 A/G of the HLA-DPB1 gene." (Abstract, Methods sentence)
- *C8* — "Neither HLA-DPB1 mismatches at allele, eplet or TerEp level nor exposure to donor's high HLA-DPB1 expression were significantly associated with the risk of developing dnDSA against HLA-DPB1." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C8* — "However, HLA-DPB1 eplet and TerEp mismatches had a significant negative impact on graft survival (p < 0.001 and p = 0.003, respectively)." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C12* — "Matching for HLA-DPB1 at epitope instead of allele level appears to have potential to improve graft survival in kidney transplantation." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. The article is not in PubMed Central (no PMCID from the NCBI ID converter), so the Results tables, the survival curves, the mismatch cut-offs, the event counts and every effect estimate are unseen. Everything recorded here is what the 250-word abstract prints.; No effect sizes at all: not a single hazard ratio, odds ratio or confidence interval is given in the abstract. Only two bare p-values (p < 0.001, p = 0.003) are printed, both for graft survival.; Whether the graft-survival analysis was multivariable-adjusted is not stated. With n = 366 and DPB1 eplet load correlated with DRB1/DQB1 mismatch through linkage, an unadjusted DP eplet effect could be carrying class II mismatch burden generally rather than DP specifically. The abstract gives no way to check.; Internally awkward result that the reviewer must not smooth over: the same eplet and TerEp exposures that predicted graft survival did NOT predict DP-directed dnDSA. The paper's own proposed mechanism (DP incompatibility -> DP-DSA -> graft loss) is therefore not demonstrated, and the graft-survival association is left without a mediating mechanism in the abstract.; The allele-level DPB1 mismatch versus graft survival result is never actually stated in the abstract. The conclusion implies it was weaker or null, but no number, p-value or explicit statement appears. Do not record an allele-level graft-survival null as if the paper reported it.; Single centre, Germany, n = 366, selected for having both serial single-antigen antibody testing and donor/recipient DPB1 high-resolution typing. That selection is not a random sample of transplants and probably enriches for monitored or higher-risk patients.; Donor type (deceased vs living) is not stated, so the paper cannot be assigned to the living-donor evidence stream. Follow-up duration and the number of graft losses are also not stated.; Every exposure requires two-field HLA-DPB1 typing of both donor and recipient. Nothing in this paper is computable from one-field or serologic typing, and the paper offers no low-resolution proxy and no imputation accuracy data.; Eplet and TerEp loads are algorithm-dependent (HLAMatchmaker / Terasaki epitope registry versions); the abstract names no software version, so the exposure is not reproducible from the abstract.; Two significant findings out of six reported tests, with no stated multiplicity correction..

### Unterrainer C 2021 — Can PIRCHE-II Matching Outmatch Traditional HLA Matching?

Unterrainer C 2021, *Frontiers in Immunology*, [DOI 10.3389/fimmu.2021.631246](https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2021.631246). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown; Frontiers in Immunology articles are normally CC BY 4.0, but no licence statement appeared in the retrieved PMC text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First European deceased-donor kidney-only transplants reported to the Collaborative Transplant Study (CTS), performed 1990-2016 at 236 centres in 24 countries; both adult and paediatric recipients (a paediatric subgroup is analysed separately); analysis limited to European transplants because the PIRCHE-II haplotype imputation was validated only in Caucasians |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 68,606 |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; multivariable Cox regression on 5-year death-censored graft survival with country-based stratification; three nested models (HLA mismatches only, adjusted PIRCHE-II only, both simultaneously) compared by AIC; cross-stratified analysis of each parameter within categories of the other; ROC/AUC for the full model |
| typing resolution | one-field split antigen level for HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 (serologic split, not two-field molecular). PIRCHE-II scores were derived from these split typings by multiple imputation of two-field types using NMDP EUR (Caucasian) haplotype frequencies from 2007; each patient's PIRCHE-II score carries an individual standard deviation reflecting that imputation uncertainty. HLA-C, -DQ and -DP were not typed or modelled. |
| outcome | 5-year death-censored graft failure (graft loss) |
| follow up | mean 6.9 years |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, donor age, recipient sex, donor sex, time on dialysis, disease leading to transplantation, latest panel reactive antibodies (PRA), donor hypertension or other reason for marginal donor, induction therapy, initial immunosuppression, transplant year, cold ischaemia time, country (stratification variable) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest head-to-head test of antigen-level HLA mismatch counting against a molecular (epitope-load) score in kidney transplantation, and it answers the review's question of whether a low-resolution mismatch count is still the right scoring primitive when two-field typing is unavailable. Its central number for us is the traditional arm: HR 1.095 (1.078-1.113) per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch for 5-year death-censored graft loss, adjusted for donor age, recipient age, cold ischaemia, PRA, era and immunosuppression, i.e. roughly a 9.5% relative increase in graft-loss hazard for each antigen mismatch added, in a cohort spanning 1990-2016. Crucially for a low-resolution pre-screen, the antigen count out-performed PIRCHE-II on certainty (Wald z 11.2 vs 9.8), stayed significant when both were fitted together (HR 1.069 per mismatch, p<0.001, versus PIRCHE-II 1.043, p=0.002), and PIRCHE-II added nothing detectable below 4 mismatches (HR 1.031, p=0.10) - which is exactly the mismatch range a living-donor pre-screen tries to reach. The paper therefore supports keeping A+B+DR antigen mismatch as the ranking variable in a system that has only one-field typing, and argues against buying a molecular score before two-field typing exists. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor setting is limited on three axes: the donors are deceased (so cold ischaemia and donor quality vary in ways living donation does not), antibody status was measured (PRA was a modelled covariate and a strong effect modifier) whereas our pre-screen assumes it unknown, and the authors state explicitly that the haplotype imputation underpinning PIRCHE-II was validated only in Caucasians and would lose accuracy in other populations - a direct warning against porting an imputation-based molecular score to an Iranian donor pool without local haplotype frequency tables.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch (linear term), model without PIRCHE-II — HR 1.095 (1.078–1.113), p=<0.001; adjusted for recipient/donor age and sex, time on dialysis, primary disease, latest PRA, marginal donor, induction, initial immunosuppression, transplant year, cold ischaemia time; country-stratified [Results; Table 2 (AIC = 150,605); Wald z = 11.2]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score point (0-6 rescaled), model without HLA mismatches — HR 1.102 (1.081–1.123), p=<0.001; adjusted for same basic confounders [Results; Table 2 (AIC = 150,629); Wald z = 9.8]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch, both parameters fitted simultaneously — HR 1.069 (1.045–1.093), p=<0.001; adjusted for same basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score [Results; Table 2 (AIC = 150,598); Wald z = 5.8]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score point, both parameters fitted simultaneously — HR 1.043 (1.015–1.071), p=0.002; adjusted for same basic confounders plus HLA mismatches [Results; Table 2 (AIC = 150,598); Wald z = 3.0]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 0 HLA mismatches — HR 0.907 (0.741–1.108), p=0.34; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 1 HLA mismatch — HR 1.033 (0.945–1.129), p=0.47; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 2 HLA mismatches — HR 1.016 (0.94–1.099), p=0.69; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 3 HLA mismatches — HR 1.029 (0.96–1.104), p=0.42; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 4 HLA mismatches — HR 1.063 (0.979–1.154), p=0.15; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 5 HLA mismatches — HR 1.179 (1.048–1.325), p=0.006; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3 (the only HLA-mismatch stratum in which PIRCHE-II was significant)]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score within 6 HLA mismatches — HR 1.074 (0.858–1.344), p=0.54; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 0-1 — HR 1.123 (0.826–1.528), p=0.46; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 2-12 — HR 0.913 (0.826–1.008), p=0.073; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 13-25 — HR 1.07 (1.021–1.122), p=0.005; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 26-43 — HR 1.055 (1.014–1.098), p=0.009; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 44-68 — HR 1.095 (1.046–1.146), p=<0.001; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score 69-102 — HR 1.11 (1.032–1.194), p=0.005; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch within PIRCHE-II score >102 — HR 1.236 (1.048–1.458), p=0.012; adjusted for basic confounders [Table 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in recipients with LOW HLA incompatibility (0-3 mismatches, n = 43,144) — HR 1.031, p=0.10; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results and Abstract; Figure 4 (CI plotted, numeric CI not printed in text)]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in recipients with HIGH HLA incompatibility (4-6 mismatches, n = 25,462) — HR 1.097, p=0.005; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results and Abstract; Figure 4 (CI plotted, numeric CI not printed in text)]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in recipients with low PIRCHE-II score 0-12 (n = 9,630) — HR 0.945, p=0.23; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 4]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in recipients with PIRCHE-II score >12 (n = 58,976) — HR 1.078, p=<0.001; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 4]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in PRESENSITISED recipients (PRA >0%) — HR 1.103, p=0.006; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 3 (CI plotted only)]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in NON-SENSITISED recipients (PRA = 0%) — HR 1.047, p=0.008; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in PRESENSITISED recipients (PRA >0%) — HR 1.014, p=0.65; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in NON-SENSITISED recipients (PRA = 0%) — HR 1.082, p=<0.001; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; Figure 3]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in PAEDIATRIC recipients — HR 1.092, p=0.18; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per adjusted PIRCHE-II score in ADULT recipients — HR 1.041, p=0.004; adjusted for basic confounders plus HLA mismatches (simultaneous model) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in ADULT recipients — HR 1.066, p=<0.001; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- 5-year death-censored graft loss: per HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch in PAEDIATRIC recipients — HR 1.028, p=0.62; adjusted for basic confounders plus adjusted PIRCHE-II score (simultaneous model) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- 5-year graft survival, model discrimination: full Cox model (basic confounders + HLA mismatches + PIRCHE-II) — AUC 0.67; adjusted for n/a (model discrimination) [Results, ROC analysis; authors note a UNOS analysis reported AUC 0.66 for 3-year graft survival]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported. HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch entered every Cox model as a SINGLE LINEAR (per-mismatch) covariate, so only one slope is printed: HR 1.095 (1.078-1.113) per mismatch alone, HR 1.069 (1.045-1.093) per mismatch alongside PIRCHE-II. No category-specific hazard ratios for 0 vs 1 vs 2 ... vs 6 mismatches, and no zero-mismatch reference contrast, appear anywhere in the paper. The category counts are given for cohort description only (0 MM: 4,469; 1: 5,297; 2: 13,282; 3: 20,096; 4: 16,171; 5: 7,401; 6: 1,890).; linearity tested: not tested for the HLA mismatch count. The log-linear per-mismatch form was imposed by model specification and never checked against a categorical alternative. For the PIRCHE-II score the authors did the opposite: they imposed a logarithmic transform a priori, citing 'the previously published logarithmic feature of the PIRCHE-II effect', and rescaled the log score onto the same 0-6 range as the mismatch count so that hazard ratios would be numerically comparable. The only hint of non-linearity in the whole paper concerns the PIRCHE-II effect ACROSS mismatch strata, not the mismatch effect itself: the authors justify dichotomising at 0-3 vs 4-6 because the per-PIRCHE HRs at 4, 5 and 6 mismatches departed from 1 while those at 0-3 sat close to 1 (Table 3).; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- adjusted PIRCHE-II score x presensitisation (PRA >0% vs PRA = 0%): PIRCHE-II effect on graft loss more than twice as large in presensitised recipients (HR 1.103 (p = 0.006) in presensitised vs HR 1.047 (p = 0.008) in non-sensitised) [Results; Figure 3]
- HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch x presensitisation (PRA >0% vs PRA = 0%): the mirror image: the antigen mismatch effect was concentrated in NON-sensitised recipients and vanished in the presensitised, once PIRCHE-II was in the same model (HR 1.014 (p = 0.65) in presensitised vs HR 1.082 (p < 0.001) in non-sensitised) [Results; Figure 3]
- adjusted PIRCHE-II score x level of HLA incompatibility (0-3 vs 4-6 mismatches): PIRCHE-II added no detectable prognostic information at low mismatch load; it only contributed above 3 mismatches. This is the paper's headline effect-modification result and the basis of its recommendation (HR 1.031 (p = 0.10) at 0-3 MM vs HR 1.097 (p = 0.005) at 4-6 MM) [Results and Abstract; Figure 4]
- HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch x PIRCHE-II score category (0-12 vs >12): symmetrically, the antigen mismatch count carried no signal inside the low-PIRCHE stratum but was strongly predictive above it (HR 0.945 (p = 0.23) at PIRCHE 0-12 vs HR 1.078 (p < 0.001) at PIRCHE >12) [Results; Figure 4]
- adjusted PIRCHE-II score x recipient age group (paediatric vs adult): PIRCHE-II effect more than twice as large in paediatric recipients, but not statistically significant there (authors attribute this to low case numbers) (HR 1.092 (p = 0.18) paediatric vs HR 1.041 (p = 0.004) adult) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- HLA-A+B+DRB1 mismatch x recipient age group (paediatric vs adult): antigen mismatch effect stronger in adults (HR 1.066 (p < 0.001) adult vs HR 1.028 (p = 0.62) paediatric) [Results; supplementary subgroup figure]
- HLA mismatch or PIRCHE-II x cold ischaemia time >18 h; x donor age >=60 years: no material effect modification reported ('did not appear to influence the impact ... greatly'); numeric hazard ratios for these strata are in a supplementary figure and are not printed in the retrieved text (not printed) [Results, final sentence of subgroup paragraph]
- PIRCHE-II effect x transplant era: PIRCHE-II effect less pronounced in 1990-2003 than later, attributed to less precise typing methods in the earlier era; the authors note that imprecise typing degrades a computed epitope load far more than it degrades a mismatch count (not printed (supplementary figure)) [Discussion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "The calculated HR per adjusted PIRCHE-II score was with 1.102 slightly higher than the 1.095 HR calculated per HLA A+B+DRB1 mismatch." (Results, paragraph 2 (Table 2))
- *C2* — "The HLA-mismatch value was a significant predictor of graft survival in all PIRCHE-II score categories above 12" (Results, paragraph 4 (Table 3))
- *C12* — "Overall, we found that the PIRCHE-II score could not outmatch the traditional HLA mismatch." (Discussion, penultimate paragraph)
- *C12* — "In order to be precise, most of the epitope matching algorithms, including PIRCHE-II, require two-field molecular HLA typing." (Discussion, opening sentence)
- *C12* — "Therefore, our results may not be representative for other ethnic groups and accuracy is expected to decrease in more diverse patient collectives or when suitable haplotype frequency tables are unavailable." (Discussion, paragraph 1)
- *C11* — "The impact of HLA mismatches on outcome was, in contrast, more pronounced in non-sensitized compared to presensitized patients" (Results, paragraph 3 (Figure 3))

**Limitations.** Deceased-donor only. Every transplant is a first European deceased-donor kidney-alone graft; there is no living-donor arm, so the per-mismatch slope is entangled with cold ischaemia (mean 16-18 h) and deceased-donor quality, both of which are largely absent in living donation.; No dose-response shape. HLA mismatch is a single linear covariate in every model; the paper prints no HR for 1 vs 0, 2 vs 0 ... 6 vs 0 mismatches and never tests linearity, so it cannot speak to a zero-mismatch premium, a threshold, or diminishing returns.; No per-locus resolution. Only A, B and DRB1 were typed; C, DQ and DP were never measured. Locus-specific analysis was performed but the authors report it produced 'no new insights' and give no locus hazard ratios, so the paper says nothing about DR vs B vs A ranking.; European/Caucasian only by design. The PIRCHE-II imputation relies on NMDP EUR haplotype frequencies from 2007 and the authors explicitly restrict the cohort because that imputation is unvalidated elsewhere; accuracy is expected to fall in more diverse populations or where haplotype tables are missing - directly relevant to Iran.; Very long era span (1990-2016) with changing typing technology and immunosuppression; the authors themselves flag that pre-2003 typing imprecision attenuated the PIRCHE-II effect, which biases the head-to-head comparison in favour of the mismatch count in the early years.; Commercial involvement: one author is an employee of PIRCHE AG (which runs the PIRCHE web portal) and the senior author declares a minor research grant from PIRCHE AG. The direction of the finding is against the sponsor's product, which if anything strengthens the negative result.; PRA was missing for 16,064 of 68,606 patients (about 23%) and missingness was handled as a separate category, so the sensitisation interaction rests on incomplete exposure data and on old lymphocytotoxic PRA rather than solid-phase single-antigen bead DSA.; Outcome is 5-year death-censored graft loss only; no rejection, dnDSA, or patient-survival endpoints, and no acute-rejection intermediate that a pre-screen might care about.; Model discrimination is modest overall (AUC 0.67), so mismatch count is a real but weak marginal predictor against the full clinical covariate set.; Several subgroup hazard ratios (Figures 3 and 4, era and paediatric strata) are given as point estimates and p-values in the text with confidence intervals only plotted, not printed - those CIs are recorded as null here rather than inferred..

### Davis S 2020 — Adequate tacrolimus exposure modulates the impact of HLA class II molecular mismatch: a validation study in an American cohort

Davis S 2020, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.16290](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.16290). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (Wiley / American Journal of Transplantation, deposited in PMC; no licence statement present in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All adult (>=18 y) kidney or kidney/pancreas recipients, University of Colorado Hospital (Denver), September 2007 - December 2013, started on tacrolimus-based triple maintenance. Excluded: simultaneous liver-kidney (N=19), previous islet cell transplant (N=5), PRE-TRANSPLANT DSA (N=272), inadequate DSA screening, inadequate donor sample for HLA typing (N=212). |
| donor type | both |
| n | 444 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; competing-risk analysis (proportional subdistribution hazards, death as competing risk); ROC validation of externally derived (Canadian/Wiebe) single-molecule eplet thresholds; univariate screening at p<0.20 then multivariable model chosen by lowest AIC; R 3.6.0 |
| typing resolution | allele-level (two-field) class II only: recipient and donor HLA-DR and -DQ typed by sequence-specific oligonucleotide (LABType SSO DRB1 [XR], DRB345, DQA1/B1) with supplemental SSP as needed; eplet load computed with HLAMatchmaker DRDQDP v2. No class I molecular mismatch analysis. Whole-antigen DR+DQ mismatch counts also used as a comparator. |
| outcome | de novo HLA-DR and/or HLA-DQ donor-specific antibody within 12 months (MFI >500 and >=2 SD above negative control mean); screening at 1, 6, 12 months and when clinically indicated. NOT graft survival, NOT biopsy-proven rejection. |
| follow up | 1 year; censored at last follow-up or 13 months post-transplant, whichever earliest |
| other factors modelled | average tacrolimus trough 0-12 months (<6.0, 6.0-7.9, >=8.0 ng/ml), age at transplant, sex, ethnic group, prior/repeat transplant, donor type (deceased vs living), thymoglobulin induction, mycophenolate dose reduction within 1 year, steroid type, delayed graft function, whole antigen HLA-DR+DQ mismatch count (0, 1-2, 3-4) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the first external validation of the Wiebe HLA-DR/DQ single-molecule eplet thresholds, so it answers the review's question of whether molecular mismatch categories out-predict antigen mismatch counts for early alloimmunisation: in the same multivariable frame, eplet risk category carried HR 15.39 and 23.81 while a whole-antigen DR+DQ mismatch of 3-4 versus 1-2 carried only HR 2.58 univariately. That is direct support for C12 (molecular thresholds, prediction versus antigen matching) and, through the tacrolimus contrast, for C11 (effect modification by immunosuppression exposure). Transfer to an Iranian pre-screen is however sharply limited by inputs: every number here depends on two-field DRB1/DRB3-4-5/DQA1/DQB1 typing, which a one-field (broad/split antigen) Iranian workup cannot produce, and the paper offers no low-resolution or imputed fallback and no accuracy estimate for one. The paper also shows why an antigen-count pre-screen cannot stand in for the molecular score: among low molecular-risk pairs only 42% had zero DR+DQ antigen mismatches, 46% had 1-2 and 12% had 3-4, so antigen counting misclassifies molecular risk in both directions. The population is the opposite of antibody-status-unknown - 272 candidates were excluded precisely because they had pre-transplant DSA - so these hazards describe a pre-screened, non-sensitised population and say nothing about the dominant risk (pre-existing DSA) that an Iranian pre-screen with unknown antibody status must handle first. Living donation is well represented (roughly 45-49% of the cohort; deceased donor carried HR 2.74, so living-donor recipients were the lower-risk half), which is mildly encouraging for C14, but no living-donor-stratified hazard ratios are reported. Finally the endpoint is 1-year dnDSA, a surrogate, and the effect is explicitly conditional on tacrolimus exposure that a pre-transplant matching algorithm does not control.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: intermediate vs low HLA-DR/DQ molecular mismatch risk category — HR (subdistribution) 15.39 (2.01–118.09), p=0.009; adjusted for average tacrolimus 0-12 months, age at transplant, deceased donor [Results 3.3 and Table 3 (multivariable); also Abstract]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: high vs low HLA-DR/DQ molecular mismatch risk category — HR (subdistribution) 23.81 (3.17–178.66), p=0.002; adjusted for average tacrolimus 0-12 months, age at transplant, deceased donor [Results 3.3 and Table 3 (multivariable); also Abstract]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: intermediate vs low molecular mismatch risk, UNIVARIATE — HR 13.92 (1.85–104.94), p=<.001; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results 3.2]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: high vs low molecular mismatch risk, UNIVARIATE — HR 21.64 (2.94–159.38), p=<.001; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results 3.2]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: WHOLE ANTIGEN DR+DQ mismatch 3-4 vs 1-2 — HR 2.58 (1.34–4.97), p=0.005; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results 3.2 - key antigen-versus-molecular comparator]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: intermediate vs low molecular mismatch risk, sensitivity analysis excluding the 11 recipients with dnDSA before 6 months — HR 12.71 (1.6–99.6), p=0.016; adjusted for other covariates (model as in Table 3) [Results 3.3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: high vs low molecular mismatch risk, sensitivity analysis excluding the 11 recipients with dnDSA before 6 months — HR 17.36 (2.3–132.9), p=0.006; adjusted for other covariates (model as in Table 3) [Results 3.3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: mean tacrolimus trough <6.0 ng/ml vs >=8.0 ng/ml — HR 2.34 (1.05–5.22), p=0.04; adjusted for molecular mismatch risk category, age, deceased donor [Results 3.3 and Table 3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: mean tacrolimus trough 6.0-7.9 ng/ml vs >=8.0 ng/ml — HR 1.09 (0.54–2.18), p=0.81; adjusted for molecular mismatch risk category, age, deceased donor [Table 3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: age at transplant, per year — HR 0.96 (0.94–0.98), p=0.0001; adjusted for molecular mismatch risk category, tacrolimus, deceased donor [Table 3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: age at transplant, per year, UNIVARIATE — HR 0.97 (0.95–0.99), p=0.002; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results 3.2]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: deceased donor vs living donor — HR 2.74 (1.47–5.1), p=0.002; adjusted for molecular mismatch risk category, tacrolimus, age [Table 3]
- de novo DR/DQ DSA by 12 months: deceased donor vs living donor, UNIVARIATE — HR 2.4 (1.27–4.53), p=0.007; adjusted for none (univariate) [Results 3.2]
- de novo DR DSA by 12 months (discrimination): HLA-DRbeta single-molecule eplet mismatch threshold >=7 — AUC 0.84; adjusted for n/a; sensitivity 100%, specificity 69% [Results 3.2 and Abstract]
- de novo DQ DSA by 12 months (discrimination): HLA-DQ alpha-beta single-molecule eplet mismatch threshold >=9 — AUC 0.82; adjusted for n/a; sensitivity 96%, specificity 58% [Results 3.2 and Abstract]
- any de novo DSA by 12 months: whole cohort incidence — percentage 18.5; adjusted for n/a; 82 of 444 patients [Results 3.1]
- de novo HLA-DR or HLA-DQ DSA by 12 months: whole cohort incidence — percentage 10.6; adjusted for n/a; 47 of 444 patients; median time 6.0 months, IQR 3.7-10.8 [Results 3.1]
- de novo HLA-A or HLA-B DSA by 12 months: whole cohort incidence — percentage 5.9; adjusted for n/a; 26 of 444 patients [Results 3.1]
- de novo HLA-C or HLA-DP DSA by 12 months: whole cohort incidence — percentage 2.0; adjusted for n/a; 9 of 444 patients [Results 3.1 - relevant to C7/C8 only as a raw rate; no eplet analysis for C or DP]
- locus attribution of the 47 DR/DQ dnDSA events: DQ alone vs DR alone vs mixed — percentage 42.6; adjusted for n/a; DQ alone 20 (42.6%), DR alone 7 (14.9%), mixed DR/DQ 20 (42.6%) [Results 3.1 - supports C4 (DQ dominance in dnDSA)]
- distribution of the 47 DR/DQ dnDSA events across molecular risk categories: low vs intermediate vs high — count and percentage of events None; adjusted for n/a; 1 (2%) low, 17 (36%) intermediate, 29 (62%) high [Results 3.2]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: None MM: reference (1.0); None MM: HR 15.39 (2.01–118.09); None MM: HR 23.81 (3.17–178.66)
- DR: HLA-DRbeta single-molecule eplet load; threshold >=7 eplets; AUC 0.84 for DR dnDSA (sens 100%, spec 69%). Table 1 as printed: Low = DRbeta 0-6; Intermediate = DRbeta 0-21; High = DRbeta 0-21.
- DQ: HLA-DQ alpha-beta single-molecule eplet load; threshold >=9 eplets; AUC 0.82 for DQ dnDSA (sens 96%, spec 58%). Table 1 as printed: Low = DQ 0-8; Intermediate = DQ 9-14; High = DQ 15 (the '>=' before 15 appears lost in the PMC text extraction).
- composite: The HLA-DR/DQ molecular mismatch score takes the greater of the patient's individual DR and DQ risks ('based on the greatest risk associated with the patient's individual HLA-DR and HLA-DQ mismatch scores'), so DQ effectively drives the category for most pairs.
- A_B_C_DP: not analysed at the molecular level; only raw dnDSA incidences reported
- Shape reported: step / graded across three ordered eplet-load categories, monotonically increasing (1.0 -> 15.39 -> 23.81 adjusted; 1.0 -> 13.92 -> 21.64 univariate). The authors describe it as 'a graded increase in risk'. The increment from intermediate to high is far smaller than the increment from low to intermediate, i.e. most of the separation is the near-absence of events in the low group.; linearity tested: not tested. Eplet load was never modelled as a continuous variable, no spline, no trend test, no p-for-trend. The thresholds (DR >=7, DQ >=9) were pre-specified from the Canadian derivation cohort and only re-validated here by ROC/AUC; the three categories were entered as an unordered factor with low as reference.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR/DQ molecular mismatch category x tacrolimus exposure: Descriptive, not formally tested. Reduced tacrolimus exposure had little apparent impact on dnDSA in the low molecular-mismatch group (the group's single dnDSA event occurred in a patient with documented non-adherence and undetectable troughs), whereas recipients with high eplet load were reported to be less able to tolerate low tacrolimus levels. In the multivariable model the tacrolimus term is a MAIN effect across the whole cohort, not an interaction term. (tacrolimus <6.0 vs >=8.0 ng/ml HR 2.34 (1.05-5.22), p=.04; 6.0-7.9 vs >=8.0 HR 1.09 (0.54-2.18), p=.81. NO interaction coefficient and NO p-for-interaction is reported anywhere in the paper.) [Results 3.3, Table 3, Discussion paragraphs 1 and 3]
- molecular mismatch category x ethnicity: No interaction tested; instead the authors argue the externally derived thresholds transported across two cohorts with very different ethnic composition (Canadian: 65% Caucasian, 13% Asian, 20% Indigenous; Denver: 71% Caucasian, 16% Hispanic, 9% African American) and still distributed patients almost identically (low 27% vs 25%, intermediate 35% vs 36%, high 39% vs 39%). (no estimate; ethnicity was not significantly associated with time-to-DR/DQ dnDSA in univariate analysis (p=.13)) [Results 3.1, Discussion paragraph 1]
- molecular mismatch category x donor type (deceased vs living): Not tested as an interaction. Donor type entered the multivariable model as an independent main effect: deceased donor HR 2.74 (1.47-5.1), p=.002. No living-donor-stratified hazard ratios for the molecular mismatch categories are reported. (HR 2.74 (1.47-5.1) for deceased donor, adjusted) [Table 3]
- factors screened and found NOT associated: In univariate analysis ethnicity (p=.13), re-transplant (p=.14), delayed graft function (p=.85) and clinical acute cellular rejection prior to DSA (p=.11) were not significantly associated with time-to-DR/DQ dnDSA; no hazard ratios are printed for these. (p-values only) [Results 3.2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "The HLA‐DRβsingle molecule eplet mismatch threshold of ≥7 associated with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 with a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 69% for development of DR DSA." (Results 3.2, Molecular mismatch and risk of donor-specific antibodies)
- *C12* — "Of the 47 patients who developed DR/DQ DSAs, there was 1 (2%) low molecular mismatch risk patient, 17 (36%) intermediate molecular mismatch risk patients, and 29 (62%) high molecular mismatch risk patients." (Results 3.2)
- *C12* — "Several traditional immunologic risk factors showed comparatively less robust associations with DR/DQ DSA development, including whole antigen DQ +DR mismatch of 3 – 4 compared to 1 – 2" (Results 3.2 (the antigen-count comparator, HR 2.58, 95% CI 1.34-4.97, p=.005))
- *C11* — "In the present study, reduced tacrolimus exposure had little impact on DSA development in patients with low molecular mismatch risk despite traditional measures of immunologic risk, including age, ethnicity, and type of donor." (Discussion, paragraph 3)
- *C11* — "In contrast, recipients with high eplet mismatch load were less likely to tolerate low tacrolimus levels without developing de novo DSAs." (Discussion, paragraph 3)
- *C4* — "Of all DR/DQ de novo DSA, 20 (42.6%) were DQ alone, 7 (14.9%) DR alone, and 20 (42.6%) mixed DR/DQ antibodies." (Results 3.1, Demographics and baseline characteristics)

**Limitations.** Very small event count: only 47 DR/DQ dnDSA events in 444 patients, and only ONE event in the low-risk reference group. Every headline hazard ratio therefore rests on a near-empty reference cell, which is why the confidence intervals are enormous (2.01-118.09 and 3.17-178.66). The point estimates (15.39, 23.81) must not be read as calibrated risk multipliers.; Single centre, retrospective, one US city (Denver), 2007-2013; the authors themselves warn of type II error from the small sample.; Heavy exclusions from an unstated source denominator: 272 excluded for pre-transplant DSA, 212 for inadequate donor sample/DSA screening, 19 liver-kidney, 5 prior islet. Selection depends on donor DNA availability and on being antibody-negative pre-transplant.; No formal interaction test between tacrolimus exposure and molecular mismatch category. The tacrolimus HR in Table 3 is a whole-cohort main effect; the authors concede power was insufficient to assess the interaction. The Abstract states the tacrolimus result as if restricted to intermediate- and high-risk patients, which the reported model does not show.; Outcome is a 1-year serological surrogate (dnDSA at MFI >500), not graft survival and not biopsy-proven rejection; the authors had no histology to evaluate T cell-mediated rejection. 14.8% of positive results were in the weak MFI 500-999 band.; Interval-censored ascertainment: DSA screened only at 1, 6 and 12 months plus for cause, so 'time to dnDSA' is coarse.; Requires allele-level (two-field) DRB1/DRB3-4-5/DQA1/DQB1 typing plus HLAMatchmaker to compute eplet load. No low-resolution, serologic or imputed-typing version of the score is presented or validated, and no misclassification estimate is given for one - this is the decisive obstacle for a one-field Iranian pre-screen.; Class I and HLA-DP are not analysed at the molecular level at all; only crude dnDSA incidences (5.9% A/B, 2% C/DP) are reported.; Only 9% of recipients were African American versus 21% of US transplants in 2019; no Middle Eastern or Iranian population represented, and the Denver cohort has a Hispanic majority-minority profile unlike Iran.; The cohort mixes kidney-alone and simultaneous kidney/pancreas recipients with no separate kidney-alone results; kidney/pancreas recipients also received different induction by protocol.; Confounding by indication for tacrolimus exposure: troughs were not randomised, and the retrospective design means clinical events (infection, toxicity, non-adherence) drove both the exposure and possibly the outcome.; Text-extraction damage in the retrieved PMC version: Table 1's threshold rows lost their '>=' signs (High DQ prints as '15'), several Table 2 percentages are corrupted ('114 (6)' for 3-4 mismatches in the high group, '50 (2)' for >=8.0 ng/ml in the high group), and inline p-value labels are missing (rendered as '= .009'). Verify Table 1 and Table 2 against the publisher PDF before quoting those cells..

### Lucisano G 2020 — Donor-specific antibodies detected by single antigen beads alone can help risk stratify patients undergoing retransplantation across a repeat HLA mismatch.

Lucisano G 2020, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.15595](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.15595). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (American Journal of Transplantation); no PMC record — convert_article_ids returned no pmcid on 2026-09-08, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult kidney retransplant recipients at a single UK centre (Imperial College Healthcare / Hammersmith Hospital), drawn from 1988 consecutive renal transplant recipients; 179 retransplants analysed, 55 of them across a repeat HLA mismatch (RMM); all recipients crossmatch negative |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract |
| n | 179 retransplant recipients (55 with a repeat mismatch), from a source cohort of 1988 consecutive renal transplant recipients |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; multivariable (Cox proportional hazards) analysis |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; the exposure is a repeat mismatched HLA antigen (antigen-level concept), and preformed DSA were defined by single antigen bead assay alone (i.e. below CDC/flow crossmatch detection) |
| outcome | antibody-mediated rejection; death-censored allograft loss; de novo DSA development |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | preformed donor-specific antibody detected by single antigen beads alone (against the repeat mismatch), prior transplant nephrectomy, HLA class II matching of the retransplant |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper speaks to review question C11 — effect modification of HLA mismatch by other factors, here by pre-existing sensitisation and by retransplant status. Its central result is that the harm of re-exposing a recipient to a previously mismatched HLA antigen is entirely conditional on whether a preformed antibody against that antigen is present: with SAB-only DSA the repeat mismatch carried an antibody-mediated rejection HR of 8.70 and a death-censored loss HR of 3.08, while without preformed DSA the same repeat mismatch was not associated with de novo DSA, rejection, or graft loss. For a living-donor pre-screen in Iran this cuts both ways. It is a warning: the population it studies (retransplant candidates, who in Iran are a real and growing group) cannot be risk-stratified on HLA antigen identity alone, because the identical mismatch means very different things depending on an antibody result the pre-screen does not have — so a system with antibody status unknown must treat a repeat mismatch as a flag for laboratory work-up, never as a computable risk score. It is also reassuring for the first-transplant majority: the whole effect is antibody-mediated, so in an unsensitised, first-graft candidate a mismatch at a given antigen does not carry this magnitude of risk. Transfer is limited by design and resolution: the cohort is single-centre UK, donor type is not reported in the retrievable abstract, typing resolution is not stated, and the exposure is binary (repeat mismatch present/absent) rather than a mismatch count, so the paper supplies no dose-response information for a one-field, count-based matching index.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- antibody-mediated rejection: preformed SAB-only DSA against a repeat HLA mismatch (RMM), vs the rest of the retransplant cohort (reference group not specified in the abstract) — HR 8.7 (3.42–22.1), p=<0.0001; adjusted for multivariable model; covariate list not visible in the abstract [Abstract (results sentence)]
- death-censored allograft loss: preformed SAB-only DSA against a repeat HLA mismatch (RMM), vs the rest of the retransplant cohort (reference group not specified in the abstract) — HR 3.08 (1.17–8.14), p=0.023; adjusted for multivariable model; covariate list not visible in the abstract [Abstract (results sentence)]
- allograft failure / favourable allograft outcome: retransplant matched at HLA class II vs not matched at HLA class II — HR 0.37 (0.14–0.99), p=0.047; adjusted for same multivariable model as above; covariate list not visible in the abstract [Abstract (results sentence)]
- allograft failure: prior transplant nephrectomy vs no prior transplant nephrectomy — HR 2.04 (1.0–4.17), p=0.0495; adjusted for same multivariable model as above [Abstract (results sentence)]
- de novo DSA development, rejection, and allograft loss: repeat HLA mismatch (RMM) without preformed DSA, vs no repeat mismatch — narrative null result None; adjusted for not stated [Abstract (results sentence)]

**Dose-response.**

- class II (DR/DQ as a block): matched retransplant at HLA class II vs unmatched: HR 0.37 (0.14-0.99), P = .047
- class I: not reported in the abstract
- DR: not reported separately
- DQ: not reported separately
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested — and not applicable: the exposure is a binary repeat mismatch (present/absent) stratified by preformed DSA status, not a count of mismatches; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- repeat HLA mismatch (RMM) x preformed SAB-only donor-specific antibody: The risk attached to a repeat mismatch is present only when a preformed DSA against that mismatch is detectable by single antigen beads; without preformed DSA the repeat mismatch was not associated with de novo DSA, rejection, or graft loss. This is the paper's central claim. (with preformed DSA: AMR HR 8.70 (3.42-22.10), P < .0001; death-censored allograft loss HR 3.08 (1.17-8.14), P = .023. Without preformed DSA: no association reported, no numeric estimate printed.) [Abstract (results and conclusion sentences)]
- retransplantation x HLA class II matching: Within retransplant recipients, receiving a graft matched at HLA class II was protective for allograft outcome, independent of the DSA/RMM exposure in the same model. (HR 0.37 (0.14-0.99), P = .047) [Abstract (results sentence)]
- retransplantation x prior transplant nephrectomy: Prior transplant nephrectomy was independently associated with allograft failure. (HR 2.04 (1.00-4.17), P = .0495) [Abstract (results sentence)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "Multivariate analysis revealed that patients with preformed DSA against an RMM were independently at risk of antibody-mediated rejection (HR 8.70 [3.42-22.10], P < .0001) and death-censored allograft loss (HR 3.08 [1.17-8.14], P = .023)." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "In the absence of preformed DSA, an RMM was not associated with de novo DSA development, rejection, or allograft loss." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "an RMM portends increased immunological risk only in the presence of a preformed DSA in patients undergoing retransplantation." (Abstract, conclusion sentence)
- *C1* — "receiving a retransplant that was matched at HLA class II was associated with a favorable outcome (HR 0.37 [0.14-0.99], P = .047)" (Abstract)
- *C11* — "From 1988 consecutive renal transplant recipients, we analyzed 179 patients undergoing retransplantation, of whom 55 had a RMM. All patients were crossmatch negative and preformed DSA were detected by single antigen beads alone." (Abstract, methods sentence)
- *C11* — "This is due to evidence derived predominantly from registry data, which lacks comprehensive information on alloantibody and rejection." (Abstract, background sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only access: no PMC record exists for this article, so the covariate list, follow-up duration, donor type, HLA typing resolution, event counts, and any figures or tables could not be inspected. Everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; Small single-centre cohort: 179 retransplants with only 55 repeat mismatches, and the DSA-positive subgroup is smaller still. Confidence intervals are correspondingly wide (AMR HR 8.70 spans 3.42 to 22.10), so the point estimates are imprecise.; Two of the four printed hazard ratios sit on the significance boundary: class II matching 0.14-0.99 with P = .047, prior nephrectomy 1.00-4.17 with P = .0495. Neither should be treated as a firm effect size.; The 'no preformed DSA' null result is narrative only — no hazard ratio, confidence interval, or P value is printed for it in the abstract, so the absence of risk is asserted rather than quantified, and the study may simply be underpowered to detect a modest effect.; No formal interaction test (P for interaction) is reported; the DSA-conditional effect is inferred from stratified/model results rather than from a printed interaction term.; Every recipient was crossmatch negative, so the findings cannot be extended to crossmatch-positive retransplantation.; The exposure is binary (repeat mismatch present or absent). The paper supplies no mismatch-count dose-response and no per-locus (A/B/C/DR/DQ/DP) breakdown; class II is analysed as a single block, so DR cannot be separated from DQ.; Retransplant-only population: results do not transfer directly to first grafts, which are the majority of a national pre-screen's traffic.; The whole risk-stratification hinges on single antigen bead DSA testing, a capability the target pre-screen explicitly does not have; the paper offers no way to reproduce its stratification from HLA typing alone..

### Sapir-Pichhadze R 2020 — Epitopes as characterized by antibody-verified eplet mismatches determine risk of kidney transplant loss.

Sapir-Pichhadze R 2020, *Kidney International*, [DOI 10.1016/j.kint.2019.10.028](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2019.10.028). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier, Kidney International); no PMC record - convert_article_ids returned no pmcid for PMID 32059998, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 118,382 United States first kidney transplant recipients (US cohort); plus an independent Canadian cohort of kidney transplant recipients for the transplant glomerulopathy analysis (size, era and centres not stated in the abstract) |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract; 'first kidney transplant recipients' in the US cohort is not broken down into living vs deceased donors in the retrieved text |
| n | 118,382 (US cohort); Canadian cohort n not stated in the abstract |
| design | retrospective cohort, multivariable Cox proportional hazards, exposure modelled as increments of ten antibody-verified eplet mismatches per locus group; sensitivity analysis in the US cohort and an independent Canadian validation cohort |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract. Eplet assignment requires two-field (allele-level) HLA, which US registry records generally do not carry; the abstract does not say whether alleles were directly typed or imputed, and this could not be verified because the full text is not in PMC |
| outcome | death-censored graft failure (US cohort); transplant glomerulopathy (Canadian cohort) |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract - the models are described only as 'multivariable Cox proportional hazard models'; no covariate list is visible in the retrieved text |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest registry test of molecular (eplet-level) HLA mismatch against hard kidney graft outcome, so it is the main quantitative anchor for the review's question of whether molecular mismatch load carries dose information that antigen counting misses (C12). It answers the locus-ranking question in molecular units: per 10 antibody-verified eplet mismatches the death-censored graft failure hazard is largest for HLA-DQB1 (1.411), then DRB1 (1.268), then class I as a block (1.231), which is the same ordering the review sees at antigen level and supports DQ as the most immunogenic locus (C4) and DR as dominant among the classical class II loci reported here (C3). Critically for the review, the authors break the DRB1/DQB1 linkage disequilibrium by fitting mutually exclusive subcohorts, and each locus remains predictive when the other contributes no eplet mismatch - direct evidence that the DQ effect is not merely DR riding on haplotype. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen is weak on the exposure side and useful on the ranking side: eplet counts cannot be computed from one-field typing at all, so this paper cannot be operationalised as a scoring rule for that setting, and it is a caution that a low-resolution pre-screen will misclassify molecular load. What does transfer is the direction and relative size of the locus weights - a pre-screen that ignores DQ is dropping the locus with the steepest measured molecular gradient. The donor mix is also not stated, so a living-donor-specific reading cannot be taken from the abstract.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: per 10 antibody-verified eplet mismatches, Class I (HLA-A, B and C) combined — HR 1.231 (1.195–1.268); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results sentence 1); US cohort n=118,382]
- death-censored graft failure: per 10 antibody-verified eplet mismatches, HLA-DRB1 — HR 1.268 (1.231–1.305); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results sentence 1); US cohort n=118,382]
- death-censored graft failure: per 10 antibody-verified eplet mismatches, HLA-DQB1 — HR 1.411 (1.331–1.495); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results sentence 1); US cohort n=118,382]
- death-censored graft failure: each additional antibody-verified HLA-DRB1 eplet mismatch, in the subcohort with NO HLA-DQB1 eplet mismatches (linkage-disequilibrium-breaking analysis) — HR 1.384 (1.293–1.48); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results sentence 2); US subcohort]
- death-censored graft failure: each additional antibody-verified HLA-DQB1 eplet mismatch, in the subcohort with NO HLA-DRB1 mismatches — HR 1.384 (1.072–1.791); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results sentence 3); US subcohort]
- transplant glomerulopathy: antibody-verified HLA-DRB1 eplet mismatches (increment not restated in the abstract for this cohort) — HR 5.511 (1.442–21.08); adjusted for described as 'autonomous/independent predictors'; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results, final sentence); independent Canadian cohort]
- transplant glomerulopathy: antibody-verified HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 eplet mismatches (increment not restated in the abstract for this cohort) — HR 3.64 (1.574–8.416); adjusted for described as 'autonomous/independent predictors'; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (Results, final sentence); independent Canadian cohort]

**Dose-response.**

- Class I (HLA-A, B, C combined): per_10_antibody_verified_eplet_mismatches MM: HR 1.231 (95% CI 1.195, 1.268)
- DRB1: per_10_antibody_verified_eplet_mismatches MM: HR 1.268 (1.231, 1.305); subcohort_with_no_DQB1_eplet_mismatch MM: HR 1.384 (1.293, 1.480) per additional antibody-verified DRB1 eplet mismatch
- DQB1: per_10_antibody_verified_eplet_mismatches MM: HR 1.411 (1.331, 1.495); subcohort_with_no_DRB1_mismatch MM: HR 1.384 (1.072, 1.791) per additional DQB1 mismatch
- DRB1/3/4/5: transplant_glomerulopathy_Canadian_cohort MM: HR 3.640 (1.574, 8.416)
- DP: not reported
- DQA1: not reported
- Shape reported: not reported. The exposure is continuous and the hazard ratio is quoted per increment of ten antibody-verified eplet mismatches, i.e. log-linearity in eplet count is assumed by the model rather than demonstrated. No 0/1/2 category series, no spline, no threshold and no zero-mismatch reference group appear anywhere in the retrieved abstract.; linearity tested: not stated in the abstract. The abstract mentions a 'sensitivity analysis' in the US cohort but does not say what it varied, and the full text is not in PMC, so whether non-linearity, thresholds or categorised eplet loads were examined could not be checked.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DRB1 eplet mismatch x HLA-DQB1 eplet mismatch (linkage disequilibrium between the two loci): Not a formal interaction test but a conditional/stratified analysis: the authors refit the model in mutually exclusive subcohorts, and each class II locus stayed an independent predictor of death-censored graft failure when the other locus contributed no eplet mismatch. This is the abstract's evidence that the DQB1 signal is not simply DRB1 carried along by haplotype linkage. (DRB1 in the DQB1-eplet-mismatch-free subcohort HR 1.384 (1.293, 1.480); DQB1 in the DRB1-mismatch-free subcohort HR 1.384 (1.072, 1.791)) [Abstract, Results sentences 2-3]
- sensitisation / PRA, recipient age, donor age or type, cold ischaemia, ethnicity, era, immunosuppression: No effect-modification result for any of these is reported in the retrieved abstract. Whether the full text tests them is unknown because the article has no PMC record. [absent from the abstract]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**
