- *C12* — "we fit multivariable Cox proportional hazard models in a cohort of 118 382 United States first kidney transplant recipients to assess risk of death-censored graft failure by increments of ten antibody-verified eplet mismatches" (Abstract, Methods sentence)
- *C3* — "independent predictors of death-censored graft failure with hazard ratios of 1.231 [95% confidence interval 1.195, 1. 268], 1.268 [1.231, 1.305] and 1.411 [1.331, 1.495] for Class I (HLA-A, B, and C), -DRB1 and -DQB1 loci, respectively" (Abstract, Results sentence 1)
- *C4* — "To address linkage disequilibrium between HLA-DRB1 and -DQB1, we fit models in a subcohort without HLA-DQB1 eplet mismatches and found hazard ratios for death-censored graft failure of 1.384 [1.293, 1.480] for each additional antibody-verified HLA-DRB1 eplet mismatch" (Abstract, Results sentence 2)
- *C4* — "In a subcohort without HLA-DRB1 mismatches, the hazard ratio was 1.384 [1.072, 1.791] for each additional HLA-DQB1 mismatch" (Abstract, Results sentence 3)
- *C12* — "In the Canadian cohort, antibody-verified eplet mismatches were independent predictors of transplant glomerulopathy with hazard ratios of 5.511 [1.442, 21.080] for HLA-DRB1 and 3.640 [1.574, 8.416] for -DRB1/3/4/5" (Abstract, Results final sentence)
- *C12* — "Thus, donor-recipient matching for specific HLA eplets appears to be a feasible and clinically justifiable strategy to mitigate risk of graft loss" (Abstract, Conclusion)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY. The article is not in PMC (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid), so no Results section, no table, no covariate list, no follow-up duration, no event counts and no figure could be read. Every number here comes from the PubMed abstract.; The exposure is continuous and modelled per ten eplet mismatches, so linearity in eplet count is an assumption of the model, not a finding. No dose-response shape, threshold, spline or category series is reported in the abstract, which limits what this paper can say about claim C2.; The two subcohort hazard ratios are worded 'for each additional' eplet mismatch while the main models are 'per increments of ten'. Whether the subcohort HRs are per 1 or per 10 eplets cannot be resolved from the abstract; the magnitudes (1.384 vs 1.268) are more consistent with per 10, but this is not verifiable and must not be assumed.; Eplet counting requires two-field HLA alleles. The abstract never states how allele-level typing was obtained for a US registry cohort of this size, so imputation cannot be confirmed or excluded from the retrieved text - and if alleles were imputed, misclassification of eplet load is a real possibility that the abstract does not quantify.; Donor type (living vs deceased) is not reported, so no living-donor-specific estimate is available. This is the single biggest gap for the review's Iranian living-donor question.; 'Antibody-verified' eplets are a curated subset of eplets defined by the HLA Eplet Registry at the time of the study; the count depends on that registry version, which the abstract does not state, so the exposure is not a fixed physical quantity across studies.; The Canadian cohort's transplant glomerulopathy hazard ratios have very wide confidence intervals (DRB1: 1.442 to 21.080), indicating few events; the point estimate of 5.511 should not be read as a precise effect size.; Transplant glomerulopathy requires protocol or indication biopsy, so the Canadian outcome is subject to ascertainment bias that the abstract does not address.; Class I is reported only as a single A+B+C block, so this paper cannot rank B against A against C and contributes nothing to claims C5, C6 or C7. HLA-DP and HLA-DQA1 are not reported at all.; Registry cohort with no randomisation; residual confounding by the covariates that co-vary with eplet load (recipient race, sensitisation, allocation priority) cannot be excluded and the abstract does not show what was adjusted for..

### Senev A 2020 — Clinical importance of extended second field high-resolution HLA genotyping for kidney transplantation

Senev A 2020, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.15938](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.15938). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (PMC deposit of a Wiley/AJT article; no licence statement returned with the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 1000 consecutive adult single kidney transplants, University Hospitals Leuven, Belgium, 1 March 2004 - 6 February 2013; all ABO-compatible with negative CDC crossmatch on T and B cells; no desensitisation. Recipients 98.4% white, mean age 53.7 y, 15.4% repeat transplants. Analytic subsets: 262 recipients with any pretransplant anti-HLA antibody; 140 with DSA suspected on low-resolution typing; 471/469 pairs for the eplet analysis. |
| donor type | both (941/1000 deceased donors, 94.1%; the remaining ~5.9% living) |
| n | 1000 (262 sensitised; 140 LR-DSA-positive; 224 individual suspected DSA) |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; donor-recipient pairs retyped by NGS at 11 loci to second-field high resolution (2F-HR) and used as the criterion standard against (a) low-resolution split-antigen typing and (b) 2F-HR genotypes inferred from LR typing by HaploStats and by the HLAMatchmaker 4-digit allele converter; agreement statistics plus Kaplan-Meier/log-rank outcome validation |
| typing resolution | mixed by design — LR split-antigen (Eurotransplant ENIS, plus SSP/Sanger for C, DQB1, DPB1) versus two-field high resolution by NGS for HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, -DRB3, -DRB4, -DRB5, -DQA1, -DQB1, -DPA1, -DPB1 (recipients N=1000, donors N=932) |
| outcome | primary: correctness of pretransplant DSA assignment (2F-HR typing as criterion standard). Secondary: 10-year death-censored graft survival; cumulative incidence of the histological phenotype of antibody-mediated rejection (ABMRh) within 5 years (3647 biopsies); agreement of eplet mismatch load and repertoire between true and inferred genotypes |
| follow up | median 7.5 years (IQR 4.9-10.0); biopsy follow-up to 5 years |
| other factors modelled | none — all outcome comparisons are unadjusted Kaplan-Meier / log-rank, donor age, cold ischaemia time, induction therapy, repeat transplantation, diabetes and recipient age are described in Table 1 but are not entered into any model |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the anchor paper for the review's low-resolution misclassification question (C12): it is the only study that takes a real kidney cohort, retypes every donor-recipient pair at two-field resolution by NGS, and then measures how often antigen-level typing gets the immunological verdict wrong AND checks that verdict against 10-year graft survival and biopsy histology, so the misclassification is shown to be genuine error rather than a laboratory artefact. Its second contribution is decisive for any programme that hopes to rescue high-resolution information statistically: HaploStats inference from LR data still left DSA assignment wrong in 23.3% of sensitised patients, and inferred genotypes reproduced the class II eplet repertoire in only 35.4% of pairs. For the Iranian living-donor pre-screen the transfer is partial but pointed in one direction. The pre-screen reads one-field (broad/serologic-level) HLA off scanned laboratory reports and has no antibody result at all, so the paper's actual endpoint — DSA assignment — cannot be computed there; what does transfer is the quantitative ceiling on inference, and it transfers pessimistically, because HaploStats was run here against a European white reference panel in a 98.4% white cohort (the best case for inference) and still recovered DQB1 in only 84.0% and DRB3/4/5 in 70.7% of donors, while Iranian haplotype frequencies are not represented in that panel. The paper therefore supports a hard design rule for the pre-screen: report antigen-level agreement as antigen-level agreement, never impute alleles or eplets from one-field typing and never present an inferred molecular score as a compatibility finding. It also supports C4 indirectly — DQ was the locus that most needed high-resolution typing, accounting for 43.1% of all misclassified DSA, and DQA1 was a named cause of misattributed reactivity — which argues for capturing DQ explicitly rather than folding it into an A/B/DR count. What the paper does NOT provide is any mismatch-count-to-outcome estimate, so it cannot be used for C1, C2, C3 or the dose-response shape.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- DSA misclassification (antibody level): suspected DSA on LR split-antigen typing, adjudicated against 2F-HR NGS typing of 11 loci — percentage 22.8; adjusted for unadjusted; 51/224 suspected DSA disproved (173/224, 77.2% confirmed) [Results 3.2]
- DSA misclassification (patient level): patients LR-DSA-positive whose DSA was entirely disproved by 2F-HR typing — percentage 22.9; adjusted for unadjusted; 32/140 patients (108/140, 77.1%, had >=1 confirmed DSA) [Results 3.3 and Abstract]
- locus distribution of misclassified DSA: share of the 51 misclassified DSA directed at HLA-DQ — percentage 43.1; adjusted for unadjusted; N=22/51. Class II overall 70.6%. Others: HLA-A 6, HLA-B 7, HLA-C 2, HLA-DRB1 8, HLA-DP 6 [Results 3.2, Figure 2A; restated in Discussion as '43% were directed against the DQ molecule']
- reasons for LR misclassification: cause of each of the 51 misclassified DSA — percentage 56.9; adjusted for unadjusted; lack of donor typing at 2F-HR level 29/51 (56.9%); lack of donor DQA1/DPA1 typing 14/51 (27.5%); incomplete recipient 2F-HR typing 9/51 (15.7%) [Results 3.2, Figure 2B]

**Dose-response.**

- note: No mismatch-count-to-outcome series exists in this paper. The only per-locus numbers are (a) mean mismatch counts by DSA-adjudication group (Table 2, descriptive, not an outcome model) and (b) per-locus accuracy of two-field inference (Figure 4). Both are reproduced below.

- haplostats_inference_accuracy_per_locus_N134: A MM: 97.5%; B MM: 90.0%; C MM: 89.6%; DRB1 MM: 83.3%; DRB3/4/5 MM: 70.7%; DQB1 MM: 84.0%
- hlamatchmaker_inference_accuracy_per_locus_N134: A MM: 87.9%; B MM: 71.5%; C MM: 50.9%; DRB1 MM: 49.5%; DQB1 MM: 57.8%
- haplostats_inference_accuracy_per_locus_N469: A MM: 96.3%; B MM: 91.3%; C MM: 95.4%; DRB1 MM: 81.7%; DRB3/4/5 MM: 67.3%; DQB1 MM: 81.5%
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested — this is a typing-resolution / DSA-misclassification study. HLA mismatch counts appear only as descriptive group means (Table 2) compared by two-sample t-test; no regression, no mismatch-count strata, no test for trend, no spline, no threshold analysis, and no hazard ratio anywhere in the paper.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA locus x typing resolution: the harm of low-resolution typing is not spread evenly across loci — it is concentrated in class II and above all in DQ. 70.6% of misclassified DSA were class II and 43.1% were anti-DQ. The named mechanisms are insufficient LR resolution of DQB1, complete absence of DQA1 donor typing (so anti-DQA1 reactivity is misattributed to DQB1), and donor DQA1/DQB1 dimers missing from the bead panel. (22/51 (43.1%) of misclassified DSA anti-DQ; class II 70.6%; DQA1/DPA1 absence caused 27.5% of all misclassifications) [Results 3.2, Figure 2; Discussion paragraph 4. Descriptive proportions — no formal interaction test.]
- HLA locus x inference method: inference accuracy also degrades by locus and by how much input the tool is given. HaploStats (A,B,C,DR,DQ input) beat the HLAMatchmaker converter (A,B,DR input) at every locus, and both did worst at the class II loci. DQA1, DPB1 and DPA1 cannot be inferred at all, which left 11 of 32 reclassified patients unresolvable. (HaploStats vs HLAMatchmaker: C 89.6% vs 50.9%; DRB1 83.3% vs 49.5%; DQB1 84.0% vs 57.8%. DRB3/4/5 worst at 70.7%.) [Results 3.4, Figure 4. Descriptive comparison — no formal interaction test.]
- inference x direction of error: inference does not merely add noise, it trades error types. Against LR typing it raised specificity (89.6% vs 81.8%) but collapsed sensitivity (58.3% vs 76.9%), so net accuracy fell (76.7% vs 79.8%). The clinically dangerous direction dominates: 20/108 patients with real DSA were wrongly reassured, and that group had the lowest 10-year graft survival in the study (44.9%) and 91.2% cumulative ABMR. (sensitivity 58.3% vs 76.9%; wrongly excluded DSA 20/108 (18.5%); 10-y survival 44.9%; ABMR 91.2%) [Results 3.4, Table 3, Figure 5]
- sensitisation status (scope restriction, not a tested modifier): the entire question is conditioned on sensitisation: only the 262 recipients with detectable pretransplant anti-HLA antibody can have a DSA misclassified, and Table 3 is computed in exactly that subset. The paper's own recommendation is likewise scoped to sensitised recipients ('for all living donor kidney transplantations in sensitized recipients, NGS ... should be done'). In an antibody-unknown or antibody-negative pre-screen this endpoint is undefined. (N=262 sensitised of 1000 (26.2%); 140 (14.0%) LR-DSA-positive) [Results 3.1, 3.4, Table 3; Discussion/summary]
- DQ heterodimer completeness x eplet score: scoring DQ from DQB1 alone rather than the whole DQA1/DQB1 molecule changes the eplet mismatch load in the majority of pairs, by up to 17 eplets — a direct warning that a molecular DQ score built on partial typing is not the same quantity as the one built on complete typing. (identical in only 37.8%; differs by 1-17 eplets in 62.2%) [Results 3.5, Figure 6B]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "we confirmed the donor specificity of the HLA antibodies in 173/224 (77.2%) cases. In the remaining 51 (22.8%) cases of suspected DSA at the LR genotyping level, we disproved the donor specificity by 2F‐HR genotyping" (Results 3.2)
- *C4* — "The majority of these misclassified DSAs (n = 51) were against HLA class II (70.6%), especially against the HLA‐DQ molecule (N = 22; 43.1%)." (Results 3.2)
- *C12* — "Therefore, we could not identify an association between misclassified DSA at LR level and ABMR or graft survival, confirming that these antibodies were also misclassified from the clinical perspective." (Results 3.3)
- *C12* — "The accuracy for assigning DSA in sensitized patients was 79.8% for LR genotyping and 76.7% for inferred 2F‐HR donor HLA genotyping using HaploStats." (Discussion, paragraph 1)
- *C12* — "the agreement between the inferred and the real 2F‐HR genotypes was 75.3% for class I and 35.4% for class II" (Results 3.5)
- *C12* — "Therefore, for all living donor kidney transplantations in sensitized recipients, NGS (or another methodology able to provide 2F‐HR typing) should be done." (Discussion, final summary paragraph)

**Limitations.** Single centre, 98.4% white European recipients, and the inference tools were run against European-white haplotype frequencies. This is the most favourable possible setting for HaploStats; accuracy in a Middle Eastern or Iranian population, whose haplotypes are not represented in that reference panel, would be expected to be lower, and the paper offers no estimate for it.; The authors state they had no donor ethnicity data at all, which they name as their first limitation; they argue this reflects real clinical practice under Eurotransplant, but it means the inference accuracy reported is for ethnicity-blind inference only.; 94.1% deceased donors. Only about 59 transplants were from living donors, and no living-donor subgroup is analysed, so the living-donor relevance rests on the authors' recommendation rather than on living-donor data.; All outcome comparisons are unadjusted Kaplan-Meier with log-rank. No Cox model, no hazard ratio, no confidence interval anywhere in the paper. Donor age, cold ischaemia, induction therapy and repeat transplantation are tabulated but never adjusted for, and the groups differ in HLA mismatch load (P=.01, P=.03), so the survival contrasts are confounded by construction.; The survival curves that carry the argument rest on very small groups: 32 patients in the reclassified-negative arm and 20 in the wrongly-excluded arm. The key null result (82.4% vs 93.8%, P=.27) is an underpowered non-significance, not a demonstrated equivalence — the paper is entitled to say it found no signal of harm, not that the risk is proven equal.; The DSA positivity cutoff was MFI >=500 with a background-corrected ratio >=4, which the authors themselves concede is low; a higher cutoff would have reduced the count of 'misclassified' DSA and changed the headline proportion.; No desensitisation was given in this era, so the outcome contrasts describe untreated natural history and may not hold in programmes that treat pretransplant DSA.; Second-vendor SAB testing was not performed, and some donor DQA1/DQB1 dimers were absent from the bead panel, so a residual of missed or under-strength DSA remains.; Complete 2F-HR typing was unavailable for 6 of the 140 transplant pairs, and Table 2's two-field rows therefore rest on 103 and 31 rather than 108 and 32.; The abstract's headline 23.3% does not appear in the Results as such; the Results and Table 3 give the complementary accuracy of 76.7%, and the Discussion rounds the residual misclassification to 'approximately 20%'. The three figures are consistent but stated at different precisions.; Several key numbers (all survival percentages, all per-locus inference accuracies) are presented in figures and figure legends rather than in a table of estimates; they are quotable from the running text but come without dispersion or interval estimates.; This paper measures whether an antibody is correctly called donor-specific. It reports no relationship between HLA mismatch count and any outcome, so it cannot be used to support or refute C1, C2, C3 or any dose-response shape..

**Why it is relevant.** This is the review's anchor paper for the molecular-mismatch question (C12) and for HLA-DQ as the dominant immunising locus (C4): in 926 pairs genotyped at high resolution across 11 loci, the antibody-verified eplet mismatch load on the DQ molecule drove dnDSA formation, both rejection phenotypes and graft failure, while mismatches at the other loci 'seem to have less effect'. Its single most decision-relevant result for this review is negative for threshold-style matching rules: the DQ eplet relationship was linear with explicitly no safe threshold below which DSA did not occur, so any pre-screen policy that declares a pair 'compatible' below a molecular cut-off is not supported by these data. The paper also directly contests the incumbent matching metric, concluding that molecular HLA-DQ matching might be more helpful than antigen matching at HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown Iranian pre-screen is nevertheless weak in three specific ways. First, the entire eplet result requires two-field genotyping of DQA1/DQB1 plus HLAMatchmaker and cannot be computed, or safely imputed, from one-field typing - so this paper tells the project what its pre-screen is blind to rather than giving it something to compute. Second, donor type is not reported in the retrievable text and no living-donor subgroup estimate is available, so C14 is not answered here. Third, dnDSA ascertainment depended on a centre antibody-screening protocol in a single European population whose allele and haplotype frequencies differ from Iran's, whereas the target setting has unknown antibody status entirely.

The 12% is converted to OR 1.12; no CI or P value is printed in the abstract.]
- T cell-mediated rejection (TCMR): per 1 antibody-verified eplet mismatch on the DQ molecule — OR 1.05; adjusted for not stated in retrieved text [Abstract, Results - the 5% in the same sentence, converted to OR 1.05; no CI or P value is printed in the abstract.]
