### Vinson AJ 2020 — Prolonged Cold Ischemia Time Offsets the Benefit of Human Leukocyte Antigen Matching in Deceased Donor Kidney Transplant

Vinson AJ 2020, *Transplantation Proceedings*, [DOI 10.1016/j.transproceed.2019.12.049](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.transproceed.2019.12.049). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier). convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 32088062, and get_article_metadata returned no pmc field, so no PMC full text exists to retrieve. Everything below comes from the PubMed abstract, cached verbatim at <scratchpad>/fulltext/32088062.txt..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Recipients with a history of kidney transplant in the United States, 2000-2016 (US registry, almost certainly SRTR/UNOS, though the abstract does not name the registry). Deceased-donor kidney transplant per the title. Recipients with 0 HLA mismatch were stratified by cold ischaemia time and each stratum compared with a single reference group of recipients with >0 HLA mismatch and CIT <10 hours. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | not stated in the abstract |
| design | retrospective US registry cohort; multivariable Cox proportional hazards model; time to graft loss compared across CIT categories against one common reference stratum |
| typing resolution | not stated. A US registry '0 HLA mismatch' in 2000-2016 is conventionally antigen-level (low-resolution) HLA-A, -B, -DR out of 6, but the abstract states neither the loci counted nor the resolution, so this is inference and is NOT recorded as a paper fact. |
| outcome | time to graft loss / 'adjusted risk of graft failure'. The abstract does not say whether graft loss was death-censored, so all-cause vs death-censored cannot be determined. |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | cold ischaemia time (the exposure of interest, in 6 categories: <10, 10-<15, 15-<20, 20-<25, 25-<30, >=30 hours), panel reactive antibody (only as a sensitivity analysis excluding PRA >98%, not as a reported model covariate), the abstract states a 'multivariable Cox proportional hazards model' but does not enumerate the adjustment covariates; they are not retrievable without the full text |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper addresses review claim C11 (effect modification of the HLA-matching benefit by another transplant factor) and, secondarily, C9 (the size of the zero-mismatch premium), in the specific form 'does the benefit of a perfect HLA match survive the logistics needed to obtain it?'. Its answer is a stratified one: with prompt transplantation (CIT <10 h) a 0-mismatch deceased-donor kidney carried an 18% lower adjusted hazard of graft failure than a mismatched kidney transplanted equally promptly (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.72-0.94), the advantage held below a 20-hour threshold, and above 20 hours it was gone. For a LIVING-donor pre-screen in Iran the transfer is unusually favourable in one direction and weak in another. Favourable: cold ischaemia in living donation is on the order of minutes to a couple of hours, so the modifier that erases the zero-mismatch premium in this cohort is effectively absent, and the paper is therefore evidence that the zero-mismatch premium is fully expressed - not attenuated - in exactly the low-CIT condition a living-donor programme operates in; it also weighs against any argument that HLA matching is worth trading for logistics, because the trade only destroyed the benefit when it cost ischaemic time, which a living-donor pre-screen never has to spend. Weak: the cohort is deceased-donor only, and the paper pools every non-zero mismatch count into a single '>0 HLA MM' reference, so it says nothing about the 1-versus-2 gradient, nothing per locus, and nothing about DR or DQ weighting that a ranking model needs. Its typing is registry-grade low resolution, which matches the one-field typing the Iranian pre-screen will have, and its exposure is antigen mismatch count rather than antibody, so it does not require the antibody status that our pre-screen lacks - but it also offers no guidance on the antibody-unknown state beyond a sensitivity analysis that merely excluded PRA >98% recipients. Net: cite it as a boundary condition on C11 and as one more estimate of the zero-mismatch premium; do not cite it for dose-response shape or locus weighting.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft failure (time to graft loss; death-censoring not stated): 0 HLA mismatch with CIT < 10 hours vs > 0 HLA mismatch with CIT < 10 hours (reference) — HR 0.82 (0.72–0.94); adjusted for multivariable Cox model; covariates not enumerated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 1]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: >0 (all non-zero counts pooled), CIT < 10 h MM: 1.0; 0 MM: 0.82 (0.72–0.94)
- Shape reported: not reported. The paper contrasts 0 mismatch against a single pooled >0 mismatch group; there is no per-count (0/1/2/.../6) and no per-locus series, so no dose-response shape can be read from it. The only graded axis in the paper is cold ischaemia time, not mismatch count.; linearity tested: not tested (no mismatch-count gradient was modelled); 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- 0 HLA mismatch x cold ischaemia time: The zero-mismatch survival advantage is present at short CIT, persists up to a threshold of < 20 hours, and is absent once CIT exceeds 20 hours. (HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.72-0.94) for 0 MM with CIT < 10 h vs > 0 MM with CIT < 10 h. The category-specific hazard ratios for the 10-<15, 15-<20, 20-<25, 25-<30 and >=30 hour strata are NOT printed in the abstract, and NO formal test of interaction (no P for interaction, no ratio of hazard ratios) is reported in any retrievable text.) [Abstract, Results sentences 1-2 and Conclusion]
- 0 HLA mismatch x cold ischaemia time, within non-highly-sensitised recipients (sensitivity analysis excluding PRA > 98%): The same pattern held after excluding highly sensitised recipients, whose organs are shipped for equitable access rather than to optimise HLA match; so the loss of the zero-mismatch benefit at long CIT is not merely an artefact of the highly sensitised, long-shipping subgroup. (no numbers reported in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C9* — "The adjusted risk of graft failure was significantly lower for 0 HLA MM with the shortest CIT compared to the reference group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval, 0.72-0.94)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "this survival advantage persisted to a threshold of < 20 hours of CIT. No survival advantage was observed for the 0 HLA MM group once CIT was > 20 hours." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "This trend persisted after excluding highly sensitized recipients (panel reactive antibody > 98%) where shipping of organs occurs to achieve more equitable access to organs rather than optimize HLA match." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "CIT > 20 hours offsets the benefit of 0 HLA MM in kidney transplantation. This may have implications in organ shipping to facilitate immunologic match." (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C9* — "Time to graft loss was compared for each CIT category to a reference group of individuals with > 0 HLA MM and short CIT (< 10 hours) using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model." (Abstract, Methods)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC deposit exists for this PMID, so the cohort size, follow-up duration, covariate list, the HRs for the 10-<15, 15-<20, 20-<25, 25-<30 and >=30 hour strata, and any confidence intervals other than the single 0.72-0.94 are unavailable. Everything about the >10 hour strata is known only from the authors' prose summary.; Every non-zero mismatch count is pooled into one reference group, so the paper contributes nothing to the 1-vs-2 mismatch question (C9's second half), nothing to dose-response shape (C2), and nothing per locus (C3-C8).; Deceased donor only. Cold ischaemia times of 10-30+ hours have essentially no analogue in living donation, where CIT is typically well under two hours; the modifier being studied is out of range for a living-donor programme.; Observational registry with non-randomised CIT. Long-CIT zero-mismatch kidneys are shipped organs, so the comparison is confounded by shipping distance, donor quality, recipient acuity and centre practice. The abstract does not state what was adjusted for, so residual confounding cannot be assessed. The authors' own sensitivity analysis addresses only one such pathway (highly sensitised recipients).; Published as a short report in Transplantation Proceedings, a proceedings journal with limited space for methodological detail; no evidence in retrievable text of a pre-specified analysis plan or a formal interaction test.; The '20 hour' threshold is a boundary between pre-specified CIT bins, not an estimated changepoint; it should not be quoted as a fitted threshold.; Neither the HLA loci counted nor the typing resolution is stated; death-censoring of graft loss is not stated; no DSA or eplet/molecular data at all, and sensitisation enters only as a PRA >98% exclusion..

### Taherkhani N 2019 — Identification and weighting of kidney allocation criteria: a novel multi-expert fuzzy method

Taherkhani N 2019, *BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making*, [DOI 10.1186/s12911-019-0892-y](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12911-019-0892-y). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (BMC Med Inform Decis Mak is fully open access); no explicit licence statement appears in the retrieved PMC prose.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Two populations. (1) Weighting panel: 10 experts who were mainly decision makers and policy makers in organ allocation in Iran, completing two face-to-face questionnaires (Fuzzy Delphi, then IF-AHP pairwise comparisons). (2) Case study: the kidney transplantation dataset of Tehran (one of Iran's 15 allocation regions, the one with the longest waiting list), October 2017 to December 2017. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 10 experts; case study 484 registered waiting-list patients and 124 deceased donors; a 30-patient sample used for the profile-matrix expert confirmation |
| design | Fuzzy Delphi Method to screen 11 candidate criteria down to 8, then Intuitionistic Fuzzy Analytic Hierarchy Process (four-level hierarchy, utility vs equity) to derive relative and global weights; the resulting point score was then re-run over a historical deceased-donor dataset and compared with the allocations the existing Iranian system actually made; sensitivity analysis by perturbing weights |
| typing resolution | not stated explicitly; the paper's own description is antigen/broad level - HLA-A, B and DR only, up to two alleles per antigen, mismatch counted from 0-0-0 to 2-2-2 (i.e. 0-6 total). Sub-criteria are named by total mismatch count (the lowest-weighted sub-criterion is '5 HLA mismatches'). No two-field/allele-level typing, no DQ, no C, no DP, no eplet or PIRCHE anywhere in the paper. |
| outcome | No clinical outcome. The paper's endpoints are allocation-process surrogates: EPTS score distribution (proportion of recipients with EPTS < 20%), mean donor-recipient age difference, mean waiting time, number of blood-type-identical allocations, number of urgent patients served, and expert agreement with the ranking shown on a utility/equity profile matrix. |
| follow up | none - no patient was followed; the dataset explicitly contained no transplant-outcome or graft-survival field |
| other factors modelled | blood type compatibility, PRA (panel reactive antibodies; high sensitisation defined as PRA > 80%), age difference between donor and recipient, waiting time, medical urgency (two-state in Iran), recipient age (paediatric priority: under 18 years in Iran), predicted survival (proposed by the authors; assumes graft survival can be predicted), rejected by the expert panel: location, a prior living donation, transplant status (first vs repeat) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's allocation-and-policy question (C13) and its Iran/regional question (C15), not the biology question: it contains no estimate of how HLA mismatch changes graft outcome, only how much weight an Iranian expert panel thinks HLA mismatch should carry relative to other criteria. Its most transferable content is the description of what Iranian deceased-donor allocation actually does today - filter the regional waiting list on blood type and medical urgency, sort by waiting time, then have a human allocator pick six priorities on distance and on donor-recipient age difference - a process in which HLA plays no formal scoring role at all, which sets the baseline our pre-screen would be improving on. The panel's conclusion that HLA belongs in the score but at the bottom of it (the '5 HLA mismatches' sub-criterion carries the lowest weight of all, and medical urgency the highest, mirroring ETKAS where 5 mismatches are worth 33.3 points against 500 for high urgency) is direct evidence on how much HLA should be allowed to move a rank order in an Iranian setting. It also confirms that the HLA construct available and acceptable in Iran is exactly the low-resolution one our pre-screen must work in: A, B and DR only, counted 0-6, with no DQ, no allele-level typing and no molecular mismatch anywhere in the criterion set. Transfer to a LIVING-donor pre-screen is nevertheless weak and indirect: the case study is deceased-donor allocation from a regional waiting list, where the scarce object is the kidney and equity between candidates is half the objective, whereas in a living-donor pre-screen the pair is already given and there is no queue to be fair to - the paper's equity half (waiting time, urgency, paediatric priority) has no analogue for us. Antibody status is handled here only as a coarse PRA > 80% sensitisation flag rather than as DSA, so the paper neither supports nor contradicts an antibody-status-unknown design; and its one direct remark on living donation is the striking policy fact that a prior-donation bonus was rejected by the panel because kidneys may lawfully be bought and sold in Iran, which is context our living-donor product sits inside rather than an outcome finding.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- criterion weight in the proposed Iranian allocation score (IF-AHP global weight): '5 HLA mismatches' sub-criterion versus all other criteria and sub-criteria — rank of derived weight (numeric weight not retrievable) None; adjusted for not applicable (expert pairwise comparison, 10 experts, intuitionistic triangular fuzzy numbers) [Results, 'Obtaining the weight of criteria and sub-criteria using IF-AHP method' - reported in prose as the LOWEST weight of all criteria/sub-criteria, with medical urgency the HIGHEST; the numeric weights sit in a table whose content is not present in the retrieved PMC text]
- ETKAS allocation points (comparator system quoted by the authors): 5 HLA mismatches versus high-urgency status in ETKAS — allocation points 33.3; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Obtaining the weight of criteria and sub-criteria using IF-AHP method': 5 HLA mismatches = 33.3 points, the lowest in ETKAS; high urgency = 500 points, the highest]
- ETKAS allocation points (comparator system quoted by the authors): high urgency patients in ETKAS — allocation points 500; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Obtaining the weight of criteria and sub-criteria using IF-AHP method']
- Eurotransplant paediatric points (quoted as an example of recipient-age scoring, NOT an HLA effect): recipients under 6 years vs 6-11 years vs 11-16 years — allocation points None; adjusted for not applicable [Methods, 'Kidney allocation criteria' - 'Recipient age': 100, 66.6 and 33.3 points respectively; in UNOS, under 11 and 11-18 years receive different points; in Iran patients under 18 have priority]
- utility surrogate in the re-allocation case study (NOT an HLA effect): proposed IF-AHP score versus the existing Iranian allocation, Tehran region, Oct-Dec 2017 — count and percentage of recipients with EPTS < 20% 18; adjusted for not applicable; EPTS calculable only for recipients over 18 years [Results, 'Model evaluation': recipients with EPTS < 20% increased from 83 to 124 (18%)]
- utility and equity surrogates in the re-allocation case study (NOT an HLA effect): proposed IF-AHP score versus the existing Iranian allocation — means (no dispersion or test reported) None; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Model evaluation': mean donor-recipient age difference fell from 8.1 to 5.3 years; mean waiting time of all recipients fell from 1.7 to 1.25 years; the existing system did better on blood-type-identical allocations and on serving urgent patients]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported - no outcome model of any kind was fitted; the HLA sub-criteria appear to be defined by total mismatch count across HLA-A, B and DR (the retrieved prose names '5 HLA mismatches' as the lowest-weighted sub-criterion, implying a graded 0-to-6 count with weight falling as mismatches rise), but the actual weight per mismatch count is in a table whose content is absent from the retrieved PMC text; linearity tested: not tested; no statistical model, no regression, no test of trend anywhere in the paper. The only robustness work is a deterministic sensitivity analysis of the weights themselves (main criteria perturbed up to 50% and sub-criteria up to ~30% with no change in patient priority); 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "To select the most suitable candidate, the waiting list is filtered based on the blood type and medical urgency. Then she/he sorts the list based on the waiting time" (Background, description of the current Iranian regional allocation process)
- *C13* — "In ETKAS, the highest point is assigned to high urgency patients (500 points) and the lowest point is assigned to 5 HLA mismatches (33.3 points)" (Results, 'Obtaining the weight of criteria and sub-criteria using IF-AHP method')
- *C15* — "From the 11 factors gathered from the literature and different allocation systems, eight essential factors were identified, and three factors (location, a prior donation and transplant status) were rejected by the experts." (Results, 'Identification of essential factor using FDM')
- *C15* — "HLA-A, B and DR are significant in kidney transplantation. Each person has up to two different alleles associated with each of the above three antigens" (Methods, 'Kidney allocation criteria' - 'HLA (human leukocyte antigen) matching')
- *C15* — "In the case of a prior donation, since it is allowed to buy and sell kidneys in Iran, therefore, considering this factor as a point for patients is not necessary." (Results, 'Identification of essential factor using FDM')
- *C13* — "The number of recipients with an EPTS < 20% has increased from 83 to 124 (18%), and the average age difference between the donor and recipient has decreased from 8.1 years to 5.3 years." (Results, 'Model evaluation')

**Limitations.** Not an outcome study: the dataset explicitly contained no field indicating transplant success or graft survival, so no HLA effect on any clinical endpoint is estimated anywhere in the paper. Every 'result' about HLA is an expert-elicited weight, not evidence.; The numeric weights are unusable from the retrieved text: the IF-AHP relative and global weights, the FDM screening values, the pairwise comparison matrices and the highest/lowest-weight comparison across allocation algorithms are all in tables that PMC returned as [TABLE CONTENT NOT IN RETRIEVED TEXT]. Only the ordinal statement (HLA lowest, medical urgency highest) and the quoted ETKAS points survive.; Elicitation base is very small and non-independent: 10 Iranian experts, and the same 10 people answered both the Delphi questionnaire and the IF-AHP pairwise comparisons. No inter-expert agreement statistic, no external validation of the weights against outcomes.; The validation is circular in an important way: the proposed model is judged better partly by EPTS (a US UNOS-derived recipient-survival score) and partly by the same experts who supplied the weights, judging a profile-matrix display of their own model's rankings.; Case study is small, single-region and three months long (484 candidates, 124 deceased donors, Tehran, Oct-Dec 2017), and is a paper re-allocation of historical records rather than a prospective or simulated-outcome comparison; no uncertainty is reported around any of the comparison numbers.; Deceased-donor waiting-list allocation only. Nothing in the design speaks to living-donor pair selection, which is the setting of our pre-screen.; HLA is treated at broad antigen level over A, B and DR only. DQ, DR51/52/53, C and DP are absent; allele-level typing, molecular/eplet mismatch and DSA are never mentioned. Sensitisation enters only as a coarse PRA > 80% flag, described as expert opinion plus 'some kidney allocation models'.; An internal inconsistency in naming: the indexed abstract calls the top-weighted criterion 'Medical emergency' while the Results and Discussion call it 'medical urgency'. They are the same criterion.; The 'predicted survival' criterion was accepted by the panel but the authors themselves record that the inputs needed to compute it are poorly recorded and followed in Iran, so its weight is aspirational.; The paper is a weighting framework by its own admission - developing an actual allocation system was declared out of scope - so nothing here has been deployed or prospectively evaluated..

### Wasik HL 2019 — A donor risk index for graft loss in pediatric living donor kidney transplantation

Wasik HL 2019, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.15360](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.15360). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown; PMC deposit is an NIH-funded author manuscript (Research Support, N.I.H., Extramural). No licence statement appeared in the retrieved PMC text, so treat as publisher copyright, author manuscript and keep quotes short..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First-time kidney-only transplant recipients aged <18 years in the United States, transplanted 1 January 2005 - 31 December 2015 (SRTR national registry). Temporal validation cohort: first-time paediatric kidney-only recipients 1999-2004. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 7,155 total (2,649 LDKT [37%], 4,506 DDKT [63%]); exclusions: 366 missing characteristics, 50 donor eGFR <60, 351 donor BMI outside 17-45. Validation cohort size not reported in the retrieved text. |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort. A single Cox proportional-hazards model of all-cause graft loss fitted across LDKT and DDKT recipients simultaneously, with living-donor characteristics set to 0 for DDKT recipients and KDPI set to 0 for LDKT recipients plus an LD/DD indicator; final living-donor covariate set chosen by lowest AIC. Beta coefficients divided by the KDPI beta to rescale onto the deceased-donor KDPI scale, producing the P-LKDPI. Validated by Kaplan-Meier/log-rank across P-LKDPI strata, by inverse-probability-weighted LDKT-vs-DDKT comparison within P-LKDPI/KDPI strata, by Harrell's C-statistic (bootstrap CI, 200 repetitions), and by temporal validation in the 1999-2004 cohort. |
| typing resolution | not stated. HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatch counts are taken from SRTR/OPTN fields, which are antigen (low-resolution) level in practice, but the paper never states the resolution and the words 'resolution', 'serologic', 'allele' and 'imputed' do not appear in the full text. |
| outcome | all-cause graft failure (all-cause graft loss); death-censored graft loss was NOT analysed |
| follow up | not reported as a median. Transplants 2005-2015 followed through SRTR; cumulative incidences reported at 5 and 10 years (development cohort), and at 5 and 10 years in the 1999-2004 validation cohort. |
| other factors modelled | donor age above 50, donor female sex, ABO incompatibility (including A2-incompatible pairs), donor systolic blood pressure, donor eGFR (CKD-EPI), deceased donor KDPI (for the DDKT arm), recipient age, sex, race, peak PRA, years of renal replacement therapy, cause of ESRD, transplant year (adjustment set), evaluated in exploratory models but not retained by AIC: donor race (black vs other), BMI, BSA, donor/recipient BSA ratio, diastolic BP, biologic relatedness, cigarette use, EBV serostatus, CMV serostatus, HLA-A mismatches |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's living-donor question (C14) more directly than any adult deceased-donor registry study: it asks which measurable donor attributes predict graft loss when a candidate has several willing living donors to choose between, which is exactly the decision a pre-screen tool in Iran automates. Its answer is that only two HLA loci survive AIC selection alongside donor blood pressure, eGFR, age, sex and ABO - HLA-B (aHR 1.27 per mismatch) and HLA-DR (aHR 1.23 per mismatch) - and that HLA-A, tested in exploratory models, does not (C5, C6). It is therefore direct evidence that a low-resolution A/B/DR mismatch count, the only kind of typing a one-field Iranian pre-screen will have, still carries prognostic signal within living donation, and it shows how a published index chooses to weight that count (44.11 index points per HLA-B mismatch, 38.83 per HLA-DR mismatch) against non-immunological donor quality (C13). The per-mismatch hazard ratios here are much larger than the ~1.03-1.05 per-mismatch estimates typical of adult registry cohorts, which is a caution rather than a bonus: the recipients are children under 18 with lower peak PRA, longer expected graft lifetimes and a different immune profile, so the magnitude should not be carried over to an adult Iranian cohort even though the direction and the B-vs-A ranking plausibly can be. Transfer is further limited because the model contains no DQ, no HLA-C and no DP term at all, and because antibody status enters only as recipient peak PRA - it cannot tell an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen anything about how the HLA effect behaves once DSA is accounted for. Its most usable output for the Iranian tool is structural rather than numerical: a validated living-donor index in which HLA mismatch is the dominant modifiable input, sitting on the same scale as deceased-donor quality, with honest reporting of weak discrimination (C-statistic 0.57).

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft loss: HLA-B, per additional mismatch (continuous count), living-donor recipients — aHR 1.27 (1.04–1.55), p=0.02; adjusted for other living-donor characteristics in the final model (donor age above 50, female sex, HLA-DR mismatches, ABO incompatibility, eGFR, SBP) plus recipient age, sex, race, peak PRA, years of RRT, cause of ESRD and transplant year [Abstract; Results 3.2 Model of donor risk]
- all-cause graft loss: HLA-DR, per additional mismatch (continuous count), living-donor recipients — aHR 1.23 (1.01–1.47), p=0.04; adjusted for other living-donor characteristics in the final model plus the recipient adjustment set [Abstract; Results 3.2 Model of donor risk]
- all-cause graft loss: HLA-A, per additional mismatch (continuous count), living-donor recipients — aHR None [Methods 2.3 Model of Donor Risk (listed among exploratory covariates) and Results 3.2 (absent from the AIC-selected final model). No estimate is printed anywhere in the paper - HLA-A was evaluated and not retained.]
- all-cause graft loss: ABO incompatible vs compatible living donor — aHR 3.26 (1.2–8.81), p=0.02; adjusted for as above [Abstract; Results 3.2]
- all-cause graft loss: donor systolic blood pressure, per 10 mmHg increase — aHR 1.08 (1.02–1.49), p=0.03; adjusted for as above [Results 3.2. NOTE: the Abstract prints aHR per 10 mm Hg = 1.07 for the same parameter, and the printed CI (1.02-1.49) is not centred on either point estimate. Internal inconsistency in the source; both values recorded exactly as printed, neither corrected.]
- all-cause graft loss: donor eGFR, per 10 mL/min/1.73m2 increase — aHR 0.94 (0.88–0.99), p=0.03; adjusted for as above [Abstract; Results 3.2]
- all-cause graft loss: donor age above 50, per 10 years — aHR 1.07 (0.99–1.14), p=0.07; adjusted for as above; retained by AIC despite not reaching significance [Results 3.2]
- all-cause graft loss: female vs male living donor — aHR 1.19 (0.97–1.46), p=0.1; adjusted for as above; retained by AIC despite not reaching significance [Results 3.2]
- all-cause graft loss: deceased-donor KDPI, per 10-unit increase (DDKT arm of the same model) — aHR 1.06 (1.01–1.1), p=0.01; adjusted for recipient adjustment set; this is the denominator coefficient used to rescale all living-donor betas onto the KDPI scale [Results 3.2]
- P-LKDPI score (index points): HLA-B, per additional mismatch — index points (beta / beta_KDPI) 44.11; adjusted for coefficient in the published P-LKDPI equation [Results 3.3, P-LKDPI equation]
- P-LKDPI score (index points): HLA-DR, per additional mismatch — index points (beta / beta_KDPI) 38.83; adjusted for coefficient in the published P-LKDPI equation [Results 3.3, P-LKDPI equation]
- P-LKDPI score (index points): ABO incompatibility (for scale comparison against the HLA terms) — index points 218.63; adjusted for coefficient in the published P-LKDPI equation; other terms: intercept -184.93, 11.87 per year of donor age above 50, 32.30 for female sex, 1.61 per mmHg SBP, -1.24 per unit eGFR [Results 3.3, P-LKDPI equation]
- cumulative incidence of all-cause graft loss at 10 years, by P-LKDPI stratum (development cohort): P-LKDPI >=20 vs 20 to -20 vs -20 to -60 vs < -60 — cumulative incidence (%) None; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier; log-rank p<0.001 [Abstract: 39% at 10 years for P-LKDPI >=20, 28% for 20 > P-LKDPI >= -20, 23% for -20 > P-LKDPI >= -60, 19% for P-LKDPI < -60]
- cumulative incidence of all-cause graft loss, highest vs lowest P-LKDPI stratum (development cohort): P-LKDPI >20 vs P-LKDPI < -60 — cumulative incidence (%) None; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier; log-rank p<0.001 [Results 3.4: 19% versus 10% at 5 years, 39% versus 19% at 10 years]
- cumulative incidence of all-cause graft loss, highest vs lowest P-LKDPI stratum (1999-2004 temporal validation cohort): P-LKDPI >20 vs P-LKDPI < -60 — cumulative incidence (%) None; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier; log-rank p<0.001 [Results 3.5: 21% versus 15% at 5 years, 39% versus 23% at 10 years]
- discrimination for all-cause graft loss: P-LKDPI among LDKT recipients (donor factors only, no recipient factors) — Harrell C-statistic 0.57 (0.54–0.6); adjusted for none; bootstrap CI, 200 repetitions [Results 3.4]
- discrimination for all-cause graft loss: deceased-donor KDPI among paediatric DDKT recipients — Harrell C-statistic 0.53 (0.51–0.55); adjusted for none [Results 3.4]
- discrimination for all-cause graft loss: P-LKDPI in the 1999-2004 temporal validation cohort — Harrell C-statistic 0.56 (0.53–0.58); adjusted for none [Results 3.5]
- composition of the worst living-donor stratum: living donors with P-LKDPI >50 (11%, N=284): proportion carrying two mismatches at each locus — percentage None; adjusted for descriptive [Results 3.3: 74% (N=210) had two HLA-B mismatches, 66% (N=188) had two HLA-DR mismatches, 67% (N=190) were female, 4% (N=12) were ABO incompatible]
- distribution of P-LKDPI: living donors vs deceased donors on the shared KDPI scale — percentage / median None; adjusted for descriptive [Abstract and Results 3.3: median P-LKDPI -25 (IQR -56 to 12), range -200 to 290; median DD KDPI 14; 68% (N=1,801) of LD had P-LKDPI <0; 25% (N=652) >14; 15% (N=393) >35; 11% (N=284) >50]

**Dose-response.**

- A: coding MM: evaluated as a continuous mismatch count in exploratory models; NOT retained in the AIC-selected final model; 0 MM: not reported; 1 MM: not reported; 2 MM: not reported; note MM: No HLA-A estimate, CI or p-value is printed anywhere in the paper. Its exclusion is a model-selection outcome (lowest AIC), not a reported test of HLA-A versus HLA-B.
- B: coding MM: continuous count of mismatches (0/1/2), single linear per-mismatch term; per_mismatch MM: aHR 1.27 (95% CI 1.04-1.55), p=0.02; 0 MM: reference by construction (count = 0); 1 MM: not separately estimated; 2 MM: not separately estimated; index_points_per_mismatch MM: 44.11
- DR: coding MM: continuous count of mismatches (0/1/2), single linear per-mismatch term; per_mismatch MM: aHR 1.23 (95% CI 1.01-1.47), p=0.04; 0 MM: reference by construction (count = 0); 1 MM: not separately estimated; 2 MM: not separately estimated; index_points_per_mismatch MM: 38.83
- C: coding MM: not modelled; HLA-C is never mentioned in the paper
- DQ: coding MM: not modelled; HLA-DQ is never mentioned in the paper
- DP: coding MM: not modelled; HLA-DP is never mentioned in the paper
- Shape reported: not reported. HLA enters as one linear per-mismatch term per locus, so a log-linear (constant per-mismatch) shape is imposed by the parameterisation rather than observed. No 0/1/2 categorical series, no total A+B+DR mismatch count, and no zero-mismatch premium are reported.; linearity tested: Not tested for HLA specifically. The only functional-form check reported is 'Continuous variables were modeled empirically using Martingale residual plots' (Methods 2.3), with no statement of whether HLA mismatch counts were among the variables so examined and no residual plot, spline, trend test or interaction shown. The words 'linear', 'spline', 'trend' and 'threshold' do not appear in the full text.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- living-donor HLA mismatch x donor type (LD vs DD): Not a tested interaction, but a structural feature of the model worth recording: all living-donor covariates (including the HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch counts) were set to 0 for DDKT recipients and KDPI was set to 0 for LDKT recipients, with an LD/DD indicator variable. The HLA coefficients are therefore estimated only within the living-donor arm and are not constrained to equal any deceased-donor HLA effect. No interaction term, no interaction p-value and no formal effect-modification test appear anywhere in the paper. [Methods 2.3 Model of Donor Risk]
- none reported: The paper reports no effect modification of the HLA mismatch effect by recipient age, peak PRA/sensitisation, race, donor age, era, or any other factor. The string 'interaction' does not occur in the full text. Recipient race, peak PRA, age, sex, years of RRT, cause of ESRD and transplant year enter only as main-effect adjustment terms; donor race (black vs other) was an exploratory covariate that AIC did not retain. [whole paper (verified by keyword search of the retrieved PMC full text)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C5* — "Among LDKT recipients, factors significantly associated with increased risk of graft loss included increased number of HLA-B mismatches (aHR per mismatch=1.27, 95% CI 1.04-1.55, p=0.02), increased number of HLA-DR mismatches (aHR per mismatch=1.23, 95% CI 1.01-1.47, p=0.04)" (Results 3.2 Model of donor risk)
- *C14* — "The LD characteristics included in the single model of DDKT and LDKT recipients, selected by AIC, were age among donors above age 50, female sex, number of HLA-B mismatches, number of HLA-DR mismatches, ABO incompatibility, eGFR, and SBP" (Results 3.2 Model of donor risk)
- *C6* — "LD characteristics used in exploratory models included age, race (modeled as black vs. other), body mass index, body surface area (BSA), donor recipient BSA ratio, ABO incompatibility, HLA-A mismatches, HLA-B mismatches, HLA-DR mismatches, systolic blood pressure" (Methods 2.3 Model of Donor Risk)
- *C13* — "44.11*(number of HLA-B mismatches) + 38.83*(number of HLA-DR mismatches) + 218.63 if ABO incompatibility + 1.61*SBP" (Results 3.3, P-LKDPI equation)
- *C3* — "In the P-LKDPI, LD characteristics associated with increased risk of graft loss include HLA-B mismatches, HLA-DR mismatches, ABO incompatibility, and increasing systolic blood pressure." (Discussion)
- *C14* — "74% (N=210) had two HLA-B mismatches, 66% (N=188) had two HLA-DR mismatches, and 4% (N=12) were ABO incompatible with their recipient." (Results 3.3 (describing the 11% of living donors with P-LKDPI >50))

**Limitations.** Recipients are children under 18 years. Every estimate is a paediatric estimate; the per-mismatch aHRs (1.27 for B, 1.23 for DR) are several times larger than the ~1.03-1.05 per-mismatch effects typical of adult registry cohorts, and should not be transported to an adult Iranian pre-screen as magnitudes.; Both HLA confidence intervals are marginal and wide (B 1.04-1.55, DR 1.01-1.47; p=0.02 and p=0.04). The DR lower bound is 1.01. These are not precise estimates and the numerical ordering B > DR is well inside the overlap of the two intervals, so the paper does not establish that B outranks DR.; HLA-A was tested and dropped by AIC with no printed estimate, so the paper gives no quantitative comparison of A against B; its exclusion is a model-selection result, not a hypothesis test, and AIC selection also makes the retained coefficients optimistically biased.; No HLA-C, HLA-DQ or HLA-DP terms exist in the model at all; the review's C4, C7 and C8 questions are simply unaddressed.; HLA is coded as one linear per-mismatch count per locus, so no 0/1/2 series, no total mismatch count, no zero-mismatch premium and no test of dose-response shape can be extracted. Constant per-mismatch increments are assumed, not demonstrated.; No interaction or effect-modification analysis of any kind is reported (no sensitisation x HLA, no age x HLA, no era x HLA).; Typing resolution is never stated. SRTR HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch counts are antigen-level in practice, but the paper does not say so, and there is no discussion of low-resolution misclassification or imputation.; Antibody status enters only as recipient peak PRA in the adjustment set. Crossmatch result and donor-specific antibody are not modelled, so the HLA coefficients cannot be separated from the DSA pathway.; Outcome is all-cause graft loss, not death-censored graft failure, so recipient death with a functioning graft is mixed in and dilutes an immunological signal.; Discrimination is weak: C-statistic 0.57 (0.54-0.60) in development and 0.56 (0.53-0.58) in temporal validation. The authors argue at length that a low C-statistic still permits useful stratification, but a pre-screen built on this index will rank individuals only coarsely.; The source contains an internal inconsistency on donor SBP: the abstract prints aHR per 10 mm Hg = 1.07 while Results 3.2 prints 1.08 with CI 1.02-1.49, a CI that is not centred on either value. Both recorded as printed; neither corrected.; Administrative registry data with centre-dependent quality control; missing, inaccurate and incompletely ascertained outcomes are acknowledged by the authors, who argue the bias is toward the null.; First-time transplants only, so nothing on retransplant or repeat mismatch (C11).; US SRTR population, developed and validated only in the US; validation is temporal (1999-2004), not external or geographic. Donor selection, immunosuppression and ABO-incompatible practice differ from Iran.; Tabular results (Tables/Figures) were not retrievable from the PMC text stream; every number recorded here comes from the abstract or the narrative Results/Discussion prose..

### Wiebe C 2019 — HLA-DR/DQ molecular mismatch: A prognostic biomarker for primary alloimmunity.

Wiebe C 2019, *American Journal of Transplantation 19(6):1708-1719 (epub 2018-12-15)*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.15177](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.15177). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown (Wiley/AJT article deposited in PMC; table captions credit John Wiley & Sons, Ltd; licence statement not present in the retrieved text).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 664 consecutive adult (n=606) and paediatric (n=58) kidney transplant recipients, single centre (Manitoba, Canada), January 1999 to July 2016, after excluding primary non-function (n=17) and pretransplant DSA (n=43); tacrolimus 87%, cyclosporin 13%, MMF and prednisone; induction in 39% |
| donor type | both (living donor 77% / 45% / 44% in molecular-mismatch groups A / B / C, Table 2; overall share not printed, about half by arithmetic on the group counts) |
| n | 664 |
| design | retrospective single-centre consecutive cohort with protocol serial dnDSA screening and first-year surveillance biopsies (79% biopsied); ROC-derived single-molecule eplet thresholds; Kaplan-Meier/log-rank; Cox univariable and multivariable models (bivariate screening P <= .2); thresholds derived and evaluated in the same cohort |
| typing resolution | two-field / high-resolution class II (HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 and HLA-DQA1/DQB1) by SSO/SSP; eplets by HLAMatchmaker DRDQDP v2.0; the antigen-level comparator (0/1/2 per DRB1 and DQB1 locus) was derived from the same typing; class I not analysed for mismatch |
| outcome | HLA-DR/DQ de novo DSA (serial screening); Banff >=1A TCMR (first year); ABMR; all-cause graft loss (death with function and moving censored); 10-year all-cause graft survival 74%, death-censored 87% |
| follow up | median 91 months (range 18-226 in Methods, 18-227 in Results) |
| other factors modelled | recipient age (significant in every multivariable model), cyclosporin vs tacrolimus (TCMR, dnDSA models), delayed graft function (TCMR, graft-loss models), nonadherence (dnDSA, ABMR, graft-loss models), candidates screened at bivariate P <= .2 from: first vs repeat transplant, donor age, living donor, ethnicity (white vs other), cold ischaemic time, induction (basiliximab/thymoglobulin), tacrolimus coefficient of variation, mycophenolate (Tables S2-S5, supplement not retrieved) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the paper that defined the HLA-DR/DQ single-molecule eplet-mismatch risk categories (Low: DR <7 and DQ <9; Intermediate: DR >=7 with DQ <=14, or DR 0-6 with DQ 9-14; High: DQ >=15) and showed that, in DSA-negative kidney recipients, the categories out-predict whole-antigen DR/DQ mismatch for dnDSA (AUC 0.84 vs 0.54/0.58) and remain independent multivariable correlates of TCMR, dnDSA, ABMR and all-cause graft loss; it is therefore the primary source for C12 (molecular thresholds, prediction versus antigen matching, two-field typing requirement). It also documents, at the antigen level, a zero-mismatch premium with no further gradient among the non-zero DR/DQ antigen-mismatch groups for dnDSA-free and TCMR-free survival (C9; the paper prints the group boundaries only in Figures 3A/4A, not in the text), and shows HLA class II mismatch still predicting outcomes in a tacrolimus/MMF era (C1). Transfer to the Iranian living-donor pre-screen is limited: the method requires two-field DRB1/3/4/5 and DQA1/DQB1 typing and HLAMatchmaker, which one-field (antigen-level) typing cannot supply; the authors do not test imputation of high-resolution alleles from low-resolution typing, so the accuracy of an imputed eplet score is not addressed here. The cohort excluded pretransplant DSA, so the risk categories describe primary (de novo) alloimmunity in antibody-negative recipients and say nothing about a recipient whose antibody status is unknown. Roughly half the cohort were living-donor transplants, and the zero-eplet-mismatch group was 77% living donors with shorter cold ischaemia, so living donation is represented but confounded with the lowest-risk group rather than analysed separately. The practical lesson for a low-resolution pre-screen is that antigen-level DR/DQ mismatch discriminates only zero versus any mismatch, and that a zero DR/DQ antigen mismatch retains value as a low-risk flag.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA-DR dnDSA (against that molecule): single-molecule HLA-DR eplet mismatch >=7 (ROC threshold) vs below — AUC 0.84; adjusted for unadjusted; sensitivity 81%, specificity 75% [Results 3.1; Table 1; Figure S2]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA (against that molecule): single-molecule HLA-DQ (alpha-beta) eplet mismatch >=9 (ROC threshold) vs below — AUC 0.84; adjusted for unadjusted; sensitivity 90%, specificity 64% [Results 3.1; Table 1; Figure S2]
- HLA-DR dnDSA: traditional whole-antigen HLA-DR mismatch (0/1/2) as correlate of dnDSA — AUC 0.54; adjusted for unadjusted; Results text and Discussion print 0.54 for DR and 0.58 for DQ, whereas Table 1 prints DR 0.58 and DQ 0.54 (internal inconsistency) [Results 3.1; Discussion; Table 1]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA: traditional whole-antigen HLA-DQ mismatch (0/1/2) as correlate of dnDSA — AUC 0.58; adjusted for unadjusted; see DR entry for the Table 1 vs text swap [Results 3.1; Discussion; Table 1]
- HLA-DR and HLA-DQ dnDSA: locus eplet-mismatch sum (previously published method) as correlate of dnDSA — AUC 0.72; adjusted for unadjusted; 0.72 for both DR and DQ [Table 1; Discussion]
- HLA-DR/DQ dnDSA-free survival: whole-antigen HLA-DR/DQ mismatch >0 vs 0 — log-rank P None, p=0.0003; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier [Results 3.2; Figure 3A]
- HLA-DR/DQ dnDSA-free survival: whole-antigen HLA-DR/DQ mismatch groups other than zero compared with each other — log-rank P None, p=0.48; adjusted for unadjusted; no statistical difference among non-zero antigen-mismatch groups; also true in locus-specific DR and DQ analysis (Figure S3) [Results 3.2; Figure 3A; Figure S3]
- HLA-DR/DQ dnDSA-free survival: eplet-mismatch sum groups using the previously published locus threshold of 11 DR or DQ eplet mismatches (printed as 'each <=11' in Results 3.2 and '>=11' in the TCMR passage) — log-rank P None, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted; printed as P < .0001; the authors call this 'a significant dose-response relationship' across the threshold groups (not a continuous or linear term) [Results 3.2; Figure 3B]
- HLA-DR/DQ dnDSA within 10 years: single-molecule DR <7 and DQ <9 (Groups A+B, n=166, 25% of cohort) — percentage 1.2; adjusted for unadjusted; 2 of 166 recipients [Results 3.2; Figure 3C]
- HLA-DR/DQ dnDSA-free survival: single-molecule DR >=7 or DQ >=9 (Group C, n=498) vs Groups A+B — log-rank P None, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.2; Figure 3C]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival, first year: whole-antigen HLA-DR/DQ mismatch >0 vs 0 — log-rank P None, p=0.0085; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 3.2; Figure 4A]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival, first year: whole-antigen HLA-DR/DQ mismatch groups other than zero compared with each other — log-rank P None, p=0.49; adjusted for unadjusted; no difference among non-zero groups [Results 3.2; Figure 4A]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival, first year: eplet-mismatch sum (>=11 DR or DQ threshold groups) — log-rank P None, p=0.0013; adjusted for unadjusted; 'trend of increased risk across eplet mismatch groups' stated qualitatively [Results 3.2; Figure 4B]
- Banff >=1A TCMR at 12 months: single-molecule DR >=7 or DQ >=9 (Group C) vs DR <7 and DQ <9 (Groups A+B, <=10%) — percentage 20, p=0.0018; adjusted for unadjusted; Groups A+B <=10% in first year [Results 3.2; Figure 4C]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: Low / Intermediate / High molecular-mismatch category (3-group log-rank) — log-rank P None, p=0.0006; adjusted for unadjusted [Results 3.3; Figure 5A]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 2.02 (1.1–3.9), p=0.023; adjusted for univariable Cox [Results 3.3]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 3.33 (1.9–6.3), p=0.0001; adjusted for univariable Cox; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 3.94 (2.2–7.5), p=0.0001; adjusted for multivariable Cox: recipient age, cyclosporin vs tacrolimus, delayed graft function; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3; Table S2]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: High vs Intermediate molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.6 (1.1–2.4), p=0.0233; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above [Results 3.3; Table S2]
- Banff >=1A TCMR-free survival: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 2.28 (1.2–4.5), p=0.0075; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above [Results 3.3; Table S2]
- dnDSA-free survival: Low / Intermediate / High molecular-mismatch category (3-group log-rank) — log-rank P None, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3; Figure 5B]
- dnDSA-free survival: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 10.18 (3.0–63.5), p=0.0001; adjusted for univariable Cox; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3]
- dnDSA-free survival: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 20.8 (6.4–127.4), p=0.0001; adjusted for univariable Cox; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3]
- dnDSA-free survival: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 18.31 (5.6–11.4), p=0.0001; adjusted for multivariable Cox: recipient age, cyclosporin vs tacrolimus, nonadherence; printed as P < .0001; the printed CI (5.6-11.4) does not contain the point estimate and is presumably a typographical error [Results 3.3; Table S3]
- dnDSA-free survival: High vs Intermediate molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.84 (1.1–3.1), p=0.0149; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above [Results 3.3; Table S3]
- dnDSA-free survival: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 9.96 (2.9–62.1), p=0.0001; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3; Table S3]
- ABMR-free survival: Low / Intermediate / High molecular-mismatch category (3-group log-rank) — log-rank P None, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3; Figure 5C]
- ABMR-free survival: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 5.06 (2.1–14.9), p=0.0001; adjusted for multivariable Cox: recipient age, nonadherence; printed as P < .0001 [Results 3.3; Table S4]
- ABMR-free survival: High vs Intermediate molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.87 (1.0–3.6), p=0.042; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above [Results 3.3; Table S4]
- ABMR-free survival: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 2.71 (1.0–8.3), p=0.0394; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above [Results 3.3; Table S4]
- all-cause graft loss: Low / Intermediate / High molecular-mismatch category (3-group log-rank) — log-rank P None, p=0.0003; adjusted for unadjusted; Results print P = .0003, Abstract prints P = .0012 (inconsistency) [Results 3.4; Figure S4; Abstract]
- all-cause graft loss: High vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.66 (1.12–2.53), p=0.012; adjusted for multivariable Cox: recipient age, delayed graft function, nonadherence [Results 3.4; Table S5]
- all-cause graft loss: High vs Intermediate molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.2 (0.9–1.7), p=0.3; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above; not significant [Results 3.4; Table S5]
- all-cause graft loss: Intermediate vs Low molecular-mismatch category — HR 1.39 (0.9–1.2), p=0.1; adjusted for multivariable Cox as above; not significant; the printed CI (0.9-1.2) does not contain the point estimate and is presumably a typographical error [Results 3.4; Table S5]
- graft survival after class I-only dnDSA: class I dnDSA alone (n=10) vs no dnDSA — log-rank P None, p=0.39; adjusted for unadjusted; class II or class I+II dnDSA vs no dnDSA P < .0001 [Results, opening paragraph; Figure S1]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: reference: whole-antigen HLA-DR/DQ mismatch = 0 had higher dnDSA-free (P = .0003) and TCMR-free (P = .0085) survival than any mismatch >0; >0 MM: groups other than zero did not differ from each other: dnDSA-free survival P = .48, TCMR-free survival P = .49
- DR: antigen 0 vs >0 MM: zero-mismatch advantage for dnDSA (Figure S3, numbers not printed); no gradient among non-zero groups; single-molecule eplet threshold MM: >=7 eplets per DRB molecule, AUC 0.84 for DR dnDSA; range 0-22; no second DR cutoff identifiable within Group C
- DQ: antigen 0 vs >0 MM: zero-mismatch advantage for dnDSA (Figure S3, numbers not printed); no gradient among non-zero groups; single-molecule eplet threshold MM: >=9 eplets per DQ alpha-beta molecule, AUC 0.84 for DQ dnDSA (sensitivity 90%, specificity 64%); second threshold >=15 defines High risk; range 0-31
- molecular categories: Low MM: DR <7 and DQ <9 (n=166; Group A DR=0 and DQ=0 n=93; Group B DR 1-6 and/or DQ 1-8 n=73); Intermediate MM: DR >=7 and DQ <=14, or DR 0-6 and DQ 9-14; High MM: DR 0-22 and DQ 15-31; graded HRs MM: TCMR multivariable 1 / 2.28 / 3.94; dnDSA 1 / 9.96 / 18.31; ABMR 1 / 2.71 / 5.06; all-cause graft loss 1 / 1.39 (ns) / 1.66
- Shape reported: step / threshold at the antigen level (zero-mismatch premium, then flat across non-zero groups); monotonic graded increase across the three molecular-mismatch categories; for graft loss only High vs Low was significant; linearity tested: not tested; thresholds chosen by ROC on dnDSA, categories compared by log-rank and Cox; the eplet-sum 'dose-response' (P < .0001) and TCMR 'trend' are across threshold groups, not a continuous or linear term; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- molecular-mismatch category x pretransplant DSA / sensitisation: not testable in this cohort: recipients with pretransplant DSA (n=43) were excluded, so all estimates describe primary alloimmunity in DSA-negative recipients; PRA was not modelled [Methods 2.1; Discussion]
- molecular-mismatch category x donor type (living vs deceased) and cold ischaemia: no interaction tested; living donation was 77% in the zero-eplet-mismatch Group A vs 45% and 44% in Groups B and C (P < .0001) with shorter cold ischaemic time (4.2 vs 6.9 vs 7.3 h, P < .0001), so donor type is confounded with the lowest-risk group; donor type was not among the significant multivariable correlates reported (living donor 77% / 45% / 44%) [Table 2; Results 3.3 (Table S1)]
- molecular-mismatch category x induction, immunosuppression, adherence: no interaction tested; induction more frequent in Group C (44% vs 20-27%), whereas nonadherence, tacrolimus vs cyclosporin and tacrolimus CV were similar across groups; cyclosporin and nonadherence entered the multivariable models as independent covariates (induction 20% / 27% / 44% (P < .0001)) [Table 2; Results 3.1, 3.3]
- molecular-mismatch category x recipient age / ethnicity: no interaction tested; recipient age was an independent covariate in every model (HR 0.97-0.98 per year for TCMR, dnDSA, ABMR; 1.03 for graft loss); ethnicity (white 79% / 62% / 65%) differed across groups but was not a retained covariate; authors call for validation in cohorts of varying ethnicity [Table 2; Results 3.3-3.4; Limitations]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "By comparison using the traditional HLA whole antigen mismatch as a correlate with dnDSA development, the AUC was only 0.54 and 0.58 for HLA‐DR, and DQ, respectively." (Results 3.1)
- *C12* — "a ROC analysis identified a molecule specific threshold of ≥7 HLA‐DR eplet mismatches and ≥9 HLA‐DQ eplet mismatches associated with an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 and 0.84 for HLA‐DR and HLA‐DQ dnDSA development, respectively" (Results 3.1)
- *C9* — "Traditional HLA‐DR/DQ whole antigen mismatch greater than zero was associated with significantly lower HLA‐DR/DQ dnDSAfree survival (= .0003). However, there was no statistical difference in HLA‐DR/DQ dnDSAfree survival between HLA‐DR/DQ whole antigen risk groups other than zero" (Results 3.2)
- *C12* — "HLA‐DR/DQ single molecule eplet mismatch risk groups with HLA‐DR <7 and HLA‐DQ <9 mismatches (Groups A and B, n = 166, 25% of the cohort) developed HLA‐DR/DQ dnDSA in only 2 recipients (1.2%) in the first 10 years posttransplant" (Results 3.2)
- *C12* — "High‐resolution Class II HLA typing (HLA‐DRβ1/3/4/5 and HLA‐DQα1/β1) was performed using sequence‐specific oligonucleotide probes or sequence‐specific primer technology" (Methods 2.2)
- *C1* — "alloimmune risk category (HR High vs Low 1.66, 95% CI 1.12‐2.53,= .0120; HR High vs Intermediate 1.20, 95% CI 0.9‐1.7,= .3; HR Intermediate vs Low 1.39, 95% CI 0.9‐1.2,= .1)" (Results 3.4)

**Limitations.** single centre, n=664, 82 dnDSA events; authors themselves warn of type II error and call for independent validation; thresholds (DR >=7, DQ >=9, DQ >=15) were derived by ROC on dnDSA in the same cohort in which the categories were then evaluated, so the AUCs and HRs are optimistic (no internal or external validation); pretransplant DSA excluded (n=43) and PRA not modelled; results apply to antibody-negative recipients only and cannot be transferred to recipients of unknown antibody status without a screen; requires two-field DRB1/3/4/5 and DQA1/DQB1 typing plus HLAMatchmaker; the paper does not evaluate imputation from one-field typing or the misclassification that would result; no formal dose-response modelling: antigen-level contrast is 0 vs >0 with a non-significant test among non-zero groups; no per-count HRs, no continuous eplet term, no linearity test, no interaction tests; the zero-eplet-mismatch group (A) is 77% living donor with shorter cold ischaemia and less induction, so donor quality is confounded with the low-risk category; supplementary bivariate tables (S1-S5) were not retrieved; class I mismatch was not assessed; class I-only dnDSA (n=10) did not affect graft survival, but class I is simply outside the model; mixed adult and paediatric (9%) cohort spanning 1999-2016 with cyclosporin in 13%; histology available in 79% in year one; retrieved text has typographic artefacts: the 'P' symbols are dropped (printed as '= .0003'), 'dnDSAfree' lacks its hyphen, the multivariable dnDSA High vs Low CI (5.6-11.4) and graft-loss Intermediate vs Low CI (0.9-1.2) do not bracket their point estimates, the Abstract gives graft-loss P = .0012 while Results give P = .0003, and Table 1 swaps the whole-antigen DR/DQ AUCs (0.58/0.54) relative to the text (0.54/0.58).

### Kamburova EG 2018 — Differential effects of donor-specific HLA antibodies in living versus deceased donor transplant

Kamburova EG 2018, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.14709](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.14709). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown; PMC open-access full text was retrieved (PMC6175247), but no explicit licence statement appears in the retrieved text. Wiley/AJT-era open access is typically CC BY-NC-ND. Treat quotes as short verbatim excerpts under fair quotation..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All kidney transplants performed in all Dutch transplant centres, January 1995 - December 2005 (6097 performed; 4787 [78%] with retrievable pretransplant serum; 4724 analysed after 17 lost to follow-up and 46 technical/non-immunological early failures excluded). Patients and donors 'primarily white'. All had a negative T-cell CDC crossmatch with current and historic highest sera. No desensitisation. SAB-defined DSA results were unknown at the time and did not influence allocation or immunosuppression. |
| donor type | both (1487 living [31.4%]; 3237 deceased [2427 DBD, 810 DCD]) - reported separately, and the living-vs-deceased split IS the paper's central contrast |
| n | 4724 transplants (4157 without DSA, 567 [12%] with DSA) |
| design | retrospective national multicentre cohort with retrospectively assayed banked pretransplant sera; adjusted Kaplan-Meier estimator via inverse probability weighting for survival curves, multivariable Cox proportional hazards for HRs; stratified (not interaction-tested) by donor type |
| typing resolution | LOW RESOLUTION. Donor HLA typing at split serological level (broad level only for 70 antigens, 47 of them HLA-DQ, in 64 transplants); antibody specificities read at serological level; mismatches counted as 'HLA-A/B/DR broad mismatches'. No two-field/allele typing, no eplet or PIRCHE analysis anywhere in the paper. |
| outcome | death-censored graft failure (return to dialysis or retransplant); recipients dying with a functioning graft censored at death. Secondary splits: failure <1 year, and failure >=1 year among grafts surviving 1 year. |
| follow up | minimum 10 years after transplant for every transplant; NOTR registry >95% complete; follow-up recorded at 3 and 12 months then yearly |
| other factors modelled | recipient age (quadratic), donor age (quadratic), donor type (living vs deceased; total-cohort model only), cold ischemia time (deceased donors: DBD and DCD), time on dialysis in years (quadratic), induction therapy with IL-2 receptor blocker |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest cohort that estimates the cost of antibody-defined HLA incompatibility separately in living-donor kidney transplantation (n=1487 living, all CDC-crossmatch-negative and none desensitised), so it is the primary source for the review's donor-type effect-modification question (angle D) and for claim C14. Its headline result is a modifier, not a main effect: the same exposure that carries HR 1.86 (1.56-2.21) and a 16-percentage-point 10-year survival penalty in deceased donors carries only HR 1.42 (0.95-2.10) and a 6-point penalty in living donors, and the authors attribute the difference to donor-organ quality and to lower HLA and adhesion-molecule expression on living-donor endothelium rather than to differences in antibody strength or immunisation. For a LIVING-DONOR pre-screen this is directly reassuring in one specific way: it bounds how much a screen that cannot see antibodies is giving up, because in living donation the antibody signal itself was weak and non-significant except when class I and class II DSA occurred together (HR 2.84, 95% CI 1.05-7.69, only 18 cases). It transfers only partially, though, because the exposure requires a single-antigen-bead assay and a CDC crossmatch, neither of which an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen has, so the paper cannot be used to score compatibility from typing alone - it can only justify weighting antibody-defined incompatibility differently by donor type once antibody data exist. The typing regime does transfer well: donor typing was split-level serological, the same one-field resolution an Iranian programme works with, and the paper documents the concrete cost of that resolution, since broad-level-only donor typing in 64 transplants forced 70 antigens (47 of them DQ) to be classified as non-DSA because the responsible split could not be resolved. Against transfer to Iran: the cohort is predominantly white, Dutch, transplanted 1995-2005 under cyclosporine/tacrolimus-era immunosuppression with only 26% induction, contains no Iranian or regional data, and its HRs are NOT adjusted for HLA mismatch load, so none of its numbers can be read as an HLA-matching effect.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: any pretransplant DSA vs no DSA, total cohort (N=4724; 567 exposed) — HR 1.77 (1.51–2.08); adjusted for recipient age (quadratic), donor age (quadratic), donor type, CIT (DBD/DCD), time on dialysis (quadratic), IL-2 receptor blocker induction [Results 3.2 and Table 2, row 'Total cohort']
- death-censored graft failure: any pretransplant DSA vs no DSA, LIVING donors (n=1487; 137 [9%] exposed) — HR 1.42 (0.95–2.1); adjusted for same covariate set (donor type dropped within strata) [Results 3.2 and Table 2, 'Living donors / All']

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported for HLA mismatch. The paper reports NO 0/1/2 mismatch series, no total-count series, and no per-locus (A, B, C, DR, DQ, DP) mismatch effect. The only graded exposure is antibody burden by class: no DSA -> class I DSA only OR class II DSA only -> class I AND class II DSA. That gradient is strikingly different by donor type. In LIVING donors it is essentially flat until both classes are present (class II only HR 1.17, class I only HR 1.46, both classes HR 2.84) - i.e. a threshold/step at the class I+II combination rather than a graded rise. In DECEASED donors it is nearly flat across all three exposed categories (1.93, 1.76, 1.96 by HR), although the absolute 10-year survival does fall stepwise (76% -> 60%/61% -> 54%), so on the survival scale there is a further decrement for the combination that the HRs do not show.; linearity tested: not tested. No trend test, no spline, no polynomial term, no P for trend anywhere in the paper. The class categories were fitted as unordered strata, not as an ordered dose.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- pretransplant DSA x donor type (living vs deceased): THE PAPER'S CENTRAL RESULT. The same antibody exposure is a clear risk factor after deceased donation and not a significant one after living donation. Estimated by stratification only. (Living HR 1.42 (95% CI 0.95-2.10) vs deceased HR 1.86 (95% CI 1.56-2.21); 10-year death-censored graft survival gap 84% vs 78% (p = .07) in living donors against 76% vs 60% (p < .0001) in deceased donors) [Results 3.2, Table 2, Figures 2B and 2C. NO formal interaction term and NO P for interaction is reported - the CIs overlap substantially, so the modification is asserted from stratum-specific significance rather than demonstrated statistically.]
- DSA class (I only vs II only vs I+II) x donor type: In deceased donors every category is significantly harmful. In living donors only the class I + class II combination reaches significance, and on 18 cases. (Living: class I only HR 1.46 (0.83-2.55), class II only HR 1.17 (0.64-2.14), class I+II HR 2.84 (1.05-7.69). Deceased: class I only HR 1.93 (1.50-2.47), class II only HR 1.76 (1.37-2.26), class I+II HR 1.96 (1.29-2.98)) [Table 2; Results 3.4; Figures 3E and 3F]
- DSA x time since transplant (early <1 y vs late >=1 y), within donor type: In deceased donors the DSA effect is present both early and late, and if anything is larger late. In living donors neither the early nor the late effect reaches significance. (Deceased: early HR 1.76 (1.33-2.33), late HR 1.97 (1.56-2.45). Living: early HR 1.69 (0.76-3.77), late HR 1.35 (0.86-2.12). Authors add that a 3-month rather than 1-year cutoff gave similar results (data not shown).) [Results 3.3, Table 2, Figure 3A-D]
- DSA x immunisation status / retransplantation, within living donors: The authors argue the living-vs-deceased difference is NOT explained by differing immunisation: DSA were no more harmful in living-donor retransplants than in living-donor first transplants despite much lower immunisation in the latter. (no numbers printed in the retrieved main text; the authors cite supplementary tables and figures not present in the PMC full text) [Discussion. Supporting numbers are in Supplementary Information, which was not retrieved.]
- DSA x DSA strength (number of DSA, maximum MFI, cumulative MFI) x donor type: Class I+II-positive transplants had higher DSA number, maximum MFI and cumulative MFI, which could partly explain their worse survival; but the authors state class I and II positivity classified risk better than any construct from the three strength parameters, and that DSA strength does not explain the living-vs-deceased difference. (no numbers printed in the retrieved main text (supplementary Table B-D)) [Discussion. Supplementary only.]
- DSA definition x MFI cutoff: Sensitivity analysis: varying the MFI cutoff for DSA positivity gave comparable effects on long-term graft survival. Positivity was defined by the manufacturer's signal:background ratio, roughly equivalent to an MFI cutoff of 750. (no numbers printed in the retrieved main text (supplementary figure)) [Methods 2.2 and Discussion. Supplementary only.]
- donor type x HLA matching (background claim, not this paper's own analysis): The authors restate the standard result that poorly HLA-matched living-donor grafts outlast well-matched deceased-donor grafts, attributing it to cold ischaemia time and to donor cardiovascular instability before nephrectomy. Their own Table 3 is consistent with it: living-donor transplants averaged MORE mismatches (2.7 vs 2.2, p<.001) and still survived better. (cited from other literature; no effect estimate computed here) [Discussion. Directly relevant to C14 but it is a citation, not a finding of this study.]
- proposed mechanism for the donor-type modification: Hypothesised, not tested: lower HLA and adhesion-molecule expression on living-donor endothelium, plus better organ quality and short cold ischaemia, may blunt DSA-mediated injury; sufficient HLA expression is needed to trigger complement effector mechanisms. (no test performed) [Discussion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "In contrast, the presence of DSAs was significantly associated with a higher risk of graft failure after deceased donor transplants" (Results 3.2, narrative (sentence continues '(HR 1.84, 95% CI 1.55-2.19)'))
- *C14* — "the presence of pretransplant DSAs had no significant influence on graft survival in living donor transplants" (Results 3.2, narrative (sentence continues '(HR 1.42, 95% CI 0.95-2.10)'))
- *C11* — "the 10-year death-censored graft survival was 60% and 76% for patients with and without DSAs, respectively" (Results 3.2, deceased donor transplants (n=3237), Figure 2C, p < .0001)
- *C14* — "The combined presence of class I and II DSAs resulted in the poorest graft survival for both donor types, with a decrease from 84% to 75% at 10 years after transplant for living donor grafts" (Results 3.4, final paragraph)
- *C14* — "In our cohort of 1487 living donor kidney transplants, the combination of class I and II antibodies occurred in only 18 cases, indicating that the prevalence of this risk factor is relatively low" (Discussion, penultimate paragraph)
- *C14* — "it is known that graft survival rates of poorly HLA-matched living donor grafts are superior to those of well HLA-matched deceased donor grafts" (Discussion (cited background, not this study's own result))

**Limitations.** NO HLA MISMATCH EFFECT IS ESTIMATED. The paper contains no HR, OR or survival estimate for number of HLA mismatches, total or per locus. Mismatch count was explicitly among the covariates 'considered for adjustment' and was then not used, so every HR reported here is UNADJUSTED for HLA mismatch load. The paper cannot support any claim about mismatch counts.; The living-vs-deceased effect modification is shown by stratification only. No interaction term was fitted and no P for interaction is reported. The living (0.95-2.10) and deceased (1.56-2.21) CIs overlap, so a formal test might not have been significant; the authors' own conclusion concedes the living-donor effect 'could not be assessed due to their low prevalence'.; The one significant living-donor result rests on 18 exposed transplants (class I + class II DSA), giving HR 2.84 with a CI from 1.05 to 7.69 - barely excluding 1 and compatible with anything from trivial to catastrophic.; Serum was retrievable for only 78% of transplants, and missingness is not random: sera are mainly missing from older transplants at 4 of 7 centres, while 3 centres contributed >90%.; Exposure ascertainment depends on low-resolution donor typing. DSA were assigned by matching serological-level antibody specificities to split-level donor typing; for 70 antigens (47 of them HLA-DQ) in 64 transplants only broad-level typing existed and the antibodies were forced to count as non-DSA. The authors report a sensitivity analysis calling them all DSA gave the same conclusions, but the numbers are not shown.; No information on post-transplant de novo DSA, so the pretransplant DSA effect may partly capture later antibody formation. The authors argue this biases toward the null because DSA-positive groups had fewer mismatches - an argument, not a measurement.; Rejection data are unusable: biopsies were not routinely performed in this era, registered rejections may not all be true rejections, and true rejections may be unrecorded. The statement that DSA-positive patients had more rejection in both donor types is 'data not shown'.; Donor organ quality is only partly captured; delayed graft function was deliberately not adjusted for (treated as a mediator), and the authors say information on donor organ quality was limited.; Era and generalisability: transplants 1995-2005, Dutch, patients and donors 'primarily white', 26% induction therapy, cyclosporine-or-tacrolimus-based regimens. No ethnicity-stratified analysis. No Iranian or Middle Eastern data.; No molecular-mismatch work of any kind: no allele-level typing, no eplet, no PIRCHE, no HLA-C or -DP mismatch analysis. Antibodies against HLA-C, DR51-53 and DP were detected but too rare (4, 13 and 19 sera) to analyse.; Several published numbers disagree between the Results narrative, Table 2 and the Abstract (see notes) - a data-integrity concern when transcribing effect sizes.; Results are conditional on a negative CDC crossmatch and no desensitisation, so they say nothing about strongly incompatible pairs, who were never transplanted..

### Leeaphorn N 2018 — HLA-DQ Mismatching and Kidney Transplant Outcomes

Leeaphorn N 2018, *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol (CJASN) 2018;13(5):763-771*, [DOI 10.2215/CJN.10860917](https://doi.org/10.2215/CJN.10860917). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright (Copyright (c) 2018 by the American Society of Nephrology); free full text in PMC, no CC licence stated.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Adult ESKD recipients of a first kidney-only transplant in the US UNOS/OPTN registry, transplanted 1 January 2005 to 3 December 2014, final follow-up 31 March 2017. Of 135,638 transplants, 18,477 (14%) were excluded for missing HLA-DQ data, 5090 (4%) for discrepancy between donor initial HLA-DQ typing and retyping, and 18,289 (14%) because recipient and/or donor carried the obsolete HLA-DQ1 and/or HLA-DQ3 broad serotypes. Final n = 93,782: 22,730 (24%) with zero HLA-DQ mismatches and 71,052 (76%) with one or two HLA-DQ mismatches. Deceased and living donor cohorts analysed separately (Table 1 columns: deceased 0 DQ MM n=12,393, deceased 1-2 DQ MM n=43,415, living 0 DQ MM n=9,791, living 1-2 DQ MM n=27,262). |
| donor type | both |
| n | 93,782 |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort. Cox proportional hazards models for death-censored graft survival; logistic regression for cumulative incidence of acute rejection at 1 year. Multiplicative interaction terms for HLA-DQ mismatch x donor type, x cold ischaemia time (continuous), and x HLA-DR mismatch. Sensitivity analyses under several cohort restrictions and levels of adjustment. Stata 13. |
| typing resolution | broad serologic antigen level (2-digit / broad specificity). HLA-DQ mismatch counted in the host-versus-graft direction when the donor expressed a DQ antigen the recipient did not. Seven single donor DQ mismatch antigens analysed: DQ2, DQ4, DQ5, DQ6, DQ7, DQ8, DQ9. Recipients or donors carrying the obsolete broad serotypes DQ1 and DQ3 were excluded. HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatches also antigen level. No DQA1, no allele-level and no eplet/epitope data. |
| outcome | primary: death-censored graft failure and cumulative incidence of acute rejection at 1 year (registry-reported, type not specified). secondary: all-cause graft failure and graft failure attributed to chronic allograft nephropathy at 10 years, per single donor HLA-DQ mismatched antigen. |
| follow up | median 4.1 years (interquartile range 2.8-6.6 years); secondary per-antigen analyses reported at 10 years |
| other factors modelled | HLA-DR mismatch, HLA-A mismatch, HLA-B mismatch, recipient race/ethnicity, recipient sex, body mass index, preemptive transplant, panel reactive antibody, diabetes, donor age, donor race/ethnicity, donor sex, donor hypertension, cytomegalovirus serostatus, immunosuppression (induction and maintenance), transplant period, expanded criteria donor status (deceased donors), cold ischaemia time (as interaction term and stratification variable) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest antigen-level test of whether HLA-DQ mismatch carries risk beyond HLA-A, -B and -DR, which is exactly the question a low-resolution pre-screen must answer before it decides whether to score DQ at all. Its central result is directly usable for a living-donor programme: after adjustment for HLA-ABDR and donor/recipient factors, one or two DQ mismatches raised death-censored graft loss in LIVING donor recipients (HR 1.18, 1.07-1.30) but not in deceased donor recipients overall (HR 1.05, 0.98-1.12), with P for interaction <0.01 - the deceased-donor null is explained by cold ischaemia, since the effect reappears at CIT <=17 h (HR 1.12) and vanishes above it (HR 0.97). An Iranian living-donor pre-screen has essentially zero cold ischaemia, so the living-donor and short-CIT estimates are the transferable ones and the pooled deceased-donor null should not be quoted as evidence that DQ does not matter. The typing here is broad antigen (2-digit) DQ, the same resolution an Iranian one-field pre-screen would have, so the effect size is achievable without allele-level or eplet typing - a rare and valuable property for this review. Two cautions limit transfer: DSA and sensitisation status were entirely unmeasured (the mechanism the authors invoke), so this cannot substitute for antibody screening in an antibody-status-unknown setting; and because DQ is not allocated in the US, DQ concordance is incidental and rides on DR linkage and donor-recipient ethnic similarity, both of which differ in a consanguineous, related-donor Iranian population where DQ concordance would arise far more often through shared haplotypes.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored graft failure: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, deceased donor — HR 1.29 (1.22–1.36), p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable) [Results, Death-Censored Graft Survival; Table 2 (events 6189/43,208 vs 1465/12,347)]
- death-censored graft failure: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, deceased donor — HR 1.05 (0.98–1.12), p=0.18; adjusted for HLA-DR, HLA-A and HLA-B mismatches, recipient race/ethnicity, sex, BMI, preemptive, PRA, diabetes, donor age, race/ethnicity, sex, donor hypertension, CMV serostatus, immunosuppression, transplant period, expanded criteria donor status [Abstract; Results, Death-Censored Graft Survival; Table 2]
- death-censored graft failure: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, living donor — HR 1.35 (1.25–1.46), p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable) [Results, Death-Censored Graft Survival; Table 2 (events 2876/27,612 vs 841/10,321)]
- death-censored graft failure: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, living donor — HR 1.18 (1.07–1.3), p=<0.001 (Results/Table 2); abstract prints P<0.01; adjusted for same multivariable set as above, including HLA-ABDR mismatches [Abstract; Results, Death-Censored Graft Survival; Table 2]
- acute rejection at 1 year: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, deceased donor — OR 1.41 (1.31–1.51), p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable) [Results, Acute Rejection at 1-Year; Table 3 (events 4540/43,415 vs 950/12,393)]
- acute rejection at 1 year: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, deceased donor — OR 1.13 (1.03–1.23), p=<0.01; adjusted for HLA-ABDR mismatches, recipient, donor and transplant factors, initial immunosuppression [Abstract; Results, Acute Rejection at 1-Year; Table 3]
- acute rejection at 1 year: 1 or 2 HLA-DQ mismatches vs 0, living donor — OR 1.66 (1.53–1.81), p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted (univariable) [Results, Acute Rejection at 1-Year; Table 3 (events 2957/27,637 vs 694/10,337)]

NOTE: the upper confidence limit is printed as 1.22, identical to the point estimate - an apparent typesetting error in the published text; recorded exactly as printed.]
