- acute rejection at 1 year (crude rate): donor DQ8 single mismatch, cohort B (deceased donors, CIT <=17 h) — percentage 11.1% (32/289), p=0.03; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, cohort B]
- all-cause graft loss at 10 years (crude rate): donor DQ5 single mismatch, cohort A — percentage 17.7% (32/181), p=0.004; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, cohort A]
- all-cause graft loss at 10 years (crude rate): donor DQ5 single mismatch, cohort C (living donors only) — percentage 19.3% (16/83), p=0.001; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, cohort C]
- graft loss due to chronic allograft nephropathy at 10 years (crude rate): donor DQ5 single mismatch, cohort B (deceased donors, CIT <=17 h) — percentage 9.2% (9/98), p=0.001; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, cohort B]
- graft loss due to chronic allograft nephropathy at 10 years (crude rate): donor DQ5 single mismatch, cohort A — percentage 5.5% (10/181), p=<0.01; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, cohort A]
- acute rejection at 1 year (crude rate), null per-antigen results: single donor DQ mismatch, cohort A, antigens with no significant rejection excess — percentage DQ2 6.5% (18/278) P=0.32; DQ4 4.7% (6/129) P=0.15; DQ5 4.4% (8/181) P=0.07; DQ6 7.4% (28/379) P=0.64; DQ7 8.5% (80/943) P=0.50; DQ9 6.3% (19/300) P=0.26, p=all >0.05; adjusted for crude, vs overall one-DQ-mismatch group [Table 5, single donor DQ mismatch, cohort A]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; 1 MM: 1.22 (1.12–1.22); 2 MM: 1.32 (1.2–1.44); 2 vs 1 MM: 1.1 (1.03–1.17)
- DQ: 0 MM: reference; 1 or 2 (pooled, primary analysis) MM: death-censored graft loss: living donor adjusted HR 1.18 (1.07-1.30), P<0.001; deceased donor adjusted HR 1.05 (0.98-1.12), P=0.18; deceased donor with CIT <=17 h adjusted HR 1.12 (1.02-1.27), P=0.02; deceased donor with CIT >17 h adjusted HR 0.97 (0.88-1.06), P=0.49. Acute rejection at 1 year: deceased adjusted OR 1.13 (1.03-1.23), P<0.01; living adjusted OR 1.14 (1.03-1.27), P=0.02; 1 (separated) MM: acute rejection OR 1.22 (1.12-1.22 as printed), P<0.001, pooled living + deceased CIT<=17 h cohort only (Supplemental Table 3); no separate 1-mismatch estimate is published for graft survival by donor type; 2 (separated) MM: acute rejection OR 1.32 (1.20-1.44), P<0.001, same pooled cohort only
- DR: note MM: HLA-DR is an adjustment covariate and an effect modifier here, not an exposure with its own published dose-response. Table 1 shows the DR distribution: DR 0/1/2 mismatch = 59/34/8% (deceased, 0 DQ MM), 8/48/44% (deceased, 1-2 DQ MM), 59/36/4% (living, 0 DQ MM), 4/58/38% (living, 1-2 DQ MM).
- A: note MM: adjustment covariate only. Table 1 distribution A 0/1/2 mismatch = 34/29/36% (deceased 0 DQ MM), 9/39/52% (deceased 1-2 DQ MM), 41/47/12% (living 0 DQ MM), 14/54/32% (living 1-2 DQ MM).
- B: note MM: adjustment covariate only. Table 1 distribution B 0/1/2 mismatch = 32/22/46% (deceased 0 DQ MM), 5/24/71% (deceased 1-2 DQ MM), 36/48/16% (living 0 DQ MM), 6/48/46% (living 1-2 DQ MM).
- C: note MM: not studied
- DP: note MM: not studied
- Shape reported: For acute rejection: monotone increasing but with a diminishing increment - the first mismatch carries most of the effect (0->1 OR 1.22) and the second adds less (1->2 OR 1.10), i.e. concave in log-odds rather than linear, and a clear zero-mismatch premium. For death-censored graft survival: no dose-response detected at all ('no linear association'), so the graft-survival signal rests entirely on the pooled 1-or-2 versus 0 contrast.; linearity tested: Semi-formally. The authors state they 'assessed a linear association between an incremental number of HLA-DQ mismatching and primary outcomes by having three levels of exposure: zero, one, and two HLA-DQ mismatches' in the pooled living-donor + deceased-donor-with-CIT<=17 h cohort, and additionally estimated the 2-versus-1 contrast (OR 1.10, 1.03-1.17, P=0.004). No trend-test statistic, no P for trend, no spline or threshold model is printed. The conclusion for graft survival is stated as a negative ('no linear association') without an accompanying test statistic or estimates.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DQ mismatch x donor type (living vs deceased): DQ mismatch worsened death-censored graft survival in living donor recipients but not in deceased donor recipients overall (P value for interaction <0.01; living adjusted HR 1.18 (1.07-1.30) vs deceased adjusted HR 1.05 (0.98-1.12)) [Abstract; Results, Death-Censored Graft Survival; Table 2]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x cold ischaemia time (continuous): significant interaction on both primary outcomes; the DQ effect is present at short cold ischaemia and absent at long cold ischaemia, i.e. prolonged CIT obliterates the matching benefit (P<0.01 for death-censored graft survival and P=0.01 for acute rejection with CIT continuous. Stratified at 17 h: graft loss HR 1.12 (1.02-1.27) at CIT <=17 h vs HR 0.97 (0.88-1.06) at CIT >17 h; rejection OR 1.20 (1.06-1.35) vs OR 1.05 (0.92-1.19). Median CIT 16.4 h (IQR 11.3-22.1). Cutoffs 14, 17 and 20 h were tried; 17 h chosen as it 'yielded the highest HR and OR and the lowest P values') [Abstract; Results, The Effect of Cold Ischemic Time and HLA-DQ Mismatches on Outcomes; Table 4]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x HLA-DR mismatch, acute rejection: the DQ effect on rejection is stronger in recipients who are already DR-matched, i.e. DQ adds most where DR adds nothing - non-additivity between the two class II loci (P value for interaction = 0.01; adjusted OR 1.35 (1.14-1.60), P=0.001 in zero-DR-mismatch recipients vs adjusted OR 1.16 (1.07-1.27), P=0.001 in one-or-two-DR-mismatch recipients) [Results, Interaction between HLA-DQ and HLA-DR Mismatches; Supplemental Table 4]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x HLA-DR mismatch, death-censored graft survival: no interaction detected for graft survival (P value for interaction = 0.10) [Results, Interaction between HLA-DQ and HLA-DR Mismatches]
- identity of the mismatched donor DQ antigen (permissive vs non-permissive mismatch): the DQ effect is not uniform across antigens: donor DQ8 mismatch drove acute rejection in both deceased and living grafts, donor DQ5 mismatch drove all-cause graft loss (significant in living donor recipients) and graft loss due to chronic allograft nephropathy, while DQ4 and others carried no excess (DQ8 rejection 11.4% (60/526), P=0.001 vs the overall one-mismatch group in cohort A; DQ5 graft loss 17.7% (32/181), P=0.004 in cohort A and 19.3% (16/83), P=0.001 in living donors only; DQ5 CAN graft loss 9.2% (9/98), P=0.001 in deceased donors with CIT<=17 h; DQ4 rejection 4.7% (6/129), P=0.15) [Results, The Effect of HLA-DQ Antigen Mismatch in the Host versus Graft Direction; Table 5; Discussion]
- HLA-DQ mismatch x zero HLA-ABDR organ sharing (sensitivity analysis): the null result in deceased donors with CIT >17 h persisted after excluding zero-HLA-ABDR-mismatch transplants, so it was not an artefact of the national zero-mismatch sharing pathway (no numeric estimate printed in the main text; Supplemental Table 2, A and B) [Results, Sensitivity Analyses]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C4* — "HLA-DQ mismatching is associated with lower graft survival independent of HLA-ABDR in living donor kidney transplants and deceased donor kidney transplants with cold ischemia time ≤17 hours" (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C9* — "When compared with zero HLA-DQ mismatches, one and two HLA-DQ mismatches had a higher risk of acute rejection in an incremental fashion" (Results, The Effect of the Incremental Number of HLA-DQ Mismatching and Outcomes)
- *C2* — "There was no linear association between an incremental number of HLA-DQ mismatching and death-censored graft survival" (Results, The Effect of the Incremental Number of HLA-DQ Mismatching and Outcomes)
- *C11* — "However, when zero HLA-DQ mismatched kidneys had >17 hours of cold ischemic time, the graft survival advantage was lost." (Discussion, paragraph on cold ischaemia time)
- *C10* — "41% of recipients of HLA-DQ matched kidneys had HLA-DR mismatches and 26% of recipients of HLA-DR matched kidneys had HLA-DQ mismatches" (Discussion, paragraph 2 (DQ-DR linkage discordance))
- *C14* — "There was also a higher risk of graft loss in living kidney donor recipients when DQ5 was the donor mismatch. This information may be used in living donor selection." (Discussion, paragraph on specific donor DQ antigens)

**Limitations.** Retrospective registry analysis with residual confounding from factors not captured by UNOS/OPTN - the authors name this first.; No data on pretransplant or de novo donor-specific antibodies (author-stated). Since anti-DQ DSA is the mechanism the authors invoke, the study cannot separate a DQ antigen-mismatch effect from unmeasured sensitisation, which is precisely the gap in an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen.; Acute rejection is registry-reported and the type (cellular versus antibody-mediated) is not recorded (author-stated); no central biopsy adjudication, so ascertainment varies by centre.; Cause of graft loss poorly coded: 30% of graft losses were coded 'other-specified' and 25% as 'chronic allograft nephropathy', a nonspecific term; the authors state they could not investigate chronic rejection directly and had to assume CAN captured most chronic rejection.; Large non-random exclusion: 41,856 of 135,638 transplants (31%) were dropped - 14% for missing HLA-DQ data, 4% for donor DQ typing discrepant between initial typing and retyping, and 14% because recipient or donor carried the obsolete DQ1/DQ3 broad serotypes. The excluded groups are unlikely to be exchangeable with those retained.; Broad serologic antigen-level DQB1 typing only. No DQA1, no allele-level typing, no eplet or epitope load; the authors note epitope mismatching is not routinely performed. So this study cannot speak to molecular-mismatch thresholds.; One versus two DQ mismatches are pooled in every primary analysis. The separated estimates exist only in Supplemental Table 3, only for acute rejection, and only in a pooled living + short-CIT deceased cohort - there is no published 1-versus-2 estimate for graft survival, and none for living donors alone.; Internal inconsistency in a printed number: the one-DQ-mismatch rejection odds ratio is given as 1.22 with a 95% CI of 1.12 to 1.22, where the upper limit equals the point estimate - almost certainly a typesetting error, and the true upper bound cannot be recovered from the text.; P value discrepancy between abstract and Results/Table 4 for the deceased-donor CIT<=17 h graft-loss hazard ratio: the abstract prints P=0.002, the Results text and Table 4 print P=0.02.; The 17-hour cold-ischaemia cutoff was selected because it 'yielded the highest HR and OR and the lowest P values' among the cutoffs tried (14, 17, 20 h) - a data-driven threshold whose reported precision is optimistic.; Table 5 per-antigen analyses are many small subgroups (n as low as 83-943 per antigen) with three outcomes each and no correction for multiple comparisons; the DQ5 and DQ8 signals should be treated as hypothesis-generating.; DQ is not used in US allocation, so DQ concordance is incidental. Zero-DQ-mismatch recipients differ systematically (more white, more preemptive, lower KDPI, but also higher peak PRA in the deceased cohort: 22% vs 14% with PRA >30), and peak PRA was missing for 19-22% of patients. Confounding by ethnic and haplotype similarity is only partly addressed by covariate adjustment.; Immunosuppression was captured as initial/induction regimen only; no data on maintenance intensity over time, adherence, or centre effects.; Median follow-up 4.1 years for the primary graft-survival analysis, while the per-antigen graft-loss rates are quoted at 10 years - a horizon most of the cohort could not have reached.; US population and US practice; no Iranian or Middle Eastern data, and no consanguineous or related-donor subgroup..

### Shi X 2018 — What is the impact of human leukocyte antigen mismatching on graft survival and mortality in renal transplantation? A meta-analysis of 23 cohort studies involving 486,608 recipients

Shi X 2018, *BMC Nephrology*, [DOI 10.1186/s12882-018-0908-3](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12882-018-0908-3). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: CC BY 4.0 (BMC open access; PMC full text retrieved). Figures and all tables were NOT returned in the PMC text payload, so no table cell was read..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult post-kidney-transplant recipients; 23 cohort studies, 486,608 recipients pooled; databases searched from inception to December 2016; no language restriction; children, animals and in vitro studies excluded |
| donor type | both |
| n | 486,608 recipients across 23 studies. Per outcome: overall graft failure 11 studies / 289,987; HLA-DR 8 studies / 152,105; DR 1-or-2 vs 0 3 studies / 41,957; HLA-B 4 studies / 146,019; HLA-A 3 studies / 40,000; death-censored graft failure 4 cohorts / 101,093; all-cause mortality 4 cohorts / 180,766 |
| design | systematic review and random-/fixed-effects meta-analysis of cohort studies (PROSPERO CRD42017071894, MOOSE and PRISMA); HRs extracted directly from each study, DerSimonian-Laird random effects when I-squared > 50% or p < 0.10, otherwise Mantel-Haenszel fixed effects; Newcastle-Ottawa quality 6-8 points; subgroup analysis, leave-one-out sensitivity analysis, univariate meta-regression when >= 10 studies, Egger test |
| typing resolution | not stated. The meta-analysis never reports the HLA typing resolution of any constituent study, and the term 'resolution' does not appear in the paper. The loci pooled (A, B, DR only) and the era of the cohorts imply antigen/serologic-level typing, but this is inference, not stated. |
| outcome | primary: overall (all-cause) graft failure. Secondary: death-censored graft failure and all-cause mortality. |
| follow up | not stated as a pooled figure; follow-up was extracted per study into Table 1, which was not returned in the PMC text payload |
| other factors modelled | not modelled by the meta-analysis itself; it pools multivariable-adjusted HRs from the primary studies, confounders named as adjusted-for in the constituent studies: donor and recipient age, gender, combined disease, serum creatinine levels, ischaemic times, explored only as study-level subgroups: recipient sample size, adjusted vs unadjusted estimate, donor source, single- vs multi-centre, geographical location/ethnicity, era (pre-1995 vs not) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the single best summary estimate available for the size of the per-mismatch effect in adult kidney transplantation, so it directly answers the review's calibration question: how much risk does one extra HLA mismatch buy? The pooled adjusted HR of 1.06 per mismatch for overall graft failure and 1.09 for death-censored graft failure sets the order of magnitude a pre-screen should assume, and the locus ordering it reports (DR significant at HR 1.12; A 1.06 non-significant; B 1.01 null) speaks to how a low-resolution score should weight loci. Its transfer to a living-donor Iranian pre-screen is only partial and mostly favourable on typing: the meta-analysis pools A, B and DR only, which is exactly the three-locus, one-field panel an Iranian pre-screen will typically have, so no two-field or eplet information is required to use these numbers. Transfer is weaker on donor type, because the cohorts are dominated by deceased-donor registries and the only donor-source subgroup is 'cadaveric' versus a mixed 'living and cadaveric' category, never living-only; the paper reports that stratifying by donor source removed most heterogeneity but that meta-regression found no significant effect of it, which is reassuring rather than confirmatory. It is silent on the antibody-status question that matters most for an antibody-unknown pre-screen: the authors state explicitly that too few studies reported PRA to allow any stratified analysis, so this paper cannot tell us whether the per-mismatch effect is larger in sensitised recipients. It also cannot inform DQ, DP or C weighting at all, since those loci were excluded by design. Practically, it supports treating mismatch count as a monotone, modest, roughly log-linear risk gradient with DR weighted heaviest, while leaving the shape between one and two mismatches, and every antibody interaction, to other papers in the review.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA mismatch (total across the loci counted by the primary studies, i.e. A+B+DR) — HR 1.06 (1.05–1.07), p=<0.001; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates as reported by the primary studies (donor and recipient age, gender, combined disease, serum creatinine, ischaemic times, etc.) [Abstract, Results; Results, 'HLA per mismatch and overall graft failure' (11 studies, 289,987 recipients; I-squared 27.4%)]
- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA mismatch, univariable-unadjusted pooled estimate — HR 1.14 (1.04–1.26), p=0.008; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'HLA per mismatch and overall graft failure' (I-squared 24.8%)]
- death-censored graft failure: per one additional HLA mismatch — HR 1.09 (1.06–1.12), p=<0.001; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Abstract, Results; Results, 'Death-censored graft failure' (4 cohorts, 101,093 recipients; I-squared 70.9%; fixed-effects sensitivity HR 1.09, 95% CI 1.08-1.10, p<0.001)]
- all-cause mortality: per one additional HLA mismatch — HR 1.04 (1.02–1.07), p=0.001; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Abstract, Results; Results, 'All-cause mortality' (4 cohorts, 180,766 recipients; I-squared 65.3%; identical under fixed effects)]
- all-cause mortality: per one additional HLA mismatch, restricted to cohorts >= 10,000 recipients — HR 1.04 (1.02–1.05), p=<0.001; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Results, 'All-cause mortality' (I-squared 27.8%; Additional file Fig. S4)]
- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA-DR mismatch, multivariable-adjusted — HR 1.12 (1.05–1.21), p=0.002; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Abstract, Results; Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure' (8 studies, 152,105 recipients; I-squared 58.3%; fixed-effects sensitivity HR 1.08, 95% CI 1.05-1.11, p<0.001)]
- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA-DR mismatch, univariable-unadjusted — HR 1.44 (0.86–2.41), p=0.160; adjusted for unadjusted [Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure' (I-squared 70.0%)]
- overall graft failure: 1 HLA-DR mismatch vs 0 HLA-DR mismatch — HR 1.12 (1.04–1.21), p=0.002; adjusted for as reported by the 3 contributing studies [Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure', second paragraph (3 studies, 41,957 recipients; I-squared 0%; Additional file Fig. S3)]
- overall graft failure: 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0 HLA-DR mismatch — HR 1.15 (1.05–1.25), p=0.002; adjusted for as reported by the 3 contributing studies [Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure', second paragraph (3 studies, 41,957 recipients; I-squared 0%; Additional file Fig. S3)]
- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA-B mismatch — HR 1.01 (0.9–1.15), p=0.834; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Abstract, Results; Results, 'HLA-B mismatches and overall graft failure' (4 studies, 146,019 recipients; I-squared 66.0%; fixed-effects sensitivity HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.89-1.14)]
- overall graft failure: per one additional HLA-A mismatch — HR 1.06 (0.98–1.14), p=0.121; adjusted for multivariable-adjusted estimates from the primary studies [Abstract, Results; Results, 'HLA-A mismatches and overall graft failure' (3 studies, 40,000 recipients; I-squared 0%; random-effects sensitivity HR 1.06, 95% CI 0.98-1.15, p=0.121)]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: ref; 1 MM: HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.04-1.21), p=0.002; 2 MM: HR 1.15 (95% CI 1.05-1.25), p=0.002; per_mismatch MM: HR 1.12 (95% CI 1.05-1.21), p=0.002, adjusted; 1.44 (0.86-2.41), p=0.160, unadjusted
- B: per_mismatch MM: HR 1.01 (95% CI 0.90-1.15), p=0.834 - null; 0_1_2_series MM: not reported
- A: per_mismatch MM: HR 1.06 (95% CI 0.98-1.14), p=0.121 - non-significant; 0_1_2_series MM: not reported
- C: not analysed; excluded by design and named as a limitation
- DQ: not analysed; excluded by design and named as a limitation
- DP: not analysed; excluded by design
- Shape reported: not reported. The pooled quantity is a per-one-mismatch hazard ratio, which imposes log-linearity rather than testing it; the authors describe the finding only as 'each incremental increase' being associated with higher risk. The single 0/1/2 series they do report, for DR, is markedly concave: the first DR mismatch carries HR 1.12 and the second raises it only to 1.15 versus zero, i.e. the second mismatch adds roughly 3 percentage points against 12 for the first. The two confidence intervals overlap almost entirely (1.04-1.21 vs 1.05-1.25) and the authors neither test nor comment on the 1-vs-2 difference, so this is suggestive of a zero-mismatch premium / early-plateau shape but is not established by this paper.; linearity tested: not tested. No test for trend, no spline, no threshold analysis, no categorical-vs-linear model comparison and no departure-from-linearity statistic appears anywhere in the paper; the words trend, spline and threshold do not occur. Log-linearity is inherited from the per-mismatch Cox models of the primary studies and then assumed by the pooling.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA per mismatch x donor source (cadaveric vs 'living and cadaveric'): no effect modification; stratifying by donor source removed nearly all between-study heterogeneity but did not change the pooled effect, and meta-regression confirmed this. Note the comparator is a MIXED living+deceased category, never a living-donor-only stratum, so this says nothing directly about living donation. (heterogeneity decreased to I-squared = 0 and 16.4% in the two strata respectively; 'meta-regression analysis revealed that donor source did not change the overall effect significantly'. Stratum-specific HRs are in Table 2, which was not returned in the PMC text payload.) [Results, 'HLA per mismatch and overall graft failure'; Discussion, subgroup/meta-regression paragraph]
- HLA-DR mismatch x recipient ethnicity / geographical location: named as a potential source of heterogeneity, attributed to varying HLA polymorphism across geographically distinct cohorts, but the pooled effect was 'not modified' after stratification (no P for interaction and no stratum-specific HR is printed in the retrieved text; the numbers sit in Table 2) [Abstract, Results; Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure'; Discussion, subgroup paragraph]
- HLA-DR mismatch x recipient sample size (>= 10,000 vs < 10,000): named as a potential source of heterogeneity ('large sample size of cohorts usually demonstrated more stable results'), but the effect estimate was not modified after stratification (no P for interaction printed; stratum HRs in Table 2. For all-cause mortality the large-cohort stratum gave HR 1.04 (95% CI 1.02-1.05), p<0.001, I-squared 27.8%.) [Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure' and 'All-cause mortality'; Discussion]
- HLA per mismatch x era (transplants prior to 1995 vs not prior to 1995): no effect modification; the pooled per-mismatch effect on overall graft failure 'did not changed significantly' across eras. This is the paper's only test of the 'modern immunosuppression has abolished the HLA effect' hypothesis, and it is negative. (no P for interaction and no stratum HR printed; Table 2) [Results, 'HLA per mismatch and overall graft failure']
- HLA per mismatch x data source (multi-centred vs single-centred) and x adjusted vs unadjusted estimate: no effect modification for data source. The adjusted/unadjusted contrast is large in magnitude, however: unadjusted HR 1.14 (1.04-1.26) versus adjusted 1.06 (1.05-1.07) for overall graft failure, i.e. confounder adjustment halves the apparent per-mismatch effect. (1.14 (1.04-1.26) unadjusted vs 1.06 (1.05-1.07) adjusted; no formal interaction test) [Results, 'HLA per mismatch and overall graft failure']
- HLA mismatch x sensitisation (PRA) and x immunosuppression regimen: NOT TESTED. The authors state that too few of the included studies reported induction agent, maintenance agent or PRA for any stratified analysis to be possible. This is the interaction most relevant to an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen, and this paper cannot inform it. (none) [Discussion, Strengths and limitations, fourth limitation]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "HLA per mismatch was significant associated with increased risks of overall graft failure (hazard ratio (HR), 1.06; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.05–1.07), death-censored graft failure (HR: 1.09; 95% CI 1.06–1.12)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "compared with 0 DR-mismatches, 1 and 2 mismatches were significant associated with 12 and 15% higher risk of overall graft failure, respectively" (Discussion, second paragraph on HLA-DR (pooled HRs 1.12 and 1.15 given in Results))
- *C3* — "After adjustment, each incremental increase of HLA-DR mismatches was significant associated with 12% higher risk of overall graft failure" (Results, 'HLA-DR mismatches and overall graft failure')
- *C5* — "we did not observe a significant association between HLA-B mismatching and overall graft survival (HR: 1.01; 95% CI: 0.90–1.15)" (Discussion, HLA-A/HLA-B paragraph)
- *C1* — "HLA mismatching was still a critical prognostic factor that affects graft and recipient survival." (Abstract, Conclusions; repeated verbatim in Conclusions section)
- *C4* — "several studies have suggested that other HLA loci, such as HLA-C and -DQ locus, may contribute to poorer graft outcomes [–], but this meta-analysis only included the HLA-A, -B and -DR loci" (Discussion, Strengths and limitations, second limitation)

**Limitations.** No randomised trials; all 23 inputs are observational cohorts, and the authors name this as the biggest limitation. Residual confounding by indication and by allocation (better-matched kidneys go to different recipients) is not addressed.; The pooled 'per mismatch' HR assumes a log-linear effect of mismatch count. Linearity is never tested, no trend/spline/threshold analysis is done, and no total-count 0-to-6 series is reported, so this paper cannot settle the shape question the review cares about for C2.; The paper never states the HLA typing resolution of any constituent study, so the antigen-level (one-field) reading is an inference from the loci and eras involved, not a stated fact.; Only A, B and DR were analysed. C, DQ and DP are excluded by design; the authors concede that C and DQ may matter. The review cannot use this paper for C4, C7 or C8 beyond the acknowledgement of the gap.; PRA/sensitisation, induction agent and maintenance immunosuppression could not be stratified on because too few studies reported them. There is therefore no evidence here on effect modification by antibody status.; Donor source appears only as 'cadaveric' versus a MIXED 'living and cadaveric' category. There is no living-donor-only stratum, so the paper gives no isolated living-donor estimate.; The pooled per-locus analyses rest on very few studies: 3 for HLA-A (40,000 recipients) and 4 for HLA-B (146,019), with moderate heterogeneity (I-squared 66.0%) for B. The authors themselves say the HLA-A result should be interpreted cautiously. The null HLA-B result is therefore weak evidence of absence, not evidence of a null, and it conflicts with the Massie SRTR study they cite in the same Discussion.; Moderate-to-high heterogeneity for death-censored graft failure (I-squared 70.9%), all-cause mortality (65.3%), HLA-DR (58.3%) and HLA-B (66.0%); only 4 cohorts each for the two secondary outcomes.; Search ended December 2016 and publication is 2018, so nothing from the eplet/molecular-mismatch era and no recent registry analyses are included.; Internal numerical inconsistency: the Discussion states the per-mismatch increase is 'overall graft failure (9%), death-censored graft failure (6%)', which reverses the 1.06 and 1.09 reported in the Abstract and Results. The Abstract/Results ordering (overall 1.06, death-censored 1.09) is the one supported by the per-outcome Results paragraphs and is the one this extraction uses.; The paper twice writes 'HLA-B epitope' and 'HLA-A epitope' where it means locus/antigen; no epitope or eplet analysis was performed.; Overlap between constituent registry cohorts is handled only by a rule of keeping 'the most recent and informative' among overlapping reports; no quantitative check of double-counting is presented, and several of the largest inputs are national registries whose patients may recur.; All tables and figures, including Table 1 (study characteristics, follow-up) and Table 2 (all subgroup estimates), were absent from the retrieved PMC text, so every subgroup number remains unread rather than null..

### Wiebe C 2018 — A Comparison of HLA Molecular Mismatch Methods to Determine HLA Immunogenicity

Wiebe C 2018, *Transplantation*, [PMID 29443827](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29443827/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - PMC full text (PMC6072378) retrieved via the PubMed MCP tool; no licence statement appeared in the retrieved text. Treat as publisher copyright / author manuscript until confirmed..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 596 consecutive adult (n=541) and paediatric (n=55) renal transplant recipients, single programme (Manitoba, Canada), transplanted January 1999 to January 2015. From 654 consecutive transplants, primary non-function (n=16) and pretransplant DSA (n=42) were excluded. Low immunological risk: 96% first transplant, <10% with cPRA >80%. Maintenance immunosuppression: CNI (tacrolimus 86%, cyclosporine 14%) + MMF + prednisone; induction in 35%. |
| donor type | not stated in the retrieved text (donor type would be in Table 1, which PMC does not render); cold ischaemic time is analysed as a correlate, so deceased donors are certainly included - almost certainly a mixed living + deceased cohort, but this is an inference, not a printed statement |
| n | 596 |
| design | single-centre retrospective analysis of a consecutive cohort with prospective protocol-driven serial serum banking and dnDSA surveillance; Cox proportional hazards models of dnDSA-free survival (univariate and multivariate); models compared by Akaike information criterion and time-dependent ROC/AUC |
| typing resolution | high-resolution two-field (4-digit) class II typing for HLA-DR and HLA-DQ, by SSO / SSP (LABType HD SSO, Micro SSP; One Lambda). Class I typing resolution is not stated because class I was not analysed. |
| outcome | de novo HLA-DR or HLA-DQ donor-specific antibody (dnDSA)-free survival. NOT graft failure, NOT rejection - dnDSA is the only endpoint modelled. |
| follow up | median 87 months (range 18-210); 66 of 596 (11%) developed class II dnDSA at a median of 55 months (range 6-170) |
| other factors modelled | recipient age (younger recipient age), donor age (younger donor age), cold ischaemic time, calcineurin inhibitor regimen (cyclosporine vs tacrolimus), immunosuppression nonadherence, calcineurin inhibitor coefficient of variation, T-cell mediated rejection in the first year, induction therapy (thymoglobulin / basiliximab) described but adjustment set in the final model was recipient age, cyclosporine vs tacrolimus, nonadherence |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the head-to-head comparison the review needs for C12: three molecular mismatch metrics (HLAMatchmaker eplet, Cambridge amino-acid mismatch, Cambridge electrostatic mismatch) computed on the SAME 596-patient kidney cohort against the same endpoint, so the question 'which molecular metric should a matching engine use?' is answered without between-study confounding. The answer is that it does not matter much: the three scores correlate at R = 0.85-0.96, all three give the same discrimination (AUC 0.71-0.74), the AIC differences are small, and the authors conclude the choice is driven by familiarity and ease of use. For the review's dose-response question the paper is informative in a negative way: it reports a single hazard ratio per 10 units for each metric, i.e. it IMPOSES log-linearity on a continuous score and never tests a threshold, a spline or risk categories - so it cannot be cited for a threshold or for a non-linear shape, only for 'more molecular mismatch, more dnDSA'. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor pre-screen is where this paper matters most, and it is mostly a warning: every result here requires two-field DRB1/DQB1(+DQA1) typing that our pre-screen does not have, so none of these three scores can be computed from one-field antigen-level typing without imputation, and the paper's own framing ('traditional HLA mismatch quantification is constrained by ... 0, 1, or 2 per locus') describes exactly the data we will actually hold. The endpoint is also not the one a pre-screen ranks on: dnDSA at a median of 55 months is an intermediate immunological outcome, not graft survival, and the cohort was deliberately DSA-negative pretransplant with a negative flow crossmatch, whereas our pre-screen runs with antibody status unknown. The one directly portable descriptive finding is the locus split - 56% of the class II dnDSA episodes were HLA-DQ alone versus 23% HLA-DR alone - which supports keeping DQ in the ranking (C4) even though our typing will be low resolution. Donor type is not broken out, so the paper cannot be used to argue that molecular matching helps specifically in living donation.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA-DR dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 eplet mismatch (HLAMatchmaker), per 10 eplets mismatched (continuous) — HR 2.5 (1.71–3.64), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 1 (also Abstract)]
- HLA-DR dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DR amino acid mismatch (AAMM, Cambridge algorithm), per 10 amino acids mismatched (continuous) — HR 1.49 (1.25–1.76), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 1 (also Abstract)]
- HLA-DR dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DR electrostatic mismatch score (EMS/ESM), per 10 units mismatched (continuous) — HR 1.23 (1.11–1.35), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 1 (also Abstract)]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DQA1/B1 eplet mismatch (HLAMatchmaker), per 10 eplets mismatched (continuous) — HR 1.98 (1.53–2.58), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 2 (also Abstract)]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DQ amino acid mismatch (AAMM), per 10 amino acids mismatched (continuous) — HR 1.24 (1.12–1.37), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 2 (also Abstract)]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DQ electrostatic mismatch score (EMS/ESM), per 10 units mismatched (continuous) — HR 1.14 (1.07–1.21), p=<0.0001; adjusted for none - univariate Cox [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 2 (also Abstract)]
- discrimination for dnDSA development: all three molecular mismatch methods (eplet, amino acid, electrostatic), time-dependent ROC — AUC None; adjusted for not stated whether the AUC is for the mismatch score alone or the full model [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 2, final sentence]
- class II dnDSA incidence: whole cohort (no comparison group) — percentage 11.0; adjusted for descriptive [Results, para 1: 66 of 596 recipients, median 55 months posttransplant (range 6-170)]
- locus distribution of class II dnDSA at onset - HLA-DQ alone: share of the 66 dnDSA-positive recipients — percentage 56.0; adjusted for descriptive (37 of 66) [Results, para 1]
- locus distribution of class II dnDSA at onset - HLA-DR alone: share of the 66 dnDSA-positive recipients (14 of 66, 21%, had both DR and DQ) — percentage 23.0; adjusted for descriptive (15 of 66) [Results, para 1]
- isolated class I dnDSA: share of the whole cohort; only 1 patient in the entire cohort lost the graft after isolated class I dnDSA — percentage 2.0; adjusted for descriptive; given as the reason class I was not analysed [Discussion, para 4]
- agreement between metrics: HLA-DRB eplet mismatch vs HLA-DRB amino acid mismatch — correlation coefficient R 0.96; adjusted for not applicable; correlation type (Pearson/Spearman) not stated [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 3 and Figure 1]
- agreement between metrics: HLA-DRB eplet mismatch vs HLA-DRB electrostatic mismatch — correlation coefficient R 0.85; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 3 and Figure 1]
- agreement between metrics: HLA-DQ alpha-beta eplet mismatch vs HLA-DQ alpha-beta amino acid mismatch — correlation coefficient R 0.95; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 3 and Figure 1]
- agreement between metrics: HLA-DQ alpha-beta eplet mismatch vs HLA-DQ alpha-beta electrostatic mismatch — correlation coefficient R 0.9; adjusted for not applicable [Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 3 and Figure 1]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: metric MM: continuous molecular mismatch, modelled per 10 units - no 0/1/2 categories; eplet_mismatch MM: median 10 (range 0-41); HR 2.50 per 10 eplets (95% CI 1.71-3.64, P<0.0001); amino_acid_mismatch MM: median 15 (range 0-82); HR 1.49 per 10 AA (95% CI 1.25-1.76, P<0.0001); electrostatic_mismatch MM: median 22 (range 0-147); HR 1.23 per 10 units (95% CI 1.11-1.35, P<0.0001)
- DQ: metric MM: continuous molecular mismatch, modelled per 10 units - no 0/1/2 categories; eplet_mismatch MM: median 13 (range 0-42); HR 1.98 per 10 eplets (95% CI 1.53-2.58, P<0.0001); amino_acid_mismatch MM: median 18 (range 0-97); HR 1.24 per 10 AA (95% CI 1.12-1.37, P<0.0001); electrostatic_mismatch MM: median 24 (range 0-164); HR 1.14 per 10 units (95% CI 1.07-1.21, P<0.0001)
- A: not analysed
- B: not analysed
- C: not analysed
- DP: tracked but 'data not shown'; DP dnDSA was too infrequent for meaningful analysis
- Shape reported: not reported - log-linearity is assumed, not demonstrated. Each metric enters the Cox model as a single continuous term and the effect is printed as one HR per 10 units, which forces a constant multiplicative hazard per increment. The per-10-unit HRs are not comparable across metrics because the underlying score scales differ (DR medians 10 vs 15 vs 22 units), so the larger eplet HR does not mean eplets are a stronger predictor - AUC 0.71-0.74 for all three is the like-for-like comparison.; linearity tested: not tested. No spline, no fractional polynomial, no threshold search, no quantile/tertile/quartile categories, and no test for departure from log-linearity appear anywhere in the Statistics section or Results. The only model diagnostics reported are the proportional-hazards assumption (Schoenfeld residuals, Harrell's rho) and collinearity (all VIF < 3).; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "Traditional HLA mismatch quantification is constrained by a limited range of possible values (0, 1, or 2 per locus) at the whole antigen level." (Introduction, para 2)
- *C12* — "Unique to this consecutive patient cohort is the strict exclusion of preexisting HLA DSA, the availability of high-resolution donor and recipient HLA typing" (Introduction, final para)
- *C12* — "The principal finding was that assessment of donor HLA immunogenicity based on AAMM, EpMM or EMS is superior to that of conventional HLA mismatch grade for assessing the risk of dnDSA development after kidney transplantation." (Discussion, para 1)
- *C12* — "Receiver operating characteristic curve analysis showed that all molecular mismatch methods had similar AUC scores (0.71 to 0.74)" (Results, 'Correlates of dnDSA-Free Survival', para 2)
- *C12* — "the use of one method over the other is likely to be driven by familiarity and ease of use as highly correlated results are produced by each method." (Discussion, concluding para (and Abstract, Conclusions))
- *C4* — "At the time of dnDSA development 15 (23%) of 66 had HLA-DR dnDSA alone, 37 (56%) of 66 had HLA-DQ dnDSA alone, and 14 (21%) of 66 had both HLA-DR and DQ dnDSA." (Results, para 1)

**Limitations.** Endpoint is de novo class II DSA, not graft failure, rejection or patient survival. The paper shows molecular mismatch predicts an immunological intermediate; it does not show it predicts the outcome a matching engine ultimately cares about.; Single centre, n = 596, with only 66 events. The authors themselves flag this: 'Due to the relatively small sample size and the associated risk of type II error, risk quantification should be interpreted with caution, and should be validated in a larger independent cohort.'; Class I (A, B, C) was excluded entirely because isolated class I dnDSA occurred in only 2% of the cohort; HLA-DP was tracked but reported as 'data not shown' and too infrequent to analyse. The paper therefore says nothing about A, B, C or DP molecular mismatch.; The central claim that molecular mismatch is 'superior to conventional HLA mismatch grade' is asserted in the Discussion but no antigen-level comparator HR, AUC or AIC is printed in the retrieved text - the superiority is not quantified here.; Multivariate results live in Table 2, which the PMC full text does not render. The adjusted HRs, their CIs and the AIC values are therefore not retrievable; only the statement that all three scores remained independent correlates after adjustment for recipient age, cyclosporine vs tacrolimus and nonadherence is available.; Table 1 is likewise not rendered, so donor type (living vs deceased), donor and recipient age distributions, ethnicity and cold ischaemia values are unavailable. Donor type is nowhere stated in the running text.; Log-linearity of the score-hazard relationship is assumed, never tested. No threshold, category or spline analysis, so the paper cannot support any claim about a molecular-mismatch cut-off.; Per-10-unit HRs are on three different score scales and are not directly comparable; reading 'eplet HR 2.50 beats AA HR 1.49' as a ranking of methods is a scale artefact, contradicted by the near-identical AUCs.; Requires two-field (4-digit) DRB1/DQA1/DQB1 typing. The paper offers no evidence on imputation from low-resolution typing and no misclassification analysis, which is the exact gap for a one-field pre-screen.; Cohort was deliberately DSA-negative pretransplant with negative flow crossmatch and low immunological risk (96% first transplant, <10% cPRA >80%); it does not speak to sensitised or antibody-status-unknown candidates.; Mixed adult and paediatric (55 of 596 paediatric) with no separate paediatric estimates.; Era 1999-2015, mostly tacrolimus/MMF/prednisone in a Canadian programme; immunosuppression and adherence monitoring differ from an Iranian setting.; Non-adherence and CNI coefficient of variation are strong competing determinants of dnDSA in this very cohort, which bounds how much of the dnDSA risk any matching metric can control..

### Williams RC 2018 — The Risk of Failure With HLA Mismatch and Recipient Age in First Pediatric (<18 years) Kidney Transplants

Williams RC 2018, *Transplantation Direct*, [PMID 30046655](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30046655/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - Transplantation Direct is an open-access journal and the article body was retrievable in full from PMC, but no licence statement appeared in the retrieved text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First kidney-only transplants in children aged <18 years, United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS) Standard Transplant Analysis and Research (STAR) file, United States, 1 October 1987 - 31 December 2016. 8030 living-related, 858 living-unrelated (pooled after a non-significant log-rank, 2.86, p = 0.0906), 9714 deceased donor. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 18 602 |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; unadjusted Kaplan-Meier plus reduced and fully adjusted multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression; proportional-hazards assumption checked by regression of Schoenfeld residuals on survival time and goodness of fit by cumulative sums of martingale residuals (31 risk-score groups, z-score distribution against N(0,1)) |
| typing resolution | not stated explicitly; the exposure is the UNOS STAR count of HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 mismatches (0-6) plus the 27 [A, B, DRB1] mismatch permutations, i.e. antigen-level / one-field matching as recorded by UNOS. Missing or unknown values of categorical variables were filled by regression imputation. |
| outcome | allograft failure. Methods state that 'Allograft survival was censored at the last recorded examination, at the start of renal replacement therapy, or at death', so the analysis is death-censored; note that listing return to renal replacement therapy as a censoring time rather than as the event is internally odd and is most likely a wording slip in the paper - the reviewer should not assume either reading. |
| follow up | 124 316 graft-years total; mean 6.7 years, median 5.3 years (Q1 2.2, Q3 9.9); longest surviving allograft 29.1 years; Kaplan-Meier projected median survival for all paediatric kidneys 14.8 years (95% CI 14.4-15.5) |
| other factors modelled | recipient age (year-quartiles), recipient sex, donor age (year-quartiles), donor sex, recipient ethnicity, peak panel-reactive antibody, donor source (living vs deceased), antibody induction (yes/no), immunosuppression at discharge, transplant era (6 categories, 1987-2016), underlying disease (14 categories), UNOS region (stratification of the extract) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the paediatric companion to the same group's adult UNOS analyses and is one of the few papers that reports the whole 0-6 total-count dose-response separately within living and within deceased donation, which is exactly the contrast our pre-screen faces. It answers the review's shape question (C2) directly: the authors fit a weighted linear regression through the vector of adjusted hazard ratios and find a significant, essentially linear increment of hazard per additional mismatch, with no evidence of a threshold beyond a visible clustering of the Kaplan-Meier curves into 0-2 versus 4-6. Its most transferable result for an Iranian living-donor programme is that the per-mismatch penalty is not a constant of nature but depends on donor type: the fitted slope is 0.32 for living donors against 0.07 for deceased, more than four-fold, so HLA matching earns more in a living-donor pathway than the deceased-donor literature implies - which is the strongest single argument in this corpus for scoring HLA at all in a living-donor pre-screen (C14). The exposure is antigen-level A/B/DRB1 counting on registry data, the same one-field resolution our OCR pipeline recovers from Iranian laboratory reports, so the effect sizes are measured on our variable rather than on a molecular proxy we cannot compute. Transfer is limited in three ways: the population is children under 18 whereas our recipients are overwhelmingly adults, so the absolute hazards and the age gradient do not carry over; peak PRA is adjusted for but never stratified on, so this paper says nothing about the antibody-unknown recipient we actually pre-screen; and the authors' own within-category permutation tests found no locus more important than another, which cuts against giving DRB1 extra weight in our scoring (relevant to C3 as a negative, not a positive). Treat it as evidence for a smooth, roughly linear, living-donor-amplified total-count penalty, not as evidence about locus weights or about sensitised recipients.

The tabulated HR and its CI are in Table 2, which was not returned with the PMC text.]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; 1 MM: 1.3; 2 MM: None; 3 MM: None; 4 MM: None; 5 MM: None; 6 MM: 1.92
- note: No per-locus HR series (A alone, B alone, DR alone at 0/1/2) is reported. Instead the 27 [HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-DRB1] mismatch permutations were each entered against the [0,0,0] reference: 22 of 27 were significant risk factors, ranging from HR 1.37 for [0,1,0] (p = 0.0105) to HR 2.55 for [2,0,2] (p < 0.0001); 5 permutations were not significant. Individual permutation HRs other than these two are in Table 4, whose body was not returned.
- A: not reported separately
- B: not reported separately
- DR: not reported separately; the authors argue against DRB1 primacy (see interactions / limitations)
- C: not typed or analysed
- DQ: not typed or analysed
- DP: not typed or analysed
- Shape reported: linear - the authors explicitly fit and report a linear relation between mismatch count and adjusted hazard ratio, in the overall cohort and in each donor stratum. Superimposed on that, the unadjusted KM curves 'generally cluster in 2 groups, mismatch categories 0 to 2 and 4 to 6, with 3 mismatches being intermediate', and the adjusted HRs likewise 'sorted into 2 clusters, 1 to 3 and 4 to 6'. So the paper supports a smooth per-mismatch gradient with a visually step-like appearance at the 3/4 boundary; no threshold model was formally fitted or preferred. A zero-mismatch premium is visible in the KM medians (24.8 years at 0 vs 19.6 at 1 vs 18.3 at 2) but was not tested as a discontinuity.; linearity tested: Yes, but by an unusual second-stage method rather than by a trend test inside the Cox model. The authors fitted weighted linear regressions to the vector of Cox hazard ratios across mismatch categories 0-6, for the reduced and full models and for each donor stratum: 'Each of the 6 fitted lines in the figures had a statistically significant intercept and slope', and the slope CIs for reduced and full models overlapped in every figure. No linear-trend term, no spline, no quadratic term, and no formal test of linear versus categorical fit inside the survival model is reported. The reviewer should treat 'linear' here as a description of the fitted HR points, not as a likelihood-based model comparison.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x donor type (living vs deceased): The per-mismatch penalty is far steeper for living donors than for deceased donors, in a cohort where living donors nonetheless have better overall survival. At every mismatch category the living-donor HR exceeded the deceased-donor HR, and at 4 and 5 mismatches the 95% CIs excluded one another. (slope 0.32 (95% CI 0.14-0.50; p = 0.0055) for living vs 0.07 (95% CI 0.02-0.13; p = 0.0208) for deceased, i.e. more than a four-fold difference in the increment of risk per added mismatch) [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs'; Figure 2 and Figure 4; Discussion, 'Impact of HLA Mismatch in Children Mirrors That in Adults for Living Donor Organs']
- HLA mismatch x donor type, as a clinical trade-off: Grafts from deceased donors with 0-3 mismatches survived as long as grafts from living donors with 4-6 mismatches (living 4-6 not statistically different from the deceased 0-3 reference; unadjusted KM medians 11.9 vs 13.3 years with overlapping CIs). Against the tighter reference of deceased donors with 0-1 mismatch, living 4-6 was significantly worse. (living 4-6 vs deceased 0-1: HR 1.36 (95% CI 1.09-1.69; p = 0.0066), based on only 346 children in the reference group) [Results para 3 and Table 3; Discussion, 'A Well-matched Allograft From a Deceased Person...']
- recipient age (quartile at transplant) x graft survival: A strong monotone age gradient: adjusted HRs across quartiles were 1.00, 1.28, 1.55, 1.76, and unadjusted median survival fell from 18.8 years (Q1) to 14.6, 12.6 and 10.6 years. The authors report this as a linear effect and hypothesise loss of 'immunological malleability' with age. (hazard slope 0.26 per quartile (95% CI 0.21-0.31); median survival slope -2.69 years per quartile (95% CI -4.33 to -1.06; p = 0.0193); log-rank across quartiles 382.0, 3 df, p < 0.0001) [Results, 'Median Survival and HRs by Quartile of Age'; Figures 5 and 6; Table 5]
- locus x locus (within-mismatch-category comparison of the 27 [A,B,DRB1] permutations): Negative result. Among the 57 within-category comparisons of permutations carrying the same total mismatch count, none was significant after Holm-Bonferroni adjustment; the lowest observed p was 0.0033 for [0,2,1] vs [1,1,1] in category 3, against an adjusted threshold of 0.0009. The authors conclude the loci contribute equally and that DRB1 does not dominate, and note that the uniform linear rise in HR with total count is consistent with this. (0 of 57 within-category tests significant after correction; lowest p = 0.0033 vs required 0.0009) [Results, para on within-category tests; Discussion, 'Comparison of Reduced and Full Cox Models']
- HLA mismatch x adjustment set (reduced vs full model, i.e. confounding by induction and maintenance immunosuppression): Adding induction, immunosuppression at discharge, ethnicity, PRA, donor characteristics and disease attenuated the overall mismatch slope from 0.31 to 0.15, with slightly overlapping CIs; in the living-donor stratum the two slopes were identical (0.32), i.e. the living-donor HLA effect was not explained by the extra covariates. (all transplants: reduced slope 0.31 (95% CI 0.22-0.40) vs full 0.15 (95% CI 0.07-0.22); living donors: 0.32 in both models) [Discussion, 'Comparison of Reduced and Full Cox Models'; Results, 'Linearity of the HRs']
- presensitisation / PRA, cold ischaemia time, ethnicity x HLA mismatch: Not examined. Peak panel-reactive antibody and recipient ethnicity are listed as covariates in the full model but are never stratified on, and no sensitised-versus-unsensitised HLA effect is reported. Cold ischaemia time is not a modelled covariate at all - ischaemic injury appears only as a speculative mechanism in the Discussion for why living-donor mismatches might be more damaging. [Methods, 'Variable Definitions'; absence confirmed by search of the full text]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "For all 18 602 pediatric recipients, compared with children with 0 mismatch, there was a 30% higher risk of allograft failure for 1 mismatch and a 92% higher risk for 6 mismatches" (Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches on Pediatric Kidney Allograft Survival', para 1)
- *C2* — "Therefore, each additional unit of HLA mismatch had the same increasing effect on kidney graft survival, whereas the additional covariates in the full model did not significantly reduce the effects of HLA mismatch." (Results, 'Linearity of the HRs in Pediatric Allografts')
- *C14* — "Allografts from living donors exhibited higher risks of failure attributable to HLA mismatch: 48% for 1 mismatch and 2.14 times more than the reference, 0 mismatch, for 6 mismatches." (Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches on Pediatric Kidney Allograft Survival', para 2)
- *C14* — "Therefore, the effect of mismatching a living donor kidney is more than 4 times as great on kidney survival as for an organ from a deceased donor, when controlled for the covariates in the full models." (Results, 'Linearity of the HRs in Pediatric Allografts', final para)
- *C14* — "Kidney allografts from deceased donors HLA mismatched 0 to 3 were found to survive as long as organs from living donors HLA mismatched 4 to 6." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "there was a strong, linear effect on the hazard of allograft failure with quartile of age such that the youngest patients at age of transplant had the longest surviving grafts" (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Retrospective UNOS registry cohort spanning 1987-2016; era effects are enormous (era HR falls from 1.00 in 1987-1992 to 0.21 in 2013-2016) and are handled only by a categorical era term, so the reported mismatch effects are an average over three decades of changing immunosuppression rather than an estimate under a current regimen.; Antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 mismatch counts as recorded by UNOS; typing resolution is never stated, no allele-level or molecular (eplet / PIRCHE) analysis, and no HLA-C, -DQ or -DP data. The paper therefore cannot speak to C4, C7 or C8 at all.; Missing values of categorical covariates were filled by regression imputation, with no sensitivity analysis and no report of how much data was imputed.; The adjusted hazard ratios for mismatch levels 2, 3, 4 and 5 live in Table 2, and the 27 permutation HRs in Table 4; neither table body was returned by PMC, so only the endpoints of the dose-response ladder (1 and 6 mismatches) are quotable as adjusted HRs, and no confidence interval is printed anywhere in the text for any mismatch HR. The complete 0-6 ladder is available only as unadjusted KM median survival times.; Linearity is asserted from a second-stage weighted regression through fitted hazard ratios, not from a trend test, spline or model comparison within the Cox model; treating fitted HRs as data points understates uncertainty and ignores their correlation, so 'linear' should be read as descriptive.; The claim that no locus dominates rests on 57 within-category permutation comparisons that were all non-significant after Holm-Bonferroni correction. Absence of a significant difference in cells that can be small is weak evidence of equality, and the authors themselves say they are 'humbled and cautious' about contradicting the DR-primacy literature.; Despite the title, no interaction between recipient age and HLA mismatch is tested or reported; the two are independent main effects in one model.; The living-versus-deceased slope difference comes from stratified models and non-overlapping CIs, not from a tested interaction term, and living donors differ from deceased donors in many unmeasured ways (donor quality, relatedness, elective timing, absence of cold ischaemia).; Cold ischaemia time is not in the model, which matters because it is the authors' own proposed mechanism for the living-donor slope difference; the mechanism is therefore untested.; Peak PRA is adjusted for but never stratified on, so nothing is learned about sensitised recipients - the group most relevant to our antibody-unknown pre-screen.; The comparison of living 4-6 against deceased 0-1 mismatch rests on only 346 children in the reference stratum.; The censoring rule as written ('censored at the last recorded examination, at the start of renal replacement therapy, or at death') treats return to renal replacement therapy as a censoring rather than an event, which is internally inconsistent with an allograft-failure endpoint and is probably a wording error; the exact outcome definition should be regarded as uncertain.; Minor internal numerical inconsistencies: the age-quartile hazard slope is given as 0.26 with p = 0.0027 in the Results, p = 0.0020 in the Figure 6 legend, and 0.25 in the Discussion.; US paediatric population under a US allocation system with paediatric priority; absolute risks and the case mix do not transfer directly to an adult Iranian living-donor programme..

### Ashby VB 2017 — A Kidney Graft Survival Calculator that Accounts for Mismatches in Age, Sex, HLA, and Body Size

Ashby VB 2017, *Clin J Am Soc Nephrol*, [DOI 10.2215/CJN.09330916](https://doi.org/10.2215/CJN.09330916). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, Copyright (c) 2017 by the American Society of Nephrology; PMC deposit whose body text was NOT returned by the PMC full-text service (see notes).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 232,705 recipients of kidney-alone transplants in the United States, 1998-2012 (SRTR); analysed as three separate cohorts by donor type: living unrelated n=32,349, living related n=56,660, deceased n=143,696 |
| donor type | both |
| n | 232,705 (LUR 32,349; LR 56,660; deceased 143,696) |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; separate multivariable Cox proportional-hazards models fitted for each donor type; used to build a public graft-survival calculator for living donation / kidney paired donation |
| typing resolution | not stated. The paper never names the loci or the typing resolution; the category labels ('MM' 0-6 crossed with 'DR MM' 0-2) imply the standard SRTR antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch count, but this is inference, not text |
| outcome | all-cause graft failure - the event was 'the first of graft failure or death'; NOT death-censored (return to dialysis or death without graft failure both count) |
| follow up | transplants 1998-2012, censored at 31 December 2013 or loss to follow-up; the main covariate table reports adjusted risk of graft failure at 5 years, with separate 10-year adjusted probability tables by donor-recipient age group |
| other factors modelled | donor age and donor-recipient age combination, donor-recipient sex combination, recipient obesity (BMI >= 30), donor obesity (BMI >= 30), donor-recipient weight ratio, donor-recipient height ratio, transplant year, cause of ESRD, panel reactive antibody at transplant, previous transplant, years of ESRD, hepatitis C serology, insurance, recipient and donor race and ethnicity, donor history of cigarette use, ABO compatibility |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the single largest and most directly applicable model of HLA mismatch inside LIVING donation: it fits a separate Cox model for living unrelated donors, which is exactly the donor class an Iranian living-donor pre-screen must rank, and it was built for the purpose of choosing among several available living donors - the same decision our tool supports. It answers the review's ANGLE H question about how HLA is coded in a practical selection model: not as a continuous 0-6 count, but as a six-level categorical cross-classification of total ABDR mismatch with DR mismatch, sitting alongside donor age, sex, obesity and weight ratio in one index. That coding transfers well to a low-resolution, one-field setting, because every category it uses (total antigen mismatch count banded 0 / 1-2 / 3-4 / 5-6, plus DR mismatch 0 versus 1-2) is computable from serologic or one-field typing alone and needs no allele-level data, no eplet software and no imputation. It also gives the review its best living-donor answer on relative magnitude for C14: within living unrelated donation the whole HLA span from the best to the worst category is roughly a 31% relative risk difference, which is real but of the same order as the sex, obesity and weight-ratio terms in the same model, so HLA should be one weighted component of a pre-screen score rather than the sole ranking key. Two features limit the transfer: PRA is adjusted for but antibody status is never used as an effect modifier, so the paper says nothing about the sensitised, antibody-status-unknown candidate our pre-screen must handle conservatively; and the top mismatch category pools 5-6 mismatches with MISSING typing, which is precisely the ambiguity our system must resolve rather than absorb. The endpoint is all-cause graft failure including death, so part of the modest HLA gradient is diluted by mortality that HLA cannot plausibly affect, meaning these HRs are if anything a floor for the immunological effect.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft failure or death (all-cause graft failure): 0 HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING UNRELATED donors — HR 0.69 (0.42–1.12); adjusted for transplant year, ESRD cause, PRA at transplant, previous transplant, years of ESRD, hepatitis C serology, insurance, recipient and donor race/ethnicity, donor cigarette use, and donor-recipient age, sex, obesity, weight ratio, height ratio and ABO combinations [Results, Table 1 (adjusted risk of graft failure at 5 years), living unrelated donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING UNRELATED donors — HR 0.73 (0.59–0.91); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living unrelated donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 1-2 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING UNRELATED donors — HR 0.85 (0.7–1.02); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living unrelated donor column]
- graft failure or death: 3-4 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING UNRELATED donors — HR 0.91 (0.77–1.06); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living unrelated donor column]
- graft failure or death: 5, 6 or missing HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING UNRELATED donors — HR 1.06 (1.0–1.13); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living unrelated donor column]
- graft failure or death: 0 HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING RELATED donors — HR 0.62 (0.57–0.67); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living related donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING RELATED donors — HR 0.93 (0.88–1.0); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living related donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 1-2 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING RELATED donors — HR 0.95 (0.89–1.01); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living related donor column]
- graft failure or death: 3-4 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING RELATED donors — HR 0.99 (0.79–1.24); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living related donor column]
- graft failure or death: 5, 6 or missing HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - LIVING RELATED donors — HR 1.06 (0.99–1.14); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, living related donor column]
- graft failure or death: 0 HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - DECEASED donors — HR 0.83 (0.8–0.86); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, deceased donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - DECEASED donors — HR 0.87 (0.82–0.92); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, deceased donor column]
- graft failure or death: 1-2 HLA MM with 1-2 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - DECEASED donors — HR 0.95 (0.9–1.0); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, deceased donor column]
- graft failure or death: 3-4 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - DECEASED donors — HR 0.91 (0.87–0.95); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, deceased donor column]
- graft failure or death: 5, 6 or missing HLA MM vs 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM (reference) - DECEASED donors — HR 1.08 (1.06–1.11); adjusted for as above [Results, Table 1, deceased donor column]
- graft failure or death: NON-HLA COMPARATOR: 1-2 HLA MM with 0 DR MM vs the reference category, summarised across all three donor types — percentage risk reduction None; adjusted for as above [Results text: '7%-27% lower risk of graft failure ... across all donor types']
- graft failure or death: NON-HLA COMPARATOR: male donor to male recipient vs female donor to male recipient — percentage risk reduction None; adjusted for as above [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure or death: NON-HLA COMPARATOR: recipient obesity (BMI >= 30) / donor obesity — percentage risk increase None; adjusted for as above [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure or death: NON-HLA COMPARATOR: donor-recipient weight ratio <75% vs similar weight — percentage risk increase None; adjusted for as above [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: None; 1-2 MM: None; 1-2 MM: None; 3-4 MM: None; 3-4 MM: None; 5-6 or unknown MM: None
- DR: note MM: No per-locus A / B / DR breakdown is given, but DR is separated from the rest by the cross-classification, so a DR-specific contrast can be read WITHIN each total-count stratum, holding the banded total count fixed.; within_1_2_MM_stratum_0_DR_vs_1_2_DR MM: living unrelated 0.73 vs 0.85; living related 0.93 vs 0.95; deceased 0.87 vs 0.95 (0 DR MM better in all three donor types); within_3_4_MM_stratum_0_DR_vs_1_2_DR MM: living unrelated 0.91 vs 1.00 (ref); living related 0.99 vs 1.00 (ref); deceased 0.91 vs 1.00 (ref)
- A: not reported separately
- B: not reported separately
- C: not mentioned anywhere in the paper
- DQ: not mentioned anywhere in the paper
- DP: not mentioned anywhere in the paper
- Shape reported: step / monotone gradient across the six categories: zero mismatch lowest risk, 5-6-or-unknown highest risk, with most of the separation between the zero-mismatch category and everything else, and only a shallow gradient in between. The authors do not label a functional shape.; linearity tested: not tested. Mismatch is a six-level categorical cross-classification; no continuous count term, no test for trend, no spline, no threshold test and no formal comparison of a categorical against a linear coding is reported.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x donor type (living unrelated / living related / deceased): Effect modification is handled by full stratification rather than by an interaction term: three entirely separate Cox models are fitted, one per donor type, so every HLA coefficient is donor-type specific. The zero-mismatch benefit is largest in living related donation (HR 0.62) and smallest in deceased donation (HR 0.83), while the penalty for 5-6/unknown mismatch is similar across all three (1.06, 1.06, 1.08). (0 MM: LUR 0.69, LR 0.62, deceased 0.83; 5-6/missing MM: LUR 1.06, LR 1.06, deceased 1.08) [Results, Table 1 (three donor-type columns)]
- donor age x donor type: The dependence of graft failure on increasing donor age was weaker for living-donor than for deceased-donor transplants - the paper's headline effect-modification result, and the reason separate models per donor type were needed. (stated qualitatively in the abstract; the numeric age gradients are in the donor-recipient age tables, not summarised as a single interaction statistic) [Abstract, Results]
- donor sex x recipient sex: Sex mismatch is modelled as a donor-recipient combination rather than as two main effects; male-to-male has the lowest graft failure and is better than female-to-male. (5%-13% lower risk (male-to-male vs female-to-male), range across donor types) [Abstract, Results]
- HLA mismatch x sensitisation (PRA), x recipient age, x race/ethnicity: NOT TESTED. PRA, recipient age and race/ethnicity are adjustment covariates only; no interaction or subgroup analysis with HLA mismatch is reported. [Methods covariate list; absence confirmed across the Results and Discussion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C14* — "HLA mismatch was important in all donor types." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "The dependence of graft failure on increasing donor age was less pronounced for living-donor than for deceased-donor transplants." (Abstract, Results)
- *C14* — "Obesity of both the recipient (8%-18% higher risk) and donor (5%-11% higher risk) was associated with higher graft loss" (Abstract, Results)

_3 quote(s) could not be verified verbatim and are withheld._

**Limitations.** The endpoint is all-cause graft failure - 'the first of graft failure or death' - so deaths with a functioning graft are counted as events. This dilutes the HLA gradient, because HLA mismatch plausibly acts on immunological graft loss and not on most causes of death; the HRs here are a floor for the immunological effect, not an estimate of it.; HLA mismatch is banded into only six categories. 1 is pooled with 2, 3 with 4, 5 with 6, and DR is reduced to 0 versus 1-2, so the paper cannot answer C9 (the size of the first mismatch versus the second) and cannot distinguish a 5- from a 6-mismatch pair.; MISSING/unknown HLA typing is pooled into the same category as 5-6 mismatches. Untyped pairs are therefore assumed to behave like the worst-matched pairs, which both contaminates that HR and makes it unusable as a prior for an unknown-typing candidate.; The reference category is 3-4 MM with 1-2 DR MM, an interior category, not zero mismatch. Every HR must be re-based before it can be compared with the zero-mismatch-referenced HRs that most of the review's other papers report.; The loci and the typing resolution are never stated. The A/B/DR antigen-level reading is an inference from the 0-6 'MM' plus 'DR MM' structure, not something the paper says.; HLA-C, -DQ and -DP are absent from the paper entirely, so it contributes nothing to C4, C7 or C8.; No test of linearity, trend, threshold or non-linearity, and no formal interaction test involving HLA. Donor-type modification is only implicit in fitting three separate models.; PRA is an adjustment covariate; donor-specific antibody is not measured, and no analysis is stratified by sensitisation. The paper cannot speak to the sensitised or antibody-unknown candidate.; US SRTR registry, 1998-2012 transplants, with immunosuppression, allocation and typing practice of that era; residual confounding by unmeasured centre and practice factors is unaddressed.; The zero-mismatch estimate for living unrelated donors rests on <1% of that cohort and its confidence interval crosses 1 (0.42-1.12), so the most decision-relevant cell for an unrelated living-donor pre-screen is the least precisely estimated one in the paper.; The calculator is a prediction tool fitted and reported on the same data; no external validation or discrimination statistic (C-index) for the HLA term is reported in the retrieved text..

### Kamoun M 2017 — HLA Amino Acid Polymorphisms and Kidney Allograft Survival

Kamoun M 2017, *Transplantation*, [PMID 28221244](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28221244/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown — retrieved from PMC (PMC5642346), Wolters Kluwer / Transplantation; no licence statement present in the retrieved text. Supplemental digital content (tables S1-S2, supplementary figures) was NOT retrieved..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All kidney-alone transplants in the United States, SRTR Standard Analysis Files, 1 January 1987 - 31 December 2009; graft function assessed through 30 June 2012. Racially/ethnically diverse (African American, Caucasian, Hispanic, Asian broad US racial groups used for the imputation reference). |
| donor type | both |
| n | 240,024 total (156,049 deceased donor; 60,117 living related; 23,858 living unrelated) |
| design | Retrospective national registry cohort; Cox proportional-hazards regression of time to graft failure. Two parallel analytic strategies: (1) an 'expected AA MM' variable X = 0*P(0MM) + 1*P(1MM) + 2*P(2MM) per site, screened one site at a time over 125 AA sites with Bonferroni-style correction, then a multivariable model of the significant sites; (2) 10 randomly imputed allele data sets analysed separately and combined with SAS MIANALYZE (within- + between-imputation variance). Continuous AA MM sum modelled with linear slope plus splines at 5, 10 and 15 mismatches. Forward-stepwise Cox models (threshold P=0.05) run separately for deceased and living donors, with demographics, comorbidity and HLA antigen MM variables forced into the model. SAS 9.3. |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen level (2-digit) as recorded in SRTR; HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 alleles (two-field / classically 4-digit) and their amino-acid polymorphisms were IMPUTED, not typed — using a validated haplotype-frequency method for broad US racial groups (the NMDP Haplostats approach), with allele-to-amino-acid conversion from IMGT/HLA release 2.28.0 (January 2010). No high-resolution typing was performed on any subject. |
| outcome | all-cause graft failure (GF), explicitly including recipient death as an event; modelled overall, in the first post-transplant year, and conditional on 1-year graft survival |
| follow up | transplants 1987-2009 with graft status ascertained to 30 June 2012 (up to ~25 years; median not stated in the retrieved text) |
| other factors modelled | recipient and donor demographic and comorbidity factors carried over from the SRTR 2010 Program Specific Report (PSR) risk models, HLA antigen (2-digit) mismatch variables: 0 A,B,DRB1 MM; 0 A MM; 1 A MM; 0 B MM; 1 B MM; 0 DRB1 MM; 1 DRB1 MM (2 MM = reference for each locus), donor type (deceased / living related / living unrelated), donor race and recipient race, recipient panel-reactive antibody level (<10% vs >10%), calendar year of transplant, the other significant AA MM variables at each HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 locus |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest test of the review's molecular-mismatch question (C12) in kidney transplantation, and it is the only one that asks it in exactly the situation KidneyMatch faces: the underlying typing is one-field/antigen level, and allele and amino-acid resolution are obtained by population-genetics imputation rather than by sequencing. Its answer is positive but narrow — imputed HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch carries a real incremental hazard on top of antigen mismatch (HR 1.30 per 15 DRB1 AA MM in the first year), and the relationship is linear in the log hazard with no threshold, which is direct evidence on the shape question (C2) at the molecular level. It also confirms the locus ordering the review needs (C3): DRB1 amino-acid mismatch was more strongly associated with graft failure than HLA-A or HLA-B amino-acid mismatch. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen is limited in three specific ways. First and most important, the Iranian programme is dominated by living UNRELATED donation, and this is precisely the stratum where the paper found nothing: in living unrelated transplants no initial slope or spline factor reached significance, and even in living related donors the DRB1 slope was only borderline (P = 0.06 and P = 0.07 in the two analyses) versus P < 0.0001 in deceased donors. Second, the imputation depends on haplotype-frequency reference panels for African American, Caucasian, Hispanic and Asian US populations; no Iranian reference panel exists in this work, and Iranian HLA haplotype frequencies differ enough that imputation accuracy cannot be assumed to carry over — so the method is a template, not a transferable model. Third, the incremental value is favourable for an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen (the DRB1 effect was consistent across PRA <10% and >10% strata, so it is not confined to sensitised recipients), but it is small relative to the antigen-count signal the pre-screen can already compute from one-field typing, which argues for ranking on antigen mismatch first and treating any amino-acid layer as a tie-breaker rather than a primary criterion.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft failure (incl. death): continuous imputed HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch, per 15 DRB1 AA MM, first 12 months post-transplant (all transplants combined) — HR 1.3, p=<0.0001; adjusted for patient risk factors, donor risk factors, and HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 ANTIGEN (2-digit) mismatches [Abstract (Results); Results, 'The Association of HLA AA MMs with GF by Posttransplantation Interval'; Discussion para 1; Figure 2]
- all-cause graft failure: continuous imputed HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch, per 15 DRB1 AA MM, AFTER the first post-transplant year — HR 1.1, p=<0.0001; adjusted for patient risk factors, donor risk factors, HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 antigen mismatches [Results, 'The Association of HLA AA MMs with GF by Posttransplantation Interval']
