- all-cause graft failure: estimated HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch, per 10 DRB1 AA MM, deceased donor transplants — first analysis (expected-AA-MM variable) — HR 1.15; adjusted for comorbidity factors, donor/recipient characteristics, HLA antigen MM variables [Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 2]
- all-cause graft failure: imputed HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch, per 10 DRB1 AA MM, deceased donor transplants — second analysis (10 imputations combined) — HR 1.1, p=0.04 (linear slope term); adjusted for comorbidity factors, donor/recipient characteristics, HLA antigen MM variables; combined across 10 imputations via SAS MIANALYZE [Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 2]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch at position 10, per site, deceased donor transplants (stepwise model, 10 imputations) — HR 1.04 (1.03–1.06), p=<0.0001; adjusted for recipient factors, donor factors, HLA antigen MMs, and the other significant AA MM variables per locus [Results, 'Joint Risk of GF Associated With HLA AA MMs at Multiple Sites'; Table 3]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch at position 74 (pocket 4), per site, deceased donor transplants (stepwise model) — HR 1.03 (1.01–1.05), p=0.003; adjusted for recipient factors, donor factors, HLA antigen MMs, other significant AA MM variables per locus [Results, 'Joint Risk of GF Associated With HLA AA MMs at Multiple Sites'; Table 3]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch at position 28 (pocket 7), per site, deceased donor transplants (stepwise model) — HR 1.02 (1.0–1.04), p=0.021; adjusted for recipient factors, donor factors, HLA antigen MMs, other significant AA MM variables per locus [Results, 'Joint Risk of GF Associated With HLA AA MMs at Multiple Sites'; Table 3. CI printed as '1-1.04'.]
- all-cause graft failure: HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch at position 13 (pockets 4 and 6), per site, LIVING donor transplants (stepwise model) — HR 1.06 (1.02–1.1), p=0.002; adjusted for recipient factors, donor factors, HLA antigen MMs, other significant AA MM variables per locus [Results, 'Joint Risk of GF Associated With HLA AA MMs at Multiple Sites'; Table 3. CI printed as '1.02-1.1'.]
- all-cause graft failure: 1 HLA-DRB1 ANTIGEN mismatch (benchmark quoted by the authors from the prior literature, NOT estimated in this study) — RR 1.15; adjusted for not stated — cited from a reference for comparison with the AA-mismatch effect size [Discussion, para 1 ('compared to 1.15 and 1.26 relative risk of GF with 1 or 2 DRB1 MMs'). CITED, not this paper's own estimate.]
- all-cause graft failure: 2 HLA-DRB1 ANTIGEN mismatches (benchmark quoted by the authors from the prior literature, NOT estimated in this study) — RR 1.26; adjusted for not stated — cited from a reference [Discussion, para 1. CITED, not this paper's own estimate.]

**Dose-response.**

- DRB1: Deceased donor: significant positive linear slope, P < 0.0001 (first analysis) and P = 0.04 (second, 10-imputation analysis); HR 1.15 per 10 AA MM (analysis 1) and 1.10 per 10 AA MM (analysis 2); HR 1.30 per 15 AA MM in year 1 and 1.10 per 15 AA MM thereafter. Living RELATED donor: initial slope borderline, P = 0.06 (analysis 1) and P = 0.07 (analysis 2). Living UNRELATED donor: no initial slope or spline factor reached significance (data not shown).
- A: Weaker than DRB1; no significant slope or spline reported in the summed-mismatch model in the retrieved text. Discussion states the imputed DRB1 AA MMs had a stronger association with GF than HLA-A and HLA-B AA MMs, referring to supplementary material for the estimates.
- B: Same as HLA-A — weaker than DRB1, no significant slope or spline reported in the retrieved text.
- C: not studied
- DQ: not studied (named as unresolved confounding and as the target of future work)
- DP: not studied
- Shape reported: linear (in the log hazard) with no threshold — splines placed at 5, 10 and 15 AA MMs did not produce a significant change in slope, so risk increases across the whole observed range of DRB1 AA mismatch; linearity tested: Yes, explicitly, and this is the paper's main shape result. A linear slope term was fitted from 0 AA MM (reference) together with restricted spline factors at 5, 10 and 15 AA MMs in a single model; a significant linear term with non-significant spline terms was read as linearity. Quote: the initial slope of HLA-DRB1 'indicates increasing risk through the entire range of AA MM with no significant change in the curve at 5 MMs'. Knot placement at 5/10/15 was chosen 'primarily due to the distribution of the number of AA MMs', i.e. data-driven rather than pre-specified biologically. The linearity claim holds for deceased donors; it is unproven for living related donors (borderline slope) and absent for living unrelated donors.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA amino-acid mismatch x donor type (deceased vs living): The effect of AA mismatch differs by donor type; the DRB1 slope is strongly significant in deceased donors, borderline in living related donors and null in living unrelated donors. (Interaction highly significant in all 10 imputations (no numeric estimate printed in text; HRs and 95% CIs referred to supplementary material). Component slopes: deceased P < 0.0001; living related P = 0.06 (analysis 1) and P = 0.07 (analysis 2); living unrelated — no slope or spline significant.) [Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', paras 1-2; Figure 1 legend]
- HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch x time since transplant: The association is markedly stronger in the first post-transplant year than afterwards — a time-varying effect, consistent with the known early dominance of DR antigen matching. (HR 1.30 per 15 DRB1 AA MM in year 1 (P < 0.0001) vs HR 1.10 per 15 DRB1 AA MM after year 1 (P < 0.0001)) [Results, 'The Association of HLA AA MMs with GF by Posttransplantation Interval'; Figure 2; Discussion para 1]
- HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch x recipient panel-reactive antibody level (<10% vs >10%): No effect modification reported — the DRB1 AA mismatch association was consistently present in both PRA strata, i.e. it is not confined to sensitised recipients. (Reported as qualitative consistency across groupings; no interaction p-value or stratum-specific estimate printed in the retrieved text.) [Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 1]
- HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch x donor race and x recipient race: Consistent direction and magnitude across donor race and recipient race groupings, with exceptions only in small categories (example given: transplants limited to deceased Asian donors with Asian recipients). (Qualitative; stratum estimates referred to supplementary material.) [Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 1]
- HLA-DRB1 amino-acid mismatch x calendar year of transplant (era / typing-technology proxy): The association is 'reasonably consistent (ie, positive and of similar magnitude)' within each transplant year once molecular typing had been introduced, arguing that changes in demographics or HLA typing methods over time did not drive the result. (Qualitative; no numbers printed.) [Results, 'The Association of HLA AA MMs with GF by Posttransplantation Interval', para 2]
- Amino-acid mismatch site x amino-acid mismatch site (linkage disequilibrium, non-additivity): Interactions between individual AA mismatch sites could NOT be evaluated because of strong linkage disequilibrium among polymorphic residues in the binding groove; highly correlated sites were collapsed rather than modelled jointly. The authors state only that the influence of AA MMs across the three loci 'may be additive as previously reported'. (Pearson r among DRB1 sites, e.g. position 11 with 13 r = 0.85, 57 with 60 r = 0.86, 28 with 30 r = 0.75, 9 with 11 r = 0.62, 74 with 73 r = 0.63.) [Results, Figure 3 legend / correlation listing; Discussion para 2 and 'computational approach' paragraph]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "A statistically significant linear relationship between the estimated number of AA MMs and risk of GF was observed for HLA-DRB1 in deceased donor and living donor transplants." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "indicates increasing risk through the entire range of AA MM with no significant change in the curve at 5 MMs" (Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 1 (initial slope of HLA-DRB1, deceased donors))
- *C12* — "with any given HLA antigen MM, there is significant variability in the degree of AA MMs at peptide-binding sites including pockets in the binding groove" (Results, 'Distribution of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 Counts...', para 1)
- *C12* — "The multiple imputation of HLA alleles we applied in this study is a well-accepted tool to use when high-resolution HLA typing is not feasible due to the high cost" (Discussion, imputation paragraph)
- *C14* — "For living unrelated donor transplants, none of the initial slopes or spline factors reached significance (data not shown)." (Results, 'The Association of HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 AA MMs With GF', para 1)
- *C3* — "the imputed HLA-DRB1 AA MMs had a stronger association with GF than that of HLA-A and HLA-B on AA MMs" (Discussion, para 1)

**Limitations.** Alleles and amino acids were never typed — they were IMPUTED from 2-digit antigen specificity using US broad-racial-group haplotype frequencies. The authors concede uncertainty at several DRB1 sites (positions 57, 71, 74 and 86 named), which inflates the standard error at exactly the pocket positions they highlight; they argue this biases towards the null rather than towards false positives, but that argument is asserted, not demonstrated.; Circularity risk: because the bulk of AA mismatch is a mechanical consequence of antigen mismatch, and antigen mismatch is also the adjustment covariate, the 'incremental' AA effect rests entirely on the residual allele-level variation within an antigen category — variation that the authors themselves say is limited to 1 to 3 additional sites.; Effect size is small and of uncertain clinical value: HR 1.10-1.15 per 10 DRB1 AA MM overall, and per-site HRs of 1.02-1.06. The authors compare it to a cited antigen-level RR of 1.15/1.26 for 1/2 DRB1 mismatches, which is a comparison across studies, not a within-model contrast.; The living-donor evidence is weak and the living-UNRELATED evidence is null: no slope or spline reached significance in living unrelated transplants; the living related slope was only P = 0.06 / P = 0.07. Only one site (DRB1 position 13) survived stepwise selection in living donors.; Only HLA-A, -B and -DRB1 were modelled. HLA-C, -DQA1, -DQB1 and -DP were absent; the authors acknowledge that DQA1/DQB1 mismatch in linkage with DRB1 could partially explain the observed DRB1 AA effect.; The outcome is all-cause graft failure INCLUDING death with a functioning graft, not death-censored graft failure, which dilutes an immunological signal with mortality unrelated to HLA.; Very long and heterogeneous era (transplants 1987-2009, follow-up to 2012) spanning several immunosuppression generations and a change from serological to molecular typing; era is addressed only by a qualitative consistency check across calendar years.; Zero HLA-A, -B, -DRB1 antigen-mismatched transplants were excluded from the dose-response analyses, so the paper says nothing about the zero-mismatch premium and the curve does not start from a true fully-matched reference.; Model building was stepwise with forward selection at P = 0.05 over 125 candidate AA sites; despite the Bonferroni-style correction on the screening step, the reported per-site HRs are post-selection estimates and are likely optimistic.; Spline knots at 5, 10 and 15 were chosen from the observed distribution of mismatch counts, not pre-specified, which weakens the linearity claim as a formal test of shape.; Many of the key quantities — antigen-mismatch coefficients, HLA-A and -B AA results, stratum-specific HRs and CIs, the donor-type interaction estimate — live in supplementary digital content that was not retrieved; the text repeatedly defers to it.; US registry population with US racial-group reference panels; no Middle Eastern or Iranian population is represented, so imputation accuracy in an Iranian cohort is unknown..

### Shi X 2017 — Effect of human leukocyte antigen mismatching on the outcomes of pediatric kidney transplantation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

Shi X 2017, *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, [DOI 10.1093/ndt/gfx259](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/gfx259). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Oxford University Press on behalf of ERA-EDTA); no PMC record returned by convert_article_ids, so no open full text. Quotes are from the PubMed abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Pediatric kidney transplant recipients pooled from 18 cohort studies, 26 018 recipients in total; databases searched from inception to 31 December 2016 |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract (cohort studies of pediatric kidney transplantation; deceased/living split not reported in the retrieved text) |
| n | 26 018 pediatric recipients across 18 studies |
| design | systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of cohort studies; pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% CI |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; the mismatch counts (HLA-DR 0-1 vs 2; HLA-A + B 0-1/0-2 vs 2-4/3-4) are antigen-level counts, consistent with serologic/one-field typing in the source cohorts |
| outcome | graft failure (primary, reported at 1, 3, 5 and 10 years); rejection; all-cause mortality |
| follow up | pooled at fixed horizons of 1, 3, 5 and 10 years post-transplant |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the few quantitative syntheses that isolates a single locus, HLA-DR, from the rest of the mismatch burden and reports its effect at four separate time horizons, which is exactly the per-locus weighting question the review must answer (C3). Its DR effect is stable and significant at 1, 3, 5 and 10 years, so DR-driven risk in children is not a purely early-rejection phenomenon that modern immunosuppression abolishes. The class I result is reported only as a combined HLA-A + B count, so the paper can say that class I burden matters at 5 years but it cannot rank B above A, and it therefore does not settle C5. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown pre-screen is partial but real in one specific way: the pooled cohorts use antigen-level mismatch counts, which is the same low-resolution currency our pre-screen will have, so the estimates are directly expressible in the units we can actually compute from a scanned lab report. Transfer is weakened by population: pediatric recipients differ from Iranian adult living-donor recipients in immune reactivity, in graft-loss mechanisms (adolescent non-adherence is a large competing cause of late failure that no HLA term captures), and in donor structure, since much pediatric transplantation is parental one-haplotype living donation that compresses the achievable mismatch range. The estimates are also pooled unadjusted or study-reported RRs rather than a single multivariable model, so they carry the confounding of the source cohorts and should inform the direction and rough order of magnitude of a DR weight in our ranking, not its exact coefficient.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft failure at 1 year: 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0-1 HLA-DR mismatch — RR 1.41 (1.11–1.8); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure at 3 years: 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0-1 HLA-DR mismatch — RR 1.28 (1.08–1.52); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure at 5 years: 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0-1 HLA-DR mismatch — RR 1.21 (1.04–1.41); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure at 10 years: 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0-1 HLA-DR mismatch — RR 1.3 (1.02–1.67); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure at 5 years: 2-4 HLA-A + B mismatches vs 0-1 HLA-A + B mismatch — RR 3.17 (1.2–8.36); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results]
- graft failure at 5 years: 3-4 HLA-A + B mismatches vs 0-2 HLA-A + B mismatches — RR 1.49 (0.79–2.8); adjusted for pooled study-reported risk ratios in a random-effects model; adjustment set not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results (non-significant)]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0-1 MM: reference (0 and 1 mismatch POOLED as the reference category); 2 MM: graft failure RR 1.41 (1.11-1.80) at 1 y; 1.28 (1.08-1.52) at 3 y; 1.21 (1.04-1.41) at 5 y; 1.30 (1.02-1.67) at 10 y
- A+B (combined, not separable): 0-1 MM: reference for the first contrast; 2-4 MM: graft failure at 5 y RR 3.17 (1.20-8.36); 0-2 MM: reference for the second contrast; 3-4 MM: graft failure at 5 y RR 1.49 (0.79-2.80), non-significant
- A alone: not reported separately
- B alone: not reported separately
- C: not reported
- DQ: not reported
- DP: not reported
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. No 0/1/2 per-locus series and no total-mismatch-count series is reported in the retrieved text; every result is a dichotomised contrast between two pooled mismatch bands, so no trend, spline or threshold test is available.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "Compared with 0-1 HLA-DR mismatch, 2 mismatches significantly increased the risk of graft failure at 1 year (RR: 1.41, 95% CI: 1.11-1.80), 3 years (RR: 1.28, 95% CI: 1.08-1.52)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "5 years (RR: 1.21, 95% CI: 1.04-1.41) and 10 years (RR: 1.30, 95% CI: 1.02-1.67)" (Abstract, Results (continuation of the HLA-DR 2 vs 0-1 series))
- *C9* — "For HLA-A + B, the 5-year graft failure risk was higher for 2-4 mismatches compared with 0-1 mismatch (RR: 3.17, 95% CI: 1.20-8.36), but not for 3-4 compared with 0-2 mismatches (RR: 1.49, 95% CI: 0.79-2.80)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "Based on pooled analysis, HLA-DR and HLA-A + B are important factors affecting post-transplant outcomes, especially graft failure, in pediatric recipients." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C9* — "Eighteen studies comprising a total of 26 018 pediatric recipients were included in the evaluation." (Abstract, Results (first sentence))

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC full text exists for this article, so the forest plots, the per-study weights, the heterogeneity statistics (I-squared), the publication-bias assessment, the rejection and mortality results and any subgroup or sensitivity analyses could not be read. Everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; Pediatric recipients only. The review population is children and adolescents, not the adult living-donor recipients of the Iranian pre-screen. Late graft loss in adolescents is heavily driven by non-adherence, a competing cause that no HLA term captures and that inflates or dilutes late RRs unpredictably.; The reference category pools 0 and 1 DR mismatch. The design therefore cannot separate a zero-mismatch premium from the first-mismatch effect, which is the exact quantity C9 asks for at the DR locus.; HLA-A and HLA-B are analysed only as a combined A + B count. The paper cannot rank B against A and so does not test C5.; The two class I contrasts use different, overlapping bands (2-4 vs 0-1, and 3-4 vs 0-2) rather than a common reference, so the apparent drop from RR 3.17 to RR 1.49 is not a dose-response gradient and must not be read as one.; The RR 3.17 (1.20-8.36) estimate has a very wide confidence interval, indicating few contributing studies or few events; its point estimate is fragile.; Pooled effect estimates are study-reported risk ratios combined in random-effects models. The abstract does not state what the source cohorts adjusted for, so residual confounding by donor type, donor age, cold ischaemia, era, immunosuppression and sensitisation is unquantified.; No DQ, DP or HLA-C result. No molecular/eplet analysis. No antibody or DSA data. Typing resolution of the source cohorts is not stated.; Cohort studies only; searches ended 31 December 2016, so the evidence base predates current induction and maintenance regimens and any recent allocation changes.; No interaction or effect-modification result is reported in the retrieved text, so C11 cannot be addressed from this paper..

### Wiebe C 2017 — Class II Eplet Mismatch Modulates Tacrolimus Trough Levels Required to Prevent Donor-Specific Antibody Development

Wiebe C 2017, *Journal of the American Society of Nephrology (JASN) 28(11):3353-3362*, [PMID 28729289](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28729289/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, PMC deposit: 'Copyright (c) 2017 by the American Society of Nephrology'. Not Creative Commons. See notes: the PMC full-text API returned an EMPTY body for PMC5661295; text was retrieved from the PMC web rendering and every numeric claim re-verified on a second independent read..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 654 consecutive adult and paediatric renal transplants at a single centre (Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada) between January 1999 and January 2015; 596 recipients analysed (adult n=541, paediatric n=55). 50,011 serial tacrolimus trough levels. |
| donor type | both |
| n | 596 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; Cox proportional-hazards models for dnDSA-free survival and graft failure (eplet mismatch entered continuously, per ten mismatches); multivariable logistic regression for dnDSA with eplet mismatch and minimum tacrolimus trough level; ROC analysis to derive an eplet mismatch threshold |
| typing resolution | two-field / high resolution for class II. 'High-resolution class II HLA typing (HLA-DRb1/3/4/5 and HLA-DQa1/b1) was performed using sequence-specific oligonucleotide probes or sequence-specific primer technology.' Eplets computed with HLAMatchmaker (HLA DRDQDP Matching, version 2.0). Class I typing resolution not stated in the retrieved text; class I loci are not part of the exposure. |
| outcome | primary: de novo HLA-DR and/or HLA-DQ donor-specific antibody (dnDSA) development; secondary: death-censored/all-cause graft failure (the retrieved text says 'graft failure' without specifying censoring) |
| follow up | median 87 months (range 18-210) |
| other factors modelled | calcineurin inhibitor type (tacrolimus vs cyclosporin), tacrolimus trough level (mean, minimum, coefficient of variation, proportion below thresholds), nonadherence, recipient age, era / transplant year (cohort 1999-2015), adult vs paediatric recipient |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the pivotal paper for claim C12 (molecular mismatch thresholds) and claim C11 (effect modification by immunosuppression), because it is the study that showed HLA class II mismatch load and drug exposure are two independent, interacting determinants of the same outcome. It answers the review question 'is HLA mismatch a fixed risk or a modifiable one?' with: modifiable - a recipient with more than 11 DR or DQ eplet mismatches who is allowed to sit below a 5 ng/ml tacrolimus trough develops dnDSA, whereas a recipient at or below 11 eplet mismatches tolerated the same low exposure without dnDSA. For a KidneyMatch pre-screen this cuts two ways. It supports ranking on class II (DR/DQ) mismatch load, because that load predicts the immunological event that precedes graft loss, and it justifies flagging high-mismatch pairs for closer post-transplant monitoring rather than exclusion. But the exposure here is an eplet count computed from two-field DRB1/3/4/5 and DQA1/B1 typing, which a one-field Iranian pre-screen cannot compute and must not impute; the >11 threshold is therefore NOT transferable to a low-resolution antigen count, and the review must not present it as one. The cohort is mixed living and deceased donor (41-50% living), so the living-donor setting is represented but not isolated. Finally, the cohort had pretransplant DSA characterised by definition (dnDSA required absence pretransplant), which is exactly the antibody information a pre-screen in Iran will not have; this paper therefore describes the ceiling of what good typing plus good antibody surveillance achieves, not what an antibody-unknown pre-screen achieves.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA-DR dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DR eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches (continuous) — HR 2.5 (1.7–3.71), p=<0.001; adjusted for reported as a significant predictor; univariable/model adjustment not specified in the retrieved sentence [Results]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA-free survival: HLA-DQ eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches (continuous) — HR 2.0 (1.54–2.61), p=<0.001; adjusted for reported as a significant correlation; model adjustment not specified in the retrieved sentence [Results]
- graft failure: HLA-DR eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches (continuous) — HR 1.35 (1.01–1.81), p=0.05; adjusted for not specified in the retrieved sentence [Results]
- graft failure: HLA-DQ eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches (continuous) — HR 1.29 (1.01–1.67), p=0.05; adjusted for not specified in the retrieved sentence [Results]
- class II (HLA-DR/DQ) dnDSA development: HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 + HLA-DQA1/B1 eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches — HR 1.37 (1.18–1.58), p=<0.001; adjusted for recipient age, nonadherence, cyclosporin vs tacrolimus (multivariate model) [Results, Table 2]
- class II (HLA-DR/DQ) dnDSA development: cyclosporin versus tacrolimus regimen — HR 2.28 (1.35–3.78), p=0.002; adjusted for recipient age, nonadherence, HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (multivariate model) [Results, Table 2]
- class II (HLA-DR/DQ) dnDSA development: nonadherence versus adherence — HR 3.09 (1.83–5.15), p=<0.001; adjusted for recipient age, cyclosporin vs tacrolimus, HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (multivariate model) [Results, Table 2]
- class II (HLA-DR/DQ) dnDSA development: recipient age (per year; younger age is the risk direction) — HR 0.97 (0.96–0.99), p=0.001; adjusted for nonadherence, cyclosporin vs tacrolimus, HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (multivariate model) [Results, Table 2]
- dnDSA development: HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (in the logistic model that also contains the minimum tacrolimus trough level) — OR 1.31 (1.1–1.56), p=0.002; adjusted for minimum recorded tacrolimus trough level; unit of the eplet term not restated in this sentence [Results]
- dnDSA development: minimum recorded tacrolimus trough level, per 1 ng/ml higher — OR 0.71 (0.57–0.88), p=0.001; adjusted for HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch [Results]
- dnDSA incidence rate: cyclosporin regimen versus tacrolimus regimen — incidence rate (per 1000 patients per year) and fold-difference 32 versus 12 per 1000 patients per year (2.7-fold higher on cyclosporin); adjusted for unadjusted incidence [Results / Abstract]
- HLA-DR or -DQ dnDSA: whole cohort event count — percentage 66 recipients (11%) of 596 developed HLA-DR or -DQ dnDSA; 57 recipients suffered allograft loss; adjusted for not applicable [Results]
- dnDSA development: tacrolimus trough-level coefficient of variation, dnDSA vs no dnDSA — mean +/- SD comparison 39.6 +/- 13.5 versus 33.7 +/- 13.3, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Results]
- dnDSA development: lowest recorded tacrolimus trough level (ng/ml), dnDSA vs no dnDSA — mean +/- SD comparison 2.76 +/- 1.71 versus 3.42 +/- 1.45, p=0.01; adjusted for unadjusted [Results]
- HLA-DR dnDSA development (discrimination of an eplet threshold): >11 HLA-DR eplet mismatches versus 11 or fewer — AUC / sensitivity / specificity AUC=0.73, sensitivity=0.90, specificity=0.53; adjusted for not applicable (ROC) [Results]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA development (discrimination of an eplet threshold): >11 HLA-DQ eplet mismatches versus 11 or fewer — AUC / sensitivity / specificity AUC=0.72, sensitivity=0.94, specificity=0.45; adjusted for not applicable (ROC) [Results]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: exposure MM: HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 eplet mismatch count (HLAMatchmaker v2.0), modelled continuously per ten mismatches; dnDSA MM: HR 2.50 per ten mismatches (95% CI 1.70-3.71; P<0.001); graft_failure MM: HR 1.35 per ten mismatches (95% CI 1.01-1.81; P=0.05); threshold MM: >11 eplet mismatches (AUC=0.73, sensitivity=0.90, specificity=0.53)
- DQ: exposure MM: HLA-DQA1/B1 eplet mismatch count (HLAMatchmaker v2.0), modelled continuously per ten mismatches; dnDSA MM: HR 2.00 per ten mismatches (95% CI 1.54-2.61; P<0.001); graft_failure MM: HR 1.29 per ten mismatches (95% CI 1.01-1.67; P=0.05); threshold MM: >11 eplet mismatches (AUC=0.72, sensitivity=0.94, specificity=0.45)
- DR_plus_DQ_combined: exposure MM: HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 + HLA-DQA1/B1 eplet mismatch, per ten mismatches; dnDSA MM: HR 1.37 per ten mismatches (95% CI 1.18-1.58; P<0.001), multivariate (Table 2)
- Shape reported: Not a classical antigen-mismatch dose-response. The exposure is a continuous eplet mismatch COUNT entered linearly on the log-hazard scale and reported per ten mismatches, i.e. log-linearity is assumed by the model rather than demonstrated. A dichotomous risk threshold at >11 DR or DQ eplet mismatches was derived by ROC and then used to define 'high alloimmune risk' for the stratified tacrolimus analysis, so the paper reports BOTH a continuous per-ten-mismatch slope and a step at >11.; linearity tested: Not tested for the eplet exposure. No spline, no quartile/category series, and no test for trend or for departure from log-linearity is reported in the retrieved text; the >11 cut-point is an ROC-optimised threshold, not a test of shape. The paper DOES make an explicit continuous-versus-threshold statement, but about the tacrolimus exposure, not the eplet exposure: 'the proportions of tacrolimus trough levels below minimum thresholds of 3, 3.5, 4, and 4.5 ng/ml correlated with dnDSA development after adjusting for HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch when considered as a continuous variable rather than a threshold'.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch load x tacrolimus trough level (the paper's central result): Effect modification in the direction of a modifiable risk: among recipients above the >11 DR or DQ eplet mismatch threshold, those who developed dnDSA had spent a significantly greater percentage of time with tacrolimus troughs <5 ng/ml than high-risk recipients who did not develop dnDSA; among recipients at or below 11 eplet mismatches, the same percentage of troughs <5 ng/ml was tolerated WITHOUT dnDSA. In other words low tacrolimus exposure is harmful only, or mainly, in high-eplet-mismatch recipients. (No formal interaction term or P-for-interaction is reported in the retrieved text; the result is a stratified comparison. Supporting adjusted estimates from the joint model: eplet mismatch OR 1.31 (95% CI 1.10-1.56; P=0.002) and minimum tacrolimus trough OR 0.71 per 1 ng/ml (95% CI 0.57-0.88; P=0.001), i.e. both remain independent predictors. The authors themselves flag the limitation of the stratum: 'Low-alloimmune risk recipients who developed dnDSA were rare (n=5), limiting comparisons.') [Results (stratified low- vs high-risk analysis) and Abstract]
- HLA mismatch x calcineurin inhibitor choice (cyclosporin vs tacrolimus): CNI class independently modifies the risk of the immunological outcome that mismatch drives: cyclosporin carried a 2.7-fold higher unadjusted dnDSA incidence, and remained significant after adjustment for eplet mismatch, age and nonadherence. (Unadjusted incidence 32 versus 12 per 1000 patients per year; multivariate HR 2.28 (95% CI 1.35-3.78; P=0.002)) [Results, Table 2 and Abstract]
- HLA mismatch x adherence: Nonadherence is the single largest independent predictor of class II dnDSA in the multivariate model, larger than the eplet mismatch term, and operates alongside it rather than through it. (HR 3.09 (95% CI 1.83-5.15; P<0.001)) [Results, Table 2]
- HLA mismatch x recipient age: Younger recipient age independently increases class II dnDSA risk in the multivariate model containing eplet mismatch. (HR 0.97 per year (95% CI 0.96-0.99; P=0.001)) [Results, Table 2]
- tacrolimus exposure x time relative to dnDSA (within-patient temporal effect modification): Within the same patients, mean tacrolimus trough levels in the 6 months immediately before dnDSA were significantly lower than at all earlier time points, while their levels more than 6 months before dnDSA were greater than or equal to those of recipients who never developed dnDSA. This is a within-person drop in exposure preceding the antibody, not a constant between-person difference. (No numeric estimate or P value for this comparison is given in the retrieved text (reported as 'significantly lower'); underlying values are in the figures, which were not extracted.) [Results and Abstract]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "HLA-DR eplet mismatch was a significant predictor of HLA-DR dnDSA-free survival post-transplant (hazard ratio [HR], 2.50 per ten mismatches; 95% confidence interval [95% CI], 1.70 to 3.71; P<0.001)." (Results)
- *C12* — "The HLA-DQ eplet mismatch threshold that best correlated with HLA-DQ dnDSA development was >11 mismatches (AUC=0.72, sensitivity =0.94, specificity =0.45)." (Results)
- *C11* — "After adjustment for HLA-DR/DQ eplet mismatch (odds ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56; P=0.002), the minimum recorded tacrolimus trough level correlated (odds ratio, 0.71 per 1 ng/ml; 95% CI, 0.57 to 0.88; P=0.001) with the risk for dnDSA development." (Results)
- *C11* — "Recipients at high alloimmune risk (>11 HLA-DR or -DQ eplet mismatches) who developed dnDSA had a significantly greater percentage of tacrolimus trough levels <5 ng/ml compared with high-risk recipients who did not develop dnDSA." (Results, stratified low- versus high-risk analysis)
- *C11* — "However, recipients with low alloimmune risk (≤11 HLA-DR and -DQ eplet mismatches) tolerated the same percentage of tacrolimus trough levels <5 ng/ml without developing dnDSA." (Results, stratified low- versus high-risk analysis)
- *C11* — "Recipients treated with a cyclosporin regimen had a 2.7-fold higher incidence of dnDSA development than recipients on a tacrolimus regimen (32 versus 12 per 1000 patients per year)." (Results)

**Limitations.** Single centre, single region (Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada), 596 recipients and only 66 dnDSA events; the authors themselves write that 'Because of the relatively small sample size and the associated risk of type II error, risk quantification should be interpreted with caution and validated in a larger independent cohort.' No external validation is presented.; The headline interaction rests on a very thin stratum: 'Low-alloimmune risk recipients who developed dnDSA were rare (n=5), limiting comparisons.' The claim that low-eplet-mismatch recipients safely tolerate troughs <5 ng/ml is therefore supported by five events and could equally reflect low power.; No formal interaction term and no P-for-interaction is reported for eplet mismatch x tacrolimus level; the central finding is a stratified comparison across an ROC-derived cut-point, which is a weaker design than a fitted interaction and inherits the optimism of a threshold chosen in the same data.; Observational and non-randomised drug exposure. Low tacrolimus troughs are not assigned; they co-travel with nonadherence (itself HR 3.09 in the same model), with dose reductions for infection, malignancy or nephrotoxicity, and possibly with early subclinical inflammation. Reverse causation and confounding by indication cannot be excluded, and the within-patient fall in troughs in the 6 months before dnDSA is equally consistent with adherence collapse as with a pharmacological threshold.; The exposure requires two-field (high-resolution) DRB1/3/4/5 and DQA1/B1 typing plus HLAMatchmaker v2.0 to compute. It cannot be derived from one-field/antigen-level typing without imputation, and the paper offers no low-resolution equivalent, no imputation accuracy data, and no antigen-mismatch comparator. The >11 threshold is not portable to an antigen count.; Only class II eplets are studied. Class I loci (A, B, C) and DP are outside the exposure, and class I dnDSA is set aside on the basis of a single event ('only one patient in this entire cohort suffering allograft failure after developing isolated class I dnDSA'), so nothing here bears on claims C5, C6, C7 or C8.; The graft-failure results are borderline and fragile: both DR (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.01-1.81) and DQ (HR 1.29, 95% CI 1.01-1.67) sit at P=0.05 with lower confidence limits at 1.01. Whether graft failure was death-censored is not stated in the retrieved text.; Incomplete ascertainment of the histological outcome: 'Histologic analysis <=12 months post-transplant was only available in 441 of 598 (74%) of the cohort'. Note that this sentence says 598 while the analysed cohort is stated as 596; the discrepancy is in the source.; Mycophenolate exposure was not measured ('Mycophenloate mofetil levels were not routinely monitored' - spelling as printed), so the total immunosuppressive exposure is only partly captured and the tacrolimus level is a proxy for it.; Mixed adult (n=541) and paediatric (n=55) cohort with a long era span (1999-2015) covering changing immunosuppression practice; results are not stratified by donor type, so no living-donor-specific estimate is available even though roughly 41-50% of the cohort received living-donor grafts.; By construction, dnDSA requires pretransplant DSA to have been measured and absent. The cohort is therefore a well-characterised, antibody-screened population, which is the opposite of the antibody-status-unknown setting the review is designing for.; Retrieval limitation on our side: the PMC full-text API returned an empty body, so figures and the full tables were not machine-extracted. Numeric values reported in figures only (for example the actual mean trough levels before versus after dnDSA, and the percentage-of-levels-below-threshold curves) are absent from this record..

### Williams RC 2017 — The Risk of Transplant Failure With HLA Mismatch in First Adult Kidney Allografts 2: Living Donors, Summary, Guide

Williams RC 2017, *Transplantation Direct*, [PMID 28573187](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28573187/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: Transplantation Direct is an open-access journal (Wolters Kluwer); PMC full text retrieved; exact CC licence not printed in the retrieved text - unknown.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All first adult (>=18 y) living-donor kidney-only transplants in the United States (UNOS/STAR), 1 Oct 1987 - 31 Dec 2013; secondary analyses on the combined deceased + living cohort of 255,737 first adult kidney-alone transplants |
| donor type | living (primary); both (secondary 'guide' analyses combining deceased and living) |
| n | 66,596 living-donor (40,596 living related; 26,000 living unrelated); 255,737 in the combined deceased+living cohort |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; Cox proportional-hazards regression, reduced (age, sex, era) and full (15-18 covariates) models; HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch count 0-6 with 0 as reference; 27 [A,B,DRB1] permutation triples; linear fit of HR on mismatch count |
| typing resolution | not stated; UNOS antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts (0-6), i.e. serologic/low-resolution by registry convention |
| outcome | kidney allograft failure (survival censored at last examination, at start of renal replacement therapy, or at death; patients dying with a functioning graft were included) - effectively death-censored graft survival |
| follow up | mean 5.24 years, median 4.18 years (Q1 1.97, Q3 7.79); 348,960 graft-years for living donors; 1,343,518 graft-years for the combined cohort; maximum 25.22 years |
| other factors modelled | donor age (year-quartiles), recipient age (year-quartiles), transplant era (5-year periods), recipient sex, donor sex, recipient ethnicity, recipient education, recipient BMI, donor BMI, recipient working for income before transplant, dialysis type, recipient years on dialysis (> median), days waiting for transplant (quartiles), COPD drug treatment, induction therapy at discharge, maintenance immunosuppression at discharge, donor relatedness (living related vs living unrelated), UNOS region (stratification) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest living-donor-only analysis of HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch count and graft survival, so it answers directly whether HLA matching matters within living donation (C14, C1) and what the total-count dose-response looks like (C2): the authors fit a straight line through the seven mismatch-count HRs and report a per-mismatch slope of about 0.15 in both reduced and full models, with 1 mismatch HR 1.44 and 6 mismatches HR 2.12 versus 0. It also gives the zero-mismatch premium and the first-mismatch step (C9): 0-mismatch living unrelated grafts were not different from 0-mismatch full siblings, and the first mismatch carries a larger jump (HR 1.44) than each subsequent one (slope 0.15). The population transfers well to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen: it is living-donor, uses low-resolution antigen-level A/B/DR mismatch counts exactly as a one-field typing pre-screen would, includes a large living-UNRELATED subset (Iran's programme is predominantly unrelated), and does not condition on antibody status, so its estimates are the 'antibody-unknown' marginal effect a pre-screen would see. Its limits for transfer are that it is a US, mostly non-Hispanic-white registry with no DQ, no DSA/sensitisation adjustment, and that the living-unrelated 0-2 mismatch cells are sparse, so the LU 1-mismatch HR is imprecise (CI 0.86-3.76). The 'guide' table (Table 9) also supports the policy position that a many-mismatch living donor is preferable to or equal to a well-matched deceased donor, which is relevant to how a living-donor scheme should weight HLA against donor source.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- allograft failure: 1 HLA-A,B,DR mismatch vs 0, all living donors (n=66,596) — HR 1.44 (1.27–1.64); adjusted for full Cox model (recipient and donor characteristics, era, induction/immunosuppression) [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2; Abstract]
- allograft failure: 6 mismatches vs 0, all living donors — HR 2.12 (1.89–2.37); adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2; Abstract]
- allograft failure: 1 mismatch vs 0, living related donors (n=40,596) — HR 1.42 (1.24–1.62); adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2]
- allograft failure: 6 mismatches vs 0, living related donors — HR 2.03 (1.73–2.38); adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2]
- allograft failure: 1 mismatch vs 0, living unrelated donors (n=26,000) — HR 1.79 (0.86–3.76); adjusted for full Cox model; authors state it did not reach statistical significance [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2]
- allograft failure: 6 mismatches vs 0, living unrelated donors — HR 2.57 (1.43–4.61); adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches', Table 2]
- allograft failure: living related 1 mismatch vs living related 0 mismatch (14-level relatedness x mismatch variable) — HR 1.43; adjusted for full Cox model; printed in text as '43% higher risk'; CI only in Table 4 (not in retrieved text) [Results, 'The Interaction of Relatedness and HLA Mismatch', Table 4]
- allograft failure: living unrelated 1 mismatch vs living related 0 mismatch — HR 1.52, p=0.0798; adjusted for full Cox model; printed as '52% increased risk ... marginal statistical significance' [Results, 'The Interaction of Relatedness and HLA Mismatch', Table 4]
- allograft failure: living unrelated 6 mismatches vs living related 0 mismatch — HR 2.14 (1.89–2.42), p=0.0001; adjusted for full Cox model; p printed as <0.0001 [Results, 'The Interaction of Relatedness and HLA Mismatch', Table 4]
- allograft failure: living related with >=1 mismatch vs 0-mismatch full siblings (combined cohort n=255,737) — HR 1.77; adjusted for full Cox model, 7-level 0-mismatch variable; CI only in Table 5 [Results, 'Quantifying the Survival Advantage', Table 5]
- allograft failure: living unrelated with >=1 mismatch vs 0-mismatch full siblings — HR 1.74; adjusted for full Cox model; CI only in Table 5 [Results, 'Quantifying the Survival Advantage', Table 5]
- allograft failure: deceased donor with >=1 mismatch vs 0-mismatch full siblings — HR 2.66; adjusted for full Cox model; CI only in Table 5 [Results, 'Quantifying the Survival Advantage', Table 5]
- allograft failure: 'living component': living vs deceased donor among grafts with 1-6 mismatches, relative hazard reduction — percentage 34; adjusted for derived as [1.0 - (1.76/2.65)] x 100 from Table 5 HRs [Results, 'Quantifying the Survival Advantage'; Abstract; Figure 7]
- allograft failure: living related 6 mismatches vs deceased donor 0 mismatch (21-level donor source x mismatch variable) — HR 1.14 (0.99–1.31); adjusted for full Cox model, combined cohort [Discussion, 'An Empirical Guide', Table 9]
- allograft failure: linear slope of HR per additional mismatch, all living donors, full model (intercept 1.28, 95% CI 0.94-1.61) — slope 0.15 (0.06–0.24), p=0.0096; adjusted for line fitted to the seven full-model HRs; Figure 1 legend prints the CI as 0.05-0.24 [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 1]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, all living donors, reduced model (intercept 1.31, 0.92-1.70) — slope 0.15 (0.04–0.26), p=0.0161; adjusted for reduced model: age, sex, transplant era [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 1]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, living related, full model (intercept 1.20, 0.92-1.48) — slope 0.19 (0.09–0.29), p=0.0043; adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 2]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, living related, reduced model (intercept 1.21, 0.91-1.51) — slope 0.21 (0.1–0.31), p=0.0037; adjusted for reduced model [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 2]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, living unrelated, full model (intercept 1.47, 0.90-2.03) — slope 0.16 (0.04–0.29), p=0.0194; adjusted for full Cox model [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 3]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, living unrelated, reduced model (intercept 1.41, 0.84-1.98) — slope 0.16 (0.04–0.28), p=0.0213; adjusted for reduced model [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', Figure 3]
- allograft failure: weighted linear slope per mismatch for the 14-level relatedness x mismatch variable, LR 0-mismatch reference (intercept 1.27, 1.07-1.47, p<0.0001) — slope 0.14 (0.09–0.2), p=0.0001; adjusted for full Cox model; p printed as <0.0001 [Results, 'The Interaction of Relatedness and HLA Mismatch', Figure 5]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, combined deceased + living cohort (n=255,737), full model with 18 covariates (intercept 1.08, 0.98-1.18) — slope 0.12 (0.1–0.15), p=0.0001; adjusted for full Cox model; p printed as <0.0001 [Results, 'Combining Deceased and Living Donor Strata', Table 6, Figure 8]
- allograft failure: linear slope per mismatch, combined cohort, reduced model (intercept 1.01, 0.94-1.07) — slope 0.19 (0.17–0.21), p=0.0001; adjusted for reduced model; p printed as <0.0001 [Results, Figure 8]
- allograft failure: weighted linear slope per mismatch within the 2009-2013 era only (combined cohort; follow-up 1.87 years per person) — slope 0.079, p=0.001; adjusted for full Cox model within era; p printed as <0.001 [Results, 'Performing the Full Cox Regressions Within 5-Year Periods', Table 8, Figure 9]
- allograft failure: deceased donors, 1 mismatch vs 0 (cited from the companion deceased-donor paper, not re-estimated here) — percentage increase in hazard 13; adjusted for full Cox model of the companion paper [Introduction]
- allograft failure: deceased donors, 6 mismatches vs 0 (cited from the companion deceased-donor paper) — percentage increase in hazard 64; adjusted for full Cox model of the companion paper [Introduction]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; 1 MM: 1.44 (1.27–1.64); 2 MM: None; 3 MM: None; 4 MM: None; 5 MM: None; 6 MM: 2.12 (1.89–2.37)
- A: no separate per-locus HR; tested via 27 [A,B,DRB1] triples
- B: no separate per-locus HR; tested via 27 [A,B,DRB1] triples
- DR: no separate per-locus HR; tested via 27 [A,B,DRB1] triples
- permutation_result_living: 22 of 26 non-zero triples had HR significantly >1.0; only [0,0,2], [2,0,0], [1,2,0] and [2,0,1] were not significantly different from [0,0,0]. Within mismatch-count categories 1-5, 57 pairwise comparisons of permutations showed no significant difference after Holm-Bonferroni, so A, B and DRB1 were judged to have equal effect per mismatch.
- permutation_result_combined_cohort: The paper's own wording is that 'each of the 27 permutations ... was significantly associated with increased graft failure when compared with the triple [0, 0, 0]' with p<0.0001 - i.e. the 26 non-reference triples, since [0,0,0] is the reference. Only 2 of 57 within-category comparisons were significant: [0,1,2] vs [2,1,0] p=0.0001 and [1,1,1] vs [2,1,0] p=0.0008 (adjusted threshold 0.0009), both in category 3.
- C: not typed / not analysed
- DQ: not typed / not analysed
- DP: not typed / not analysed
- Shape reported: linear (in HR, not log-hazard) with a positive intercept above 1.0, i.e. a first-mismatch step (HR 1.44 at 1 mismatch) followed by roughly equal increments of about 0.15 per additional mismatch; linearity tested: A straight line was fitted to the observed HRs against mismatch count (0-6) for reduced and full models, with slope and intercept, 95% CIs and p-values; a weighted linear regression (weights = number in each mismatch category) was used for the relatedness-combined and combined-cohort variables and within each 5-year era. Goodness of fit of the Cox model was checked with Schoenfeld residuals and martingale residuals. No spline, quadratic or formal test against a nonlinear alternative is reported; linearity is asserted from the fit of the line to the seven points.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x donor relatedness (living related vs living unrelated): Penalty per mismatch reported as least for deceased donors, intermediate for living related and largest for living unrelated (Figure 4 weighted fits); with LR 0-mismatch as reference, LU 1 mismatch HR 1.52 (p=0.0798) and LU 6 mismatches HR 2.14 (1.89-2.42); LU 0- and 1-mismatch categories were not significantly different from LR 0-mismatch (full-model slopes: LR 0.19 (0.09-0.29), LU 0.16 (0.04-0.29); intercepts LR 1.20, LU 1.47; combined 14-level variable slope 0.14 (0.09-0.20), intercept 1.27 (1.07-1.47)) [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs', 'The Interaction of Relatedness and HLA Mismatch'; Figures 2-6; Table 4]
- HLA mismatch x donor source (deceased vs living related vs living unrelated), combined cohort: Within each mismatch category living grafts had lower HRs than deceased grafts with the same count; any living kidney with 2 mismatches was significantly better than a 0-mismatch deceased kidney; at 3 mismatches living HRs were not different from the deceased 0-mismatch reference; LR 6-mismatch HR 1.14 (0.99-1.31) vs deceased 0-mismatch (21-level variable, deceased 0-mismatch reference; per-cell HRs in Table 9 (not in retrieved text) except LR 6 = 1.14 (0.99-1.31)) [Results, 'The Interaction of HLA Mismatch With Donor Source'; Discussion, 'An Empirical Guide'; Table 9]
- living component vs deceased, conditional on >=1 mismatch (0-mismatch full siblings as reference): LR and LU grafts with >=1 mismatch had similar HRs (1.77, 1.74) vs 2.66 for deceased; 0-mismatch LR and LU grafts were not significantly different from 0-mismatch full siblings (LU 0-mismatch N=146) (34% hazard reduction = [1 - 1.76/2.65] x 100) [Results, 'Quantifying the Survival Advantage'; Table 5; Figure 7; Discussion]
- HLA mismatch x transplant era (five 5-year periods, combined cohort): Every era had a significant positive slope; the 2009-2013 slope was lowest (0.079, p<0.001) but follow-up was only 1.87 years/person versus 7.15, 7.39, 6.81 and 5.15 in earlier eras, so the authors treat a declining HLA effect as unresolved (slope 0.079 (2009-2013); other era slopes in Table 8 only) [Results, 'Performing the Full Cox Regressions Within 5-Year Periods'; Table 8; Figures 9-10; Discussion]
- covariate adjustment (reduced vs full model): Slopes and intercepts of the reduced (age, sex, era) and full models were nearly identical (about 0.15), so ethnicity, clinical, induction and immunosuppression covariates add little to the HLA effect in living donors (0.15 (0.04-0.26) reduced vs 0.15 (0.06-0.24) full) [Results, 'Linearity of the HRs'; Discussion, 'Nearly Identical Slopes']
- locus identity within a mismatch count (A vs B vs DRB1): No significant within-category differences among permutations after Holm-Bonferroni in living donors (57 comparisons); authors conclude each locus contributes equally (no significant tests (living); 2 of 57 significant in combined cohort) [Results, 'HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 Have Equal Roles'; 'Combining Deceased and Living Donor Strata']

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "there was a 44% higher risk (HR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.27-1.64) of allograft failure for 1 mismatch and more than twice the risk (HR, 2.12; 95% CI, 1.89-2.37) for 6 mismatches" (Results, 'Impact of Number of HLA Mismatches on Living-Donor Kidney Allograft Survival')
- *C2* — "Linearity shows that the risk of failure increases by the same amount for each mismatch of HLA." (Discussion, 'Nearly Identical Slopes of Reduced and Full Models')
- *C9* — "This implies that, within mismatch categories 1 to 5, all single HLA mismatches have equal effect irrespective of the locus where the difference appears." (Results, 'HLA-A, -B, and -DRB1 Have Equal Roles in the Failure of Living-Donor Allografts')
- *C14* — "The penalty in HR for HLA mismatch appears to be least for deceased donors, more for the LR fitted line, and largest for the LU stratum." (Results, 'Linearity of the HRs in Living Donor Allografts')
- *C14* — "In other words, any living donor kidney with 2 mismatches is significantly better than a kidney from a deceased donor with 0 mismatches." (Discussion, 'An Empirical Guide to Matching Recipient and Donor')
- *C9* — "0-mismatch allografts from unrelated living donors were equal in their survival to kidneys from related donors, which suggests an insignificance of mismatching for minor histocompatibility antigens" (Discussion, '0-mismatch VARIABLE Parses the Living Component')

**Limitations.** Registry (UNOS/STAR) analysis with antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts only; typing resolution not stated; no HLA-C, -DQ or -DP; No adjustment for sensitisation (PRA/cPRA), donor-specific antibody, or crossmatch; the effect is the marginal, antibody-status-unknown effect; Missing or unknown covariate values were imputed by regression; extent of missingness not reported in the retrieved text; Spans 1987-2013, so the pooled HRs mix eras with very different immunosuppression; the era-stratified analysis shows a lower slope in 2009-2013 (0.079) with only 1.87 years follow-up per person, leaving the modern-era effect size unresolved; Living-unrelated 0-2 mismatch categories are sparse (LU 0-mismatch N=146 in the combined analysis), so LU 1-mismatch HR 1.79 has CI 0.86-3.76 and the LU dose-response at the low end is imprecise; The per-count HRs for 2-5 mismatches (Table 2), the Table 4/5/9 cells and the era-specific slopes (Table 8) are in tables whose cells are not present in the retrieved PMC text; only the values quoted in the prose could be extracted; Linearity is asserted from a straight-line fit to seven HR points (HR scale, not log-hazard); no spline, quadratic or formal nonlinearity test; the intercept above 1.0 implies a first-mismatch step that the linear description understates; No per-locus HRs; locus equality is inferred from the absence of significant within-category permutation differences after Holm-Bonferroni, which is a null result of limited power in category 1-2 cells; Outcome censors death with a functioning graft, so all-cause graft loss is not reported; US population, mostly non-Hispanic white recipients; no ethnicity-specific HLA effect reported; Minor internal inconsistencies in the retrieved text: full-model slope CI 0.06-0.24 (text) vs 0.05-0.24 (Figure 1 legend); the 34% reduction uses 1.76/2.65 whereas the printed HRs are 1.77, 1.74 and 2.66; italic P symbols were stripped in the PMC extraction so some p-values appear as '= 0.0003'.

### Yacoub R 2017 — Analysis of OPTN/UNOS registry suggests the number of HLA matches and not mismatches is a stronger independent predictor of kidney transplant survival.

Yacoub R 2017, *Kidney International*, [DOI 10.1016/j.kint.2017.07.016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.kint.2017.07.016). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier, Kidney International); no PMC record for this PMID or DOI (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid, checked 2026-09-07), so no open-access full text was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients in the United Network for Organ Sharing (UNOS/OPTN) database, 1995-2012; sensitivity subgroup restricted to recipients transplanted after 2003 ('more uniform HLA nomenclature'); bootstrap resampling on complete data from 96,236 recipients |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 96,236 recipients with complete data (the only cohort figure the abstract gives, used for the bootstrap resampling); the size of the full 1995-2012 analytic cohort is not stated in the abstract |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; multivariable models entering HLA match count and HLA mismatch count individually and then simultaneously; sensitivity analysis in the post-2003 subgroup; bootstrap resampling |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen level (registry HLA-A, -B, -DR); the abstract flags that HLA nomenclature was more uniform only after 2003; the number of loci counted is not stated in the abstract |
| outcome | delayed graft function; 1-year acute rejection; death-censored graft survival |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract (transplant years 1995-2012) |
| other factors modelled | not named in the abstract; the abstract states only 'combined multivariable models including HLA matching and mismatching' |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is the review's cleanest statement that the 0-6 mismatch count is not a symmetric, self-sufficient encoding of HLA compatibility: in a large deceased-donor UNOS cohort the authors show that match count and mismatch count, although inversely related, are 'not exact opposites', and that when both enter the same model the mismatch term loses significance while the match term keeps predicting delayed graft function, 1-year acute rejection and death-censored graft survival. For ANGLE A (shape of the dose-response) it therefore bears on the coding question rather than on the curve itself: it argues that the information the review attributes to 'number of mismatches' may travel with 'number of matches', which is a different variable whenever a donor or recipient is homozygous or incompletely typed. For a low-resolution, one-field, antigen-level Iranian pre-screen this is directly actionable, because exactly that setting produces homozygous and partially typed records in which the match count and 6-minus-mismatch-count diverge; the safe implementation is to compute and store both counts and to keep the number of antigens actually typed as provenance rather than assuming the pair is redundant. Transfer is nevertheless indirect and weak in three ways: the cohort is deceased-donor only, so it says nothing about the living-donor selection setting the pre-screen serves; there is no antibody or DSA information, so it cannot inform an antibody-status-unknown workflow; and because no PMC full text exists, the review can take only the direction of the finding, not a single hazard ratio, confidence interval or per-count series. The paper should therefore be cited as a caution about how the count is coded (C2, C9) and never as a source of a numeric dose-response.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported in the retrieved text; the abstract gives only a direction-of-association result (match count retains, mismatch count loses, statistical significance when both are modelled together) and no per-count or per-locus series; linearity tested: not stated in the abstract; the abstract does not say whether match and mismatch counts entered the models as continuous ('degree of HLA mismatching') or as categories, and reports no test of linearity, no spline and no test for trend; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "HLA matching and mismatching, while inversely related, are not exact opposites." (Abstract, first sentence)
- *C1* — "Individually, both HLA matching and mismatching showed significant associations with graft survival." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "Adjusting the model to take into account both matching and mismatching simultaneously, the degree of HLA mismatching lost significance while matching continued to have a significant prediction for delayed graft function, the one-year acute rejection rate, and graft survival." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "Future analyses should preferentially utilize HLA matching as a covariate over mismatching for accurately reflecting impact on graft outcomes." (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C2* — "Sensitivity analyses were performed using the subgroup of deceased donor kidney transplant patients after 2003 with more uniform HLA nomenclature and resampling analyses using bootstrapping on complete data available from 96,236 recipients." (Abstract, Methods)

**Limitations.** No PMC full text exists for this PMID or DOI, so every number in the paper - hazard ratios, odds ratios, confidence intervals, p-values, any per-count or per-locus series, the covariate list and the total cohort size - was unavailable. Only the abstract's qualitative direction-of-effect statements could be extracted.; Deceased-donor recipients only. The review's target setting is living-donor selection, so the finding transfers only as a coding principle, not as a quantitative estimate.; Registry antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR data. No DQ, DP or C, no allele-level or eplet-level mismatch, and the authors themselves restrict a sensitivity analysis to post-2003 transplants because HLA nomenclature before then was not uniform.; Match count and mismatch count are collinear by construction. Entering both in one model is a demanding design, and the abstract reports no collinearity diagnostics, no variance inflation factors and no coefficient magnitudes, so a reader cannot tell whether the mismatch term's loss of significance reflects a real absence of independent effect or only a loss of precision.; The mechanism that makes matches and mismatches non-equivalent - donor or recipient homozygosity, and antigens never typed or never reported - is not stated in the abstract and could not be verified from the retrieved text. Reviewer inference, not a claim of the retrieved text: because an untyped or homozygous locus lowers the match count without raising the mismatch count, the match variable may partly encode typing completeness and homozygosity rather than immunological distance.; No sensitisation, PRA or donor-specific antibody information appears in the abstract, so the result cannot be read as antibody-adjusted.; Retrospective registry analysis: residual confounding by allocation policy (zero-ABDR-mismatch national sharing), centre effects, immunosuppression era and cold ischaemia is not addressable from the abstract.; Delayed graft function and 1-year acute rejection are registry-reported outcomes with known misclassification; no biopsy adjudication is described.; No effect modification or interaction result is reported in the abstract, so the paper contributes nothing to C10 or C11..

### Kosmoliaptsis V 2016 — Alloantibody Responses After Renal Transplant Failure Can Be Better Predicted by Donor-Recipient HLA Amino Acid Sequence and Physicochemical Disparities Than Conventional HLA Matching

Kosmoliaptsis V 2016, *American Journal of Transplantation 2016;16(7):2139-47*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.13707](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.13707). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: unknown - PMC full text retrieved (Wiley / John Wiley & Sons, Ltd author manuscript or open-access deposit); explicit licence statement not present in the retrieved text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 131 consecutive patients (87 male, 44 female, median age 38) who received a primary kidney allograft in Cambridge, UK between 1995 and 2010 and returned to the transplant waiting list after failure of that first graft; 56 (43%) had a transplant nephrectomy; 66 (50.4%) continued immunosuppression after relisting. 671 donor-recipient HLA mismatches analysed at the mismatch level. |
| donor type | not stated (first kidney allografts 1995-2010; the allocation discussion is framed around deceased-donor allocation, and living-donor transplants are neither excluded nor reported separately) |
| n | 131 patients; 671 donor-recipient HLA mismatches |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; univariate and multivariate logistic regression; HLA immunogenicity scores (AMS, EpMS, EMS) de-correlated from conventional HLA mismatch grade by linear regression before entry into the models; likelihood-ratio tests; R |
| typing resolution | not explicitly stated. Conventional mismatch grade was counted at HLA specificity (antigen) level - the Introduction states that in the companion study 'mismatches were based on HLA specificities and the number of donor mismatches within each locus was enumerated as 0, 1, or 2'. The AMS/EpMS/EMS scores require allele-level amino-acid sequences (inter-locus subtraction for HLA-A/-B/-C and HLA-DRB1/3/4/5, intra-locus for HLA-DQA1/DQB1), i.e. two-field typing or its equivalent. HLA-DP was not routinely typed in this era. |
| outcome | (1) post-graft-failure HLA-specific sensitisation measured as calculated reaction frequency (cRF) against 10,000 consecutive UK deceased donors, dichotomised at cRF>15% (sensitised) and cRF>=85% (highly sensitised); (2) development of donor-specific antibody (DSA) against each individual donor HLA mismatch, at Luminex single-antigen-bead MFI thresholds >2000 and >8000. NOT graft survival, rejection or patient survival. |
| follow up | peak reactive serum taken within a median (SD) follow-up of 2539 (1605) days since first transplantation; sera screened 3-monthly while on the list |
| other factors modelled | time on the waiting list (per year), maintenance dual-agent immunosuppression after graft failure, transplant (allograft) nephrectomy, pre-transplant sensitisation level (sensitivity adjustment) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's molecular-mismatch question (C12) in the one setting where the alloantibody read-out is cleanest: patients whose first kidney graft has failed, where every mismatched donor HLA can be scored for immunogenicity and then checked against the antibody that actually appeared. Its central result is a warning rather than an endorsement for a low-resolution pre-screen: amino-acid (AMS), eplet (EpMS) and electrostatic (EMS) disparity each added predictive value OVER conventional antigen-level mismatch counting for both breadth of sensitisation and per-mismatch DSA, which means that counting 0/1/2 antigen mismatches per locus systematically misclassifies how dangerous a given mismatch is. For the KidneyMatch Iranian pre-screen this matters twice over. First, the superior scores are simply not computable from one-field (antigen-level) typing - AMS, EpMS and EMS all require allele-level donor and recipient sequences, so the honest position for a low-resolution tool is that it must use the inferior-but-available antigen count while stating that the residual immunological risk within a mismatch grade is real and unmeasured. Second, the outcome studied is exactly the harm a living-donor pre-screen should care about beyond graft survival: sensitisation that later closes off retransplantation - and the authors note that HLA matching is 'particularly important in recipients who are likely to require repeat transplantation in the future', which in a young Iranian living-donor population is most of them. Transfer is limited by design: this is a deceased-donor-era UK cohort of retransplant candidates, donor type is not reported, antibody status was measured (not unknown), and the outcome is antibody rather than graft failure, so the paper cannot be used to weight a graft-survival score - only to justify treating DR/DQ mismatches as the highest-immunogenicity loci and to disclose the ceiling on precision imposed by one-field typing.
