**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: conventional HLA mismatch grade entered as a single CONTINUOUS per-mismatch term, not as 0/1/2 categories MM: OR 1.29 (1.05, 1.62) per additional mismatch for cRF 16-100%, p = 0.02 (AMS model); 1.39 (1.05, 1.63) EpMS model; 1.30 (1.05, 1.64) EMS model; same continuous term, outcome cRF >= 85% MM: OR 1.29 (1.07, 1.59) p = 0.01 (AMS model); 1.30 (1.07, 1.59) p = 0.01 (EpMS and EMS models)
- note: This paper reports per-locus results in terms of IMMUNOGENICITY SCORES per mismatch, not in terms of 0/1/2 antigen-mismatch counts. Ranking of per-10-unit DSA odds ratios (MFI > 2000): HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 strongest (AMS 5.42, EpMS 6.30, EMS 2.77), then HLA-DQ (AMS 1.79, EpMS 1.99, EMS 1.46), then HLA-A/-B (AMS 2.02 borderline, EpMS 2.04 non-significant, EMS 1.81 significant), with HLA-C showing no association at all.
- HLA-A and -B: only EMS predicted DSA independently: OR 1.81 (1.16, 2.86) p = 0.01 at MFI > 2000 and 1.62 (1.01, 2.59) p = 0.04 at MFI > 8000; AMS and EpMS did not reach significance on univariate analysis
- HLA-C: DSA infrequent (16.8% of C mismatches) and NOT associated with donor HLA-C alloantigen immunogenicity; the companion analysis also found the HLA-C locus contribution to sensitisation 'less pronounced'
- HLA-DRB1/3/4/5: all three scores independently predictive at both MFI thresholds; largest effect sizes in the paper
- HLA-DQ: all three scores independently predictive at MFI > 2000 but none at MFI > 8000; authors state the cohort had too few mismatched DQ specificities for in-depth DQ analysis
- locus-specific cRF: AMS, EpMS and EMS were independently associated with HLA class I (cRF > 15% and cRF >= 85%) and HLA-DQ (cRF > 15%) sensitisation; for HLA-DR it was the conventional mismatch grade that correlated with locus-specific sensitisation, with an additional effect of HLA-DR EMS only at cRF >= 85% (Table S2, supplement not retrieved)
- mean (SD) score burden: HLA class I AMS 20 (11.1), EpMS 17 (9.4), EMS 31 (20.8); HLA-DR AMS 5 (7.2), EpMS 8 (10.0), EMS 7 (9.3); HLA-DQ AMS 11 (15.4), EpMS 12 (13.9), EMS 15 (22.8)
- Shape reported: not reported for antigen mismatch count. Conventional mismatch grade was modelled as one continuous per-mismatch term (implicitly log-linear); no separate 0 vs 1 vs 2 estimates and no zero-mismatch reference category are printed in this paper. The incremental 0/1/2 per-locus dose-response is asserted in the Introduction/Discussion but is cited to the authors' earlier companion study and its numbers are NOT reproduced here. For the immunogenicity scores, AMS/EpMS/EMS were entered as continuous absolute values (per 10 units); Figures 1 and 2 present them grouped into quantiles/bands and Figure 2 shows fitted logistic curves, but those figure-level numbers are not in the retrieved text.; linearity tested: not tested. No spline, no trend test, no test of departure from linearity, and no 'P for interaction' anywhere in the paper. Categorisation (cRF bands 0-15%, 16-50%, 51-84%, 85-100%; score quantiles) was used only 'for presentation'; the regression models used absolute continuous values.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA locus x type of immunogenicity metric (class I vs class II): For HLA-A and -B mismatches only the physicochemical/electrostatic score predicted DSA; amino-acid and eplet counts did not. For HLA-DR and HLA-DQ all three scores predicted DSA and none outperformed the others. This is the paper's core heterogeneity result. (HLA-A/-B MFI>2000: EMS OR 1.81 (1.16-2.86) p=0.01 vs AMS 2.02 (1.01-4.12) p=0.05 and EpMS 2.04 (0.90-4.69) p=0.09; HLA-DR MFI>2000: AMS 5.42 (2.23-15.01), EpMS 6.30 (2.30-19.30), EMS 2.77 (1.52-5.52), all p<=0.002) [Results, DSA section, and Table 2; restated in Discussion. NOT a formal interaction test - the loci were modelled in separate stratified regressions and no P for interaction is reported.]
- HLA-C mismatch x immunogenicity score: No association of any kind: HLA-C DSA responses were infrequent and unrelated to donor HLA-C immunogenicity, so no HLA-C model is presented in Table 2. (16.8% of HLA-C mismatches provoked DSA; no OR reported) [Results, DSA section]
- immunogenicity score x DSA strength threshold (MFI > 2000 vs > 8000): For HLA-DR the scores predicted both moderate and high-level DSA; for HLA-DQ they predicted only MFI > 2000 and all three lost significance at MFI > 8000; for HLA-A/-B only EMS survived at the high threshold. (HLA-DQ AMS 1.79 (1.19-2.71) p=0.005 at >2000 vs 1.49 (0.92-2.47) p=0.11 at >8000; HLA-A/-B EMS 1.81 (1.16-2.86) p=0.01 vs 1.62 (1.01-2.59) p=0.04) [Table 2]
- immunogenicity score x severity of sensitisation outcome (cRF > 15% vs cRF >= 85%): AMS, EpMS and EMS predicted BECOMING sensitised but had no independent effect on becoming HIGHLY sensitised; at cRF >= 85% only conventional mismatch grade, immunosuppression and waiting time remained significant. (AMS 1.44 (1.02-2.10) p=0.04 for cRF 16-100% vs 1.22 (0.91-1.65) p=0.18 for cRF 85-100%; EMS 1.27 (1.02-1.62) p=0.04 vs 1.13 (0.94-1.37) p=0.20) [Table 1 and Results text]
- maintenance immunosuppression after graft failure x DSA development, by class: Continued dual-agent immunosuppression was strongly protective against HLA-DR DSA and moderately protective against HLA-A/-B DSA; no HLA-DR DSA in immunosuppressed patients reached MFI > 8000 (the parameter was not estimable). This is the largest effect modifier in the paper and is not an HLA property. (HLA-DR DSA MFI>2000: OR 0.05 (0.01-0.21) p<0.001; HLA-A/-B DSA MFI>2000: OR 0.34-0.36, p=0.02; highly sensitised cRF>=85%: OR 0.28 (0.08-0.81) p=0.03) [Table 2 (and footnote a), Table 1]
- transplant nephrectomy x HLA class: Nephrectomy was independently associated with DSA against HLA-A and -B but not with class II DSA; the authors interpret this as class I alloantibody being absorbed by the retained graft. No effect on overall sensitisation once immunosuppression withdrawal was accounted for. (HLA-A/-B DSA MFI>2000: OR 2.15-2.27 (1.20-4.15), p = 0.006 to 0.01; at MFI > 8000 non-significant (1.13-1.19)) [Table 2 and Discussion, limitations paragraph]
- time on the waiting list x HLA class: Longer waiting time raised class I DSA and overall sensitisation but had no effect on class II DSA (point estimates around 0.9-1.0 for DR and DQ). (HLA-A/-B DSA per year 1.29-1.31 (1.15-1.48) p<0.001; HLA-DR 1.00 (0.83-1.19) p=0.96; HLA-DQ 0.91 (0.70-1.15) p=0.43; overall cRF 16-100% 1.54 (1.21-2.07) p=0.001) [Tables 1 and 2]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "assessment of donor HLA immunogenicity based on AMS, EpMS, or EMS offers additional value to that of conventional HLA mismatch grade for predicting sensitization to HLA in patients awaiting retransplantation" (Discussion, paragraph 2 ('The principal finding was that ...'))
- *C12* — "We did not, however, demonstrate an advantage in using an eplet approach to assess HLA immunogenicity over simply enumerating the number of amino acid polymorphisms between donor and recipient HLA molecules." (Discussion, paragraph 3)
- *C12* — "Importantly, donor HLA EMS, but not AMS or EpMS, predicted the development of DSA (at MFI > 2000 and >8000) against HLA‐A and ‐B mismatches." (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C4* — "Moreover, donor HLA‐DR and ‐DQ alloantigens with high AMS, EpMS, or EMS were more likely to induce DSA responses, which in the case of HLA‐DR were more likely to be of high level (MFI > 8000)." (Discussion, paragraph 2)
- *C7* — "DSA responses against HLA‐C mismatches were infrequent (16.8%) and not associated with donor HLA‐C alloantigen immunogenicity." (Results, 'Influence of donor HLA immunogenicity on development of posttransplant DSA')
- *C2* — "the level of sensitization in this cohort increased incrementally with the number of donor HLA mismatches of their failed transplant, and all HLA loci assessed (HLA‐A, ‐B, ‐C, ‐DRB1, ‐DRB3/4/5, and DQB1) contributed independently to sensitization" (Results, first paragraph (reported as a prior finding of the authors' companion study))

**Limitations.** Small single-centre cohort: 131 patients and 671 mismatches, from one UK unit (Cambridge), transplanted 1995-2010. Several key confidence intervals are very wide (e.g. HLA-DR EpMS at MFI > 8000: 6.97, 2.24-25.58) and one is exactly at the null boundary (EpMS for cRF 16-100%: 1.41, 1.00-2.05, p = 0.05).; The outcome is alloantibody, not graft survival, rejection or patient survival. The paper cannot be used to weight a graft-outcome score; it speaks only to sensitisation and DSA risk.; Antibody was measured only AFTER graft failure and after immunosuppression withdrawal. The authors state their findings 'would be strengthened if they were confirmed in patients with functioning grafts'. Whether the same immunogenicity ranking holds under maintenance immunosuppression is untested here.; HLA-DP was not routinely typed in this era, so DP could not be scored at all, even though the authors note many patients become DP-sensitised after graft failure. Nothing in this paper supports or refutes claim C8.; The cohort was deliberately well matched at HLA-DR and -DQ by the allocation policy of the day (49% had 0-1 DR mismatch), which left too few mismatched DQ specificities for in-depth DQ analysis - the DQ estimates are the least well powered in the paper despite DQ being a locus of high interest.; The conventional-mismatch comparator is entered as a single continuous per-mismatch term rather than as 0/1/2 categories, so this paper contributes NO usable dose-response shape, no zero-mismatch premium and no first-vs-second-mismatch contrast. Linearity is never tested.; AMS, EpMS and EMS are strongly collinear with each other and with mismatch grade; the authors handled this by residualising the scores against mismatch grade with linear regression and by fitting the three scores in separate models. That procedure changes the interpretation of the score coefficient (it is the effect of the score component orthogonal to mismatch count) and gives no head-to-head statistical comparison of the three metrics.; No formal interaction tests. Every locus- and class-specific contrast in this record is a comparison of separately fitted stratified models, so 'EMS works for class I but AMS does not' is an informal, underpowered contrast, not a tested effect modification.; No external validation and no calibration or discrimination statistics (no c-statistic, no AUC, no reclassification measure). 'Better predicted' in the title rests on likelihood-ratio significance of an added term, not on demonstrated predictive performance in new data.; cRF is computed against a panel of 10,000 UK deceased donors, so both the sensitisation outcome and its clinical meaning are calibrated to UK HLA frequencies; the same antibody profile maps to a different cRF in an Iranian donor pool.; Selection: only patients who returned to the waiting list are included. Patients who died, were never relisted, or were not screened are absent, and the retained-graft/nephrectomy split is observational.; Sera were EDTA-treated for prozone but not titrated; DSA strength rests on two MFI cut-offs (2000, 8000) rather than titre.; Donor type (living vs deceased) is not reported anywhere in the paper, and the discussion is framed entirely around deceased-donor allocation. There is no living-donor subgroup..

### Lim WH 2016 — HLA-DQ Mismatches and Rejection in Kidney Transplant Recipients

Lim WH 2016, *Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology (CJASN) 11(5):875-883*, [DOI 10.2215/CJN.11641115](https://doi.org/10.2215/CJN.11641115). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright (Copyright 2016 by the American Society of Nephrology); free full text at PMC, not CC BY. The PubMed MCP full-text call returned an empty full_text field; the article text was captured from the PMC article page (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4858494/) through the Browser pane and saved to fulltext/27034399.txt, so every quote below was verified with ft_extract.py check..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Primary (first) kidney-alone transplant recipients, live and deceased donor, Australia and New Zealand 2004-2012, restricted to the 788 of 6107 (13%) with donor-recipient HLA-DQ molecular typing available; multiple-organ and prior-graft recipients excluded |
| donor type | both |
| n | 788 (321 with 0 DQ mismatches, 393 with 1, 74 with 2); 245 (31.1%) live donor |
| design | retrospective registry cohort (ANZDATA); adjusted Cox and random-effects Cox (clustered by state/country); two-way interaction terms for effect modification; linear regression for eGFR |
| typing resolution | Molecular HLA typing (introduced 1997; all ANZ laboratories reporting molecular typing from 2002), but the exposure is the count of BROAD-ANTIGEN HLA-DQ mismatches (0/1/2) supplied to ANZDATA by the National Organ Matching system. The Discussion calls for 'future studies evaluating both broad antigen and epitope HLA-DQ mismatches', confirming the antigen-level exposure. The DQ locus analysed (DQA1 vs DQB1) and the field resolution used to call a mismatch are never stated; DQB1/DQA1 appear nowhere in the text. |
| outcome | acute rejection (any; early <=6 months; late >6 months; antibody-mediated rejection defined by at least 2 of C4d, DSA, histology), overall graft loss, death-censored graft loss, eGFR at 1 and 5 years |
| follow up | median 2.8 years (IQR 1.2-6.6), 2891 person-years |
| other factors modelled | recipient age, donor age, donor type (live vs deceased), BMI, HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatches (0 vs 1-2 each), peak PRA, transplant era (2004-2006, 2007-2009, 2010-2012), race (white / nonwhite / Indigenous), total ischaemic time, waiting time, induction antibody therapy, initial immunosuppression (CNI, antimetabolite, prednisolone), transplant state/country as random effect (cluster) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the registry study behind the claim that HLA-DQ mismatch carries rejection risk that is not captured by HLA-A, -B, -DR matching (C4): in 788 ANZ recipients with DQ typing, 1-2 DQ mismatches versus 0 raised any rejection (adjusted HR 1.54), late rejection (2.85) and AMR (2.33) after adjustment for ABDR mismatches, peak PRA, donor type and initial immunosuppression, while graft loss and eGFR were not affected within 2.8 years. It is also the clearest published test of a DQ x DR interaction (C10): DR was an effect modifier for AMR (P for interaction 0.02), with the DQ effect on AMR confined to DR-mismatched recipients in the text, which argues that the DQ signal is not simply DR linkage but also that DQ matching cannot be read as independent of DR. For the Iranian living-donor pre-screen the transfer is partial: the exposure is a broad-antigen 0/1/2 DQ count, which is what one-field (low-resolution) DQB1 typing yields, so the effect sizes are on the right scale; 31% of the cohort were living-donor and donor type was adjusted for, but no living-donor subgroup estimate is printed. Pre-transplant DSA status was unknown to the analysis (only peak PRA was available), which matches an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen, but it also means the observed early-rejection excess may partly reflect pre-formed DQ-DSA rather than the mismatch itself. One and two DQ mismatches were pooled (only 74 recipients had two), so the paper cannot say whether a second DQ mismatch adds risk; 87% of the source population was excluded for missing DQ typing; and the population is 80% white, so allele/haplotype frequencies differ from Iran. One descriptive number carries most of the operational weight for a DR-only, one-field pre-screen: of the kidneys with zero HLA-DR mismatches, 15% were still mismatched at HLA-DQ, and only 3% of the whole cohort were matched at A, B, DR and DQ together. So a screen that matches on DR alone leaves roughly one in seven DR-matched pairs carrying the DQ mismatch that this paper links to a 2.3-fold AMR hazard - but the same paper's interaction result says that residual DQ risk is concentrated where DR is ALSO mismatched, so DQ typing adds most where the DR match is already imperfect.

**Effect sizes reported.**

**Limitations.** Only 788 of 6107 eligible recipients (13%) had HLA-DQ typing; the excluded 87% were older, had older donors and were more often living-donor recipients (44.6% vs 31.1%), so selection is by typing practice, not random; 1 and 2 DQ mismatches pooled a priori; only 74 recipients had two DQ mismatches, so no 1-vs-2 or per-mismatch estimate exists and no dose-response shape can be inferred; AMR events are few (12 vs 38); stratified AMR estimates are imprecise (DR-matched stratum CI 0.20-9.99) and the interaction rests on a single P value of 0.02; Table 2 labels the AMR-by-DR strata the opposite way from the Abstract and Results text; the text assignment (effect in DR-mismatched, n=616) was used here but the discrepancy is unresolved in the paper; Two versions of the adjusted early-rejection CI are printed (0.95-2.01 in text, 0.90-2.01 in Table 2); Pre- and post-transplant DSA are not held by ANZDATA; only peak PRA was adjusted, so pre-formed DQ-DSA cannot be separated from mismatch per se; roughly 80% of rejections were early; Registry-coded rejection and AMR (2 of 3 criteria) without central biopsy review; possible outcome misclassification; Median follow-up 2.8 years; no association with graft loss or eGFR, so the paper informs rejection risk, not long-term graft survival; Broad-antigen DQ mismatch count; DQ locus (DQA1/DQB1), typing field level, and the mismatch-calling rule are not stated; HLA-DP not collected; ANZ cohort, ~80% white; donor type adjusted for but no living-donor subgroup reported; deceased-donor allocation context (ABDR-matched allocation) shapes the mismatch distribution (only 3% zero-ABDR+DQ mismatch); eGFR analyses rest on subsets, not the full cohort (1-year eGFR n=585, 5-year eGFR n=214 of 788), and are adjusted only for sex, donor and recipient age and BMI - a thinner model than the Cox models; the null eGFR result is therefore weakly powered; Effect modification was screened with two-way interaction terms across many covariates but only the DR x DQ interaction for AMR is reported with a statistic; the other interaction tests are asserted as null with no numbers, so multiplicity cannot be assessed.

### Massie AB 2016 — A Risk Index for Living Donor Kidney Transplantation

Massie AB 2016, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.13709](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.13709). Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, author manuscript (NIH Public Access deposit, PMC6114098). Body text retrieved is the accepted author manuscript; tables and the LKDPI equation are images and were not in the retrieved text..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult first-time kidney-only transplant recipients in the United States (SRTR/OPTN national registry), 1 January 2005 - 31 December 2013; 69,994 deceased-donor and 36,025 living-donor recipients modelled jointly |
| donor type | both |
| n | 106,019 (69,994 DDKT + 36,025 LDKT); exclusions: missing donor characteristics N=255, donor BMI outside 17-45 N=1407 |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; single Cox proportional-hazards model of DDKT and LDKT recipients together (KDPI set to 0 for LDKT, living-donor covariates set to 0 for DDKT, plus an LDKT indicator), adjusted for recipient characteristics; LKDPI built by dividing each living-donor log HR by the per-unit KDPI log HR; validated by KM/logrank and matched analyses within KDPI/LKDPI strata and by a 200-replicate bootstrap C-statistic |
| typing resolution | not stated. The paper reports only counts of HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatches from OPTN data (in practice antigen/serologic level, 0-2 per locus); the words allele, antigen, serologic, resolution and imputation do not appear anywhere in the retrieved text. |
| outcome | all-cause graft loss |
| follow up | not stated in the retrieved text (transplants 2005-2013; follow-up duration and median follow-up are not printed in the body text) |
| other factors modelled | deceased-donor KDPI (per 10 units), living donor age (spline for years over 50), living donor eGFR (CKD-EPI), living donor BMI, living donor African-American race, living donor history of cigarette use, living donor systolic blood pressure, male donor to male recipient, ABO incompatibility, biological unrelatedness to recipient, donor/recipient weight ratio (spline for D/RWR < 0.9), recipient peak PRA, BMI, age, HCV status, private insurance, race, sex, years of renal replacement therapy |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the anchor paper for the living-donor half of the review: it is the only large national derivation of a donor-quality index that is estimated inside living-donor transplantation, and it answers the question of how much an HLA mismatch is worth relative to the non-HLA donor factors a pre-screen also sees. The population is exactly the decision KidneyMatch supports - a candidate choosing among several potential living donors, or weighing a living offer against a deceased-donor kidney - and the authors frame it that way explicitly (kidney paired donation, choosing between multiple potential donors). It transfers well on typing: only HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch counts are used, which is precisely one-field/antigen-level information, and no allele-level, eplet or DSA data are required, so the model is computable from the low-resolution typing available in Iran. It transfers well on antibody status too, in the sense that the model needs no antibody measurement to run - recipient peak PRA enters only as a recipient-side adjustment covariate, not as an effect modifier - so an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen can still apply the HLA terms, though it inherits the paper's silence about sensitisation. It transfers badly in three ways: the cohort is US, mostly Caucasian, and 100% crossmatch-negative and clinically cleared (ABO-incompatible pairs here went through desensitisation), the outcome is all-cause graft loss over a registry follow-up rather than rejection or dnDSA, and the absolute effect sizes are small enough that they sit inside the residual confounding the authors themselves concede. For the review it supplies C14 directly (HLA matters within living donation, but donor-quality and match terms are of comparable or larger magnitude), C5 in a weak form (B is retained and A is not), and C3 in a weak form (DR is retained and is of the same size as B, not larger).

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft loss (LDKT recipients): per HLA-B mismatch (continuous count) — HR 1.08 (1.03–1.14), p=<0.05 (stated for all abstract estimates collectively); adjusted for recipient peak PRA, BMI, age, HCV status, private insurance, race, sex, years of RRT; all other living-donor terms and KDPI [Abstract (published version). CIs printed in Louis-Zeger low-point-high format: '1.03 1.081.14'.]
- all-cause graft loss (LDKT recipients): per HLA-DR mismatch (continuous count) — HR 1.09 (1.04–1.15), p=<0.05 (stated for all abstract estimates collectively); adjusted for recipient peak PRA, BMI, age, HCV status, private insurance, race, sex, years of RRT; all other living-donor terms and KDPI [Abstract (published version). CIs printed as '1.04 1.091.15'.]

NOTE: body text gives B=1.09 and DR=1.08, i.e. the B and DR values are transposed relative to the published abstract.]

**Dose-response.**

- A: modelling MM: tested as a mismatch count in exploratory models, p=0.4, excluded from the index; no HR printed; 0 MM: not reported; 1 MM: not reported; 2 MM: not reported
- B: modelling MM: continuous count of mismatches, single per-mismatch coefficient; per_mismatch MM: HR 1.08 (1.03-1.14) in the abstract; aHR 1.09, p<0.01 in the body text; 0 MM: reference (implicit); 1 MM: not reported separately; 2 MM: not reported separately
- DR: modelling MM: continuous count of mismatches, single per-mismatch coefficient; per_mismatch MM: HR 1.09 (1.04-1.15) in the abstract; aHR 1.08, p<0.01 in the body text; 0 MM: reference (implicit); 1 MM: not reported separately; 2 MM: not reported separately
- C: not examined
- DQ: not examined
- DP: not examined
- Shape reported: not reported. HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatches enter the model as continuous counts, so a constant hazard ratio per mismatch (log-linear in the mismatch count) is imposed by the model specification, not demonstrated. No 0/1/2 category series and no total-mismatch-count series is printed anywhere in the retrieved text.; linearity tested: not tested for HLA. The authors did use Martingale residual plots to justify departures from linearity, but only for donor age (spline for years over 50) and donor/recipient weight ratio (spline for D/RWR < 0.9); no equivalent check is reported for the HLA-B or HLA-DR mismatch counts, and no spline, threshold or category alternative for HLA is mentioned.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x anything (sensitisation/peak PRA, recipient age, donor age, race, related vs unrelated): No effect-modification or interaction analysis involving HLA is reported. The words 'interaction' and 'sensitisation' do not appear in the retrieved text; recipient peak PRA enters only as an adjustment covariate in the Cox model and as a matching variable in the validation, never as a modifier of the HLA terms. [absence verified by grep over the full retrieved text (Methods 'Model of donor risk'; Results)]
- biological relatedness x HLA mismatch (confounding rather than interaction): Biologically unrelated donors were associated with LOWER risk (aHR=0.90, p<0.01) once HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch were in the model; the authors read this as HLA compatibility, not relatedness per se, carrying the effect, and cite their own paediatric work where an unrelated-donor HR of 1.24 (p<0.01) fell to 1.04 (p=0.7) after adjusting for HLA mismatch. (aHR 0.90, p<0.01 (this cohort); prior paediatric study HR 1.24, p<0.01 unadjusted vs aHR 1.04, p=0.7 HLA-adjusted) [Results 'Model of donor risk'; Discussion para 4. The 1.24 -> 1.04 figures are quoted by the authors from a previous publication, not estimated here.]
- LDKT vs DDKT within strata of LKDPI/KDPI (index-equivalence check, not an HLA interaction): Within strata of KDPI/LKDPI (0-20, 20-40, 40-60, 60-80, 80-100), the adjusted HR for LDKT versus DDKT was not statistically significantly different from 1 in any stratum, and matched cumulative incidence of all-cause graft loss was similar - i.e. a living kidney with LKDPI x behaved like a deceased kidney with KDPI x. (no stratum-specific numbers printed in the retrieved text (results are in figures/tables that were not retrieved)) [Results, 'LKDPI validation']

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C14* — "HLA-B mismatches with recipient (aHR per mismatch =1.09, p<0.01), and HLA-DR mismatches with recipient (aHR per mismatch =1.08, p<0.01) were associated with increased risk of all-cause graft loss" (Results, 'Model of donor risk')
- *C5* — "donor history of cancer (p=0.5), donor proteinuria (p=0.2), donor/recipient HLA-A mismatch (p=0.4), donor diastolic blood pressure (p=0.6)" (Results, 'Model of donor risk' - list of exploratory variables evaluated for the LKDPI but found not to be statistically significant)
- *C14* — "In a large, national population, older donor age (among donors older than 50 years), African-American race, ABO incompatibility, and HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatches were associated with worse graft survival" (Discussion, para 1)
- *C14* — "Our study showed that a biologically unrelated donor was associated with decreased risk, after adjusting for other characteristics. Notably, our adjustment included HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch." (Discussion, para 4)
- *C13* — "A related donor with better HLA compatibility may confer less risk than an unrelated donor with worse HLA compatibility." (Discussion, para 4)
- *C14* — "recipient characteristics are the major driver of LDKT outcomes; even the healthiest living-donor organ will have a shorter graft life in an old or sick recipient" (Discussion, para 7)

**Limitations.** The published abstract and the body text disagree on which locus carries the larger coefficient: the abstract prints HLA-B HR 1.08 (1.03-1.14) and DR HR 1.09 (1.04-1.15), while the Results text prints HLA-B aHR 1.09 and HLA-DR aHR 1.08. The two loci are statistically indistinguishable here, and this paper cannot be used to rank B against DR.; Confidence intervals for the HLA terms exist only in the abstract; the body text gives p-values only, and Table 2 (which would carry the full model with CIs) is an image that was not retrieved. Several other point estimates also differ between abstract and body (donor age 1.24 vs 1.19; BMI 1.09 vs 1.12; ABO 1.27 vs 1.30; LKDPI<0 24.2% vs 26.5%; LKDPI>50 4.4% vs 5.0%), consistent with a PMC author manuscript that predates the final published version.; HLA-B and HLA-DR are entered as continuous mismatch counts, so the model cannot show the shape of the dose-response, cannot show a zero-mismatch premium, and cannot show whether the second mismatch at a locus costs the same as the first. Linearity for the HLA terms is assumed, never tested.; HLA-A was tested and dropped at p=0.4 with no estimate printed, so the paper gives no usable size for the A effect - only that it was smaller than the detection threshold in this cohort. HLA-C, DQ and DP were never examined; eplet/molecular mismatch and DSA were never examined.; Typing resolution is never stated. The mismatch counts come from OPTN reporting, which is antigen-level in practice, but the paper offers no description, so the transfer to a one-field typing pre-screen is by assumption rather than by evidence.; Outcome is all-cause graft loss only. No death-censored graft failure, no rejection, no dnDSA - so this paper says nothing about the immunological mechanism by which mismatch acts, and death with function dilutes the HLA signal.; Sensitisation is handled only as a recipient-side adjustment (peak PRA); there is no analysis of whether the HLA mismatch effect is larger in sensitised recipients. A pre-screen with unknown antibody status inherits that silence.; The cohort is US registry data 2005-2013 with 72.3% Caucasian LDKT recipients. No Middle Eastern or Iranian population; HLA haplotype frequencies, consanguinity rates and the resulting mismatch distribution differ materially from Iran, where related donation and consanguineous pairs are more common.; Discrimination is weak in absolute terms (C-statistic 0.59 for LKDPI vs 0.58 for KDPI); the authors attribute this to recipient factors dominating. An index this weak ranks donors only coarsely.; The authors concede residual confounding from unmeasured recipient characteristics (cardiovascular risk, frailty) and heterogeneous reporting from hundreds of centres, and argue this biases toward the null - which, for effect sizes as small as HR 1.08-1.09, is a material caveat in both directions.; ABO-incompatible transplants in this cohort proceeded after desensitisation at experienced US centres; the ABO term is therefore not transportable to a setting without that infrastructure.; The LKDPI equation itself (the point weights assigned to each factor) is printed as an image/formula and was not present in the retrieved text, so the published coefficients cannot be quoted from this retrieval..

### Tinckam KJ 2016 — Re-Examining Risk of Repeated HLA Mismatch in Kidney Transplantation.

Tinckam KJ 2016, *J Am Soc Nephrol*, [PMID 26888475](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26888475/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown; a PMC record exists (PMC5004649) but get_full_text_article returned an empty body on two attempts (prefixed and bare id), so only the PubMed/PMC abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | recipients of a SECOND kidney transplant, 1995-2011; registry not named in the retrievable abstract |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract |
| n | 13,789 second kidney transplants; 3868 had one or more repeated mismatches |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; multivariable Cox proportional hazards; predefined subgroup analyses |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; a repeated-mismatch definition of this registry era implies serologic/antigen-level HLA, but this is not confirmed in the retrievable text |
| outcome | all-cause graft loss and death-censored graft loss |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | panel-reactive antibody (PRA) before the second transplant - subgroup definer, nephrectomy of the first allograft - subgroup definer, multivariable Cox adjustment stated but the covariate list is not visible in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review's effect-modification question (C11): whether the harm of an HLA mismatch depends on the recipient's immunological history rather than on the mismatch count alone. Its headline result is a null - in a contemporary cohort of 13,789 second kidney transplants, repeated mismatches from the first donor carried no overall excess risk of all-cause or death-censored graft loss - which directly weakens the historical assumption that a repeated antigen is automatically a high-risk mismatch. The risk reappears only inside two named recipient categories: detectable PRA before the second transplant (class 2 repeated mismatch, death-censored graft loss HR 1.15) and prior nephrectomy of the first allograft (HR 1.30 all-cause, 1.41 death-censored). For a LIVING-donor, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran this is the crucial transfer: the modifiers that make a repeated mismatch dangerous are exactly the two facts a pre-screen cannot observe, so a repeat-transplant candidate with unknown PRA and unknown nephrectomy history must be routed to serological/DSA assessment rather than scored as low risk on antigen matching alone. The exposure is defined at antigen level (a repeated mismatched HLA antigen), which is compatible with one-field low-resolution typing and so does not require two-field data to apply. Transfer is limited, however, because the population is retransplantation only, the donor type is not stated (a registry of this size and era is deceased-donor dominated), and no per-count or per-locus dose-response is available in the retrievable text.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft loss and death-censored graft loss: repeated HLA mismatch (present vs absent) at second transplant, whole cohort — HR None; adjusted for multivariable Cox proportional hazards; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (qualitative null: 'revealed no effect'; no numeric HR or CI printed in the retrievable abstract)]
- death-censored graft loss: any class 2 repeated mismatch vs none, in recipients with detectable PRA before the second transplant — HR 1.15 (1.02–1.29); adjusted for multivariable Cox; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (predefined subgroup analysis)]
- all-cause graft loss: any class 2 repeated mismatch vs none, in recipients who had nephrectomy of the first allograft — HR 1.3 (1.07–1.58); adjusted for multivariable Cox; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (predefined subgroup analysis)]
- death-censored graft loss: any class 2 repeated mismatch vs none, in recipients who had nephrectomy of the first allograft — HR 1.41 (1.12–1.78); adjusted for multivariable Cox; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract (predefined subgroup analysis)]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested in the retrievable text; no linear, trend, spline or threshold test is mentioned in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- class 2 repeated mismatch x sensitisation (detectable PRA before the second transplant): the repeated-mismatch effect on death-censored graft loss appears in recipients with detectable PRA, whereas the whole-cohort effect is null (HR 1.15 (95% CI 1.02-1.29) for death-censored graft loss in the detectable-PRA subgroup; no formal interaction p-value is reported in the abstract) [Abstract, predefined subgroup analysis]
- class 2 repeated mismatch x nephrectomy of the first allograft: in recipients whose first allograft was removed, class 2 repeated mismatches are associated with both all-cause and death-censored graft loss (HR 1.30 (95% CI 1.07-1.58) all-cause; HR 1.41 (95% CI 1.12-1.78) death-censored; no formal interaction p-value is reported in the abstract) [Abstract, predefined subgroup analysis]
- HLA class of the repeated mismatch (class 2 vs class 1): every signal reported in the abstract is specific to class 2 repeated mismatches; no class 1 repeated-mismatch estimate is given, so a class 1 effect can be neither confirmed nor excluded from the retrievable text (not reported for class 1) [Abstract]
- repeated mismatch x era / HLA testing method: the paper is framed as a re-examination of historical repeated-mismatch findings in a modern era (1995-2011) with evolved HLA testing; the contemporary null is contrasted with the historical positive literature, but no formal era interaction term is reported in the abstract (not reported) [Abstract, background and conclusion]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "We conducted a contemporary registry analysis of data from 13,789 patients who received a second kidney transplant from 1995 to 2011, of which 3868 had one or more repeated mismatches." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "Multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling revealed no effect of repeated mismatches on all-cause or death-censored graft loss." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "any class 2 repeated mismatch increased the hazard of death-censored graft loss, particularly in patients with detectable panel-reactive antibody before second transplant (hazard ratio [HR], 1.15; 95% confidence interval [95% CI], 1.02 to 1.29)" (Abstract)
- *C11* — "in those who had nephrectomy of the first allograft, class 2 repeated mismatches specifically associated with all-cause (HR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.07 to 1.58) and death-censored graft loss (HR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.12 to 1.78)" (Abstract)
- *C11* — "These updated data redefine the effect of repeated mismatches in retransplantation and challenge the paradigm that repeated mismatches in isolation confer increased immunologic risk." (Abstract, conclusion)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT-ONLY ACCESS: the PMC record PMC5004649 returned an empty full-text body, so Methods, covariate list, tables, figures, per-locus results, class 1 estimates, subgroup sizes and any interaction tests could not be read. Only the four abstract findings are extractable.; The whole-cohort result is a qualitative null with no HR or CI printed in the abstract, so the precision of the null (and whether a clinically relevant effect was excluded) cannot be judged from the retrievable text.; Multiple predefined subgroups are reported without any interaction p-value in the abstract; the two positive subgroup findings sit close to the null boundary (lower CI limits 1.02, 1.07, 1.12) and are vulnerable to multiplicity.; Observational registry design: repeated mismatches are not randomly assigned. Clinicians and allocation systems avoid repeated mismatches for the patients judged highest risk, so confounding by indication plausibly biases the overall effect toward the null.; Sensitisation is captured by PRA before the second transplant, a coarse proxy; no donor-specific antibody, single-antigen-bead, eplet or PIRCHE data are mentioned, so the mechanism (memory response to the repeated antigen) is not directly measured.; Era 1995-2011 predates current induction/maintenance practice and routine SAB-based virtual crossmatching; the authors' own argument is that HLA testing evolution changes the answer, which also limits extrapolation forward from 2011.; Donor type (living vs deceased), follow-up duration, HLA typing resolution and the identity of the registry are not stated in the retrievable abstract.; Applies only to RETRANSPLANTATION. It says nothing about the mismatch-outcome relation in first transplants, which is the dominant case in a living-donor pre-screen.; No per-count or per-locus dose-response is retrievable, so this paper cannot inform the shape of the mismatch-count gradient (C2) or locus weighting (C3-C8)..

### Williams RC 2016 — The Risk of Transplant Failure With HLA Mismatch in First Adult Kidney Allografts From Deceased Donors

Williams RC 2016, *Transplantation*, [PMID 26901078](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26901078/) — DOI omitted: its digits trip the repository PII scanner. Access: pmc_full_text; licence: publisher copyright, author manuscript (PMC8086563 is the NIH author-manuscript version; no CC licence stated in the retrieved text; tables, figures and supplementary content are NOT included in the PMC text, and in-text citations to them appear as empty parentheses).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | all first adult kidney-alone transplants from deceased donors with complete data in the UNOS STAR registry, United States, 1 October 1987 to 31 December 2013 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 189,141 transplants; 994,558 allograft-years of follow-up; 74,049 female / 115,092 male recipients, mean recipient age 49.8 y; donor mean age 36.6 y; 43,656 died with a functioning kidney |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; Cox proportional-hazards regression with a reduced model (recipient age, sex, era) and a full model (17 variables, all covariates above); HLA mismatch entered both as a 7-level categorical variable (0 = reference) and as 27 ordered A/B/DR triples (0/1/2 per locus); proportional-hazards assumption checked by OLS regression of Schoenfeld residuals (beta never >0.0001, R-square <=0.0016) and by a 100-group martingale-residual goodness-of-fit test; a straight line was fitted to the seven category HRs with SAS TRANSREG; 57 within-category permutation comparisons with sequential Holm-Bonferroni correction |
| typing resolution | not stated. The registry records antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts (0-2 per locus, 0-6 total); the manuscript never mentions typing method, allele/two-field typing, or resolution |
| outcome | kidney allograft failure, defined for living patients as the start of renal replacement therapy; survival censored at last recorded examination or at death, i.e. death-censored graft failure. Persons with a functioning kidney at death were included and censored |
| follow up | 994,558 allograft-years total (given as 994,557 in the Strengths section). Median follow-up is not stated; Kaplan-Meier projected median survival times by mismatch category exist only in a table/figure absent from the PMC text |
| other factors modelled | recipient age (quartiles: 18-40, >40-51, >51-60, >60), donor age (quartiles: <=22, >22-38, >38-50, >50), transplant era (five periods: 1987-1993, 1994-1998, 1999-2003, 2004-2008, 2009-2013), recipient sex, recipient ethnicity (Hispanic, non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic black, American Indian, Pacific Islander, Asian), cold ischaemia time (<=25 h vs >25 h), PRA (<=50% vs >50%), recipient education (high school or less vs greater), recipient BMI >30, donor BMI >30, recipient diabetes, recipient working for income before transplant, drug treatment for COPD at transplant, recipient dialysis type (haemodialysis, peritoneal, none), induction therapy (anti-thymocyte globulin, muromonab CD3 [printed 'macomonab CD3' in the manuscript], basiliximab, daclizumab, alemtuzumab, other, steroids only, no induction), maintenance immunosuppression at discharge (permutations of six drug groups), recipient age x donor age interaction (16-level variable) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest single total-count dose-response series for antigen-level HLA-A/B/DR mismatch in kidney-alone transplantation, and it addresses two review questions directly. For C1 it shows the mismatch effect survives full adjustment for induction and maintenance immunosuppression across an era in which baseline graft survival improved dramatically (era HRs falling 0.80, 0.67, 0.50, 0.37), so mismatch still predicts outcome under modern regimens. For C2 it is the strongest available statement of shape: the authors fit a straight line to the seven category hazard ratios and report a constant increment of 0.11 HR units per additional mismatch after full adjustment (0.16 unadjusted), bounded by HR 1.13 at one mismatch and 1.64 at six. Its 27-permutation analysis is the clearest published test of whether locus identity matters within a fixed mismatch count (C10): 56 of 57 within-category comparisons were non-significant after Holm-Bonferroni, which the authors read as equality across loci. The weighted fit through the 27 triples has intercept 1.04 (1.00-1.08), meaning the zero-mismatch group sits essentially on the extrapolated line rather than far below it, i.e. no large zero-mismatch premium beyond what the additive count already predicts (C9) - a direct counterpoint to the US allocation policy the Introduction describes as putting a premium on zero mismatch while ignoring the number of mismatches. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen is partial: the cohort is deceased-donor, US, 1987-2013, so absolute hazards, cold ischaemia and donor quality differ, and the paper is silent on living donors, DQ, HLA-C, DP, antibody status and typing resolution. What does transfer is that the antigen-level A/B/DR count is exactly what a low-resolution one-field Iranian report can reproduce, and that a simple unweighted additive count is defensible as a first-pass ranking signal while antibody status is unknown. Because no HLA x PRA or HLA x DSA interaction was tested, the paper cannot say how that count should be modified once sensitisation becomes known.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death-censored kidney allograft failure: 1 HLA-A,B,DR mismatch vs 0 — HR 1.13 (1.06–1.21); adjusted for full model: all recipient and donor covariates listed in scope_check [Abstract; Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches on kidney allograft survival', para 1]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: 6 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches vs 0 — HR 1.64 (1.56–1.73); adjusted for full model [Abstract; Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 1]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: 1 HLA-A,B,DR mismatch vs 0 — HR 1.17 (1.1–1.25); adjusted for reduced model: recipient age, recipient sex, transplant era only [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 1]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: 6 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches vs 0 — HR 1.98 (1.88–2.08); adjusted for reduced model (age, sex, era) [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 1]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: linear fit of the category HRs on mismatch count 1-6: slope (HR units per additional mismatch), reduced model — OLS slope of HR on mismatch count (SAS TRANSREG) 0.16 (0.15–0.17); adjusted for reduced model (age, sex, era) [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 1; Discussion, 'The Risk of Kidney Failure is Linear with HLA Mismatch']
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: linear fit of the category HRs on mismatch count 1-6: slope (HR units per additional mismatch), full model — OLS slope of HR on mismatch count (SAS TRANSREG) 0.11 (0.09–0.12); adjusted for full model [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 1; Discussion, 'The Risk of Kidney Failure is Linear with HLA Mismatch']
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: weighted general linear model of the 27 A/B/DR permutation HRs on total mismatch count: intercept — regression intercept (HR units) 1.04 (1.0–1.08); adjusted for full model; weighted by number of persons in each triple [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 2]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: weighted general linear model of the 27 A/B/DR permutation HRs on total mismatch count: slope — regression slope (HR units per mismatch) 0.11 (0.09–0.12), p=<0.0001 (stated in Discussion for the weighted 27-triple fit); adjusted for full model; weighted by number of persons in each triple [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 2; Discussion, 'First, ...' para]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: triple [A=0, B=1, DR=2] vs [0,0,0] (3 total mismatches, the 2 at DR) — HR 1.57 (1.41–1.75), p=the only one of 57 within-category comparisons significant after Holm-Bonferroni (vs triple [2,1,0]); exact p not printed; adjusted for full model with 26 triple index variables [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 3]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: triple [A=2, B=1, DR=0] vs [0,0,0] (3 total mismatches, the 2 at A) — HR 1.27 (1.18–1.36), p=see previous entry; adjusted for full model with 26 triple index variables [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 3]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: triple [A=0, B=0, DR=1] vs [0,0,0] (a single DR mismatch alone) — HR None, p=described only as 'only marginally significant'; no number in the retrieved text (table absent from PMC); adjusted for full model with 26 triple index variables [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 2]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: recipient ethnicity: non-Hispanic black vs reference — HR 1.62; adjusted for full model [Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects on Kidney Survival']
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: recipient ethnicity: Asian vs reference — HR 0.81; adjusted for full model [Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects on Kidney Survival']
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: donor age quartiles Q2, Q3, Q4 vs Q1 — HR None, p=<0.0001 for each; 95% CIs non-overlapping; adjusted for full model [Results, last para: values 1.11, 1.37, 1.90]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: recipient age quartiles Q2, Q3, Q4 vs Q1 — HR None, p=<0.0001 for each; adjusted for full model [Results, last para: values 0.74, 0.65, 0.61]
- death-censored kidney allograft failure: transplant era: 1994-1998, 1999-2003, 2004-2008, 2009-2013 vs 1987-1993 — HR None; adjusted for full model [Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects': values 0.80, 0.67, 0.50, 0.37]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 1.0; 1 MM: 1.13 (1.06–1.21); 2 MM: None; 3 MM: None; 4 MM: None; 5 MM: None; 6 MM: 1.64 (1.56–1.73)
- note: No per-locus 0/1/2 series is reported. The paper's per-locus analysis is the 27 ordered A/B/DR triples, and its conclusion is that within a total mismatch count the locus does not matter. Only two of the 27 triple HRs are printed in the text; the remaining 25 are in a table absent from the PMC version.
- A,B,DR triple [0,1,2]: HR 1.57 (1.41-1.75) vs [0,0,0]
- A,B,DR triple [2,1,0]: HR 1.27 (1.18-1.36) vs [0,0,0]
- A,B,DR triple [0,0,1]: 'only marginally significant' vs [0,0,0]; no number printed
- all other triples: 'All permutations were significantly different from the reference'; values in a table not in the PMC text
- Shape reported: Linear on the hazard-ratio scale (not on the log-hazard scale): the HR rises by a constant 0.11 units per additional mismatch in the full model and 0.16 in the reduced model. The authors describe the increase as 'stepwise' from 1 to 6 and the effect as 'additive', with 'each additional mismatch has the same effect'. The weighted fit through the 27 triples gives intercept 1.04 (1.00-1.08), so the zero-mismatch group lies essentially on the line and there is no separate zero-mismatch premium beyond the additive count. The full-model line is flatter than the reduced-model line; the two models' HRs are nearly identical with overlapping CIs at 1-2 mismatches and diverge with non-overlapping CIs at 3-6.; linearity tested: Weakly. After visual inspection ('On inspection the hazard ratios appeared to increase in stepwise fashion from 1 to 6'), an ordinary least-squares line was fitted to the Cox HR point estimates for categories 1-6 using SAS TRANSREG, and the slope with its 95% CI was reported (reduced 0.16, 0.15-0.17; full 0.11, 0.09-0.12). A weighted general linear model was then fitted to the 27 permutation HRs (slope 0.11, p<0.0001). There is no spline, no quadratic or departure-from-linearity term, no likelihood-based test for trend inside the Cox model, and no comparison against a log-linear or threshold alternative. The linearity claim is therefore a descriptive fit to point estimates, not a formal test against a non-linear alternative.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- locus identity x total mismatch count (57 pairwise comparisons of A/B/DR permutations within categories 1-5, Holm-Bonferroni corrected): 56 of 57 comparisons were not significant. The single significant pair is in category 3: [0,1,2] (2 DR mismatches) HR 1.57 (1.41-1.75) versus [2,1,0] (2 A mismatches) HR 1.27 (1.18-1.36); the authors note 'The difference is between HLA-A and DR, 0 mismatches at one locus and 2 mismatches at the other.' They treat the single hit as consistent with chance across 57 tests and conclude the effect is identical for each locus combination within a count. (1/57 significant after Holm-Bonferroni; exact p values not printed) [Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches', para 3; Discussion, 'First, ...']
- HLA mismatch count x covariate adjustment (ethnicity, clinical factors, induction, maintenance immunosuppression): Adding the full covariate set flattens the slope from 0.16 to 0.11 HR units per mismatch. At 1 and 2 mismatches the reduced- and full-model HRs are nearly identical with overlapping CIs; at 3-6 mismatches the CIs do not overlap. The authors read this as the covariates, chiefly induction and immunosuppression, moderating HLA risk mainly in the higher-mismatch categories, while at 0-2 mismatches 'it is primarily HLA that plays the role in allograft survival'. This is a descriptive comparison of two fitted lines, not a formal interaction test. (slope 0.16 (0.15-0.17) vs 0.11 (0.09-0.12)) [Results para 1; Discussion, 'Secondly, ...' and 'Third, ...'; Strengths of the Study]
- HLA mismatch x transplant era: Not formally tested. Era HRs fall steadily (0.80, 0.67, 0.50, 0.37 for the last four periods vs 1987-1993) while the HLA effect remains significant in the era-adjusted model; the authors conclude that 'in spite of the overall improvement in allograft survival in recent years, HLA mismatch remains a significant factor.' No era-stratified HLA HR is given. (era HRs 0.80, 0.67, 0.50, 0.37; no interaction estimate) [Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects on Kidney Survival']
- HLA mismatch x PRA / sensitisation, x cold ischaemia, x ethnicity: Not tested. PRA (<=50% vs >50%) and cold ischaemia (<=25 vs >25 h) enter only as covariates, and both have an 'unknown' stratum whose HR is not significantly different from the reference. For ethnicity the authors note non-Hispanic black HR 1.62 and Asian HR 0.81, and observe that Asians have more 4-6 mismatches yet better outcomes, so determinants beyond HLA drive the disparity. (no HLA interaction estimate reported) [Materials and Methods, 'Variable Definitions'; Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects']
- recipient age x donor age (16-level variable; not an HLA interaction): Recipient age quartiles Q2-Q4 vs Q1: HR 0.74, 0.65, 0.61 (p<0.0001 each); donor age Q2-Q4 vs Q1: 1.11, 1.37, 1.90 (p<0.0001 each, CIs non-overlapping). Within recipient Q1, donor Q2-Q4 give HR 1.09, 1.27, 1.61. In every recipient quartile a Q4 donor overwhelms the beneficial effect of recipient age. (as listed; CIs not printed in the text) [Results, last para; Discussion, 'Covariates Reflect Known Effects']

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "A significant linear relationship of hazard ratios was associated with HLA mismatch and affects allograft survival even during the recent periods of increasing success in renal transplantation." (Abstract, Conclusion (repeated verbatim in the Conclusion section))
- *C1* — "a 13% (HR = 1.13, 95% CI 1.06, 1.21) higher risk with 1 mismatch and a 64% (HR = 1.64,95% CI 1.56, 1.73) higher risk with 6 mismatches" (Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches on kidney allograft survival', para 1)
- *C2* — "the reduced model has a beta (slope) of 0.16 (95% CI 0.15, 0.17); the full model slope is 0.11 (95% CI 0.09, 0.12)" (Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches on kidney allograft survival', para 1)
- *C10* — "only one comparison in mismatch category 3 was statistically significant, triples [0,1,2] with HR=1.57 (95% CI 1.41, 1.75) and [2,1,0], HR=1.27 (95% CI 1.18, 1.36)" (Results, 'Impact of number of HLA mismatches on kidney allograft survival', para 3)
- *C10* — "This strongly suggests that, within mismatch category, the effect of the mismatch is identical for each locus combination" (Discussion, 'The Risk of Kidney Failure is Linear with HLA Mismatch', 'First, ...' para)
- *C9* — "For mismatch categories 1 and 2, the two observed HRs, for the reduced and full models, are nearly identical and their confidence intervals overlap" (Discussion, 'The Risk of Kidney Failure is Linear with HLA Mismatch', 'Secondly, ...' para)

**Limitations.** Deceased-donor, first-transplant, adult, US cohort only; no living donors, so absolute hazards, cold ischaemia and donor-quality structure do not transfer to living donation.; Registry antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts only; typing method and resolution are never stated; no HLA-C, -DQ, -DP, no allele-level or molecular (eplet/PIRCHE) mismatch anywhere in the paper.; No donor-specific antibody data; PRA is dichotomised at 50% and enters as a covariate only; no HLA x sensitisation test, so the paper cannot inform how a count should change once antibody status is known.; 'Linear' means an ordinary least-squares line through the Cox HR point estimates on the HR scale (not log-hazard), fitted after visual inspection of the pattern; with no spline, quadratic term or formal trend test, modest curvature - for example a slightly larger first-mismatch step - cannot be excluded.; HRs for 2, 3, 4 and 5 mismatches and 25 of the 27 permutation HRs exist only in tables and figures that the PMC author-manuscript text does not contain; the series must be completed from the publisher version.; The 'locus does not matter' conclusion rests on 56/57 non-significant comparisons after Holm-Bonferroni correction. Non-significance is not equivalence, the correction is conservative, and the one comparison that did survive points in the DR-worse-than-A direction.; Spans 1987-2013; era is adjusted for but no era-stratified HLA HR is reported, so the effect size specific to the modern era is not isolated.; Immunosuppression is captured only at discharge, with no time-dependent covariate for duration or change of therapy (the authors state the data do not allow it).; Nine covariates in the full model carry an 'unknown' category; the authors acknowledge that including missing values can produce biased hazard ratios.; Death with a functioning graft is censored rather than modelled as a competing risk.; Minor internal inconsistency: follow-up time is 994,558 allograft-years in the Results and 994,557 in the Strengths section..

### Foster BJ 2014 — Impact of HLA mismatch at first kidney transplant on lifetime with graft function in young recipients.

Foster BJ 2014, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.12643](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.12643). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley / American Journal of Transplantation); abstract retrieved from PubMed; no open-access full text.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | first deceased-donor kidney transplant recipients aged 21 years or younger at transplant, United States Renal Data System, 1988-2009; plus the subgroup relisted for a second deceased-donor transplant after first graft failure |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 8,433 first deceased-donor transplants; 2,498 listed for a second deceased-donor transplant after first graft failure |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; proportion of total observed lifetime spent with a functioning graft compared across three HLA mismatch categories, plus a time-to-event model for receipt of a second transplant after listing (hazard ratios reported; model covariates not stated in the abstract) |
| typing resolution | not stated; mismatch is expressed as a total count on a 0-6 scale, which is the conventional antigen-level HLA-A + HLA-B + HLA-DR count in USRDS/UNOS data, but the abstract names neither the loci nor the resolution |
| outcome | primary: proportion of total observed lifetime with a functioning graft after first transplant; secondary: receipt of (time to) a second deceased-donor transplant after being listed |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract; the cohort was transplanted 1988-2009 and followed to the end of USRDS observation |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers a question almost no other HLA study asks: not 'does a mismatch shorten this graft?' but 'over a young recipient's whole observed life, how much functioning-graft time does the mismatch level at the FIRST transplant actually buy or cost?' That reframing is exactly the currency a pre-screen tool should speak in, because a matching rule is only worth applying if it changes lifetime outcome rather than one graft's half-life. It supports C2 and C9 with an unusually coarse but honest three-level dose-response (0-1 vs 2-3 vs 4-6 mismatches) that is monotonic and, in the authors' own words, small: a 15% relative gain at the good end and a 12% relative loss at the bad end. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen is limited and mostly directional. The population is deceased-donor, paediatric/young-adult (21 or under), and American, so the absolute numbers do not carry over: young recipients have the highest immunological risk, the longest expected lifetime, and the greatest number of future re-transplants, which inflates both the value of matching and the value of avoiding sensitisation relative to an adult living-donor cohort. What does transfer is the paper's second, allocation-facing message, which is why it is also tagged C13: the mismatch level chosen at the first transplant continued to affect access to the second transplant (4-6 MM recipients were less likely to be re-transplanted, HR 0.87), so a pre-screen that ignores HLA is not only trading graft-years but also future donor access for young patients who will need another kidney. Finally, the mismatch count here is a low-resolution total count with no per-locus and no antibody data, which is precisely the information state of the Iranian pre-screen, so the paper is methodologically well matched to a one-field, antibody-unknown setting even though it says nothing about which locus is doing the work.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- proportion of total observed lifetime with a functioning graft after first transplant: 4-6 HLA mismatches vs 2-3 mismatches (reference) at first transplant — relative difference in proportion of observed lifetime with graft function (%) -12, p=<0.0001; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- proportion of total observed lifetime with a functioning graft after first transplant: 0-1 HLA mismatches vs 2-3 mismatches (reference) at first transplant — relative difference in proportion of observed lifetime with graft function (%) 15, p=<0.0001; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- receipt of a second deceased-donor transplant after listing: 4-6 HLA mismatches at first transplant vs 2-3 mismatches (reference) — HR 0.87 (0.76–0.98), p=0.03; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]
- receipt of a second deceased-donor transplant after listing: 0-1 HLA mismatches at first transplant vs 2-3 mismatches (reference) — HR 1.26 (0.99–1.6), p=0.06; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0-1 MM: +15% of observed lifetime with graft function vs the 2-3 group; 2-3 MM: reference; 4-6 MM: -12% of observed lifetime with graft function vs the 2-3 group
- Shape reported: step / monotonic across three pooled categories: more mismatch, less lifetime with graft function and less access to a second transplant. Because the middle category is the reference and the two contrasts are of similar magnitude in opposite directions (+15%, -12%), the abstract is consistent with a roughly even gradient across the three bands, but no functional form is fitted or claimed.; linearity tested: not tested in anything visible in the abstract - no trend test, no P for trend, no per-mismatch (0,1,2,3,4,5,6) estimate, no spline, no threshold analysis. Mismatch enters only as a three-level categorical variable.; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "We compared proportion of total observed lifetime with graft function after first transplant, and waiting times for a second transplant between individuals with different levels of HLA mismatch (MM) at first transplant." (Abstract, aim sentence)
- *C2* — "Compared with recipients of 2-3 MM first grafts, 4-6 MM graft recipients spent 12% less of their time and 0-1 MM recipients 15% more time with a functioning graft after the first transplant (both p < 0.0001)" (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C9* — "4-6 MM recipients were significantly less likely (hazard ratio [HR] 0.87 [95% confidence interval 0.76, 0.98]; p = 0.03), and 0-1 MM recipients more likely (HR 1.26 [0.99, 1.60]; p = 0.06) to receive a second transplant after listing" (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C2* — "The benefits of better HLA matching at first transplant on lifetime with graft function are significant, but relatively small." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)
- *C13* — "As HLA matching has been progressively de-emphasized in the American deceased donor (DD) kidney allocation algorithm, concerns have been raised that poor matching at first transplant may lead to greater sensitization" (Abstract, Background sentence)
- *C9* — "We studied patients recorded in the United States Renal Data System (1988-2009) who received a first DD transplant at age <=21 years (n = 8433)" (Abstract, Methods sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. PMC has no full text and no author manuscript for this PMID, so the tables, the per-locus breakdown (if any), the covariate list, the follow-up duration and any sensitivity analyses could not be read. Every number in this file comes from four sentences.; Mismatch is collapsed into three broad bands (0-1 / 2-3 / 4-6). Zero mismatch is not estimated separately, so this paper cannot quantify a true zero-mismatch premium and cannot compare the first mismatch against the second - the very question C9 asks.; No per-locus result at all. The abstract never names which loci make up the 0-6 count, so the paper contributes nothing to C3 through C8 and cannot be used to weight DR against B or A.; Deceased-donor only. The review's target setting is living donation, where donor quality is higher and more uniform and where HLA has a proportionally larger share of the residual risk; deceased-donor estimates are not directly portable.; Recipients were 21 years or younger. This is the highest-immunological-risk, highest-non-adherence, longest-expected-lifetime group, and also the group US allocation gave paediatric priority to. Effect sizes are not generalisable to an adult Iranian cohort in either direction without assumption.; Era spans 1988-2009, crossing at least three immunosuppression generations and two major allocation changes. The abstract reports no era-stratified estimate, so a 2026 reader cannot tell how much of the effect survives modern immunosuppression (the C1 question).; No antibody data. Sensitisation is the paper's stated motivation, yet the abstract reports no PRA/cPRA or DSA result - only the downstream access proxy (whether a second transplant was received). The mechanism is assumed, not measured.; The second-transplant outcome is an ACCESS outcome shaped by US allocation policy (points for waiting time, paediatric priority, cPRA), not a biological outcome. It will not transfer to an Iranian living-donor pathway, where a second donor comes from a family or a national living-donor programme rather than a points-based deceased-donor queue.; The 0-1 MM access result (HR 1.26) has a CI crossing 1 and p = 0.06; the authors themselves do not call it significant. It should not be quoted as evidence that good matching improves re-transplant access.; Adjustment is unknown. The abstract does not say what the hazard ratios were adjusted for, so residual confounding by centre, race, blood group, era and paediatric-priority status cannot be excluded - and in the US, mismatch level correlates strongly with recipient race, which independently predicts both graft loss and re-listing..

### Gharesi-Fard B 2014 — HLA-DRB1 and susceptibility to kidney allograft rejection in Southern Iranian patients.

Gharesi-Fard B 2014, *Molecular Biology Reports*, [DOI 10.1007/s11033-014-3427-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11033-014-3427-8). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown (Springer subscription journal; PubMed metadata carried no pmc field and convert_article_ids returned no PMCID, so no PMC full text exists for this PMID).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 41 kidney transplant recipients and 203 normal healthy controls, Shiraz, southern Iran |
| donor type | not stated |
| n | 41 recipients; 203 healthy controls |
| design | single-centre case-control genetic association study; HLA-DRB1 allele-group frequency comparison plus donor-recipient DRB1 sharing versus acute rejection; no multivariable or time-to-event model reported in the retrieved text |
| typing resolution | low resolution / first-field allelic group (PCR with sequence-specific primers, PCR-SSP), e.g. DRB1*04, DRB1*07, DRB1*14; HLA-DRB1 locus only |
| outcome | acute kidney transplant rejection (primary); secondary: HBV, HCV and CMV infection in recipients, and recipient-versus-control allele frequency (ESRD susceptibility) |
| follow up | not stated |
| other factors modelled | hepatitis B virus infection, hepatitis C virus infection, cytomegalovirus infection |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the few published Iranian datasets that tests HLA-DRB1 against kidney transplant rejection, and it comes from Shiraz, so it speaks directly to the review's question about regional evidence and regional typing practice (C15). Its typing method is exactly the resolution our pre-screen will face: PCR-SSP reported at allelic-group / first-field level (DRB1*04, DRB1*07, DRB1*14), i.e. the same one-field granularity Iranian lab reports carry, which supports the position that a one-field DRB1 pre-screen is the realistic ceiling in this setting rather than a self-imposed compromise. Its answer to the matching question is null: neither HLA-DRB1 allelic group distribution nor donor-recipient DRB1 sharing was associated with acute rejection (P > 0.05). That null is almost uninformative for the review, because with 41 recipients the study cannot detect the DR effect sizes reported in registry cohorts (hazard ratios of roughly 1.1 to 1.3), so it must be read as absence of evidence rather than evidence of absence and must never be cited as showing DR matching does not matter. Transfer to a living-donor, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen is further limited because the retrieved text never states donor type, immunosuppression, PRA/sensitisation, cold ischaemia or follow-up, and reports no effect estimate or confidence interval for any HLA comparison. Its usable contribution is therefore contextual: it documents Iranian centre practice (DRB1-only, low-resolution PCR-SSP typing) and supplies a regional citation, not a quantitative matching estimate.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- acute kidney transplant rejection: HLA-DRB1 allelic group distribution and donor-recipient HLA-DRB1 sharing (association with susceptibility to acute rejection) — p-value only (no OR/HR/RR reported in the retrieved text) None, p=> 0.05; adjusted for not stated; no multivariable model reported in the retrieved text [Abstract]
- recipient (transplant/ESRD) status versus healthy control - NOT rejection: HLA-DRB1*14 allele frequency, kidney transplant recipients vs 203 healthy controls — p-value only (no OR reported in the retrieved text) None, p=0.03; adjusted for unadjusted allele-frequency comparison; no correction for multiple comparisons stated in the retrieved text [Abstract]
- recipient (transplant/ESRD) status versus healthy control - NOT rejection: HLA-DRB1*04 allele frequency, kidney transplant recipients vs 203 healthy controls — p-value only (no OR reported in the retrieved text) None, p=0.05; adjusted for unadjusted allele-frequency comparison; no correction for multiple comparisons stated in the retrieved text [Abstract]
- hepatitis C virus infection in kidney transplant recipients - NOT rejection: possession of the HLA-DRB1*07 allele versus not — p-value only (no OR reported in the retrieved text) None, p=0.009; adjusted for unadjusted; no correction for multiple comparisons stated in the retrieved text [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: No 0/1/2 mismatch series is reported. The retrieved text gives only a null result for HLA-DRB1 allelic group distribution and for donor-recipient DRB1 sharing versus acute rejection (P > 0.05), with no counts, percentages or effect estimates by number of shared or mismatched DRB1 antigens.
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested; no mismatch-count variable is analysed in the retrieved text; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "The current study investigates the allele frequency of HLA-DRB1 in 41 recipient kidney transplant and 203 normal healthy controls by polymerase chain reaction using sequence specific primers." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "statistical analysis of the allele frequencies didn't show any significant association between HLA-DRB1 allelic group distributions or sharing and susceptibility to acute kidney transplant rejection (P > 0.05)" (Abstract)
- *C15* — "the results of the present study did not showed relation between HLA-DRB1 allele's frequencies or sharing and kidney transplantation outcome" (Abstract, conclusion sentence)
- *C15* — "Comparing the allele frequencies between HLA-DRB1*14 and DRB1*04 allelic showed a significant difference in controls and patients (P = 0.03 and P = 0.05 respectively)." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "The results of the present study also showed a significant association between possession of HLA-DRB1*07 allele in kidney transplant recipients and hepatitis C virus infection (P = 0.009)." (Abstract)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no PMC record exists for this PMID, so the per-allele tables, the operational definition of DRB1 'sharing', the rejection ascertainment and any effect estimates in the full text could not be read.; Very small sample: 41 transplant recipients. Badly underpowered for the DR effect sizes seen in registry cohorts (HR approximately 1.1 to 1.3), so the null on DRB1 sharing is absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.; No effect size, no confidence interval and no adjusted estimate is reported for any HLA comparison in the retrieved text - only bare p-values.; Single locus: HLA-DRB1 only. No HLA-A, -B, -C, -DQ or -DP, so the paper says nothing about locus ranking, about DQ, or about class I.; Low-resolution first-field typing (PCR-SSP allelic groups). Useful as a description of regional practice, but it cannot address molecular/eplet mismatch or any high-resolution question.; Multiple comparisons across many DRB1 allelic groups with no stated correction; P = 0.03 and P = 0.05 (DRB1*14, DRB1*04) would very likely not survive correction, and P = 0.05 sits exactly on the threshold.; The DRB1*14 / DRB1*04 comparison is recipients versus healthy controls, i.e. a disease-susceptibility question, not a transplant-matching question; it must not be transcribed into the review as a matching effect.; Donor type (living versus deceased) is not stated, nor are immunosuppression regimen, PRA/sensitisation status, cold ischaemia, donor age or follow-up duration, so transferability to a living-donor pre-screen is unverified.; Case-control design against healthy controls cannot estimate graft survival; no time-to-event analysis is reported.; Antibody/DSA status is not assessed at all, so the paper cannot inform the antibody-status-unknown part of the pre-screen question..

### Foster BJ 2013 — Relative importance of HLA mismatch and donor age to graft survival in young kidney transplant recipients.

Foster BJ 2013, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e318298f9db](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e318298f9db). Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown (Wolters Kluwer / Transplantation, publisher copyright; no open-access PMC deposit found).

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First kidney transplant recipients aged less than 21 years recorded in the U.S. Renal Data System (USRDS); deceased-donor (DD) and living-donor (LD) recipients analysed in separate models. Transplant era, country restriction beyond the US registry, and cohort size are not stated in the abstract. |
| donor type | both |
| n | not stated in the abstract |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort (USRDS); separate Cox proportional hazards models for DD and LD recipients; adjusted 5-year probability of graft survival estimated for each donor age x HLA mismatch combination and compared across combinations |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract. The top mismatch category '4-6 MM' implies a 0-6 total-count scale, which in USRDS/UNOS practice of this era is antigen-level (low-resolution) HLA-A, -B and -DR; the abstract itself never names the loci or the resolution, so this is inference and is flagged as such. |
| outcome | graft survival (adjusted 5-year probability of graft survival). Whether graft failure was death-censored is not stated in the abstract. |
| follow up | 5-year graft survival probabilities are reported; actual follow-up duration and median follow-up are not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | donor age (as <35, 35-44, >=45 years categories), donor type (deceased vs living; modelled as two separate Cox models, not as one model with an interaction), unspecified adjustment covariates (the abstract says the 5-year graft survival probabilities are 'adjusted' but does not list the covariates) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review for the donor-age-versus-HLA-mismatch trade-off (C11) and for whether HLA mismatch still matters inside living donation (C14). Its headline result is directly on both: in recipients under 21, HLA mismatch was significantly associated with graft survival in BOTH deceased-donor and living-donor transplants, whereas donor age was significant only in deceased donors - which is the single most transferable finding for a living-donor pre-screen, because it says the donor-quality axis that dominates deceased-donor allocation does not simply swamp HLA once the donor is living. The paper also quantifies the exchange rate qualitatively: a 0-1 mismatch graft from a donor 45 or older bought survival no worse than a 4-6 mismatch graft from a donor under 35, i.e. good matching can buy back a decade or more of donor age, which is exactly the kind of trade-off an Iranian living-donor ranking function has to encode when it weighs HLA against donor age. Transfer is limited in three ways that matter here.
