First, the population is paediatric and young-adult recipients (<21 years), the most immunologically responsive group, so the HLA effect measured here is probably an upper bound for a general adult Iranian recipient pool. Second, HLA mismatch is collapsed into 0-1, 2-3 and 4-6, so the paper cannot tell a pre-screen anything about per-locus weighting (no DR, DQ, B, A or C breakdown at all) and cannot separate a zero-mismatch premium from a one-mismatch result - both of which are core questions of this review. Third, the abstract-only access means no hazard ratio, confidence interval, p-value or sample size is available, so this paper can support the direction and the qualitative trade-off but must not be used as a numeric weight anywhere; the antigen-level, one-field typing implied by the 0-6 scale is at least well matched to the low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown setting the pre-screen targets.

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0-1 MM: None; 2-3 MM: None; 4-6 MM: None
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested, or at least not reported in the abstract; the three-category grouping precludes any within-category assessment of shape; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x donor type (deceased donor vs living donor): HLA mismatch was significantly associated with graft survival in both the deceased-donor and the living-donor model, whereas donor age was significantly associated with graft survival only among deceased donors. This is the paper's central effect-modification claim and the one that supports C14: HLA matching continues to matter within living donation, where the donor-age gradient does not. (no numeric estimate, interaction coefficient or interaction p-value printed in the abstract) [Abstract, results sentence]
- HLA mismatch x donor age (within deceased donors): The two offset one another. Relative to grafts from donors under 35 with 4-6 mismatches, survival was not significantly different for 0-1 and 2-3 mismatch grafts from donors aged 35-44, nor for 0-1 mismatch grafts from donors aged 45 or older. Better matching therefore compensates for older donor age and younger donor age compensates for worse matching. (no numeric estimate or p-value printed in the abstract; the comparisons are reported only as 'not significantly different') [Abstract, results sentence]
- donor type x donor age x HLA mismatch (living donors versus all deceased donors): The most poorly matched grafts from the oldest living donors had survival similar to or better than any deceased-donor graft, including well-matched grafts from young deceased donors. Donor type dominates the comparison across the DD/LD boundary even though HLA still discriminates within each donor type. (no numeric estimate printed in the abstract) [Abstract, results sentence]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "The American deceased-donor (DD) kidney allocation algorithm for children emphasizes the importance of younger donors and shorter waiting times over human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching." (Abstract, background sentence)
- *C11* — "we estimated the adjusted 5-year probability of graft survival for each donor age-HLA MM combination" (Abstract, methods sentence)
- *C14* — "Both donor age and HLA MM were significantly associated with DD graft survival, whereas only HLA MM had a significant association with LD graft survival." (Abstract, results sentence)
- *C11* — "Compared with DD grafts from less than 35-year-old 4-6 MM donors, survival was not significantly different for 0-1 and 2-3 MM grafts from 35- to 44-year-old donors or for 0-1 MM grafts from donors 45 years old or older." (Abstract, results sentence)
- *C14* — "The most poorly matched grafts from the oldest LD had survival similar to or better than any DD." (Abstract, results sentence)
- *C11* — "The advantages of younger donors offset the disadvantages of poorer HLA matching, and better HLA matching offsets the disadvantages of older donor age." (Abstract, conclusion sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only access. No PMC deposit exists (no pmcid returned for the PMID or the DOI), so no hazard ratio, confidence interval, p-value, cohort size, covariate list or per-locus result could be extracted. The paper can support direction and the qualitative trade-off but must never be used as a source of a numeric weight.; HLA mismatch is collapsed into three coarse categories (0-1, 2-3, 4-6). Zero mismatch is pooled with one mismatch, so the zero-mismatch premium cannot be isolated, and the shape of the dose-response cannot be assessed.; No per-locus analysis whatsoever. DR, DQ, B, A, C and DP are never separated in the abstract, so the paper contributes nothing to the locus-weighting questions (C3-C8) of this review.; Recipients are under 21 years old. Paediatric and young-adult recipients are the most immunologically responsive group and also have distinct adherence-driven late graft loss, so the measured HLA effect is likely larger than it would be in a general adult recipient pool.; Deceased-donor and living-donor recipients were fitted in separate Cox models, so 'HLA mismatch matters in LD but donor age does not' is a stratified observation, not a tested interaction; no interaction p-value is reported in the abstract.; The graft survival endpoint is not defined in the abstract (death-censored versus all-cause graft failure), and follow-up duration and transplant era are not stated.; No sensitisation/PRA, donor-specific antibody, cold ischaemia time, ethnicity or immunosuppression regimen information appears in the abstract, so none of the standard effect modifiers can be checked and residual confounding by these factors cannot be excluded.; US registry data with an allocation algorithm that itself prioritises young donors over HLA matching; the resulting donor-age/HLA joint distribution is allocation-driven and does not resemble an Iranian living-donor pool.; The PubMed abstract text renders the deceased-donor inclusion rule as 'a DD 5 years old or younger', which is inconsistent with the donor age strata the same abstract uses (<35, 35-44, >=45 years). This looks like an inequality symbol lost in the abstract rendering; the true inclusion rule could not be confirmed without the full text and has not been guessed at..

### Süsal C 2013 — Current role of human leukocyte antigen matching in kidney transplantation.

Süsal C 2013, *Curr Opin Organ Transplant*, [DOI 10.1097/MOT.0b013e3283636ddf](https://doi.org/10.1097/MOT.0b013e3283636ddf). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Lippincott Williams & Wilkins); no PMC deposit. convert_article_ids returned no pmcid for PMID 23838649, so no open full text exists to quote from..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | not stated in the abstract; a narrative review of published kidney-transplant series, predominantly Collaborative Transplant Study (CTS) registry analyses from the authors' own centre (Heidelberg). Donor type, era, country mix, sample size and follow-up are all unretrievable from the abstract. |
| donor type | both |
| design | narrative (non-systematic) review; no pooled analysis, no search strategy, no new primary data reported in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated; the MeSH term 'Alleles' hints that allele-level typing is discussed, but the abstract does not say at what resolution any cited result was produced |
| outcome | graft survival; immunosuppressive drug dosage; side-effects of immunosuppression (non-Hodgkin lymphoma, hip fracture, death from infection); degree of sensitisation after graft loss and relisting |
| follow up | not stated |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a position review by the Heidelberg/CTS group written specifically to answer the review question 'does HLA matching still matter now that graft survival has improved?' — which is the exact objection an Iranian living-donor programme will face when it is asked to spend effort on HLA at all. Its contribution to our review is C1 (matching still predicts outcome under modern immunosuppression) and, more distinctively, C11-adjacent effect modification: it is one of the few sources arguing that the benefit of matching is not only graft survival but the downstream consequences of needing less immunosuppression (lower drug dosage, fewer malignancies/fractures/infectious deaths) and a lower degree of sensitisation if the graft is lost and the patient is relisted. That second argument transfers well to Iran: a living-donor pre-screen that picks a better-matched donor from among several willing relatives buys a re-transplantable, less-sensitised patient later, which matters more in a programme with limited deceased-donor backup. The transfer is nevertheless weak in three ways: the review is deceased-donor-allocation-centric ('organ sharing', 'kidney exchange'), so it does not speak to choosing among living donors; it reports no numbers at all in the retrievable text, so it cannot calibrate any weight in our matching score; and it says nothing about typing resolution, so it neither supports nor contradicts the use of one-field (antigen-level) typing. It also does not address antibody status, so it cannot inform an antibody-unknown pre-screen. Treat it as a citable framing/justification source for C1 and C11, never as a source of an effect size.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested; the retrievable text (abstract) contains no mismatch-count series, no per-locus breakdown and no test of trend, linearity, spline or threshold. The review's underlying CTS analyses report such series, but they are not visible here and must be taken from the primary papers.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching × immunosuppressive burden: Better-matched recipients are reported to receive lower dosages of immunosuppressive agents, i.e. the benefit of matching is partly mediated by (and modifies) the amount of immunosuppression needed. Stated qualitatively only. [Abstract, Recent findings]
- HLA matching × side-effects of immunosuppression: Better matching is associated with a lower incidence of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, hip fractures and death from infection — outcomes outside graft survival that follow from the lower drug burden. Stated qualitatively only. [Abstract, Recent findings]
- HLA matching × graft loss and relisting (future sensitisation): Patients who lose a better-matched graft and are relisted for retransplant show a lower grade of sensitisation, i.e. the value of matching extends into the retransplant window. Stated qualitatively only. [Abstract, Summary/Recent findings]
- HLA matching × ethnic minority status: NOT RETRIEVABLE. The MeSH indexing includes 'Minority Groups', which strongly suggests the full review discusses the allocation disadvantage that HLA matching imposes on ethnic minorities, but no such statement appears in the abstract and nothing may be attributed to this paper on that point without the full text. [MeSH terms only, not in retrievable text]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "With graft survival rates steadily improving during the recent years, there is debate whether donor kidneys should still be allocated according to compatibility for human leukocyte antigens (HLA)." (Abstract, Purpose of review)
- *C1* — "Recent studies argue for continued kidney exchange efforts for achieving better HLA compatibility." (Abstract, Recent findings)
- *C11* — "In this modern era of immunosuppression, better HLA matching is associated not only with better graft survival, but also with the administration of lower dosages of immunosuppressive agents" (Abstract, Recent findings)
- *C11* — "a lower incidence of side-effects of immunosuppression such as non-Hodgkin lymphoma, hip fractures, and death from infection" (Abstract, Recent findings)
- *C11* — "a lower grade of sensitization if a patient has lost a kidney graft and is relisted for a retransplant" (Abstract, Recent findings)
- *C1* — "Despite the overall improved graft survival rates in the recent years, the data continue to support organ sharing based on HLA matching in kidney transplantation." (Abstract, Summary)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no PMC deposit, publisher copyright. Every field below the bibliography rests on ~120 words of structured abstract.; No effect size of any kind is retrievable: no HR, OR, RR, percentage, confidence interval or p-value appears in the abstract, so this paper can contribute no number to a pooled or calibrated estimate.; Narrative, non-systematic review by the group that generated much of the evidence it reviews (Collaborative Transplant Study, Heidelberg); no search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no risk-of-bias assessment, and a foreseeable direction of interest in favour of continued HLA-based allocation.; The claimed associations (lower drug dosage, fewer side-effects, less sensitisation) are observational and confounded by indication: better-matched recipients are also, in registry data, less sensitised, more often first grafts and often better-matched because they are of the commoner haplotypes — the abstract reports no adjustment.; Deceased-donor allocation framing ('organ sharing', 'kidney exchange'); it does not address selecting among candidate living donors, which is our use case.; Typing resolution is never stated, so the paper cannot be used to argue for or against one-field/antigen-level typing.; No antibody/DSA dimension in the retrievable text, so it does not inform an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen.; No per-locus (A/B/C/DR/DQ/DP) discrimination and no mismatch-count series in the retrievable text, so it supports none of C2-C10.; 2013 vintage: 'modern era of immunosuppression' means tacrolimus/MMF-era cohorts; it predates the eplet/PIRCHE molecular-mismatch literature entirely..

### Wiebe C 2013 — Class II HLA epitope matching-A strategy to minimize de novo donor-specific antibody development and improve outcomes.

Wiebe C 2013, *American Journal of Transplantation (Am J Transplant) 13(12):3114-22*, [DOI 10.1111/ajt.12478](https://doi.org/10.1111/ajt.12478). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley/AJT). Re-checked 2026-09-07: convert_article_ids returns no pmcid for PMID 24164958 and get_article_metadata returns no pmc identifier, so there is no PMC deposit and no full text. Everything below is from the PubMed abstract and the PubMed metadata record..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | renal transplant recipients, 286 donor-recipient pairs, single centre (University of Manitoba, Winnipeg, Canada, per the first author's affiliation in the PubMed record); transplant era not stated in the abstract; PubMed MeSH age terms are Adult and Middle Aged only |
| donor type | not stated in abstract |
| n | 286 donor-recipient pairs |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; HLAMatchmaker software used to count epitope (eplet) mismatches across 395 potential HLA-DR/DQ/DP conformational epitopes; dnDSA detected and epitope specificities assigned by single-antigen HLA bead analysis, correlated with known monoclonal alloantibody epitope targets; an optimal per-locus threshold was derived, plus a multivariate analysis of individual epitope specificities |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract. HLAMatchmaker eplet counting requires allele-level (two-field) DR/DQ/DP typing or imputation, but the abstract does not say how typing was obtained; the abstract explicitly contrasts the method with 'traditional low-resolution antigen-based matching' |
| outcome | de novo donor-specific antibody (dnDSA) against HLA-DR and HLA-DQ (Class II dnDSA); graft survival is invoked in the title and background but no graft-survival analysis is reported in the abstract |
| follow up | median 6.9 years (stated for the below-threshold groups) |
| other factors modelled | not stated in abstract; the only multivariate analysis described is of individual epitope specificities as predictors of Class II dnDSA, with no clinical covariates named |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the origin paper for the Class II eplet-mismatch thresholds (10 for HLA-DR, 17 for HLA-DQ) that the same Manitoba group later developed into the molecular-mismatch risk categories, so it is the primary source for C12: molecular mismatch expressed as thresholds, and the authors' claim that epitope matching outperforms antigen-level matching. It also bears on C4, because the DQ eplet load separating dnDSA formers from non-formers was higher than the DR load (27.5 vs 17.3 for DQ against 21.4 vs 13.2 for DR), and below the derived threshold DR dnDSA fell to zero while 2.7% still formed DQ dnDSA, which is consistent with DQ being the harder Class II locus to render safe. The outcome is de novo DSA, so the paper speaks to recipients who start without donor-specific antibody; that is the assumed but unverified state of the Iranian pre-screen population, and with antibody status unknown the paper cannot distinguish de novo from pre-existing sensitisation. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field pre-screen is weak on the mechanics: eplet counting needs two-field donor and recipient typing or imputation, which a one-field pre-screen cannot supply, so the 10/17 thresholds cannot be applied directly, and the paper positions low-resolution antigen matching as the inferior comparator rather than validating it. The usable transfer is directional, not numeric: it supports weighting DQ at least as heavily as DR in a Class II pre-screen, and supports treating antigen-level Class II matching as a coarse proxy for an epitope load the pre-screen cannot measure. The absolute numbers should not be carried over, given a single Canadian centre of 286 pairs, thresholds derived and tested in the same cohort, and no stated donor type, immunosuppression or baseline antibody status.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA-DR dnDSA alone: HLA-DR locus-specific epitope mismatch count, patients who developed HLA-DR dnDSA alone vs those who did not — epitope (eplet) mismatch count, two-group comparison; the abstract does not say whether these are means or medians 21.4 vs. 13.2, p=<0.02; adjusted for not stated in abstract [Abstract]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA alone: HLA-DQ locus-specific epitope mismatch count, patients who developed HLA-DQ dnDSA alone vs those who did not — epitope (eplet) mismatch count, two-group comparison; the abstract does not say whether these are means or medians 27.5 vs. 17.3, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated in abstract [Abstract]
- HLA-DR dnDSA: patients at or below the derived HLA-DR epitope mismatch threshold of 10; cumulative incidence after a median of 6.9 years — percentage 0.0; adjusted for unadjusted crude incidence [Abstract]
- HLA-DQ dnDSA: patients at or below the derived HLA-DQ epitope mismatch threshold of 17; cumulative incidence after a median of 6.9 years — percentage 2.7; adjusted for unadjusted crude incidence [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: threshold MM: 10 eplet mismatches; below_threshold_dnDSA MM: 0% developed HLA-DR dnDSA after a median of 6.9 years; dnDSA_former_vs_non_former_load MM: 21.4 vs. 13.2 (p < 0.02); 0 MM: None; 1 MM: None; 2 MM: None
- DQ: threshold MM: 17 eplet mismatches; below_threshold_dnDSA MM: 2.7% developed HLA-DQ dnDSA after a median of 6.9 years; dnDSA_former_vs_non_former_load MM: 27.5 vs. 17.3 (p < 0.001); 0 MM: None; 1 MM: None; 2 MM: None
- DP: note MM: DP conformational epitopes were included in the 395 HLA-DR/DQ/DP epitopes characterised, but no DP threshold and no DP dnDSA result appear in the abstract
- Shape reported: threshold. The abstract reports a derived optimal per-locus eplet-count threshold (10 DR, 17 DQ) below which Class II dnDSA development is minimal, not a graded per-count curve. No antigen-level 0/1/2 mismatch series is reported.; linearity tested: not reported in the abstract. The abstract states only that an optimal threshold was defined for each locus; the method used to select the threshold, and any test of whether risk rises smoothly rather than stepwise, are not described in the abstract.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "An optimal threshold for epitope mismatches (10 for HLA-DR, 17 for HLA-DQ) was defined that was associated with minimal development of Class II dnDSA." (Abstract)
- *C12* — "Applying these thresholds, zero and 2.7% of patients developed dnDSA against HLA-DR and HLA-DQ, respectively, after a median of 6.9 years." (Abstract)
- *C4* — "Locus-specific epitope mismatches were more numerous in patients who developed HLA-DR dnDSA alone (21.4 vs. 13.2, p < 0.02) or HLA-DQ dnDSA alone (27.5 vs. 17.3, p < 0.001)." (Abstract)
- *C12* — "HLA-DR and DQ epitope matching outperforms traditional low-resolution antigen-based matching and has the potential to minimize the risk of de novo Class II DSA development, thereby improving long-term graft outcome." (Abstract)
- *C4* — "Epitope specificity analysis revealed that 3 HLA-DR and 3 HLA-DQ epitopes were independent multivariate predictors of Class II dnDSA." (Abstract)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no PMC deposit exists, so the Results tables could not be read. Group sizes for the below-threshold strata, confidence intervals, the multivariate model coefficients, the DP results, and the numeric comparison against antigen-level matching are all unavailable.; Single centre (University of Manitoba), 286 donor-recipient pairs. Donor type (living vs deceased), transplant era, immunosuppression protocol, induction, and baseline antibody status are not stated in the abstract.; The outcome is dnDSA, a surrogate, not graft failure. The 'improve outcomes' claim in the title rests on the background statement that dnDSA carries 40% lower graft survival at 10 years, which is prior literature, not a graft-survival analysis reported here.; The 10 and 17 thresholds were derived in the same 286-pair cohort in which their performance is reported, so the 0% and 2.7% figures are in-sample and optimistic; no external validation appears in the abstract.; No confidence intervals anywhere in the abstract, and the abstract does not state whether 21.4/13.2 and 27.5/17.3 are means or medians, so the comparisons cannot be re-analysed.; HLAMatchmaker eplet definitions and the software version have been revised repeatedly since 2013, so the exact threshold counts are version-dependent and are not interchangeable with eplet loads computed by current software.; Eplet counting requires allele-level (two-field) DR/DQ typing or imputation. The abstract does not state how donor and recipient typing was obtained, and the method cannot be applied to a one-field pre-screen without an imputation step that carries its own error.; Age range is not stated in the abstract; PubMed MeSH lists Adult and Middle Aged, but whether paediatric recipients were included cannot be determined from the retrieved text.; Recipients with pre-existing DSA are, by the definition of a de novo outcome, outside the question this paper answers, so it says nothing about an antibody-status-unknown population where prevalent sensitisation cannot be excluded..

### Lim WH 2012 — Human leukocyte antigen mismatches associated with increased risk of rejection, graft failure, and death independent of initial immunosuppression in renal transplant recipients.

Lim WH 2012, *Clinical Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/j.1399-0012.2012.01654.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1399-0012.2012.01654.x). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley); no PMC record exists for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned pmid only, no pmcid), so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | live-donor and deceased-donor renal transplant recipients in Australia and New Zealand transplanted 1998-2009, captured by the Australia and New Zealand Dialysis and Transplant Registry (ANZDATA) |
| donor type | both |
| n | 8036 |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; multivariable adjusted models comparing outcomes by number of HLA mismatches and by HLA-loci mismatches. The regression family (Cox vs other) and the covariate list are NOT stated in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved text. The analysis uses HLA-AB and HLA-DR mismatch counts with a 0-6 total, which is the classic serologic/antigen-level (broad or split antigen) A/B/DR scheme, but the abstract never states the resolution and no full text was available to confirm it. |
| outcome | acute rejection; all-cause graft failure; death-censored graft failure; patient death |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract; transplants performed 1998-2009 with registry follow-up of unstated duration |
| other factors modelled | initial immunosuppressive regimen (explicitly examined; 'no consistent association ... between initial immunosuppressive regimen and outcomes'), transplant era (claimed in the conclusion: effects 'independent of immunosuppression and transplant era'), unspecified further covariates - the abstract says only 'the adjusted models' and never lists them |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the few large registry cohorts that deliberately pools LIVING and deceased donor kidney transplants and then asks whether HLA mismatch still predicts outcome under contemporary (1998-2009, tacrolimus/MMF-era) immunosuppression, which is exactly review question C1, and it answers yes. It matters more than its size suggests for a living-donor pre-screen because the one piece of effect modification it reports runs in the living-donor direction: the incremental rejection risk per mismatch was reportedly HIGHER in live donor transplants, i.e. HLA matching is not rendered irrelevant by the donor-quality advantage of a living graft, which is the central worry behind claim C14. The mismatch metric it uses - a total count over HLA-A, B and DR with per-locus 'HLA-AB' and 'HLA-DR' groupings - is a low-resolution, one-field-compatible metric, so it transfers directly to an Iranian pre-screen that has only antigen-level typing and cannot compute eplet or PIRCHE loads. Its reference category is 0 mismatch and the reported direction is monotonic, which is the qualitative form of C2. The transfer is nonetheless weak in three ways: the abstract publishes no HR, no CI and no per-count series, so this paper can corroborate the DIRECTION of the dose-response but cannot contribute a single number to a pooled estimate; the ANZDATA population is predominantly European-ancestry with different haplotype frequencies from an Iranian donor pool; and antibody/DSA status is not mentioned at all, so it neither supports nor refutes the antibody-unknown assumption of the pre-screen. Its practical value to this review is as a modern-era, living-donor-inclusive corroboration of C1/C2/C14, not as a source of effect sizes.

**Dose-response.**

- AB: HLA-A and HLA-B are POOLED by the authors into a single 'HLA-AB' mismatch variable; increasing HLA-AB mismatch reported as associated with greater risk of acute rejection, graft failure, death-censored graft failure and/or death. No estimates, CIs or p-values in the abstract.
- DR: Increasing HLA-DR mismatch reported as associated with greater risk of acute rejection, graft failure, death-censored graft failure and/or death. No estimates, CIs or p-values in the abstract.
- DQ: not examined / not mentioned
- C: not examined / not mentioned
- DP: not examined / not mentioned
- Shape reported: monotonic increase described in words only ('increasing HLA mismatches were associated with a higher risk'; 'an incremental risk of rejection'), with 0 mismatch as the reference. The abstract gives no numeric series, so the shape (linear in log-hazard vs concave vs step vs zero-mismatch premium) CANNOT be determined from the retrieved text.; linearity tested: not stated in the abstract. No test for trend, no linear term, no spline, no threshold analysis is mentioned. Whether the full text tests linearity is unknown because no PMC full text exists.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch count x donor type (live vs deceased donor): The incremental risk of rejection per additional HLA mismatch was reported as larger in live donor kidney transplants than in deceased donor transplants. The abstract states this as a comparison of relative risks; it does NOT report a formal P for interaction. [Abstract, Results sentence]
- HLA mismatch x initial immunosuppressive regimen: The authors examined whether the HLA mismatch effect depended on the initial immunosuppressive regimen and report no consistent association between regimen and outcomes; the title and conclusion frame the HLA effect as 'independent of initial immunosuppression'. This is reported as a null/no-modification result, but no interaction estimate or P value appears in the abstract. [Abstract, Results and Conclusion sentences; also the article title]
- HLA mismatch x transplant era: The conclusion asserts the HLA mismatch effect is independent of transplant era. No era-stratified estimate or interaction test is shown in the abstract. [Abstract, Conclusion sentence]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "Compared with 0 HLA mismatch, increasing HLA mismatches were associated with a higher risk of graft failure and patient death in the adjusted models." (Abstract, Results)
- *C14* — "HLA mismatches were associated with an incremental risk of rejection although the relative risk was higher for live donor kidney transplants." (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "Increasing HLA-AB and HLA-DR mismatches were associated with a greater risk of acute rejection, graft failure, death-censored graft failure, and/or death." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "There was no consistent association between initial immunosuppressive regimen and outcomes." (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "Our results corroborate and extend the previous registry analyses demonstrating that HLA mismatches are associated with poorer transplant outcomes independent of immunosuppression and transplant era." (Abstract, Conclusion)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY. No PMC record exists for this PMID, so no full text could be retrieved. Every effect size, confidence interval, p-value, per-count series and covariate list is therefore unavailable. This paper contributes direction, not magnitude.; The abstract reports zero numeric estimates for HLA mismatch. effect_sizes is empty by necessity, not by oversight. Anyone quoting an HR from this paper must obtain the full text (Clin Transplant 2012;26(4):E428-37) from the publisher.; HLA-A and HLA-B are pooled into a single 'HLA-AB' variable, so the paper cannot rank A against B (claims C5, C6) and cannot separate a class I effect into its loci.; Only A, B and DR are considered. HLA-C, DQ and DP are not examined, so it says nothing about C4, C7 or C8 - a real gap given that DQ is the locus most implicated in dnDSA in living-donor cohorts.; The dose-response shape is unresolvable from the abstract: no per-count estimates, no test for trend, no spline, no threshold analysis. It supports C2 only in its weak qualitative form ('risk rises'), not in its strong form (the shape).; Retrospective registry cohort: residual confounding by indication and by allocation is likely, since better-matched deceased-donor recipients are selected by the allocation algorithm itself, and better-matched living donors are disproportionately siblings (who differ in other ways from unrelated living donors).; The adjustment set is not stated. 'The adjusted models' could mean anything; cold ischaemia, donor age, PRA/sensitisation and recipient ethnicity are never mentioned in the abstract, so it is unknown whether the mismatch effect survives adjustment for donor quality.; No antibody data (PRA, DSA) is mentioned, so the paper cannot address whether the mismatch effect is mediated by pre-existing or de novo antibody.; HLA typing resolution is not stated. Assuming antigen-level typing is an inference from the A/B/DR 0-6 scheme, not something the retrieved text says.; Follow-up duration is not stated, and the cohort is a mixed live/deceased population reported partly in aggregate, so the living-donor-specific estimates that would matter most to this review are not separable from the abstract.; Australia/New Zealand population, predominantly European ancestry; HLA haplotype frequencies and the achievable match distribution differ from an Iranian donor pool, limiting direct transfer of the mismatch distribution (though not necessarily of the per-mismatch effect)..

### Opelz G 2012 — Association of HLA mismatch with death with a functioning graft after kidney transplantation: a collaborative transplant study report.

Opelz G 2012, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/j.1600-6143.2012.04226.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-6143.2012.04226.x). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley / American Journal of Transplantation); no PMC record, convert_article_ids returned no pmcid, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | deceased-donor kidney transplants performed 1990-2009 and reported to the Collaborative Transplant Study (CTS), a multinational (predominantly European) registry; no further restriction stated in the abstract |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 177,584 |
| design | retrospective multinational registry cohort; Kaplan-Meier incidence plus multivariable analysis (model type not named in the abstract; CTS analyses of this kind are Cox proportional hazards, but that is not confirmable from the retrieved text) |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract |
| outcome | death with a functioning graft (DWFG), overall and by cause of death (infection, cardiovascular disease, malignancy); secondary outcome: hospitalization for viral or bacterial infection |
| follow up | analysed in two windows, year 1 posttransplant and years 2-5; total follow-up length not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | not retrievable from the abstract; the abstract states only that a 'Multivariable analysis' was performed and does not list the covariates, cause of death category (infection, cardiovascular disease, malignancy) is analysed as a separate outcome, not as a covariate, time since transplant (year 1 vs years 2-5) is stratified |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers a question the rest of the review mostly leaves open: whether HLA mismatch harms the recipient and not only the graft. In 177,584 deceased-donor kidney transplants it links HLA-A+B+DR mismatch to death with a functioning graft, and it locates the mechanism in the immunosuppression burden mismatch creates - the excess deaths are from infection and cardiovascular disease, not malignancy, and mismatch also predicts hospitalization for viral and bacterial infection. That matters for a pre-screen tool because it means the cost of a poorly matched pairing is not fully captured by graft-survival curves; part of it lands on patient survival, and the excess is concentrated in the first year. It supports C1 (mismatch still predicts outcome), C11 (effect modification - the association is strong in year 1 and weaker though still present in years 2-5, and is present for infectious and cardiovascular death but absent for malignancy), and partially C3 (class II mismatch was more strongly associated with both hospitalization and DWFG than class I). Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown Iranian pre-screen is indirect and should be treated as directional only: the cohort is entirely deceased-donor, the era is 1990-2009, and the abstract gives no per-locus or per-mismatch-count estimates, no hazard ratios and no confidence intervals, so nothing here can be used to calibrate a weight. Its usable content for the tool is qualitative - a reason to keep favouring lower total mismatch, and specifically class II mismatch, even when the stated goal is patient rather than graft outcome.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- death with a functioning graft (DWFG): whole cohort baseline (not an HLA contrast) — cumulative incidence, Kaplan-Meier 4.8; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- death with a functioning graft (DWFG): whole cohort baseline (not an HLA contrast) — cumulative incidence, Kaplan-Meier 7.7; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- death with a functioning graft (DWFG), all causes: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch (mismatch categories not printed in the abstract) - association test, year 1 — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated at this point in the abstract [Abstract]
- death with a functioning graft (DWFG), all causes: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test, years 2-5 — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated at this point in the abstract [Abstract]
- DWFG due to infection: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=<0.001 during year 1; 0.043 during years 2-5; adjusted for not stated [Abstract]
- DWFG due to cardiovascular disease: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=<0.001 during year 1; 0.030 during years 2-5; adjusted for not stated [Abstract]
- DWFG due to malignancy: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test — null result, no estimate and no p-value printed None; adjusted for not stated [Abstract]
- hospitalization for viral infection: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated [Abstract]
- hospitalization for bacterial infection: HLA-A + B + DR mismatch - association test — significance test only, no point estimate printed None, p=0.002; adjusted for not stated [Abstract]
- DWFG and hospitalization: HLA class II mismatch vs HLA class I mismatch (relative strength of association) — direction only, no point estimate printed None; adjusted for multivariable analysis (covariates not listed in the abstract) [Abstract, final sentence]
- distribution of causes of DWFG: cause-of-death composition (not an HLA contrast) — proportion of DWFG events, percent None; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported in the retrievable text; linearity tested: not determinable from the abstract. The abstract reports only overall p-values for the association between HLA-A + B + DR mismatch and DWFG; it does not state whether mismatch was modelled as a count, as ordered categories, or as a trend test, and prints no per-count estimates.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-A + B + DR mismatch x time since transplant (year 1 vs years 2-5): the association with DWFG was strongest during the first posttransplant year and weakened, without disappearing, during years 2-5 (p < 0.001 in year 1 and p < 0.001 in years 2-5; the authors describe the year 2-5 correlation as 'diminished but persisted'. No formal interaction test and no P-for-interaction is reported in the abstract.) [Abstract]
- HLA mismatch x cause of death: mismatch predicted death from infection and from cardiovascular disease but not death from malignancy - consistent with the authors' proposed mechanism of heavier immunosuppression and more antirejection therapy in mismatched recipients (infection p < 0.001 (year 1) and p = 0.043 (years 2-5); cardiovascular disease p < 0.001 (year 1) and p = 0.030 (years 2-5); malignancy not significant, no p printed) [Abstract]
- HLA class II vs HLA class I mismatch: class II mismatch was more strongly associated with both hospitalization and DWFG than class I mismatch (direction only; no estimates, confidence intervals or p-values printed in the abstract) [Abstract, final sentence]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "Deceased-donor kidney transplants (n = 177 584) performed 1990-2009 and reported to the Collaborative Transplant Study were analyzed." (Abstract)
- *C1* — "HLA-A + B + DR mismatches were significantly associated with DWFG during year 1 (p < 0.001), a correlation that diminished but persisted during years 2-5 (p < 0.001)." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "HLA mismatch was associated with DWFG because of infection (p < 0.001 during year 1, p = 0.043 during years 2-5) or cardiovascular disease (p < 0.001 during year 1, p = 0.030 during years 2-5) but not malignancy." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "There was also a significant association between HLA mismatch and hospitalization for viral (p < 0.001) or bacterial (p = 0.002) infection." (Abstract)
- *C3* — "Multivariable analysis showed that mismatches for HLA class II were more strongly associated with both hospitalization and DWFG than mismatches for HLA class I." (Abstract, final sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract-only access. The paper is not in PMC (convert_article_ids returned no PMCID) and is under publisher copyright, so no tables, figures, hazard ratios, confidence intervals or per-mismatch-count numbers could be retrieved. Every quantitative claim below the level of a p-value is therefore unavailable.; No effect sizes at all: the abstract prints p-values and incidence percentages but not a single HR, OR or RR for HLA mismatch. The paper cannot be pooled or used to calibrate a mismatch weight from the retrievable text.; Deceased-donor only. Nothing in the paper speaks directly to living donation, which is the Iranian pre-screen's setting; living donors differ in cold ischaemia, donor quality and recipient selection, all of which plausibly modify a mechanism that runs through immunosuppression burden.; Era 1990-2009. Immunosuppression, viral prophylaxis (CMV, BK) and cardiovascular risk management have all changed since; the infection-mediated component in particular may be smaller today.; Confounding by indication is the central threat and cannot be assessed from the abstract: recipients who receive more mismatched grafts are also more likely to be sensitised, re-transplanted, longer on dialysis and older, and all of those independently raise infectious and cardiovascular death. The abstract does not list the covariates in the multivariable model.; The proposed mechanism - higher immunosuppression doses and more antirejection therapy - is stated as a rationale, not measured. No immunosuppression exposure data are reported in the abstract.; HLA typing resolution is not stated. The mismatch definition (HLA-A + B + DR, broad vs split antigens, how unknowns were handled) is not retrievable.; 'Class II' is not defined in the abstract. It may mean DR alone or DR plus DQ, so the class II > class I finding supports C3 only weakly and cannot separate DR from DQ.; The outcome, death with a functioning graft, is not the review's primary outcome (graft failure). It is a competing risk for graft failure, so this paper complements rather than duplicates the graft-survival literature - but it also means the numbers here must not be mixed into a graft-failure synthesis.; Single registry (CTS), predominantly European centres; no Iranian or regional data, and no ethnicity-stratified results in the abstract..

### Willicombe M 2012 — De novo DQ donor-specific antibodies are associated with a significant risk of antibody-mediated rejection and transplant glomerulopathy.

Willicombe M 2012, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e3182543950](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e3182543950). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wolters Kluwer / Lippincott, Transplantation 2012;94(2):172-7); convert_article_ids returned no PMCID, so there is no PMC full text and no open licence. All extracted content comes from the PubMed abstract record..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 505 recipients of a renal-alone transplant at a single UK centre (Imperial College Kidney and Transplant Centre, Hammersmith Hospital, London), 2005-2010; ABO-incompatible and HLA-incompatible grafts excluded, the latter defined as positive crossmatch or preformed DSAbs detected by single-antigen beads only |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract |
| n | 505 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; incidence of de novo DSAbs and of DQ DSAbs, and comparison of class II DSAb / AMR risk across DR and DQ match categories; significance reported as P values without effect estimates in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract (DR and DQ reported dichotomously as matched or mismatched at each locus) |
| outcome | de novo DSAb development (any HLA; class II; DQ), antibody-mediated rejection, transplant glomerulopathy, allograft loss |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract (transplants performed 2005-2010) |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract - the abstract reports crude group comparisons with P values only; no covariate-adjusted model is described |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is one of the primary sources for claim C4: it shows that DQ is the dominant target of de novo class II DSA (50 of 92 DSAb-positive patients, 54.3%) and that DQ dnDSA carries a significant risk of AMR, transplant glomerulopathy and allograft loss. Crucially for a pre-screen, its exposure is a purely pre-transplant, typing-derived variable - whether the pair is matched or mismatched at DR and at DQ - and mismatch at BOTH loci predicted class II dnDSA and AMR better than mismatch at either locus alone (P=0.001 for each), which is the kind of joint DR x DQ term a matching engine can actually compute (C10). Because the exposure is dichotomous matched/mismatched at antigen level rather than an eplet or PIRCHE load, it transfers to a LOW-RESOLUTION (one-field) Iranian pre-screen without needing two-field typing - but only if DQ is typed at all, which is the practical decision this paper forces. The cohort excluded positive crossmatches and preformed DSAbs, so it describes de novo antibody formation starting from an essentially unsensitised baseline; that is the closest available analogue to an ANTIBODY-STATUS-UNKNOWN pre-screen used to pick a donor before any DSA workup, though it cannot speak to candidates who already carry DSA, which an Iranian pre-screen cannot exclude. Transfer to LIVING donation is the weak link: the abstract never states the donor mix, and a 2005-2010 London cohort's immunosuppression, biopsy policy and donor pool differ from Iranian living-donor practice. Finally, the abstract reports no hazard ratios or confidence intervals, so this paper supplies direction and a DQ-typing rationale but no magnitude that can be used to weight DQ against DR in a scoring rule.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- de novo DSAb (any HLA): crude cohort incidence over follow-up — percentage 18.2; adjusted for unadjusted (raw proportion, 92 of 505) [Abstract, Results]
- DQ de novo DSAb: share of DSAb-positive patients whose DSAb included DQ — percentage 54.3; adjusted for unadjusted (raw proportion, 50 of 92) [Abstract, Results]
- antibody-mediated rejection, transplant glomerulopathy and allograft loss (the three outcomes reported together with a single P value): patients who developed DQ DSAbs vs those who did not — p-value only (no point estimate printed in the abstract) None, p=<0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results]
- development of class II DSAbs: mismatched at BOTH DR and DQ vs mismatched at either DR or DQ alone — p-value only (no point estimate printed in the abstract) None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results]
- antibody-mediated rejection: mismatched at BOTH DR and DQ vs mismatched at either DR or DQ alone — p-value only (no point estimate printed in the abstract) None, p=0.001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results]
- cohort composition by class II match category: matched at both the DR and DQ loci — percentage 21.4; adjusted for not applicable (distribution, 108 of 505) [Abstract, Results]
- cohort composition by class II match category: mismatched at both DR and DQ loci — percentage 56.2; adjusted for not applicable (distribution, 284 of 505) [Abstract, Results]
- cohort composition by class II match category: matched at DR alone (i.e. DR matched, DQ mismatched) — percentage 7.5; adjusted for not applicable (distribution, 38 of 505) [Abstract, Results]
- cohort composition by class II match category: matched at DQ alone (i.e. DQ matched, DR mismatched) — percentage 14.9; adjusted for not applicable (distribution, 75 of 505) [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- DR and DQ jointly (four match categories, exactly as printed): matched at both DR and DQ MM: 108 of 505 (21.4%); matched at DR alone (DQ mismatched) MM: 38 of 505 (7.5%); matched at DQ alone (DR mismatched) MM: 75 of 505 (14.9%); mismatched at both DR and DQ MM: 284 of 505 (56.2%)
- reported comparison: mismatched at BOTH DR and DQ vs the pooled single-locus-mismatch groups ('those mismatched at either DR or DQ alone', i.e. the 38 + 75 patients): higher risk of class II DSAbs, P=0.001, and higher risk of antibody-mediated rejection, P=0.001. NOTE the comparator is the single-mismatch groups, NOT the fully matched group; the abstract prints no comparison against the 108 doubly matched patients.
- DR alone: no separate DR-only effect estimate is printed in the abstract
- DQ alone: no separate DQ-only effect estimate is printed in the abstract
- A, B, C, DP: not reported in the abstract
- Shape reported: step / joint-effect across DR x DQ match categories; no mismatch-count dose-response of any kind is reported; linearity tested: not tested - no mismatch-count model, trend test, spline or threshold analysis is described in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR mismatch x HLA-DQ mismatch (joint class II mismatch): Mismatch at both DR and DQ carried a greater risk of developing class II DSAbs, and a greater risk of antibody-mediated rejection, than mismatch at either DR or DQ alone. This is a joint-category comparison; no formal statistical test of interaction (e.g. a multiplicative interaction term or 'P for interaction') is reported in the abstract. (P=0.001 for class II DSAb development; P=0.001 for antibody-mediated rejection) [Abstract, Results]

- *C4* — "De novo DQ donor-specific antibodies (DSAbs) are the predominant HLA class II DSAb after transplantation." (Abstract, Background)
- *C4* — "Of 505 patients, 92 (18.2%) developed DSAbs, with 50 (54.3%) of these 92 patients having DQ DSAbs." (Abstract, Results)
- *C4* — "Patients who developed DQ DSAbs were at significant risk for antibody-mediated rejection, transplant glomerulopathy, and allograft loss (P<0.0001)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C10* — "108 (21.4%) were matched at both the DR and DQ loci, 284 (56.2%) were mismatched at both loci, 38 (7.5%) were matched at DR alone, and 75 (14.9%) were matched at DQ alone." (Abstract, Results)
- *C10* — "Patients mismatched at both DR and DQ were at risk for developing class II DSAbs when compared with those mismatched at either DR or DQ alone, P=0.001, and were at risk for antibody-mediated rejection, P=0.001." (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 22735711, so no PMC full text was available; everything in this record comes from the PubMed abstract and nothing from the paper's tables, figures or Methods could be checked.; No effect sizes for the HLA-mismatch comparisons. The two key mismatch results are reported as bare P values (P=0.001 each) with no HR, OR, RR, risk difference or confidence interval, so the MAGNITUDE of the DR+DQ double-mismatch effect cannot be extracted and cannot be used to weight DQ relative to DR in a scoring rule.; No evidence of covariate adjustment in the abstract; the comparisons appear crude, so confounding by recipient age, retransplant status, PRA, immunosuppression regimen and adherence is unaddressed in what can be read.; Donor type (living vs deceased, or the mix) is never stated in the abstract, which is the single biggest obstacle to transferring this to a living-donor pre-screen.; Typing resolution is not stated. DR and DQ are treated as matched/mismatched without saying whether this is serological/antigen level, DRB1/DQB1 two-field, or whether DQA1 was considered at all.; Exposure is dichotomised per locus (matched vs mismatched), so 1 and 2 mismatches at a locus are pooled; no 0/1/2 count series and no test of linearity, trend or threshold is reported. This paper therefore contributes nothing to C2 or C9.; The stated comparator for the double-mismatch result is the pooled single-locus-mismatch group, not the fully matched group, so the abstract does not quantify the fully-matched (0 DR, 0 DQ) advantage.; DR and DQ are in strong linkage disequilibrium and the group sizes reflect it (56.2% mismatched at both loci vs 7.5% matched at DR alone), so with n=505 the independent contribution of DQ over DR cannot be isolated from these data; the abstract reports no attempt to do so.; Single centre, n=505, transplants 2005-2010, one UK immunosuppression protocol (not described in the abstract). Ascertainment of AMR and transplant glomerulopathy depends on the centre's biopsy policy (protocol vs indication), which is not stated, and DSAb screening frequency is likewise not stated - both bias incidence estimates.; Patients with a positive crossmatch or preformed DSAbs were excluded, so the results do not describe sensitised recipients and do not support any claim about pre-existing DSA.; The opening claim that 'HLA-DR compatibility [has] the greatest influence' is background assertion, not a result of this study, and must not be cited as this paper's finding.; Follow-up duration is not stated, so the 18.2% dnDSA incidence has no time denominator and is not comparable with other cohorts..

### Ashby VB 2011 — Transplanting kidneys without points for HLA-B matching: consequences of the policy change.

Ashby VB 2011, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/j.1600-6143.2011.03606.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-6143.2011.03606.x). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley / American Journal of Transplantation); no PMC record returned by convert_article_ids, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | solitary deceased donor kidney transplant recipients in the United States, in the 6 years before and the 6 years after the May 2003 elimination of allocation priority for HLA-B similarity (Scientific Registry of Transplant Recipients) |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 108 701 solitary deceased donor kidney recipients |
| design | retrospective national registry before/after (policy natural experiment); chi-square comparison of the racial/ethnic distribution of recipients between eras, Cox models for graft failure |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; the HLA-B matching that the US allocation system awarded points for was antigen (serologic broad/split) level, i.e. low resolution |
| outcome | two co-primary outcomes: (a) access - racial/ethnic distribution and number of deceased donor kidney transplants; (b) graft failure / 2-year graft survival |
| follow up | graft survival reported at 2 years; eras are the 6 years either side of the 2003 policy change |
| other factors modelled | not stated in the abstract; the abstract says only that graft failures were analysed with Cox models and does not list the covariates |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the policy-outcome paper for claim C13: it is the national evaluation of what happened when an allocation system deliberately stopped scoring one HLA locus (HLA-B), and it is therefore the cleanest available real-world test of how much a class I locus is worth when it is traded against access. For claim C5 it supplies evidence in the limiting direction rather than the confirming one: B is conventionally ranked above A among class I loci, yet the abstract reports that after B points were removed two-year graft survival improved in every racial/ethnic group and that there was no adverse effect on graft survival, so whatever survival value B-matching carried at the population level was small enough to be outweighed by other era changes. The design is a deceased-donor, US, antigen-level registry cohort, so it transfers to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen only at the level of policy logic, not of effect size: living-donor pairs are self-selected and are not allocated by a points system, cold ischaemia and donor quality are far more favourable, and the immunological gradient across a living-donor pool is much narrower than across a national deceased-donor pool. What it does transfer is the design lesson for a low-resolution, one-field, antibody-status-unknown screen: a locus that is cheap to type at antigen level can be dropped from a scoring rule without a detectable graft-survival penalty, and dropping it materially widens access for groups whose HLA distribution differs from the majority. For an Iranian pre-screen the analogue is that HLA-B weighting should be justified by a demonstrated outcome gain rather than assumed, and that any B weighting must be checked for the access penalty it imposes on ethnic groups (Azeri, Kurd, Baluch, Arab, Turkmen) whose antigen frequencies differ from the majority Persian donor pool. The paper cannot inform DQ, DP, eplet or DSA questions at all, and it says nothing about antibody status, so it constrains the scoring rule's HLA-B weight and its equity audit, not its immunological core.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- number of deceased donor kidney transplants performed: 6 years after removal of HLA-B matching points vs the 6 years before, all recipients — percentage change 23; adjusted for unadjusted count comparison [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- number of deceased donor kidney transplants performed: post- vs pre-policy, minority recipients — percentage change 40; adjusted for unadjusted count comparison [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- number of deceased donor kidney transplants performed: post- vs pre-policy, non-Hispanic white recipients — percentage change 8; adjusted for unadjusted count comparison [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- proportion of transplants going to non-whites versus whites: post- vs pre-policy era — p-value only (chi-square) None, p=<0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted (chi-square on the recipient racial/ethnic distribution) [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- 2-year graft survival: post- vs pre-policy, within each racial/ethnic group — direction only, no number printed None; adjusted for Cox models (covariates not listed in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 3 and Conclusion]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested; no mismatch-count or per-locus mismatch series appears in the retrievable text; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- removal of HLA-B allocation priority x recipient race/ethnicity: the policy change increased transplant numbers far more for minorities than for non-Hispanic whites, reducing but not eliminating the access deficit for minorities (+40% for minorities vs +8% for whites; chi-square for the change in the non-white versus white proportion p < 0.0001) [Abstract, Results and Conclusion]
- removal of HLA-B allocation priority x recipient race/ethnicity, for the graft-survival outcome: no differential harm: 2-year graft survival improved in every racial/ethnic group after the policy change, so the access gain was not bought with a survival loss in any group (direction only; no hazard ratio or percentage printed in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "In 2003, the US kidney allocation system was changed to eliminate priority for HLA-B similarity." (Abstract, opening sentence)
- *C13* — "Analyses were based on 108 701 solitary deceased donor kidney recipients during the 6 years before and after the policy change." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C13* — "the overall number of deceased donor transplants rose 23%, with a larger increase for minorities (40%) and a smaller increase for non-Hispanic whites (whites) (8%)" (Abstract, Results sentence 1)
- *C5* — "Two-year graft survival improved for all racial/ethnic groups after implementation of this new policy." (Abstract, Results sentence 3)
- *C5* — "Following elimination of allocation priority for HLA-B similarity, the deficit in transplantation rates among minorities compared with that for whites was reduced but not eliminated; furthermore, there was no adverse effect on graft survival." (Abstract, Conclusion)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no PMC full text, so every quantitative claim below the abstract level (hazard ratios, confidence intervals, covariate lists, the HLA-B mismatch distribution itself) is unavailable and must not be inferred.; The specific quantity the review wanted - how much HLA-B mismatch actually increased after B points were removed - is not in the retrievable text.; Before/after design over two 6-year eras: the policy change is fully confounded with secular trends in immunosuppression, induction therapy, donor selection, expanded-criteria and donation-after-cardiac-death use, and recipient case mix. 'Two-year graft survival improved' is therefore an era observation, not an effect of the policy.; The conclusion 'no adverse effect on graft survival' is an absence-of-evidence statement at national level; it does not exclude a real but small HLA-B effect, and the abstract gives no confidence interval that would bound how small.; Deceased-donor only, US only, antigen-level (low-resolution) HLA typing, 2-year graft-survival horizon; the eras end in roughly 2009, before the 2014 Kidney Allocation System and before routine solid-phase DSA monitoring.; No data on sensitisation, PRA, donor-specific antibody, cold ischaemia, DR/DQ/DP mismatch, eplet or molecular mismatch, retransplantation, or immunosuppression regimen in the retrievable text.; Race/ethnicity here is a US classification (non-Hispanic white versus minorities) and is a proxy for HLA haplotype frequency differences; it does not map onto Iranian ethnic structure.; Ecological/policy-level inference: individual recipients were not randomised to a matching rule, so the paper supports statements about an allocation system, not about the immunological value of a B mismatch in a given pair..

### Tran TH 2011 — Deleterious impact of mismatching for human leukocyte antigen-C in presensitized recipients of kidney transplants.

Tran TH 2011, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e318224c14e](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e318224c14e). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wolters Kluwer / Transplantation); no PMC record exists for this PMID, so only the PubMed abstract was retrieved.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | adult deceased-donor kidney transplants from centres participating in the Collaborative Transplant Study (CTS, coordinated at Heidelberg), restricted to transplants with DNA available for retrospective HLA-C typing; transplant years, countries and ethnicity not stated in the abstract |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 2260 |
| design | retrospective multicentre registry cohort (CTS) with retrospective HLA-C DNA typing; graft survival compared by HLA-C mismatch status separately within presensitised and non-presensitised strata; the statistical model (Cox vs log-rank) is not stated in the abstract |
| typing resolution | HLA-C typed by DNA PCR-SSP (field/resolution level not stated in the abstract); an HLA-C epitope-matching approach was also tested; presensitisation determined by lymphocytotoxicity (CDC) |
| outcome | renal allograft (graft) survival; whether death-censored is not stated in the abstract |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | presensitisation (lymphocytotoxic antibody status) used as the stratifying factor; no other covariate list is given in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the reference CTS paper for the review question of whether HLA-C, a locus that conventional A/B/DR allocation ignores, carries risk of its own: across 2,260 deceased-donor kidney transplants HLA-C mismatch was associated with worse graft survival in presensitised recipients (P<0.001) but not in non-presensitised recipients (P=0.75). That contrast is the core of claim C7 and a clean instance of effect modification by sensitisation (C11): the locus is not universally important, it is important conditional on recipient antibody status. The finding that some HLA-C epitope mismatches mattered more than others points to an antibody/epitope mechanism rather than a generic T-cell alloresponse, which is why the authors argue for identifying donor-specific HLA-C antibodies. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor, one-field, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen is limited on three counts: the cohort is deceased-donor; HLA-C was typed by DNA methods that routine Iranian one-field reports frequently omit altogether; and the entire result is conditional on knowing presensitisation status, which is exactly what the pre-screen does not have. The operational reading is therefore that HLA-C should carry weight only when a candidate is known or likely to be sensitised (retransplant, pregnancy, transfusion history), and that a C mismatch in an unsensitised candidate should not by itself downgrade a living-donor pair. Because HLA-C sits in strong linkage disequilibrium with HLA-B (the paper is MeSH-indexed under Linkage Disequilibrium, and the abstract does not show the C effect to be independent of B), a B-matched living donor will often be C-matched as well, so much of the C signal is already captured by B in a one-field scheme.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft survival: HLA-C mismatch vs no HLA-C mismatch, presensitised recipients — P value only (no point estimate or CI printed in the abstract) None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated in the abstract; analysis stratified by presensitisation [Abstract, Results]
- graft survival: HLA-C mismatch vs no HLA-C mismatch, non-presensitised recipients — P value only (no point estimate or CI printed in the abstract) None, p=0.75; adjusted for not stated in the abstract; analysis stratified by presensitisation [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- C: 0 MM: reference; the abstract reports only mismatch vs no mismatch; 1 MM: not separated in the abstract; 2 MM: not separated in the abstract
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-C mismatch x presensitisation (lymphocytotoxic antibodies): HLA-C mismatch reduced graft survival only in presensitised recipients; there was no detectable effect in non-presensitised recipients. Reported as two stratum-specific P values, not as a formal interaction test. (P<0.001 (presensitised) vs P=0.75 (non-presensitised)) [Abstract, Results]
- HLA-C epitope identity x presensitisation: Mismatch of certain HLA-C epitopes seemed to be more influential than others, with a negative impact on graft survival in presensitised patients; the epitopes and their effect sizes are not named in the abstract. (not given in the abstract) [Abstract, Results]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "HLA-C mismatch was found to be associated with significantly decreased graft survival in presensitized (P<0.001) but not in non-presensitized (P=0.75) recipients." (Abstract, Results)
- *C7* — "Mismatch of certain HLA-C epitopes seemed to be more influential than others, with mismatches showing a negative impact on graft survival in presensitized patients." (Abstract, Results)
- *C7* — "HLA-C mismatch has a substantial deleterious effect on graft survival in presensitized kidney recipients." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C7* — "A cohort of 2260 deceased donor kidney transplants were typed for HLA-C using polymerase chain reaction-sequence specific primer method." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C13* — "Allocation of deceased donor kidneys is commonly based on matching for human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-A, -B, and -DR, whereas HLA-C is currently disregarded." (Abstract, Background)
- *C7* — "matching for HLA-C may provide a reasonable approach to improve transplant outcomes in presensitized kidney transplant recipients." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no hazard ratios, confidence intervals, survival percentages, follow-up length, covariate list or statistical model could be retrieved; the article has no PMC record.; Deceased-donor CTS cohort throughout; no living-donor data, which is the review's target setting.; Only the subset of CTS transplants with DNA available was retyped for HLA-C (2,260), so how this subset was selected relative to the full registry is unknown and possibly non-random.; Presensitisation is defined by lymphocytotoxicity (CDC PRA), not by solid-phase HLA-C donor-specific antibody, so the proposed C-DSA mechanism is inferred rather than measured; the authors themselves call for studies identifying donor-specific HLA-C antibodies.; HLA-C appears to be analysed as mismatch vs no mismatch; no 0/1/2 dose-response for HLA-C is reported in the abstract, so whether one and two C mismatches were pooled cannot be determined.; The abstract does not show the HLA-C effect to be independent of HLA-B mismatch; given strong B-C linkage disequilibrium, confounding by B is unresolved from the retrievable text.; Effect modification is presented as two stratum-specific P values rather than a formal interaction test; a significant result in one stratum and a null in the other is not itself evidence that the two effects differ.; The epitope-level result is stated qualitatively ('seemed to be more influential') with no numbers, epitope names, or multiplicity correction in the abstract.; 2011 publication; transplant era and immunosuppression predate current practice, and the antibody assays criticised in the conclusion have since changed..

### Fuggle SV 2010 — Impact of the 1998 UK National Allocation Scheme for deceased heartbeating donor kidneys.

Fuggle SV 2010, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e3181c90270](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e3181c90270). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation, Lippincott Williams and Wilkins). convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 20177337, so PMC has no full text; only the PubMed abstract was retrievable..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | deceased heartbeating (DHB) donor kidney transplants performed in the United Kingdom under the 1998 National Kidney Allocation Scheme; adult and paediatric (younger than 18 years) recipients; scheme impact assessed over 5 years. Exact cohort size, era boundaries and first-versus-repeat transplant status are not stated in the abstract. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | not stated in abstract |
| design | description of an allocation policy plus a before/after comparison of national HLA-matching and access distributions; no multivariable survival model is reported in the abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; mismatch is counted as HLA-A, -B and -DR (000 mismatch terminology), i.e. broad/split antigen (serologic-equivalent, one-field) level as used in UK allocation - inferred from the mismatch notation, not asserted by the retrieved text |
| outcome | HLA matching achieved by allocation (proportion of transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatched) and equity of access (blood group, rare HLA type, HLA homozygosity, sensitisation, paediatric access). Graft or patient survival is NOT reported in the abstract. |
| follow up | 5 years of scheme operation from 1998; no recipient outcome follow-up reported in the abstract |
| other factors modelled | points score based on six factors (the six factors are NOT named in the abstract), paediatric recipient status (younger than 18 years) - explicit priority, local/regional versus national listing - explicit priority, sensitisation (reported as an equity beneficiary, not stated to be a scored factor), recipient blood group (reported as an equity outcome), rareness of recipient HLA type (reported as an equity outcome), recipient HLA homozygosity (reported as an equity outcome) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is the policy-design half of claim C13: it documents an allocation scheme built on three tiers of patients defined by HLA mismatch, with a points score based on six factors setting the specific priority order for allocation in tiers 1 and 2. The abstract does not say how the tiers are constructed from the individual loci, so this paper establishes only that the scheme is TIERED; it does not establish that the scheme scores HLA non-additively rather than by summing per-locus penalties, and it says nothing about later UK schemes. A tiered scheme is nevertheless the concrete precedent for any KidneyMatch ranking that groups donor-recipient pairs into mismatch bands before ranking inside a band, which is exactly the shape a low-resolution pre-screen can support. Its access findings also transfer: the scheme improved equity for patients with rare HLA types and for HLA-homozygous patients, which is the matchability problem an Iranian registry will face with a differently structured HLA haplotype distribution and a small donor pool. Transfer is nevertheless limited in three ways that matter here. The population is deceased heartbeating donors allocated from a national waiting list, where the scheme's whole purpose is to route a single kidney among many candidates; a living-donor pre-screen instead evaluates a small number of known, self-presenting pairs, so the tier machinery informs how to band a pair but not how to allocate scarce organs. The abstract reports no graft-survival validation at all, so this paper can support how a scheme scores HLA and what matching it achieved, but it cannot on its own justify that any particular tier boundary improves outcome. Finally, the scheme presupposes national HLA typing and a maintained sensitisation/antibody register; in an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen the sensitisation and highly-sensitised-patient components of this design have no counterpart and must not be simulated from mismatch counts.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- proportion of adult transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatched: before the 1998 NKAS (pre-scheme baseline) — percentage 7; adjusted for unadjusted crude national proportion [Abstract, Results ('more than doubling the proportion of transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, and -DR mismatched from 7% to 16% for adults')]
- proportion of adult transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatched: after the 1998 NKAS (5 years of scheme operation) — percentage 16; adjusted for unadjusted crude national proportion; abstract states the improvement in HLA matching was 'significant' but prints no test statistic or p-value [Abstract, Results ('more than doubling the proportion of transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, and -DR mismatched from 7% to 16% for adults')]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The abstract reports no survival or rejection model, so no per-count or per-locus risk series exists to test for linearity. The scheme itself imposes a STEP structure on HLA mismatch for allocation purposes - three tiers defined by HLA mismatch, with national allocation for tiers 1 and 2 and regional allocation for tier 3 - but that is a policy design, not an estimated dose-response, and the abstract does not state how the tiers are defined in terms of the individual loci. That detail was not retrievable here and must not be filled in from memory or from other papers.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "The 1998 NKAS was based on three tiers of patients defined by human leukocyte antigen (HLA) mismatch." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C13* — "This involved national allocation of well-matched kidneys in tiers 1 and 2, with regional allocation for less well-matched patients in tier 3." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C13* — "Pediatric patients (younger than 18 years) and regional patients were prioritized in tiers 1 and 2, with a points score based on six factors determining the specific priority order for allocation." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C13* — "resulted in significantly improved HLA matching, more than doubling the proportion of transplants that were 000 HLA-A, -B, and -DR mismatched from 7% to 16% for adults" (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "The scheme also benefited highly sensitized patients and improved equity with regard to patient blood group, rareness of HLA type, and HLA homozygosity." (Abstract, Results)
