**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC deposit exists for this PMID, so the Methods, Results tables and Discussion could not be read; every field here is bounded by roughly 300 words of abstract.; No graft or patient survival outcome is reported in the abstract. The paper as retrieved validates the scheme against HLA matching achieved and equity of access, not against transplant outcome, so it cannot support any claim that the tier boundaries improve graft survival.; No effect estimate, confidence interval or p-value is printed. The word 'significantly' appears without a test statistic; the two percentages (7 and 16) are unadjusted crude national proportions.; Before/after national comparison with no concurrent control. Secular trends over the 5-year window - changes in donor and recipient case mix, typing practice, immunosuppression, listing behaviour - are not separable from the effect of the scheme.; The six factors of the points score are not named in the abstract, so the relative weight this scheme gave to HLA versus waiting time, age matching or other criteria cannot be recovered from the retrieved text.; The tier definitions themselves are not given in the abstract beyond 'three tiers defined by HLA mismatch'. Whether the tiers are built DR-first, or from a summed HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch count, is not stated anywhere in the retrieved text; the full text must be obtained before this paper is cited for locus ordering or for non-additivity.; Deceased heartbeating donors allocated from a national waiting list. The scheme's logic is competition among many candidates for one kidney and does not directly describe living-donor pair evaluation.; United Kingdom HLA and blood-group distribution circa 1998-2003. Matchability, rare-HLA-type and homozygosity findings are population-specific and will not carry numerically to an Iranian donor pool.; Typing resolution is not stated. The 000 A-B-DR mismatch notation implies antigen-level (one-field) counting, but this is an inference from notation, not a statement in the retrieved text.; The scheme depends on a national sensitisation/antibody register and virtual crossmatch infrastructure that an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen does not have..

### Johnson RJ 2010 — A New UK 2006 National Kidney Allocation Scheme for deceased heart-beating donor kidneys.

Johnson RJ 2010, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e3181c9029d](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e3181c9029d). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation, Wolters Kluwer); only the PubMed abstract was retrieved, no PMC full text exists.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | UK national waiting list for kidneys from deceased heart-beating donors, adult and paediatric patients; scheme introduced 2006, impact described after 3 years |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | not stated in abstract |
| design | national allocation policy description: review of HLA matching criteria, simulation of alternative schemes, then descriptive 3-year registry impact (no multivariable outcome model in abstract) |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen-level specificities implied (rare specificities defaulted to common, related specificities); resolution not otherwise stated in abstract |
| outcome | equity of access to transplantation, achievement of well-matched transplants, waiting-time benefit; graft or patient survival not reported in the abstract |
| follow up | 3 years after introduction of the scheme |
| other factors modelled | waiting time (most influential points component), recipient age (points linked to HLA mismatch), paediatric status (<18 years, well-matched priority), HLA-DR homozygosity (equity of access), rare HLA specificities (defaulted to common related specificities), geography (regional equity of access) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper answers the review question of how a national allocation scheme scores HLA (C13): the UK 2006 NKAS gives absolute priority to 000 HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatches and to well-matched children, then ranks by a points score in which waiting time dominates and the HLA-mismatch points are linked to recipient age so that younger patients are steered towards well-matched kidneys. It also documents a practical low-resolution matching device, defaulting rare specificities to common related specificities, which is directly transferable to a one-field antigen-level pre-screen because it reduces false mismatches created by rare or split antigens. The age-HLA linkage is a policy embodiment of effect modification by recipient age (C11), justified by the lower likelihood of retransplantation in older recipients, and the same logic can be reused as a tunable weight in a living-donor pre-screen. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor setting is only partial: the scheme allocates deceased heart-beating donor kidneys within a national waiting list, its weights were tuned for equity of access rather than for individual graft survival, and the abstract reports no hazard ratios and no antibody data, so it cannot calibrate the magnitude of any HLA effect or the handling of unknown sensitisation. Its value to the review is as a worked example of how a mature registry translated antigen-level matching evidence into a points scheme with a zero-mismatch premium and an age-conditional HLA weight, and as an early report that the observed results after 3 years tracked the pre-implementation simulations.

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested / not reported (abstract only; the scheme is a policy description, not an outcome model); 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch points x recipient age: Policy design, not an outcome estimate: points for age and HLA mismatch are linked so that younger patients are steered towards well-matched transplants while HLA matching is given less weight for older patients, on the rationale that retransplantation is less likely to be required in older recipients. [Abstract (Algorithm for 2006 NKAS)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "Points for age and HLA mismatch are linked in a novel approach to ensure well-matched transplants for younger patients while recognizing that HLA matching is less important for older patients as retransplantation is less likely to be required." (Abstract (Algorithm for 2006 NKAS))
- *C13* — "To improve equity for difficult to match patients, rare HLA specificities were defaulted to more common, related specificities." (Abstract (Algorithm for 2006 NKAS))
- *C13* — "preparatory work included a review of the criteria for human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching and simulation evidence about the effectiveness of alternative schemes." (Abstract (background))
- *C13* — "After 3 years, the scheme is already making good progress in achieving its objectives, with overall results similar to those observed in the simulations." (Abstract (Impact of 2006 NKAS))
- *C13* — "including the achievement of equity of access to transplant for HLA-DR homozygous patients, but geographical inequity of access will take a number of years to address fully." (Abstract (Impact of 2006 NKAS))

**Limitations.** abstract only: no PMC full text, so the mismatch-level definitions (which DR and B combinations form each level), the age-linked points table and the list of defaulted specificities could not be retrieved or verified; policy description, not an outcome study: no hazard ratios, odds ratios, confidence intervals or p-values for HLA mismatch are reported in the abstract; deceased heart-beating donor allocation in the UK; no living-donor data; outcomes after 3 years are descriptive measures of equity of access and matching, compared with pre-implementation simulations; graft survival is not reported in the abstract; the one statistical claim in the abstract, a significant benefit for patients waiting more than 5 years, is stated without any number, denominator, comparator or p-value; no information on sensitisation, antibody status, cold ischaemia, donor age or immunosuppression in the abstract; typing resolution not stated; antigen-level specificities implied by the defaulting rule; the scheme's HLA weights were chosen for equity of access and simulated performance, not fitted to a graft-survival model, so they are not evidence for the size of any HLA effect.

Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation, Lippincott Williams and Wilkins); convert_article_ids returned no PMCID, so no PMC full text exists and no author manuscript was found. All quotes are taken from the PubMed abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | US candidates listed 1988-2007 (SRTR) who were relisted after loss of a primary kidney transplant |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract; first kidney transplants from the US registry, living- and deceased-donor recipients are not separated in the retrieved text |
| n | 15,980 |
| design | retrospective registry cohort; absolute change in PRA modelled in general linear models, new sensitisation in logistic models |
| typing resolution | not stated; registry antigen-level (serologic) HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch counts are implied by the reported mismatch categories |
| outcome | change in panel reactive antibody (PRA) from before the first transplant to relisting; and the probability of becoming newly sensitised |
| follow up | not stated; the interval is from listing for the first transplant to relisting after graft loss, inside a 1988-2007 listing window |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the sensitisation-cost paper for the review: it answers what a poorly matched first kidney transplant costs the patient later, not what mismatch does to this graft. The exposure is the mismatch count of the first transplant and the outcome is alloantibody at relisting, so it supplies dose-response evidence (C2/C9) for a harm that a graft-survival-only analysis cannot see, and it is the mechanistic bridge to the retransplant arm of C11. For an Iranian living-donor, low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen the transfer is unusually good in one respect and poor in two. Good: the exposure is exactly what such a pre-screen can measure, a broad HLA-A, -B, -DR antigen-level mismatch count, so the paper argues that a one-field count is worth acting on even when this graft's survival difference is small, which is the core justification for ranking on mismatch at all. Poor: the cohort is a US deceased-donor-era registry whose mismatch distribution and immunosuppression era do not match Iranian living donation, and the abstract does not separate living from deceased first transplants. Also poor: the outcome is PRA, and a programme that cannot measure antibody status before transplant cannot use this paper to stratify its current candidates; it can only use it prospectively, to argue that today's mismatch choice determines tomorrow's PRA and therefore tomorrow's access to a second graft. Because the paper carries no DQ, DP or HLA-C data, it cannot support C4.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- became newly sensitised by relisting: first transplant with 0 HLA-A, -B mismatch — proportion (%) 10; adjusted for none stated; reported as a raw proportion in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- became newly sensitised by relisting: highest HLA mismatch category of the first transplant (the abstract does not name the mismatch count) — proportion (%) 37; adjusted for none stated; reported as a raw proportion in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- absolute change in PRA from before the first transplant to relisting: first transplant with 0 HLA-A, -B, -DR or 0 HLA-A, -B mismatch, versus increasing mismatch — direction only (no number printed in the abstract) None; adjusted for general linear model; covariates not listed in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 1. The abstract states 'no appreciable change' at zero mismatch and 'a significant increase in PRA by increasing HLA mismatch' but prints no coefficient, CI or p-value.]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 (HLA-A, -B) MM: 10%; increasing, highest category; count not stated in the abstract MM: up to 37%
- Shape reported: monotone increasing in mismatch count, with a zero-mismatch premium: no appreciable PRA rise at 0 HLA-A, -B, -DR or 0 HLA-A, -B mismatch, then a rise across increasing mismatch, 10% to 37% newly sensitised. Only the two endpoints are printed in the abstract; the intermediate 1/2/3/4-mismatch points exist only in the paper's tables and figures, which are not retrievable without full text.; linearity tested: not tested in the retrieved text. The abstract reports general linear models for PRA change and logistic models for new sensitisation, but no test for trend, no linearity test, no spline and no threshold analysis is reported.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- first-transplant HLA mismatch x recipient age; first-transplant HLA mismatch x race (African American): The abstract reports younger age and African American race as additional contributors to a higher PRA at relisting. These are reported as independent contributors (main effects in the models), NOT as tested effect-modification/interaction terms; no interaction test appears in the retrieved text. [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "There was no appreciable change in PRA for patients receiving a first 0 HLA-A, -B, -DR, or 0 HLA-A, -B-mismatched kidney transplant; contrariwise, there was a significant increase in PRA by increasing HLA mismatch of the first transplant." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "Only 10% of patients became sensitized after a 0 HLA-A, -B-mismatched transplant, whereas the proportion rose up to 37% with increasing HLA mismatches." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "Other factors, notably younger age and African American race, also contributed to a higher PRA at relisting." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "Although there might be a limited impact of HLA matching on acute rejection and graft survival, many patients might be negatively impacted from poor HLA matching of their first kidney transplant when needing a second transplant." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C13* — "An unforeseen consequence of poorer matching could be increased sensitization for candidates pursuing retransplantation." (Abstract, Background)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC deposit exists for this PMID, so the adjusted model output - the odds ratios, coefficients, confidence intervals and p-values for each mismatch count - could not be retrieved. Every number in this record is a raw proportion printed in the abstract.; The per-count dose-response series (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 mismatches) is not in the abstract; only the 0-mismatch value and the top category are given. The shape between them is asserted as 'increasing' but cannot be characterised as linear, concave, convex or step from the retrieved text.; Registry data with antigen-level (serologic) HLA-A, -B, -DR typing only. No HLA-C, no DQ, no DP, no allele-level or molecular (eplet/PIRCHE) mismatch. The paper therefore cannot speak to C4.; The outcome is PRA measured across 1988-2007, a period spanning CDC, AHG-CDC and solid-phase/flow assays. Assay drift over twenty years is a serious threat to a 'change in PRA' outcome and is not addressed in the retrieved text.; Selection: the cohort is restricted to patients who lost a first graft AND were relisted. Patients who died with function, or who lost a graft and were never relisted, are excluded. Sensitisation itself reduces the chance of being relisted, which can bias the exposure-outcome relation.; Graft loss itself, transplant nephrectomy, transfusions, pregnancy and immunosuppression withdrawal at graft failure are all routes to sensitisation that correlate with mismatch; the abstract does not state whether these were adjusted for.; Donor type is not separated in the abstract, so the living-donor-specific dose-response - the case the Iranian programme needs - cannot be read from this record.; The outcome is sensitisation, not graft or patient survival. The paper argues an indirect harm; it does not itself estimate the graft-survival cost of mismatch..

### Rao PS 2009 — A comprehensive risk quantification score for deceased donor kidneys: the kidney donor risk index.

Rao PS 2009, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/TP.0b013e3181ac620b](https://doi.org/10.1097/TP.0b013e3181ac620b). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wolters Kluwer/Lippincott). No PMC record: get_article_metadata returned no pmc identifier, and convert_article_ids returned no pmcid from either the PMID or the DOI. No open-access or author-manuscript version was located, so no full text could be retrieved..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | first-time, kidney-only, deceased-donor adult transplants, United States national data 1995-2005 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 69,440 |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; Cox proportional-hazards regression on donor and transplant factors, adjusting for recipient factors; the fitted donor/transplant coefficients are combined into a continuous donor risk index (KDRI) scaled to a healthy 40-year-old donor |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved abstract. US registry data of this era are serologic/antigen (one-field) level in practice, but the retrieved text does not state this and it must not be asserted from this paper. |
| outcome | composite all-cause graft failure: 'the risk of death or graft loss' (death is NOT censored); adjusted 5-year graft survival reported by KDRI quintile |
| follow up | not stated in the retrieved abstract; outcomes summarised at 5 years |
| other factors modelled | donor age, donor race, donor history of hypertension, donor history of diabetes, donor serum creatinine, cerebrovascular cause of death, donor height, donor weight, donation after cardiac death (DCD), hepatitis C virus status, cold ischemia time, double or en bloc transplant, recipient factors (adjusted for, not part of the index; not itemised in the abstract) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the canonical deceased-donor kidney risk index, and the review needs it for two distinct questions. First, as a locus-ranking datapoint (C5/C3): out of a candidate set of donor and transplant variables, the only HLA terms that survived into the final 14-factor index were HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch - HLA-A mismatch is absent from the published list. That is model-selection evidence that B and DR carry the independently detectable signal and A does not, at antigen-level typing, once donor quality is in the model; it is weaker than a head-to-head effect comparison, and A's absence is equally consistent with A's effect being absorbed by B through A-B haplotype linkage rather than with A having no effect. Second, as the reference case for C14, the claim that donor-quality factors dominate composite indices: HLA supplies only 2 of 14 terms, while the index as a whole separates adjusted 5-year graft survival by 63% versus 82%, and the abstract gives no decomposition, so this paper shows HLA is a real but minority component of donor-quality scoring without quantifying its share. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor, low-resolution, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen is indirect and should be treated as directional only. The population is deceased-donor, where the dominant KDRI terms - DCD, cold ischaemia, cerebrovascular death, donor creatinine, HCV - either vanish or collapse to near-constant in elective living donation, so the donor-quality variance that swamps HLA here is largely absent there and HLA's relative weight should rise, not fall, in a living-donor setting. The outcome is a death-inclusive composite, which dilutes the immunological signal that a matching pre-screen is trying to capture. Most importantly for this review's immediate need, the per-locus HLA-B and HLA-DR coefficients that are the stated reason for including this paper are not in the abstract and could not be retrieved.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- adjusted 5-year graft survival: highest KDRI quintile (>1.45) - COMPOSITE 14-factor donor index, NOT an HLA-specific contrast — adjusted 5-year graft survival (%) 63; adjusted for recipient factors (Cox model adjusting for recipient characteristics; not itemised in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- adjusted 5-year graft survival: lowest KDRI quintile (<0.79) - COMPOSITE 14-factor donor index, NOT an HLA-specific contrast — adjusted 5-year graft survival (%) 82; adjusted for recipient factors (Cox model adjusting for recipient characteristics; not itemised in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- adjusted 5-year graft survival: second-lowest KDRI quintile (0.79-<0.96) - COMPOSITE 14-factor donor index, NOT an HLA-specific contrast — adjusted 5-year graft survival (%) 79; adjusted for recipient factors (Cox model adjusting for recipient characteristics; not itemised in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 1]

**Dose-response.**

- B: entered the final 14-factor KDRI as 'human leukocyte antigen-B ... mismatch'; no coefficient, hazard ratio, CI or p-value is given in the retrieved abstract
- DR: entered the final 14-factor KDRI as 'human leukocyte antigen- ... DR mismatch'; no coefficient, hazard ratio, CI or p-value is given in the retrieved abstract
- A: ABSENT from the published 14-factor list; the abstract does not say whether HLA-A mismatch was tested and dropped or never entered as a candidate
- C: not mentioned
- DQ: not mentioned
- DP: not mentioned
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not stated. The abstract does not say whether HLA-B and HLA-DR mismatch were entered as a 0/1/2 count, as ordered categories, or as a collapsed binary, and reports no test of linearity, no spline and no threshold analysis. This is the single most important gap: the paper is in the review specifically for its per-locus coefficients and mismatch coding, and both are in the full text only.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C5* — "cerebrovascular cause of death, height, weight, donation after cardiac death, hepatitis C virus status, human leukocyte antigen-B and DR mismatch, cold ischemia time, and double or en bloc transplant" (Abstract, Methods/Results - the enumerated 14-factor list (sentence fragment, continues the list begun at 'donor age, race, ...'))
- *C3* — "The proposed KDRI includes 14 donor and transplant factors, each found to be independently associated with graft failure or death" (Abstract, Methods)
- *C14* — "Transplants of kidneys in the highest KDRI quintile (>1.45) had an adjusted 5-year graft survival of 63%, compared with 82% and 79% in the two lowest KDRI quintiles" (Abstract, Results)
- *C14* — "By using national data from 1995 to 2005, we analyzed 69,440 first-time, kidney-only, deceased donor adult transplants" (Abstract, Methods)
- *C14* — "Cox regression was used to model the risk of death or graft loss, based on donor and transplant factors, adjusting for recipient factors" (Abstract, Methods)

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY. Not in PMC; no full text could be retrieved. The per-locus HLA-B and HLA-DR coefficients, the mismatch coding (count vs category), and any test of linearity - the exact reasons this paper is in the review - are all in the full text and are NOT reported here. This record cannot settle the questions it was pulled to answer.; The outcome is a death-inclusive composite ('death or graft loss'), not death-censored graft failure, so the HLA terms are diluted by patient death from non-immunological causes.; HLA-A is absent from the 14-factor list, but the abstract does not state whether it was tested and dropped or never a candidate; absence from a selected model is not evidence of no effect, especially given A-B haplotype linkage.; The index is deliberately a DONOR index: it is adjusted for recipient factors rather than modelling them, so it says nothing about the donor-recipient interaction (sensitisation, PRA, DSA, repeat mismatch) that dominates a matching decision.; No sensitisation, PRA, DSA or antibody data are mentioned anywhere in the retrieved text; no interaction or effect-modification analysis is reported.; Typing resolution is not stated; antigen-level typing is implied by the era and data source but is not confirmed by the retrieved text.; Deceased-donor only, US only, 1995-2005 era immunosuppression and allocation - two decades before the target setting.; The 63% vs 82% quintile spread is the effect of the whole composite index, not of HLA. The abstract gives no decomposition, so HLA's share of that spread is unknown and must not be inferred from these numbers.; Derivation cohort only in the retrieved text; no external validation is described in the abstract..

### Gritsch HA 2008 — Should pediatric patients wait for HLA-DR-matched renal transplants?

Gritsch HA 2008, *American Journal of Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1111/j.1600-6143.2008.02320.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-6143.2008.02320.x). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Wiley, American Journal of Transplantation); no PMC record, no author manuscript. convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 18839440, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable. All extraction below is from the abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | all primary (first) paediatric kidney transplant recipients in the United States, 1996-2004, receiving kidneys from deceased donors aged 35 years or less; a separate analysis covers PRA at the time of second waitlisting after a first transplant |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | not stated in the abstract |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; graft-survival comparison across DR mismatch strata plus a relative-rate model for donor age, and a logistic-type analysis of the odds of PRA >30% at re-listing. The modelling approach, covariate set and n are not described in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; the 1996-2004 US OPTN era implies serologic/antigen-level (one-field) typing, but the paper does not say so in the retrieved text |
| outcome | primary: 5-year graft survival (all-cause; death-censoring not stated). Secondary: allograft failure rate by donor age; odds of panel-reactive antibody (PRA) >30% at the time of second waitlisting (post-transplant sensitisation). |
| follow up | not stated; 5-year graft survival is the reported horizon, transplants performed 1996-2004 |
| other factors modelled | donor age (<35 vs >=35 years), pre-transplant HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatch of the first graft (as exposure for later sensitisation) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is deliberate counter-evidence for the review: it is one of the few registry analyses that isolates the DR locus inside a stratum where donor quality is already excellent, and finds nothing. Within US paediatric recipients of kidneys from deceased donors aged 35 or under, 5-year graft survival was flat across 0, 1 and 2 DR mismatches (71%, 69%, 71%), which bears directly on C3 (is DR the dominant single locus?) and on C9 (is there a zero-mismatch premium?). It bears on C11 because it is an effect-modification result by construction: the DR effect is estimated only inside a young-donor stratum, and in the same analysis donor age >=35 carried a relative allograft failure rate of 1.32 (p = 0.0326) - donor quality moved the outcome where DR did not. It also supplies the review's only paediatric evidence on the sensitisation argument for matching: the degree of HLA-A, -B or -DR mismatch of the first transplant did not raise the odds of PRA >30% at re-listing, and no dose effect was seen. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown pre-screen in Iran is limited and mostly cautionary. The population is deceased-donor and paediatric, so the donor-age axis this paper exploits (young deceased donors) is not the axis that varies in a living-donor pool. The typing resolution is never stated in the retrieved text; the 1996-2004 US registry era makes antigen-level typing likely but that is an inference, not a fact the paper supplies. The correct use of this paper is as a bound on how much a pre-screen should be allowed to penalise a DR mismatch when the alternative is a worse donor or a longer wait: in this one registry stratum, DR matching bought no 5-year graft survival and no protection against sensitisation. The abstract reports no sample size, no confidence interval and no test statistic for the DR comparison, so the strength of that null cannot be judged from the retrieved text.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- 5-year graft survival: 0 HLA-DR mismatch (deceased donors aged <=35, paediatric recipients) — percentage (5-year graft survival) 71; adjusted for unadjusted stratum estimate as far as the abstract states; restricted to deceased donors aged <=35 and to primary paediatric transplants [Abstract]
- 5-year graft survival: 1 HLA-DR mismatch (deceased donors aged <=35, paediatric recipients) — percentage (5-year graft survival) 69; adjusted for as above; authors describe the three DR strata as 'statistically comparable' but print no test statistic or p value in the abstract [Abstract]
- 5-year graft survival: 2 HLA-DR mismatches (deceased donors aged <=35, paediatric recipients) — percentage (5-year graft survival) 71; adjusted for as above [Abstract]
- allograft failure: donor age >=35 years vs donor age <35 years — relative rate (term used by the authors; the underlying model is not named in the abstract) 1.32, p=0.0326; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract]
- panel-reactive antibody (PRA) >30% at the time of second waitlisting: increasing degree of HLA-A, -B or -DR mismatch of the first transplant (and increasing total number of mismatched HLA antigens) — odds (reported as a null result; no numeric estimate printed in the abstract) None; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: 5-year graft survival 71%; 1 MM: 5-year graft survival 69%; 2 MM: 5-year graft survival 71%; note MM: reported as three separate strata (1 and 2 mismatches are NOT pooled); the authors call the three 'statistically comparable' but print no p value, no CI and no hazard ratio in the abstract. No A, B, DQ, C or DP per-locus series is reported.
- Shape reported: flat / no dose-response. For graft survival the DR series is non-monotonic and essentially flat (71% / 69% / 71%). For post-transplant sensitisation the authors state explicitly that there was no 'dose effect' as more HLA antigens were mismatched.; linearity tested: not formally tested in the retrieved text. No trend test, spline, threshold model, categorical-vs-linear comparison or P-for-trend is reported in the abstract; the claim of no dose-response rests on the three flat DR percentages and on a stated absence of a 'dose effect' on PRA >30%, neither of which is accompanied by a printed statistic.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR mismatch x donor age (by restriction, not by a tested interaction term): The whole DR analysis is conducted inside the stratum of deceased donors aged 35 years or less. Within that young-donor stratum DR mismatch showed no graft-survival gradient, while donor age itself did move the outcome. The authors did not report a formal interaction test between DR mismatch and donor age, so this is stratified evidence, not a measured effect modification. (DR 0/1/2 mismatch: 71% / 69% / 71% 5-year graft survival within donors <=35; donor age >=35 vs <35: relative rate of allograft failure 1.32 (p = 0.0326)) [Abstract]
- degree of HLA-A, -B or -DR mismatch of the first transplant x subsequent sensitisation (PRA >30% at second waitlisting): No statistical increase in the odds of PRA >30% at re-listing with greater HLA-A, -B or -DR mismatch of the first graft, and no 'dose effect' as the number of mismatched antigens rose. This undercuts the standard argument that matching the first graft protects the paediatric recipient's chance of a second one. (no numeric estimate, CI or p value printed in the abstract) [Abstract]
- recipient age (paediatric population) x HLA matching policy: The paper's conclusion is an effect-modification claim at the policy level: for paediatric recipients specifically, donor age should outrank HLA-DR matching in allocation, because the DR benefit was absent while the donor-age penalty was measurable. (qualitative; rests on the two results above) [Abstract (conclusion)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "Zero HLA-DR-mismatched kidneys had statistically comparable 5-year graft survival (71%), to 1-DR-mismatched kidneys (69%) and 2-DR-mismatched kidneys (71%)." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "When compared to donors less than 35 years of age, the relative rate of allograft failure was 1.32 (p = 0.0326) for donor age greater than or equal to age 35." (Abstract)
- *C11* — "There was no statistical increase in the odds of developing a panel-reactive antibody (PRA) greater than 30% at the time of second waitlisting, based upon the degree of HLA-A, -B or -DR mismatch of the first transplant" (Abstract)
- *C2* — "nor was there a 'dose effect' when more HLA antigens were mismatched between the donor and recipient" (Abstract)
- *C13* — "should not turn down such kidney offers to wait for a better HLA-DR-matched kidney" (Abstract (conclusion))

**Limitations.** Abstract only. PMC has no full text and no author manuscript exists, so the sample size, the model specification, the covariate set, all confidence intervals and every p value except the donor-age one are unavailable. Nothing in the Results or Tables could be read.; The central claim is an accepted null. With no n, no CI and no power statement, a clinically meaningful DR effect cannot be excluded; 'statistically comparable' is asserted without a printed test statistic.; The DR analysis is restricted to deceased donors aged 35 or less, i.e. the best-quality deceased donors. The result therefore says DR matching adds little on top of an already-excellent donor, not that DR matching is irrelevant in general. It cannot be extrapolated to older or marginal donors.; Deceased-donor only, and paediatric only. Neither the donor type nor the recipient age band matches an adult living-donor pre-screen. Paediatric recipients receive different immunosuppression and have different rejection and adherence profiles than adults.; Typing resolution is never stated. The 1996-2004 US registry era implies antigen-level typing, but this is an inference, not a retrieved fact.; Only A, B and DR are considered. DQ, C and DP are absent, so the paper cannot speak to the possibility that the apparent DR null is confounded by unmeasured DQ mismatch travelling with DR.; Graft survival is reported at 5 years and is not stated to be death-censored. A flat curve at 5 years does not rule out divergence later, which matters for paediatric recipients who need decades of graft function.; The sensitisation analysis conditions on reaching a second waitlisting, which selects on graft failure and can bias the mismatch-to-PRA relationship toward the null.; Era effects: 1996-2004 immunosuppression and the absence of routine solid-phase (Luminex) antibody testing mean sensitisation was measured by PRA, a cruder and less mismatch-specific instrument than modern dnDSA assays.; Published 2008; the OPTN allocation policy it endorses has since been revised, so its policy conclusion is historical..

### Doxiadis IIN 2007 — Simpler and equitable allocation of kidneys from postmortem donors primarily based on full HLA-DR compatibility.

Doxiadis IIN 2007, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/01.tp.0000261108.27421.bc](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.tp.0000261108.27421.bc). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Lippincott Williams & Wilkins); no PMC record returned by convert_article_ids for PMID 17496537 or for the DOI, so no open full text was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Two datasets. (1) Single centre (Leiden University Medical Center), n=456 kidney transplants performed 1985-1999. (2) Eurotransplant database, n=39,205 transplants performed 1985-2005. Recipient age, retransplant status, sensitisation and immunosuppression era are not described in the retrieved abstract. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 456 (single centre) and 39,205 (Eurotransplant) |
| design | retrospective cohort in two tiers: single-centre biopsy-confirmed rejection analysis plus registry graft-survival analysis; Kaplan-Meier product limit survival estimates and Cox proportional hazards regression |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved abstract; serologic/antigen (broad and split) level is implied by the 1985-2005 Eurotransplant era and by the HLA-A/-B/-DR antigen MeSH indexing, but this is not confirmed in the retrieved text |
| outcome | biopsy-confirmed acute rejection within the first 180 posttransplant days (single centre); graft survival (Eurotransplant) |
| follow up | not stated in the retrieved abstract; transplant accrual spans 1985-1999 (single centre) and 1985-2005 (Eurotransplant) |
| other factors modelled | not specified in the retrieved abstract; the abstract states only that Cox proportional hazard regression was used 'for the estimation of relative risks (Hazard-ratios) for different variables' without naming them |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the rationale paper for DR-first ('DR-gated') deceased-donor kidney allocation and is the cleanest published statement of the locus interaction the review needs for C10: HLA-A,B matching bought an additional benefit only inside the fully HLA-DR compatible stratum, and a single HLA-DR incompatibility was enough to abolish the HLA-A,B effect entirely. That is a non-additivity claim, not a per-locus main-effect claim, and it is the direct evidence for treating DR as a gate rather than as one more term in a 0-6 mismatch sum. It also supports C3 (DR dominance) with two outcomes at once: biopsy-confirmed acute rejection in the first 180 days at a single centre, and graft survival in a 39,205-transplant registry. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field, antibody-unknown pre-screen in Iran is partial. The direction transfers well and is arguably conservative: the population is deceased-donor with the long cold ischaemia and allocation-driven travel that this paper is trying to reduce, so a living-donor setting removes noise rather than adding it, and the DR-gate logic is exactly the kind of rule a low-resolution pre-screen can execute, since broad HLA-DR antigen assignment is the part of one-field typing that is least often ambiguous and DR polymorphism is the lowest of the three loci. The transfer fails in three places: the paper pools 1 and 2 DR mismatches into a single 'incompatible' group, so it cannot tell a pre-screen how to rank one DR mismatch against two (C9 is not answered here); it reports no HLA-C, -DQ or -DP result, so it cannot inform the class II loci that dominate dnDSA risk in living donation; and, critically for our use, the retrieved abstract carries no hazard ratios, confidence intervals or interaction p-values at all, so this paper can justify the SHAPE of a rule but must not be used to set any weight or threshold number.

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: reference: 'full HLA-DR compatible' - lower incidence of biopsy-confirmed acute rejection in the first 180 days (single centre) and significantly better graft survival (Eurotransplant); 1_or_2_pooled MM: 'incompatible' - worse on both outcomes; no hazard ratio, confidence interval or p-value appears in the retrieved abstract; 1 MM: not reported separately; 2 MM: not reported separately
- A_and_B_combined: within_DR_compatible MM: additional positive effect of HLA-A,B matching present; magnitude not given in the retrieved abstract; within_DR_incompatible MM: no HLA-A,B matching effect - 'a single HLA-DR incompatibility eliminates the HLA-A,B matching effect'; note MM: HLA-A and HLA-B are treated jointly throughout the abstract; the paper as retrieved does not separate an A effect from a B effect, so it cannot support C5 (B outranks A)
- C: not reported
- DQ: not reported
- DP: not reported
- Shape reported: threshold / step at HLA-DR, conditional on the class I effect: 0 versus >=1 DR mismatch is the operative split, and the HLA-A,B gradient exists only in the 0-DR-mismatch stratum. No 0-6 total-count series and no per-count estimates are reported in the retrieved abstract.; linearity tested: not reported in the retrieved abstract; no test of linearity, trend, spline or threshold is described, and no per-count series is shown from which one could be inferred; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-A,B matching x HLA-DR compatibility (0 vs >=1 DR mismatch): The benefit of HLA-A,B matching was present only among fully HLA-DR compatible transplants; introducing a single HLA-DR incompatibility abolished the HLA-A,B matching effect. Reported as consistent in both the single-centre (n=456, rejection) and the Eurotransplant (n=39,205, graft survival) analyses. [Abstract, Results and Conclusions sentences (no interaction p-value or stratum-specific hazard ratio in the retrieved abstract)]
- HLA-DR compatibility x recipient ethnic origin (asserted, not tested): The authors argue that a DR-primary allocation rule would benefit patients irrespective of ethnic origin because HLA-DR polymorphism is far lower than HLA-A,B polymorphism. This is a stated expectation about equity of access under the proposed rule, not a measured effect-modification result. [Abstract, Conclusions]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "A single center study (n=456 transplants, performed between 1985 and 1999) showed that full HLA-DR compatibility leads to a lower incidence of biopsy confirmed acute rejections in the first 180 posttransplantation days." (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "graft survival in the full HLA-DR compatible group was significantly better than in the incompatible" (Abstract, Results (Eurotransplant database, n=39,205))
- *C10* — "An additional positive effect of HLA-A,B matching was only found in the full HLA-DR compatible group." (Abstract, Results)
- *C10* — "In both studies, the introduction of a single HLA-DR incompatibility eliminates the HLA-A,B matching effect." (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "We propose to allocate postmortem kidneys only to patients with full HLA-DR compatibility, and use HLA-A,B compatibility as an additional selection criterion." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C13* — "the polymorphism of HLA-DR is by far lower than that of HLA-A,B" (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. PMC holds no full text for this article (convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for the PMID or the DOI), so no table, figure, hazard ratio, confidence interval or p-value could be retrieved. Every quantitative statement below the level of 'significantly better' is unavailable.; No effect sizes at all: zero hazard ratios, zero confidence intervals, zero percentages in the retrieved text. The paper can support the existence and direction of the DR gate but cannot supply a single number for weighting or thresholding.; The interaction is asserted as a stratified observation ('only found in the full HLA-DR compatible group') with no formal test of interaction reported in the retrieved abstract, and with no adjustment described. A stratum where the effect is not significant is not the same as a significant difference between strata.; One and two HLA-DR mismatches are pooled into a single 'incompatible' group, so the paper cannot address C9 (size of the first versus the second mismatch at a locus).; HLA-A and HLA-B are analysed jointly as 'HLA-A,B' throughout; no separate A and B estimates are reported, so this paper does not support C5 (B outranks A) despite being tagged for it.; Deceased-donor only. No living-donor transplants, which is the review's target setting.; Historical cohorts (1985-1999 and 1985-2005), predating current induction and maintenance immunosuppression; the size of any HLA effect in that era is an upper bound on the contemporary effect.; Observational and allocation-confounded: in Eurotransplant, DR-matched kidneys were preferentially allocated and therefore differ systematically in travel distance, cold ischaemia time, waiting time and recipient phenotype rarity from unmatched kidneys. The abstract does not say which covariates the Cox models adjusted for.; No HLA-C, -DQ or -DP result, and no antibody or DSA data, so nothing here informs the class II loci that drive de novo DSA in living donation.; Single-centre rejection cohort is small (n=456) for a stratified interaction analysis; the interaction claim rests mainly on the registry arm.; European (Eurotransplant) population; HLA haplotype frequencies and the achievability of full DR compatibility differ in an Iranian donor pool, and the paper's equity argument was made for a European allocation system..

### Opelz G 2007 — Effect of human leukocyte antigen compatibility on kidney graft survival: comparative analysis of two decades.

Opelz G 2007, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/01.tp.0000269725.74189.b9](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.tp.0000269725.74189.b9). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Lippincott Williams & Wilkins); no PMC deposit (convert_article_ids returns no PMCID); abstract only via PubMed.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Kidney transplants reported to the Collaborative Transplant Study (international multicentre registry), transplanted 1985-1994 versus 1995-2004, with the last 5 years (2000-2004) analysed separately |
| donor type | not stated in abstract (CTS collects both deceased- and living-donor transplants; the conclusion refers to 'kidney exchange programs', i.e. deceased-donor allocation, and CTS era analyses of this kind are predominantly deceased-donor) |
| n | not stated in abstract |
| design | retrospective registry cohort, era comparison, multivariate Cox regression |
| typing resolution | not stated in abstract (CTS matching of this era is serologic/antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR) |
| outcome | graft survival (censoring not specified in abstract); need for posttransplant rejection treatment |
| follow up | not stated in abstract |
| other factors modelled | confounders adjusted by multivariate Cox regression (specific covariates not named in the abstract) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is the Collaborative Transplant Study's direct answer to the UNOS-based claim that the HLA-matching effect on kidney graft survival had weakened under modern immunosuppression: it compares the decades 1985-1994 and 1995-2004 (plus 2000-2004 alone) with multivariate Cox adjustment and reports that the relative effect of HLA matching on graft survival and on the need for rejection treatment stayed strong and highly significant (P<0.001) in every interval. It therefore supports claim C1 (persistence of the HLA effect under improving immunosuppression) and, as an era-stratified analysis, addresses C11 (effect modification by era/immunosuppression, with the finding that era did not abolish the effect). Only the abstract is available, so the per-mismatch-count graft-survival series that the full paper presents cannot be extracted here; the abstract prints no HRs, CIs or 0-6 mismatch figures, so C2 is supported only in the weak qualitative sense that 'HLA mismatches significantly influence outcome' and is not recorded as supported. For transfer to an Iranian living-donor, one-field-typing, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen: the CTS population is international and largely deceased-donor with antigen-level typing, so the typing resolution matches the target setting well, but the donor type and the allocation-driven mismatch distribution do not, and living-donor transplants carry lower baseline risk in which a fixed relative HLA effect translates into a smaller absolute one. The paper's usable contribution to the pre-screen is a licence to keep counting antigen-level HLA-A, -B, -DR mismatch as prognostically meaningful in the modern era; it supplies no weights, no per-locus ranking and no threshold.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft survival: HLA matching (mismatch grade; categories not given in abstract), analysed separately in 1985-1994, 1995-2004 and 2000-2004 — no HR printed in abstract (multivariate Cox); significance only None, p=<0.001; adjusted for confounders via multivariate Cox regression (not itemised in abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- need for posttransplant rejection treatment: HLA matching (mismatch grade; categories not given in abstract), all intervals analysed — no OR/RR printed in abstract; significance only None, p=<0.001; adjusted for not stated in abstract [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported in the abstract; the full paper's per-mismatch graft-survival curves are not accessible here; linearity tested: not stated in abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching x transplant era (1985-1994 vs 1995-2004 vs 2000-2004): The relative impact of HLA matching on graft survival and on the need for rejection treatment remained strong and highly significant in every interval; no attenuation by era was found. This is a comparison of separately analysed era strata, not a formal interaction test - no P for interaction is reported in the abstract. (P<0.001 in each interval) [Abstract, Results]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C1* — "the influence of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) matching in renal transplantation has diminished in recent years, prompting the suggestion that donor kidney allocation algorithms should be revised" (Abstract, Background - this is the prior UNOS-based claim the paper set out to test, NOT this paper's finding)
- *C11* — "We compared the impact of HLA matching on kidney graft survival during the decades 1985-1994 and 1995-2004 using the data of the Collaborative Transplant Study." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C11* — "Multivariate Cox regression analysis was used to account for the influence of confounders." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C1* — "while graft survival rates have improved overall over time, the relative impact of HLA matching on the graft survival rate has remained strong and highly significant" (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "Both the need for posttransplant rejection treatment and the graft survival rates showed statistically highly significant associations with HLA matching regardless of the interval analyzed (P<0.001)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "We conclude that HLA mismatches significantly influence the outcome of kidney transplants and that kidney exchange programs for the purpose of achieving better HLA matches continue to be meaningful." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no HRs, CIs, sample size, follow-up, mismatch categories or per-locus results could be extracted; the full paper's 0-6 mismatch graft-survival series is not available here; Registry cohort with (almost certainly) antigen-level serologic typing; typing resolution is not stated in the abstract; Donor type not stated in the abstract; CTS era analyses are dominated by deceased-donor transplants and the conclusion concerns deceased-donor kidney exchange, so transfer to living donation is indirect; Covariates in the multivariate Cox model are not itemised in the abstract; adjustment for sensitisation, donor age and cold ischaemia cannot be confirmed; No formal HLA x era interaction test is reported in the abstract; 'remained strong' is a qualitative comparison of separately analysed era strata; Graft-survival censoring (all-cause vs death-censored) is not specified in the abstract; Registry analysis by the group that runs the registry and that has long argued for HLA matching; the paper is an explicit rebuttal of a competing UNOS analysis, so it is not a neutral adjudication of the question; Era ends in 2004; says nothing about practice, immunosuppression or outcomes after 2004; A constant RELATIVE effect across eras is compatible with a shrinking ABSOLUTE effect as baseline graft survival improves; the abstract reports only the relative claim.

### Persijn GG 2006 — Allocation of organs, particularly kidneys, within Eurotransplant.

Persijn GG 2006, *Human Immunology (Hum Immunol) 2006;67(6):419-23*, [DOI 10.1016/j.humimm.2006.03.008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.humimm.2006.03.008). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier); no PMC record, convert_article_ids returned no PMCID for PMID 16728263.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Deceased-donor kidney recipients allocated through the Eurotransplant Kidney Allocation System (ETKAS) across the six Eurotransplant countries; the first 9 years of ETKAS, i.e. from its introduction in 1996 to approximately 2005 |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | almost 30,000 deceased donor kidneys allocated during the first 9 years of ETKAS (abstract gives no recipient-level denominator for the survival figures) |
| design | Descriptive policy / allocation-system report with aggregate programme statistics. No multivariable model, no adjusted estimate, no confidence interval and no p-value appears anywhere in the retrieved abstract; the phrase 'a significant HLA-matching effect' is asserted without a test statistic. |
| typing resolution | not stated. The abstract names only HLA-A, -B and -DR as the matched loci (no C, DQ or DP) and does not state whether typing is serological/antigen (one-field) or allele level. |
| outcome | kidney graft survival at 3 years; plus allocation-process outcomes (share transplanted with 0 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches, transplantation of long-waiting patients, access for children and highly sensitised patients, national import/export balance) |
| follow up | 3 years for the graft-survival figures; the programme experience described spans the first 9 years of ETKAS (1996 to approximately 2005) |
| other factors modelled | mismatch probability (HLA phenotype frequency / chance of a matched offer), waiting period, i.e. time on dialysis, distance between donor centre and transplant centre, balance between import and export of the six participating countries, high urgency status (extra points), paediatric status (extra points) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is a first-hand description of how a large multinational allocation scheme converts HLA matching into an allocation decision, so it answers the review's C13 question — how do real allocation systems score HLA, and does the scoring deliver an outcome benefit? It is directly useful for the design of a scoring pre-screen because it shows that ETKAS does not use HLA mismatch alone: it scores the HLA-A,B,DR mismatch count together with mismatch probability (a correction so that patients with rare phenotypes are not penalised by their own genetics), dialysis waiting time, distance and inter-country balance, with bonus points for urgency and for children. The mismatch-probability term is the single most transferable idea for Iran, because an Iranian donor pool with strong founder haplotypes will otherwise systematically starve patients with uncommon phenotypes of any acceptable offer. The paper also gives the yield figure a scheme designer needs: with A,B,DR-based points and a pool of that size, only 22.3% of transplants reached 0 mismatches, which sets a realistic ceiling on how often a matching-driven scheme can deliver a full match. Transfer to the intended Iranian use case is nevertheless weak in three ways: the cohort is deceased-donor while the target is living-donor, where donor quality and the recipient-donor relationship dominate and where a waiting-time term has no meaning; antibody status is explicitly handled in Eurotransplant by a separate Acceptable Mismatch Program for the highly sensitised, whereas the Iranian pre-screen assumes antibody status is unknown; and the reported matching effect is a crude unadjusted 3-year survival contrast with no adjustment for donor age, cold ischaemia or sensitisation, so it cannot be used as an effect estimate, only as an existence claim. Its correct role in the review is as a design precedent for the points structure (C13) and as weak, unadjusted corroboration of a zero-mismatch premium (C9), not as a source of an effect size.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- share of transplants achieving a full HLA-A,B,DR match (allocation yield, not a clinical outcome): 0 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches vs any mismatch, among all kidneys allocated by ETKAS — percentage 22.3; adjusted for unadjusted; simple proportion of almost 30,000 allocated deceased donor kidneys over the first 9 years of ETKAS [Abstract]
- kidney transplant survival at 3 years (graft survival; the abstract does not say whether death-censored): overall ETKAS cohort, all mismatch levels combined (reference value for the matched-group comparison) — percentage 78; adjusted for unadjusted crude survival [Abstract]
- kidney transplant survival at 3 years (graft survival; the abstract does not say whether death-censored): HLA-A,B,DR matched combinations. WORDING CAUTION: the retrieved abstract literally reads '83% at 3 years for the HLA-A,B,DR mismatched combinations', which is internally inconsistent with the same sentence's claim of 'a significant HLA-matching effect' and with the 78% overall figure. The 83% can only belong to the favourably matched (0-mismatch) group; the printed word 'mismatched' appears to be a typographical error for 'fully matched' / 'non-mismatched'. The direction is NOT independently confirmed in the retrieved text. — percentage 83; adjusted for unadjusted crude survival; no adjustment for donor age, cold ischaemia, sensitisation or waiting time is reported [Abstract]
- transplantation of long-waiting patients (waiting more than 5 years) — allocation-process outcome: ETKAS era vs the pre-ETKAS period — ratio (stated in words as 'Twice as many') 2.0; adjusted for unadjusted before/after era comparison; no denominator, no CI, no test reported [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. No mismatch-count categories (0/1/2/3/4/5/6) and no per-locus breakdown appear in the retrieved abstract; the only matching contrast given is the fully-matched group against the overall cohort. The allocation points formula itself is described only qualitatively ('HLA-A,B,DR mismatch' as a scored factor), so the shape of the points-per-mismatch function cannot be recovered from the retrieved text either.; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "This point-scoring system takes the following factors into account: HLA-A,B,DR mismatch, mismatch probability, waiting period, i.e., time on dialysis, distance between donor/transplantation center, and balance between import/export of the six participating countries." (Abstract (PMID 16728263))
- *C13* — "Extra points are given to high urgency patients and to children." (Abstract (PMID 16728263))
- *C13* — "During the first 9 years of the new ET kidney allocation system (ETKAS) almost 30,000 deceased donor kidneys have been allocated of which 22.3% have been transplanted without HLA-A,B,DR mismatches." (Abstract (PMID 16728263))
- *C9* — "overall kidney transplant survival was 78% after 3 years and a significant HLA-matching effect was noticed, i.e., 83% at 3 years for the HLA-A,B,DR mismatched combinations" (Abstract (PMID 16728263). Quoted exactly as printed; see effect_sizes entry 3 and notes on the apparent typographical error in the word 'mismatched'.)
- *C11* — "Also substantially more children and highly sensitized patients received kidney transplants." (Abstract (PMID 16728263))
- *C13* — "All kidneys are offered to the pool and are allocated according to the degree of HLA matching, mismatch probability, waiting time, distance from the donor center, and balance between the countries participating in ET." (COMPANION PAPER, not the target paper: Doxiadis et al., 'It takes six to boogie', Transplantation 2004;77(4):615-7, PMID 15084947, Abstract)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. PMID 16728263 has no PMC record (convert_article_ids returned no PMCID), so the Results section, any table, the exact mismatch-count strata and any statistical test could not be read. Everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; No effect estimate in the epidemiological sense: no HR, OR, RR or SHR, no confidence interval and no p-value anywhere in the retrieved text. The claim of 'a significant HLA-matching effect' is asserted without a reported test.; The survival contrast is crude and unadjusted. Better-matched deceased-donor recipients in ETKAS also differ systematically in waiting time, sensitisation, donor origin and travel distance, precisely because the same points system allocated them; the 83% vs 78% gap therefore carries allocation-induced confounding and cannot be read as a causal matching effect.; The comparator is the overall cohort, which itself contains the matched group, so the 5-percentage-point gap understates the matched-vs-mismatched contrast by an unknown amount and is not a clean two-group comparison.; The sentence reporting the 83% figure is internally inconsistent as printed ('for the HLA-A,B,DR mismatched combinations'); the group label had to be read from context rather than from the text.; No per-locus decomposition. A, B and DR are scored as a bundle, so the paper says nothing about the relative weight of DR versus B versus A, and C, DQ and DP are absent from the scheme entirely.; Typing resolution is not stated, so it cannot be confirmed from this source whether ETKAS matching was at broad antigen, split antigen or allele level.; Deceased-donor allocation only. Two of the six scored factors (dialysis waiting time and inter-country import/export balance) and a third (donor-to-centre distance) have no analogue in a living-donor pre-screen.; Era effect: immunosuppression, induction practice and antibody detection (CDC-era crossmatching rather than single-antigen bead testing) in 1996-2005 differ substantially from current practice, so the magnitude of the matching benefit is not directly portable.; Single-author descriptive report by the allocating organisation itself, describing the performance of its own system; no independent validation and an evident institutional interest in a favourable evaluation ('the new ETKAS has reached its aims and goals')..

### Tajik N 2006 — The Predictive Value of HLA-DR Matching and Cytokine Gene Polymorphisms in Renal Allograft Acute Rejection: a Living-unrelated Donor (LURD) Study.

Tajik N 2006, *Iranian Journal of Immunology (Iran J Immunol) 2006 Dec;3(4):150-6*, PMID 18685174. Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown; PubMed record only. No PMCID and no DOI returned by PubMed or by the PMID/PMCID/DOI converter, so no open-access full text was retrievable. All extraction below is from the PubMed abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 42 living-unrelated donor (LURD) kidney transplant recipient/donor pairs transplanted at Hashemi Nejad Kidney Hospital, Tehran, Iran; adult status, retransplant status, sensitisation/PRA, immunosuppression protocol and cold ischaemia are not stated in the abstract |
| donor type | living |
| n | 42 |
| design | single-centre observational cohort of 42 LURD kidney transplants with 3 months of follow-up; rejector vs nonrejector group comparison of HLA-DR mismatch counts and cytokine genotypes. No multivariable model, no HR/OR reported in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | low resolution / one-field allele-group level: HLA-DR typed by PCR-SSP for DR1-18 (DRB1 allele groups, serologically equivalent). DR51/52/53, DQ, DP and class I loci were not typed or not reported. |
| outcome | biopsy-status-unspecified acute rejection within 3 months post-transplant (11/42, 26.2%). No graft survival or death-censored graft failure outcome. |
| follow up | 3 months post-transplantation |
| other factors modelled | recipient cytokine gene polymorphisms: TNF-alpha, TGF-beta1, IL-10, IL-6, IFN-gamma, combined recipient cytokine genotype considered jointly with HLA-DR matching |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the few published Iranian living-unrelated-donor series that reports HLA-DR mismatch against a clinical outcome, so it speaks directly to claim C15 (regional evidence and typing practice) and, secondarily, to C14 (does HLA matter within living donation). Its exposure measurement is almost exactly the exposure the KidneyMatch pre-screen will have: HLA-DR by PCR-SSP at DR1-18 allele-group (one-field, antigen-equivalent) resolution, in an Iranian LURD population, with recipient antibody/PRA status not reported. Its answer to the review's question is a null one: DR mismatch counts did not differ significantly between rejectors and nonrejectors (1.82 vs 1.52 mean mismatches, P=0.069), and more than half of the patients who did NOT reject were fully DR-mismatched, which the authors read as evidence that DR mismatch predicts acute rejection less reliably in LURD than in deceased-donor transplantation. Transfer to the pre-screen is nevertheless weak in one crucial respect: with n=42 and 11 events the study has almost no power (a P of 0.069 with a mean difference of 0.30 mismatches is an underpowered near-miss, not a demonstrated absence of effect), the outcome is 3-month acute rejection rather than graft survival, and the authors themselves say HLA compatibility still influences allograft survival. For KidneyMatch it is therefore best used as a caution that a DR-only, one-field score will not cleanly separate rejectors in an Iranian LURD population and must not be presented as a rejection predictor, rather than as evidence that DR matching can be dropped.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- acute rejection within 3 months (whole cohort incidence): all 42 LURD recipients — percentage 26.2; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results sentence 1 ("Acute rejection was observed in 11(26.2%) of 42 renal recipients.")]
- acute rejection: proportion of REJECTORS with one HLA-DR mismatch (2/11) — percentage 18.2; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- acute rejection: proportion of REJECTORS with two HLA-DR mismatches (9/11) — percentage 81.8; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- acute rejection: proportion of NONREJECTORS with one HLA-DR mismatch (13/31) — percentage 41.9; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- acute rejection: proportion of NONREJECTORS with two HLA-DR mismatches (17/31) — percentage 54.8; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- acute rejection: mean number of HLA-DR mismatches, rejectors (1.82, SD 0.40) vs nonrejectors (1.52, SD 0.57) — mean difference in HLA-DR mismatch count (rejector minus nonrejector) 0.3, p=0.069; adjusted for unadjusted; two-group comparison, statistical test not named in the abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 3. NOTE: the mean difference 0.30 is arithmetic on the two printed means (1.82 and 1.52); only the two means, the two SDs and P=0.069 are printed. The PubMed abstract text has lost its plus-minus signs, rendering these as "(1.820.40)" and "(1.520.57)".]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: not printed as a category; 0 rejectors and (by subtraction from the printed denominators) 1 nonrejector fall outside the 1-MM and 2-MM counts. See notes - this is derived, not printed.; 1 MM: rejectors 2 (18.2% of 11); nonrejectors 13 (41.9% of 31); 2 MM: rejectors 9 (81.8% of 11); nonrejectors 17 (54.8% of 31); mean_mismatch_count MM: rejectors 1.82 (SD 0.40) vs nonrejectors 1.52 (SD 0.57), P=0.069
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested. The authors report the DR mismatch distribution as 1-MM and 2-MM categories by rejection status, and separately compare the MEAN mismatch count between the two groups (which treats the 0/1/2 count as a continuous score), but no trend test, no per-mismatch estimate, no spline and no threshold analysis is reported. No risk model (HR/OR/RR) is fitted at all.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-DR matching x combined recipient cytokine genotype (TNF-alpha, TGF-beta1, IL-10, IL-6, IFN-gamma): null: no association of the combined cytokine genotype together with HLA-DR matching with acute rejection could be demonstrated. Cytokine polymorphisms alone also showed no correlation with acute rejection. (no estimate, no P value and no interaction test statistic printed; reported narratively as a failure to demonstrate an association) [Abstract, Results sentence 4 and Conclusion sentence 3]
- HLA-DR mismatch x donor type (living-unrelated vs deceased/cadaveric): asserted, not tested within this study: the authors postulate from the high DR mismatch frequency among nonrejectors that LURD immunogenicity differs from cadaveric transplantation, so that DR mismatch is a less reliable predictor of acute rejection in LURD. No deceased-donor comparison group was included and no formal interaction was estimated. (no estimate; narrative inference from the within-cohort distribution) [Abstract, Conclusion sentence 1]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "A total of 42 renal transplants that were performed at Hashemi Nejad Kidney Hospital (Tehran/Iran) and then followed up for 3 months post-transplantation were included in our study." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C15* — "Using PCR-SSP, HLA-DR alleles (DR1-18) of recipient and donor pairs" (Abstract, Methods)
- *C15* — "The frequency of one and two HLA-DR mismatches in rejector and nonrejector groups were 2(18.2%), 9(81.8%) and 13(41.9%), 17(54.8%) respectively." (Abstract, Results)
- *C15* — "more than half of nonrejectors had completely mismatched HLA-DR antigens with their donors" (Abstract, Results)
- *C15* — "we can postulate that the immunogenecity of LURD renal transplant is not similar to the cadaveric one, and predictive value of HLA-DR mismatching for acute rejection is not as reliable as in cadaveric transplant" (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C15* — "Polymorphisms associated with all the cytokines mentioned above were found to have no correlation with acute rejection." (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMCID and no DOI exist in the PubMed record or the ID converter, so the Methods, Results tables and the statistical test used could not be inspected; everything here is from the ~300-word abstract.; Very small: n=42 with only 11 rejection events. P=0.069 for a mean difference of 0.30 DR mismatches is an underpowered near-miss and must not be read as evidence of no effect. No confidence interval, no OR/HR/RR, and no power calculation is reported.; Single centre, single country, single donor type (LURD only), and no deceased-donor comparison group, so the paper's central claim that LURD immunogenicity differs from cadaveric transplantation is a postulate rather than a tested contrast.; Outcome is acute rejection within 3 months only. No graft survival, no death-censored graft failure, no dnDSA. A 3-month window misses late rejection and all chronic injury, which is where HLA mismatch effects are largest.; Rejection ascertainment is not described in the abstract: biopsy-proven versus clinically treated rejection is unstated, and Banff grading is not mentioned.; Only HLA-DR was typed and reported. No HLA-A, -B, -C, -DQ, -DP, and no total mismatch count, so nothing in this paper bears on any locus other than DR or on the total-count dose-response.; Typing is PCR-SSP at DR1-18 allele-group (one-field) level, so DRB1 allele-level and eplet/molecular mismatch effects are invisible; no imputation, no eplet or PIRCHE analysis.; No adjustment for anything: recipient/donor age, sex, PRA/sensitisation status, prior transplant, induction and maintenance immunosuppression, and cold ischaemia are not reported in the abstract and are not modelled. In an Iranian LURD programme, unmeasured confounding by immunosuppression protocol is plausible.; The exposure is analysed two incompatible ways (as 1-MM/2-MM categories and as a mean count) with no linearity or trend test, so the shape of any DR dose-response is unknowable from this report.; The PubMed abstract text has lost Greek letters and plus-minus signs; the cytokine names and the two mean-plus-or-minus-SD figures had to be reconstructed from context and are annotated as such rather than quoted..

|---|---|
