| follow up | not stated in abstract |
| other factors modelled | race / ethnicity (whites vs nonwhites), HLA-B and DR antigen profiles (transplantation-rate model, per abstract), waiting time (allocation criterion, described), covariates of the graft-failure Cox model are not stated in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the analysis that underpinned the 2003 US decision to drop HLA-B points from deceased-donor kidney allocation, so it is direct evidence for C13: it quantifies the trade-off between HLA-B priority and access, projecting that removing B priority while keeping DR priority would raise the rate of graft loss by 2.0 percent while increasing transplants among nonwhites by 6.3 percent and reducing them among whites by 4.0 percent (166 fewer in a year). Its message for any locus-weighting scheme is that at antigen level DR matching was judged worth keeping and B matching dispensable at a small outcome cost; the abstract, however, gives no per-locus hazard ratio, so the size of the B effect relative to A or DR cannot be read from the retrieved text. Transfer to a living-donor, one-field-typing, antibody-status-unknown pre-screen in Iran is indirect: the population is US deceased-donor recipients under pre-2003 immunosuppression, the outcome numbers are model projections of a policy change rather than observed between-group differences, and living-donor selection carries none of the waiting-list queueing that drives the equity result here. The equity lesson does transfer in principle, because HLA antigen frequencies differ across Iran's ethnic groups, so any pre-screen that weights B heavily will systematically favour candidates from the groups whose antigens are common in the donor pool. The typing level is the one point of good fit: the whole analysis is antigen-level (one-field) matching, the same resolution the Iranian pre-screen will have. The paper says nothing about HLA-A effect size, -C, -DQ, -DP, sensitisation, or high-resolution typing.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- rate of graft loss (projected): allocation without HLA-B matching priority (HLA-DR priority retained) vs current policy — percentage increase (projected from Cox graft-failure model; relative vs absolute not stated) 2.0; adjusted for Cox model for time from first transplantation to graft failure; covariates not stated in abstract [Abstract, Results]
- number of kidney transplantations among nonwhites (projected, one year): allocation without HLA-B matching priority (HLA-DR priority retained) vs current policy — percentage increase (projected) 6.3; adjusted for Cox model for time from listing to transplantation, adjusted for HLA-B and DR antigen profiles [Abstract, Results]
- number of kidney transplantations among whites (projected, one year): allocation without HLA-B matching priority (HLA-DR priority retained) vs current policy — percentage decrease (projected) -4.0; adjusted for Cox model for time from listing to transplantation, adjusted for HLA-B and DR antigen profiles [Abstract, Results]
- number of kidney transplantations among whites (projected, one year): allocation without HLA-B matching priority (HLA-DR priority retained) vs current policy — absolute difference in transplant count over one year (projected); the same result as the -4.0 percent row, not an independent estimate -166; adjusted for Cox model for time from listing to transplantation, adjusted for HLA-B and DR antigen profiles [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported (abstract only); linearity tested: not tested in the retrieved text; the paper fits a Cox graft-failure model on HLA matching but reports no coefficients in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "HLA typing and the time a patient has spent on the waiting list are the primary criteria used to allocate cadaveric kidneys for transplantation in the United States." (Abstract, Background)
- *C13* — "Candidates with no HLA-A, B, and DR mismatches are given top priority, followed by candidates with the fewest mismatches at the HLA-B and DR loci; this policy contributes to a higher transplantation rate among whites than nonwhites." (Abstract, Background)
- *C13* — "We also investigated the effect of HLA matching on the risk of graft failure, using a Cox model for the time from the first transplantation to graft failure." (Abstract, Methods)
- *C5* — "Eliminating the HLA-B matching as a priority while maintaining HLA-DR matching as a priority would decrease the number of transplantations among whites by 4.0 percent (166 fewer transplantations over a one-year period)" (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "it would increase the number among nonwhites by 6.3 percent and increase the rate of graft loss by 2.0 percent" (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "Removing HLA-B matching as a priority for the allocation of cadaveric kidneys could reduce the existing racial imbalance by increasing the number of transplantations among nonwhites, with only a small increase in the rate of graft loss." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** abstract only: no PMC full text (convert_article_ids returns no PMCID for PMID 14762181); per-locus hazard ratios, confidence intervals, sample size, calendar years and the graft-failure model covariates are not in the retrieved text; US deceased-donor registry population under pre-2003 immunosuppression; no living-donor data; antigen-level (serologic) HLA typing implied by 'HLA antigen profiles', not explicitly stated; the outcome effects are model projections of a hypothetical policy change, not observed differences between matched and mismatched groups; definition of graft loss (death-censored or all-cause) not stated in abstract; the 2.0 percent graft-loss figure is reported without a confidence interval, and whether it is a relative or an absolute increase is not stated in the abstract; ethnicity categories (whites vs nonwhites) are US-specific and do not map onto Iranian ethnic groups; no information on the size of the HLA-A effect, or on HLA-C, DQ, DP, sensitisation, or high-resolution typing; the second simulated scenario (removing both HLA-B and DR priority) is described in the Methods but not quantified in the abstract.

### Rees MT 2003 — HLA-A, B, C, DRB1, DQB1 matching heterogeneity in 'favourably matched' kidney recipients.

Rees MT 2003, *Transplant Immunology (Transpl Immunol) 12(1):73-8*, [DOI 10.1016/S0966-3274(03)00017-0](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0966-3274(03)00017-0). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Elsevier); no PMC record exists for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned pmid only, no pmcid), so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable. All quotes below are from the PubMed abstract..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 237 cadaveric (deceased) donor/recipient renal transplant pairs classified as 'favourably matched' according to United Kingdom Transplant criteria; typed at the Welsh Transplantation and Immunogenetics Laboratory, UK |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 237 donor/recipient pairs |
| design | cross-sectional descriptive study: pairs already graded 'favourably matched' on broad HLA-A, -B, -DR were re-typed at higher resolution and the residual (hidden) mismatch at HLA-A, -B, -C split level and HLA-DRB1/-DQB1 allele level was counted. Comparisons are unadjusted proportions with chi-square-type P values. No multivariable model, no survival analysis. |
| typing resolution | mixed and explicitly stratified by resolution: allocation used broad specificities for HLA-A, -B, -DR; the study re-typed at split specificity level for HLA-A, -B, -C and at allele level for HLA-DRB1 and -DQB1. 'Allele level' is as stated by the 2003 authors and is not necessarily today's two-field high resolution. HLA-DP and DQA1 were not typed. |
| outcome | prevalence of residual HLA mismatch at higher resolution and at unmatched loci (HLA-C, -DQ, DRB1/DQB1 alleles) within pairs already labelled 'favourably matched'. NO clinical outcome (no graft survival, no rejection, no DSA) is reported. |
| follow up | none - no clinical follow-up reported; this is a typing/exposure-misclassification study, not an outcome study |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is the mechanism evidence for what a low-resolution HLA match grade conceals, which is exactly the question a one-field, antigen-level pre-screen has to answer about itself. It shows that a pair labelled 'favourably matched' on broad HLA-A, -B, -DR is not a matched pair: two thirds (66.7%) still carried at least one HLA-C mismatch, 30.4% an HLA-DQ mismatch, and 50.6% at least one DRB1 or DQB1 allele mismatch, while only 4.6% showed a DR split mismatch. It supports C7 and C10 directly by quantifying the linkage between B and C: an HLA-C mismatch was present in 36.9% of B-matched pairs but 85.5% of B-mismatched pairs (P<0.0001), so matching B captures most but by no means all of C, and C mismatch is not an independent free-standing exposure. It supports C12 by measuring low-resolution misclassification empirically - the same broad-level label covers pairs that are allele-identical and pairs carrying several allele mismatches - which is the reason a one-field pre-screen must be reported as a screening grade and not as a compatibility finding. Transfer to a living-donor Iranian pre-screen is partial: the direction transfers (broad A/B/DR matching leaves substantial hidden C, DQ and allele mismatch, and C mismatch is conditional on B status), but the magnitudes do not, because B~C and DR~DQ linkage disequilibrium is population-specific and these are unrelated UK deceased-donor pairs, whereas Iranian living donors are frequently biologically related and share haplotypes, which would make the hidden-mismatch fractions here an upper bound for related pairs. Because the paper reports no outcome at all, it can be used to calibrate what our pre-screen may claim and how it must label residual uncertainty, but it cannot be used to set any weight, threshold or risk estimate; and since HLA-C matters clinically mainly through DSA in sensitised recipients, an antibody-status-unknown screen can only flag the hidden C mismatch, never resolve it.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- presence of at least one HLA-C split-specificity mismatch (donor vs recipient): all 237 'favourably matched' pairs (overall prevalence) — percentage of pairs 66.7; adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- presence of at least one HLA-C split-specificity mismatch: pairs MATCHED for HLA-B (stratum of the 237) — percentage of pairs 36.9, p=<0.0001 (for the B-matched vs B-mismatched contrast, as printed); adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence within stratum) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- presence of at least one HLA-C split-specificity mismatch: pairs MISMATCHED for HLA-B (stratum of the 237) — percentage of pairs 85.5, p=<0.0001 (for the B-matched vs B-mismatched contrast, as printed); adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence within stratum) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- presence of an HLA-DR SPLIT specificity mismatch: all 237 'favourably matched' pairs (overall prevalence) — percentage of pairs 4.6; adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- presence of an HLA-DQ mismatch: all 237 'favourably matched' pairs (overall prevalence) — percentage of pairs 30.4; adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- presence of at least one HLA-DRB1 or -DQB1 ALLELE mismatch: all 237 'favourably matched' pairs (overall prevalence) — percentage of pairs 50.6; adjusted for unadjusted (raw prevalence) [Abstract, Results sentence]

**Dose-response.**

- _units: These are PREVALENCES OF MISMATCH among 237 'favourably matched' pairs, NOT risk estimates. The paper reports no outcome, so there is no dose-response in the effect sense.
- C: at_least_one_split_mismatch MM: 66.7% overall; 36.9% if B matched, 85.5% if B mismatched (P<0.0001)
- DR: split_specificity_mismatch MM: 4.6% overall
- DQ: antigen_mismatch MM: 30.4% overall
- DRB1_or_DQB1: at_least_one_allele_mismatch MM: 50.6% overall
- A: note MM: no standalone prevalence printed in the abstract; only the conditional statement that a broad HLA-B mismatch influenced the presence of an HLA-A split mismatch (P<0.05)
- B: note MM: no standalone prevalence printed in the abstract; B match status is used as the stratifier for HLA-C and a broad HLA-A mismatch influenced the presence of an HLA-B split mismatch (P<0.05)
- Shape reported: not reported - no outcome model of any kind; the paper measures how much mismatch is hidden inside a match grade, not how risk scales with mismatch count; linearity tested: not tested - no trend test, no spline, no categorical outcome model. The only statistical tests reported are unadjusted between-stratum comparisons of mismatch prevalence (P<0.0001 for C by B status; P<0.05 for the A/B broad-to-split relations).; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-C mismatch x HLA-B match status (class I haplotype linkage): HLA-C mismatch is strongly conditional on HLA-B: uncommon-to-moderate when B is matched, near-universal when B is mismatched. B matching therefore captures much of C by linkage disequilibrium but leaves roughly a third of B-matched pairs C-mismatched. (36.9% (B matched) vs 85.5% (B mismatched), P<0.0001; 66.7% overall) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- broad-specificity HLA-A mismatch x presence of an HLA-B SPLIT mismatch, and broad-specificity HLA-B mismatch x presence of an HLA-A SPLIT mismatch: A broad mismatch at one class I locus significantly increased the chance of a split-level mismatch at the other class I locus (non-independence across A and B, consistent with haplotype linkage). (P<0.05 (both directions, as printed; no proportions given in the abstract)) [Abstract, Results sentence]
- broad-specificity HLA-A or -B mismatch x presence of an HLA-DR SPLIT mismatch (class I to class II): No significant effect: class I broad mismatch did not predict a DR split mismatch, i.e. the class I / class II non-independence seen within class I does not extend to DR splits in this sample. (reported as 'no significant difference'; no P value or proportion printed) [Abstract, Results sentence]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C7* — "66.7% of the patients had at least one HLA-C mismatch with their donors; 36.9% of those matched for HLA-B and 85.5% of those mismatched for HLA-B (P<0.0001)." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C12* — "4.6% of the patients were mismatched for HLA-DR split specificities but 30.4% were mismatched at HLA-DQ and 50.6% had at least one HLA-DRB1 or -DQB1 allele mismatch." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C10* — "A broad specificity HLA-A or -B mismatch influenced the presence of an HLA-B, or HLA-A split specificity mismatch, respectively, (P<0.05) but made no significant difference to the presence of an HLA-DR split mismatch." (Abstract, Results sentence)
- *C12* — "Two hundred and thirty-seven cadaveric donor/recipient pairs, 'favourably matched', according to United Kingdom Transplant criteria, were typed at the split specificity level for HLA-A, -B, -C and at the allele level for HLA-DRB1 and -DQB1." (Abstract, Methods sentence)
- *C13* — "Considerable HLA-A, -B, -C, -DR, -DQ matching heterogeneity exists even amongst 'well matched' renal transplant patient groups." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)
- *C10* — "Little is known about the effects of combinations of mismatched specificities on graft survival. Thus, further investigation is merited particularly for HLA-C and -DQ mismatching." (Abstract, Conclusion sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC full text exists for this PMID, so tables, per-stratum denominators, the exact UK Transplant definition of 'favourably matched', the typing methods and any figures could not be read. Every number recorded here is from the PubMed abstract.; Purely descriptive: the paper reports NO clinical outcome - no graft survival, no rejection, no DSA, no follow-up. It quantifies hidden exposure, not risk, and the authors themselves state that the effect of these mismatch combinations on graft survival is little known.; Small sample (n=237 pairs), one laboratory, one national allocation scheme (UK), 2003. Percentages have no confidence intervals and the P values are unadjusted pairwise comparisons with no multivariable modelling and no correction for multiple testing.; Deceased-donor only. No living-donor pairs, and no related pairs, so the haplotype sharing that dominates living related donation in Iran is absent; the hidden-mismatch fractions are therefore an upper bound for related living pairs.; Population-specific linkage: the 36.9% vs 85.5% C-by-B split depends on UK (largely northern European) haplotype frequencies and cannot be assumed to hold in an Iranian population.; 'At least one mismatch' pooling throughout means 1 vs 2 mismatches at a locus cannot be separated; there is no dose information at all.; 'Allele level' DRB1/DQB1 typing as performed in 2003 is not necessarily equivalent to modern two-field high-resolution typing, and the abstract does not state the method or the nomenclature version.; HLA-DP is named in the introduction as a locus of interest but was NOT typed; DQA1 and eplet/molecular mismatch were also not assessed.; Selection: only pairs already graded 'favourably matched' were studied, so the results describe residual mismatch inside a favourable grade and say nothing about the full mismatch distribution of the transplant population..

### Thompson JS 2003 — Human leukocyte antigens DR and AB and kidney retransplantation.

Thompson JS 2003, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/01.TP.0000048376.79803.C1](https://doi.org/10.1097/01.TP.0000048376.79803.C1). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation / Lippincott Williams & Wilkins); no PMC full text exists (convert_article_ids returns no PMCID); abstract retrieved from PubMed.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | kidney retransplants (regrafts) performed in Southeastern Organ Procurement Foundation (SEOPF) centres, USA, January 1988 to December 1997, with ABDR typing on both donor and recipient and pretransplant PRA data |
| donor type | not stated in abstract |
| n | 2,574 |
| design | retrospective multicentre registry cohort (SEOPF), Cox regression of multiple variables |
| typing resolution | antigen level ('ABDR typing', serologic era 1988-1997); resolution not explicitly stated in abstract |
| outcome | regraft (retransplant kidney graft) survival; death-censored vs all-cause not stated in abstract |
| follow up | not stated in abstract |
| other factors modelled | recipient race (white vs non-white), donor sex (female donor), pretransplant PRA as a continuous variable, cold ischaemia time, other variables in the Cox model not named in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is in the review for the locus-hierarchy and non-additivity questions (C3, C10): in 2,574 kidney retransplants it ranks DR mismatch as the top risk factor and shows that A+B mismatches carry no significant effect when DR is matched and only a minimal effect when DR is mismatched, so a flat 0-6 ABDR count blends a weak (AB) and a strong (DR) signal. The typing is antigen-level (serologic era), which matches the one-field typing of an Iranian living-donor pre-screen, so the ranking of DR over AB transfers at the same resolution without any high-resolution imputation. It also gives a retransplant-specific and race-specific effect-modification result (C11): DR mismatch matters in both white and non-white recipients but much more in the latter, and graft survival falls progressively with PRA, which the authors attribute to undetected class II sensitisation. Transfer is limited: retransplants are a sensitised, higher-risk population with PRA measured, whereas the Iranian pre-screen targets mostly first transplants with antibody status unknown; donor type is not stated in the abstract and the SEOPF era with cold ischaemia modelled points to a predominantly deceased-donor cohort, so living-donor transfer is by analogy only; and the 1988-1997 era predates modern immunosuppression. Because only the abstract is accessible, the paper contributes ordering and interaction structure (weight DR above AB; do not treat mismatches as an additive 0-6 count) rather than coefficients.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- regraft survival: DR mismatching (ranked first among risk factors: DR mismatching > non-white recipient > female donor > PRA continuous > cold ischaemia time) — qualitative ranking from multivariable Cox model; no HR/CI/p printed in abstract None; adjusted for multiple variables including recipient race, donor sex, PRA (continuous), cold ischaemia time [Abstract, Results]
- regraft survival: 0-4 AB mismatches vs 0 AB, within DR-matched retransplants (both white and non-white) — qualitative: no significant effect; no HR/CI/p printed in abstract None; adjusted for stratified by DR match status and recipient race; other adjustment not stated [Abstract, Results]
- regraft survival: 0-4 AB mismatches vs 0 AB, within DR-mismatched retransplants (both white and non-white) — qualitative: only a minimal effect; no HR/CI/p printed in abstract None; adjusted for stratified by DR match status and recipient race; other adjustment not stated [Abstract, Results]
- regraft survival: 0 ABDR mismatch vs 1-4 AB mismatches with 0 DR mismatch — qualitative: no significant difference; no numbers printed in abstract None; adjusted for not stated (Conclusions statement) [Abstract, Conclusions]
- regraft survival: 1-4 AB mismatches with 0 DR mismatch vs 1 or 2 DR mismatches — qualitative: survival of the 0-DR groups exceeded that of the 1-2 DR mismatched groups; no numbers printed in abstract None; adjusted for not stated (Conclusions statement) [Abstract, Conclusions]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: ref (DR matched); 1 MM: pooled with 2 in the abstract comparisons ('one or two DR mismatched retransplants' had lower survival than any 1-4 AB / 0 DR group); no numbers; 2 MM: pooled with 1; no numbers
- AB (A and B combined): 0 MM: ref; 1-4 MM: pooled; no significant effect if DR matched, minimal effect if DR mismatched; no numbers
- Shape reported: not reported numerically in the abstract; the authors state that the stepwise decrease with total 0-6 ABDR mismatches reported elsewhere is explained by the mixture of AB mismatches (little effect) and DR mismatches (major effect), i.e. the total-count gradient is not an additive per-mismatch effect; linearity tested: not tested / not reported in the abstract for HLA; PRA was modelled as a continuous variable and survival is described as decreasing progressively with PRA; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- AB mismatch (0-4) x DR match status: AB mismatches had no significant effect on regraft survival when DR was matched and only a minimal effect when DR was mismatched; the AB effect is conditional on DR (not printed in abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- DR mismatch x recipient race (white vs non-white): DR mismatching had a significant effect in white recipients and a much greater impact in non-white recipients (not printed in abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- total 0-6 ABDR count vs locus composition: the stepwise fall in regraft survival with total 0-6 ABDR mismatches is attributed to the DR component; the AB component contributes little (not printed in abstract) [Abstract, Results]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C3* — "Cox regression of multiple variables demonstrated that the most important risk factors in descending order were DR mismatching, non-white recipient, female donor, PRA as a continuous variable, and cold ischemia time." (Abstract, Results)
- *C11* — "Although DR mismatching demonstrated a significant effect in white recipients, the impact was much greater in non-white recipients." (Abstract, Results)
- *C10* — "In both groups, zero to four AB mismatches demonstrated no significant effect on regraft survival if DR was matched and only a minimal effect when DR was mismatched." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "the zero to six ABDR mismatches are a combination of AB mismatches with little effect and DR mismatches with a major effect." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "There was no significant difference in survival of zero ABDR mismatched retransplants compared with one to four AB and zero DR mismatched retransplants." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C3* — "kidney graft survival of all one to four AB and zero DR mismatches exceeded that of one or two DR mismatched retransplants." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** abstract-only access: no hazard ratios, confidence intervals, p-values, tables or Kaplan-Meier figures could be extracted; all effect statements are directional; retransplants only (a sensitised, higher immunological-risk population); does not describe first transplants; era 1988-1997, before modern immunosuppression; C1 not addressed; antigen-level (serologic era) ABDR typing; DQ, C and DP not typed, so C4, C7, C8 not addressable; A and B are pooled as 'AB' mismatches, so B vs A (C5) and the size of the A effect alone (C6) cannot be separated; 1 and 2 DR mismatches are pooled and 1-4 AB mismatches are pooled in the reported comparisons; per-count DR series not available from the abstract; donor type (deceased vs living) not stated in the abstract; cold ischaemia time modelled, so the cohort is probably predominantly deceased-donor; race dichotomised as white vs non-white; single US regional organ-sharing registry (SEOPF); outcome definition (death-censored vs all-cause) and follow-up length not stated in the abstract; key comparisons in the Conclusions are stated without indicating whether they are adjusted.

### Zafar MN 2003 — HLA-matching by DNA methods: impact on a living related renal transplantation programme.

Zafar MN 2003, *Exp Clin Transplant*, PMID 15859908. Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright; PubMed abstract only. convert_article_ids returned no PMCID and no DOI for this PMID, so no PMC full text and no open-access licence applies..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 585 living-related renal transplants (LRRT) at a single Pakistani centre (SIUT, Karachi), split into three sequential HLA-typing groups: Group I n=159 serology only; Group II n=172 serology + PCR-SSP for HLA-DR; Group III n=254 serology + PCR-SSP for HLA-A and -B and PCR-SSP only for HLA-DR |
| donor type | living |
| n | 585 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort comparing three sequential HLA-typing eras; unadjusted between-group comparisons with p-values. No multivariable model, no covariate adjustment and no confidence intervals are reported in the abstract, which is the only text available. |
| typing resolution | mixed - serologic/antigen level (CTS and Terasaki antisera trays) versus low-resolution (one-field, 'two-digit') PCR-SSP with 24 primers for HLA-A, 48 for HLA-B and 24 for HLA-DR. No two-field/high-resolution typing anywhere in the study. |
| outcome | (a) serology-vs-PCR-SSP typing discordance ('error') rate per locus; (b) acute rejection; (c) graft function, serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL at 1 year; (d) graft survival at 1 and 3 years |
| follow up | graft survival reported to 3 years; median or mean follow-up not stated in the abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the closest published analogue to the KidneyMatch setting the review could hope for: a large living-related kidney programme in a lower-resource South Asian country, where matching had to be done with whatever typing technology was actually affordable locally - the same constraint the Iranian pre-screen operates under. It answers the review's typing-resolution question (C12/C15) with direct measurement rather than assertion: it quantifies how often antigen-level serology disagrees with low-resolution PCR-SSP (24% at HLA-A, 16% at HLA-B, 35% at HLA-DR), showing that the typing method feeding the pipeline, not only the mismatch count computed from it, determines who is called matched. It is also direct evidence for C14 in the living-donor setting: within living-related donation, improving the accuracy of HLA assignment tracked with less acute rejection (39% to 26% across the three groups), better 1-year function (26% vs 48% with creatinine <1.5 mg/dL) and 12-18 percentage points more graft survival. It transfers unusually well to a low-resolution, one-field pre-screen because the better arm here IS one-field PCR-SSP, not high-resolution typing - the demonstrated benefit sits at exactly the resolution KidneyMatch works at, so the paper supports 'move from serology to one-field DNA' rather than 'you need two-field typing'. It does not transfer to the antibody-status-unknown half of the problem: no PRA, DSA or crossmatch data are reported, so nothing here informs sensitisation handling. Its causal claim is weak - the three groups are sequential calendar eras at one centre with no adjustment - so it should be cited for the misclassification rates and the direction of effect, not for the magnitude as an unbiased estimate.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- HLA-A typing discordance (serology vs low-resolution PCR-SSP): serology assignment vs PCR-SSP assignment, PCR-SSP taken as reference — percentage 24.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- HLA-B typing discordance (serology vs low-resolution PCR-SSP): serology assignment vs PCR-SSP assignment, PCR-SSP taken as reference — percentage 16.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- HLA-DR typing discordance (serology vs low-resolution PCR-SSP): serology assignment vs PCR-SSP assignment, PCR-SSP taken as reference — percentage 35.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- acute rejection: Group I (serology only, n=159) — percentage 39.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- acute rejection: Group II (serology + PCR-SSP for HLA-DR, n=172) — percentage 30.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- acute rejection: Group III (serology + PCR-SSP for A/B, PCR-SSP only for DR, n=254); p is for the three-group comparison — percentage 26.0, p=0.02; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft function: serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL at 1 year: Group I (serology only) — percentage 26.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft function: serum creatinine <1.5 mg/dL at 1 year: Group III (serology + PCR-SSP A/B, PCR-SSP DR) vs Group I; p is for that contrast — percentage 48.0, p=<0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft survival at 1 year: Group II (serology + PCR-SSP for HLA-DR) — percentage 93.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft survival at 1 year: Group I (serology only); p is for the Group II vs Group I survival comparison — percentage 81.0, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft survival at 3 years: Group II (serology + PCR-SSP for HLA-DR) — percentage 87.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft survival at 3 years: Group I (serology only); p is for the Group II vs Group I survival comparison — percentage 69.0, p=0.0001; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract]
- graft survival at 1 year, absolute improvement: serology + PCR-SSP vs serology alone (authors' summary statement) — absolute risk difference (percentage points) 12.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, concluding sentence]
- graft survival at 3 years, absolute improvement: serology + PCR-SSP vs serology alone (authors' summary statement) — absolute risk difference (percentage points) 18.0; adjusted for unadjusted [Abstract, concluding sentence]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C12* — "Error rates in serology as compared to PCR-SSP were 24% for HLA A , 16% for HLA B and 35% for HLA DR." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "Of the 585 transplants, 159 (Group I) were serology based, 172 serology and PCR-SSP for HLA DR (Group II) and 254 on serology and PCR-SSP for HLA A and B and only PCR-SSP for HLA DR (Group III)." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "Acute rejection in Group I were 39% Group II 30% and Group III 26% (p 0.02)." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "Graft function of serum creatinine<1.5 mg/dl at 1 year was found in 26% of Group I patients as compared to 48% of Group III (p<0.0001)." (Abstract)
- *C14* — "One and three year graft survival was 93% and 87% for Group II as compared to 81% and 69% for Group I respectively (p 0.0001)." (Abstract)
- *C15* — "Matching by this combination of serology and PCR-SSP is not only economical for a developing country but also improves graft survival by 12% at 1 and 18% at 3 years." (Abstract, concluding sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. The article has no PMC record and no DOI was returned, so the Methods, Results tables and Discussion could not be read; every number in this file comes from the PubMed abstract.; Non-randomised sequential-era design: the three groups are consecutive periods at one centre, so the typing change is fully confounded with calendar time, evolving immunosuppression, surgical and clinical practice, and possibly with donor/recipient selection. The paper reports no adjustment for any covariate.; No confidence intervals anywhere; only bare p-values (p 0.02, p<0.0001, p 0.0001). No hazard ratios, odds ratios or relative risks are reported, so the effect sizes cannot be pooled with regression-based studies.; Internally inconsistent group usage: acute rejection and 1-year function are compared using Group III, but graft survival is reported for Group II versus Group I. Group III graft survival is not reported in the abstract, so the headline '12% at 1 and 18% at 3 years' rests on the DR-only DNA-typing group.; No mismatch counts are given at all: it is impossible to tell how much of the benefit came from better-matched pairs actually being selected versus from correcting mis-assignments in pairs that would have been transplanted anyway.; The 'error rate' is discordance with low-resolution PCR-SSP treated as ground truth; PCR-SSP itself was not validated against sequencing, and one-field PCR-SSP has its own ambiguity and null-allele blind spots.; No sensitisation data: PRA, DSA, crossmatch method and results are not reported, so the paper says nothing about antibody-mediated risk or about the antibody-status-unknown pre-screen problem.; Living-RELATED donors only. Haplotype sharing among relatives makes the mismatch distribution narrow and non-representative of the Iranian living-unrelated donor (LURD) programme, where donor and recipient are genetically unrelated.; Single centre in Pakistan, 1990s-early 2000s era immunosuppression; graft-survival levels are not transportable to current practice.; Small absolute numbers per group (159/172/254) and no reporting of censoring or of patient versus graft survival definitions..

### Frohn C 2001 — The effect of HLA-C matching on acute renal transplant rejection.

Frohn C 2001, *Nephrol Dial Transplant*, [DOI 10.1093/ndt/16.2.355](https://doi.org/10.1093/ndt/16.2.355). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Oxford University Press / ERA-EDTA); no PMC record returned by convert_article_ids, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 104 consecutive donor/recipient pairs transplanted at a single university unit (Institute of Immunology and Transfusion Medicine, University of Luebeck, Germany); transplant era and recipient age range not stated in the abstract |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract; MeSH indexing includes 'Cadaver', which points to deceased-donor transplants |
| n | 104 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; the HLA-C effect is tested inside groups of pairs with a homogeneous number of HLA-B mismatches, to break the HLA-B/HLA-C linkage disequilibrium; significance testing only, no multivariable model or effect estimate reported in the abstract |
| typing resolution | HLA-C by allele-specific PCR (allele-group / low-to-intermediate resolution) combined with serology; resolution used for HLA-A, -B and -DR is not stated in the abstract |
| outcome | acute graft rejection (acute rejection episode); rejection definition, biopsy confirmation and ascertainment window are not stated in the abstract |
| follow up | not stated |
| other factors modelled | HLA-B mismatch (used as the stratifying variable), HLA-A mismatch, HLA-DR mismatch, cold ischaemia time, warm ischaemia time, previous transplantations, pre-existing HLA antibodies |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the earliest dedicated tests of whether an HLA-C mismatch adds acute-rejection risk beyond HLA-B, which is precisely the C7 question of whether HLA-C matters in its own right or only rides on HLA-B through linkage disequilibrium. Its design attacks that confound structurally rather than statistically: the HLA-C comparison is made inside groups of pairs that carry the same number of HLA-B mismatches, so the reported association is explicitly conditional on B, which is the form a matching pre-screen actually needs (does a score that already counts B need to count C separately?). Against that, the paper supplies direction only and not magnitude - a single p-value from one stratum of a 104-pair single-centre series published in 2001 - so the review can cite it as supportive but cannot pool it. Transfer to a living-donor Iranian pre-screen is weak on three counts: the donors appear to be deceased (MeSH 'Cadaver'), the immunosuppression is pre-2001 and therefore not the modern tacrolimus/MMF baseline, and HLA-C here was typed by allele-specific PCR, a better resolution than the one-field typing a low-resolution Iranian screen would hold. On the antibody question the paper is silent in the way that matters most: pre-existing HLA antibodies were examined and reported not to explain the finding, but no sensitised-versus-unsensitised subgroup effect is given, so it cannot tell an antibody-status-unknown screen whether the HLA-C effect is confined to sensitised recipients - the half of C7 that would decide whether C belongs in the score at all. Taken alone it is hypothesis-generating support for including HLA-C in matching, and the authors themselves ask for larger cohorts; it is not a basis for assigning HLA-C a numeric weight in a deterministic score.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- acute graft rejection: HLA-C mismatch vs no HLA-C mismatch, within the group of donor/recipient pairs carrying one additional mismatch at the HLA-B locus — p-value only (no HR, OR, RR or rejection percentage is given in the abstract) None, p=0.004; adjusted for stratified on the number of HLA-B mismatches (homogeneous distribution) rather than statistically adjusted; HLA-A and DR mismatch, cold and warm ischaemia time, previous transplantations and pre-existing HLA antibodies were analysed separately and reported not to explain the finding [Abstract, results paragraph (third paragraph)]

**Dose-response.**

- C: 0 MM: reference (implied; not quantified); 1 MM: not reported separately; 2 MM: not reported separately; note MM: the abstract reports only 'HLA-C mismatch' versus no mismatch inside a B-stratum, with P=0.004; it does not print a 0/1/2 series for HLA-C
- B: note MM: HLA-B mismatch count is the stratifying variable, not an estimated exposure; the significant HLA-C result is reported for the stratum with one additional B mismatch, and no HLA-B effect estimate is given
- A: note MM: analysed as a potential explanation only; no estimate reported in the abstract
- DR: note MM: analysed as a potential explanation only; no estimate reported in the abstract
- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - no per-count HLA-C series, no trend test, no spline or threshold analysis appears in the abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-C mismatch x number of HLA-B mismatches (linkage disequilibrium control): the HLA-C effect on acute rejection is reported as significant in the stratum of pairs with one additional HLA-B mismatch; the abstract does not report the result in the zero-additional-B-mismatch or two-B-mismatch strata, so it is not stated whether the effect is absent there or merely untested/underpowered (P=0.004 in the one-additional-B-mismatch group; no estimate or p-value printed for the other B strata) [Abstract, results paragraph (third paragraph)]
- HLA-C mismatch x pre-existing HLA antibodies (presensitisation): pre-existing HLA antibodies were analysed as a possible alternative explanation and reported not to explain the HLA-C finding; no sensitised-versus-unsensitised subgroup estimate, and no formal interaction test, is reported in the abstract [Abstract, results paragraph (third paragraph)]
- HLA-C mismatch x cold/warm ischaemia, previous transplantation, HLA-A or DR mismatch: each was analysed and reported as unable to explain the HLA-C finding; these are described as confounding checks, not as effect modifiers, and no numbers are printed [Abstract, results paragraph (third paragraph)]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C7* — "HLA-C mismatch turned out to be significantly correlated with acute transplant rejection in pairs with one additional mismatch on the B locus (P=0.004)" (Abstract, results paragraph)
- *C10* — "By analysing groups of donor/recipient pairs with a homogeneous distribution of HLA-B mismatches in order to exclude an effect of the linkage disequilibrium between HLA-B/C" (Abstract, results paragraph)
- *C7* — "Additional parameters that may hypothetically influence acute rejection episodes (HLA-A or DR mismatch, time of cold and warm ischaemia, previous transplantations, pre-existing HLA antibodies) were also analysed but cannot explain this finding." (Abstract, results paragraph)
- *C7* — "In 104 consecutive patient/donor pairs from our transplantation unit, we retrospectively analysed whether acute graft rejection is influenced by HLA-C match status between donor and recipient." (Abstract, methods paragraph)
- *C12* — "For typing HLA-C alleles, we used an allele-specific PCR protocol in combination with serology." (Abstract, methods paragraph)
- *C7* — "HLA-C matching of all kidney donors and recipients seems to be an option to reduce the probability of acute rejection episodes." (Abstract, conclusion paragraph)

**Limitations.** Abstract only: no PMC full text exists (convert_article_ids returns no PMCID), so the Methods, tables and any numeric effect estimates could not be read; everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; No effect size of any kind is reported in the abstract - only P=0.004. There is no HR, OR, RR or even a rejection percentage per HLA-C mismatch group, so the paper cannot be meta-analysed and cannot support a numeric weight for HLA-C.; Very small single-centre series (n=104 pairs), then split into HLA-B mismatch strata, so each stratum is small and the analysis is underpowered; a significant result in one stratum of several raises a multiple-comparison concern that the abstract does not address.; The significant result is reported only for the stratum with one additional HLA-B mismatch. Whether the effect was absent or simply untestable in the other B strata is not stated, so the finding may be a subgroup artefact rather than a B-conditional effect.; The confounders (HLA-A/DR mismatch, cold and warm ischaemia, previous transplantation, pre-existing HLA antibodies) are said to be analysed and to 'not explain' the finding, but no multivariable model, adjusted estimate or test statistic is shown for any of them.; Outcome definition is not given: 'acute graft rejection' is not stated to be biopsy-proven, and no follow-up window, rejection grading or censoring rule appears in the abstract.; Published 2001 from a German centre, so the immunosuppression era predates routine tacrolimus/MMF and current induction practice; the absolute acute-rejection rate would have been far higher than today, which inflates power for rejection but limits transferability.; Donor type is not stated in the abstract; MeSH indexing ('Cadaver') suggests deceased donors, so this does not directly address living donation.; HLA-C was typed by allele-specific PCR plus serology, a higher resolution than one-field serological typing; a low-resolution pre-screen would misclassify some of these pairs, and the paper gives no data on that misclassification.; Sensitisation is handled as a nuisance variable rather than an effect modifier, so the paper cannot confirm or refute the central C7 proposition that the HLA-C effect acts mainly in sensitised recipients through DSA. No DSA measurement is mentioned at all..

### Ghoneim MA 2001 — Live-donor renal transplantation at the Urology & Nephrology Center of Mansoura: 1976-1998.

Ghoneim MA 2001, *Clinical Transplants (Clin Transpl), 2001:167-78*, PMID 12211779. Access: abstract_only; licence: unknown - publisher copyright; Clinical Transplants is a book series that is not deposited in PMC, and convert_article_ids returned no PMCID and no DOI for this PMID.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | living-donor kidney transplant recipients at the Urology & Nephrology Center, Mansoura University, Egypt; more than 1,200 transplants performed 1976-1998 |
| donor type | living |
| n | more than 1,200 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; multivariable analysis of graft-survival predictors. The statistical model (Cox vs logistic), the covariate list and the candidate-variable set are NOT stated in the retrieved abstract |
| typing resolution | not stated. Only HLA-A, -B and -DR are counted, and the transplants date from 1976-1998, so serologic/antigen-level (one-field) typing is the near-certain resolution, but the abstract does not say so |
| outcome | graft survival (all-cause graft failure; the abstract does not say whether death-censored) |
| follow up | not stated. Transplants performed 1976-1998; graft survival reported to 10 years, with a projected half-life of 10.7 years |
| other factors modelled | number of acute rejection episodes, post-transplant hypertension (uncontrolled or newly developed), bilharziasis (schistosomiasis) - tested, reported null |

**Why it is relevant.** This is one of the largest single-centre living-donor kidney series from the wider region (Egypt, >1,200 transplants) that reports HLA mismatch as an independent predictor of graft survival, so it speaks directly to the review's living-donor question (C14) and to the regional-evidence question (C15). Its design is the closest available analogue to an Iranian living-donor programme: living donors only, a mix of related and unrelated/consanguineous pairs, antigen-level HLA-A/-B/-DR counting, and no molecular or eplet-level matching, which is exactly the low-resolution one-field setting the KidneyMatch pre-screen must operate in. The clinically usable content is a single dichotomy - grafts with 2 or fewer HLA-A/-B/-DR mismatches survived significantly better - which supports the idea that a coarse total-count cut is discriminating even when only one-field typing exists. Transfer is limited in three ways that matter: the era is pre-modern immunosuppression (1976-1998, so azathioprine/steroid and early cyclosporine regimens dominate), antibody status is not reported at all (no PRA, no crossmatch, no DSA), and the abstract publishes no effect estimate, confidence interval or p-value for the HLA term, so it cannot contribute a number to any pooled analysis. It should therefore be used as qualitative, direction-only regional corroboration that HLA mismatch count matters within living donation, and never as a source of an effect size. The same centre's later and larger analysis of the same series did not retain HLA in its multivariable model (see notes), so this paper's HLA finding is not stable within its own programme and must be reported with that caveat.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft survival: 2 or fewer vs more than 2 HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatches (0-6 antigen scale) — none reported - direction and statistical significance only None; adjusted for multivariable analysis in which the number of HLA mismatches, the number of acute rejection episodes and post-transplant hypertension were the three independent predictors of graft survival; the full covariate list and model type are not given in the abstract [Abstract, numbered points 2 and 2a]
- graft survival at 5 years: whole cohort - NOT stratified by HLA mismatch — percent 75.8; adjusted for unadjusted crude cohort rate [Abstract, numbered point 1]
- graft survival at 10 years: whole cohort - NOT stratified by HLA mismatch — percent 51.9; adjusted for unadjusted crude cohort rate [Abstract, numbered point 1]
- projected graft half-life: whole cohort - NOT stratified by HLA mismatch — years 10.7; adjusted for unadjusted projection [Abstract, numbered point 1]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported. The only functional form published in the abstract is a single dichotomy at 2 or fewer vs more than 2 mismatches summed across HLA-A, -B and -DR. No per-count (0/1/2/3/4/5/6) series, no reference category, no estimate at any count; linearity tested: not tested, or at least not reported. The abstract calls 'the number of HLA mismatches' an independent variable influencing graft survival, which implies the count entered the model, but it then reports only the dichotomised result; no test of linear trend, no spline, no categorical-vs-linear comparison and no threshold test is described; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C15* — "Based on more than 1,200 living donor transplants performed at the Urology & Nephrology Center at Mansoura University between 1976-1998" (Abstract, opening sentence)
- *C15* — "The overall graft survival rate was 75.8% and 51.9% at 5 and 10 years, respectively, with a projected half-life of 10.7 years." (Abstract, numbered point 1)
- *C14* — "Three factors acted as independent variables that significantly influenced graft survival: the number of HLA mismatches, the number of acute rejection episodes and the presence of posttransplant hypertension." (Abstract, numbered point 2)
- *C14* — "Grafts with 2 or fewer HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatches had a significantly better survival rate." (Abstract, numbered point 2a)
- *C14* — "Despite improvements in tissue matching and immunosuppression, an important proportion of grafts is still lost following living-donor kidney transplantation." (Abstract, numbered point 4)
- *C15* — "Bilharziasis had no impact on the outcome." (Abstract, numbered point 3)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC full text, no PMCID and no DOI; Clinical Transplants is a book series that is not deposited in PMC, so the Results tables, the survival curves and the multivariable model output could not be read.; No effect size of any kind for HLA: no HR, OR or RR, no confidence interval and no p-value for the mismatch term. The paper contributes direction and claimed significance only and cannot enter a quantitative synthesis.; The HLA result is published only as a dichotomy (2 or fewer vs more than 2 mismatches across A, B and DR). No per-count dose-response, no zero-mismatch category, and no test of the functional form.; A, B and DR are summed into a single count, so no per-locus effect can be recovered and the review's DR-versus-A/B ranking question (C3, C5, C6) cannot be addressed from this paper.; HLA-C, -DQ and -DP are not typed or not reported, so nothing bears on C4, C7 or C8.; Typing resolution is not stated; antigen-level serology is inferred from the era and the locus set rather than read from the text.; Antibody status is entirely absent: no PRA, no crossmatch method, no DSA. The review's antibody-unknown pre-screen question cannot be informed, and confounding by sensitisation cannot be excluded.; Era effects are severe and unmodelled in the reported output: transplants span 1976-1998, crossing azathioprine/steroid, cyclosporine and later regimens. The abstract does not say whether transplant era was a candidate covariate, so the HLA effect may be partly an era proxy.; The statistical model is not identified (Cox vs logistic), the covariate list is not given, and it is not stated whether graft survival is death-censored. Selection of the reported 'three independent variables' from an unstated candidate set raises a real risk of model-selection bias.; Single centre, single country, historical. Donor relatedness and consanguinity are not broken out in the abstract even though they drive the mismatch distribution in this kind of programme.; Internal instability: the same centre's later, larger report of the same series (PMID 18202512) did not retain HLA in its multivariable model - see notes. The 2001 HLA finding is therefore not reproduced within its own programme..

### Meier-Kriesche HU 2001 — Interaction of mycophenolate mofetil and HLA matching on renal allograft survival.

Meier-Kriesche HU 2001, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/00007890-200102150-00010](https://doi.org/10.1097/00007890-200102150-00010). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Lippincott Williams & Wilkins / Transplantation, 2001); no PMC deposit - get_article_metadata returned no pmc field and convert_article_ids returns pmid only, no pmcid. Everything below comes from the PubMed abstract, cached at <scratchpad>/fulltext/11233900_abstract.txt..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | All primary, solitary renal transplants registered in the United States Renal Data System (USRDS) between January 1995 and June 1997 whose initial immunosuppression included either MMF or azathioprine; followed until June 1998. Retransplants and multi-organ recipients excluded by the 'primary, solitary' restriction. |
| donor type | not stated in the abstract. USRDS kidney transplants of 1995-1997 include both deceased- and living-donor recipients, but no split, and no living-donor subgroup, is reported in the abstract. |
| n | 19,675 (8,459 MMF; 11,216 AZA) |
| design | retrospective national registry cohort; Kaplan-Meier graft survival by HLA mismatch within each immunosuppression arm; Cox proportional hazards models fitted specifically to test the HLA mismatch x (MMF vs AZA) interaction, adjusted for 13 pretransplant confounders |
| typing resolution | serologic / antigen level. The abstract counts 'antigen mismatches' on a 0-6 scale, which in USRDS/UNOS data of this era is HLA-A + HLA-B + HLA-DR broad antigen mismatch; the abstract itself never names the loci (only MeSH carries 'HLA-A Antigens' and 'Histocompatibility Testing'). No allele-level, two-field, eplet or PIRCHE data. |
| outcome | primary endpoints graft survival and patient survival; all reported HLA results are all-cause (not death-censored) 3-year graft survival / relative risk of graft loss |
| follow up | transplants accrued Jan 1995 - Jun 1997, all followed to June 1998, i.e. maximum ~3.5 years and minimum ~1 year of observation; the reported 3-year graft survival figures are Kaplan-Meier estimates, not 3 years of observed follow-up in every patient |
| other factors modelled | intention-to-treat initial immunosuppression (MMF-containing vs AZA-containing) - the effect modifier of interest, 13 potential confounding pretransplant variables, NOT itemised in the abstract (so it is unknown whether PRA/sensitisation, cold ischaemia, donor age, donor type or race were among them) |

**Why it is relevant.** This paper is the canonical test of review question C11 for the immunosuppression axis: it asks whether a more potent antiproliferative agent erases the HLA-matching gradient, and answers no. In 19,675 US primary kidney recipients the 3-year graft survival gap between 0 and 6 antigen mismatches was essentially the same under azathioprine (92.4% -> 80.6%) and under MMF (95.2% -> 82.9%), and the authors conclude the two act as additive, not competing, factors - so a pre-screen that scores HLA mismatch does not become redundant because the centre uses a modern antiproliferative. It also supplies the two endpoints of the total-count series for C2, though only the endpoints. The exposure transfers well to a KidneyMatch pre-screen: 'antigen mismatch' counted 0-6 across A, B and DR is exactly the one-field, low-resolution quantity an Iranian pre-screen can compute from a serologic or two-digit report, with no allele-level typing assumed. Transfer is weaker in three ways. First, donor type is not reported, and a US 0-mismatch kidney in 1995-1997 was typically a nationally shared deceased-donor organ with its own selection and long cold ischaemia, whereas an Iranian 0-mismatch living donor is almost always an HLA-identical sibling - so the size of the zero-mismatch step here is not directly transportable to living donation. Second, the comparator drug era is obsolete: both arms are cyclosporine-era, and the transferable inference is the qualitative one (a stronger drug leaves the gradient intact), not the 2001 percentages, since Iranian practice today is tacrolimus plus mycophenolate. Third, it says nothing about antibody status: sensitisation is not reported as a modifier and no DSA data exist, so it cannot tell an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen how mismatch counts behave in a sensitised candidate.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft survival at 3 years (Kaplan-Meier): MMF vs AZA overall, not stratified by HLA mismatch (reference AZA 84%) — percent surviving 87, p=<0.001; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier comparison as printed in the abstract [Abstract, Results, sentence 2]
- all-cause graft survival at 3 years (Kaplan-Meier): 0 antigen mismatches, AZA arm (this is the favourable end of the 0-6 series) — percent surviving 92.4; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier within the AZA arm [Abstract, Results, sentence 4]
- all-cause graft survival at 3 years (Kaplan-Meier): 6 antigen mismatches, AZA arm — percent surviving 80.6; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier within the AZA arm [Abstract, Results, sentence 4]
- all-cause graft survival at 3 years (Kaplan-Meier): 0 antigen mismatches, MMF arm — percent surviving 95.2; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier within the MMF arm [Abstract, Results, sentence 4]
- all-cause graft survival at 3 years (Kaplan-Meier): 6 antigen mismatches, MMF arm — percent surviving 82.9; adjusted for unadjusted Kaplan-Meier within the MMF arm [Abstract, Results, sentence 4]
- graft loss: increasing HLA matching (fewer mismatches) within the AZA arm — relative risk from Cox proportional hazards model - NO point estimate, CI or p-value is printed in the abstract, only the word 'significantly' None; adjusted for 13 unnamed pretransplant confounders including intention-to-treat immunosuppression [Abstract, Results, final sentence]
- graft loss: increasing HLA matching (fewer mismatches) within the MMF arm — relative risk from Cox proportional hazards model - NO point estimate, CI or p-value is printed in the abstract, only the word 'significantly' None; adjusted for 13 unnamed pretransplant confounders including intention-to-treat immunosuppression [Abstract, Results, final sentence]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 92.4; 6 MM: 80.6; 0 MM: 95.2; 6 MM: 82.9
- Shape reported: not reported. Only the two endpoints of the 0-6 antigen-mismatch scale are printed, and only as survival percentages within each drug arm. Mismatch counts 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are not given in the abstract, so nothing can be said about whether the gradient is linear, concave, stepped, or whether a discontinuous zero-mismatch premium exists. The abstract's only shape statement is the direction: 'three-year graft survival improved with fewer HLA donor-recipient mismatches' in both arms.; linearity tested: not tested, or at least not reported. The abstract describes Cox models fitted to test the HLA-mismatch x immunosuppression interaction, not the functional form of the mismatch term; no trend test, spline, threshold analysis or per-mismatch coefficient is mentioned. Whether mismatch entered the Cox model as a continuous 0-6 count or as categories is not stated.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA antigen mismatch (0-6) x initial immunosuppression (MMF-containing vs AZA-containing): No effect modification. The 0-vs-6-mismatch survival gap is of similar magnitude in both arms, and MMF shifts the whole curve upward rather than flattening it. The authors' stated conclusion is that HLA matching and MMF are additive, and that neither obviates the other. (NO interaction term, ratio-of-hazard-ratios or 'P for interaction' is printed in the abstract. The only supporting numbers are the four Kaplan-Meier percentages: AZA 92.4% (0 MM) vs 80.6% (6 MM); MMF 95.2% (0 MM) vs 82.9% (6 MM). The abstract calls the relative improvement 'comparable'.) [Abstract, Methods (Cox models 'used to investigate the interaction'), Results sentence 4, and Conclusions]
- HLA matching x era of immunosuppression (the background hypothesis being tested): The paper was designed against the hypothesis that stronger, more specific pharmacologic immunosuppression makes HLA matching vanish; the result rejects that hypothesis for the AZA-to-MMF step. This is the C1/C11 payload of the paper. (no numeric estimate printed for this framing) [Abstract, Background and Conclusions]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C11* — "Comparing zero antigen mismatches to six antigen mismatches, the relative improvement was comparable for both patients on AZA (92.4% vs. 80.6%) and MMF (95.2% vs. 82.9%)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "For both AZA and MMF three-year graft survival improved with fewer HLA donor-recipient mismatches." (Abstract, Results)
- *C1* — "By Cox proportional hazard model the relative risk for graft loss decreased significantly in both the AZA and MMF treated patients with increased HLA matching." (Abstract, Results (final sentence))
- *C11* — "The use of MMF does not obviate the benefits of HLA matching, while HLA matching does not minimize the benefits of MMF on long term graft survival." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C11* — "Our study would suggest that HLA matching and MMF therapy are additive factors in decreasing the risk for renal allograft loss." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C1* — "Overall three year graft survival was higher in the MMF group when compared to the AZA group (87% vs. 84% respectively P<0.001)." (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC full text and no author manuscript exist for this 2001 Transplantation paper, so the mismatch-stratified table, the Cox coefficients and any interaction p-value cannot be read. Everything here is limited to what the abstract prints.; The central 'no interaction / additive' conclusion is asserted without a printed interaction estimate or P for interaction. Absence of evidence of interaction is not evidence of absence, and the abstract gives no way to bound how large a missed interaction could be.; Only the 0 and 6 mismatch categories are reported. The intermediate counts 1-5 are absent, so the paper contributes the endpoints of the dose-response but not its shape, and cannot address a discontinuous zero-mismatch premium (C9).; No per-locus analysis. HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR are aggregated into a 0-6 antigen count, so the paper says nothing about the relative weight of DR vs B vs A (C3, C5, C6), and nothing at all about DQ, DP or C.; Short follow-up. Accrual ran Jan 1995 - Jun 1997 with censoring in June 1998, so 3-year survival is a Kaplan-Meier extrapolation from at most ~3.5 years of observation; the paper cannot speak to the long-term divergence where HLA effects are usually largest.; Obsolete immunosuppression comparison. Both arms are cyclosporine-era; the modern question is whether the gradient survives tacrolimus + mycophenolate + induction, which this design cannot answer.; Non-randomised drug assignment. MMF vs AZA was clinician-chosen in a registry, adjusted only by 13 unnamed pretransplant covariates; residual confounding by centre, era-within-period and unmeasured recipient risk is unaddressed, and the 87% vs 84% overall difference is especially exposed to it.; All-cause, not death-censored, graft survival, so death with a functioning graft is mixed into the endpoint and dilutes an immunological exposure.; Donor type is not reported and no living-donor subgroup is given, which is the single biggest gap for a living-donor pre-screen: in US data of this era the 0-mismatch group is dominated by nationally shared deceased-donor kidneys, a population with different selection and cold ischaemia from an Iranian related living donor.; Sensitisation, PRA, cold ischaemia, donor age and race are not reported as modifiers; they may or may not be inside the 13 unnamed confounders, so no C11 conclusion can be drawn for any factor other than the antiproliferative drug.; Antigen-level typing only, with the loci not even named in the abstract; no allele-level, eplet or PIRCHE comparison, so the paper is silent on C12..

| typing resolution | not stated anywhere in the retrieved abstract. No resolution, locus set or matching definition is printed; any assumption that this is serologic/antigen-level (one-field) typing comes from era knowledge, not from this paper's retrieved text. |
| outcome | all-cause graft survival (10-year, half-life); functional (death-censored) graft survival; rejection episodes; graft loss from rejection |
| follow up | up to 12 years (Oct 1987 - Sep 1999); 10-year actuarial estimates and projected half-lives |
| other factors modelled | demographic characteristics (stated as the adjustment set; the individual covariates are not itemised in the abstract), cold ischaemia (mean 23 h matched vs 22 h mismatched; addressed by the paired-donor design rather than by modelling) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the largest outcome validation of an allocation policy built around a full HLA match: the US national sharing programme shipped kidneys the programme classed as HLA-matched to matched recipients, and the paper compares them against every mismatched cadaveric transplant in the same registry window. It answers the review's zero-mismatch-premium question (C2, C9) at the coarsest possible grain, matched versus mismatched with all mismatch grades pooled, so it constrains the size of the premium but says nothing about the shape between one and six mismatches. The paired-donor design (3562 pairs) is its strongest transferable feature, because it holds donor quality fixed by construction and still shows the matched kidney beating its own mate, which is the answer to the standard objection that matched recipients simply receive better organs. Transfer to an Iranian living-donor pre-screen is limited: donors were deceased, immunosuppression was of the cyclosporine era, and the matched cohort was selected by a policy that also shortened waiting time. What does transfer is the message that a full A,B,DR-level match carries a large and durable survival advantage, which supports giving zero-mismatch living donors a distinct premium rather than scoring mismatch as purely additive. What does not transfer is any per-locus or per-count guidance, and the paper is silent on sensitisation, DQ, DP and C, so it cannot inform an antibody-status-unknown screen beyond the count of A,B,DR antigens.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- all-cause graft survival at 10 years (actuarial, unadjusted): HLA-matched cadaveric transplants (n=7614) — percent surviving 52; adjusted for none (crude actuarial estimate) [Abstract, Results]
- all-cause graft survival at 10 years (actuarial, unadjusted): HLA-mismatched cadaveric transplants (n=81,364) — percent surviving 37; adjusted for none (crude actuarial estimate) [Abstract, Results]
- graft half-life (projected): HLA-matched cadaveric transplants — half-life, years 12.5; adjusted for none [Abstract, Results]
- graft half-life (projected): HLA-mismatched cadaveric transplants — half-life, years 8.6; adjusted for none [Abstract, Results]
- overall (all-cause) graft survival at 10 years, adjusted: HLA-matched vs HLA-mismatched — difference, printed as '10 percent higher' (unit ambiguous in the abstract; read as percentage points) 10; adjusted for demographic characteristics [Abstract, Results]
- functional graft survival at 10 years (censored at death with functioning graft), adjusted: HLA-matched vs HLA-mismatched — difference, printed as '11 percent higher' (unit ambiguous in the abstract; read as percentage points) 11; adjusted for demographic characteristics [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 52; 1-6 pooled (all HLA-mismatched) MM: 37
- Shape reported: step: a zero-mismatch premium against all mismatched grades pooled. No intermediate mismatch counts are reported, so no shape between 1 and 6 can be read from this paper.; linearity tested: not tested; the abstract reports only a binary matched-versus-mismatched comparison, which cannot test linearity; 1 and 2 pooled: True

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA matching x cold ischaemia (national shipping of matched kidneys): the matched-kidney advantage persisted despite a slightly longer mean cold ischaemia (23 h vs 22 h), and within 3562 donor pairs the matched kidney had higher survival, fewer rejection episodes and lower rejection-related loss. This is a design control that holds donor quality constant, NOT a formal effect-modification test. (no numeric estimate and no interaction p-value in the abstract) [Abstract, Methods and Results]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C9* — "The estimated 10-year rate of graft survival was 52 percent for HLA-matched transplants, as compared with 37 percent for HLA-mismatched transplants." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "The estimated half-lives of the transplants were 12.5 years and 8.6 years, respectively, and the mean duration of cold ischemia was 23 hours and 22 hours, respectively." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "the overall rates of graft survival and the rates of functional-graft survival (with data censored on patients who died with a functioning graft) were 10 percent and 11 percent higher, respectively, for HLA-matched transplants" (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "Among 3562 pairs of kidneys, HLA-matched transplants had higher rates of survival, a lower incidence of episodes of rejection, and a lower risk of loss as a result of rejection." (Abstract, Results)
- *C13* — "A superior graft outcome with little increase in the duration of cold ischemia justifies national sharing of HLA-matched kidney transplants." (Abstract, Conclusions)

**Limitations.** abstract only: no PMC full text exists for this PMID, so confidence intervals, p-values, adjusted hazard ratios, the itemised adjustment covariates and the paired-analysis numbers are not retrievable; binary comparison: every mismatched grade (1-6 A,B,DR mismatches) is pooled into one arm, so the paper cannot describe the dose-response shape or separate the first mismatch effect from the second; the abstract never defines 'HLA-matched'; the UNOS programme criterion (six-antigen match, later zero A,B,DR mismatch) is not printed in the retrieved text, so the exact contrast is assumed rather than read; deceased donors only, USA, 1987-1999, cyclosporine-era immunosuppression; neither a modern-immunosuppression nor a living-donor cohort; 10-year survival and half-lives are actuarial projections for a cohort still accruing follow-up at the time of analysis, and half-life projection assumes a constant attrition rate; matched recipients were selected by an allocation policy that also shortened waiting time and shipped nationally; adjustment is limited to unspecified 'demographic characteristics', and sensitisation/PRA is never mentioned; no confidence interval or p-value appears anywhere in the abstract, so every number here is a point estimate with no printed precision; typing resolution, loci and matching algorithm are not stated; no DQ, DP or C information.

### Reisaeter AV 1998 — A strong impact of matching for a limited number of HLA-DR antigens on graft survival and rejection episodes: a single-center study of first cadaveric kidneys to nonsensitized recipients.

Reisaeter AV 1998, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/00007890-199808270-00018](https://doi.org/10.1097/00007890-199808270-00018). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation, 1998); no PMC full text; abstract only via PubMed.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | first (primary) cadaveric kidney grafts to nonsensitized recipients, single centre (Institute of Transplantation Immunology, The National Hospital, Oslo, Norway); transplant years not stated in the abstract. PubMed MeSH indexing for this record spans Infant, Child, Preschool, Child, Adolescent, Adult, Middle Aged, Aged and Aged 80-and-over, so the cohort is not adult-only; the abstract gives no age breakdown. |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 655 |
| design | retrospective single-centre cohort; graft survival at 1 and 5 years and acute rejection within 3 months by number of HLA-DR antigen mismatches (0/1/2); statistical test not named in abstract |
| typing resolution | serologic/antigen level for HLA-A, -B and DR 1-10; subgroup analyses for DR 11-14 and for 'some DR alleles only detectable by genomic typing' |
| outcome | graft survival at 1 and 5 years (death-censoring not stated); acute rejection episodes within the first 3 months |
| follow up | up to 5 years reported (graft survival at 1 and 5 years); median not stated |
| other factors modelled | none stated in the abstract (crude percentages; no multivariable adjustment described) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the classic single-centre demonstration that DR (antigen-level, serologically defined DR 1-10) matching alone carries most of the HLA effect on both graft survival and early acute rejection in first, nonsensitized deceased-donor kidney recipients, and that HLA-A and -B matching adds no significant further benefit for overall survival or rejection. It answers review question C3 (DR is the most important single locus) and C9 (the 0/1/2 DR-mismatch gradient: graft survival 90/82/73% at 1 year and 76/62/56% at 5 years, rejection 48/64/82% within 3 months). The 0/1/2 series is reported without pooling, so the size of the first versus the second DR mismatch can be read off directly, although no formal linearity test or hazard ratio is given in the abstract. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor pre-screen is favourable on typing resolution: the effect was seen with serologic (one-field-equivalent) DR typing, exactly the low-resolution data the pre-screen will hold, and the recipients were nonsensitized, matching an antibody-status-unknown pool better than a sensitized one. Transfer is weaker on donor type (deceased donors with presumably longer cold ischaemia than living donation) and era (1980s-1990s immunosuppression), so the absolute percentages should not be carried over; only the ranking of DR above A/B and the stepwise gradient should.

- graft survival at 1 year: 1 HLA-DR antigen mismatch vs 0 — percentage 82, p=0.004; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- graft survival at 1 year: 2 HLA-DR antigen mismatches vs 0 — percentage 73, p=0.001; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- graft survival at 5 years: 0 HLA-DR antigen mismatches (reference) — percentage 76; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- graft survival at 5 years: 1 HLA-DR antigen mismatch — percentage 62; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- graft survival at 5 years: 2 HLA-DR antigen mismatches — percentage 56; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- acute rejection episodes within the first 3 months: 0 HLA-DR antigen mismatches (reference) — percentage 48; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- acute rejection episodes within the first 3 months: 1 HLA-DR antigen mismatch vs 0 — percentage 64, p=<0.001; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- acute rejection episodes within the first 3 months: 2 HLA-DR antigen mismatches vs 0 — percentage 82, p=<0.001; adjusted for none stated (crude percentage; abstract) [Abstract, Results]

**Dose-response.**

- DR: 0 MM: 1-yr graft survival 90% (ref); 5-yr 76%; acute rejection <3 mo 48%; 1 MM: 1-yr graft survival 82% (P=0.004); 5-yr 62%; acute rejection <3 mo 64% (P<0.001); 2 MM: 1-yr graft survival 73% (P=0.001); 5-yr 56%; acute rejection <3 mo 82% (P<0.001)
- A: note MM: reported only pooled with B: 'did not significantly further improve overall graft survival'; 'no significant correlation to acute rejection episodes'; no numbers in abstract
- B: note MM: reported only pooled with A: see A
- Shape reported: step (0/1/2 DR reported as three separate strata; each added DR mismatch worsened both outcomes; the authors do not characterise the shape); linearity tested: not tested (abstract reports stratum percentages with P-values against the 0-mismatch stratum only; no trend test, HR or model described); 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA-A/B matching x time after transplant (grafts surviving at least 1 year): A/B matching did not significantly improve overall graft survival, but 'some effects for grafts surviving at least 1 year were observed' (conditional/late effect; no numbers in abstract) (not reported in abstract) [Abstract, Results]
- DR matching x typing resolution (serologic DR 1-10 vs DR 11-14 and genomic-typing-only DR alleles): matching additionally for DR 11-14 or for DR alleles detectable only by genomic typing 'further improved graft survival, but the differences did not reach statistical significance' (not reported in abstract (stated non-significant)) [Abstract, Results]

- *C9* — "The corresponding figures at 5 years were 76%, 62%, and 56%, respectively." (Abstract, Results)
- *C9* — "Among recipients of grafts mismatched for zero, one, or two HLA-DR antigens, acute rejection episodes were experienced in 48%, 64% (P<0.001), and 82% (P<0.001), respectively, within the first 3 months." (Abstract, Results)
