### Opelz G 1997 — Impact of HLA compatibility on survival of kidney transplants from unrelated live donors.

Opelz G 1997, *Transplantation*, [DOI 10.1097/00007890-199711270-00017](https://doi.org/10.1097/00007890-199711270-00017). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Transplantation 1997, Lippincott); no PMC record exists for this PMID, abstract retrieved via PubMed.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | 2281 kidney transplants from unrelated LIVE donors (spouses and non-spouses), grafted 1986-1995, reported by 198 transplant centres to the Collaborative Transplant Study (predominantly European/multinational registry) |
| donor type | living |
| n | 2281 |
| design | multicentre registry cohort; 5-year graft ('transplant') success rate compared across HLA-A+B+DR mismatch categories and by locus. The abstract reports significance tests only; the statistical method (log-rank, trend test, or Cox model) is not named in the retrieved abstract. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved abstract (1986-1995 CTS data, so serologic broad-antigen / one-field typing is the era-typical method, but the paper's own statement of resolution was not retrieved) |
| outcome | 5-year graft survival, described as '5-year transplant success rate'; whether it is death-censored or all-cause graft failure is not stated in the abstract |
| follow up | 5 years (5-year success rate is the reported endpoint) |
| other factors modelled | cold/ischaemic preservation time (discussed as the competing explanation, not reported as a modelled covariate), donor relationship: spouse vs non-spouse (reported as a stratification of the matching-distribution analysis) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the closest published analogue to the Iranian programme's structural situation: kidney grafts from LIVING but genetically UNRELATED donors, where donor-recipient HLA sharing is near-random rather than haplotype-driven, and where cold ischaemia is minimal by construction. It directly answers the review's living-donor question (C14): the paper was written to rebut the claim that excellent living-unrelated results prove HLA matching is superfluous once ischaemia is short, and it finds the opposite - 5-year success still tracks the number of HLA-A+B+DR mismatches at P<0.0001. That matters for a pre-screen in Iran because the standard local counterargument ('these are live donors with short ischaemia, so matching does not pay') is exactly the argument this cohort tests and rejects. It also speaks to C2 in shape terms only weakly: the abstract confirms an association with mismatch COUNT but the per-count 0/1/2...6 series lives in the paper's figures/tables, which are not in PMC, so the dose-response shape cannot be read from the retrieved text. Transfer to the Iranian setting is partial: typing is antigen-level (one-field), which matches a low-resolution Iranian pre-screen well, but the era's immunosuppression (1986-1995, largely cyclosporine-based, pre-tacrolimus/MMF) inflates the absolute HLA effect relative to today, and recipient antibody status (PRA/DSA) is not reported at all, so this paper cannot tell an antibody-status-unknown screen anything about how much of the mismatch effect is antibody-mediated. It does NOT provide Iranian or regional data (C15); it is a design analogue only.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- 5-year graft survival ('transplant success rate'): across the number of HLA-A, -B and -DR mismatches (mismatch count categories; the category boundaries are not given in the abstract) — significance test only - no HR/OR/RR or per-category percentage appears in the retrieved abstract None, p=<0.0001; adjusted for not stated in the retrieved abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- graft survival: mismatches at the class I HLA-A and HLA-B loci (A and B taken together, not separated) — significance test only - no effect size in the retrieved abstract None, p=0.001; adjusted for not stated in the retrieved abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- graft survival: mismatches at the class II HLA-DR locus — significance test only - no effect size in the retrieved abstract None, p=0.005; adjusted for not stated in the retrieved abstract [Abstract, Results sentence 2]
- distribution of HLA-DR mismatch (not a survival outcome): observed frequency of 0 HLA-DR mismatch vs the frequency expected under chance donor selection, in spouse and in non-spouse donor pairs — excess of 0-DR-mismatch pairs over chance expectation; no numeric excess, ratio or p-value is given in the retrieved abstract None; adjusted for not applicable [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Dose-response.**

- A_and_B_combined: class I A+B mismatch effect on graft survival, P=0.001; no per-count (0/1/2) estimates in the retrieved abstract
- DR: class II DR mismatch effect on graft survival, P=0.005; no per-count (0/1/2) estimates in the retrieved abstract
- Shape reported: not reported in the retrieved text; linearity tested: Not determinable from the abstract. The abstract states only that the 5-year success rate 'was significantly associated with the number of HLA-A, -B, and -DR mismatches (P<0.0001)', which is consistent with a trend/ordered test across mismatch counts, but no test name, no per-category estimates and no formal linearity or trend statistic are given. The 5-year survival by mismatch-count series that the review wants is in the paper's figure/table, which is not accessible (no PMC record).; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch effect x cold/warm ischaemia time (living donation implies very short ischaemia): The paper's central claim is that the HLA matching effect is NOT abolished by the very short ischaemia of living donation - i.e. no effect modification by short preservation time. This is asserted as the study's conclusion; no formal interaction test, and no direct statistical comparison against a cadaver-donor cohort, is reported in the retrieved abstract. (no interaction statistic reported; supported only by the significant HLA effects (P<0.0001 overall, P=0.001 class I, P=0.005 DR) observed within the living-unrelated cohort itself) [Abstract, Background and Conclusion]
- HLA effect x donor relationship (spouse vs non-spouse): Spouse and non-spouse pairs are analysed separately, but only for the DISTRIBUTION of HLA-DR mismatch (both groups show more 0-DR-mismatch pairs than chance would give). No spouse-vs-non-spouse comparison of the HLA effect ON GRAFT SURVIVAL is reported in the retrieved abstract. [Abstract, Results sentence 3]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C2* — "The 5-year transplant success rate was significantly associated with the number of HLA-A, -B, and -DR mismatches (P<0.0001)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C3* — "There was a significant impact on graft survival of mismatches at the class I HLA-A, and -B loci (P=0.001) as well as at the class II HLA-DR locus (P=0.005)." (Abstract, Results)
- *C14* — "The outcome of kidney transplants from unrelated live donors is strongly influenced by HLA compatibility." (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C11* — "Short exposure of donor kidneys to ischemia does not eliminate the influence of HLA matching on graft survival." (Abstract, Conclusion)
- *C13* — "In transplants from both spouses and nonspouses, cases with no HLA-DR mismatch were found more often than would be expected if transplant donors were selected by chance" (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. This 1997 Transplantation paper has no PMC record, so the per-mismatch-count 5-year survival series - the single number the review most wants from it - could not be retrieved. Everything below the locus level is unavailable.; No effect sizes of any kind in the retrieved text: no hazard ratios, no risk differences, no per-category survival percentages, no confidence intervals. Only three p-values (P<0.0001 overall, P=0.001 class I A+B, P=0.005 DR).; Adjustment is not stated. It is unclear from the abstract whether the HLA effects are crude or adjusted for recipient age, donor age, transplant year, centre, or immunosuppression - a serious concern in a 198-centre registry where matched pairs may cluster in better-resourced centres.; Class I is reported as A and B combined (P=0.001), so this paper cannot separate B from A and gives no evidence on the review's C5/C6 ordering.; No HLA-C, -DQ or -DP data; the analysis is A/B/DR only, matching the era but leaving the review's C4, C7 and C8 untouched.; No sensitisation data. PRA and DSA are not mentioned, so the mechanism (antibody-mediated vs cellular) cannot be separated - directly limiting transfer to an antibody-status-unknown pre-screen.; Era effect. Transplants 1986-1995 were performed under cyclosporine-era immunosuppression, largely before tacrolimus and mycophenolate; the absolute size of the HLA effect is expected to be larger than under current regimens (relevant to C1's modern-era question).; Confounding by indication in donor selection: the paper itself shows that 0-DR-mismatch pairs occur more often than chance, i.e. centres were prospectively matching. Pairs that reached transplantation with good matches may differ systematically from poorly matched pairs in ways not captured.; Typing resolution is not stated in the retrieved text; antigen-level serology is inferred from the era rather than read from the paper.; The claim that short ischaemia does not eliminate the HLA effect is a conclusion drawn within a living-donor cohort; no formal interaction test against a cadaver cohort is reported in the abstract.; Survival definition (death-censored vs all-cause graft loss) is not stated..

### Held PJ 1994 — The impact of HLA mismatches on the survival of first cadaveric kidney transplants.

Held PJ 1994, *N Engl J Med*, [DOI 10.1056/NEJM199409223311203](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJM199409223311203). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (New England Journal of Medicine); no PMC record, convert_article_ids returned a PMID only.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | first cadaveric (deceased-donor) kidney transplants in 30,564 Medicare patients, United States, transplanted 1984-1990; a separate simulated allocation of a sample of organs to a sample of 20,000 waiting candidates |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | 30,564 transplants (plus a 20,000-candidate simulation sample) |
| design | retrospective registry cohort, proportional-hazards (Cox) models adjusted for patient and donor characteristics, plus a policy simulation of national mandatory sharing |
| typing resolution | not stated in the abstract; HLA-A, B and DR only, transplants 1984-1990 (serologic antigen-level typing is the era's practice, but the paper's own wording is not in the retrieved text) |
| outcome | all-cause graft survival (adjusted 1-year graft survival; projected 5-year graft survival) |
| follow up | not stated in the abstract; results reported at 1 year and projected to 5 years |
| other factors modelled | patient characteristics (unspecified in the abstract), donor characteristics (unspecified in the abstract), recipient race/ethnicity (reported as an allocation consequence, not as a covariate list) |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the classic quantification of HOW BIG the antigen-level HLA-A/B/DR mismatch gradient actually is in kidney transplantation, and it is in the review to calibrate ANGLE A rather than to establish direction. It answers the magnitude half of C2 and C9: the adjusted 1-year graft survival premium for a zero-mismatch graft over a four-mismatch graft is 7.3 percentage points (84.3 vs 77.0), and driving the national mean mismatch count from 3.6 down to 1.2 buys only 4.4 percentage points of projected 5-year graft survival. That is the single most useful number for a pre-screen tool: HLA matching is real but is a modest, gradual effect, not a gate. Transfer to a LIVING-donor Iranian pre-screen is partial and must be stated as such. The direction and the antigen-level, one-field HLA-A/B/DR counting scheme transfer well, because this paper is itself low-resolution and uses exactly the 0-6 count our pre-screen can compute from serologic typing; it needs no two-field data, no eplet load and no DSA result, so it is one of the few effect sizes our antibody-status-unknown setting can actually claim. The population does not transfer: these are deceased-donor grafts from 1984-1990 under azathioprine/cyclosporine-era immunosuppression, where absolute graft survival was far lower and cold ischaemia and donor quality varied in ways living donation removes, so the ABSOLUTE percentages are obsolete and the paper should be cited for the shape and the modest size of the gradient, never for a predicted survival number quoted to an Iranian patient. Its equity finding is directly relevant to how the tool is allowed to rank: the same simulation that gained 4.4 points cut the share of kidneys going to Black recipients from 22.2 to 15.0 percent, which is the historical demonstration that a matching-maximising ranker imposes an access cost on genetically less-represented groups - a warning that applies to any Iranian ranker that would weight HLA heavily across ethnic groups.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft survival at 1 year (all-cause): 0 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches — adjusted survival percentage 84.3; adjusted for patient and donor characteristics (proportional-hazards model; covariates not enumerated in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- graft survival at 1 year (all-cause): 4 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches — adjusted survival percentage 77.0; adjusted for patient and donor characteristics (proportional-hazards model; covariates not enumerated in the abstract) [Abstract, Results sentence 1]
- graft survival at 5 years (projected, current allocation): status quo, mean 3.6 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches — projected survival percentage 58.5; adjusted for simulated allocation of a sample of organs to a sample of 20,000 candidates, using the adjusted proportional-hazards model [Abstract, Results sentence 3]
- graft survival at 5 years (projected, maximal matching): national rationing for minimal mismatch, mean 1.2 HLA-A,B,DR mismatches — projected survival percentage 62.9; adjusted for simulated allocation of a sample of organs to a sample of 20,000 candidates, using the adjusted proportional-hazards model [Abstract, Results sentence 3]
- graft survival at 5 years (projected): maximal matching (mean 1.2 MM) vs status quo (mean 3.6 MM) - the whole-policy gain — absolute risk difference (percentage points) 4.4; adjusted for as above; the authors state the actual benefit is likely to be smaller [Abstract, Conclusions]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: 84.3; 4 MM: 77.0
- Shape reported: not reported in the retrieved text. Only two points of the 0-6 count series (0 and 4 mismatches) appear in the abstract; the counts 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 and any HLA-A vs B vs DR breakdown are in the full text, which PMC does not hold. The two available endpoints span 7.3 percentage points over four mismatches, but no per-count series, no hazard ratios and no test of linearity are visible, so the shape must be recorded as unknown from this source.; linearity tested: not stated in the abstract; no trend test, spline, categorical-vs-linear comparison or threshold analysis is visible in the retrieved text; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C9* — "The adjusted one-year graft survival was 84.3 percent for grafts with no mismatches and 77.0 percent for grafts with four mismatches." (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "decrease the average number of HLA mismatches from 3.6 to 1.2" (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "projected five-year graft survival could potentially increase from 58.5 percent to 62.9 percent" (Abstract, Results)
- *C2* — "a policy of maximal matching of cadaveric renal transplants would increase five-year graft survival by a comparatively small 4.4 percentage points, but the actual benefit is likely to be smaller." (Abstract, Conclusions)
- *C13* — "a decrease in the proportion of kidneys allocated to black recipients from 22.2 to 15.0 percent" (Abstract, Results)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. The New England Journal of Medicine 1994 paper is not in PMC (convert_article_ids returned no PMCID), so the per-count 0-6 series, the locus-specific HLA-A vs B vs DR results, all hazard ratios, all confidence intervals and all p-values are unavailable and are recorded as null rather than estimated.; The discovery note that motivated including this paper promises locus-specific results; none could be verified from the retrieved text. Any locus claim from Held 1994 needs the publisher PDF before it may be cited.; Era: transplants 1984-1990, pre-tacrolimus and pre-mycophenolate immunosuppression. Absolute graft survival (84.3 percent at one year, 58.5 percent at five years) is far below contemporary results, so the absolute percentages are obsolete even if the relative gradient is informative.; Deceased-donor only, and first grafts only. Nothing here speaks to living donation, to retransplants, or to repeat-mismatch effects.; Antigen-level HLA-A, B, DR only. No DQ, no C, no DP, no molecular or eplet mismatch, and no DSA or PRA data are reported in the abstract, so the estimate is a broad serologic-mismatch effect that will partly be a proxy for unmeasured antibody risk.; The 4.4-percentage-point figure is a projection from a simulated allocation, not an observed randomised or even observed cohort contrast; the authors themselves warn the real benefit would be smaller.; Adjustment covariates are not enumerated in the retrieved text, so residual confounding by cold ischaemia time, centre, donor quality and sensitisation cannot be assessed.; United States Medicare population; the ethnic composition that drives the equity result differs from Iran's, so the direction of the access cost transfers but its size does not..

### Zhou YC 1993 — Effect of HLA matching on renal transplant survival.

Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Clinical Transplants annual volume); no PMC record and no DOI exist for this 1993 book chapter, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable. Actuarial (life-table) graft survival at 1 and 3 years with a projected 10-year rate, compared across HLA-A,B,DR mismatch levels; early rejection compared as an incidence proportion. Statistical testing is reported only as p-values for group comparisons. A multivariate model is mentioned only for RANKING centres, not for adjusting the mismatch effect. All 27 possible HLA-A,B,DR mismatch combinations were examined for the per-locus analysis. |

| follow up | not stated; 1- and 3-year actuarial rates are observed, the 10-year figure is explicitly 'projected' |
| other factors modelled | transplant centre quality (top 20 vs bottom 20 US centres by multivariate ranking), era / year of transplant (1987-1992 trend in the share of HLA-matched grafts), no other covariate adjustment of the matching effect is reported in the retrieved abstract |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the earliest registry-scale statement of the two features the review's ANGLE A asks about at once: a discrete zero-mismatch premium and a graded gradient above it. It answers the shape question directly, because in 30,139 first cadaver kidneys the 0-antigen-mismatch group is set apart from every other match level ('superior result compared with any other match level'), yet survival still falls stepwise as mismatches accumulate to 6 - i.e. the curve is a step at zero followed by a slope, not a pure threshold and not a clean straight line. Its typing resolution is exactly the resolution a low-resolution, one-field Iranian pre-screen has: broad serologic HLA-A, -B and -DR antigens, so the mismatch counts here are the same objects the pre-screen would compute, with no allele-level inflation. It transfers only partly, however. The cohort is deceased-donor, so its zero-mismatch group was assembled by national sharing across centres and carries longer cold ischaemia and a different case mix than a living-donor pair, while the review's target is living donation, where donor quality is high and uniform and HLA is one of the few remaining discriminants. It is also pre-tacrolimus, pre-mycophenolate and pre-solid-phase-antibody: the absolute gaps (11 points at 1 year, 19 at 3) are almost certainly larger than what modern immunosuppression would show, so the paper should be cited for the SHAPE of the dose-response and for the ordering of loci, not for the magnitude. Finally, antibody status is unmodelled here, which happens to mirror the antibody-status-unknown pre-screen, but it means the estimates are unadjusted associations rather than the causal effect of mismatch alone.

A discrete zero-mismatch premium (0 mismatches 'yielded a superior result compared with any other match level', and 'even a single HLA antigen mismatch resulted in substantially poorer survival') sitting on top of a monotone gradient ('there was a stepwise decline in graft survival with increasing numbers of mismatched HLA antigens'). The authors explicitly present these as coexisting, joined by 'Nevertheless'.; linearity tested: Not tested. No trend test, spline, or linear-vs-categorical comparison is reported in the retrieved abstract; the only statistics given are p-values for pairwise group comparisons (p<0.001 for 1 vs 0 mismatches; p<0.01 for the 0 vs 5-6 rejection contrast; p<0.05 / p<0.01 for the centre-stratified best-vs-worst contrasts). 'Stepwise decline' is a descriptive statement about the ordering of the actuarial curves, not a fitted model.; 1 and 2 pooled: False

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA mismatch x transplant centre quality (top 20 vs bottom 20 US centres by multivariate ranking): The matching effect was present in both strata but the absolute best-vs-worst gap was LARGER at the bottom-20 centres than at the top-20 centres, at every time point. The authors attribute the bottom-20 pattern partly to those centres placing more emphasis on matching (34% of their first cadaver transplants had fewer than 3 mismatched antigens, vs 26% at the top-20 centres). (top 20: 9% (1 yr) / 16% (3 yr) / projected 25% (10 yr), p<0.05. bottom 20: 16% / 22% / projected 36%, p<0.01.) [Abstract, numbered points 5 and 6]
- locus x time since transplant (effect modification of the locus ranking by follow-up duration): The locus that matters changes with time: DR mismatches dominated graft outcome at 3 months, whereas B mismatches had the most influence on long-term outcome; A had the smallest effect throughout. (qualitative; derived from examining all 27 HLA-A,B,DR mismatch combinations. No numeric estimate or interaction p-value printed.) [Abstract, numbered point 7]
- HLA matching x era (1987-1992): Not an outcome interaction but a practice-pattern trend: the share of HLA-matched first cadaver transplants rose from 2% (1987) to 6% (1992) after the UNOS national 6-antigen-match sharing programme began in 1987 and was extended to phenotypically matched kidneys in 1990. (2% -> 6% of first cadaver transplants) [Abstract, numbered point 3]

**Limitations.** ABSTRACT ONLY. Clinical Transplants 1993 is a book-style annual volume with no PMC deposit and no DOI; convert_article_ids returned no PMCID. Everything above comes from the PubMed abstract, which is itself flagged '(ABSTRACT TRUNCATED AT 400 WORDS)' - so numbered point 7 is cut off mid-argument and any further points (8, 9, ...) are lost.; No hazard ratios, no relative risks, no confidence intervals anywhere. Only absolute actuarial percentages and threshold p-values (p<0.05, p<0.01, p<0.001). Any HR the review wants must come from a different paper.; The matching effect is UNADJUSTED. The multivariate model mentioned is used to rank centres, not to adjust the mismatch-survival association. No adjustment for donor age, cold ischaemia time, PRA/sensitisation, race, retransplant status, or delayed graft function is reported - and the zero-mismatch group is precisely the group assembled by national sharing, so it differs systematically (longer cold ischaemia, wider geographic distribution, and plausibly a different sensitised/regraft mix) from locally allocated kidneys. Confounding in both directions is unquantified.; The per-count series is incomplete: only 0 and 1 mismatch have printed survival rates. Counts 2, 3, 4 are never given numerically, and 5 and 6 are pooled in the rejection analysis. 'Stepwise decline' therefore cannot be checked against numbers from this record, and the shape between 1 and 6 cannot be characterised as linear or otherwise.; Linearity was never formally tested - no trend test, no spline, no comparison of a linear against a categorical mismatch term.; The 10-year figures (32%, 25%, 36%) are explicitly PROJECTIONS from short follow-up, not observed 10-year outcomes, and projected differences from 1- and 3-year life-table data are fragile.; DECEASED-DONOR ONLY. No living-donor stratum at all, which is the review's actual target population.; Era: 1987-1992, cyclosporine/azathioprine/prednisone immunosuppression, before tacrolimus, mycophenolate, modern induction, and before solid-phase (Luminex) antibody detection. Effect magnitudes from this era are widely held to overstate what modern immunosuppression shows; the ordering and shape are the transferable part.; Serologic broad-antigen typing at A, B and DR only. No HLA-C, -DQ or -DP, no allele-level (two-field) data, and no eplet or molecular mismatch - so the paper says nothing about C4, C7, C8 or C12.; Antibody/sensitisation status is not modelled or reported, so C7 and C11 (sensitisation modification) cannot be addressed.; The centre-stratified contrast is confounded by design: the bottom-20 centres both matched more aggressively AND had worse baseline outcomes, so the larger absolute gap there could reflect a higher event rate rather than a stronger biological effect of matching. No interaction test is reported.; Registry data, self-reported by centres; no central audit of HLA typing is described in the retrieved text.; Single-source registry, US population; no Iranian or regional data (C15 unaddressed)..

### Opelz G 1992 — Strength of HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-DR mismatches in relation to short- and long-term kidney graft survival. Collaborative Transplant Study.

Opelz G 1992, *Transplant International (Transpl Int) 5 Suppl 1: S621-4*, [DOI 10.1007/978-3-642-77423-2_182](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-77423-2_182). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Springer); no PMC record exists for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid), so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable.

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | First cadaver (deceased-donor) kidney transplant recipients reported to the Collaborative Transplant Study, an international multicentre registry; transplant era not stated in the abstract (paper published 1992, so predominantly 1980s to early-1990s ciclosporin-era transplants) |
| donor type | deceased |
| n | over 40,000 |
| design | retrospective multicentre registry cohort; actuarial graft-survival curves compared across mismatch categories separately for each of HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR, plus a total HLA-A+B+DR mismatch count; for the long-term analysis the survival computation was re-based to 100% at 6 months, i.e. conditional on 6-month graft survival. No regression model, no test statistic and no variance estimate are described in the abstract. |
| typing resolution | serologic / broad antigen level (one field) at HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR - not stated explicitly, but the abstract speaks of 'antigens' and the 1992 CTS era predates routine molecular typing. No HLA-C, DQ or DP. |
| outcome | kidney graft survival (all-cause graft failure); reported both for the early post-transplant period and for the 6-month-to-5-year period conditional on survival to 6 months |
| follow up | 5 years post transplant (the long-term contrast covers 6 months to 5 years) |
| other factors modelled | not reported in the retrieved abstract - no covariate list and no statement of adjustment for donor age, cold ischaemia, PRA/sensitisation, recipient age, centre or immunosuppression |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the classic Collaborative Transplant Study per-locus ranking: more than 40,000 first cadaver-donor kidney transplants analysed locus by locus, and one of the few sources that puts HLA-A, HLA-B and HLA-DR side by side on a single common metric (absolute 5-year graft-survival difference). It answers the review's per-locus question (ANGLE B) directly, and it answers the locus-interaction question (ANGLE C) in the negative: over the 6-month-to-5-year window the three loci behaved additively, since three times the per-locus 6% approximately reproduces the 17% observed for 0 versus 6 mismatches, so it is evidence for additivity rather than for locus-by-locus interaction. The most transferable finding for a pre-screen tool is the time dependence: DR dominates early and A is almost irrelevant early, but from 6 months to 5 years A, B and DR carry the same weight, so a tool aimed at long-term graft survival cannot down-weight HLA-A the way an early-rejection tool could. Transfer to the Iranian setting is partial, but the typing resolution matches unusually well: broad serological one-field antigens at A, B and DR are exactly what an Iranian living-donor pre-screen will have, so the effect sizes are measured on the same scale the tool will operate on. The population, however, is deceased-donor rather than living, the immunosuppression is that of the 1980s and early 1990s, antibody and sensitisation status are not reported at all, and there is no DQ, DP or HLA-C information, so nothing here informs the antibody-unknown aspect of the pre-screen. The numbers should therefore be carried into the review as a ranking and a functional shape - roughly equal, additive per-locus weights for long-term survival - rather than as calibrated absolute risks for a contemporary living-donor programme.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- graft survival at 5 years, conditional on graft survival at 6 months (curve re-based to 100% at 6 months): 2 HLA-A mismatches vs 0 HLA-A mismatches — absolute difference in graft survival (percentage points) 6; adjusted for not stated in the abstract; it is not clear whether the per-locus comparison is adjusted for mismatch at the other two loci or for any donor/recipient covariate [Abstract (only retrievable source; no PMC full text)]
- graft survival at 5 years, conditional on graft survival at 6 months (curve re-based to 100% at 6 months): 2 HLA-B mismatches vs 0 HLA-B mismatches — absolute difference in graft survival (percentage points) 6; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract]
- graft survival at 5 years, conditional on graft survival at 6 months (curve re-based to 100% at 6 months): 2 HLA-DR mismatches vs 0 HLA-DR mismatches — absolute difference in graft survival (percentage points) 6; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract]
- graft survival at 5 years: 6 total HLA-A + HLA-B + HLA-DR mismatches vs 0 — absolute difference in graft survival (percentage points) 17; adjusted for not stated in the abstract [Abstract. The figure is stated immediately after the sentence describing the 6-month re-based computation, and the abstract does not say explicitly whether the 17% is the 6-month-conditional or the from-transplant difference; the arithmetic (3 x 6% = 18%, close to 17%) is consistent with the conditional analysis.]

**Dose-response.**

- Total mismatch count: 0 MM: reference; 6 MM: 17 percentage points lower 5-year graft survival than 0 mismatches
- A: 0 MM: reference; 1 MM: not reported in the abstract; 2 MM: 6 percentage points lower 5-year graft survival than 0 (conditional on 6-month survival)
- B: 0 MM: reference; 1 MM: not reported in the abstract; 2 MM: 6 percentage points lower 5-year graft survival than 0 (conditional on 6-month survival)
- DR: 0 MM: reference; 1 MM: not reported in the abstract; 2 MM: 6 percentage points lower 5-year graft survival than 0 (conditional on 6-month survival)
- C: not studied
- DQ: not studied
- DP: not studied
- Shape reported: additive across loci, and approximately linear in the total mismatch count over the 6-month-to-5-year window: the authors state the influence of the three loci was additive, and three loci times a 6% per-locus 0-vs-2 step approximately reproduces the 17% observed for 0 vs 6. Early post transplant the shape is NOT equal across loci: DR > B >> A. Intermediate categories (1 mismatch per locus; 1-5 total) are not given in the abstract, so the within-locus shape - whether the first mismatch costs more than the second, and whether there is a distinct zero-mismatch premium - cannot be read from the retrieved text.; linearity tested: Not formally tested in the retrieved text - no interaction term, no trend test, no spline, no p-value. Additivity is asserted descriptively by comparing the summed per-locus 0-vs-2 differences (3 x 6% = 18%) against the observed 0-vs-6 total-count difference (17%).; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- HLA locus (A vs B vs DR) x time since transplant: The relative strength of the loci changes with follow-up period. Early post transplant, DR mismatches had a stronger influence than B, and A had a very small influence. From 6 months to 5 years all three loci had approximately the same influence, and the authors conclude that the long-term influence of HLA-A is comparable to that of HLA-B and HLA-DR. (Qualitative for the early period (no numbers given). For 6 months to 5 years: 6 percentage-point 0-vs-2 survival difference at each of A, B and DR. No formal test of the time-by-locus interaction is reported.) [Abstract]
- HLA-A x HLA-B x HLA-DR mismatch (locus-by-locus interaction / additivity): No interaction between loci was found: the effects of the three loci were described as additive, so that the 0-vs-6 total mismatch difference (17% at 5 years) approximately equals the sum of the three per-locus 0-vs-2 differences (3 x 6% = 18%). (17% observed for 0 vs 6 mismatches versus 18% expected under strict additivity. No interaction p-value reported.) [Abstract]

- *C9* — "the difference between grafts with zero or two mismatches at the end of 5 years was 6%, regardless of whether HLA-A, HLA-B, or HLA-DR antigens were analyzed" (Abstract)
- *C2* — "The influence of the three loci was additive so that the survival rate difference between transplants with zero or six mismatches for HLA-A, -B, -DR was 17% at 5 years." (Abstract)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. PMC holds no full text for this PMID (convert_article_ids returned no pmcid), so the per-locus survival curves, tables, figures and methods were not retrievable. Everything recorded here comes from the PubMed abstract.; No hazard ratios, relative risks, confidence intervals or p-values appear anywhere in the retrieved text. Only absolute graft-survival percentage differences are given, with no measure of precision, so the paper cannot be pooled with HR-based studies without recovering the original figures.; The 1-mismatch category is not reported. The abstract gives only the 0-vs-2 contrast per locus, so the size of the first mismatch relative to the second, and the existence of a distinct zero-mismatch premium, cannot be established from this paper. Claim C9 is therefore only partially supported.; Conference-supplement / proceedings short paper (Transpl Int 5 Suppl 1, S621-4, four pages). Not a full methods report; no statistical model is described.; No statement of adjustment. It is unclear whether the per-locus comparisons are mutually adjusted for mismatch at the other two loci, or adjusted for PRA/sensitisation, donor and recipient age, cold ischaemia time, centre or immunosuppressive regimen. Confounding by these factors, and by the preferential allocation of well-matched kidneys, is not excluded.; Deceased-donor (cadaver) transplants only, and first transplants only. The paper says nothing about living donation - the target setting for the Iranian pre-screen - nor about retransplants or repeat mismatch.; 1980s to early-1990s immunosuppression (predominantly ciclosporin-based, before tacrolimus, mycophenolate and modern induction). Absolute effect sizes from this era are widely held to overstate the HLA effect achievable today, so these percentages should be read as a ranking rather than as calibrated modern risks.; Serological broad-antigen typing at A, B and DR only. No HLA-C, DQ, DP or DRB3/4/5; no allele-level or molecular (eplet / PIRCHE) mismatch; no assessment of low-resolution misclassification.; Antibody status, dnDSA and rejection are not reported; the only outcome is graft survival. Nothing here informs the antibody-unknown aspect of a pre-screen.; The 17% figure for 0 vs 6 mismatches is stated immediately after the 6-month re-basing sentence, and the abstract does not make explicit whether it is the 6-month-conditional or the from-transplant difference. Recorded as ambiguous rather than resolved.; Registry study with no external validation and no reported handling of centre heterogeneity or of missing typing data..

### Gilks WR 1988 — Matchability in kidney transplantation.

Gilks WR 1988, *Tissue Antigens*, [DOI 10.1111/j.1399-0039.1988.tb01647.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1399-0039.1988.tb01647.x). Access: abstract_only; licence: publisher copyright (Munksgaard/Wiley, 1988). No PMC record exists: convert_article_ids on PMID 3064360 returned no pmcid, so only the PubMed abstract was retrievable..

| Scope | |
|---|---|
| population | Patients awaiting kidney transplantation, UK Transplant Service. Country, era (1980s UK) and the 'well-matched' definition are named in the abstract; the cohort size, dates and inclusion criteria are not stated in the retrieved abstract. |
| donor type | not stated in the retrieved abstract (the UK Transplant Service national scheme of the era was deceased-donor allocation, but the abstract does not say so and this was not assumed) |
| design | Methodological paper: defines matchability as a waiting-list patient's propensity to be 'well-matched', presents two estimation methods, and compares the resulting matchability estimates with HLA phenotype frequency; also examines ABO type and HLA homozygosity as determinants of matchability. |
| typing resolution | not stated in the retrieved abstract (serologic/antigen-level, one-field typing is what UK Transplant Service used in 1988, but this is not stated in the text retrieved and was not assumed) |
| outcome | matchability - the probability/propensity that a listed patient is offered a 'well-matched' kidney, using the UK Transplant Service definition of 'well-matched'. NOT graft survival, rejection or dnDSA. |
| other factors modelled | ABO blood group, HLA homozygosity, HLA phenotype frequency |

**Why it is relevant.** This is the origin paper for the 'matchability' concept that later became the matchability score inside the UK 1998 and 2006 kidney allocation schemes, so it speaks directly to claim C13 (how allocation schemes score HLA) and to claim C10 (non-additivity, because matchability is a property of the whole phenotype and of the donor pool, not a sum of per-locus terms). Its central result is negative and structural: HLA phenotype frequency - the naive, easy-to-compute quantity - is a poor proxy for how matchable a patient actually is, with a correlation of only 0.3 under the UK Transplant Service definition of 'well-matched'. That matters for a KidneyMatch-style pre-screen because it says a ranking or a 'hard to match' flag cannot be derived from allele or phenotype frequencies in the Iranian population alone; matchability depends on the joint distribution of the available donor pool and on the matching rule in force. The paper also identifies ABO type and HLA homozygosity as modifiers of matchability, which is the mechanism behind the later observation that DR-homozygous or rare-phenotype candidates face unequal access. Transfer to the Iranian living-donor setting is partial and must be stated honestly: matchability as defined here is a waiting-list/donor-pool quantity computed against a national deceased-donor allocation scheme, whereas a living-donor pre-screen evaluates a small set of specific volunteer donors, so the operative question becomes 'given this candidate's phenotype, how likely is any of these donors to reach the match threshold' rather than 'how likely is the national pool to offer a well-matched kidney'. It carries no graft-outcome effect estimate, so it can support scheme-design and equity-of-access claims but must not be cited for any statement that HLA mismatch changes graft survival, and it says nothing about high-resolution typing, eplets or antibody status.

**Effect sizes reported.**

- matchability (propensity of a listed patient to be 'well-matched'): matchability vs HLA phenotype frequency (agreement between the two quantities) — correlation coefficient 0.3; adjusted for not stated; unadjusted correlation using the UK Transplant Service definition of 'well-matched' [Abstract]

**Dose-response.**

- Shape reported: not reported; linearity tested: not tested - the paper reports no mismatch-count or per-locus risk series; its outcome is matchability, not graft failure, and no 0/1/2 mismatch gradient is given in the retrieved abstract; 1 and 2 pooled: None

**Effect modification / interactions.**

- matchability x ABO blood group: ABO type is reported to affect matchability, i.e. the propensity of being well-matched is not a function of the HLA phenotype alone but is modified by a non-HLA, allocation-relevant recipient attribute (no numeric estimate in the retrieved abstract) [Abstract (final sentence)]
- matchability x HLA homozygosity: HLA homozygosity is reported to affect matchability - the structural modifier this review tracks for DR-homozygous and rare-phenotype candidates and their unequal access to a well-matched organ (no numeric estimate in the retrieved abstract) [Abstract (final sentence)]
- matchability x HLA phenotype frequency (non-equivalence, not an effect modification in the statistical sense): Phenotype frequency, commonly supposed to predict matchability, correlates with it only weakly - so matchability is not reducible to the marginal frequency of the patient's own antigens and must be computed against the donor pool and the matching rule (correlation 0.3) [Abstract]

**Verbatim support (verified against the source).**

- *C13* — "The matchability of a patient awaiting kidney transplantation is his propensity for being 'well-matched'." (Abstract, sentence 1)
- *C13* — "We present two methods for estimating matchability." (Abstract, sentence 2)
- *C13* — "We show a correlation of only 0.3 between matchability and phenotype frequency using the definition of 'well-matched' used by the UK Transplant Service." (Abstract, sentence 4)
- *C10* — "We also show that ABO type and HLA homozygocity can affect matchability." (Abstract, final sentence)

**Limitations.** Abstract only. No PMC full text exists for this 1988 Tissue Antigens paper (convert_article_ids returned no PMCID), so the two estimation methods, the cohort, the exact 'well-matched' definition, the size and direction of the ABO and homozygosity effects, and any tables or figures were NOT read and are not represented here.; No graft-outcome estimate of any kind: no HR, OR, RR or survival percentage for HLA mismatch. The paper cannot support C1, C2, C3 or any per-locus risk claim.; The single number available (correlation 0.3) has no confidence interval, no p value and no stated sample size in the retrieved text.; Matchability is defined relative to one national scheme's threshold for 'well-matched' at one point in time; the value is therefore not portable across allocation rules, donor pools or populations without recomputation.; 1988 UK population and 1988 serological typing practice. Neither the population's HLA distribution nor the typing resolution is stated in the abstract, and neither resembles the Iranian donor pool; the paper's method transfers, its numbers do not.; Deceased-donor national-waiting-list framing. Matchability as defined here presupposes a pool of organs allocated centrally, which is not the structure of a living-donor pre-screen where a candidate has a handful of named volunteers.; Pre-dates DQ/DP typing, molecular typing, eplet-level matching and virtual crossmatch entirely; says nothing about sensitisation or antibody status..
